raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute the hepatic injury in the reported 52-yr-old woman to an idiosyncratic allergic reaction to oral carbamazepine that manifested as acute severe cholangitis with histology of vanishing ducts mixed with mild hepatocellular injury, based on a compatible temporal profile, improvement of liver enzymes after carbamazepine withdrawal, transient peripheral eosinophilia and fever, and exclusion of primary biliary cirrhosis, sclerosing cholangitis, and extrahepatic obstruction. The patient had jaundice and markedly elevated cholestatic enzymes about 4 weeks after starting carbamazepine, and a biopsy showed severely damaged bile ductules with only a few identifiable ductules.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral carbamazepine 200 mg t.i.d.; liver enzymes normal at start except pre-existing elevated GGT (155 U/ml). Four weeks later admitted with fever, jaundice, AST 166, ALT 122, ALP 2906, GGT 4026 U/ml, total/direct bilirubin 4.2/4.0 mg/dl, PT 20 s (INR 1.9), peripheral eosinophils 14%; serum CBZ 11 mg/dl. Biopsy: portal expansion with lymphocytes/eosinophils, mild piecemeal necrosis, severely damaged bile ductules with only a few identifiable, canalicular bile plugging, mild lobular inflammation, focal severe hepatocyte ballooning. Enzymes gradually improved after discontinuation; aminotransferases returned to normal. Patient later died of a massive stroke (unrelated to liver injury). Concurrent long-term (>6 months) aspirin, gliburide, and nifedipine; prior phenytoin for seizures.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of carbamazepine-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) in the English literature. The patient presented with jaundice, cholestasis (bilirubin 212 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 1030 IU/L, AST 99 IU/L), a liver biopsy showing an activated T-lymphocyte portal infiltrate with damaged and destroyed interlobular bile ducts, and had no large-duct obstruction, PBC, PSC, or sarcoidosis. Ductal loss and portal fibrosis progressed after CBZ withdrawal, and the immunoallergic/hypersensitivity mechanism (eosinophilia, rash, fever) is invoked for CBZ hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported CBZ-induced VBDS case. Patient had fever, rash, pruritus, eosinophilia (20% of WBC), elevated bilirubin 212 micromol/L, alkaline phosphatase 1030 IU/L, AST 99 IU/L, prolonged PT corrected by vitamin K. Biopsy showed activated T-lymphocyte portal infiltration with damaged/destroyed interlobular bile ducts; loss of bile ducts and portal fibrosis progressed on follow-up biopsies. PBC, PSC, sarcoidosis, large-duct obstruction, CMV and HIV excluded. Hypersensitivity/immunoallergic mechanism proposed. Treated with prednisolone and ursodeoxycholic acid; recovered clinically with persistent abnormal liver biochemistry.

raw_record.support_text: Two 38-year-old women developed elevated transaminases with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms after receiving carbamazepine (CBZ) for eye pain (Case 1, trigeminal neuralgia) and for epilepsy (Case 2). In Case 1, a small rechallenge dose of CBZ reproduced a multi-peaked rise in transaminases that took about 2 months to normalize. Case 2 developed progressive jaundice and impaired consciousness and died of fulminant hepatic failure on day 63. The authors add 17 reported Japanese and Western cases and characterize CBZ liver injury: onset typically 3-4 weeks after starting the drug with fever, jaundice, and GI symptoms; mechanisms proposed include direct action of CBZ or its metabolites and a delayed-type allergic reaction; granulomatous hepatitis has been reported; after drug withdrawal most resolve within 1 week, but 4 deaths have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 38yo woman with trigeminal neuralgia; initial CBZ 400 mg/day led to elevated GOT 363 U/l, GPT 309 U/l, ALP 504 U/l, γ-GTP 396 U/l, T-bil 0.7 mg/dl, normalizing ~2 weeks after discontinuation; rechallenge with CBZ 600 mg produced chills, fever (39.5°C), and recurrent hepatic dysfunction with a bimodal transaminase peak normalizing in ~1 month. Case 2: 38yo woman with epilepsy; progressive jaundice and impaired consciousness, fulminant hepatic failure, died on day 63. Literature review adds 17 reported cases (Japan and Western): typical onset 3-4 weeks after start with fever, jaundice, GI symptoms; proposed mechanisms include direct action of CBZ or its metabolites and delayed-type hypersensitivity; granulomatous hepatitis reported; 4 deaths reported, some cases protracted. CBZ is a dibenzoazepine used for epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia; liver injury is rare (17 published cases before this report).

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based cohort study of 11,141 persons starting isoniazid preventive therapy for latent tuberculosis infection (1989-1995), the study identified 11 cases of hepatotoxicity attributable to isoniazid, a rate of 1.0 per 1000 persons starting therapy. The authors observed an increasing risk of isoniazid hepatotoxicity with increasing age and a greater frequency in women than in men, and a borderline association with white race. They concluded that isoniazid is less toxic than previously believed.
raw_record.extra_details: Population-based cohort, 1989-1995, 11,141 persons starting isoniazid preventive therapy for latent TB; 11 cases of hepatotoxicity (rate 1.0 per 1000). Rates by subgroup: males 0.5 (3/6066), females 1.6 (8/5075, adjusted OR 3.30, 95% CI 0.87-12.45); age 15-34 0.8 (reference), 35-64 2.1 (OR 3.17, 0.94-10.70), >=65 2.8 (OR 3.62, 0.43-30.42), 0-14 0 cases; white 2.2 (OR 2.60, 0.75-8.95), nonwhite 0.8. Authors note these findings were based on a small number of cases (n=11).

raw_record.support_text: In the IUAT study (Thompson 1982), hepatotoxicity was prospectively assessed as the most serious adverse effect of isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy, in which patients took 0, 3, 6, or 12 month INH regimens. The first-year placebo rate of hepatitis was 0.12%, whereas rates for 3, 6, and 12 month INH courses were 0.25%, 0.36%, and 0.52% respectively. A total of 95 of 20,840 patients receiving INH developed hepatitis and 3 died; no serum liver enzyme monitoring or discontinuation for biochemical or clinical hepatotoxicity signs was done in this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective hepatitis assessment in the IUAT preventive-therapy trial (0, 3, 6, 12 month INH regimens). Hepatitis rates increased with INH duration: placebo 0.12%, 3-month 0.25%, 6-month 0.36%, 12-month 0.52% in the first year. 95 of 20,840 INH recipients developed hepatitis and 3 died. No serum liver enzyme monitoring or medication discontinuation for biochemical/clinical hepatotoxicity was performed.

raw_record.support_text: A prospective study of 174 patients receiving isoniazid, examined monthly for SGOT and bilirubin elevations, found that about 20% showed abnormal values that subsided while patients continued the drug. The paper concludes that isoniazid was hepatotoxic in a large proportion of individuals, though most adapted to the insult and recovered rather than progressing to severe hepatic injury; no correlation with slow acetylation or anti-isoniazid antibodies was found.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective study of 174 isoniazid recipients; ~20% had abnormal SGOT/bilirubin that subsided on continued therapy ('adaptation'). A second retrospective USPHS surveillance program on 13,838 isoniazid recipients (224 with possible isoniazid-related hepatic injury) showed the injury was biochemically (SGOT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase) and morphologically indistinguishable from iproniazid-induced liver damage or viral hepatitis, with no evidence of a hypersensitivity mechanism; ~30% of hepatic reactors were Honolulu residents of Oriental ancestry, so up to 90% would be expected to be fast acetylators. No correlation with acetylation rate or anti-isoniazid antibodies.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of the overt hepatic disease that developed in 114 patients while taking isoniazid for chemoprophylaxis of tuberculosis showed it to be mainly hepatocellular. Severity was manifested by 13 fatalities (12.3%) and by histologic demonstration of submassive necrosis in 9 and massive necrosis in 4 patients; among 20 others, 16 had moderately severe acute hepatocellular injury (4 with a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern) and 4 had chronic hepatic diseases (1 with cirrhosis). The study concluded that the observations offer no support for the view that isoniazid-induced hepatic disease results from hypersensitivity, while considering data supporting hepatotoxic metabolites of isoniazid as responsible for the injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Ischemic/isoniazid-induced hepatic injury assessed in 114 patients from the US Public Health Service surveillance program (13,838 patients enrolled July 1971-Nov 1972, receiving isoniazid 300 mg/day) plus additional reported patients. Hepatotoxicity manifested as submassive necrosis (9) and massive necrosis (4); 16 moderate acute hepatocellular injury (4 mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic), 4 chronic liver disease (1 cirrhosis). Hepatic injury recognized in 15% during month 1 and an additional 31% during month 2; in 54% after 2-11 months. Fatal outcome more likely when injury presented after 2 months, especially with bilirubin >20 mg/100 ml. Case fatality rate significantly higher in black females than in black males or whites of either sex. Premonitory complaints: vague digestive complaints (55%), 'viral'-like complaints (35%); jaundice presenting in 10%; fever and rash in <4%; modest eosinophilia in ~10%. Fever/rash/eosinophilia present in few, offering no support for hypersensitivity mechanism; hepatotoxic metabolites implicated instead.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that daily isoniazid for 6-9 months for latent tuberculosis is one of the most commonly prescribed regimens, that its most common adverse effect is drug-induced abnormal aminotransferases, and that its most worrisome toxicity, though extremely rare (less than 0.01%), is fatal hepatitis, noting that mortality rates in patients with acute liver failure due to idiosyncratic drug reactions such as those from isoniazid approach 80-90%. Reported cofactors for hepatotoxicity include older age, concurrent alcohol, acetaminophen or injection drug use, hepatitis B infection, lower body mass index, and lower albumin levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Used daily for 6-9 months for latent tuberculosis. Drug-induced abnormal aminotransferases is the most common adverse effect; fatal hepatitis is extremely rare (<0.01%). Mortality in acute liver failure from idiosyncratic drug reactions such as isoniazid approaches 80-90%. Reported cofactors for hepatotoxicity: older age, concurrent alcohol, acetaminophen or injection drug use, hepatitis B infection, lower BMI, lower albumin. Patel & Voigt case cohort study (327 of 743 Vietnamese immigrants, 9 yr): isoniazid hepatotoxicity defined as jaundice with transaminases >5x ULN resolving after withdrawal, per gastroenterologist evaluation excluding other causes; hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation rates were 3% (HBsAg-negative), 6% (HBsAg-positive/HBeAg-negative), and 48% (HBsAg-positive/HBeAg-positive). Another study in Southeast Asian immigrants in Philadelphia found no significant difference in isoniazid hepatotoxicity rates between HBV carriers and controls.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes isoniazid as the cause of a rare hepatitis reaction and reports a case in which severe cirrhosis, esophageal varices, hemorrhage, and death followed prolonged administration of isoniazid, coupled with failure to recognize hepatic necrosis secondary to its use. Hepatitis from isoniazid is described as allergic in nature and had been reported in only four patients in the English literature, none with permanent liver damage, whereas this case progressed to fatal hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for presumed tuberculosis of the spine, given concurrently with para-aminosalicylic acid (12 g daily) and streptomycin (1 g twice weekly). The patient developed a rash after 37 days of therapy, received a blood transfusion, and two days later developed clinical jaundice that persisted until discharge. The authors note the diagnosis of superimposed infectious hepatitis was initially suspected but the hepatic necrosis was attributed to isoniazid. Prolonged administration resulted in severe cirrhosis, esophageal varices, hemorrhage, and death.

raw_record.support_text: A case of apparent INH (isoniazid)-induced jaundice resulting in fulminating submassive necrotic hepatitis with hepatic coma and death is reported. Jaundice with laboratory and histologic findings of hepatocellular necrosis first appeared after starting INH and subsided with cessation of the medication; it recurred with reinstitution of the drug, and continued INH therapy was associated with the fatal hepatitis. The liver at necropsy resembled that seen in fatal viral hepatitis or iproniazid hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice recurred on rechallenge with INH and subsided upon cessation, supporting causality. The injury was a fulminating submassive necrotic hepatitis with hepatic coma and death. Necropsy findings resembled fatal viral hepatitis or iproniazid hepatitis. INH is an anti-tuberculosis agent used therapeutically.

raw_record.support_text: A case of isoniazid hypersensitivity is presented, manifesting with fever, malaise, headache, anorexia, dermatitis, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and anicteric hepatitis. After an oral desensitization period of fifty-two days, the patient became able to tolerate full doses of the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Hypersensitivity reaction in a single patient presenting with fever, malaise, headache, anorexia, dermatitis, lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilia together with anicteric hepatitis. After a 52-day oral desensitization, the patient tolerated full doses of isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: In an open-label randomized trial comparing 4 months of daily rifampin with 9 months of daily isoniazid (5 mg/kg, up to 300 mg/day) for latent tuberculosis infection, three patients developed drug-induced hepatitis, and all three were taking isoniazid. Adverse events resulted in permanent discontinuation of therapy for eight (14%) patients taking isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Three of 58 patients randomized to 9 months of daily isoniazid (5 mg/kg, up to 300 mg/day) for latent tuberculosis infection developed drug-induced hepatitis, all in the isoniazid arm; eight (14%) isoniazid patients permanently discontinued due to adverse events.

raw_record.support_text: In an analysis of UNOS liver transplant database, one-year graft survival for liver transplantation for acute liver failure from isoniazid (n=24), propylthiouracil (n=13), and phenytoin (n=10) was 78, 84, and 60%, respectively. The study captured patients who developed acute liver failure from any drug and underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation, from UNOS database. 24 liver transplants for isoniazid-induced ALF with 1-year graft survival 78%. Isoniazid was among the 4 drugs (with propylthiouracil, phenytoin, valproate) accounting for 42% of liver transplants for non-APAP injury; severe liver injury due to these drugs described as well described. African-American women over-represented (16% vs 4% of Caucasian women; OR 4.2, 95% CI 1.4-12.7, P=0.02).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 3,377 patients treated with isoniazid (INH) for latent tuberculosis, 19 patients developed hepatotoxicity, defined as serum AST >5 times the upper limit of normal; INH was immediately discontinued. The incidence was 5.63 hepatotoxic events per 1,000 patients started on therapy. The events were attributed to INH therapy, with peak AST elevations peaking 1 to 6 months after treatment start, and some affected patients were icteric with elevated total bilirubin.
raw_record.extra_details: 19/3,377 patients (0.56%) had hepatotoxicity (AST >5x ULN), 5.63 events per 1,000 patients started. Risk factors: age >49 years (bivariate OR 4.814, 95% CI 1.400-16.551, p=0.02; multivariable OR 3.699, 95% CI 1.428-9.584, p=0.008) and baseline AST > ULN (bivariate OR 4.832, 95% CI 1.884-12.394, p=0.0003; multivariable OR 5.398, 95% CI 2.081-13.999, p=0.0005). No association with gender, race/ethnicity, alcohol consumption, or prior liver disease. Only 1 of 19 had prodromal symptoms; two icteric patients had total bilirubin 5.8 and 6.4 mg/dL with malaise/nausea. Peak AST ranged 212-1602 U/L, 1-6 months after starting INH. Population was predominately African-American men <50 years with no reported alcohol use or prior liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of sheltered homeless men, the frequency of hepatotoxic reactions (2.1%) requiring cessation of isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy was similar to that reported by Stead and coworkers in nursing home residents (hepatotoxicity 4.4%, other drug intolerance 6.0% among nearly 2,000 residents). Isoniazid was not considered to have contributed to deaths among those elderly persons. By contrast, Moulding and colleagues controversially implicated INH in 20 deaths from hepatitis in California residents over a 14-yr period.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of directly observed INH preventive therapy in sheltered homeless men. Hepatotoxic reactions caused cessation of therapy in 2.1% of all men who began therapy; the one incident occurred in a reportedly alcoholic man, representing hepatotoxic effects in 3.7% of the 27 men with reported alcoholism. The paper concludes directly observed INH preventive therapy largely removes the threat of fatal INH hepatotoxicity even in high-risk populations (alcoholic homeless men, elderly nursing home residents, methadone-treated addicts). Stead and coworkers reported 4.4% hepatotoxicity among nursing home residents. Moulding and colleagues controversially implicated INH in 20 deaths from hepatitis in California over 14 years, noting infrequent medical follow-up in fatal cases.

raw_record.support_text: Of 104 cases of acute hepatic failure in two steroid trials, 12 were attributable to a drug; isoniazid was implicated in one of those patients. Isoniazid is also listed among drugs for which anecdotal cases show benefit from drug withdrawal and steroid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 1 of 12 drug-attributable acute hepatic failure cases among 104 acute liver failure cases in two steroid trials. Anti-tuberculosis drug also highlighted in monitoring recommendations (isoniazid alone in patients older than 35 years) because the risk is significant.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the most important adverse effect of isoniazid is hepatitis, and reports hepatotoxicity risk of 0.5% to 1% in the International Union Against Tuberculosis trial (20,840 subjects) and the US Public Health Service (PHS) multicentre study (13,838 persons). Increasing age and daily alcohol consumption are important risk factors, and hepatotoxicity usually occurs in the first 3 months of treatment. PHS data showed isoniazid-associated hepatitis in 0% under 20 years, 0.3% from 20-34, 1.2% from 35-49 and 2.3% from 50-64 years, with hospitalization rates up to 5.0 per 1000 treatment initiations and a mortality rate of 0.6 per 1000 persons (with liver cirrhosis possibly confounding).
raw_record.extra_details: Given at 5 mg/kg daily (max 300 mg) or 15 mg twice weekly (max 900 mg) for 6-12 months of LTBI treatment. Hepatotoxicity risk 0.5-1% (IUAT trial), usually within first 3 months. Age-dependent incidence (0% <20 y, 0.3% 20-34 y, 1.2% 35-49 y, 2.3% 50-64 y). Hospitalization up to 5.0/1000; recent symptomatic hepatitis estimated 1-3/1000, hospitalization 0.1-0.2/1000, mortality 0.0-0.3/1000. Risk factors: increasing age and daily alcohol consumption.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 46 individual case reports; median age 39 y; 25 female/21 male; median treatment duration 5 weeks; HC 93%, Cs/mixed 7%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 18% (44/46 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 24% (34/46 reported); hepatic necrosis 65%; inflammatory reaction 68%; death or liver transplant 35%; liver biopsy reported in 33/46 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) causes drug-related hepatitis in humans. After initial sporadic reports, a 1971 retrospective study reported clinical hepatitis in 19 of 2,321 patients (1 percent) taking INH for chemoprophylaxis, 13 of whom developed overt jaundice and 2 of whom died; the USPHS prospective multicenter surveillance study of 13,838 persons receiving INH chemoprophylaxis found an overall hepatitis rate of 10.3 per 1,000 (1 percent) with eight deaths (0.06 percent), leading to termination of the study because of the high mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: INH given for chemoprophylaxis ('INH-related hepatitis'), based on overt clinical hepatitis not merely chemical liver-test abnormality. Garibaldi et al: 19/2,321 (1%), 13 with overt jaundice, 2 deaths (0.1%). CDC ad-hoc advisory committee estimated 0-10 serious hepatotoxicity cases/1,000 persons/year. USPHS surveillance study: 13,838 persons, rate 10.3/1,000 (1%), 8 deaths (0.06%), terminated due to unexpected mortality; deaths mostly in Baltimore raised speculation about non-INH hepatotoxic factors, but study not supplanted. Scharer and Smith (1969) reported liver function abnormalities in 10.3% of INH patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 755 patients with latent tuberculosis infection treated with isoniazid for 9 months, 94 patients (12.4%) had adverse effects, and treatment was withdrawn in 50 (6.6%): 2 for hypersensitivity and 48 for hepatic toxicity. Of these, 25 (3.3% of the total) met the criteria for isoniazid withdrawal due to hepatotoxicity. Viral hepatitis markers were negative and liver function normalized in all cases. Table 4 tabulates hepatic toxicity by grade: grade I 49 (6.50%), grade II 23 (3.04%), grade III 5 (0.66%), and grade IV 11 (1.45%).
raw_record.extra_details: Nine-month isoniazid therapy (270 doses) for latent tuberculosis infection in a retrospective cohort of 755 patients. Hepatic toxicity grades (n, %): grade I 49 (6.50), grade II 23 (3.04), grade III 5 (0.66), grade IV 11 (1.45). Adverse effects occurred in 94 (12.4%; 95% CI 10.1-14.7%); treatment withdrawn in 50 (6.6%), 2 for hypersensitivity and 48 for hepatic toxicity, of whom 25 (3.3%; 95% CI 2.0-4.6%) met explicit isoniazid-hepatotoxicity withdrawal criteria. Viral hepatitis markers negative; liver function normalized in all; 47 of 48 patients with hepatic toxicity discontinued before 6 months.

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including nine cases of isoniazid hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test the reliability of RUCAM causality scores.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of isoniazid hepatotoxicity. Median time to onset across the cohort was 42.5 days, 73% were hospitalized, and 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: The author discusses Public Health Service data on isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity, clarifying the incidence of hepatotoxicity established by criteria from a panel of hepatic-disease experts. The rate was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age, 0.8% for persons over 64, and 1.7% per year for all persons 50 years or older, correcting an earlier letter's misstatement.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity computed from Public Health Service study using criteria established by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported rates: 2.3% per year for persons 50-64 years, 0.8% for persons >64 years, and 1.7% per year for all persons ≥50 years. The paper corrects claims that figures underestimate incidence, noting half the patients discontinued the year of therapy and that excluding persons not known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed tends to overestimate incidence; if not excluded, calculated incidence would be 0.2% for ages 20-34, 0.7% for 35-49, 1.6% for 50-64, and 0.6% for >64, so the true age-specific incidence likely lies between the high and low figures. Also discusses that it is not known whether high-dose isoniazid given twice weekly for preventive therapy of tuberculosis would reduce isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity risk; standard 300 mg daily adult dosing recommended.

raw_record.support_text: During treatment of genitourinary tuberculosis, the authors encountered INH (isoniazid)-induced liver injury, which they note occurs in about 0.5% of all (TB treatment) cases, with liver toxicity only rarely proven by histology. Adverse drug reactions, most commonly hepatotoxicity, occur in about 20% of TB treatments. The case was histologically proven INH liver toxicity and the patient was treated successfully.
raw_record.extra_details: Histologically proven INH liver toxicity. INH-induced liver injury occurs in about 0.5% of all TB treatment cases; adverse drug reactions (most commonly hepatotoxicity) occur in about 20% of TB treatments. Occurred in a patient with TB of the female genital tract (genitourinary TB), who was treated successfully. The case highlights the diagnostic work-up of extrapulmonary TB using the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA).

raw_record.support_text: The study assesses genetic variation in the candidate genes CES1, CES2 and CES4 in subjects with and without INH (isoniazid)-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper repeatedly refers to 'INH-induced hepatotoxicity' as the liver-injury phenotype under investigation, i.e., isoniazid is the molecular agent implicated in causing the hepatotoxicity events, and the pharmacogenetic analyses (e.g., of CES1/CES2/CES4 variants) test whether genetic factors modify this drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: INH (isoniazid) is used as the anti-tuberculosis drug whose hepatotoxicity (INH-induced hepatotoxicity) is the study phenotype. The paper catalogued variants in CES1, CES2 and CES4 in subjects with and without hepatotoxicity (n=170 all subjects for association tests) and found no significant association of genetic variation in CES2, or SNPs and haplotypes in CES1/CES4, with INH-induced hepatotoxicity; no trend P values remained significant after adjustment for multiple testing using the false discovery rate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a rare case of hepatitis with skin implication selectively caused by Isoniazid, with a positive epicutaneous test, suggesting both a type IV mechanism of immunologic hypersensitivity and drug-induced toxicity. The alternative regimen without Isoniazid was established with total recovery of liver function.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis was accompanied by skin involvement; epicutaneous (patch) test was positive to Isoniazid, suggesting a type IV immunologic hypersensitivity mechanism plus drug-induced toxicity. Dechallenge: switching to a regimen without Isoniazid led to total recovery of liver function.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) is well-known to cause hepatotoxicity, described as its most concerning adverse effect, and has been shown to cause asymptomatic transaminase elevation and frank liver injury. In the 1970 Capitol Hill outbreak investigation, 19 of 2321 TB contacts treated with INH developed hepatotoxicity, including two deaths, with no cases in a matched control group. A subsequent USPHS surveillance study of nearly 14,000 persons taking INH identified 174 (1.3%) probable and possible cases of INH hepatotoxicity, including eight deaths; age (>35 years) and daily alcohol consumption were associated risk factors.
raw_record.extra_details: INH used to treat latent TB infection (LTBI). A meta-analysis of six studies (including the Capitol Hill investigation, the USPHS surveillance study, and the Eastern European IUAT trial) with >38,000 INH-treated persons found 0.6% overall developed hepatotoxicity (range by study 0-2.9%). More recent observational studies with routine monitoring reported lower incidence: Seattle (~11,000 patients) 0.1% and San Diego (~3,800 patients) 0.3%, with no deaths and one hospitalization. Risk factors for INH hepatotoxicity: age >35 years and daily alcohol consumption. INH also causes asymptomatic transaminase elevation and frank liver injury; peripheral neuropathy (<0.2%, preventable/treated with pyridoxine) is a separate adverse effect.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is recognised as a cause of hepatotoxicity in latent tuberculosis treatment. The USPHS surveillance study of 13,838 persons reported isoniazid-related hepatitis frequency of 10.3 per 1,000 participants (1%), most cases occurring within the first 3 months, with eight fatalities (mortality 0.6 per 1,000) and hospitalisation up to 5.0 per 1,000 treatment initiations; an earlier outbreak produced 19 cases of hepatitis with two deaths among 2,321 contacts treated with isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Surveillance of isoniazid-treated contacts: overall hepatitis 10.3/1000 (1%), most within first 3 months; risk increased with age (0%, 0.3%, 1.2%, 2.3% for <20, 20-34, 35-49, 50-64 yrs); daily alcohol consumption was an important risk factor; hospitalisation up to 5.0/1000; 8 fatalities (mortality 0.6/1000). Earlier outbreak: 19 hepatitis cases with 2 deaths among 2,321 contacts. Meta-analysis of 38,257 subjects: clinical hepatitis 0.0-2.9%, combined 0.6% unadjusted for age. Recent estimates of symptomatic hepatitis 1-3/1000, hospitalisation 0.1-0.2/1000, mortality 0.0-0.3/1000; serum transaminase elevations and other hepatic abnormalities recognised during latent TB treatment. Also listed as hepatitis (uncommon reaction) in Table 4.

raw_record.support_text: In a consecutive series of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) and tuberculosis admitted to a liver intensive care unit between 1986 and 2008, 14 of 16 patients had an established diagnosis of anti-TB drug-induced ALF. The paper states that hepatitis was caused by isoniazid (INH) treatment in 4 patients and by pyrazinamide (PZA) in 10 patients. Mean time from initiation of anti-TB treatment to the development of jaundice was 3.5 ± 3.1 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to INH in 4 of 14 patients with anti-TB drug-induced ALF. Patients were receiving anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) for tuberculosis, some immunosuppressed (renal transplant recipients, HIV infection). Two additional patients (miliary TB presenting as liver failure; carbamazepine-induced ALF in DRESS syndrome) were excluded from the study.

raw_record.support_text: Within this DILI ALF cohort, isoniazid, as monotherapy or in combination, is stated to commonly cause hepatotoxicity leading to liver transplantation, followed by sulfur drugs, nitrofurantoin, other antibiotics, and antifungals. For isoniazid the median latency was 5 months, with 6-8 months in one-third of cases. The paper also lists isoniazid among drugs carrying warnings of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Used as monotherapy or in combination; median latency 5 months, 6-8 months in one-third of cases; carries hepatotoxicity warning; noted as a common cause of liver transplantation due to hepatotoxicity in this cohort.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 1039 patients treated prophylactically for latent TB with isoniazid (6H or 9H regimens), hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation occurred in 49 (4.7%) on 6H and 54 (5.2%) on 9H, and transient ALT elevation occurred in 39 (3.8%) on 6H and 70 (6.7%) on 9H. Liver toxicity receded when isoniazid was suspended, and normal liver function was confirmed on follow-up after withdrawal; no patient was hospitalised for hepatotoxicity or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 1039 patients at risk of developing TB; 6H and 9H isoniazid regimens (6 or 9 months). Hepatotoxicity requiring treatment discontinuation: 6H 49 (4.7%, 95%CI 3.4-6.1), 9H 54 (5.2%, 95%CI 3.8-6.6). Transient ALT elevation not causing discontinuation: 6H 39 (3.8%), 9H 70 (6.7%). Liver toxicity receded and liver functions normalized after isoniazid withdrawal; no hospitalization for hepatotoxicity and no liver transplantation. Costs of these adverse effects were maintained based on maximum probable incidence.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid treatment is a recognized cause of clinical hepatitis in the general population. Symptomatic hepatitis was first described in the early 1970s with 19 cases of clinical intolerance (0.8%) and two deaths among 2312 treated contacts. A US multicenter study of 13,838 subjects reported 1% probable hepatitis (up to 2.3% after age 50), higher with alcohol use, requiring hospitalization in 0.5%. In the UICT study, 95 of 20,840 isoniazid-treated subjects developed hepatitis, three of whom died (0.14/1000 treated). Meta-analyses found 0.36% hepatotoxicity at six months and 0.52% at 12 months of treatment, and hepatitis was seen in 6/545 subjects receiving 12 months of isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis risk increased with age (up to 2.3% after 50 years) and alcohol use. Mortality: Ferebee reported 3 deaths/20,840 treatments; two studies reported no deaths among 11,141 treatments or among 1600 elderly institution residents; a US study of 13,838 patients had 8 deaths (0.6/1000), 7 in Baltimore where liver cirrhosis prevalence was above average. A Canadian retrospective matched-cohort study (1998-2003): 9145 LTBI-treated subjects (92.8% isoniazid monotherapy), 45 (0.5%) hospitalized for acute liver disease vs 15/18,290 (0.1%) controls; risk rose per decade of age and with co-morbidities, reaching 2.6% over age 65; 7 treated subjects died (treatment attribution uncertain); 3 liver transplants but all had pre-existing liver disease. Meta-analysis of 38,257 subjects: 0.6% clinical hepatitis (0.0-2.9% by age). Transaminase surveillance: 0.3% abnormalities (3x ULN with symptoms or 5x without); in 3377 adults (5x ULN criterion) risk factors were age >50 or prior transaminase elevation; meta-analysis of 7 articles/18,610 participants: 1.8% biological+clinical toxicity, worse if age >35 (1.7% vs 0.2%), prior transaminase elevation, or alcoholism; hepatitis C and treatment duration (9 vs 6 months) not associated; 15,229 treatments hospitalized, no deaths in 15,644. Prognosis worsened by continuing treatment despite prodromal symptoms (anorexia, asthenia, malaise). Isoniazid is a first-line agent for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatic insufficiency due to isoniazid toxicity during antituberculosis treatment is a rare condition with high mortality, and describes a clinical case in which, after ruling out other etiologies, isoniazid was attributed as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of acute/fulminant hepatic failure during tuberculosis treatment with isoniazid; severe hepatic impairment with coagulopathy (Quick time <60%) unresponsive to vitamin K; other etiologies ruled out per drug hepatotoxicity diagnostic guidelines and fulminant hepatic failure prognostic criteria; liver transplant indicated; antituberculosis treatment continued with alternative drugs due to risk of reactivating infection under post-transplant immunosuppression; condition described as rare with high mortality (reference 11).

raw_record.support_text: The study investigates human patients with INH (isoniazid)-induced liver failure, presenting a series of 20 acute liver failure (ALF) patients attributed to isoniazid therapy. Sera from these patients were analyzed for anti-INH and anti-CYP antibodies; the paper frames the injury as 'INH-induced liver failure' and reports that elevated peak ALT, bilirubin, and INR values occurred in these patients following isoniazid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 patients with INH-induced acute liver failure were studied; isoniazid dosed typically at 300 mg/day for durations up to ~8 months for tuberculosis prophylaxis/treatment. Peak ALT up to 144 U/L was recorded in milder cases; liver-failure patients showed markedly elevated ALT, bilirubin, and INR. Sera were tested for anti-INH antibodies (positive in patients ALF-2, ALF-3, ALF-7, ALF-9, ALF-10, ALF-14, ALF-18, ALF-19) and for autoantibodies against CYP2E1, CYP3A4, and CYP2C9. Many ALF patients also took concomitant medications (rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and others), but the paper attributes the liver failure to isoniazid. In vitro covalent binding of INH to CYP2E1, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 was shown, and patients with liver failure displayed antibodies against INH-modified CYP2E1.

raw_record.support_text: In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) analysis of non-acetaminophen drug-induced ALF, isoniazid (INH) was implicated in 21 cases, 15 as monotherapy and 6 when used in combination, as one of the most common antimicrobial causes.
raw_record.extra_details: ALFSG 1998-2007: 21 drug-induced ALF cases (15 INH monotherapy, 6 in combination). US DILIN registry: n=13 suspected single-agent DILI. UNOS database: n=48 INH alone and n=2 with another antituberculosis drug as causes of emergency liver transplant for drug-induced ALF. Spain (n=9) and Sweden (n=7) also list INH as an implicated antimicrobial.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid was used as a positive control, described as one drug known to be a causative agent of acute liver injury. In the disproportionality analysis, the association between isoniazid and acute liver injury was consistently among the largest effects observed, with all 5 claims databases generating IRR between 3 and 5 with very tight confidence intervals.
raw_record.extra_details: Used as a positive control drug. Across 5 US claims databases (CCAE, MDCD, MDCR, MSLR, GE), disproportionality analysis gave IRRs between 3 and 5 with very tight confidence intervals for the isoniazid–acute liver injury pair.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) causes human drug-induced liver injury with a delayed onset; anti-INH and/or anti-P450 antibodies were found in 15 of 19 patients with INH-induced liver failure, and covalent INH binding was identified in a human liver biopsy from a patient with INH-induced liver failure. In five patients with mild INH-induced liver injury there was an increase in Th17 cells and IL-10-producing cells, whereas patients taking INH without liver injury showed none of these findings. The authors conclude the mechanism is immune-mediated idiosyncratic injury rather than 'metabolic idiosyncrasy.'
raw_record.extra_details: Delayed-onset liver injury; mild injury can resolve despite continued treatment. Anti-INH and/or anti-P450 antibodies detected in serum of 15/19 patients with INH-induced liver failure, but no anti-drug or anti-P450 antibodies in patients who received INH without severe liver injury. Increased Th17 and IL-10-producing cells in 5 patients with mild INH-induced liver injury. Covalent binding of INH identified in a human liver biopsy from a patient with INH-induced liver failure. Authors reject prior 'metabolic idiosyncrasy' mechanism attributed to acetylhydrazine (AcHz) bioactivation.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, isoniazid was the second most common individual DILI agent, accounting for 48 of 899 adjudicated cases. Isoniazid is classified under antimicrobials, the class responsible for most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 48 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry; second most common individual agent.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is listed among drugs with very well documented hepatotoxicity with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge (reproduced DILI), and is identified among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in DILIN and as a top-ten drug in multiple DILI registries.
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculosis agent; among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in the DILIN cohort (with amoxicillin–clavulanate, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole); in the ten most frequent drugs of the DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish registries; rechallenge has reproduced the DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Among 60 isoniazid (INH) hepatotoxicity patients, patterns of liver injury at presentation were predominantly hepatocellular, with 55 (92%) patients having an R ratio greater than 5, and 4 (7%) having a mixed pattern (R ratio 2-5); no patient had a cholestatic pattern. The mean days from INH initiation to increased ALT was 97 days, and from DILI onset to peak ALT was short (mean 6.6 days).
raw_record.extra_details: 60 INH hepatotoxicity patients from the DILIN registry. 55/60 (92%) hepatocellular (R ratio >5); 4 (7%) mixed (R ratio 2-5); none cholestatic. Mean days INH initiation to increased ALT 97 d (SD 64); to ALT ≥5x ULN 103 d (SD 59); DILI onset to peak ALT mean 6.6 d (SD 9). DILIN Severity Index scores reported; 12 patients required liver transplant (1 died post-transplant) and another patient died without transplant; 37 (62%) hospitalized; 14 (23%) encephalopathy. Mean peak ALT 1385 IU/L, bilirubin 12.7 mg/dL, INR 2.6. Delay in stopping INH after ATS stopping criteria correlated with higher SIS (P=.05); among those continuing INH >1 week, 49% had severe/fatal course vs 22% stopping within 7 days; higher BMI correlated with increased SIS (P=.02).

raw_record.support_text: A patient admitted with markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 1,581 IU/L, ALT 2,540 IU/L, ALP 734 IU/L, γ-GTP 553 IU/L, T-Bil 7.82 mg/dL), prolonged prothrombin time, and slight liver atrophy on CT had negative viral and autoimmune markers. A drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) for isoniazid (INH) was positive [249 S.I. (>180%)], and the patient was diagnosed with INH-induced hepatitis. Despite discontinuing INH and starting ursodeoxycholic acid, the injury progressed to acute liver failure with Grade II hepatic encephalopathy; the patient rejected proposed liver transplantation and died of liver failure four months after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of INH-induced hepatitis in a latent tuberculosis patient. Elevated serum IgE (1,739 mg/dL). DLST for INH positive [249 S.I. (>180%)]. Illness progressed despite INH discontinuation and ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day: advancing liver atrophy on CT, sepsis with Enterobacter aerogenes (blood culture positive), Grade II hepatic encephalopathy, PT 30% (INR 2.05), acute liver failure (subacute type, Japanese criteria), and death from liver failure four months after admission. Review context: INH hepatotoxicity ranges from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to severe hepatitis; AST >5x ULN reported in 0.56% (19/3,377) and >10x ULN in 0.30% (10/3,377) of INH-treated patients; US Public Health Service reported 8 hepatitis deaths among ~14,000 patients; higher INH hepatotoxicity incidence reported in patients over 35 years, those with daily alcohol consumption, and HCV/HIV carriers; slow-acetylator NAT2 and CYP2E1 C/D or C/C genotypes associated with higher hepatotoxicity frequency.

raw_record.support_text: During isoniazid chemoprophylaxis for tuberculosis, chemoprophylactic agents can cause a wide range of liver side effects, from a slight increase in transaminases to diffuse necrosis of the liver; liver damage is dose related and usually of a hepatocellular type, with most cases developing in the first 4-8 weeks of treatment, and progression to irreversible liver failure is very rare.
raw_record.extra_details: A 32-year-old woman admitted with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting for 2 days; initial diagnosis was fulminant toxic hepatitis due to isoniazid chemoprophylaxis at 300 mg/day for 5 months (given because the patient's father was being treated for active pulmonary tuberculosis). Reduced consciousness and delirium developed on the seventh day of treatment. Treated successfully with living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) because she refused cadaveric transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial reports an analysis of hepatotoxicity from the PREVENT TB study in patients treated for latent tuberculous infection (LTBI). Among 6862 patients who took at least one dose, hepatotoxicity was lower in the once-weekly rifapentine-plus-isoniazid (3HP1) group than in the daily isoniazid for 9 months (9H) group (0.4% vs 1.9%, P<0.001), for both symptomatic and asymptomatic cases. The editorial also states generally that hepatotoxicity limits completion of daily isoniazid LTBI therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Daily isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months (9H) for LTBI preventive chemotherapy. In the PREVENT TB study (6862 patients taking at least one dose), hepatotoxicity was 1.9% in the 9H group vs 0.4% in the 3HP1 (weekly rifapentine+isoniazid) group, P<0.001, seen in both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; monitoring of liver enzymes varied by site (baseline AST measured for 76% of participants; repeat AST for 40% on 9H and 35% on 3HP1). Multivariable risk factors: abnormal baseline AST (relative risk 5.57, 95% CI 3.31–9.37), increased age, female sex, white race, non-Hispanic ethnicity, history of chronic liver disease; nested case-control identified hepatitis C as a risk factor (OR 3.24, 95% CI 1.12–9.34). Editorial notes hepatotoxicity limits completion rates of daily 6–9 month isoniazid LTBI therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In 1975, Mitchell et al. prospectively followed psychiatric hospital patients treated with isoniazid (INH) during a tuberculosis outbreak, collecting blood before starting INH and up to 1 week after study termination. INH (isoniazid) resulted in elevated liver enzymes in 38% of patients, which subsided in the majority despite continued INH treatment, including several who developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law cases). The text notes that although INH toxicity can result in severe liver injury and even liver failure, no cases of liver failure were reported in this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Classic example of adaptation: 38% of patients developed elevated liver enzymes, resolving in the majority despite continued INH; several developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law). Though INH toxicity can cause severe liver injury and even liver failure, no liver failure cases occurred in this study. Patients were psychiatric hospital patients treated during a tuberculosis outbreak; liver enzymes followed every 4 weeks. Figure 1 shows AST and bilirubin trends (AST >60 and bilirubin >1.2 mg/dl, with three Hy's Law cases having bilirubin >2x ULN) plotted by Dr John Senior (FDA).

raw_record.support_text: In an ALFSG cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF and APAP-ALF groups, isoniazid was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity progressing to acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 71 tuberculosis patients on a conventional antituberculosis regimen, 11 (15.4%) patients developed isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity (IIH), diagnosed according to Benichou et al. A high isoniazid serum concentration (C3, measured 3 h after the morning dose) was a risk factor for IIH (AUC 0.74, P=0.007, 95% CI 0.56–0.93), with a cutoff at 3.69 mg/L (OR 13.2, P=0.0007, 95% CI 2.9–59). A combined CYP2E1 Dral(C/D)/slow-acetylator NAT2 genotype also increased IIH risk (OR 8.41, P=0.01, 95% CI 1.54–45.76).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity reported as 11/71 (15.4%) in Tunisian tuberculosis patients on a conventional antituberculosis regimen; diagnosed per Benichou et al. Risk factor analysis: isoniazid serum concentration C3 > 3.69 mg/L (AUC 0.74, P=0.007, 95% CI 0.56–0.93; OR 13.2, P=0.0007, 95% CI 2.9–59) was the only independent multivariate risk factor; combined CYP2E1 Dral C/D plus slow-acetylator NAT2 genotype increased risk (OR 8.41, P=0.01, 95% CI 1.54–45.76) vs other combined profiles, while NAT2 and CYP2E1 variants analyzed separately did not increase risk. Demographic factors (age, weight, gender) were not associated with hepatotoxicity. Introduction notes INH causes a range of 1–36% incidence of hepatotoxicity depending on study criteria.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as a leading cause of hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. In a study from the US DILI Network (DILIN), isoniazid was the second most frequently reported hepatotoxic agent in the registry, with cases likely under-reported. Investigators found a significant delay in discontinuing isoniazid after hepatitis-related symptoms developed: over 50% of patients who met criteria that would warrant immediate drug cessation continued isoniazid for more than 7 days, and 24 patients (40%) continued for more than 14 days; 9 of 13 patients who continued for more than 7 days were listed as having died or needing a liver transplant.
raw_record.extra_details: Leading cause of hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. Second most frequently reported hepatotoxic agent in the US DILIN registry; cases likely under-reported. Self-reported symptom monitoring was relied upon rather than formal ALT testing. Delay in discontinuation: over 50% of patients meeting symptom criteria for immediate drug stop continued isoniazid >7 days, 24 patients (40%) >14 days; 9 of 13 patients continuing >7 days died or needed liver transplant. Symptoms: nausea, abdominal pain, jaundice, unexplained fatigue.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old female with latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection receiving oral isoniazid 300 mg daily was admitted for epigastric and right-sided flank pain of one-week duration; laboratory results and imaging confirmed hepatitis. After ruling out all other possible causes, she was diagnosed with isoniazid-induced acute hepatitis, rated a probable association by the Naranjo scale. She was readmitted with severe coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, hepatic encephalopathy, and cardiorespiratory arrest and, despite maximal hemodynamic support, did not survive. The paper also reviews literature from European countries and the USA reporting a low incidence of mortality due to isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity when isoniazid is used as a single agent for latent tuberculosis infection, and notes that withdrawal of isoniazid is the first management step and rechallenge is usually discouraged.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dose 300 mg daily for latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; presented with epigastric and right-sided flank pain for one week; hepatitis confirmed by labs and imaging; later severe coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, hepatic encephalopathy, and cardiorespiratory arrest requiring two rounds of CPR; patient died despite maximal hemodynamic support. Naranjo scale rated probable. Patient was 65 years old (age is a well-confirmed risk factor per the paper's discussion). Literature review (European countries and USA) indicates a low incidence of mortality when isoniazid is used as single-agent therapy for latent TB; management is withdrawal of isoniazid and rechallenge is usually discouraged. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncratic reactions; CYP2E1 c1/c1 homozygous slow acetylators at increased risk. Historical context: 1970 Capitol Hill TB outbreak, 19 prophylaxis workers developed signs/symptoms of liver damage and 2 died.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that among INH (isoniazid)-associated fatal hepatitis cases, deaths predominated in women: 16 of 20 deaths in this series were female, and 12 of 16 overall and eight of nine in the 15-49 age group were women when postpartum deaths are excluded. This is consistent with 23 published INH hepatitis deaths of which 16 were in women, making 32 of 43 reported deaths female. An epidemiologic study showed a 3-fold excess mortality from cirrhosis among females exposed to INH but not among males, and a prior study found roughly equal incidence of INH-associated hepatitis in men and women but higher female case fatality (6 of 8 deaths in women).
raw_record.extra_details: INH used as tuberculosis preventive/prophylactic treatment; 20 fatal INH-associated hepatitis cases in this series with 16 female deaths (including 8 of 9 in reproductive ages 15-49); combined with 23 published deaths gives 32 of 43 deaths in women; epidemiologic study reported 3-fold excess cirrhosis mortality among exposed females but not males; prior study showed approximately equal hepatitis incidence in men and women but higher female case fatality (6 of 8 deaths were women). Racial distribution of the 20 deaths: 14 Hispanic, 4 white, 2 black, no Oriental deaths despite a large Oriental population (55.31% Hispanic, 7.98% white, 2.8% black, 21.35% Oriental among INH recipients); total 36 reported INH hepatitis deaths without an Oriental death.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN Prospective Study cohort (1198 participants with definite, highly likely, or probable DILI), the frequency of liver injury due to isoniazid was not different between the heavy alcohol consumption group and those without alcohol consumption (6.3% vs 5%, p=0.8). The text attributes isoniazid as a cause of DILI in these adjudicated human cases.
raw_record.extra_details: From the DILIN Prospective Study; frequency of isoniazid-attributed DILI was 6.3% in the heavy alcohol consumption group (n=80 heavy drinkers) versus 5% in those without alcohol consumption, p=0.8. Part of adjudicated DILI cases (definite, highly likely, or probable).

raw_record.support_text: Among people receiving tuberculosis preventive therapy in Tibetan schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 11 schoolchildren (1.4%) and 1 staff member (1.0%) experienced hepatotoxicity attributed to isoniazid, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms that regressed after the drug was discontinued. Preventive therapy was permanently stopped for 2 people with hepatotoxicity; 10 others completed treatment. Separately, 1 of 20 individuals with latent TB and HBV coinfection who received preventive therapy with isoniazid and rifampicin developed hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Recipients were schoolchildren and staff with latent TB infection receiving TB preventive therapy in Tibetan boarding/day schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 2017. Of those treated, 227 (25%) people developed at least 1 treatment side effect, almost all attributed to isoniazid; fatigue, drowsiness, and gastrointestinal complaints were reported by 8%-10% of schoolchildren and 5%-13% of staff. Isoniazid-attributed hepatotoxicity occurred in 11/799 (1.4%) schoolchildren and 1/101 (1.0%) staff, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms regressing after drug discontinuation; preventive therapy was permanently stopped in 2 people. One of 20 (44%) HBV-coinfected latent TB individuals receiving isoniazid + rifampicin developed hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation. Isoniazid was used both as part of a regimen with rifampicin (isoniazid-rifampicin) and alone for 4-6 months in some individuals.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs. The causative drug was identified as isoniazid in eight patients, rifampicin in 14 and pyrazinamide in 16 per next-generation sequencing analysis framed around the hypothesis that mtDNA variants are risk factors for isoniazid-, rifampicin- or pyrazinamide-induced DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, isoniazid was the attributed causative drug in 8. DILI was defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. Isoniazid-induced liver injury cases had more variants in complex I NADH subunit 5 and 1 genes, more nonsynonymous mutations in NADH subunit 5, and a higher nonsynonymous/total substitution ratio, consistent with the hypothesis that hydrazine, an isoniazid metabolite and complex II inhibitor, predisposes to injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of healthcare workers receiving latent tuberculosis infection treatment, hepatotoxicity occurred in 17/43 (39.5%) on the 9-month isoniazid (9H) regimen, with hepatotoxicity ≥grade 2 in 8 (18.6%). Hepatotoxicity incidence was higher in 9H than in 3HR (39.5% vs 17.2%). Seven workers had to change or discontinue their LTBI treatment because of hepatotoxicity, all in the 9H group, with LFT (ALT/AST) elevations with or without hepatitis symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: 9-month isoniazid (9H) LTBI regimen; 43 recipients among healthcare workers. Hepatotoxicity 17/43 (39.5%), ≥grade 2 in 8 (18.6%); median time to hepatotoxicity 102 days (IQR 96-105). Seven cases caused regimen change/discontinuation: LFT elevation ALT grade 1-3 with/without hepatitis symptoms, sample AST/ALT 84/212, 105/126, 129/135, 338/670, 100/106, 102/140, 105/678. Major adverse event hepatotoxicity: ALT >3x ULN with symptoms in 4 (9.3%) and ALT >5x ULN without symptoms in 3 (7.0%).

raw_record.support_text: In the European American subset, 32 DILI patients were due to isoniazid, two of whom carried HLA-B*14:01 (carriage frequency 0.063). The paper groups these as DILI patients attributed to isoniazid in the DILIN cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN registry DILI cohort; 32 European American isoniazid DILI patients (2/32 carrying HLA-B*14:01, CF=0.063); 19 African American isoniazid DILI patients (2/19 carrying HLA-B*35:01, CF=0.105).

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid causes mild liver injury (increased serum transaminases) in approximately 10% of persons taking it, usually transient and asymptomatic, and occasionally clinically apparent hepatitis that mimics acute viral hepatitis, often with severe hepatitis showing bridging and/or multilobular necrosis. In a study of 14 patients with isoniazid hepatitis, 3 died with fulminant hepatic failure and bridging/multilobular necrosis was found in 8 of the 11 survivors; one patient who died after 6 months of drug had cirrhosis at postmortem.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild transaminase elevations occur in ~10% of users, generally unassociated with clinical symptoms and usually subsiding despite continued administration; clinically apparent hepatitis is infrequent and mimics acute viral hepatitis; severe hepatitis with bridging and/or multilobular necrosis common among clinically apparent cases. In a study of 14 isoniazid hepatitis patients, 3 died of fulminant hepatic failure and 8 of 11 survivors had bridging/multilobular necrosis; one 6-month-treated fatal case had cirrhosis at postmortem; no clinical or biochemical evidence of continuing disease in surviving patients, with follow-up biopsy in 2 showing mild residual scarring but no ongoing necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: In the survey, isoniazid was the most frequently incriminated anti-tuberculosis drug in drug-induced liver damage, accounting for 16.3% of total DILI cases, and the paper notes pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin are known for their hepatotoxicity. The mechanism table additionally describes isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity as idiosyncratic and most probably caused by toxic metabolites.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed in 16.3% of total DILI cases in the Maghrebian survey; considered idiosyncratic, most probably caused by toxic metabolites; used for tuberculosis treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists isoniazid with 19 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Hopley (99).
raw_record.extra_details: 19 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); HLA pharmacogenetic association noted in some patients (p32).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the most severe side effect associated with antituberculosis medications such as isoniazid, and describes a study by Lee et al. (2019) in which 38 patients with tuberculosis who had experienced DILI (16 attributed to pyrazinamide, 14 to rifampin, 8 to isoniazid) were compared with 38 sex- and age-matched non-DILI TB-positive controls. Patients presenting with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity were explicitly identified, making isoniazid the attributed liver-injuring agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Lee et al. (2019) case-control study (38 TB patients with DILI, including 8 isoniazid-attributed cases, vs 38 matched non-DILI controls) using PacBio SMRT sequencing of the mitochondrial genome. The paper's focus was mtDNA variant associations: patients with isoniazid-induced DILI had more mtDNA variants in complex I ND1 (p=0.025) and ND5 (p=0.028), more non-synonymous ND5 mutations (1.5±1.6 vs 0.7±0.8; p=0.033), and a higher ratio of non-synonymous to total substitutions than non-DILI controls. The authors hypothesized variation in complex I subunits predisposes to isoniazid-induced DILI via the primary metabolite hydrazine, a complex II inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: In the Toxic Hepatitis group (D), three patients had biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis caused respectively by diphenylhydantoin, INH (isoniazid), and methyldopa. Liver biopsies in each case showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation, and all three had extremely high GGTP values (1018, 980, and 645 mU/ml) with alkaline phosphatase values of 284, 560, and 251 IU.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis attributed to INH (isoniazid); histology showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation; GGTP 980 mU/ml and AP 560 IU.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute liver failure in a middle-aged woman who had taken isoniazid for five months for latent tuberculosis, which progressed despite withdrawal of the drug and required liver transplantation, with a favorable outcome. The case is presented as a rare example of progression to acute liver failure despite isoniazid discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Middle-aged woman treated with isoniazid for 5 months for latent tuberculosis; acute liver failure developed despite drug withdrawal; required liver transplantation with favorable outcome. Authors caution on isoniazid hepatotoxicity and the need for tight monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies hepatitis as the risk of greatest concern from isoniazid chemoprophylaxis. A CDC cooperative surveillance study following 13,838 people in 21 health departments found 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases, with the authors judging the true incidence best approximated by the probable cases. Age-specific rates (per 1000 persons) were used: one possible and no probable for those under age 20 years; seven possible and three probable for ages 20-34; 11 possible and 12 probable for ages 35-49; 18 possible and 23 probable for ages 50-64; and 18 possible and eight probable for those over 64 years. The probability of terminating chemoprophylaxis because of hepatitis used combined possible and probable rates.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid given as tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis, assumed 70% effective in preventing activation (varied 30%-90% in sensitivity analysis). Hepatitis led to termination of prophylaxis in the analysis. In a CDC cooperative surveillance study of 13,838 people in 21 health departments there were 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases; incidence rates per 1000 persons by age (possible/probable): under 20 y: 1/0; 20-34 y: 7/3; 35-49 y: 11/12; 50-64 y: 18/23; over 64 y: 18/8. Rates varied by 75%-125% in sensitivity analysis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 680 trial participants receiving isoniazid preventive therapy, hepatotoxicity resulting in isoniazid discontinuation occurred in 47 (7%) participants. Isoniazid discontinuation due to a grade 3 or higher adverse event occurred in 53 (8%) participants, and there was significant heterogeneity in hepatotoxicity by study site, with one rural site having significantly greater hepatotoxicity rates.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity resulting in isoniazid discontinuation occurred in 47 (7%) of 680 participants during isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT); 53 (8%) discontinued isoniazid due to a grade 3 or higher adverse event overall. No significant association between randomisation group (alcohol reduction and/or isoniazid adherence incentives) and hepatotoxicity leading to isoniazid discontinuation after adjusting for sex and site; significant site heterogeneity, with one rural site showing greater hepatotoxicity rates.

raw_record.support_text: In an adjudicated IDILI patient cohort, 4 single drugs caused IDILI in at least 3 patients each, and only INH (isoniazid)-induced liver injury showed significant DEGs compared to IDILI not due to INH. All three patients with INH-induced IDILI were in the 'fatal' IDILI group: two died because of their injury and one required a liver transplant. Of 25 DEGs associated with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, 80% were elevated in the INH patients, and 40% overlapped with the DEGs related to IDILI severity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with INH-induced IDILI were in the fatal IDILI group: two died from their injury and one required liver transplant. Of 25 DEGs associated with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, 80% were elevated in INH patients, 40% overlapped with general IDILI-severity DEGs; TRBV7-2, encoding a TCR subunit, was reduced in INH patients. No canonical pathways were significant. No differences in circulating T-cell percentages or concentration were observed between INH-related and other severe/all IDILI patients. Study note: patients frequently take multiple medications/supplements concurrently, complicating culprit identification; INH-induced injury was the drug-attributable subgroup analyzed.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient on isoniazid (INH), a liver biopsy revealed severe acute hepatitis with features suggestive of drug-induced immune-mediated injury, including prominent interface hepatitis, a lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate, and multiple foci of lobular confluent necrosis. Given the severity and progressive course despite INH discontinuation and a low TB reactivation risk, the patient was started on prednisone for presumed INH-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis. Two months after starting INH he had developed jaundice, markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2126 U/L, ALT 2617 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 15.7 mg/dL) and mild coagulopathy (INR 1.4), and his liver tests met DILI Network grade 3 severity criteria; he improved on prednisone and had normalized liver enzymes at 6-month follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper frames this as drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-ALH), a subgroup of DILI recognized by AASLD Practice Guidance and an expert group report ('liver injury with laboratory or/and histological evidence of autoimmunity'). Latency was 2 months after starting INH; presentation included jaundice, RUQ pain, fatigue, ALT 2617 U/L, AST 2126 U/L, total bilirubin 15.7 mg/dL, INR 1.4; on readmission liver injury met DILI Network grade 3 severity criteria. Biopsy showed interface hepatitis, lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate, lobular confluent necrosis, and no fibrosis on trichrome. Viral hepatitis, CMV, EBV and autoimmune (ANA, ASMA) markers were negative. Patient was treated with prednisone 40 mg daily with tapering over 1 month, with no recurrence and normal enzymes at 6-month follow-up. INH was discontinued (dechallenge) with worsening before steroid therapy. Indication was latent TB treatment/prophylaxis; no TB reactivation occurred.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes clinically meaningful human liver injury to isoniazid. Scharer and Smith reported that 10% of patients receiving isoniazid alone for preventive tuberculosis therapy developed elevated serum transaminases (SGOT and SGPT) during the first 2 months of treatment, with liver biopsies in 5 patients showing focal hepatic necrosis and transaminases generally returning to normal with continued therapy. In a Capitol Hill cohort, 19 of 2,321 employees given isoniazid developed hepatitis (attack rate 8.2 per 1,000), 13 were jaundiced, and 2 died, versus attack rates of 0.5 per 1,000 in matched non-isoniazid controls and 0 per 1,000 in tuberculin reactors who refused treatment. A subsequent prospective Public Health Service surveillance of 13,838 patients, including 3,196 in Baltimore, recorded 41 isoniazid-associated cases of liver dysfunction with 7 deaths (rate 12.83 per 1,000) and 133 probable/possible hepatitis cases with 1 fatality in the other 20 health departments (rate 12.50 per 1,000). The paper concludes that the new evidence shows isoniazid can produce liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Preventive-therapy setting for tuberculosis. Elevated serum transaminases (SGOT and SGPT) in 10% of patients in the first 2 months, with focal hepatic necrosis on biopsy in 5 patients and enzyme return to normal despite continued isoniazid in most instances. Capitol Hill study: 19/2,321 developed hepatitis, 13 jaundiced, 2 died; hepatitis attack rate 8.2/1,000 vs 0.5/1,000 in matched non-treated controls and 0/1,000 in untreated tuberculin reactors. Symptom onset 3-31 weeks after therapy initiation; 2 fatal cases began at 22 and 30 weeks. Prospective PHS surveillance: 41 isoniazid-associated liver-dysfunction cases with 7 deaths in Baltimore (3,196 patients, rate 12.83/1,000) and 133 probable/possible hepatitis cases with 1 fatality across 20 health departments (10,642 patients, rate 12.50/1,000). CDC Ad Hoc Committee on Isoniazid and Liver Disease recommended continued use with monthly questioning for symptoms of liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: In an isoniazid-treated patient, an open liver biopsy showed thick fibrous capsule, dense connective tissue septa, periportal necrosis with ballooning and condensed liver cells and spotty focal necrosis, judged most consistent with a chronic progressive, precirrhotic drug-related form of hepatitis. Three months after cessation of isoniazid, splenomegaly and varices resolved and serum values returned to normal, supporting isoniazid as the cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic progressive precirrhotic hepatitis with ascites, edema, portal hypertension, palpable spleen and esophageal varices; gradual improvement after isoniazid cessation with normalization of SGOT, bilirubin, albumin and platelet count. Biopsy showed fibrosis with mononuclear inflammation, erosion of limiting plates, ballooning hepatocytes and spotty focal necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents 5 patients with 'isoniazid-associated hepatitis' who received prophylactic isoniazid (INH) for 3 weeks to 3 months before symptoms developed. In all 5 patients serum contained no hepatitis-associated antigen, and all drugs except INH (including indomethacin) were restarted without clinical exacerbation, supporting INH as the causal agent. INH rechallenge was not performed because a prior rechallenge of INH had been fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 patients reported; duration of INH therapy before symptoms 3 weeks to 3 months; cases presented after the hospital changed to its current pharmaceutical supplier of INH. Other medications (indomethacin, phenobarbital, chloral hydrate, nitroglycerine, meprobamate, aspirin, etc.) were restarted without exacerbation; INH rechallenge avoided due to a prior fatal rechallenge report. Histology varied from classic viral hepatitis to portal inflammation, portal noncaseating granulomas, and portal/periportal eosinophil infiltration. Earlier literature: 6 cases before 1960, scattered reports including fatal cases, and 2,321 Capitol Hill INH prophylactic recipients with clinical hepatitis in 19 (2 died); Scharer and Smith prospective study found 10% asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 90 patients. The paper notes INH-associated hepatitis is apparently idiosyncratic and not dose-related, with severity ranging from transient transaminase elevations to fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that although toxic hepatic injury from isoniazid has been produced in animals and man with large doses, it has not occurred at the usual dose range of 3-5 mg/kg/day; nevertheless, the drug at standard doses clearly and occasionally causes hepatitis, presumably by a hypersensitivity mechanism. The authors note the literature contains 17 detailed, adequately documented case reports of isoniazid-induced hepatitis, often complicated by serious underlying disease and concurrent antituberculous drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Standard doses of 3-5 mg/kg/day for tuberculosis treatment or prophylaxis. Serum transaminase elevations occur in approximately 10% of prophylaxis patients, usually mild and resolving despite continuation; such cases showed mild focal hepatitis on biopsy. Authors found 17 detailed documented case reports (with concomitant adverse reactions to aminosalicylic acid in 11 and streptomycin in 2), requiring rechallenge to distinguish reactions; rechallenge was positive in many. In a group of 2300 government employees given prophylaxis there were 2 deaths from hepatitis and 19 other cases (~1% incidence); Berté series reported only 1.3% adverse reactions to isoniazid. Eight deaths from isoniazid hepatitis were reported including three in the authors' series. Mechanism presumed hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report another case to add to the literature on isoniazid-induced hepatitis: a patient who died in hepatic failure 2 months after beginning isoniazid therapy. The patient was given isoniazid 300 mg daily (with pyridoxine 50 mg daily) following a positive PPD test, became icteric ~6 weeks later, and isoniazid was withdrawn. She deteriorated and died in hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of 53-year-old woman treated for latent tuberculosis infection; isoniazid 300 mg daily with pyridoxine 50 mg daily; latency ~2 months (isoniazid withdrawn 4 days before admission when icteric); died in hepatic failure. Antemortem labs: total bilirubin 35.4 mg/100 ml (direct 24 mg/100 ml), SGOT 1000 IU, LDH 582 IU, alkaline phosphatase 84.6 Babson units, prothrombin time 38.5 s vs control 12.5 s, BUN 23 mg/100 ml. Postmortem: shrunken soft green liver; histology showed diffuse destruction of hepatic tissue with preservation of irregular islands of hepatocytes in a pseudoacinar pattern within broad bands of fibrous tissue, bile duct proliferation, and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells; no Dane particles on EM. Concurrent exposures included earlier ablative radioiodine (5.3 mCi 131I) and propranolol 10 mg qid; causality is attributed to isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: Of 249 patients treated with prophylactic isoniazid, three (1.2%) developed hepatitis. All three cases had elevated SGOT, negative hepatitis B antigen tests, and resolved abnormal laboratory values after isoniazid was withdrawn (dechallenge), consistent with isoniazid-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Prophylactic use (indications prioritized as close contact, recent conversion, positive PPD in child/adolescent, inadequately treated TB, reinfective X-ray with positive PPD, positive PPD with risk factors). Incidence 3/249 (1.2%). Latency: Patient 1 after ~2 years on isoniazid (then 300 mg/day; lethargy, 6 kg weight loss, SGOT 450 Karmen units [normal 8-40], LDH 600 IU, normal bilirubin, negative HBsAg; enzymes normal within a month after withdrawal and weight regained within 3 months). Patient 2: 6 weeks after starting, dark urine, abdominal discomfort, jaundice; SGOT 1600 Karmen units, bilirubin 9.0 mg/100 ml, negative HBsAg; lab values normalized within a month after withdrawal. Patient 3: 7 weeks after starting, jaundice and itching; SGOT 2000 Karmen units, bilirubin 26 mg/100 ml, negative HBsAg; values normal 6 weeks after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 40-year-old merchant seaman who developed hepatitis shortly after beginning isoniazid (INH) 300 mg daily for a recent tuberculin skin-test conversion. Challenge with INH was followed by a recurrence of hepatitis that was confirmed by histologic study, and after rises in SGOT each time INH was restarted with return to normal on discontinuation, the authors concluded INH was causing the hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single patient; INH taken at 300 mg daily starting one month before presentation (February 13, 1968) with anorexia, epigastric pain, gray stools, dark urine and jaundice. Serial SGOT rose to 1885 and 1750 U and total bilirubin to 18.4 and 24.2 mg/100 ml; rechallenge with INH (restarted and stopped) produced recurrent SGOT rises (151, 734, 526 U) with return to normal on discontinuation. Liver biopsy showed moderate mononuclear, rare polymorphonuclear and eosinophilic infiltrate in periportal and centrolobular regions with necrosis and reticulin-fiber collapse. Patient denied fever, skin rash, peripheral eosinophilia, prior jaundice, transfusions and recent injections; consumed only moderate social whiskey. PAS concurrently noted as a well-known potential hepatotoxin in other reported cases, but only INH was administered here.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient in whom hepatitis developed shortly after he began taking isoniazid (INH) for a recent tuberculin skin-test conversion, and challenge with INH was followed by a recurrence of hepatitis confirmed by histologic study. The paper notes that INH is thought to be a rare cause of jaundice but that its precise role has previously been unclear, as most patients in earlier cases also received para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), a known hepatotoxin.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 40-year-old merchant seaman with no prior jaundice who took isoniazid 300 mg daily for a positive tuberculin test; hepatitis (with 1 week of anorexia, epigastric pain, loose gray stools, dark urine and jaundice) developed one month after starting INH. Serial SGOT peaked at 1885 U (2/14/68) and bilirubin at 24.2 mg/100 ml; jaundice recurred on INH rechallenge (4/17/68, then again 8/1/68-8/5/68), with elevation confirmed and biopsy performed; INH was stopped on 8/5/68 and SGOT fell to 37 U by 8/16/68. Galbumin 3.5 gm/100 ml, total protein 6.5 gm; no history of blood transfusions or recent injections, only moderate social whiskey drinking. Author affiliation: Alaska Native Medical Center.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 113 patients taking preventive isoniazid (INH) for at least 8 weeks, 19 of 101 patients with initially normal liver tests developed significant liver dysfunction, mostly hepatocellular, with three developing overt hepatitis. After excluding 12 patients who drank alcohol, 15 of 89 still developed significant liver dysfunction, 12 of whom were slow acetylators (p<0.05), and age was the only other risk factor. The paper concludes that fast acetylation is not a risk factor for INH-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Preventive INH 300 mg orally daily (or 5 mg/kg for children) in outpatients, followed prospectively; the paper cites an ~1% incidence of overt and 10-20% incidence of subclinical liver damage with INH therapy.
