Among 113 completing 2 months, 19/101 with normal initial tests developed significant liver dysfunction (3 overt hepatitis); excluding 12 alcohol drinkers, 15/89 remained affected, 12 being slow acetylators. Risk of INH-induced liver enzyme elevation by acetylator phenotype and age (alcohol excluded): under 35 fast acetylators 3.7%, slow 13%; over 35 fast 13.2%, slow 37% (p<0.02). Slow acetylation and older age were risk factors; fast acetylation was not a risk factor. Mitchel evidence on monoacetylhydrazine (P-450 mediated acylating agent causing liver necrosis) is discussed as a proposed mechanism, not an independent human DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 15 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) and massive hepatic necrosis who underwent orthotopic liver transplantation, the etiology of FHF was classified on the basis of molecular and immunohistochemical findings as HBV infection in six patients, HCV infection in one patient, isoniazid toxicity in one patient (case 9, a 69-year-old man), and unknown in seven patients. Case 9 had a history of isoniazid toxicity and the inflammatory infiltrate in the explant was scanty.
raw_record.extra_details: 78-year... correction: 69-year-old male (case 9) with fulminant hepatic failure and massive hepatic necrosis (MHN) requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Explant showed MHN with prominent regenerative nodules and scanty inflammatory cells (plasma cells not conspicuous). Final diagnosis assigned as isoniazid toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that 'hepatic disease in most of these patients undoubtedly was induced by isoniazid.' They argue the uniformly negative HbAg results in 57% of patients tested early in the illness weigh against viral hepatitis as the cause, and that isoniazid liver injury is primarily a disease of the middle-aged and elderly, unlike sporadic viral hepatitis. Alcoholic liver disease was largely excluded because the study required an SGOT above 250 Karmen units or comparable SGPT elevation, and liver biopsy in 33 patients confirmed the absence of alcoholic liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 114 patients with isoniazid hepatotoxicity; 13 deaths. Most patients who became ill within the first 8 weeks of therapy had milder and usually nonfatal disease, with only 2 deaths in that subgroup versus 11 deaths among those ill after >8 weeks. Race/sex/age distribution: White 55, black 36, Oriental 23; female 60, male 54; most patients aged 41-60. Deaths among black women were disproportionately prevalent (9 of 13). Mean age did not differ between fatal and nonfatal groups. Peak bilirubin exceeded 20 mg/dl in 11 of 13 fatal but only 19 of 101 surviving patients. After stopping isoniazid, transaminase values fell an average of 63% within 1 week and 87% by the third week (30 patients); peak bilirubin fell 44% by week 1 and 72% by week 3 (22 patients). Viral hepatitis and alcohol-related liver injury were considered and largely excluded as competing causes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors, responding to a critique, discuss the incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatitis and isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity in persons receiving isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis. They explain that their previously reported age-specific incidence rates were computed by excluding from the denominator persons not known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed, which tends to overestimate incidence. If excluded persons were included, the calculated incidence of hepatotoxicity would have been 0.2% for ages 20-34, 0.7% for ages 35-49, 1.6% for ages 50-64, and 0.6% for ages >64, and they conclude the true age-specific incidence lies between the high and low figures.
raw_record.extra_details: Letters/correspondence discussing incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatitis during preventive therapy for tuberculosis. Age-specific incidence of hepatotoxicity: 0.2% for persons 20-34 years, 0.7% for 35-49, 1.6% for 50-64, 0.6% for >64 years (when excluded, probably still-medicated persons are included in the denominator); true incidence considered to lie between the high and low figures. Standard adult dosing of 300 mg daily is mentioned. The authors note that about half of patients discontinued isoniazid during the year of therapy. A separate paragraph mentions future consideration of high-dose isoniazid given twice weekly, without making an additional DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: The letter presenting Public Health Service data on isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity states that, using criteria established by a panel of experts in hepatic disease, the incidence of hepatotoxicity was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age and 0.8% for persons over 64 years of age, and 1.7% per year for all persons 50 or more years of age. The discussion refers to 'isoniazid hepatitis' and reports age-specific incidence of 'isoniazid-induced hepatitis' for adults taking isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Data from the Public Health Service isoniazid hepatitis surveillance study adjudicated by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported incidence of hepatotoxicity, computed excluding from the denominator persons not clearly at risk, was per year: about 0.2% for ages 20-34, about 0.7% for ages 35-49, about 2.3% (high) / 1.6% (low) for ages 50-64, about 0.8% (high) / 0.6% (low) for ages >64, and 1.7% per year for all persons 50 or more years of age. The author argues the method tends to overestimate incidence because some excluded persons were probably taking the drug; the 'true' age-specific incidence likely lies between the high and low figures. Context is isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis; the standard method discussed is 300 mg daily in adults. Whether high-dose twice-weekly isoniazid would reduce the incidence of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity is stated as not known.

raw_record.support_text: The letter, titled 'Isoniazid-Related Hepatotoxicity', corrects statements about Public Health Service data on isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity. Using criteria established by a panel of experts in hepatic disease, the PHS study showed the incidence of hepatotoxicity was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age and 0.8% for persons over 64, and the rate for all persons 50 or more years of age was 1.7% per year.
raw_record.extra_details: DISCUSSION OF PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICE (PHS) STUDY INCIDENCE DATA FOR ISONIAZID HEPATOTOXICITY. REPORTED INCIDENCE: 2.3% PER YEAR IN PERSONS 50-64 Y; 0.8% PER YEAR IN PERSONS >64 Y; 1.7% PER YEAR FOR ALL PERSONS >=50 Y. LETTER CORRECTS EARLIER CLAIMS (MOULDING ET AL., ANN INTERN MED 85:398-399, 1976). TRUE AGE-SPECIFIC INCIDENCE (IF ALL EXCLUDED FROM DENOMINATOR INCLUDED) WOULD BE LOWER: 0.2% FOR 20-34 Y; 0.7% FOR 35-49 Y; 1.6% FOR 50-64 Y; 0.6% FOR >64 Y. CONTEXT: ISONIAZID PREVENTIVE THERAPY FOR TUBERCULOSIS; STANDARD DOSE NOTED AS 300 MG DAILY IN ADULTS. CASE NUMBER: APPROXIMATELY HALF OF PATIENTS DISCONTINUED ISONIAZID DURING THE YEAR OF THERAPY. CRITERIA ESTABLISHED BY A PANEL OF EXPERTS IN HEPATIC DISEASE.

raw_record.support_text: Using criteria established by a panel of experts in hepatic disease, the Public Health Service study reported that the incidence of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age and 0.8% for persons over 64 years of age, and the overall rate for all persons 50 or more years of age was 1.7% per year.
raw_record.extra_details: Data from the US Public Health Service isoniazid preventive-therapy study, with hepatotoxicity identified using criteria established by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported incidence was 2.3%/year (age 50-64), 0.8%/year (>64), and 1.7%/year for all persons >=50. When the denominator was not restricted to persons known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed, the calculated incidence was lower: 0.2% (age 20-34), 0.7% (35-49), 1.6% (50-64), and 0.6% (>64); the authors state the 'true' age-specific incidence lies between the high and low figures. Correspondence concerns isoniazid used as preventive therapy for tuberculosis, standard adult dosing of 300 mg daily.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of employees treated with isoniazid (INH), 32 subjects developed SGOT levels above the upper limit of normal. In one patient (Case 29), marked SGOT and bilirubin elevations developed after four weeks of INH administration, with preceding fatigue and jaundice; she was thought to have developed INH hepatitis and the drug was discontinued, after which bilirubin and SGOT promptly returned to normal. Elevation of SGOT levels in all but two subjects returned to normal within three to eight weeks after discontinuation of the drug, and the discussion notes concern about toxic hepatitis during treatment with INH.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of employees in a tuberculosis control program treated with INH; 32 of an unstated denominator developed elevated SGOT (>65 Karmen units). Case 29 developed jaundice with SGOT 898 Karmen units, SGPT 200, and bilirubin >10.0 mg/100 ml after 4 weeks of therapy; drug discontinued and tests normalized. INH was stopped in patients with rapid/progressive SGOT rise, bilirubin >1.5 mg/100 ml, or symptoms. Two subjects with persistently elevated SGOT had been drinking alcohol heavily during therapy (competing exposure); SGOT elevations ranged up to 898 units and developed from within 2 months to after 6 months of therapy. No positive HBsAg or rheumatoid factor was found in tested patients; some patients demonstrated antinuclear factor.

raw_record.support_text: The 74-year-old patient was given 150 mg of isoniazid (INH) daily for tuberculosis prophylaxis. One month later she developed INH-induced hepatic injury, and INH was replaced by rifampicin and streptomycin.
raw_record.extra_details: Given 150 mg daily for pulmonary tuberculosis prophylaxis; hepatic injury developed one month after starting INH and resolved after the drug was replaced by rifampicin (450 mg daily) and streptomycin (1 g intramuscularly twice weekly). No liver-test values, biochemical pattern, or severity level were reported.

raw_record.support_text: The main toxic side effect associated with isoniazid chemoprophylaxis is the development of hepatitis. A US study of nearly 14,000 persons between 1971 and 1972 (Kopanoff et al., 1978) found an overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis of 1%, which was age-related (no cases in those aged <20 years, 2.3% in those aged >50 years) and also related to alcohol consumption.
raw_record.extra_details: Epidemiologic study of ~14,000 persons on isoniazid chemoprophylaxis (1971-1972, Kopanoff et al.). Overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis 1%; age-related with no cases under 20 years and 2.3% in persons >50 years; development of hepatitis also related to alcohol consumption. Discussed in the context of isoniazid preventive therapy for TB.

raw_record.support_text: Among a group of 114 patients with isoniazid-induced hepatocellular disease, 13 died (about a 12% case-fatality rate). The authors compare this to 2 deaths out of 19 hepatitis patients reported by Garibaldi among 2300 patients receiving isoniazid, and 3 deaths out of 14 isoniazid hepatitis patients reported by Maddrey and Boitnott, noting that of 65 cases of isoniazid hepatitis reported in the literature prior to their publication, 8 were fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: 114 patients with isoniazid-induced hepatocellular disease with 13 deaths (~12% case fatality). 87 patients from the USPHS surveillance trial, of whom 7 died (~8%); the authors note the 27 additional non-trial patients likely came to attention because they were severely ill. Literature review: 65 pre-publication cases of isoniazid hepatitis with 8 fatalities; Garibaldi and associates 2/19 deaths among 2300 isoniazid recipients; Maddrey and Boitnott 3/14 deaths. Authors regard even surveillance-trial hepatitis/death rates as low estimates because >50% of patients dropped out during the year of treatment, inflating the at-risk denominator.

raw_record.support_text: Guidelines for isoniazid administration aim to identify hepatotoxicity as early as possible; at the first suggestion of hepatitis-like symptoms isoniazid should be discontinued and liver function tests performed. A reported series of 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis showed prodromal fatigue, weakness, and anorexia, and the severity of subsequent hepatitis was related to the duration of continued isoniazid consumption: patients with histologic patchy hepatitis continued isoniazid an average of 2.2 weeks, while those with multilobular or bridging necrosis continued it an average of 4.6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis (Maddry and Boitnott report); prodromal symptoms fatigue, weakness, anorexia; severity proportional to duration of continued isoniazid intake despite symptoms; histologic patchy hepatitis observed after ~2.2 weeks continued use versus multilobular or bridging necrosis after ~4.6 weeks; severity of isoniazid-induced hepatitis judged best by onset of hepatitis-like symptoms; routine LFT monitoring considered impractical.

raw_record.support_text: Donepezil was evaluated in 3 double-blind, placebo-controlled trials randomising 1102 patients over age 50 years with mild or moderate Alzheimer's disease, of 12 to 24 weeks duration, at donepezil doses of 5 to 10 mg; the paper states there is no evidence of hepatotoxicity at the dosages used in the trials.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 double-blind placebo-controlled trials, 1102 patients aged over 50 years with mild or moderate Alzheimer's disease, 12-24 weeks duration, donepezil 5-10 mg/day; explicit statement that there is no evidence of hepatotoxicity at the dosages used in the trials.

raw_record.support_text: In the safety assessment of donepezil in this open-label extension study in Alzheimer's disease patients, the authors report no clinically significant treatment-related effects on laboratory test values or vital signs. They state that there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity occurring during the study, as assessed by laboratory measures of liver function, and that six deaths were all considered by investigators to be unrelated to donepezil treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label extension study in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease patients; hepatotoxicity assessed via laboratory measures of liver function; no evidence of hepatotoxicity during the study. Six deaths occurred (4 during study, 2 within 30 days of discontinuation; myocardial infarction, motor vehicle accidents, cardiopulmonary arrest, unknown natural causes) and were all considered unrelated to donepezil.

raw_record.support_text: In a trial of 161 patients receiving 1-5 mg/day donepezil for Alzheimer's disease, adverse events such as nausea/vomiting, diarrhoea, gastric upset and constipation appeared more frequently in the high-dose group, but the study reported that no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity was seen with donepezil.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial of 161 patients (96% Caucasian) with Alzheimer's disease, donepezil 1-5 mg/day, 12 weeks of dosing plus 2-week washout; explicitly stated that no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity was seen in this study. Dose-related reduction in ADAS-cog seen.'

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a combined hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury that was probably related to initiation of donepezil treatment, with liver function tests gradually returning to normal after cessation of therapy. The authors conclude that laboratory monitoring should be considered in patients receiving donepezil.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient treated with donepezil from September 22 to October 13 (2005); liver tests rose (ALT peaked 363 U/L on 02/11, AlkPhos 1343 U/L, GGTP 426 U/L, total bilirubin 22.60 mg/dL) and normalized after withdrawal; liver biopsy showed mild cholestatic hepatitis with mildly active moderately severe inflammation and absence of fibrosis; the Maria & Victorino diagnostic scale for DILI was applied to assess causality; injury resolved, supporting a causal relationship.

raw_record.support_text: In an open-label extension study of 133 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease receiving donepezil (up to 10 mg/day) for up to 98 weeks, donepezil was well tolerated with no evidence of hepatotoxicity reported in the safety analysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label extension study of 133 Alzheimer's disease patients (mild to moderate) who completed a previous 14-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial; donepezil up to 10 mg/day; interim analysis at 98 weeks; safety monitored by physical examinations, laboratory tests and vital sign measurements.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase II dose-ranging study of donepezil in patients with Alzheimer's disease, the drug at 5 mg/day was reported to be well tolerated, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II dose-ranging study of donepezil in Alzheimer's disease patients, 5 mg/day dose; tolerability conclusion stated as 'no evidence of hepatotoxicity'; the paper's explicit conclusion does not support a human DILI relationship.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 44 patients classified as having drug related hepatotoxicity by International Consensus Group criteria (with suggestive/compatible onset, suggestive dechallenge course, exclusion of alternatives incl. liver biopsy, and positive rechallenge where available), table 1 lists the responsible drugs. Diclofenac was implicated in four patients (cases 1, 6, 7, 8): one presented with liver failure on a histology of acute hepatitis, and three with raised enzymes on chronic hepatitis, with follow-up ranging 3.5-7.7 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic/NSAID class. Case 1: liver failure, acute hepatitis, follow-up 5.2 y; cases 6,7,8: raised enzymes, chronic hepatitis, follow-ups 4, 3.5, 7.7 y. Initial presentation most commonly jaundice (n=24) or abnormal liver blood tests (n=17); 3 patients presented with hepatic failure manifest as encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The study group comprised 24 patients (18 female, six male; aged 24-70 years, median 54) with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity. Six presented with jaundice, three with hepatic failure and 15 with raised liver enzymes on routine monitoring; diagnoses included 13 acute cytolytic hepatitis, two acute cholestatic injury, eight chronic hepatitis (biopsy proven) and one subacute hepatic necrosis. Ten patients were taking other drugs concomitantly, including other CYP2C9 substrates.
raw_record.extra_details: 24 diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity patients (18 female, six male; age 24-70 y, median 54). Presentations: six with jaundice, three with hepatic failure, 15 with raised liver enzymes on routine monitoring. Diagnoses: 13 acute cytolytic hepatitis, two acute cholestatic injury, eight chronic hepatitis (biopsy proven), one subacute hepatic necrosis. Ten patients took other drugs concomitantly, six of them other CYP2C9 substrates (sulphamethoxazole, indomethacin, ibuprofen) and another cimetidine (a general P450 inhibitor). Study also reported CYP2C9 genotyping and kinetic analysis of diclofenac 4'-hydroxylation in human liver microsomes (no difference in Km among CYP2C9*1/*2/*3; Vmax lower in CYP2C9*3 heterozygotes, P=0.057).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most frequently prescribed NSAID, causes minimal serum transaminase elevations in about 15% of patients; severe hepatic dysfunction is rare but 27 case reports of severe diclofenac-induced hepatitis have been described worldwide, including four fatalities. This report describes the second case of diclofenac-induced liver failure successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac produces a type II idiosyncratic liver injury; most cases are thought to occur by a metabolic mechanism, though hypersensitivity cases occur. In this case the mechanism was probably a hypersensitivity reaction, evidenced by short exposure duration, dramatic response to rechallenge, and eosinophils in the liver biopsy. Repeated hepatotoxicity on rechallenging with diclofenac has been described, while challenge with a different NSAID was not hepatotoxic, indicating an idiosyncratic rather than class effect. About 15% of patients show minimal transaminase elevations; 27 reported cases of severe hepatitis include 4 fatalities; this is only the second liver-failure case successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the NSAID most often responsible for DILI, with 14 of 77 cases. The ascribed pattern distribution was seven hepatocellular, five cholestatic and two mixed, and six of the cases had jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: 14 of 77 DILI cases; 7 female/7 male; pattern 7 hepatocellular/5 cholestatic/2 mixed; duration of treatment mean 24 (2-60) days; time to biochemical resolution mean 52 (10-150) days. Six jaundice cases detailed (bilirubin 2.1-16 ULN), some with very high AST/ALT.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-four patients (19 female, 79%) aged 24–70 years who had suffered diclofenac hepatotoxicity between 1990 and 1999 were identified from hospital records and adverse hepatotoxicity reaction reports to the Committee on Safety of Medicines (North East region, UK). The causal relationship of liver injury to diclofenac was established using international consensus criteria. Six patients presented with jaundice, 3 with liver failure, and the rest had nonspecific symptoms associated with raised liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Twenty-four patients; causality adjudicated using international consensus criteria. Six patients presented with jaundice, 3 with liver failure, and the rest had nonspecific symptoms with raised liver enzymes. Clinical details including laboratory values, liver biopsy findings, and diagnoses previously described in reference 11.

raw_record.support_text: Among reported cases, 26 met inclusion criteria where diclofenac was the sole suspected drug, the patient recovered after drug withdrawal, no other treatment or probable cause of hepatic dysfunction was found, and serial liver function tests were available including a recovery-phase value. Serology for hepatitis A and B was negative in 15 tested, and imaging ruled out biliary obstruction in 7 cases; one liver biopsy favored drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 cases analyzed; average age 64 years (range 37-84), 70% female. Main features included jaundice (total bilirubin deviate ratio >2) in half, hepatomegaly (sometimes painful), anorexia, nausea; itch, malaise, or vomiting less common; 25% asymptomatic; mild thrombocytopenia in 2 reports; no extrahepatic hypersensitivity phenomena reported. Onset within first 6 months in 18/21 reports; median duration of exposure 76 days (range 6-417 days); median cumulative dose 8.7 g (1.4-63.5 g). Dominant biochemical feature was raised transaminases with lesser rises in alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and bilirubin; severity ranged to fortyfold transaminase elevations. Significant log dose vs log peak AST (r²=0.68, slope 0.91, p=0.0001) and ALT (r²=0.71, slope 1.04, p=0.001) relations. Transaminases fell exponentially after withdrawal with post-peak half-lives of 13.7 days (AST) and 13.2 days (ALT).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 60 individual case reports; median age 56 y; 49 female/11 male; median treatment duration 8 weeks; HC 58%, Cs/mixed 42%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 13% (55/60 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 37% (27/60 reported); hepatic necrosis 54%; inflammatory reaction 93%; death or liver transplant 18%; liver biopsy reported in 32/60 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Aithal et al. investigated the relationship between CYP2C9 genotype and susceptibility to hepatotoxicity in 24 patients with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity, compared with 100 healthy controls for the CYP2C9*2 and *3 alleles, and found that the frequencies of these alleles were similar in patients and controls. This explicitly attributes a human hepatotoxic response to diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 24 patients with diclofenac-induced hepatotoxicity vs 100 healthy controls; CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C9*3 allele frequencies did not differ between patients and controls, indicating no association between these CYP2C9 genotypes and diclofenac hepatotoxicity susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes diclofenac hepatitis as an idiosyncratic drug reaction in humans whose mechanism remains controversial (hypersensitivity vs toxic-metabolic), describing 13 cases (12 literature cases and the present patient) of diclofenac-induced hepatitis with jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and outcomes ranging from recovery to death in 2 of 13 patients. A typically mixed cholestatic/hepatocellular biochemical profile was reported after prolonged exposure, and hepatotoxicity recurred after reintroduction of diclofenac in patients 1, 6, and 11.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 diclofenac-induced hepatitis cases compiled from 8 biopsy studies and 2 autopsies plus the present case; latency about 1-48 weeks (present case 26 weeks); outcome recovery in most, progression in 1, death in 2 (patients 5 and 6, massive/fatal hepatic necrosis; end-stage fulminant hepatitis with small, shrunken liver). Histology ranged from mild acute lobular hepatitis to massive necrosis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, ballooning degeneration, acidophil bodies, perivenular hepatocyte dropout, canalicular cholestasis and bile thrombi, and possible reactive Kupffer cell hyperplasia and noncaseating granulomas. Ultrastructurally shows lamellated bodies, bizarre mitochondria, complex phagolysosomes, and other criteria for drug-induced liver injury; eosinophilia in some patients; recurrence after reintroduction in patients 1, 6, 11; reversible after withdrawal in most, but not always (2 deaths).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most widely used NSAID in the world, is discussed as a cause of human hepatotoxicity. Banks and co-workers analyzed 180 cases referred to the FDA (1988-1991), finding liver disease in 85% of patients within the first 6 months, jaundice in 90 of 120 patients, and 7 jaundiced patients who died from liver disease; LFTs showed a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern in 66% of cases and cholestatic in 8%. In the prospective, randomized, double-blind MEDAL program (17,289 patients), hypertransaminasemia >3xULN occurred in over 3% of arthritis patients on diclofenac 150 mg daily, ALT >10xULN in 0.5%, liver-related hospitalizations at 16 per 100,000 patient-years (0.023%), and Hy's cases at 0.012%. The authors conclude diclofenac bears a low liver toxicity rate while still causing hepatic reactions.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; Banks 1995 analysis of 180 FDA-referred cases (1988-1991): liver disease in 85% within 6 mo, higher latency >6 mo in 12%; jaundice in 90 of 120 patients, 7 jaundiced deaths; LFTs mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic in 66%, cholestatic in 8%, indeterminate remainder. MEDAL program: prospective randomized double-blind, 17,289 osteoarthritis/rheumatoid arthritis patients >50 y on diclofenac 150 mg daily vs etoricoxib (60/90 mg); excluded prior liver disease and >14 weekly alcoholic drinks; hypertransaminasemia >3xULN in >3%; ALT >10xULN in 0.5%; liver-related hospitalizations 16/100,000 patient-years (0.023%); Hy's cases 0.012%. Authors concluded diclofenac has a low liver toxicity rate. Mechanistic context: metabolic idiosyncrasy or immunologic injury via drug adduct formation, reactive metabolite formation and clearance.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, diclofenac accounted for 13 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, one of the top 10 individual agents.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is noted as the only non-antibiotic among the top ten drugs in the DILIN registry and is one of the five drugs present among the ten most common DILI-causing drugs in at least two of three prospective studies (DILIN, Iceland, Spain).
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; top-ten drug in DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish registries; in the ten most frequently implicated drugs across three DILI registries; listed in Table 1 with >100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox); strongly associated with DILI in GPRD studies.

raw_record.support_text: In the U.S. Drug Induced Liver Injury Network prospective registry, 30 of 1221 adjudicated cases were attributed to eight different NSAIDs, with a mean latency of 67 days, most showing a hepatocellular pattern of injury. Diclofenac was the most frequently implicated NSAID (16/30 cases) characterized by hepatocellular injury; 17 cases resulted in hospitalization or prolongation of hospitalization and one patient died from complications of Stevens–Johnson syndrome attributed to diclofenac. The Network studies idiosyncratic drug hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: DICLIN prospective registry of 1221 adjudicated cases; 30 total cases attributed to eight NSAIDs, of which diclofenac accounted for 16/30 (most frequent). Mean age 52 y, 24/30 (80%) women, 21/30 (70%) Caucasian; mean latency 67 days. Presenting features: nausea 73%, jaundice 67%, dark urine 67%; peak AST 898 U/L, ALT 1060 U/L, total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl, ALP 326 U/L; hepatocellular pattern most common (70%); autoantibodies detected in 33% of cases. Seventeen cases resulted in hospitalization or prolongation; one death from complications of Stevens-Johnson syndrome attributed to diclofenac.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac is listed as the second most frequent drug, n = 13, among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The study included 16 patients with liver injury initially suspected of idiosyncratic DILI (iDILI), diagnosed by clinical causality assessment including RUCAM. Subgroup DicloDILI comprised patients suffering from iDILI due to Diclofenac. All DicloDILI patients had a causality likelihood of at least "highly likely" for iDILI due to Diclofenac, and the MH cell test was positive for Diclofenac only in DicloDILI patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients were diagnosed with iDILI due to Diclofenac (DicloDILI) based on clinical causality assessment including RUCAM, all with causality likelihood of at least 'highly likely'. MH cell test was positive for Diclofenac only in DicloDILI patients, while co-medications tested negative. Among DicloDILI patients, DicloDILI2 had the lowest ITGB3-positive cell level and the worst outcome, requiring liver transplantation; DicloDILI3 recovered within a few weeks after cessation of Diclofenac administration. Diclofenac is a suspected inducer of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In UK patients with idiosyncratic DILI (iDILI) due to diclofenac, an increased frequency of the MRP2 C‐24T allelic variant was observed, proposed to arise because of MRP2‐mediated biliary excretion of glucuronide metabolites of the drug. The passage explicitly attributes human idiosyncratic drug‐induced liver injury to diclofenac.
raw_record.extra_details: UK patients with iDILI due to diclofenac showed an increased frequency of the MRP2 C‐24T (ABCC2 c.-24T) allelic variant, proposed to arise because of MRP2‐mediated biliary excretion of glucuronide metabolites of the drug.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists two patients (cases 1 and 12) with DILI attributed to diclofenac taken therapeutically for pain. The first case was a 76-year-old woman on diclofenac 50 mg/day who developed jaundice with ASMA 1/80, hepatocellular-type injury (TB 2.9xULN, ALT 24xULN, ALP 2.6xULN), classified Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The second was an 80-year-old woman on diclofenac 75 mg/day with jaundice, hepatocellular injury (TB 4.9xULN, ALT 38xULN, ALP 1.9xULN), Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases. Case 1 (76/F, lumbar pain), 50 mg/day for 93 days, onset 30 days, co-meds levothyroxine and metamizole, jaundice, ASMA 1/80, TB 2.9xULN, ALT 24xULN, ALP 2.6xULN, Moderate severity, resolution at 221 days. Case 12 (80/F), 75 mg/day for 171 days, onset 171 days, co-meds telmisartan, allopurinol, glibenclamide, ebastine, troxerutin, jaundice, TB 4.9xULN, ALT 38xULN, ALP 1.9xULN, Moderate, hospitalized, resolution at 348 days. CIOMS 'Highly probable' for both. Indication: pain.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the most common offending agent in this study, responsible for DILI in 31 (41.3%) patients. Diclofenac injury was hepatocellular in 54.8% of cases and equally cholestatic or mixed in the remaining cases, with a mean time interval between intake and symptoms of 11.2 ± 5.3 days.
raw_record.extra_details: 31 cases (41.3%); hepatocellular 17 (54.8%), cholestatic 7 (22.6%), mixed 7 (22.6%); acute 10, chronic 21; time interval 11.2 ± 5.3 days; 4 of the 7 deceased cases had diclofenac-induced injury (all with chronic liver disease); liver biopsies showed focal necrosis with lymphocytes and plasma cells in 5 cases, cholestatic hepatitis in 1, and autoimmune with abundant eosinophilia in 1; RUCAM causality assessment applied.

raw_record.support_text: In a Brazilian study of acute liver failure (ALF) across 12 transplant centers, drug-related ALF causes included NSAIDs (21%), with diclofenac reported in n=5 attributed cases of DILI leading to ALF.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF in a cohort of patients undergoing liver transplantation for ALF; n=5 cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was attributed to 15 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (93%). Seven cases (50%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria but had favourable outcomes without fatalities or liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 15 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 93%/Chol 6.7%/Mix 0%; female 40%, lymphopenia 14%, eosinophilia 7.7%; 7 (50%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law with no fatalities/liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists diclofenac with 46 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Zanger (116). Separately (p29), peripheral blood monocytes from patients suspected to have diclofenac-induced DILI converted to hepatocyte-like cells increased ITGB3 when incubated with diclofenac, framed as a suspected cause.
raw_record.extra_details: 46 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); aryl glucuronides proposed as responsible reactive metabolites in diclofenac DILI, evidence not compelling (p32); biomarker (ITGB3) study on patients suspected of diclofenac-induced DILI (p29).

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac was the most incriminated drug in the DILI group (16 patients, 40%). Of 28 hepatocellular patients, 14 (50%) were caused by diclofenac, and of 4 mixed-injury patients, 2 (50%) were caused by diclofenac. Diclofenac accounted for 66.6% (4 patients) of the mortality cases. Exposure duration was 10.5 ±1.5 days with 13.5 ±1.4 days to symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 of 40 DILI patients (40%); hepatocellular injury in 14 cases, mixed injury in 2; duration 10.5±1.5 days, time to symptoms 13.5±1.4 days; accounted for 66.6% (4 patients) of the 6 mortality cases (p=0.28). RUCAM-based DILI classification.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old man taking diclofenac for painful pseudogout developed nausea, vomiting, dark urine, pale stools, and jaundice, with an enlarged liver; liver function tests were consistent with acute hepatitis (bilirubin 126 µmol/l, aspartate aminotransferase 1375 IU/l). Hepatitis B and A serology were negative and he took no other regular medication. Diclofenac was withdrawn and the jaundice resolved completely over seven days. Rechallenge with diclofenac five weeks later produced vomiting and jaundice again (bilirubin 201 µmol/l, aspartate aminotransferase 1150 IU/l); liver biopsy specimens showed moderately severe acute hepatitis with canalicular cholestasis, Kupffer-cell proliferation, and plasma cells and eosinophils in the inflammatory infiltrate. Diclofenac was stopped and symptoms and liver function test results normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report with positive dechallenge-rechallenge; symptoms recurred on rechallenge. Liver biopsy showed moderately severe acute hepatitis with canalicular cholestasis, Kupffer-cell proliferation, plasma cells and eosinophils. Relevant laboratory values: bilirubin 126 µmol/l (7.4 mg/100 ml) initially and 201 µmol/l (11.8 mg/100 ml) on rechallenge; aspartate aminotransferase 1375 IU/l initially and 1150 IU/l on rechallenge. Enlarged liver (4 cm and later 2 cm below right costal margin). Viral hepatitis excluded (HBsAg, HAV IgM, EBV, CMV negative). Indication: painful pseudogout of right knee; no alcohol abuse or other regular medication. Jaundice resolved within days of withdrawal in both episodes, liver function normal within six weeks and at three months.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of 180 patients with possible adverse hepatic reactions to diclofenac reported to the FDA found predominantly hepatocellular or mixed hepatocellular biochemical injury (66% of cases), with only 8% cholestatic; 75% of symptomatic patients were jaundiced and 7 of 90 icteric patients died. Injury appeared by 1-6 months in most patients, and the absence of rash, fever, or eosinophilia combined with long latency led to the inference that the mechanism is probably metabolic idiosyncrasy. The authors concluded diclofenac-related liver injury is particularly likely to involve osteoarthritic females presenting with jaundice and predominantly hepatocellular injury caused by presumed metabolic idiosyncrasy.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective FDA spontaneous-report case series, Nov 1988-Jun 1991 (434 initial reports, 180 retained after excluding duplicates, foreign sources, other causes, and inadequate data). Patients: 79% female, 71% aged >=60 years, 77% had osteoarthritis (139 OA, 22 RA, 1 ankylosing spondylitis, 1 psoriatic arthritis, 15 miscellaneous, 2 unknown). 67% of cases detected by symptoms and remainder by abnormal labs; 75% of symptomatic patients (90/120) were jaundiced; 7 of 90 icteric patients died. Biochemical pattern: hepatocellular or mixed in 66%, cholestatic in 8%, remainder 'indeterminate'. Hepatocellular defined as ALT peak >=8x ULN with ALP <3x ULN; cholestatic as ALP >=3x ULN with transaminases <8x ULN; mixed as both elevated. 21 liver sections available. Latency: injury apparent by 1 month in 24%, by 3 months in 63%, by 6 months in 85%; 12% at 6-12 months, 3% >12 months. No case had rash, fever, and eosinophilia combined (hypersensitivity); mechanism presumed metabolic idiosyncrasy. Diclofenac approved in US 1988 for OA/RA/ankylosing spondylitis; available in Europe since 1974. Approximately 60 prior literature cases of diclofenac-associated hepatic injury, mostly acute hepatocellular, several chronic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A case of diclofenac-induced hepatitis in a 53-year-old Indian woman with recurrent jaundice is presented. The diagnosis was suspected from the liver biopsy appearance and confirmed by the temporal association with drug usage and cure on withdrawal of the drug. Diclofenac, a widely used NSAID, is described as having documented but rare hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic hepatic enzyme elevation to symptomatic hepatic injury and even fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old Indian woman with recurrent jaundice; liver biopsy showed diffuse hepatocellular degeneration, extensive bridging necrosis, a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, many eosinophils), acidophilic bodies, and mild hepatocytic cholestasis. Labs: total bilirubin 17.8 mg/dl, direct 12.8 mg/dl, SGOT 1448 IU/l, SGPT 862 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 622 U/l; prolonged prothrombin time (6 s over control) normalized after vitamin K; transient ANA positivity with negative repeat and LE-cell tests; HBsAg (ELISA) and anti-HCV (2nd-gen Abbott ELISA) negative; liver palpable 5 cm below costal margin. No peripheral eosinophilia or rash; patient not alcoholic. The agent was taken for joint pain. Case highlights awareness of this entity, first suspected on examination of the liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: During the first phase of the ADR Monitoring Program, the authors observed a patient who underwent liver transplant because of severe liver toxicity from diclofenac. A second liver transplant was ultimately necessary, and the patient subsequently died. The finding is listed among scientifically and clinically important reports as 'severe liver toxicity from diclofenac resulting in liver transplantations and death.'
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient observed while taking diclofenac developed severe liver toxicity requiring liver transplant, then a second transplant, and subsequently died; reported as an example of a scientifically and clinically important finding from the hospital ADR Monitoring Program.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac appears to be the inciting agent for the liver disease in the three reported patients. Alcohol, viral, and other genetic causes of liver disease were excluded, and transaminases returned to and remained normal after discontinuation of therapy; the biochemical abnormalities reappeared on reintroduction of diclofenac (or another anthranilic acid derivative). Two hepatic reactions were observed: patients 1 and 2 had serologic and histologic features of autoimmune chronic active hepatitis (ACAH) that were initially misdiagnosed, and patient 3 presented with features of acute hepatitis with elevated transaminases, jaundice, low-grade fever, nausea, marked peripheral eosinophilia, and low-titer ANA. The paper states it is likely that diclofenac can induce several types of hepatotoxicity and classifies the reactions as idiosyncratic (type II), with patients 1 and 2 falling into the metabolic-aberration category and patient 3 showing a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three new patients (Scully, this study) treated for osteoarthritis or back pain. Causality supported by dechallenge with normalization of transaminases and rechallenge with reappearance of biochemical abnormalities. Patients 1 and 2: autoimmune chronic active hepatitis features, elevated ANA (1/640, 1/40), negative ASMA, normal IgG, no fibrosis on biopsy, initially treated with corticosteroids without relapse after withdrawal; patient 1 also had presumed isoniazid hepatotoxicity and vitiligo, patient 2 had high-titer antithyroglobulin antibodies; none developed SLE. Patient 3: acute hepatitis with jaundice, low-grade fever, nausea, marked peripheral eosinophilia, low-titer ANA, background multiple sclerosis. Type II idiosyncratic classification: patients 1-2 metabolic aberration, patient 3 hypersensitivity. Review table of 26 published diclofenac-induced liver disease cases (22F/4M, age 58 ± 11 yr, treatment duration 12.6 ± 10.6 weeks): 4 died, 20 improved, 2 steroid-treated; 13 jaundiced; phenotypes included periportal/lobular inflammation, hepatic necrosis, mixed hepatitis with cholestasis, fatty change with centrilobular hepatocyte loss, multilobular necrosis, bridging fibrosis; maximum reported severity includes fatal cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman developed fulminant hepatic failure after taking Arthrotec (containing diclofenac and misoprostol) 50 mg three times per day for two months for a painful left heel. Viral and autoimmune etiologies and other drugs or chemical exposures were excluded, and the paper reports this as diclofenac-induced fulminant hepatic failure, the first such case successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. Four similar previously reported diclofenac-induced cases died without transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient took the fixed combination product Arthrotec (diclofenac plus misoprostol) 50 mg three times daily for two months at a therapeutic dose. Developed jaundice, dark urine and constipation after a flu-like prodrome; had five out of five poor prognostic criteria for non-paracetamol drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure and underwent successful orthotopic liver transplantation with excellent recovery. History of immune hemolytic anemia treated with prednisolone that had been discontinued six months prior. Co-medications Coproxamol and Amoxil (jaundice noted a week before Amoxil started) and no paracetamol overdose were reported and excluded as causes. Described as the first reported successful treatment of diclofenac-induced fulminant hepatic failure; four previously reported similar cases died without liver transplantation. Putative mechanisms of diclofenac toxicity reviewed.

raw_record.support_text: Dextropropoxyphene was listed as the responsible drug in four patients (cases 26, 27, 28, 44) in the drug-related hepatotoxicity series, all presenting with jaundice and cholestasis histology, with follow-ups ranging 1-12.4 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic; associated with 4 cases. Cases 26,27,28,44: all jaundice with cholestasis histology.

raw_record.support_text: In three patients, symptoms of severe malaise and abdominal pain began within 24 hours after rechallenge with a low dose of dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride (32.5 mg). In patients 1 and 2, liver function tests became abnormal within 24 hours and were predominantly hepatitic initially, followed by a more prolonged cholestatic phase; abnormalities returned completely to normal. The authors state that hepatic toxicity reliably attributable to dextropropoxyphene is rare, and that incrimination of the drug was proven by rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 new patients (plus 12 previously reported literature cases) presenting with epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, fever/rigors, jaundice, pale stools and dark urine, commonly leading to a misdiagnosis of biliary tract disease (two patients underwent laparotomy/cholecystectomy). Hepatic injury proven by rechallenge: symptoms within 24 hours of a single 32.5 mg oral dose of dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride; LFTs predominantly hepatitic initially then a prolonged cholestatic phase, all returning to normal. Liver histology (postchallenge) showed centrilobular/intrahepatic cholestasis with bile thrombi, oedematous portal tracts infiltrated by eosinophils and lymphocytes, and dilated bile canaliculae with granular material, suggestive of a drug hypersensitivity reaction; ultrastructural changes compared to chlorpromazine jaundice. Clinical diagnosis was cholestatic hepatitis with mixed LFTs.

raw_record.support_text: A case report documents a cholestatic hepatitis attributed to propoxyphene (Darvon), an agent not previously reported as hepatotoxic, with recurrence of clinical and chemical abnormalities on rechallenge at a later date.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old white male (JB) developed cholestatic hepatitis after taking propoxyphene with acetylsalicylic acid (Darvon Compound) as required for occipital headache. Recurrence of clinical and chemical abnormalities occurred on rechallenge. Findings included malaise, daily fever to 101.8 deg F, dark brown urine, tender liver edge 4 cm below costal margin, urinalysis positive for bile, total bilirubin 3.3 mg/100 ml, atypical lymphocytes.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-yr-old woman developed subacute hepatitis and liver failure after a 1-month course of treatment with the NSAID bromfenac. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative, as were antinuclear antibodies and ceruloplasmin, and a transjugular liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis. The course was complicated by encephalopathy, fluid retention, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, prompting consideration for liver transplantation. The authors conclude that prolonged bromfenac use was the etiological agent and that this drug can cause severe hepatotoxicity resulting in liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 40-yr-old woman; bromfenac sodium 25 mg t.i.d.; prior short courses (10 days and ~3 wk) with pain recurrence after discontinuation and reinstitution; jaundice and nausea/vomiting/fever developed, jaundice and biochemical hepatitis followed. Initial labs: total bilirubin 5.2 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 223 IU/L, ALT 2001 IU/L; admission labs total bilirubin 15.0 mg/dl, ALT 1966 U/L, AST 2144 U/L, INR 1.7. Transjugular biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; subacute hepatic failure with consideration for liver transplant; supportive management led to resolution of jaundice and fluid retention over ~3 months. Negative hepatitis A/B/C serologies, ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody; normal ceruloplasmin; no acetaminophen, ethanol, prior liver disease, or other co-medications at the time. Prior agents tramadol and cyclobenzaprine were discontinued and ibuprofen stopped 7 days before reinstating bromfenac and are not attributed as causes.

raw_record.support_text: In the randomized part of the study, one case of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) was observed in a 43-year-old white female admitted for acute liver failure secondary to the use of Duract (Wyeth Ayerst, St. Davids, PA) (bromfenac sodium). The patient's baseline coagulation parameters were suggestive but not conclusive of DIC, and after taking bromfenac she required a successful liver transplantation and recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Bromfenac (brand name Duract, Wyeth Ayerst) was reported as the cause of acute liver failure in a 43-year-old white female. The patient's DIC/coagulation abnormalities were suspected post-liver biopsy after a drop in hematocrit and were not considered related to rFVIIa treatment. The patient recovered after a successful liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 43-year-old female with no prior history of liver disease was transferred to the hepatology service with acute liver failure secondary to the use of Duract (bromfenac) taken for arthritis/club foot over approximately 5–6 months. After treatment with rFVIIa and laparoscopic liver biopsy, the biopsy revealed 60–80% necrosis, and the patient was referred for and successfully underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Duract brand); a 43-year-old female without prior liver disease with acute liver failure secondary to bromfenac used ~5–6 months for arthritis/club foot. Post-biopsy haematocrit fell from 34.3 to 28.5 and platelets from 129,000 to 119,000 with no identified bleeding source; no fibrinogen or PT values available. Liver biopsy showed 60–80% necrosis; patient successfully underwent liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Bromfenac, shortly after its introduction, produced acute liver failure in several patients and was subsequently withdrawn from the market. The severe reactions were thought to be precipitated by bioactivation to a reactive metabolite, with three potential sites (bromphenol moiety to an epoxide, aniline ring to reactive nitroso compounds, and an arylacetic acid moiety).
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; caused acute liver failure in several patients shortly after market introduction and was withdrawn; injury attributed to bioactivation to a reactive metabolite at three potential toxicophore sites: a bromphenol moiety (possible epoxide), an aniline ring (reactive nitroso compounds), and an arylacetic acid moiety.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed raised liver enzyme activity, chronic hepatitis lesions, raised serum IgG, and anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle autoantibodies after 21 months of mesalazine treatment; idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis was reasonably excluded. Liver tests and serum IgG became normal and autoantibodies disappeared without immunosuppressive therapy, and the liver disease never relapsed. The authors conclude mesalazine probably caused chronic hepatitis and autoimmune manifestations in this patient; no other cause of liver disease was detected. Simvastatin was withdrawn without improvement, and the five remaining drugs did not prevent recovery once mesalazine was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported after 21 months of mesalazine treatment. Raised liver enzymes, chronic hepatitis lesions, elevated serum IgG, anti-nuclear (peak 1:500) and anti-smooth muscle (peak 1:200) autoantibodies. Liver biopsy at three weeks after mesalazine discontinuation showed portal and periportal fibrosis, mild cholangiolar proliferation, mild perisinusoidal fibrosis, mononuclear portal infiltrates with some neutrophils and rare eosinophils, piecemeal necrosis around portal fibrosis, and acidophilic bodies surrounded by inflammatory cells; mild iron deposits in Kupffer cells; wedge-free hepatic vein gradient moderately increased (6 mm Hg; N 1-4). Liver tests improved quickly after mesalazine withdrawal and returned to normal by 12 Aug 1997 without relapse; autoantibodies declined and disappeared, IgG normalized. Patient had received six other drugs; simvastatin was withdrawn earlier without improvement and the remaining five drugs continued did not prevent recovery after mesalazine cessation. Patient never had inflammatory bowel disease.

raw_record.support_text: Deltenre et al. reported the first case of mesalazine-induced autoimmune hepatitis. Laboratory changes indicative of hepatocellular inflammation were observed in a 65-year-old man during 8 months of treatment with mesalazine, 3 grams daily. High titer smooth muscle antibodies (SMA) and ANA, abnormal serum immunoglobulin G concentration, and histologic features of interface hepatitis and fibrosis of the portal, periportal, and perisinusoidal areas supported the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis, and laboratory abnormalities fully resolved within 2 months after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of mesalazine-induced autoimmune hepatitis; 65-year-old man, 8 months treatment at 3 grams daily; high titer SMA and ANA, abnormal serum IgG, histologic interface hepatitis with portal/periportal/perisinusoidal fibrosis; laboratory abnormalities fully resolved within 2 months after discontinuation. Mesalazine (5-aminosalicylic acid) was developed to deliver 5-ASA to inflamed GI mucosa and avoid sulphasalazine toxicity, but the report and others indicate 5-aminosalicylic acid has its own potential for liver injury and should be discontinued in patients with liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors performed a PubMed literature review (January 2023) for case reports of liver dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, or liver injury caused by 5-ASA (mesalazine), excluded cases not associated with 5-ASA-induced liver injury, and identified 7 published case reports plus their own case (8 total). All events occurred after initiation of 5-ASA, with onset ranging from 1 week to 8 months; one case was classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type) and the others as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). The paper concludes that although mesalamine is generally safe, serious 5-ASA-related liver injury can occur and regular monitoring of liver function is needed.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 human case reports of DILI attributed to 5-ASA (mesalazine) at therapeutic doses (800-4,000 mg/day); onset 1 week to 8 months after initiation. One case classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type; Hautekeete et al., CTCAE grade 4), the rest as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). CTCAE grades ranged 3-4. Patients had ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease; treatment included withdrawal of 5-ASA, PSL, UDCA, and SNMC. Literature search limited by small number of reports suggesting possible publication bias; pathogenesis and timing not well understood. Authors note 5-ASA-related DILI is typically classified as a blood-test abnormality with a median onset of about 55 days (~2 months), but can present in various ways including mimicking IBD exacerbations or lupus-like symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 29-year-old patient who developed liver failure during valproic acid (VPA) therapy; the patient tested negative for hepatitis viruses A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus, and the valproate level was 97.1 µM (below the therapeutic range of 350-700 µM). Autopsy showed subacute liver dystrophy with an organ weight of 860 g, microvesicular steatosis and bridging hepatocellular necrosis predominantly in the centrolobular zone, signs of cholestasis, and marked fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 29-year-old patient with Friedreich's disease on VPA therapy who died. Laboratory abnormalities included bilirubin 14.3 mg/dl conjugated at admission, AST 113 U/L, ALT 109 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L, GGT 34 U/L, NH3 150 µM; before death bilirubin 33.7, AST 50, ALT 63, ALP 182, NH3 281. Autopsy: subacute liver dystrophy (860 g), microvesicular steatosis, bridging hepatocellular necrosis in centrolobular zone, cholestasis, marked fibrosis, plus generalized hemorrhage, bronchopneumonia, aspiration, and pancreatitis. Viral hepatitis (A,B,C), EBV, and CMV excluded.

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, valproate was implicated in 10 of 137 (7.3%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Tied with phenytoin at 10 of 137 non-APAP cases (7.3%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes VPA (valproic acid)-associated hepatic failure established across multiple reports: Dreifuss et al. found most patients developed symptoms within 90 days of starting therapy, Zimmerman and Ishak reported 23 fatal cases of VPA-associated hepatic failure (19 within four months of treatment), and symptoms appeared in the present patient within approximately 45 days. Histology showed massive hepatic necrosis with collapse, hepatocellular ballooning, steatosis, and cholestasis, and the report notes microvesicular steatosis and necrosis consistent with prior reports.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as an idiosyncratic reaction with no dose-dependency and absent usual hypersensitivity markers (rash, fever, eosinophilia); supported by the small number of cases relative to the many patients using the drug and a delay in onset. Zimmerman and Ishak reported 23 fatal VPA-associated hepatic failure cases, most within 4 months of drug initiation; latency in the present patient was about 45 days. Histology: massive necrosis with collapse, hepatocellular ballooning, steatosis, and cholestasis; microvesicular steatosis and necrosis consistent with prior reports. Proposed mechanisms (not independently established as causal): a 4-ene-VPA metabolite mediating mitochondrial/fatty-acid beta-oxidation disruption, polytherapy with microsomal P-450 inducers (e.g., phenobarbital, phenytoin) as a risk factor, carnitine deficiency, and impaired ketogenesis in malnourished or fasting children. Mortality has also occurred in patients treated up to four years.

raw_record.support_text: In table 2, valproate (VPA 400 mg) was marked as the RUCAM highly-suggestive DILI drug (score 11) in a single patient (case 19), with non-attributed co-medication milnacipran 60 mg.
raw_record.extra_details: Single RUCAM-adjudicated case (case 19) at 400 mg, RUCAM score 11; psychiatric inpatient; DILI moderate in severity.

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including 11 cases of valproate hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test RUCAM causality score reliability.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of valproate hepatotoxicity. Cohort-wide median time to onset was 42.5 days, 73% hospitalized, 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: Eighteen days after starting valproic acid (VPA) prophylactic treatment and 11 days after discharge, the 58-year-old patient was admitted with massive elevations of liver enzymes (AST 8747 U/L, ALT 7184 U/L, GGT 153 U/L), elevated creatinine, INR 2.4 and a VPA serum level of 81 mg/L. Hepatitis serology and auto-antibodies were negative, and the diagnosis of an acute toxic liver failure most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine was made. The patient developed progressive hepatic encephalopathy and underwent urgent liver transplantation, followed by a second transplant after primary graft dysfunction; she died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months later.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA given as Ergenyl chrono prophylactic treatment (300 mg OD day 1, 300 mg three times day 2, then 300 mg 1-0-2-0). Liver function tests were normal on day 7 of VPA (serum level 73 mg/L); on admission VPA level was 81 mg/L. Histology showed massive necrosis with less than 5% of liver tissue preserved, plasma cell infiltration and slight fatty degeneration, consistent with acute drug-induced liver failure due to VPA. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale scored the causative role of valproate as probable. Possible cytochrome P450 polymorphism was not tested. Generalized toxicity attributed to toxic metabolites such as 4-en VPA via impaired beta-oxidation. Co-suspect duloxetine was initially mentioned ('most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine') but the final diagnosis and histology attributed the liver failure to VPA. Multi-organ involvement included renal failure, pancolitis and lymphadenopathy. Patient died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months after transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A study in 17 patients with valproate hepatotoxicity found that heterozygous genetic variation within the POLG gene correlated significantly with valproate-induced liver injury. In vitro analyses showed therapeutic concentrations of valproate suppressed hepatocyte proliferation and high doses led to non-apoptotic cell death.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 17 patients with valproate hepatotoxicity; heterozygous genetic variation in the POLG gene correlated significantly with valproate-induced liver injury. In vitro, therapeutic concentrations of valproate suppressed hepatocyte proliferation while high doses caused non-apoptotic cell death.

raw_record.support_text: High-confidence DILI cases due to valproate (n=13) from the DILIN studies were analyzed. The rare HLA class 2 risk allele DRB1*10:01 was increased among valproate-induced DILI (n=12, OR=13.9, 95% CI 2.8-43.9, P=0.004, FDR=0.14).
raw_record.extra_details: High-confidence DILI cases (n=13, n=12 analyzed) from DILIN. Associated with HLA-DRB1*10:01 (AF cases=0.08, AF controls=0.008). Antiepileptic drug class.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old female patient with Friedreich's ataxia and grand-mal epilepsy died after therapy with valproic acid (valproate) from acute liver failure with massive lactacidosis. Clinical symptoms were hyperventilation, increasing loss of consciousness and shock, leading to treatment-resistant hepatic coma. Pathoanatomy showed extensive confluent lytic necroses of the liver acini (centrolobular and intermediary accentuation) and small-to-medium droplet fatty degeneration increasing from periphery to centre. The paper states the disease picture is quite characteristic for being caused by valproic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: 19-year-old female with Friedreich's ataxia and grand-mal epilepsy; died of acute liver failure with massive lactacidosis; hyperventilation, loss of consciousness, shock and treatment-resistant hepatic coma; histology: extensive confluent lytic necroses with centrolobular/intermediary accentuation plus small-to-medium droplet fatty degeneration increasing from periphery to centre; authors recommend monitoring liver function with prodromal symptoms (anorexia, weakness, apathy), dose reduction or drug discontinuation, and keeping serum valproate in the lower half of the therapeutic range. Paralanguage note: valproate considered a relatively complication-free drug despite known side effects; prior reported cases of acute liver failure after valproate (18 published with detail, 11 fatal).

raw_record.support_text: This study collected medical data from patients treated with valproic acid (VPA) between January 2020 and October 2023; prescription sequence analysis identified 64 patients with suspected VPA-induced liver injury versus 192 controls (incidence 5.3%), and the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method was used to confirm the VPA-induced liver injury diagnosis. Multivariate logistic regression found dysglycemia, hyperlipidemia, surgery, and hypokalemia to be significant independent risk factors, and a nomogram model predicted the likelihood of VPA-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 64 VPA-induced liver injury cases among 256 VPA-treated patients (incidence 5.3%); diagnosis confirmed by prescription sequence analysis plus RUCAM causality assessment. Significant independent risk factors in multivariate logistic regression: dysglycemia (OR 5.171; 95% CI 1.254-21.325), hyperlipidemia (OR 4.903; 95% CI 1.400-17.173), surgery (OR 10.020; 95% CI 1.737-57.805), and hypokalemia (OR 10.407; 95% CI 2.398-45.173). Nomogram model AUC 0.904 (95% CI 0.860-0.947); Hosmer-Lemeshow P=0.2671. VPA is a first-line antiepileptic, also used for migraine, mood disorders, anxiety, and bipolar disorder.

raw_record.support_text: The first case is a 24-year-old woman who developed a reversible hepatic lesion attributed to valproate (VPA) treatment, described as 'liver lesion due to VPA treatment.' Liver biopsy showed liver tissue with drug-induced changes. The authors recommend stopping VPA if symptoms of hepatic toxicity appear to prevent irreversible injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-year-old woman on valproate for primary generalized epilepsy with absences and tonic-clonic seizures; medication changed from carbamazepine and primidone to carbamazepine and VPA; VPA 900 mg daily, serum level 220 (350-450) µmol/l just below therapeutic range; liver parameters normal one month after starting VPA; both cases were reversible; indication: epilepsy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that evidence that their two patients had fluoxetine-induced acute hepatitis is convincing. No other cause was identified from history, physical examination, or laboratory tests; viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and obstructive liver disease were excluded. After fluoxetine was discontinued, both patients had prompt symptomatic improvement and steady normalization of liver biochemistry test results. Liver biopsy and fluoxetine rechallenge were not performed because symptoms diminished and liver tests normalized after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (case series). Case 2: 45-year-old woman, fluoxetine 40 mg/d for 3 months, also on levothyroxine sodium 0.122 mg/d, no acetaminophen/alcohol use; presented with 3-day RUQ pain, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, jaundice. Labs: total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL, AST 168 U/L, ALT 641 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L, GGT 92 U/L; normal prothrombin time and TSH. Jaundice present, no cirrhosis/ascites. Tests excluded viral (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV), autoimmune, metabolic, cholelithiasis, and obstructive causes. After fluoxetine discontinuation, patient 1 normalized in ~6 months, patient 2 near-normal in ~2.5 months. Liver biopsy and fluoxetine rechallenge were not performed.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 2, a 55-year-old female, was started on fluoxetine 20 mg once daily; about 1 week later she developed dark urine, pale stools, itching, and jaundice. Intrahepatic cholestasis was diagnosed, and a liver biopsy revealed a centrolobular cholestatic hepatitis typical for drug-induced cholestasis. Because other medications had been discontinued before the cholestasis emerged, the authors concluded that fluoxetine must be regarded as the causative agent. The cholestasis was refractory to prednisolone, ursodeoxycholic acid, and naltrexone, and extracorporeal albumin dialysis (MARS) was started.
raw_record.extra_details: 55-year-old female with a 6-year history of depression; 20 mg once daily; symptoms appeared ~1 week after starting fluoxetine; jaundice with bilirubin 18.7 mg/dl falling to 8.3 mg/dl after MARS; liver biopsy showed centrolobular cholestatic hepatitis; failed treatment with prednisolone, ursodeoxycholic acid, naltrexone; treated with MARS albumin dialysis.

raw_record.support_text: A female patient treated with fluoxetine (Tab Fluoxetine) developed liver cirrhosis (with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, activity score 6, fibrosis stage 4), jaundice, ascites, and elevated bilirubin (1.41 mg/dl). Fluoxetine was discontinued, and liver enzyme levels subsequently improved. Application of the Naranjo algorithm gave a score of 8, indicating a 'probable' role of fluoxetine in causing this adverse drug reaction (psychotropic drug-induced liver cirrhosis), since she had no history of alcohol, liver infection, or other medication. The report also notes prior cases/case series of fluoxetine-induced hepatitis and acute liver injury and cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality score 8. Presentation: right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, pruritus, jaundice, engorged veins, serum bilirubin 1.41 mg/dl, ascites, mild splenomegaly, left pleural effusion. Liver biopsy showed non-alcoholic steatohepatitis with cirrhosis, NAFLD activity score 6, fibrosis stage 4. Fluoxetine was stopped; liver enzymes improved within a month; hepatoprotective medications given; psychiatric treatment continued with ERP sessions. No alcohol, liver infection, or other drugs. Reference is made to prior reports of fluoxetine-induced hepatitis, acute liver injury with cutaneous reaction (Soni et al.), acute cholestatic hepatitis in a 49-year-old man, and transaminitis in a patient on citalopram and olanzapine after fluoxetine was added as an adjuvant.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first drug for improving insulin resistance, was reported to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients shortly after its introduction in Japan and the U.S. in March 1997. Following this, the Japanese government recommended monthly liver function assessment and the U.S. FDA recommended ALT monitoring. The authors report on a patient who developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment, highlighting uncertainty about how long liver-function tests should be continued to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity reported in patients soon after market introduction in Japan and the U.S. (March 1997). Regulatory responses: the Japanese government recommended monthly liver-function assessment; the U.S. FDA recommended ALT measurement before therapy, monthly for the next 8 months, every 2 months for the remainder of the first year, and periodically thereafter. Case report: patient developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment; authors note the unknown duration of monitoring needed to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with elevated liver chemistries (ALT 653 U/L, AST 413 U/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl) that appeared 5 months after beginning troglitazone therapy, in the absence of other prescription medications, alcohol, viral hepatitis, or autoimmune markers. She was told to stop troglitazone. The paper collectively reports this as part of 'troglitazone hepatotoxicity' in two patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient continued taking troglitazone in error after initially instructed to stop; 4 weeks later aminotransferases further elevated with increased total bilirubin and prothrombin time and decreased albumin, and she appeared jaundiced/icteric. Urgent liver biopsy showed zone 3 necrosis with hemorrhage and hepatocyte dropout, occasional foci of bridging necrosis to triads, active cell injury (acidophilic bodies, cell swelling, lobular disarray), minimal macrovesicular steatosis, mild non-prominent cholestasis, enlarged Kupffer cells, diffuse mononuclear infiltrate, and early pericentral and bridging fibrosis on trichrome stain. Histology reflected severe hepatocellular injury; improvement (decreased aminotransferases and bilirubin, normal prothrombin time) occurred within 18 days after stopping troglitazone with oral vitamin K supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes an autopsy case of fatal subacute hepatic failure after administration of troglitazone in a 63-year-old woman. Liver dysfunction developed about five months after initial troglitazone treatment, and the patient died despite hepatic auxiliary treatments such as plasmapheresis. Autopsy revealed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis and steatosis with lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration and lack of regenerative activity. The authors state the fatal subacute hepatic failure was 'due unequivocally to troglitazone' and proposed metabolite aberration with accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), categorized as idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal subacute hepatic failure in a 63-year-old woman with a history of non-insulin-dependent diabetes and hypothyroidism and no prior liver disease, treated for NIDDM. Dose: troglitazone 200 mg twice a day (400 mg/day), increased to 600 mg/day, then reduced to 400 mg/day. Latency about 5 months before liver dysfunction; presented with jaundice and hepatic failure and died despite plasmapheresis, FFP, and methylprednisolone pulse. Autopsy showed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis, and steatosis with lymphocyte and neutrophil infiltration and lack of regenerative activity. Proposed mechanism is accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s) as an idiosyncratic liver injury. Markers of viral hepatitis were negative; co-prescribed glibenclamide (2.5 mg/day) and thyroxine (0.05 mg/day). FDA and MHW in Japan had issued warnings about troglitazone-related liver function side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 47-year-old man who developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after consuming only four doses of troglitazone. He experienced vomiting and dehydration, and despite prompt discontinuation of troglitazone his symptoms progressed to jaundice and fatigue; he had no history of exposure to other hepatotoxins. Evaluation revealed transaminitis without underlying liver disease, and liver biopsy showed patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation, consistent with severe drug-induced hepatitis; the patient was managed supportively and liver function returned to normal. Earlier reports (Gitlin, Neuschwander-Tetri and colleagues, 1998) described severe hepatotoxicity associated with troglitazone in patients who consumed it for at least 1 month and received supportive care or liver transplantation. The authors emphasize the unpredictable nature of troglitazone hepatotoxicity and its potentially life-threatening effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Current case: acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only four doses, with vomiting, dehydration, jaundice, fatigue, transaminitis, no other hepatotoxins, no underlying liver disease. Biopsy: patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation; no chronic liver disease. Managed supportively with eventual normalization of liver function. Earlier 1998 reports (Gitlin and Neuschwander-Tetri, respectively) described severe troglitazone hepatotoxicity after at least 1 month of use treated with supportive care or liver transplantation. Authors highlight the unpredictable (idiosyncratic) nature and potentially life-threatening effects and call for vigilant monitoring of liver enzyme levels.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old diabetic man presented with progressive liver dysfunction after 1 year of troglitazone therapy. His overall presentation was considered consistent with troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity; liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis, transaminase and bilirubin levels were markedly elevated, and viral serologic test results were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient had taken troglitazone for 1 year with normal baseline liver enzymes; troglitazone and simvastatin were stopped upon presentation. ALT rose from 8350 to 21667 nkat/L and bilirubin increased from normal to 308 µmol/L (18 mg/dL). On evaluation, total bilirubin 444 µmol/L (26 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 7.36 µkat/L, ALT 10583 nkat/L, AST 5.26 µkat/L; prothrombin time normal; mild ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positivity (1:80); negative viral serology; unremarkable ultrasound and CT. Liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis. Treated with prednisone 20 mg twice daily; at 5-month follow-up liver enzymes were normal. Concurrent medications included ramipril, diltiazem, furosemide, insulin, glyburide; alcohol intake insignificant.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that in this patient the time course of hepatic dysfunction and subsequent improvement after use and withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No other viral or autoimmune causes were identified, and the authors believe the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. On jaundice, troglitazone was stopped; tests showed total bilirubin 7.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 5.9 mg/dl, ALT 2,040 mg/dl, normal alkaline phosphatase, and negative ANA, AMA, and hepatitis A/B/C panels; symptoms disappeared and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with type 2 diabetes on troglitazone. Jaundice with total bilirubin 127 µmol/l (7.5 mg/dl), direct bilirubin 100.8 µmol/l (5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2,040 mg/dl (given in text as mg/dl), normal serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, normal prothrombin time/INR, negative antinuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, normal α1 antitrypsin, mildly elevated ceruloplasmin 61.0 mg/dl, nonreactive hepatitis A/B/C panel, normal iron and transferrin saturation. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of discontinuation (dechallenge); no rechallenge with troglitazone. Metformin and escalated insulin were used around the time; the authors attributed dysfunction to troglitazone. Troglitazone is a first-generation PPAR-γ agonist (thiazolidinedione) metabolized by cytochrome P4503A4 to a quinone derivative; 3% excreted in urine.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that in this patient, the time course of hepatic dysfunction and its improvement after use and withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; no viral or autoimmune causes were identified, and they state that 'We believe that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity.'
