raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a female type 2 diabetes patient on troglitazone who developed clinical jaundice with elevated total/direct bilirubin (127 and 100.8 µmol/l; 7.5 and 5.9 mg/dl) and ALT 2,040; serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, prothrombin time, and INR were normal. Antinuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were negative, α1-antitrypsin was normal, ceruloplasmin mildly elevated (61.0 mg/dl), and hepatitis A/B/C panel nonreactive. After stopping troglitazone, symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months (favorable dechallenge). Subsequent rosiglitazone 4 mg twice a day was well tolerated with normal liver tests for up to 10 months.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was the first thiazolidinedione and has been associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that included cases of liver failure, liver transplantation, and death; it was voluntarily withdrawn from the U.S. market in March 2000. A 36-year-old woman developed jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain four months after starting troglitazone 400 mg/day (increased to 800 mg/day), with elevated bilirubin and ALT.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated hepatotoxicity included cases of liver failure, liver transplantation, and death; voluntarily withdrawn from the U.S. market in March 2000. Case: 36-year-old woman with severe insulin resistance on 35 U U-500 insulin twice daily, glyburide and acarbose previously; troglitazone 400 mg/day from March 1997, increased to 800 mg/day April 1997; jaundice, malaise, crampy abdominal pain developed 4 months after start. Total bilirubin 127 µmol/l (7.5 mg/dl), direct bilirubin 100.8 µmol/l (5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2,040 mg/dl, normal serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, normal PT/INR; ANA and AMA negative; hepatitis A/B/C nonreactive.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes developed clinical evidence of jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain 4 months after starting troglitazone (increased from 400 to 800 mg/day); her liver function tests were normal before and 2 months after starting the drug. On presentation, total and direct bilirubin were elevated (127 and 100.8 µmol/l) and ALT was 2,040 mg/dl with normal alkaline phosphatase; viral, autoimmune, ceruloplasmin, and α1 antitrypsin work-up did not identify other causes. After troglitazone was stopped, her symptoms disappeared and liver tests normalized within several months. The authors state that the time course and improvement after withdrawal were consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity and that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity, with no other viral or autoimmune cause identified.
raw_record.extra_details: 36-year-old woman with uncomplicated type 2 diabetes; troglitazone dosed 400 mg/day starting March 1997, increased to 800 mg/day in April 1997; jaundice developed about 4 months after initiation, 2 months after a normal 2-month liver-function check. On evaluation total and direct bilirubin 127 and 100.8 µmol/l (7.5 and 5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2,040 mg/dl, normal serum/leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, normal prothrombin time and INR, normal blood count and platelets; ANA and AMA negative, α1 antitrypsin normal, ceruloplasmin mildly elevated (61.0 mg/dl), hepatitis A/B/C panel nonreactive, iron/transferrin saturation normal. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping troglitazone; concurrent use of insulin and later metformin; no other medications at time of hepatotoxicity, no alcohol use. Authors note a favorable dechallenge response consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first thiazolidinedione, has been associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that included cases of liver failure, liver transplantation, and death, and was voluntarily withdrawn from the U.S. market in March 2000. In the presented case, a 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes developed jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain four months after starting troglitazone 400 mg/day (increased to 800 mg/day), with elevated bilirubin and alanine aminotransferase and a normal alkaline phosphatase; her symptoms and liver tests normalized within several months after troglitazone was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Class-level history: cases of liver failure, liver transplantation, and death; voluntarily withdrawn from the U.S. market in March 2000. Case specifics: jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain at 4 months of use; total bilirubin 127 umol/l, direct bilirubin 100.8 umol/l, ALT 2040 mg/dl, normal serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and INR; antinuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies negative; symptoms and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping drug; insulin requirements increased after cessation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that troglitazone has been associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that included cases of liver failure, liver transplantation, and death, and was voluntarily withdrawn from the US market in March 2000. In the presented case, the patient developed classic troglitazone-induced liver disease with jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain about 4 months after starting troglitazone 400 mg/day (increased to 800 mg/day), with total/direct bilirubin 127/100.8 µmol/l and ALT 2,040; symptoms and liver tests normalized within months of discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: First TZD in a class of antidiabetic drugs; voluntarily withdrawn from the US market in March 2000. Presented patient: 36-year-old woman, type 2 diabetes with extreme insulin resistance, taking no other medications and denying alcohol; jaundice appeared 4 months after starting 400 mg/day (increased to 800 mg/day); total bilirubin 127 µmol/l, direct 100.8 µmol/l, ALT 2,040, normal alkaline phosphatase, normal prothrombin time/INR, negative antinuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, nonreactive hepatitis A/B/C panel; recovered with normalization of liver tests within months of stopping drug. Broad association included cases of liver failure and liver transplantation in addition to death.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that in this patient the time course of hepatic dysfunction and subsequent improvement after use and withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, and that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. No other viral or autoimmune cause for the hepatic dysfunction was identified.
raw_record.extra_details: 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes. Troglitazone started at 400 mg/day in March 1997, increased to 800 mg/day in April 1997; jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain developed 4 months after initiation, with normal liver function tests 2 months after start. Total/direct bilirubin 127/100.8 µmol/l (7.5/5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2040 (printed as mg/dl), serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase normal, prothrombin time/INR normal, negative ANA/AMA, normal α1 antitrypsin, nonreactive hepatitis A/B/C panel. Symptoms and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping troglitazone; no rechallenge. Background: gallstone-induced pancreatitis history, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, oligoamenorrhea; denied alcohol and other medications.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that in this patient the time course of hepatic dysfunction and subsequent improvement after use and withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity, and that no other viral or autoimmune causes were identified. They concluded: We believe that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient developed jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain four months after starting troglitazone (400 mg/day, increased to 800 mg/day), with total bilirubin 127 µmol/l, ALT 2040 mg/dl, and normal alkaline phosphatase; symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping troglitazone.
raw_record.extra_details: 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes; troglitazone 400 mg/day added March 1997, increased to 800 mg/day April 1997. Jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain developed 4 months after starting troglitazone; liver function was normal before and 2 months after initiation. Total and direct bilirubin 127 and 100.8 µmol/l (7.5 and 5.9 mg/dl); ALT 2040 mg/dl; normal serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase; normal prothrombin time/INR. ANA, AMA negative; normal α1 antitrypsin; mild ceruloplasmin elevation (61.0 mg/dl); hepatitis A/B/C panel nonreactive. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of withdrawal (dechallenge). No other medications or alcohol; history of gallstone-induced pancreatitis. No rechallenge with troglitazone. Subsequent rosiglitazone 4 mg twice daily was well tolerated with normal liver tests up to 10 months.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone (marketed as Rezulin), the first thiazolidinedione made available for clinical use, is no longer available for clinical use after the reporting of several cases of liver failure and death directly related to its use. It is an orally active insulin-action enhancer for type 2 diabetes that lowers fasting serum glucose and HbA1c.
raw_record.extra_details: Several reported cases of liver failure and death were directly related to use of the drug, leading to its withdrawal from clinical use. Marketed as Rezulin. Used clinically for type 2 diabetes (therapeutic oral insulin-action enhancer).

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was associated with ALT elevations in premarketing clinical studies, including rare cases of severe idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury leading to death or liver transplantation. Neither rosiglitazone nor pioglitazone was associated with an increase in ALT values compared with placebo or with drug-related hepatotoxicity in premarketing trials.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT elevations seen in premarketing clinical studies; rare cases of severe idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury leading to death or liver transplantation. In light of the troglitazone experience, liver enzyme monitoring is recommended for both rosiglitazone and pioglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the major issue with the thiazolidinediones was the rare occurrence of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity leading to liver failure and death in a small number of individuals treated with troglitazone. Clinical trial data showed 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients (vs 0.6% placebo) developed liver enzyme elevations at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, and some patients developed jaundice or enzyme elevations 10 times the upper limit of normal, described as a clear signal of liver toxicity. Troglitazone was removed from the market in March 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity leading to liver failure and death in a small number of treated individuals; 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients (vs 0.6% placebo) developed enzyme elevations >=3x upper limit of normal, with some patients developing jaundice or enzyme elevations 10x ULN; described as a clear signal of liver toxicity; removed from the US market in March 2000; FDA recommended intermittent liver-function monitoring for other thiazolidinediones.

raw_record.support_text: Post-marketing FDA reporting linked troglitazone use with liver failure and death (reported October 1997), and an FDA advisory committee on 26 March 1999 adjudicated 38 cases of acute liver failure as probably related to troglitazone, 5 as possibly related, and 81 cases of hepatitis as related. Troglitazone was removed from the US market in March 2000. Clinical features included jaundice as the first symptom in 62% of liver-failure cases and progression from jaundice to encephalopathy over a mean 19 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione (glitazone) antidiabetic agent (Rezulin, Parke-Davis/Sankyo) for type 2 diabetes; removed from US market March 2000 and denied reintroduction in Britain. FDA-meeting adjudication: 38 ALF probably related, 5 possibly related, 81 hepatitis cases related; 70% of initial liver-failure cases were women, mean age 63 y (43-91), mean treatment duration 116 d (4-236 d), jaundice first symptom in 62%, LFT abnormalities first sign in 14%, jaundice-to-encephalopathy progression mean 19 d (0-70 d). A non-diabetic National Institutes of Health Diabetes Prevention Trial patient died of liver failure after liver transplant. Approval-trial data: ALT>3xULN in 1.9% of troglitazone subjects vs 0.6% placebo; severe LFT abnormalities (ALT>30xULN) in 0.2%; two patients had reversible jaundice and two had liver biopsies consistent with idiosyncratic drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The case report states 'Our patient developed liver injury from troglitazone', which was administered for about 2.25 years (25 September 1997 to 9 January 2000) without elevated ALT or AST. In January 2000 she presented with mild jaundice (total serum bilirubin 42.5 µM, 2.5 mg/dl) and increased alkaline phosphatase (4.84 µkat/L, 290 IU/L), and other possible causes of liver injury were excluded by history, course, laboratory, imaging, and hepatic histopathology.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy showed hepatitis and cholangitis with a likely immune-mediated component (nonnecrotizing granulomas in portal triads and a distorted bile duct), treated with prednisone, azathioprine, and ursodiol. The paper also notes troglitazone proved to be a frequent and severe hepatotoxin, leading to its withdrawal from the US market in March 2000 and earlier voluntary withdrawal in the UK. Latency to recognition about 2.25 years with biochemically silent injury; patient recovered over the ensuing 8 months.

raw_record.support_text: During clinical trials, troglitazone (TRG) proved to be hepatotoxic in 1.9% of patients receiving therapy for Type II diabetes; hepatic failure and death were reported in a few cases, and as a consequence of safety concerns TRG was withdrawn from the US market in March 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapy with troglitazone has been associated with severe hepatic injury in a small percentage of patients; hepatotoxic in 1.9% of patients during clinical trials; hepatic failure and death reported in a few cases; withdrawn from the US market in March 2000 due to safety concerns. Indication: Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus; first thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent.

raw_record.support_text: The Diabetes Prevention Programme (DPP), which showed lifestyle intervention and metformin reduced progression from impaired glucose tolerance to overt diabetes, originally included a troglitazone arm. This treatment arm of ~1000 people had to be discontinued after a fatal case of troglitazone-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity occurred in the DPP diabetes-prevention arm (impaired glucose tolerance/prediabetic population, ~1000 participants), which led to discontinuation of the troglitazone treatment arm of the trial.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone's major adverse effect is hepatotoxicity. Among 2500 patients prescribed troglitazone, 2.2% had more than a 3-fold elevation of serum aminotransferase levels, and two of these had reversible jaundice, developing within 1 to 4.5 months of starting the drug. Liver biopsies in these two cases showed hepatocyte necrosis, bridging necrosis, portal inflammation, and evidence of cholestasis, with recovery 3 months after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 2.2% of 2500 patients had >3-fold aminotransferase elevation; two cases of reversible jaundice within 1-4.5 months; biopsies showed hepatocyte necrosis, bridging necrosis, portal inflammation, and cholestasis; recovery 3 months after discontinuation. High incidence of liver failure leading to liver transplantation or death prompted removal from the market in Great Britain and the United States.

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials of troglitazone, 48 (1.9%) of 2510 treated patients had ALT over three times the upper limit of normal versus 3 (0.6%) of 475 placebo patients; 12 (0.6%) of 2510 had peak ALT over 10 times ULN versus none on placebo; only two patients developed jaundice and clinically overt hepatitis. The actual number of acute liver failure cases was nearly 100 among 2 million patients treated, i.e., about 1 in 20,000, as predicted from the trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Combined North American trials: ALT>3x ULN in 48/2510 (1.9%) vs 3/475 (0.6%) placebo; ALT>10x ULN in 12/2510 (0.6%) vs none. Two patients had jaundice and clinically overt hepatitis. Predicted ~1/2000 jaundice and ~1/20,000 ALF; nearly 100 ALF cases in 2 million treated patients (Graham 2003). Withdrawn; example of rapidly progressing hepatotoxicity resistant to monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first glitazone approved by the US FDA, proved to be hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from the market after reports of several dozen deaths and cases of severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. An observational retrospective inception cohort using US claims data confirmed that troglitazone use was associated with a marked increase in the risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled clinical trials, troglitazone was associated with a ~3-fold greater incidence of significant (>3x ULN) ALT elevations than placebo.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market after reports of several dozen deaths and severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. Retrospective inception cohort assembled from claims data of a large multistate US healthcare organisation showed marked increase in risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled trials, troglitazone showed a ~3-fold greater incidence of ALT elevations >3x ULN than placebo. In a troglitazone-insulin combination study, 3 patients on troglitazone 600mg had ALT >3x ULN during the 26-week treatment period; one patient discontinued permanently due to jaundice and hyperbilirubinaemia. Hepatotoxicity is not a glitazone class effect.

raw_record.support_text: The thiazolidinediones rosiglitazone (Avandia) and pioglitazone (Actos) act on PPAR and decrease insulin resistance. Troglitazone, another drug in this class, was withdrawn from the market after a number of cases of fatal hepatotoxicity were reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone is a thiazolidinedione antidiabetic (PPAR agonist, decreases insulin resistance); it was withdrawn from the market after a number of cases of fatal hepatotoxicity were reported.

raw_record.support_text: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, the study initially included a fourth arm using troglitazone, 400 mg/d. This arm was discontinued in 1998 because of hepatotoxicity that resulted in liver failure and the death of one DPP participant.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone was the fourth arm of the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) at 400 mg/day in adults with impaired glucose tolerance; the arm was discontinued in 1998 because hepatotoxicity resulted in liver failure and the death of one DPP participant.

raw_record.support_text: In controlled clinical trials, 1.3% of subjects given troglitazone developed ALT values >3× the ULN and 1% developed ALT >8× ULN, representing a mild reversible hepatotoxicity that appeared in <2% of subjects. After drug approval, several cases of severe and sometimes fatal liver failure were reported, in subjects showing elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin and signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; histologically troglitazone elicits hepatocellular necrosis with bridging necrosis and fibrosis and/or collapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reactions in man; reactive quinone/quinone epoxide/quinone methide and reactive isocyanate/thiazolidine sulfoxide intermediates implicated; induces CYP3A4 which bioactivates it. ALT >3× ULN in 1.3% and >8× ULN in 1% of trial subjects; post-marketing severe and sometimes fatal liver failure; acute liver failure incidence ~1:20,000; signs appeared at inconsistent times with no consistent dose relationship; monthly monitoring insufficient; histology shows hepatocellular necrosis with bridging necrosis, fibrosis and/or collapse.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, a thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent, was withdrawn from the market in 2000 due to its association with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Two female patients (47- and 70-year-old) with type II diabetes mellitus stopped taking troglitazone (400 mg/day) after 23.5 and 16 weeks, respectively, due to increased serum ALT, and autoantibodies to aldolase B were detected in their sera.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent for type II diabetes; withdrawn from market in 2000. During clinical trials 1.9% of patients had ALT increases greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal; fulminant hepatic failure reported in some patients after long-term treatment (>4 weeks). In the present case series, two female patients (47 and 70 years old) ceased 400 mg/day after 23.5 and 16 weeks due to increased serum ALT; anti-aldolase B autoantibody titer remained high for several weeks after stopping. Aldolase B was identified as an autoantigen by 2D electrophoresis and amino acid sequencing; anti-aldolase B autoantibodies also elevated in chronic hepatitis (n=40) and liver cirrhosis (n=40) patients versus healthy subjects (n=80). Hepatotoxicity not reproduced in experimental animals. Troglitazone brands Noscal (Sankyo) and Rezulin (Parke-Davis).

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was withdrawn in 1999 after spontaneous reports of 94 cases of acute liver failure. In a cohort of 7568 new troglitazone users, the point estimates for hospitalization and acute liver failure were 1244 and 240 per million person-years of exposure, respectively, versus background rates of 10-22 per million person-years. In pre-approval controlled clinical trials in type 2 diabetes, troglitazone was associated with ALT elevations above three times the upper limit of normal in 1.9% versus 0.60% in placebo-treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn in 1999 after spontaneous reports of 94 cases of acute liver failure; cohort of 7568 users gave hospitalization rate 1244 and acute liver failure 240 per million person-years vs background 10-22 per million. Pre-approval trials: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% (vs 0.60% placebo, 0.60% ALT >10x ULN); jaundice in 0.5%; acute liver failure ~1 in 20,000 treated patients; broad post-approval use associated with acute liver failure, liver transplantation, and death at intolerable frequency. Used in type 2 diabetes mellitus (thiazolidinedione).

raw_record.support_text: The incidence of acute liver failure (ALF) for troglitazone is conservatively estimated at about one case in 10 000 persons exposed, a figure serving as a benchmark incidence for other drugs. The text notes that the risk of ALF from existing diabetes treatment options is roughly 1 in 10 000 person-years, an incidence 'not dissimilar to the frequency calculated for ALF attributed to troglitazone.'
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the market over concerns about an excessive risk of liver failure. Estimated ALF incidence ~1 in 10,000 exposed; listed in Acute Liver Failure Study Group (1998-2003) series as a well-known hepatotoxin; compared with the benchmark incidence of 1 in 2300 for Exanta.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, an oral hypoglycemic drug withdrawn from the market due to numerous post-marketing reports of acute liver failure, had ALT >3× ULN in 1.9% of subjects in pre-approval trials, with two cases of elevated bilirubin and ALT among approximately 2600 subjects. After approval, 1 case of ALF requiring liver transplantation occurred among 585 subjects in a post-marketing trial, and 3 possible cases of drug-induced acute liver failure occurred in a database of roughly 9000 people; the paper estimates life-threatening hepatotoxicity rate between 1:585 and 1:3000.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market due to post-marketing reports of acute liver failure; ALT>3× ULN in 1.9% of ~2600 pre-approval subjects; two cases of elevated bilirubin and ALT; one ALF requiring liver transplantation among 585 subjects in a post-marketing trial; 3 possible cases of drug-induced ALF in a database of roughly 9000 people; retrospective analysis showed 1.7% ALT>5× ULN and 0.3% ALT>8× ULN; precise event rate cannot be calculated, estimated life-threatening hepatotoxicity rate between 1:585 and 1:3000.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was withdrawn from the market because of its association with fulminant hepatic failure; it was withdrawn in Europe in 1997 due to reports of liver toxicity, and was linked to at least 90 cases of liver failure with 70 patients requiring liver transplantation or dying, before withdrawal from the U.S. market in March 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione anti-diabetic; introduced in the U.S. and Europe in 1997, withdrawn from Europe that year and from the U.S. in March 2000 due to liver toxicity; linked to at least 90 cases of liver failure with 70 patients requiring liver transplantation or dying (reference 118). Phenotype is fulminant hepatic failure/liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: At least 10 cases of hepatitis due to troglitazone, a thiazolidinedione used to treat diabetes mellitus, were reported in 2000, contributing to its removal from the marketplace. Most studies showed severe lesions with zone 3 necrosis, bridging and confluent necrosis, or submassive necrosis with reactive bile ductules; portal infiltrates were mononuclear or mixed lymphocytic-plasmacytic with eosinophils, and hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis, and cholestasis were frequent; portal and lobular granulomas were present in one case.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiazolidinedione antidiabetic; at least 10 cases reported in 2000 leading to market withdrawal; severe lesions with zone 3, bridging, confluent or submassive necrosis with reactive bile ductule formation (neocholangioles); portal infiltrates mononuclear or mixed lymphocytic-plasmacytic with eosinophils; hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis and cholestasis; one case with portal and lobular granulomas.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone was introduced in 1997 but was withdrawn in 2000 due to cases of idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity, including fatalities and the need for liver transplants. In the UK, troglitazone was available for only a few weeks in 1997 before being withdrawn by its distributor as reports of hepatotoxicity accumulated.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn in 2000 due to idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity; reported cases included fatalities and need for liver transplants. In the UK the drug was available only for a few weeks in 1997 before withdrawal by its distributor as hepatotoxicity reports accumulated. Successor thiazolidinediones (rosiglitazone, pioglitazone) showed no evidence of similar hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: After troglitazone, the first thiazolidinedione, was launched in 1997, cases of acute liver failure were reported with its use, leading to its withdrawal from the Japanese and US markets in March 2000. In a North American clinical study, the troglitazone group showed a 1.9% incidence (48/2510 patients) of ALT ≥3x upper limit of normal versus 0.63% (3/475) in the placebo group, and two patients in the troglitazone group had liver disorder with jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of acute liver failure reported with troglitazone use after 1997 launch; withdrawn from Japanese and US markets in March 2000. North American clinical study: ALT ≥3x ULN incidence 1.9% (48/2510) in troglitazone group vs 0.63% (3/475) in placebo; two patients in the troglitazone group had liver disorder with jaundice (icterus).

raw_record.support_text: The first thiazolidinedione, troglitazone, was studied in 10 patients who had NASH and was associated with improved aminotransferase levels, but the drug was withdrawn from clinical use because of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone was withdrawn from clinical use because of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Studied as a NASH treatment in 10 patients; although steatohepatitis was unchanged in control subjects, four of seven treated subjects showed a 1-point improvement in necroinflammatory grade.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a series of 11 patients with liver injury attributed to troglitazone therapy for type 2 diabetes. For example, Patient 1, a 65-year-old woman, developed mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic jaundice after 6 weeks of troglitazone 400 mg/day, with alternative causes methodically excluded, and liver biopsy showing bridging necrosis and fibrosis. Patient 4's first biopsy was explicitly labeled 'troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity' showing chronic active hepatitis with bridging fibrosis, progressing to cirrhosis in several patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 11 patients (personal patients treated by an author plus additional cases) on troglitazone for type 2 diabetes: mean age 61±9 years, mean time on drug 10.4±9.9 months, with clinically apparent liver injury sometimes arising within months after drug discontinuation. Histology spanning bridging necrosis/fibrosis, cirrhosis, micro- and macrovesicular steatosis, submassive hepatic necrosis, chronic active hepatitis, and portal hypertension complications. Patient 3 died while awaiting liver transplantation; Patients 5 and 6 died from complications of liver disease years after drug cessation; Patient 8 presented with acute liver failure, ascites and myositis and later developed cirrhosis/portal hypertension; Patient 1 showed mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic jaundice with ALT/AST elevations; troglitazone 400 mg/day in Patient 1. Eosinophils noted in some biopsies.

raw_record.support_text: Patients (n=7,658) receiving troglitazone provided 4,020 person-years; 5 were hospitalized with acute liver injury, an incidence of 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900), far greater than the expected 10–22/million. Case reports documented idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after ≥1 month of treatment, and one patient developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only 4 doses with biopsy showing patchy cholestatic hepatitis, recovering after palliative treatment. Because of the high incidence of liver injury, troglitazone was withdrawn from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 7,658 patients (4,020 person-years); 5 hospitalized with acute liver injury; incidence 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900) vs expected 10–22/million. Case reports of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after ≥1 month; one case of acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after 4 doses whose biopsy showed patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant cell transformation, and fat accumulation; patient recovered after palliative treatment. Withdrawn from market. Proposed mechanisms: reactive intermediates, apoptosis (potentially irreversible in acute liver failure), oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, bile salt transporter inhibition, fibrosis. Injury described as idiosyncratic and not dose-related at clinically meaningful doses; low PPARγ affinity necessitates higher doses.

raw_record.support_text: The paper contrasts pioglitazone with troglitazone (Rezulin, Pfizer), a thiazolidinedione removed from the drug market due to severe liver toxicity. In clinical trials of troglitazone, elevations in serum ALT at least three times the upper limit of normal occurred in 1.9% of treated patients versus 0.6% of placebo controls, whereas the corresponding ALT elevation incidence for pioglitazone was low and comparable to placebo (0.26% vs 0.25%).
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone (Rezulin, Pfizer Inc), a thiazolidinedione (TZD) used for Type 2 diabetes, was removed from the drug market due to severe liver toxicity. In clinical trials, serum ALT elevations at least 3x the upper limit of normal were observed in 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients versus 0.6% of placebo controls, in contrast to pioglitazone which showed a low incidence comparable to placebo (0.26% vs 0.25%).

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials, ALT elevations more than three times the upper limit of normal were seen in 48 of 2,510 patients (1.9%) treated with troglitazone versus 0.6% on placebo, and two patients were confirmed to have suffered serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic drug reaction. Troglitazone was associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, with some patients showing severe or fatal liver damage, leading to its withdrawal from the US and Japanese markets in March 2000. The recommended therapeutic dose was 200-600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% (48/2,510) troglitazone-treated patients vs 0.6% placebo; two patients confirmed to have serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic reaction; some patients showed severe or fatal liver damage; withdrawn from US and Japanese markets March 2000; recommended dose 200-600 mg/day; hepatotoxicity was not predicted in conventional animals or cynomolgus monkeys (300-1200 mg/kg/day for 52 weeks).

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials, 1.9% of subjects who received troglitazone (vs 0.6% of placebo) had threefold ALT elevations, and 2 of 2510 subjects developed overt liver disease with jaundice. A signature injury incompatible with T2DM became clear, and troglitazone was withdrawn from the UK market in 1999 and the US market in March 2000. Later, 2% of patients developed liver injury and 94 of the 1.92 million exposed patients developed liver failure, with the incidence of troglitazone-induced liver failure estimated at the FDA Advisory Committee as 1 in 15,154 and an overall incidence of liver mortality of 0.0035% a year.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial data: 1.9% vs 0.6% placebo had ≥3x ULN ALT elevations; 2/2510 developed overt liver disease with jaundice. Market withdrawals: UK 1999, US March 2000. Retrospective figures: 2% developed liver injury; 94 of 1.92 million exposed patients developed liver failure; FDA Advisory Committee estimated liver-failure incidence of 1 in 15,154 and overall liver mortality of 0.0035%/year. TZD class member; injury described as a signature injury incompatible with type 2 diabetes.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first glitazone-class drug, was launched in the USA in March 1997 and reached Europe later that year only to be withdrawn within weeks on the grounds of liver toxicity. It caused at least 90 cases of liver failure (70 resulting in death or transplantation) before it was withdrawn in March 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: First glitazone-class drug, launched in the USA in March 1997; withdrawn on grounds of liver toxicity; at least 90 cases of liver failure, 70 resulting in death or transplantation; withdrawn March 2000.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first thiazolidinedione approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in January 1997, was followed by numerous reports of severe liver injury and several published reports of acute liver failure. Clinically significant liver injury was estimated to occur in ~1:10,000 recipients, and the drug was withdrawn from the US market in March 2000. In combined North American clinical trials, ALT elevation >3x ULN occurred in 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients versus 0.6% of placebo recipients, and two troglitazone-treated patients had ALT >3x ULN plus total bilirubin >2x ULN consistent with Hy's law.
raw_record.extra_details: First thiazolidinedione approved in the US, licensed for type 2 diabetes January 1997; numerous reports of severe liver injury and published reports of acute liver failure; clinically significant liver injury estimated ~1:10,000 recipients; withdrawn from US market March 2000. Retrospective analysis of combined North American clinical trials: ALT>3x ULN in 1.9% (48/2510) vs 0.6% (3/475) placebo; ALT>10x ULN in 0.5% (none in placebo); ALT>20x ULN in 5 patients (0 placebo); peak ALT typically delayed to 3rd-7th months; treatment discontinued for abnormal liver tests in 20 patients (0.8%); 2 patients met Hy's law criteria; placebo group had higher incidence of any ALT elevation, possibly due to beneficial effect on steatosis.

raw_record.support_text: During the preclinical testing phase of troglitazone efficacy, approximately 1.9% of patients receiving troglitazone developed severe hepatic problems with elevated serum transaminase activities. In the severe cases, troglitazone caused fulminant hepatic failures, leading to multiple human deaths. Due to the severity of troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity and the availability of structural derivatives such as rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, troglitazone was removed from the market in 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Approximately 1.9% of patients developed severe hepatic problems with elevated serum transaminase activities; fulminant hepatic failures leading to multiple human deaths; removed from the market in 2000. Proposed mechanisms include electrophilic reactive intermediates, direct PPARγ binding, mitochondrial injury, and BSEP inhibition by troglitazone (paragraphs 0 and 4); a chromane-containing glitazone predicted as an apoptotic agonist activating p53 via the intrinsic pathway, confirmed by immunoblot.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first derivative of the thiazolidinedione family, was withdrawn from the market in 2000. It induced several cases of fatal acute liver injury with massive hepatic cytolysis, cholestasis and microvesicular steatosis in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone is the first thiazolidinedione derivative, withdrawn from the market in 2000. Reported injury comprised fatal acute liver injury with massive hepatic cytolysis, cholestasis and microvesicular steatosis. Antidiabetic agent.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man contracted severe hepatitis 2 months after troglitazone was started for type 2 diabetes; the liver damage progressed after drug withdrawal, became fulminant, and the patient died 8 weeks after onset. Autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis and cholestasis with inflammatory cell infiltration. A positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for troglitazone indicated the liver damage was mediated by hypersensitivity to troglitazone.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~2 months after starting troglitazone; disease progressed after withdrawal; death occurred 8 weeks after onset of liver damage. Positive drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test for troglitazone; hypersensitivity-mediated mechanism. Autopsy: massive hepatic necrosis and cholestasis with inflammatory cell infiltration. Reported as the first autopsy case of troglitazone-induced fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Histological examination of the liver showed a marked periportal acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate with increased eosinophils and lobular hepatocyte necrosis, consistent with a severe drug-induced hepatitis. Skin biopsy showed toxic epidermal necrolysis and lymph node features were consistent with phenytoin-induced pseudolymphoma, all attributed to the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Case presented with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, leucocytosis, eosinophilia, toxic epidermal necrolysis and hypersensitivity myocarditis. Phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome typically onsets 3 weeks to 3 months after initiation of therapy and is more common in blacks. Drug-induced hepatitis with or without hepatocyte necrosis is a potentially fatal complication carrying a mortality of up to 50%. Liver histology showed periportal acute and chronic inflammation with eosinophils and lobular hepatocyte necrosis. The patient died and autopsy revealed Alzheimer's disease, amyloid angiopathy, extracellular amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles and Hirano bodies. Cross-reactivity with other aromatic anticonvulsants (phenobarbital, carbamazepine) has been reported in patients with a history of phenytoin hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old African-American woman with Alzheimer's disease was prescribed phenytoin 100 mg three times daily after two seizures. Four weeks after starting the drug she was hospitalized with high fever, confusion, altered mental status, and a diffuse maculopapular pruritic rash. Laboratory values showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (peak 96 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (peak 77 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (peak 521 IU/L), and eosinophilia, consistent with an anticonvulsant hypersensitivity reaction with hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) in a 73-year-old woman; onset ~4 weeks after starting phenytoin 100 mg 3 times/day. AHS features included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, and laboratory abnormalities with eosinophilia (eosinophils up to 19%). Selected laboratory values: AST up to 96 IU/L, ALT up to 77 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase up to 521 IU/L, total bilirubin <1 mg/dl, phenytoin level 11.7 µg/ml on admission. Phenytoin was discontinued on hospital day 3 as the rash persisted and elevated eosinophils indicated an allergic drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, phenytoin was implicated in 10 of 137 (7.3%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Tied with valproate at 10 of 137 non-APAP cases (7.3%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 100 individual case reports; median age 28 y; 53 female/47 male; median treatment duration 4 weeks; HC 36%, Cs/mixed 64%; highest incidence of peripheral and hepatic eosinophilia of the studied drugs (peripheral present in 77%, 81/100 reported; hepatic present in 72%, 43/100 reported); hepatic necrosis 31%; inflammatory reaction 89%; death or liver transplant 13%; liver biopsy reported in 50/100 cases.

raw_record.support_text: There were 9 DILI cases due to phenytoin alone. The mean age of these patients was 37.2 yr (median 39, range 2–70), only 2 (22.2%) occurred in children, there was an equal proportion of men and women, and 4 (44%) required hospitalization. The most frequent ICD-9-CM code was 573.3 whereas 3 patients had 572.8.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 DILI cases due to phenytoin alone; mean age 37.2 yr (median 39, range 2–70); only 2 (22.2%) in children; equal men/women; 4 (44%) required hospitalization; most frequent code 573.3, 3 patients had 572.8.

raw_record.support_text: The ILIAD reliability study enrolled its first 40 patients including five cases of phenytoin hepatotoxicity. The paper describes these as cases of drug-induced liver injury used to test RUCAM causality score reliability.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 40 DILI cases in the ILIAD study cohort; patients with a diagnosis of phenytoin hepatotoxicity. Cohort-wide median time to onset was 42.5 days, 73% hospitalized, 15% overall required liver transplantation (not drug-specific).

raw_record.support_text: Our patient presented approximately four weeks after beginning phenytoin therapy with physical signs and laboratory findings consistent with an acute inflammatory reaction and severe liver dysfunction, typical of the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by fever, exanthems, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, lymphadenopathy, and leukocytosis with eosinophilia, and usually begins within six weeks of the onset of phenytoin therapy if there has been no prior exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome with an acute inflammatory reaction and severe liver dysfunction; syndrome usually begins within six weeks of therapy onset, has no sex or age predilection, and at increased risk in blacks, patients with prior reactions who are reexposed, and those who continue drug after unrecognized hypersensitivity. Mechanism attributed to allergic hypersensitivity (no dose linearity, induction period, recurrence on rechallenge) via direct antigen/hapten action, altered lymphocyte function, or toxic arene-oxide metabolites from reduced epoxide hydrolase detoxification; some patients have circulating IgG antibodies without proven causation. Reported morphologic types of hepatic injury include active and chronic hepatitis, granulomatous hepatitis, mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic hepatitis, submassive and massive necrosis, with fatty infiltration, monocyte/eosinophil infiltration, necrotizing vasculitis; mortality estimated at 30-40%, mostly from massive or submassive necrosis. Our patient's liver function tests peaked on days 3-5 and then decreased; rash and hepatosplenomegaly resolved after drug discontinuation with supportive prednisone tapering; intradermal phenytoin skin test weakly positive and phenytoin stimulation test negative; patient later placed on mexiletine. This is the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome rather than the false phenytoin labeling in the entity list.

raw_record.support_text: Of the neuropsychiatric drugs, phenytoin use (eight cases) was frequent among causes of drug-induced liver injury acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases; rash occurred in four phenytoin cases, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome was caused by phenytoin in one subject.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients died of hepatic failure; both had massive hepatic necrosis induced by phenytoin and chlorpropamide respectively. The remaining 51 patients recovered clinically and biochemically after a mean interval of 63 days.
raw_record.extra_details: One of two fatal cases in the study; massive hepatic necrosis with death from hepatic failure. Also listed in the morphological table under massive/submassive necrosis and under hepatocanalicular cholestatic injury, indicating varied reactions.

raw_record.support_text: Anticonvulsants were the most common offending drugs (21 of 27 definite DRESS/DIHS cases; 77.7%). Phenytoin was the most common individual drug (12 cases; 44.4%), followed by carbamazepine (8 cases; 29.6%). Other drugs such as allopurinol, dapsone, and nevirapine were also identified. Hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement, present in 23 patients (85.1%), with ALT (mean ± SD) 569 ± 911.5 U/L and AST 474 ± 743.0 U/L.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenytoin identified as culprit drug in 12 of 27 definite RegiSCAR-scored DRESS/DIHS cases (44.4%); most common indications were epilepsy and prophylaxis after neurological surgery or cranioencephalic trauma; hepatitis with elevated ALT/AST was the most common visceral involvement (23/27 patients, 85.1%) in this cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 4 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of severe phenytoin hepatitis in a patient with seizures who initially presented with fever, pharyngitis, rash, and atypical lymphocytosis resembling infectious mononucleosis. After phenytoin was stopped she was inadvertently rechallenged with 1 g of intravenous phenytoin, which was followed by nausea, abdominal pain, edema, exfoliative dermatitis, markedly elevated transaminases (peak SGOT 2900 U, SGPT 1530 U), rising bilirubin (peak 16.0 g/liter), prolonged prothrombin time, and hepatic coma, before recovery. Negative viral serologies and the response to rechallenge supported phenytoin reaction as the etiology. The authors also reviewed 44 additional adequately documented cases of phenytoin hepatitis, in which rash, eosinophilia, and jaundice were typical.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: initial presentation mimicked infectious mononucleosis (fever, pharyngitis, malaise, mild hepatitis, atypical lymphocytosis). Inadvertent rechallenge with 1 g IV phenytoin produced nausea, abdominal pain, facial/oral edema, and severe hepatic necrosis; laboratory findings on day 3 post-rechallenge: total bilirubin 5.6 g/liter, SGOT 2355 U, SGPT 1530 U, alkaline phosphatase 267 IU; peak SGOT 2900 U and SGPT 1530 U on Jan 18; total bilirubin reached 16.0 g/liter with prothrombin time 20.4/11.8 sec and arterial NH3 144 mg; lapsed into hepatic coma, then recovered with resolution of liver tests. Viral serologies and cultures (CSF, blood, urine, cervix) negative, including monospot, EBV titers, ANA, HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HAV-IgM, toxoplasmosis, Brucella, tularemia, and CMV. Authors reviewed 44 additional adequately documented phenytoin hepatitis cases plus this one (45 total); in that series morbiliform rash 90%, exfoliative rash 44%, eosinophilia 56%, jaundice 88%, leukocytosis 70%, lymphadenopathy 70%. Phenytoin was stopped on admission; discharged on valproic acid for seizure disorder.

raw_record.support_text: In comparative monotherapy studies, none of the valproate-treated patients developed evidence of hepatotoxicity, but one patient in the authors' study (Turnbull et al., 1985) and one patient in the study by Wilder et al. (1983) experienced phenytoin-induced hepatitis that necessitated discontinuation of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Two separately reported patients (one from Turnbull et al., 1985, and one from Wilder et al., 1983) developed phenytoin-induced hepatitis in comparative epilepsy monotherapy studies; the hepatitis necessitated discontinuation of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: High-confidence DILI cases due to phenytoin (n=17) from the DILIN prospective and retrospective studies were analyzed for HLA risk alleles. DILI due to phenytoin was associated with HLA-A*68:01 in European-ancestry individuals (n=9, OR=8.4, 95% CI 2.7-21.8, P=0.001, FDR=0.03) and with HLA-B*53:01 in African Americans (n=8, OR=8.4, 95% CI 3.2-22.8, P=2.7x10^-5, FDR=0.0009).
raw_record.extra_details: High-confidence DILI cases (n=17 total; n=9 EA and n=8 AA analyzed) from DILIN prospective and retrospective studies. Novel population-specific HLA risk alleles identified: HLA-A*68:01 (EA, AF cases=0.22) and HLA-B*53:01 (AA, AF cases=0.56). Antiepileptic drug class.

raw_record.support_text: Phenytoin was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with seizures was changed to phenytoin 300 mg daily, with liver function tests normal prior to commencement. Six weeks after starting phenytoin she developed a generalised pruritic rash, dark urine, fever and malaise. On admission she was icteric and febrile with a confluent maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy and 8% eosinophilia; liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis with numerous well-formed granulomas, portal/periportal and focal lobular inflammation, and minimal hepatocytic degeneration with individual cellular necrosis. Phenytoin was ceased on admission and the patient made a slow clinical and biochemical recovery, with temperature and liver function tests returning to normal, implicating phenytoin as the cause of the granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Anticonvulsant given at 300 mg/day for seizures; latency of about 6 weeks. Admission labs: bilirubin 41 µmol/l (<17), ALP 639 u/l (100-350), AST 212 u/l (6-42); 8% eosinophilia; transient atypical lymphocytosis (14%, 1792 x 10^6/l). Liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis (granulomata with giant/epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, few eosinophils, no necrosis or caseation), portal/periportal and focal lobular inflammation. Dechallenge: phenytoin ceased on admission with gradual clinical and biochemical recovery (temperature normal by day 8, liver function tests by day 25); no recurrence at 12-week follow-up after restarting methylphenobarbitone. Serology negative for hepatitis A/B, toxoplasma, CMV and streptococcus; negative antimitochondrial antibodies. Reported phenotype: granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: An asymptomatic 52-year-old woman who received phenytoin sodium for 11 years was found to have elevated serum aminotransferases; assays for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative and a liver biopsy showed chronic persistent hepatitis. The authors report this as documentation of phenytoin-induced chronic persistent hepatitis, proven by histology and with its etiology confirmed by drug withdrawal and by rechallenge with phenytoin.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old woman; phenytoin sodium for 11 years; asymptomatic with elevated serum aminotransferases; negative serology for hepatitis A, B, and C; liver biopsy showed chronic persistent hepatitis; etiology confirmed by drug withdrawal and rechallenge with phenytoin (phenytoin therapy alone). Phenytoin had previously been associated with acute hepatotoxicity, with chronic liver enzyme abnormalities attributed to enzyme induction and no prior reports of chronic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Six years earlier the same patient developed cholestatic hepatitis to flucloxacillin; she had been diagnosed with flucloxacillin-induced hepatitis when she presented with jaundice and pruritus.
raw_record.extra_details: Episode 6 years earlier, presenting with jaundice and pruritus; predominantly obstructive picture: bilirubin 178 µmol/L (NR 3–18), alkaline phosphatase 312 U/L (NR 60–119), AST 59 U/L (NR 12–36), ALT 150 U/L (NR 5–40), GGT 238 U/L (NR 6–65). Hepatitis A/B/C serologies negative, ultrasound showed no calculi or intrahepatic bile duct dilatation; no biopsy; liver tests gradually returned to normal. Reported hepatitis frequency in Australia 1:10,000 to 1:100,000 prescriptions.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of drug-induced liver injury, flucloxacillin was one of the most common antibiotics responsible, with eight of 77 DILI cases. Among the flucloxacillin-attributed cases the injury was predominantly cholestatic (seven cases) with one mixed case, and seven of the cases were associated with jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: Eight of 77 DILI cases; causality held via highest International Consensus Criteria score. Pattern distribution 7 cholestatic/1 mixed; duration of treatment median 10 (2-21) days; time to biochemical resolution median 120 (2-540) days with some chronic courses. Seven jaundice cases detailed (bilirubin 2.3-11.2 ULN).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin accounted for 7 of 28 cases (25%) of drug-induced jaundice presenting to the Jaundice Hotline after application of consensus criteria for DILI. Flucloxacillin cases were mostly cholestatic (6/7) with the remainder mixed, more common in women (M:F 2:5), mean age 76 years, with mean time to normalization of liver function tests of 49 days.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 28 DIJ cases (25%); annual incidence of flucloxacillin-induced jaundice 3.2 per million in Cornwall vs 0.6 per million national CSM rate; jaundice onset on average at 20.4 days (range 7–40); marked jaundice, mean peak bilirubin 267 µmol/l; cholestatic pattern in 6/7, mixed in remainder; M:F 2:5; mean age 76 (range 56–81); prescribed mainly for cellulitis (6/7) or one breast abscess.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 36 individual case reports; median age 54 y; 24 female/12 male; median treatment duration 2 weeks; HC 11%, Cs/mixed 89%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 21% (24/36 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 31% (26/36 reported); hepatic necrosis 7%; inflammatory reaction 50%; death or liver transplant 14%; liver biopsy reported in 29/36 cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman (Table 2) had flucloxacillin as the drug associated with the first DILI (treatment duration 10 days, presentation with jaundice, cholestatic pattern). At follow-up 48 months later she had persistent cholestatic-pattern liver test abnormalities not explained by alternative diagnoses: ALT 1.04 × ULN and GGT 4.6 × ULN, but no jaundice and no itching.
raw_record.extra_details: First DILI treatment duration 10 days; presentation with jaundice and cholestatic pattern; follow-up 48 months. Persistent unexplained abnormalities at follow-up: ALT 1.04 × ULN, GGT 4.6 × ULN; no jaundice or itching.

raw_record.support_text: Seven individuals with DILI exposed to co-amoxiclav in addition to flucloxacillin and 16 recently recruited individuals with flucloxacillin DILI were genotyped for HLA-B*5701 for replication; 20 of these 23 additional subjects (87%) were HLA-B*5701 positive (P = 6.62 × 10^-13). The paper is a genome-wide association study of a human DILI cohort that treats flucloxacillin-induced liver injury as an established clinical entity, additionally reporting that HLA-B*5701 did not correlate with pattern of injury and that four subjects with low ICC causality scores were all HLA-B*5701 positive.
raw_record.extra_details: Genome-wide association study of flucloxacillin DILI. Causality supported by Hill causality/HLA cohort with ICC causality scores (four subjects had low ICC scores). HLA-B*5701 genotype did not correlate with pattern of injury. Only 1 in every 500-1000 HLA-B*5701 carriers develops DILI when treated with flucloxacillin; population attributable fraction (PAF) of HLA-B*5701 estimated at 0.64. Additional genetic factors suspected; a chromosome 3 SNP (rs10937275) reached P = 1.4 × 10^-8 (allelic OR = 4.1, minor allele frequency 0.29 vs 0.09) in 48 risk-allele-carrying cases. Most subjects (65%) had at least one extrahepatic manifestation; no common CNV associated with DILI. Co-amoxiclav exposure was present in some subjects as a co-medication.

raw_record.support_text: Daly et al. identified HLA-B*5701 as a potent risk factor for drug-induced liver injury (DILI) owing to flucloxacillin, based on the DILIGEN study of 51 cases and 289 controls. The accompanying table further lists flucloxacillin-DILI associations with HLA-B*5701 (odds ratio 81, PPV 91%, NPV 88%) and TNF-α (-238G/A) (odds ratio 31).
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*5701 identified as a potent risk factor for flucloxacillin DILI from the DILIGEN study (51 cases, 289 controls; OR 81, PPV 91%, NPV 88%); additional reported associations for flucloxacillin DILI include TNF-α (-238G/A) (OR 31) and HLA-DRB1*0107-DQB1*0103 (OR 17).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin is a narrow-spectrum β-lactam antibiotic of the penicillin class used for Gram-positive infections. The incidence of flucloxacillin-induced hepatotoxicity in the UK is 8.5 per 100,000 patients in days 1 to 45 during treatment. A GWA study with 51 flucloxacillin DILI cases and 282 controls identified HLA-B*5701 as a major genetic risk factor (OR=80.6, P=9.0 x 10^-19), although only 1 in every 500 to 1,000 individuals with this genotype develops flucloxacillin-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Narrow-spectrum β-lactam penicillin for Gram-positive bacterial infections. Incidence 8.5 per 100,000 in the UK during days 1-45 of treatment. HLA-B*5701 GWA study: 51 DILI cases vs 282 controls, OR=80.6, P=9.0x10^-19; allele common in Northern Europe, rare in Africa/Asia; only 1 in 500-1,000 carriers develop hepatotoxicity; no significant difference in disease severity between HLA-B*5701-negative and carrier individuals.

raw_record.support_text: Table 2 lists flucloxacillin among the most common drugs implicated in DILI (75/9.6% of the discovery cohort; absent from the US replication cohort). The MHC risk allele rs2395029 for flucloxacillin-DILI is used as a covariate.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 75 (9.6%) of 783 discovery cases; 0 in the replication cohort. Known high-impact MHC DILI risk allele rs2395029 used as covariate. An additional 8 discovery cases were co-implicated with amoxicillin/clavulanate.

raw_record.support_text: PBMCs were isolated from six patients who developed cholestatic liver injury following flucloxacillin therapy to characterize the drug-specific T-cell response. PBMC activation with flucloxacillin was detected in five patients (including one HLA-B*57:01-negative individual). Flucloxacillin-responsive CD8+ T-cell clones from four HLA-B*57:01 ELISpot-positive patients and CD4+ clones (in low numbers) were isolated; activation was concentration-dependent and provoked IFN-γ and cytolytic molecule secretion. The authors conclude that immune phenomena contribute to the development of flucloxacillin-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic liver injury phenotype. Six patients with DILI following therapy; five showed PBMC activation (including one HLA-B*57:01-negative patient). Flucloxacillin-responsive CD8+ clones restricted by HLA-B*57:01 and HLA-B*58:01; clones expressed CCR2, CCR4, CCR9, CXCR3. Concentration-dependent activation, peak serum ~60 μM, estimated achievable liver concentration ~100 μM. Clones secreted IFN-γ, granzyme B, FasL, perforin. Flucloxacillin-responsive clones were not activated by abacavir. In p:47 responses were dependent on MHC class I (anti-HLA class I blocking antibody inhibited activation).

raw_record.support_text: The review describes a landmark genome-wide association study of flucloxacillin-induced liver injury, a drug mostly associated with cholestasis. Direct genotyping for HLA-B*5701 in 51 cases and 63 drug-exposed controls revealed a strong relationship between this allele and flucloxacillin-induced liver injury (odds ratio 80.6), with the strongest GWAS association at rs2395029 in the major histocompatibility complex region.
raw_record.extra_details: Daly and colleagues' GWAS; strongest association rs2395029 in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*5701; HLA-B*5701 genotype in 51 cases and 63 drug-exposed controls OR 80.6. Additional SNPs (HLA-DRB1*0701, TNF rs361525, TNF rs1799964, HSPA1L rs2227956) were not independent of HLA-B*5701.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a semi-synthetic penicillin used for staphylococcal infection, has been known to be associated with cholestatic hepatitis with a prevalence of 10.3 per 100,000 new users in the United Kingdom. A GWAS of 866,399 SNPs in 51 flucloxacillin-related DILI cases vs 282 matched controls found the strongest association with rs2395029 (OR=45, P=8.7e-33), in complete linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B*57:01.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis attributed (prevalence 10.3 per 100,000 new users in the UK). GWAS: strongest association rs2395029 (in complete LD with HLA-B*57:01) OR=45 (P=8.7e-33); ORs vs tolerant controls 80.6 (51 exploration cases) and 100 (23 replication cases); other HLA-region SNPs (e.g., TNF rs361525) not significant after conditioning on HLA-B*57:01; HLA-B*57:01 frequency 0.01–0.03 in Northern Europeans but <0.001 in Japanese; not approved in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: The strongest single risk factor for idiosyncratic DILI is the association of the HLA-B*5701 genotype in flucloxacillin-induced DILI. A GWAS on well-defined European and North American cases of flucloxacillin-induced DILI found HLA-B*5701 associated with an odds ratio of 80.6; because flucloxacillin-induced DILI is rare, the estimated absolute risk for genotype carriers treated with flucloxacillin was only 1 in 500-1000.
raw_record.extra_details: GWAS on well-defined European/North American flucloxacillin-induced DILI cases; HLA-B*5701 odds ratio 80.6; absolute risk for HLA-B*5701 carriers about 1 in every 500-1000 individuals treated with flucloxacillin.

raw_record.support_text: Patient B, a 53-year-old female, developed DILI with jaundice and pruritus one week after a 3-week course of flucloxacillin. Liver histology showed mild portal inflammation, portal fibrosis, ductopenia, and extensive cholestasis compatible with flucloxacillin-induced liver injury. She had persistent hepatocellular secretory failure and responded to rifampicin 300 mg daily.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and pruritus began 1 week after a 3-week flucloxacillin course; bilirubin 278 µmol/L, AP 298 U/L, γGT 39 U/L, AST 43, ALT 51; AMA positive, ANA/ANCA negative; histology showed ductopenia and portal fibrosis; treated with rifampicin 300 mg od for 4 weeks followed by budesonide; incomplete biochemical recovery possibly due to ductopenia.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients with flucloxacillin-induced and amoxicillin-clavulanate-induced liver injury were enrolled from the DILIGEN (Pharmacogenetics of drug induced liver injury) study. Causality assessment used the Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment method (RUCAM), and HLA types were determined for the patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients with flucloxacillin-induced liver injury were enrolled from the DILIGEN (Pharmacogenetics of drug induced liver injury) study; causality was assessed with the Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment method (RUCAM). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were cultured with flucloxacillin to generate drug-specific T-cell clones and to prime naive T cells from healthy donors.

raw_record.support_text: The background states that the antibiotic flucloxacillin is an established cause of liver injury, with age over 60, prolonged use, and gender identified as possible risk factors. A population-based cohort study using UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink data (1,046,696 people; 861,959 exposed to flucloxacillin) compared flucloxacillin against oxytetracycline and reported a 45-day risk of laboratory-confirmed liver injury of 6.15 per 100,000 users (95% CI 4.61-8.04), 14.15 per 100,000 for symptom-defined injury, and a multivariable-adjusted rate ratio of 3.79 (95% CI 1.19-12.13).
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort study, UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 1 Jan 2000 - 1 Jan 2012, 1,046,696 people (861,959 exposed). Compared against oxytetracycline. 45-day risk of laboratory-confirmed injury 6.15 per 100,000 users (95% CI 4.61-8.04); symptom-defined injury 14.15 per 100,000 (95% CI 11.75-16.90); multivariable adjusted rate ratio 3.79 (95% CI 1.19-12.13). Highest risk subgroup: age 70+ with more than two consecutive prescriptions (72.78 per 100,000 users, 95% CI 19.87-185.96). Background risk factors: age over 60, prolonged use, gender.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a β-lactam antibiotic used as first-line treatment for Staphylococcal infections, causes drug-induced cholestatic liver injury with an incidence of 8.5 per 100,000 patients and delayed onset of clinical symptoms 1-45 days after starting therapy (and 1.8 per 100,000 following 46-90 days). The cholestasis involves bile duct injury and Vanishing Bile Duct Syndrome (ductopenia); an immune-mediated response with a genetic pre-disposition is generally accepted to account for the DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: β-lactam antibiotic, first-line for Staphylococcal infections; cholestatic liver injury incidence 8.5 per 100,000 patients, delayed onset of clinical symptoms 1-45 days and 1.8 per 100,000 for 46-90 days after starting therapy; cholestasis with bile duct injury and Vanishing Bile Duct Syndrome (ductopenia); small amounts form metabolites via CYP3A4, possibly under genetic control; generally accepted immune-mediated response with genetic predisposition; mechanism 5.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin-induced DILI is studied as an established clinical entity. A genome-wide association study showed that 84.3% of patients with flucloxacillin-induced DILI carry the HLA-B*57:01 genotype, with an 80-fold increased risk (OR 80.6, 95% CI 22.8-284.9), though this yields low positive predictive value because most HLA-B*57:01 carriers treated with flucloxacillin do not develop DILI. Female sex, age over 60 years, and treatment duration longer than 2 weeks have previously been proposed as additional risk factors, and this retrospective case-control study aims to validate and identify new clinical risk factors for flucloxacillin-induced DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: A genome-wide association study showed that 84.3% of patients with flucloxacillin-induced DILI carry HLA-B*57:01 (OR 80.6, 95% CI 22.8-284.9), an 80-fold increased risk; the association implies low positive predictive value because most treated HLA-B*57:01 carriers do not develop DILI. Previously proposed risk factors include female sex, age older than 60 years, and treatment duration longer than 2 weeks. The study is a retrospective case-control study using the SWEDEGENE database of suspected ADR cases (1990-2016) collected from the Swedish MPA spontaneous ADR reports, with TWINGENE controls.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of mixed hepatotoxicity due to flucloxacillin that caused prolonged hospitalization and comprehensive etiological study. Despite the moderate to severe analytical presentation and histological findings indicative of poor prognosis, there was favorable evolution, without clinical evidence of coagulopathy or encephalopathy; analytical normalization was slow, with progression to chronicity. Studies associating the HLA-B*5701 allele with susceptibility to flucloxacillin toxicity have been reported in the literature.
raw_record.extra_details: Flucloxacillin hepatotoxicity is rare and classified as idiosyncratic, dependent on individual susceptibility, unpredictable and dose-independent. Case presented with moderate to severe analytical presentation and histological findings indicative of poor prognosis, favorable evolution without coagulopathy or encephalopathy, slow analytical normalization with progression to chronicity, and prolonged hospitalization requiring comprehensive etiological study. HLA-B*5701 allele has been associated with susceptibility to flucloxacillin toxicity in the literature.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies HLA-B*5701 as associated with flucloxacillin-induced drug-induced liver injury (DILI). A single study (Daly et al., 2009) met inclusion criteria, comprising 51 DILI cases and 64 tolerant controls, reporting 84.3% sensitivity and 93.8% specificity for the HLA-B*5701 test, with low PPV (0.11%), high NPV (99.99%), an incidence of 0.000085, and a number needed to genotype (NNG) of 13,953.
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*5701 pharmacogenetic association; Daly et al. (2009) case-control study with 51 DILI cases + 64 tolerant controls; sensitivity 84.3%, specificity 93.8%, PPV 0.0011 (0.11%), NPV 0.9999 (99.99%), incidence 0.000085, NNG 13,953.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 294 human DILI cases, flucloxacillin was causal in 79 cases (26.9%), one of the two most frequently implicated drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Causal in 79 of 294 DILI cases (26.9%); second most frequently implicated drug. In the flucloxacillin subgroup, higher bilirubin at onset was associated with prolonged recovery time, whereas longer time to DILI onset was not.

raw_record.support_text: A table of the top 48 drugs worldwide causing idiosyncratic DILI with verified causality assessed by RUCAM lists flucloxacillin with 130 RUCAM-based DILI cases, categorized as a CYP substrate (CYP+), referenced to Dekker (91).
raw_record.extra_details: 130 RUCAM-verified DILI cases; CYP substrate (CYP+); HLA pharmacogenetic associations also noted in some patients (p32).

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin was one of the most commonly implicated conventional drugs in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry, adjudicated as the single cause of liver injury in 23 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 adjudicated single-cause cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry; ATC J01CF05; over 90% of cases came from the United Kingdom.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists flucloxacillin as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 8 conferring a probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 8, probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [20].

raw_record.support_text: In the described flucloxacillin cohort, three patients experienced acute kidney injury, but the paper explicitly reports that there were no cases of hepatotoxicity or haematological side effects (neutropenia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) observed during flucloxacillin treatment, including in the three acute kidney injury cases.
raw_record.extra_details: No cases of hepatotoxicity were observed during flucloxacillin outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT); adverse events reported included acute kidney injury in three patients, axillary vein thrombosis in one, maculopapular rash in one, and other non-hepatic events.

raw_record.support_text: Eleven cases of hepatic injury were attributed to the intake of flucloxacillin and reported to the Netherlands Center for Monitoring of Adverse Reactions to Drugs between 1982 and 1992. The biochemical pattern was compatible with cholestatic hepatitis in seven cases, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury in one, hepatocellular pattern in two, and mild liver enzyme elevations in one. Two patients died, one from fatal bleeding from the liver after biopsy and one from combined hepatic and cardiac failure; the rest recovered. In paragraph 9, the causal relationship was assessed as 'probable' in eight cases and 'possible' in three.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven patients (4 men, 7 women; mean age 57 years) treated for staphylococcal infection; oral flucloxacillin 1500-4000 mg/day for 2-28 days; symptoms appeared about 10-30 days after start. Causal relationship 'probable' in 8 cases (no. 1-8) and 'possible' in 3 (no. 9-11) using temporal-relationship plus exclusion-of-other-causes criteria. Biochemical patterns: cholestatic hepatitis in 7, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular in 1, hepatocellular in 2, mild liver enzyme elevations in 1; peripheral eosinophilia in 3; autoantibodies absent; hepatitis A/B (and some C), CMV, and infectious mononucleosis serologically excluded; extrahepatic cholestasis excluded by ultrasonography. Histology in 7 cases showed cholestatic hepatitis in 5 (with cholangitis/cholangiolitis in 4), centrilobular cholestasis with bridging fibrosis, and portal-central bridging necrosis in the others. Two deaths: fatal liver bleeding after biopsy, and combined hepatic and cardiac failure; survivors recovered on average 72 days (range 17-180) after peak aminotransferases. Case 4 developed injury on three occasions after flucloxacillin; her second-biopsy hepatocellular damage had initially been attributed to ranitidine and diclofenac before flucloxacillin causality was recognized. Nine patients used other drugs concurrently but, except case 11, continued them without recurrent injury.

raw_record.support_text: The study found 10 cases of cholestatic hepatitis of uncertain origin diagnosed within 45 days of receiving flucloxacillin that were characteristic of or consistent with a syndrome recently described as associated with this drug. The conclusion states that flucloxacillin is a likely cause of cholestatic hepatitis, with the risk estimated at 7.6 per 100,000 users (95% confidence interval, 3.6-13.9).
raw_record.extra_details: Epidemiologic study; 10 cases of cholestatic hepatitis diagnosed within 45 days of flucloxacillin and 1 case 46-90 days after prescription. Risk estimate 7.6 per 100,000 users (95% CI 3.6-13.9). Cholestatic hepatitis with deep jaundice, highly elevated bilirubin, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and prolonged recovery; onset within a few weeks of starting therapy and possibly up to two or three weeks after completion. ADRAC spontaneous reports accumulated from 17 to 73-77 cases of flucloxacillin-associated liver toxicity. Flucloxacillin is a semi-synthetic penicillinase-resistant penicillin indicated for suspected staphylococcal infections.

raw_record.support_text: Among the patients with non-alcoholic liver disease controls, one patient had flucloxacillin hepatotoxicity characterized by pruritus and jaundice beginning soon after drug treatment started, with bilirubin reaching a peak over 200 µmol/l and jaundice resolving gradually after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient with flucloxacillin hepatotoxicity presenting with pruritus and jaundice soon after start of treatment; bilirubin peaked above 200 µmol/l; jaundice resolved gradually after drug discontinuation; patient enrolled in the drug-induced hepatotoxicity subset of the non-alcoholic liver disease control group.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes flucloxacillin as a cause of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis in humans, describing 30 individual case reports of cholestasis across twelve publications. Most patients were women (77%) with a mean age of 61, predominant symptoms being jaundice (95%) and pruritus (77%), and characteristic biochemical abnormalities of elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase. The authors add flucloxacillin to the list of drugs responsible for the vanishing bile duct syndrome, an established cause of protracted severe cholestasis, and note fibrosis in one case and cirrhosis in another.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 individual case reports in twelve publications; predominantly women (77%), mean age 61; symptoms jaundice (95%), pruritus (77%), dark urine, pale faeces, nausea, abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, lethargy, anorexia, weight loss; pruritus refractory to prednisone, cholestyramine, antihistamines, phenobarbitone; elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma glutamyl transferase with lesser aminotransferase elevations. Onset after cessation of flucloxacillin in 68% (mean 16.6 days, range 1-42); course averaging ~11 weeks; LFTs abnormal after symptoms in 42% for ~5 more weeks; one case of severe cholestasis persisting >7 years after an 18-day course. Pathology: moderate to severe cholestatic hepatitis with centrilobular bile stasis with canalicular dilatation, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, mild to moderate fatty infiltration, interlobular bile duct damage (oedema, degenerate epithelium, duct disappearance); vanishing bile duct syndrome attribution; fibrosis in one case; cirrhosis in another. First flucloxacillin-induced hepatitis case reported 1982; data from literature, Australia spontaneous ADR reporting, and WHO Collaborative Centre for International Drug Monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that during the first year tolcapone was marketed, a fulminant and fatal hepatopathy was documented in 3 patients, with an estimated 60,000 patients having received tolcapone by the time of the third fatal hepatopathy. Because of this hepatotoxicity, tolcapone was relegated to a secondary-choice adjunctive therapy, with pharmaceutical-company directives requiring monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase values at baseline and at regular intervals during treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant and fatal hepatopathy documented in 3 patients during tolcapone's first year on the market; estimated 60,000 exposed by the time of the third fatal case (suggesting a rare problem). Tolcapone relegated to secondary-choice adjunctive therapy.
