Pharma directives mandate monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase at baseline, every 2 weeks for the first year, every 4 weeks for the next 6 months, and every 2 months thereafter. Context: adjunctive treatment of levodopa-related fluctuations in Parkinson's disease.

raw_record.support_text: Three deaths due to fulminant hepatitis were reported in 1998 among tolcapone-treated patients. The deaths prompted a black box warning in the United States along with stricter liver monitoring guidelines. A postmarketing surveillance analysis later found no deaths among 1725 patients treated with tolcapone for up to 2 years or longer, and transaminase elevations were rare and transient, which led the FDA to relax hepatic enzyme monitoring guidelines in February 2006.
raw_record.extra_details: Three deaths due to fulminant hepatitis reported in 1998 among tolcapone-treated patients; prompted a black box warning in the US and stricter liver monitoring guidelines (Olanow and Tasmar Advisory Panel 2000). A postmarketing surveillance analysis reported no deaths among 1725 patients treated for up to 2 years or longer, with rare and transient transaminase elevations (Lew and Kricorian 2007). FDA relaxed hepatic enzyme monitoring in February 2006: ALT/AST every 2-4 weeks for first 6 months then at clinically relevant intervals, discontinue if AST/ALT exceeds 2x ULN (prior label was stricter); EU monitoring requirements unchanged. Proposed mechanism involves uncoupling of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation reducing ATP generation at concentrations higher than those needed to inhibit COMT (Borges 2005). Used as adjunctive therapy with levodopa/carbidopa for Parkinson's disease.

raw_record.support_text: After about one year of clinical use, tolcapone was found to induce liver toxicity among parkinsonian patients, with three fatal cases reported within a short time span. In 1998 tolcapone was withdrawn from the European Union and Canadian markets due to liver problems, and it was later reintroduced in the EU with use limited in both the EU and USA and liver function monitoring required.
raw_record.extra_details: Three fatal cases reported within a short time span (~1 year after clinical use began). Withdrawn from EU and Canadian markets in 1998 due to liver problems, later reintroduced in EU with use limited in both EU and USA with liver function monitoring. In clinical trials raised ALT or AST >3× ULN was reported in about 2–3% of patients, usually within the first 3 months and latest by 6 months; elevations were transient and returned to normal after discontinuation. Diarrhea was the most frequent non-dopaminergic reason for withdrawal (developed usually during first 3 months).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that potential hepatotoxicity is the most serious safety issue associated with COMT inhibitors and that liver toxicity has been observed with tolcapone. In clinical trials elevations of liver enzyme levels were reported for 1-3% of tolcapone-treated patients, and soon after tolcapone's market introduction four cases of fulminant liver failure were reported, three of which resulted in death, in patients who had received tolcapone for 2-4 months. These reports led to a temporary withdrawal of tolcapone from the market in Europe and Canada and a black box warning in the USA; tolcapone was later reintroduced in the EU and now requires prior failure of other COMT inhibitors and regular liver enzyme monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: COMT inhibitor used to treat Parkinson disease. Liver enzyme elevations in 1-3% of treated patients in clinical trials; four cases of fulminant liver failure reported soon after market introduction, three fatal, after 2-4 months of treatment. Led to temporary European/Canadian market withdrawal and US black box warning; reintroduced in EU with requirement to try other COMT inhibitors first and regular liver enzyme monitoring. Mechanism open, possibly uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation or toxic metabolite accumulation in genetically prone patients; less likely COMT inhibition per se since not seen with entacapone.

raw_record.support_text: The COMT inhibitor tolcapone is an effective adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients. In clinical trials, elevated liver enzymes were notable in tolcapone-treated patients and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme testing as a condition for drug approval. After approximately one year on the market, three cases of fatal hepatotoxicity and one case of reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. Later reports described three additional cases of severe hepatocellular liver injury (including one with hepatocellular jaundice, one after 3 years of treatment, and one developing 17 months after starting), as well as less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST elevations three times the upper limit of normal; the majority of these elevations were transient, asymptomatic, and resolved spontaneously (median time to elevation 81 days, median duration 22 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients with Parkinson disease. Clinical trials showed elevated liver enzymes, and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme monitoring as a condition of approval. After ~1 year on market, three fatal hepatotoxicity cases and one reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. In these four cases recommended liver-monitoring guidelines were not followed, and in two cases the drug was continued despite clear clinical evidence of hepatic dysfunction. Consequence: 7-year marketing suspension in Europe and Canada and a US black box warning; tolcapone currently carries a black box warning in all countries on the risk of hepatotoxicity. Over a decade later, no further tolcapone-induced hepatic fatalities, but three additional reports of severe hepatocellular injury: one case of hepatocellular jaundice (duration unknown), one severe hepatocellular injury after 3 years, one developing hepatotoxicity 17 months after starting. Olanow and Watkins reported less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST three times ULN; majority transient, asymptomatic, spontaneously resolved; median time to elevated levels 81 days, median duration 22 days.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that COMT inhibitors harbor the potential for liver toxicity, and that in the case of tolcapone—but not entacapone—this constitutes a safety risk. Following tolcapone's market authorization in 1997, three patients died from acute liver failure, which led to withdrawal of the drug from the European market; after further safety evaluations it was re-approved in 2004, and it is now considered a second-choice COMT inhibitor for advanced Parkinson's disease with fluctuations, with regular liver enzyme monitoring mandated.
raw_record.extra_details: Market authorized 1997; three patients died from acute liver failure leading to European market withdrawal; re-approved 2004 after safety evaluation; considered second-choice COMT inhibitor for advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations; regular liver enzyme monitoring mandated. Causal claim is presented as a known safety risk documented by the fatal cases and attendant regulatory action.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone is a potent, blood-brain-barrier-permeable COMT inhibitor, but its clinical use is currently very restricted because of the risk of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). It was associated with three fatal cases of fulminant hepatitis and was briefly withdrawn from the market, only to be later reintroduced because of a lack of equally effective drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated with three fatal cases of fulminant hepatitis; briefly withdrawn from the market and later reintroduced due to a lack of equally effective drugs; clinical use currently very restricted because of DILI risk. Mechanistically, a lipophilic p-tolyl moiety (cLogP=3.17) facilitates mitochondrial uncoupling and possible bioactivation to reactive quinone-imines, though most evidence points to mitochondrial toxicity via uncoupling as the cause of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report of a single patient, the diagnosis of trazodone-induced hepatotoxicity was supported by a liver biopsy showing no significant inflammation or fat and, more importantly, by the biochemical response to inadvertent rechallenge with trazodone (given on 8/10/98 and 8/11/98). Viral and serological markers were negative, there was no biliary radiographic abnormality, and the liver tests essentially normalized approximately 2 weeks after discontinuation of trazodone and again after stopping the inadvertent challenge. The atypical rapid rise in AST on rechallenge was considered consistent with (but not diagnostic of) an idiosyncratic mechanism, described as an idiosyncratic, possible immune reaction. The reaction occurred almost 18 months after drug initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case proven by inadvertent rechallenge (2 days of drug, 8/10-8/11/98); onset ~18 months after drug initiation. Liver biopsy showed bile plugs with intracanalicular cholestasis and modest periportal lymphocytic infiltrate without interface, with feathery degeneration and ballooning of hepatocytes. Lab values at hospitalization: total bilirubin 11.0 mg/dL, AST 625 U/L, ALT 1092 U/L, Alk Phos 206 U/L; values rose on rechallenge (AST 824, ALT 1476) then normalized. Patient hospitalized 8/2/98, all drugs stopped, discharged after 3 days, no other meds taken. Five prior reports of trazodone hepatotoxicity noted (latencies from 14 days to 8 months); one reported fatal hepatic necrosis (Hull et al.) occurred in a patient concurrently taking a neuroleptic drug. Patient was on low-dose steroids and still had a severe idiosyncratic reaction. Trazodone bears structural similarity to fluorobutyrophenone antipsychotics; major metabolite is m-chloro-4-phenylpiperazine.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to trazodone have been well described, one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Three cases occurred within 9 weeks of starting treatment with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular histological pattern; two other cases developed jaundice after 7-8 months of use with liver function tests increased until 6 months after withdrawal (one showing a chronic active hepatitis pattern on histology); and one occurred after 18 months of use while on low-dose steroids. Liver injury was self-limited upon discontinuation. The mechanism seems immunoallergic/hypersensitivity given associated exanthema/rash or leukonychia, positive antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils in liver specimens, and a rapid response on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Six well-described cases; one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Latency 9 weeks to 18 months. Histology mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular; one case chronic active hepatitis (jaundice after 7-8 months, LFTs elevated up to 6 months post-withdrawal); one case after 18 months of use on low-dose steroids. Immunoallergic/hypersensitivity mechanism (exanthema, leukonychia, antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils, rapid response on rechallenge). Liver injury self-limited on discontinuation. p49: main psychoactive metabolite is mCPP via CYP3A3/4 hydroxylation, further metabolized by polymorphic CYP2D6; poor metabolizers have higher mCPP steady-state concentrations; thioridazine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) increased mCPP plasma concentrations ~50%; the only fatal liver failure case involved combined trazodone and trifluoperazine (neuroleptic) treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular liver injury in a patient on trazodone at the recommended starting dose. They state: 'We believe our patient also had an idiosyncratic drug reaction to trazodone, characterized by both a cholestatic and hepatocellular resemblance and profound hyperbilirubinemia.' The reaction peaked 2 weeks after drug discontinuation and resolved over 8 weeks, and they advise monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin during the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone, regardless of dosage.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient presenting with what appeared to be obstructive jaundice with hepatocellular inflammation; extensive evaluation was negative. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and inflammatory response consistent with a drug reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 29 mg/dL two weeks after drug discontinuation; aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase decreased to 235 IU/L and 152 IU/L, respectively, and all liver enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal eight weeks after trazodone was discontinued. The reaction occurred at the recommended starting dose. A prior published case (Chu et al., reference 1) of a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic reaction at trazodone 500 mg/d was the first published case of liver toxicity. Trazodone is a triazolopyridine derivative (nontricyclic antidepressant); its primary side effects are drowsiness and dizziness. Authors recommend monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin for the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old man treated for Parkinson disease with levodopa and pergolide and who had a prior major depressive episode was admitted on 15 April 1999 with icteric acute hepatitis. He had started venlafaxine at 37.5 mg/d on 6 March and increased to 150 mg/d on 9 April. On admission his liver tests were abnormal (ALT 3.97 µkat/L, AST 4.36 µkat/L, GGT 12.17 µkat/L, ALP 11.33 µkat/L, total bilirubin 87 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 86 µmol/L), versus normal prior chemistry, and serology for hepatitis A, B, and C was negative. The authors conclude it is well justified to identify venlafaxine as the culprit in the patient's acute liver toxic insult, stating that all other possible causes of toxic hepatic injury were excluded and that liver function returned to normal within 5 weeks after venlafaxine was progressively discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of icteric acute hepatitis attributed to venlafaxine in a 78-year-old man; venlafaxine titrated from 37.5 mg/d (started 6 March 1999) to 150 mg/d (9 April 1999); admission liver tests: ALT 3.97 µkat/L, AST 4.36 µkat/L, GGT 12.17 µkat/L, ALP 11.33 µkat/L, total bilirubin 87 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 86 µmol/L; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C; improvement and normalization of liver function within 5 weeks of progressive venlafaxine discontinuation; authors excluded other causes of toxic hepatic injury; co-medication was levodopa and pergolide for Parkinson disease; authors support routine liver-function monitoring for patients on venlafaxine, concurring with Horsmans and colleagues.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old man treated for Parkinson disease and a prior depression episode presented on 15 April 1999 with icteric acute hepatitis. He had begun venlafaxine on 6 March at 37.5 mg/d, increased to 150 mg/d on 9 April, while continuing regular therapy. Admission showed elevated alanine aminotransferase (3.97 µkat/L), aspartate aminotransferase (4.36 µkat/L), γ-glutamyltransferase (12.17 µkat/L), alkaline phosphatase (11.33 µkat/L), total bilirubin (87 µmol/L) and direct bilirubin (86 µmol/L), with negative serology for hepatitis A, B, and C and normal abdominal ultrasonography.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient also had Parkinson disease treated with levodopa and pergolide and a prior major depression treated with electroconvulsive therapy, but the authors excluded all other possible causes of toxic hepatic injury. Venlafaxine was progressively discontinued while other therapy continued; liver function tests returned to normal within 5 weeks (dechallenge recovery). Authors concluded it is well justified to identify venlafaxine as the culprit in the acute liver toxic insult and supported monitoring of liver function in venlafaxine patients. Onset/report: venlafaxine started 6 March at 37.5 mg/d, increased to 150 mg/d on 9 April; presented 15 April 1999.

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old woman taking 75 mg of venlafaxine daily for vasomotor symptoms presented one month after starting treatment with abdominal pain, an enlarged liver, and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 372 U/L, AST 99 U/L, GGT 962 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 758 U/L). After all potentially hepatotoxic medications including venlafaxine were stopped, liver function improved markedly; rechallenge at 37.5 mg produced renewed rises (ALT 269, AST 49, GGT 256, ALP 263 U/L) within six days, which resolved when venlafaxine was withdrawn. The authors concluded that an objective causality evaluation revealed a probable causal link between venlafaxine and the adverse effect, describing the hepatotoxic effects as rare and idiosyncratic.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced hepatitis at low therapeutic dose: 60-year-old woman, 75 mg/day for vasomotor symptoms; onset ~1 month after start. Positive rechallenge: on rechallenge with 37.5 mg, elevated ALT (269), AST (49), GGT (256), ALP (263) U/L within 6 days. Initial labs: ALT 372, AST 99, GGT 962, ALP 758 U/L, enlarged liver, abdominal pain, nonspecific symptoms. Liver enzymes returned to normal after withdrawal. Hepatotoxicity characterized as rare and idiosyncratic; objective causality assessment deemed the reaction probably due to the drug.

raw_record.support_text: The present report describes a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis occurring in a 39-year-old woman after administration of venlafaxine. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3 of the hepatic lobule with portal inflammation and abundant eosinophils. The clinical course rapidly improved after cessation of venlafaxine and administration of corticosteroid; liver toxicity recurred with a medium dose upon initiation of therapy and with increase of dosage after reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine. The positive rechallenge clearly supports the association between venlafaxine and liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old woman; liver biopsy (Nov 17, 2011) showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3, perivenular feathery degenerated hepatocytes with cytoplasmic bile pigment, intrasinusoidal lymphocytes, activated Kupffer cells, occasional apoptotic bodies and single liver cell necrosis, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils; no bile duct lesions or bile plugs. Diagnosed as venlafaxine-associated cholestatic hepatitis. Positive rechallenge: toxicity recurred with reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine and dose increase; improved after cessation with methylprednisolone 50 mg/day tapering. Elevated AST 734 U/L, ALT 805 U/L, AP 167 U/L, γGT 102 U/L, bilirubin 11.2 mg/dL on readmission.

raw_record.support_text: Venlafaxine was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: The authors summarize a case of severe hepatocellular jaundice most likely caused by nefazodone, noting this represents the fourth case and second report of severe liver toxicity with the drug despite no liver toxicity seen in premarketing studies. The liver panel returned to normal after cessation of nefazodone, and they recommend frequent liver panel evaluation and early drug withdrawal, with complete recovery expected with early recognition.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as severe hepatocellular jaundice; fourth case and second report of severe liver toxicity; no liver toxicity observed in premarketing studies; liver panel returned to normal after cessation; complete recovery after early drug withdrawal; authors recommend liver panel evaluation in the first six months of therapy and immediate drug withdrawal if liver toxicity occurs. Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte dropout on reticulin stain.

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of early onset, nefazodone-induced acute liver failure are reported, presenting as early as 4 weeks after initiation of therapy. The paper also notes that nefazodone has well established potential hepatotoxic side effects, and symptoms of liver failure have previously been reported within 6 weeks of institution of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Nefazodone (Serzone; Bristol-Myers Squibb) prescribed for reactive depression and work-related anxiety/depression. Patient 1 (61-yr-old woman) developed malaise, fatigue, jaundice 4 weeks after starting therapy, with raised liver enzymes/bilirubin and coagulopathy; over 48 h developed grade III encephalopathy and underwent successful liver transplantation; explanted liver showed submassive parenchymal necrosis without fatty changes or fibrosis. Patient 2 (46-yr-old man) developed fatigue and jaundice within 4 weeks of nefazodone, with coagulopathy and elevated liver enzymes/bilirubin; transjugular biopsy showed massive parenchymal necrosis in centrilobular areas extending to portal tracts; after discontinuation of nefazodone coagulopathy corrected and liver enzymes normalized over 3 months (dechallenge evidence). Hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, and infectious or autoimmune hepatitis were excluded in both patients; both denied other drug ingestion. This is described as the shortest reported duration before onset of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 2 was a 46-yr-old man who developed progressive fatigue and jaundice within 4 wk of starting nefazodone for work-related anxiety and depression, progressing to acute liver failure with marked coagulopathy and elevated enzymes/bilirubin. Hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, and infectious or autoimmune hepatitis were excluded, and the patient denied other drug ingestion. Transjugular biopsy showed massive centrilobular parenchymal necrosis extending to portal tracts; the patient improved upon nefazodone discontinuation, with coagulopathy correcting over 2 wk and liver enzymes normalizing over 3 months. The accompanying letter notes both reported patients presented with acute liver failure within 4 wk of therapy, one requiring liver transplantation and this patient requiring prolonged hospitalization, representing the shortest onset time reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Two reported cases of acute liver failure within 4 weeks of starting nefazodone; duration of therapy before onset is noted as the shortest ever reported. Patient 2 (46-yr-old man, anxiety/depression) had massive centrilobular parenchymal necrosis on biopsy, marked coagulopathy and elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin; recovered after drug withdrawal (coagulopathy corrected over 2 wk, enzymes normalized over 3 months). The other patient required liver transplantation. The letter states nefazodone has well established potential hepatotoxic side effects generally apparent 3-6 months after starting therapy. Competing causes (hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, infectious/autoimmune hepatitis) excluded and no co-medication.

raw_record.support_text: A life-threatening ADR, fulminant hepatic failure, has been reported with lamotrigine. A 22-year-old woman developed a maculopapular rash and hepatic failure; lamotrigine was stopped and liver function gradually improved after admission to hospital, but the patient died unexpectedly of a massive pulmonary embolus 2 months after admission. Biopsy confirmed a diagnosis of fulminant hepatic failure and, in the absence of other causes, it was concluded that the fulminant hepatic failure was due to lamotrigine.
raw_record.extra_details: 22-year-old woman on lamotrigine therapy developed maculopapular rash and hepatic failure; fulminant hepatic failure confirmed by biopsy; causality concluded in absence of other causes; liver function improved after lamotrigine cessation, but the patient died of a massive pulmonary embolus 2 months after admission (death not directly attributed to the liver injury).

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of acute hepatitis patients, toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis was attributed to intake of nitrofurantoin, efavirenz, amphetamine, prophylthiouracil, sirolimus, flumatid, lamictal (lamotrigine), and opipramol.
raw_record.extra_details: Referenced under the brand name 'Lamictal'. Listed among drugs causing toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis in a case series of acute hepatitis patients; liver stiffness measured with FibroScan.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's commentary refers to a case reported by Ouellet et al of fulminant hepatitis induced by lamotrigine in a 40-year-old female patient who presented with features characteristic of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS). Causality was attributed to lamotrigine because signs appeared shortly after a dosage escalation and clinical improvement followed drug discontinuation, with evidence of fever and rash without another identifiable cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 40-year-old female presenting with features of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (fever and rash, rash noted on the torso); signs appeared shortly after a lamotrigine dosage escalation and clinical improvement followed drug discontinuation. The commentary frames this as a serious, potentially life-threatening hypersensitivity syndrome and highlights considering drug-induced injury in acute hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors note that although lamotrigine causes skin eruptions in about 3% of cases, it had not previously been reported to cause hepatotoxicity. They report a case of fulminant hepatic failure induced by lamotrigine, making an explicit causal attribution of liver injury to this drug in a single patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the first case of hepatotoxicity caused by lamotrigine (skin eruptions occur in about 3% of cases). Clinical outcome was fulminant hepatic failure. Details of dose, duration, latency, laboratory values, histology, and recovery/outcome are not provided in the available text.

raw_record.support_text: A percutaneous liver biopsy performed on day 54 after the first Ticlopidine intake showed preserved liver architecture with edema of the portal fields and mild lymphocytic/granulocytic infiltrates containing eosinophils, an excessive cholestasis with dilated canaliculi filled with bile thrombi, vacuolar cytoplasmic transformation of hepatocytes, and small focal parenchymal necroses. The overall pattern of severe intrahepatic cholestasis with mild parenchymatous hepatitis was interpreted as drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Cholestatic hepatitis: severe intrahepatic cholestasis with bile thrombi and mild parenchymatous hepatitis on biopsy. Clinically presented with icterus and pruritus (controlled by antihistamines). Transaminases normalized rapidly after discontinuation, while cholestasis parameters returned to normal only 79 days after stopping Ticlopidine. No rechallenge was performed. Biopsy also showed vacuolar hepatocyte transformation, small focal parenchymal necroses, mild parenchymal siderosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-yr-old female was admitted to hospital with a 2-month history of weakness, anorexia, pruritus, and abnormal liver function tests; physical exam showed jaundice. Her history was unremarkable except for treatment with ticlopidine (Ticlid, 250 mg daily) until 2 wk before hospitalization. Labs showed total bilirubin 16.5 mg/dl (direct 11.1), ALP 209 U/L, AST 768 U/L, and ALT 575 U/L; ANA and hepatitis A/B/C serologies were negative; gallbladder ultrasound and ERCP were normal; the patient declined liver biopsy. Combined with the title labeling this 'Ticlopidine-Induced Cholestatic Hepatitis,' the report attributes ticlopidine as the cause, and in the preceding paragraph the authors note that 1% or less of patients treated with ticlopidine develop cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiplatelet medication (Ticlid, Hoffmann-La Roche) used to prevent thrombosis in coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease; case of a 68-yr-old female with 2-month history of weakness, anorexia, pruritus, abnormal LFTs and jaundice; ticlopidine 250 mg daily stopped 2 wk before admission; total bilirubin 16.5 mg/dl (direct 11.1), ALP 209 U/L, AST 768 U/L, ALT 575 U/L, Hb 11.8 g; ANA and hepatitis A/B/C negative; gallbladder ultrasound and ERCP normal; liver biopsy declined; cholestatic hepatitis successfully treated with corticosteroids. Background: only 1% or less of treated patients develop cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that this patient was likely to have ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis because of the temporal relationship with commencement of the medication and resolution with its withdrawal; the liver biopsy was consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon, and there was an absence of other possible aetiologies on laboratory testing and imaging. They recommended that ticlopidine be considered as a cause of intrahepatic cholestasis in patients presenting with jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic hepatitis attributed to ticlopidine in a patient presenting with jaundice. Causality was based on temporal relationship to drug start, resolution (dechallenge) on withdrawal, a liver biopsy consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon (portal tract fibrosis, inflammation, and florid bile ductule proliferation highlighted by cytokeratin 7, with mixed inflammation including eosinophils and neutrophils), and exclusion of other aetiologies. The paper notes hepatotoxicity has been reported in up to 4.4% of cases, mainly as asymptomatic elevations of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, and that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare side-effect; typically jaundice appears after a latent period of about 6 weeks and lasts approximately 4 months, and the condition is generally benign with resolution after drug withdrawal. Pathogenesis is unknown, with both direct intrinsic hepatotoxicity and immuno-allergic mechanisms proposed.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents ticlopidine as a recognized cause of drug-induced hepatotoxicity, analyzing 49 reports of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity patients (47 previously published cases described in table I plus two new cases described in this paper). A Bayesian causal-assessment method based on analytical and demographic traits was applied to attribute abnormal liver function to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine was given at 250 mg twice daily. Case 2 (76-year-old man) had abnormal liver function emerging after 21 weeks and severe enzyme elevations (AST 91 IU/L, ALT 134 IU/L, GGT 1029 IU/L, ALP 754 IU/L) with total bilirubin rising to 11.5 mg/dl by week 28; enzymes and bilirubin improved after ticlopidine discontinuation at week 64. The Danan causality assessment gave a suggestive relationship, and the Bayesian method assigned ticlopidine a posterior probability (PsP) of 87.30% at week 21 and 81.89% at week 64. The analytical profile emphasized alkaline phosphatase (ALP >720 IU/L had a likelihood ratio of 109.50); alcohol, viral hepatitis, mononucleosis, and drug-associated/uncertain etiologies had statistically different PsP from ticlopidine. Published ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases (47 in table I plus the 2 new cases) were used to build the model.

raw_record.support_text: Ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis is described as a rare serious but reversible adverse effect of the drug, with more than 40 cases reported in the literature plus 2 additional cases reported in this paper. The latent period, severity, and duration after discontinuation are highly variable, but cholestasis resolved after the drug was discontinued in all cases. In vitro T-cell stimulation studies at therapeutic ticlopidine concentrations support a possible T-cell-mediated mechanism, and the authors recommend monitoring liver function tests in patients receiving ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (cholestasis with jaundice) attributed to ticlopidine used as part of pharmacological management of percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA). More than 40 published cases plus 2 new reported cases; latent period from drug introduction to hepatotoxicity, its severity, and duration after discontinuation are highly variable, and remission was complete in all cases. In vitro T-cell stimulation assay showed therapeutic ticlopidine concentrations stimulated T cells from the two cholestatic patients but not from healthy individuals, supporting a possible immune/T-cell-mediated mechanism; underlying mechanism otherwise unknown. Recommendation to include liver function tests in routine blood monitoring for ticlopidine recipients.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man developed jaundice, pruritus, and liver dysfunction (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dl, gamma-GTP 806 IU/L) after starting ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction. Serology for hepatitis B and C and ANA were negative, and abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver without obstruction, so the patient was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine. After ticlopidine discontinuation liver enzymes and bilirubin improved; a later liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and the case was reported as acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine was given for cerebral infarction. Markers for HBsAg, HBsAb, HBeAg, HBeAb, IgM-HBc Ab, HCV Ab and IgM-HA Ab were negative; anti-nuclear antibody negative; ultrasound showed no obstructive jaundice. Dechallenge led to improvement of liver enzymes and T-bilirubin. Liver biopsy on day 43 showed intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with drug-induced liver damage. The case was accompanied by pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), whose etiologic attribution to ticlopidine was raised. The text also notes ticlopidine-induced mild serum liver enzyme elevations at 1-2% incidence in some studies and an estimated 0.0013% incidence of severe hepatitis, with only a few reported cases of a severe cholestatic pattern of liver injury showing centro-acinar cholestasis on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man on ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction developed malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus with marked liver dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dL, γ-GTP 806 IU/L). Hepatitis serologies (HBV, HCV, HAV) and ANA were negative, and ultrasound showed no obstruction. He was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis induced by ticlopidine; enzymes improved after discontinuation, and he also developed pure red cell aplasia. Liver biopsy on day 43 showed intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with drug-induced liver damage, and he was diagnosed with acute intrahepatic cholestasis associated with pure red cell aplasia due to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 69-year-old man with acute intrahepatic/acute cholestatic hepatitis plus pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), both attributed to ticlopidine. Ticlopidine was given for cerebral infarction. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis; liver enzymes and bilirubin improved after drug discontinuation. Serologies for HBV/HCV/HAV and ANA negative; ultrasound showed normal liver and no obstruction. The paper notes ticlopidine causes mild serum liver enzyme elevations in ~1-2% in some studies, with severe hepatitis incidence estimated at 0.0013% and only a few cases of a severe cholestatic pattern, with biopsies showing centro-acinar cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presenting with jaundice, cholestatic liver tests, and marked hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol 1,666 mg/dl) had a liver biopsy showing moderate spotty necrosis, moderate steatosis and slight bile stasis compatible with drug-induced cholestasis. The drug-induced leukocyte stimulating test (DLST) was positive for ticlopidine hydrochloride, and the liver damage and hyperlipidemia were diagnosed as ticlopidine hydrochloride-induced cholestatic hepatitis with associated abnormal lipidemia (LP-X). Values increased even after withdrawal of the causative drug, then declined.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Admission labs: total bilirubin 7.8 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 5.5 mg/dl, GOT 94 IU/l, GPT 243 IU/l, ALP 842 IU/l, γ-GTP 2,418 IU/l, LAP 156 IU/l; LP-X test positive; total cholesterol rose from 257 mg/dl before onset to 1,682 mg/dl with cholestasis. DLST positive for ticlopidine hydrochloride. Liver biopsy (Dec 12) showed moderate spotty necrosis, moderate steatosis and slight bile stasis, compatible with drug-induced cholestasis. Phenotype: cholestatic hepatitis with associated abnormal (LP-X) lipoproteinemia. Total bilirubin peaked at 30.2 mg/dl and took 80 days to normalize; GPT and γ-GTP remained elevated ~140 days after jaundice. Patient recovered without transplantation or death. Structural pattern: cholestasis/bile stasis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a rare case of agranulocytosis associated with hepatic toxicity, probably related to the use of ticlopidine, a platelet inhibitor. More serious but less frequent adverse effects of ticlopidine are hematological dyscrasia and cholestatic hepatitis. In the presented patient, ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily was given after a vertebrobasilar stroke, and about four weeks later she developed agranulocytosis and hepatic toxicity; after ticlopidine was discontinued, liver tests progressively normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was a 70-year-old Caucasian woman with no prior hematological or liver disease and no prior history of blood or liver disorders. Hepatic toxicity and agranulocytosis developed about 4 weeks after starting ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily; ticlopidine was discontinued and she was treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, with rapid rise in white blood count and progressive normalization of liver tests. Cholestatic hepatitis is described as a recognized serious, less frequent ticlopidine adverse effect. The paper recommends monitoring complete blood count and liver function tests in the first three months of ticlopidine therapy for early detection of serious and unpredictable side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a patient who developed drug-induced cholestatic liver injury attributed to ticlopidine. Histopathology showed mild periportal inflammation with neutrophils and eosinophils, foci of piecemeal necrosis, and mild collagen deposition, and MRP2 immunoreactivity was reduced and cytosolic. Ticlopidine therapy was stopped and liver biochemistry normalized 6 weeks after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine is an anti-platelet drug described as inducing idiosyncratic DILI, typically cholestatic hepatitis occurring 2-12 weeks after therapy initiation. In this case the calculated R value was 0.85, confirming a cholestatic injury. Histology showed periportal inflammation (neutrophils and eosinophils), piecemeal necrosis with inflammatory infiltrate, and mild collagen deposition, with no iron or copper accumulation. MRP2 immunoreactivity was weaker and mainly cytosolic. Liver biochemistry normalized 6 weeks after stopping ticlopidine. This is noted as the first human evidence of abnormal hepatic MRP2 immunoreactivity in drug-induced cholestasis, consistent with pre-clinical DILI models.

raw_record.support_text: The objective of the paper is to report a case of probable ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis. A 76-year-old man without liver disease developed painless jaundice approximately three weeks after starting ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily; jaundice and elevated serum liver enzyme concentrations resolved after ticlopidine was discontinued, and the patient was not rechallenged. A diagnosis of probable ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (jaundice, elevated serum liver enzymes). Ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily; jaundice appeared approximately 3 weeks after starting therapy. On admission, ticlopidine had already been discontinued, and jaundice and abnormal enzymes resolved over months after withdrawal without other treatment except discontinuation; no rechallenge. A literature review found six case reports describing seven patients with probable ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis, of which only one in the US literature; jaundice developed one to three months after starting at or below the recommended daily dose and resolved after discontinuation. Symptom onset with jaundice reported about 1 month after initiating recommended dosage; monitoring of serum liver enzymes not recommended, with patient instructions to watch for jaundice, dark urine, and light-colored stools.

raw_record.support_text: Liver disease has been implicated to result from therapy with 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP). Definitive drug-induced hepatitis was reported in one patient with ulcerative colitis treated with 6-MP, in whom hepatitis developed 6 months after initiation of treatment. Liver biopsy revealed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis, and the diagnosis was confirmed by the response to drug withdrawal and rechallenge (Present et al. 56).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a patient with ulcerative colitis; hepatitis developed 6 months after initiation of 6-MP treatment. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with inflammation suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis. Diagnosis confirmed by response to drug withdrawal and rechallenge (Present et al. 56).

raw_record.support_text: In the histopathologic study of human drug-induced liver injury, Group I (zonal injury) included eight cases, among which two were associated with the therapeutic administration of mercaptopurine. The lesion showed severe centrolobular fatty metamorphosis with intracytoplasmic coarse or medium-sized lipid globules, necrotic liver cells or loss of cytoplasmic basophilia and nuclear pyknosis, occasional PAS-positive pigmented macrophages in necrotic zones, and minimal portal inflammation with occasional bile ductule proliferation; cholestasis was noted in two of the group's cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Zonal injury (Group I) with severe centrolobular fatty metamorphosis characterized by intracytoplasmic coarse or medium-sized lipid globules; liver cells necrotic or showing loss of cytoplasmic basophilia and nuclear pyknosis; occasional pigmented macrophages containing PAS-positive material in necrotic zones; inflammation not conspicuous except for enlarged Kupffer cells; minimal portal inflammation and occasional proliferation of bile ductules; cholestasis was noted in two cases of the group. Two cases reported.

raw_record.support_text: Over the initial ten-year period of the prospective DILIN cohort study, 1434 cases of drug-induced liver injury were enrolled and underwent causality assessment, of which 27 were attributed, at least in part, to a thiopurine, including 12 to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) and 15 to azathioprine. After excluding 5 cases in which liver injury was considered only possibly related to the thiopurine, 22 cases (10 attributed to 6-MP and 12 to Aza) fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria and were analyzed.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 of 22 included DILIN cases were attributed to 6-mercaptopurine (10-year prospective DILIN cohort, total 1434 DILI cases). Combined 6-MP/Aza expert DILIN causality was definite in 2 (9%), very likely in 12 (54%), and probable in 8 (36%); RUCAM median 6.5 with 4 highly probable, 14 probable, and 4 possible. One 11-year-old boy received 6-MP for acute lymphocytic leukemia. Most patients were adults with autoimmune conditions, most commonly inflammatory bowel disease (55%). Presenting features included symptoms attributable to liver injury in all but one patient (jaundice 73%, nausea 64%, fatigue and abdominal pain 50%); viral serologies negative except one patient with stable pre-existing chronic hepatitis C; imaging showed no biliary obstruction.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 396 patients with inflammatory bowel disease (120 ulcerative colitis, 276 Crohn disease) treated with 6-mercaptopurine over 18 years and followed for a mean of 60.3 months, toxicity directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine included drug hepatitis in 1 patient (0.3%). These complications were reversible in all cases with no mortality.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug hepatitis reported as directly induced by 6-mercaptopurine in 1 of 396 patients (0.3%) with inflammatory bowel disease (120 ulcerative colitis, 276 Crohn disease); complication reversible with no mortality. Disease indication was steroid-dependent or intractable inflammatory bowel disease, fistulas, or need to avoid resection.

raw_record.support_text: In this placebo-controlled study, pioglitazone was found to be generally well tolerated; there were no cases of jaundice and no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity or drug-induced elevations of ALT levels. This result is consistent with all placebo-controlled clinical studies of pioglitazone, in which the incidence of patients with ALT ≥3 × ULN was low and comparable between pioglitazone (4 of 1,526 [0.26%]) and placebo (2 of 793 [0.25%]).
raw_record.extra_details: No cases of jaundice and no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity or drug-induced ALT elevations were observed in the study. Consistent with pooled placebo-controlled studies: ALT ≥3 × ULN incidence was 0.26% (4/1,526) for pioglitazone versus 0.25% (2/793) for placebo. ALT elevations and hepatotoxicity were not attributed to pioglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: In discussing the study results, the authors state that pioglitazone once daily as monotherapy significantly improved HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose in patients with type 2 diabetes, with no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity. This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion regarding pioglitazone and human DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: In the safety analysis of the randomized trial (197 patients), no patient who received pioglitazone experienced increases in ALT or AST > 3x the upper limit of normal, and no patients developed jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: A second case of reversible cholestatic liver injury was reported in a 49-year-old woman. Mild AST and ALT elevations developed 22 days after starting pioglitazone and, after 6 weeks of continued therapy, she developed jaundice, pale-colored stools, dark urine, pruritus, and pedal edema. At the time pioglitazone was stopped, AST was 94, ALT 84, alkaline phosphatase three times normal, and total bilirubin 21.5 mg/dL. CT and MRCP were normal and hepatitis virus serology was negative. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis with bile duct injury, regenerative changes, and focal apoptosis without fibrosis. Serum bilirubin peaked at 34 mg%, then all liver chemistries normalized over 8 weeks; at 12 months follow-up the patient was asymptomatic with normal liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Second of two reported reversible pioglitazone-induced jaundice cases. Latency: mild AST/ALT elevations at 22 days after start; jaundice noted after 6 weeks of continued therapy. Labs at stop: AST 94, ALT 84, alkaline phosphatase 3x, total bilirubin 21.5 mg/dL; bilirubin peaked at 34 mg%. CT/MRCP normal; hepatitis virus serology negative. Liver biopsy: cholestasis with bile duct injury, regenerative changes, focal apoptosis, no fibrosis. All liver chemistries normalized over 8 weeks; asymptomatic with normal enzymes at 12 months.

raw_record.support_text: Pioglitazone monotherapy significantly improves hemoglobin A1c and fasting plasma glucose while producing beneficial effects on serum lipids in patients with type 2 diabetes, with no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients with type 2 diabetes; pioglitazone monotherapy improved HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and serum lipids; authors report no evidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports cases of rosiglitazone- and pioglitazone-induced liver failure reported to the FDA from 1997-2006. For pioglitazone (n=10 cases), the maximum recorded hepatic enzyme levels reflected a pattern expected with severe hepatocellular injury; 9/10 cases were acute and nearly all had jaundice and encephalopathy. Outcomes were 8/10 death, 0 transplant, and 2/10 spontaneous recovery. Negative viral serologies and absence of significant alcohol use were documented in most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 FDA-reported cases. Median age 65, 70% male. Daily dose 15 mg (n=2), 30 mg (n=1), 45 mg (n=5). Median treatment duration 10 weeks (IQR 5-16, n=10). Acute in 9/10; jaundice 9/10; encephalopathy 7/8. Max AST median 604 IU/L (n=8), max ALT 1130 IU/L (n=8), max AP 400 IU/L (n=9), max total bilirubin 13.3 mg/dL (n=10). Pathology available 7/10, necrosis present 4/7. Outcomes: death 8/10, transplant 0, spontaneous recovery 2/10. 2/10 published in literature.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (D-FIAU) demonstrated potent anti-HBV activity in clinical trials for chronic HBV infection, but also induced severe delayed toxicity associated with lactic acidosis and hepatic failure that resulted in the death of several patients. This is contrasted with L-FMAU, which the authors note does not induce the increase in lactic acid production in HepG2 cells observed with D-FMAU and D-FIAU.
raw_record.extra_details: Agent aliases: D-FIAU, fialuridine. Injury described as severe delayed toxicity associated with lactic acidosis and hepatic failure, occurring during clinical trials of chronic HBV infection; resulted in death of several patients. Reported as context/reference in a woodchuck antiviral-efficacy study; no primary patient data presented.

raw_record.support_text: A 1993 trial of the antiviral nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) for chronic hepatitis B was halted after 13 weeks when several patients developed severe hepatotoxicity, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis. Of the seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity, five died and two required transplantation. The toxic reaction was believed to be caused by marked accumulation of hepatic microvesicular and macrovesicular fat as well as widespread mitochondrial damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 1993 trial in chronic hepatitis B treatment halted after 13 weeks; 7 patients with severe hepatotoxicity, 5 died and 2 required transplantation; concurrent lactic acidosis and pancreatitis; attributed to marked accumulation of hepatic microvesicular and macrovesicular fat and widespread mitochondrial damage.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a nucleoside analogue drug developed to treat hepatitis B, suppresses mitochondrial DNA synthesis, causing hepatic failure, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis in patients, which resulted in discontinuation of clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue developed to treat hepatitis B. Mechanism attributed to suppression of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) synthesis, also causing lactic acidosis and pancreatitis in patients, leading to discontinuation of clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: The nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU) reached Phase II trials before its toxic side effects were discovered. The study was terminated as an emergency at week 13 when seven of 15 patients were discovered to have developed severe hepatotoxicity and progressive lactic acidosis that progressed despite the drug being stopped. Three other patients showed mild hepatotoxicity; of the seven worst affected, only two survived following orthotopic liver transplantation, three died despite receiving a transplant, and two succumbed before transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Experimental anti-HBV nucleoside analogue evaluated in a Phase II clinical trial; study terminated at week 13 when 7/15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with progressive lactic acidosis that worsened after drug discontinuation; other adverse events included pancreatitis, myopathy and neuropathy; 3 additional patients showed mild hepatotoxicity; 5 of 15 were symptom-free (short exposure); of the 7 severe cases, 2 survived after orthotopic liver transplantation, 3 died after transplant, and 2 died before transplantation; outcome progressed despite stopping the drug.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials for treatment, the pyrimidine nucleoside analog fialuridine (FIAU; 1-[2-deoxy-2-fluoro-β-D-arabinofuranosyl]-5-iodouracil) showed promising early results but was later found to be extremely toxic to the liver in treated patients. Profound mitochondrial toxicity, lactic acidosis and hepatic failure required heroic clinical interventions, necessitated early termination of the trials, and deaths occurred. The hepatic toxicity was subsequently confirmed in animal models and in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Lactic acidosis and hepatic failure occurred, requiring heroic interventions; trials were terminated early and deaths occurred. FIAU was also toxic to skeletal and cardiac muscle, pancreas and peripheral nerve. Mechanism attributed to profound mitochondrial toxicity via DNA polymerase-γ inhibition. Confirmed by mitochondrial toxicity findings in animal models and in humans.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analogue developed for treatment of hepatitis B, was removed from the market after several reported cases of fatal microvesicular steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue (FIAU) developed for hepatitis B; removed from the market after several reported cases of fatal microvesicular steatosis (McKenzie et al., 1995).

raw_record.support_text: A six-month fialuridine course began in March 1993 and was terminated on an emergency basis 13 weeks later when hepatic failure and lactic acidosis occurred in one of 15 patients; three patients had already discontinued therapy between weeks 10 and 12. Seven of the 15 patients showed varying degrees of hepatic failure and lactic acidosis, with symptoms including fatigue, nausea, constipation, abdominal pain, worsening jaundice, decreasing hepatic synthetic function, worsening prothrombin times, and rising serum ammonia and lactate.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 trial patients developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis. Two patients with rapidly progressive hepatic failure died 22 and 36 hours after emergency liver transplantation; two others died of hemodynamic collapse due to pancreatitis and lactic acidosis before transplantation; one died of pancreatitis complications after transplantation; the remaining two underwent successful liver transplantation and survived with only little residual toxicity over 24 months follow-up. The seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity had biochemical evidence of pancreatitis, and all five who died showed pancreatitis at autopsy. Earlier-reported side effects included crampy abdominal pain, foot paresthesia, fatigue, nausea, numbness/tingling of feet or hands, lower abdominal pain, constipation, and mild thrombocytopenia.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), an antiviral nucleoside analogue tested against chronic hepatitis B virus infection, halted HBV in Hep G2 cells and in animals. However, in 1993, patients with chronic HBV infection treated with FIAU for 9.5 to 13 weeks developed signs of severe and, in some cases, fatal hepatotoxicity associated with lactic acidosis and multiple organ failures. Histopathology showed clear microvesicular steatosis in the liver and pancreas, now known to be due to mitochondrial DNA damage disturbing the electron transport chain; this outcome was not seen in preclinical studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, or cynomolgus monkeys.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiviral nucleoside analogue (1-[2-deoxy-2-fluoro-beta-D-arabinofuranosyl]-5-iodouracil) tested for chronic HBV infection; injury attributed to mitochondrial DNA damage disturbing the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Microvesicular steatosis in liver and pancreas; lactic acidosis and multiple organ failure; fatal in some cases. Treatment duration 9.5-13 weeks. Outcome was not seen during preclinical animal studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, and cynomolgus monkeys.

raw_record.support_text: In 1993, 15 participants in a phase II trial received the nucleoside analogue fialuridine to treat hepatitis B virus infection. Seven participants developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; analysis of liver tissue revealed steatosis (fatty degeneration), intracellular fat droplets, and swollen mitochondria. Five participants subsequently died, and two required liver transplantation. The paper states that human-specific mitochondrial toxicity underlies fialuridine's human hepatotoxicity, which was not predicted by preclinical animal testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Two hepatotoxins: 7 of 15 phase II participants (treated for hepatitis B virus infection) developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; histology showed steatosis with intracellular fat droplets and swollen mitochondria; 5 died and 2 required liver transplantation. Toxicity attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity of the nucleoside analogue. Preclinical testing in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication of hepatotoxicity, and a 1,600-fold dose over 4 days produced liver failure and lactic acidosis only in chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers (toxicity in human-hepatocyte regions).

raw_record.support_text: In a 1993 Phase II clinical trial of fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analogue for treatment of hepatitis B, 7 of 15 subjects unexpectedly developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and subsequently died by week 13. Liver histology revealed steatosis and cholestasis, and electron microscopy showed hepatocytes with cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with a reduced number of cristae.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial conducted in 1993 in 15 subjects with HBV infection; trial terminated by week 13. 7 subjects developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and died. Histology: steatosis and cholestasis; electron microscopy: cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and monkeys provided no indication of such toxicity; rats tolerated 510 mg/kg-day (2,000-fold the maximum human dose) for 10 weeks. The paper concludes FIAU has a direct toxic effect on human hepatocytes that does not require a comorbidity (e.g., viral infection) and is not immune mediated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that fialuridine caused acute liver failure during clinical trials: 7 of 15 patients treated with fialuridine developed acute liver injury, of which 5 died, an outcome not observed in preclinical toxicology studies. Damaged liver tissue showed steatosis, cholestasis, cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae, and mitochondrial toxicity and intracytoplasmic lipid droplets were also reported as mechanisms related to fialuridine hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude that fialuridine-induced hepatotoxicity has several underlying mechanisms.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 patients treated with fialuridine developed acute liver injury, of which 5 died, during clinical trials; injury not observed in preclinical toxicology studies. Histological marks in damaged liver tissue: steatosis, cholestasis, cytoplasmic fat droplets, swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. Mitochondrial toxicity and intracytoplasmic lipid droplets reported as mechanisms; the paper states fialuridine-induced hepatotoxicity has several underlying mechanisms. In the in vitro DIC assay fialuridine gave borderline DICI 0.80 ± 0.08 with high safety margins for both DIC and general cytotoxicity, and it was found to cause ATP depletion.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials, 7 of 15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity several weeks after beginning fialuridine treatment, and five of them died. No indication of fialuridine hepatotoxicity was observed in any pre-clinical testing, and the in vitro PHH spheroid model described here predicted fialuridine toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: In the referenced clinical trials, 7 of 15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity several weeks after beginning fialuridine treatment, and five of the 15 patients died. No hepatotoxicity was observed in pre-clinical testing; toxicity was later reproduced in chimeric TK-NOG mice carrying human hepatocytes and in long-term PHH spheroid cultures (cytotoxicity only after long-term dosing, EC50 > 100 uM at 48 h vs. 0.1 uM at 28 days).

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine was developed as antiviral therapy for hepatitis B infection. In a phase II study, fialuridine caused severe toxicity: irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7 out of 15 patients, myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment. Five out of 7 participants with severe hepatotoxicity died and two survived after liver transplantation. Preclinical toxicology studies in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication that FIAU would be hepatotoxic in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II study in hepatitis B patients; irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7/15 patients, with myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment; 5 of 7 patients with severe hepatotoxicity died, 2 survived after liver transplantation. Histology showed prominent microvesicular fat with chronic active hepatitis and variable macrovesicular steatosis, little hepatocellular necrosis, without substantial serum aminotransferase elevations; electron microscopy showed markedly swollen mitochondria with loss of cristae, matrix dissolution, and vesicular inclusions. Mechanism (mechanism 1, mitochondrial impairment): inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma by the triphosphate metabolite leading to mtDNA depletion. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and primates showed no hepatotoxicity signal.

raw_record.support_text: In the paper's context, fialuridine toxicity was mentioned as an example: although fialuridine hepatotoxicity was not detected in any preclinical study (including 2D primary hepatocyte cultures and rat, mouse, dog, and cynomolgus monkey in vivo studies), in clinical trials severe hepatotoxicity was observed after multiple weeks, and 7 of 15 patients developed progressive lactic acidosis and worsening jaundice, 5 of whom died.
raw_record.extra_details: In clinical trials severe hepatotoxicity was observed after multiple weeks of dosing; 7 of 15 patients developed progressive lactic acidosis and worsening jaundice, 5 of whom died. Notably, the hepatotoxicity was not detected in any preclinical study, including primary hepatocyte 2D cultures and rat, mouse, dog, and cynomolgus monkey in vivo studies.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analog for therapy of hepatitis B infections, did not show toxicity in preclinical test systems, yet in clinical trials 7 of 15 participants developed severe hepatic dysfunctions, five of whom died.
raw_record.extra_details: Indicated for hepatitis B. 7 of 15 trial participants developed severe hepatic dysfunctions; 5 died. No toxicity seen in preclinical test systems.

raw_record.support_text: The review notes that fialuridine (FIAU), despite the absence of hepatotoxicity in nonclinical studies, caused liver failure in seven patients during early clinical trials, of whom five died. This toxicity was subsequently attributed to incorporation of FIAU by mitochondrial DNA polymerase and was reported to depend on a nucleoside uptake transporter present in human but not rat or mouse mitochondria.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 patients in early clinical trials developed liver failure, 5 died; no hepatotoxicity observed in nonclinical (animal) studies; attributed to incorporation by mitochondrial DNA polymerase; dependent on a human-specific mitochondrial nucleoside uptake transporter; effects on urea synthesis reported as a sensitive mitochondrial function assessment in HepatoPac.

raw_record.support_text: The PHH 3D spheroid platform is presented as a predictive model for human drug response, exemplified by fialuridine (FIAU), which caused the deaths of 5 of 15 participants in a clinical trial by inducing acute liver failure. Toxicity was not detected in any preclinical model (rat, mouse, dog, cynomolgus monkey), yet the PHH spheroid system indicated that FIAU toxicity was already present at therapeutic exposure levels (spheroid EC50 = 100 nM; FIAU serum Cmax = 639 nM).
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU caused acute liver failure leading to death in 5 of 15 clinical trial participants; the therapeutic-use setting was highlighted because spheroid-predicted toxicity occurred at therapeutic exposure levels (spheroid EC50 = 100 nM; FIAU serum Cmax = 639 nM). FIAU hepatotoxicity was not detected in rat, mouse, dog, or cynomolgus monkey preclinical models. Agent referenced with alias FIAU.

raw_record.support_text: In Table 2, FIAU (fialuridine) is described with side effects including severe lactic acidosis, liver failure, and steatosis, kidney failure, myopathy and peripheral neuropathy; it is noted as discontinued due to severe hepatotoxicity and death, with in vitro inhibition of Polγ as experimental evidence.
raw_record.extra_details: Undine analog with a 3' OH, not a chain terminator; impairs DNA elongation at adenosine tracts. Used in trials for chronic hepatitis B. Severe lactic acidosis, liver failure and steatosis, kidney failure, myopathy, peripheral neuropathy; discontinued due to severe hepatotoxicity and death. In clinical trials, mitochondrial toxicity severe enough that hepatic failure and death in some patients necessitated discontinuation. FIAUppp strongly incorporated by Polγ in vitro.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a nucleoside analog developed for the treatment of viral hepatitis, showed no hepatotoxicity in any preclinical species. Despite this, 7 out of 15 volunteers in a phase I clinical trial exhibited lactic acidosis and acute liver failure a few weeks after commencing therapy, and 5 of them died.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 phase I trial volunteers exhibited lactic acidosis and acute liver failure a few weeks after commencing therapy, 5 of whom died (McKenzie et al., 1995). Nucleoside analog developed for viral hepatitis treatment; did not show hepatotoxicity in rat, mouse, dog, or cynomolgus monkey in preclinical species (Manning and Swartz, 1995). PHH spheroids detected fialuridine hepatotoxicity at clinically relevant concentrations.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that human micropatterned co-cultures (MPCCs), but not conventional primary human hepatocyte monolayers, detected the toxicity of fialuridine, a nucleoside analog drug used for hepatitis B viral infection. The text states that fialuridine caused liver failure and the deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials, and that these deaths resulted from lactic acidosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analog drug for hepatitis B viral infection; attributed injury manifested as liver failure with lactic acidosis, resulting in the deaths of 5 patients in clinical trials. In the in vitro component, human MPCCs, but not conventional PHH monolayers, detected fialuridine toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a nucleoside analogue used for the treatment of hepatitis B virus infection, caused acute liver failure in several clinical trial participants. Preclinical toxicology studies in conventional mice, rats, dogs, and non-human primates provided no indication of hepatotoxicity, whereas chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers were able to mirror the hepatotoxicity seen in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue used for treatment of hepatitis B virus infection; caused acute liver failure in several clinical trial participants. Preclinical toxicology in conventional mice, rats, dogs, and non-human primates showed no hepatotoxicity, but chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers mirrored the human hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a pyrimidine nucleoside analogue developed for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, is presented as an exemplar of drug hepatotoxicity that caused severe human injury. A subsequent phase II trial was terminated in the 13th week of treatment due to sudden onset of multi-system mitochondrial toxicity involving liver, muscle, nerve, and pancreas. Progressive lactic acidosis and severe hepatotoxicity resulted in five deaths and two emergency liver transplants; liver biopsies revealed hepatocellular lipid accumulation, cholestasis, and mitochondrial abnormalities presumed to result from mitochondrial toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial terminated in the 13th week of treatment for multi-system mitochondrial toxicity involving liver, muscle, nerve, and pancreas; progressive lactic acidosis and severe hepatotoxicity resulted in five deaths and two emergency liver transplants. Liver biopsies revealed hepatocellular lipid accumulation, cholestasis, and mitochondrial abnormalities. Mechanism attributed to mitochondrial toxicity via human ENT1-mediated mitochondrial transport and inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma; retrospective rodent studies (10 weeks at doses 1000 times higher) showed no toxicity, while chimeric mice with humanized livers detected the hepatotoxicity. Fialuridine is 1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-1-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil, developed for chronic hepatitis B virus infection.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies fialuridine as a clear example of drug-induced mitochondrial hepatotoxicity that caused several deaths during clinical trials, with toxicity appearing only after about 13 weeks of exposure due to inhibition of mitochondrial DNA replication. This is presented as a human clinical outcome.
raw_record.extra_details: Mitochondrial hepatotoxicity attributed to inhibition of mitochondrial DNA replication; toxicity induced after ~13 weeks of exposure; caused several deaths during clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: Phase II clinical trials with the anti-HBV drug fialuridine, which inhibits mtDNA replication, were prematurely interrupted due to serious adverse effects including unmanageable lactic acidosis, microvesicular steatosis and liver failure requiring liver transplantation, or even leading to death.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-HBV drug; phase II clinical trials prematurely interrupted; adverse effects included unmanageable lactic acidosis, microvesicular steatosis and liver failure requiring liver transplantation or leading to death; attributed mechanism is inhibition of mtDNA replication. References 7,8,9.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), a uracil nucleoside analogue, was evaluated in a clinical trial (NCT01337466) with fifteen HBV patients. The paper states that FIAU caused hepatic toxicity owing to mitochondrial damage, resulting in the death of five patients, which led to discontinuation of the trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Uracil nucleoside analogue originally developed as an anti-herpes drug; FIAU monophosphate is converted intracellularly to FIAU triphosphate, which enters viral DNA causing HBV DNA chain termination, and showed antiviral properties in the woodchuck model. In the clinical trial with 15 HBV patients, hepatic toxicity was attributed to mitochondrial damage and resulted in the death of five patients, leading to discontinuation of further trials.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a 1993 phase II clinical trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) evaluating fialuridine as an anti-HBV antiviral drug. Although the preliminary results reduced HBV DNA in patients, the study was terminated on an emergency basis by week 13 because of serious hepatotoxicity in seven patients, of whom five died and two required emergency liver transplantation. The paper attributes the human-specific toxicity to mitochondrial toxicity through a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria, and notes fialuridine toxicity was recapitulated in human liver organoids but not in HepG2 cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) terminated emergently at week 13; serious hepatotoxicity in 7 patients, 5 deaths and 2 emergency liver transplants. Mechanism attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity via a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria. Fialuridine passed preclinical toxicity studies; its toxicity was significant and quantifiable in primary human liver organoids but not observed in HepG2 hepatoma cells.

raw_record.support_text: The paper cites fialuridine as an anti-hepatitis B drug developed in the 1990s, tested in five animal models yet failing during 9-week human clinical trials due to unexpected induction of liver failure, with the trial terminated following the deaths of five volunteers, and elsewhere describes fialuridine as a discontinued anti-hepatitis B drug known for causing severe liver toxicity in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-hepatitis B drug discontinued; developed in the 1990s and extensively tested in mice, rats, dogs, monkeys, and woodchucks; failed during a 9-week clinical trial with unexpected induction of liver failure; trial terminated following deaths of five volunteers.

raw_record.support_text: Patients 8 to 10 were treated for FIAU (fialuridine) toxicity, described by the authors as a previously undescribed cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF). FIAU is a nucleoside analogue that becomes incorporated into mitochondrial DNA, affecting many organs, and the liver is unable to clear the lactic acid generated throughout the body; serial lactate levels were measured in Patients 8 and 10.
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU is a nucleoside analogue incorporated into mitochondrial DNA and described as a mitochondrial toxin; toxicity was dominated by multisystem disease and lactic acidosis with the liver unable to clear lactic acid. All 3 affected patients (Patients 8-10) were treated for fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) and were eventually transplanted, as their mitochondria did not recover once FIAU was withdrawn. The FIAU patients had higher baseline hepatic galactose elimination capacity (GEC) than expected in advanced FHF.

raw_record.support_text: In two patients with fialuridine toxicity from the Hepatix ELAD pilot trials (23 patients total), fialuridine is described as an agent that causes mitochondrial damage, and affected patients present with acute liver failure and lactic acidosis. ELAD therapy provided the liver function needed to control lactate levels, although cartridge function was overwhelmed toward the end of treatment. The same two patients (nos. 8 and 10) had received liver transplantations.
raw_record.extra_details: Fialuridine causes mitochondrial damage; patients present with acute liver failure and lactic acidosis. Two affected patients (nos. 8 and 10) were treated with the Hepatix ELAD (single cartridges, 200 g of metabolic function each); serum lactic acid decreased at onset of ELAD therapy but rose when cartridge capacity was overwhelmed. Both received liver transplantations.

raw_record.support_text: Research development of fialuridine (FIAU, 1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-beta-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil) suffered a setback with reports of unanticipated lethal toxicity in an NIH phase II study using 0.1-0.25 mg/kg/day. The trial, stopped in June 1993 after 15 patients were enrolled, saw 7 of the 15 develop severe liver toxicity, including hepatic failure with lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy, and neuropathy. Of those seven, five died and two survived after liver transplantation. Liver histology showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular fat accumulation with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II NIH study of fialuridine (FIAU) for hepatitis B; doses 0.1 mg/kg/day and 0.25 mg/kg/day; trial stopped June 1993 after 15 patients enrolled; 7 of 15 developed severe liver toxicity including hepatic failure with lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy, and neuropathy; 5 died and 2 survived after liver transplantation; liver histology showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular fat accumulation with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural changes; possible mechanism: incorporation into mitochondrial DNA (McKenzie et al, 1995); clinical course described in McKenzie et al 1995 and Stevenson et al 1995.

raw_record.support_text: Serious hepatotoxicity developed in 7 of 15 patients given the nucleoside analogue fialuridine for 8 to 12 weeks; five of these patients died. Cell-culture studies showed fialuridine is incorporated into nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, causing marked mitochondrial dysfunction, and it contains a free 3'-hydroxyl group. These findings are presented as contrast to lamivudine, for which no serious hepatotoxicity and no mitochondrial effects were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious hepatotoxicity developed in 7 of 15 patients given fialuridine for 8-12 weeks as an investigational nucleoside analogue; 5 of these 15 patients died. Supporting cell-culture findings: fialuridine is incorporated into nuclear and mitochondrial DNA causing marked mitochondrial dysfunction, attributed to its free 3'-hydroxyl group permitting inter-nucleotide incorporation. Presented in contrast to lamivudine (which lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group and is not incorporated into DNA).

raw_record.support_text: In the phase II fialuridine trial, 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B received oral fialuridine 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses. After 13 weeks one patient developed sudden-onset hepatic failure, shock and lactic acidosis, and the study was terminated; during follow-up 7 patients exhibited varying degrees of hepatic failure, jaundice, lactic acidosis and biochemical signs of pancreatitis. Five patients died and the other 2 survived after emergency liver transplantation, with severe toxicity attributed to the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral pyrimidine nucleoside analogue [1-(2'-deoxy-2'-fluoro-1-β-D-arabinofuranosyl-5-iodo)-uracil] for chronic hepatitis B; dosed 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses; toxicity developed after 9-13 weeks of treatment (p0). 7 of 15 patients affected; 5 died and 2 survivors required emergency liver transplantation; signs of hepatic failure, jaundice, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis. Histology of liver explants showed microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis and cholestasis, and electron microscopy showed swollen, misshapen mitochondria with fewer cristae and fat droplets, suggesting multisystem mitochondrial injury; steatosis appeared to be an early sign. Patients receiving <4 weeks (cumulative dose 200 mg) showed no overt toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical studies, FIAU (fialuridine) was evaluated as a treatment for chronic HBV infection. Trials with a longer treatment period were stopped after 12 weeks when signs of multi-organ toxicity involving muscle, nerve, liver, and pancreas appeared. The delayed toxicity included myopathy, lactic acidosis, peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, microvesicular fat infiltration of the liver, and liver failure resulting in five fatalities.
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU (fialuridine) was evaluated as a treatment for chronic HBV infection.
