Pilot studies with a 4-week oral course demonstrated significant but unsustained inhibition of viral DNA replication; further trials with longer treatment were stopped after 12 weeks when delayed multi-organ toxicity appeared, including myopathy, lactic acidosis, peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, microvesicular fat infiltration of the liver, and liver failure resulting in five fatalities. Mechanism was proposed to be mitochondrial dysfunction mediated through FIAU incorporation into DNA at internucleotide positions, lowest Ki of FIAU-TP for DNA polymerase gamma, and lactate elevation in cultured human liver cells.

raw_record.support_text: The concern of toxicity in prolonged antiviral therapy was exemplified by the results of a phase II clinical trial with fluoroiodoauracil (FIAU) in chronic hepatitis B patients, which had to be stopped because several patients developed severe liver and kidney dysfunction associated with lactic acidosis. Mitochondrial toxicity was shown to be responsible for these dramatic side effects, and the trial's unfortunate outcome emphasized the need for extensive preclinical studies of both antiviral effect and toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II clinical trial in chronic hepatitis B patients that was stopped because several patients developed severe liver and kidney dysfunction associated with lactic acidosis; mitochondrial toxicity was shown to be responsible for these dramatic side effects.

raw_record.support_text: In November 1995 a 40-year-old white male with no past medical history was diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis on liver biopsy after two months of pravastatin therapy. His total serum bilirubin reached 43 mg/dl and transaminases 2000 U/l. The hepatitis resolved spontaneously over a 3-month period.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis diagnosed on liver biopsy after two months of pravastatin therapy. Total serum bilirubin reached 43 mg/dl; transaminases reached 2000 U/l. Hepatitis resolved spontaneously over a 3-month period, after which the patient's blood counts declined and a subsequent diagnosis of severe aplastic anemia was made.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, pravastatin was implicated in 0.4% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 0.4% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases in the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted after adjudication as true statin-induced DILI, described as mostly mild-moderate, self-limited injury with idiosyncratic timing as a likely class effect. Pravastatin accounted for 2 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated pravastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=2; Swedish 1988-2010 n=2; Spanish Registry n=2 (4.3%). DILIN aggregate (all statins): hepatocellular 12/22, cholestatic 9/22, 4 severe, 1 fatal; latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to halothane in 2 cases. The mean age of patients with fulminant drug-induced hepatitis was significantly higher than those with fulminant hepatitis type B (p<0.001) and fulminant hepatitis of unknown etiology (p<0.05).
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 2 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999). Drug group survival rate 36%.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 94 reports to the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction Committee of patients with liver injury after surgery and halothane anaesthesia (including 13 fatal cases) revealed no other factors responsible for the liver injury than the halothane administration. Eighty-two percent of the total material and 12 of 13 fatal cases had multiple exposures, and the liver injury appeared more severe after repeated exposures, with higher maximum serum bilirubin and SGOT values after an increasing number of halothane exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: 94 ADR reports evaluated in three steps by the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction Committee (medical officer, working party, full committee) with complete medical records; 13 fatal cases; 82% of the total and 12/13 fatal cases had multiple halothane exposures; injury more severe after repeated exposures with higher maximum serum bilirubin and SGOT values; reports from 1966-1972 (Böttiger et al. 1973) plus 1973 cases.

raw_record.support_text: In-vitro sensitization (inhibition or stimulation of leukocyte migration) in response to a liver homogenate obtained from rabbits pre-treated with halothane was found in eight of 12 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis in 1975. After this first report on involvement of an immune-mediated mechanism in halothane hepatitis, it is established today that antibodies against trifluoroacetylated proteins are responsible for the development of this rare but sometimes deleterious sequel of anaesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Immune-mediated halothane hepatitis; antibodies against trifluoroacetylated proteins responsible; reported clinical features include fever (~88%, onset 4-7 days), jaundice (~100%, onset 4-11 days up to 4 weeks), eosinophilia 8-32%, serum auto-antibodies 25-44%; diagnostic ELISA using purified trifluoroacetylated liver microsomal proteins reported sensitivity 79%.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 57-year-old man who underwent two operations (femoral hernia repair followed by ligation of a saphenous varix three days later), with anesthesia maintained by halothane during both procedures. Six days after the second operation he developed spiking fevers up to 105°F, jaundice, and markedly deranged liver chemistries, which returned to normal or near-normal forty-five days after the second operation. A liver biopsy on day 21 showed fatty metamorphosis, liver-cell necrosis, and round-cell infiltration of the portal tracts. The authors add this as a case of hepatitis apparently due to halothane, having reasonably excluded hypoxia, hypotension, pre-existing liver disease, and exposure to other toxins as causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case added to those reported by Lindenbaum and Leifer and by Bunker and Blumenfeld. Patient exposed to halothane anesthesia during two procedures (femoral hernia repair and, three days later, ligation of a saphenous varix). Onset six days after the second operation with spiking fevers to 105°F, jaundice, and markedly deranged liver chemistries; values normal or near-normal by forty-five days after the second operation. Day-21 liver biopsy showed fatty metamorphosis, liver-cell necrosis, and round-cell infiltration of portal tracts. Hypoxia, hypotension, pre-existing liver disease, and other toxin exposure were reasonably excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports patients afflicted with halothane hepatitis, some of whom died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure. Patients 3 and 5 exhibited normal levels of cross-reactive proteins yet both died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure and exhibited very large elevations in plasma AST indicating massive hepatic necrosis. Seven patients with halothane hepatitis were analyzed for expression of 52-kDa and 64-kDa cross-reactive proteins, while patient 6, who did not develop encephalopathy and survived, exhibited very low amounts of these proteins.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients with halothane hepatitis were studied (patients 1-7). Patients 3 and 5 died from complications of fulminant hepatic failure with very large elevations in plasma AST indicating massive hepatic necrosis. Patient 6 survived without encephalopathy. Liver samples were collected at least 17 days after halothane exposure for six patients and 6 days for the remaining patient. This record reflects the halothane-induced hepatitis attribution in a human case series; the paper's main focus is on the immunochemical characterization of cross-reactive 52-kDa and 64-kDa proteins and epoxide hydrolase, which are not themselves the injuring agents.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' study of patients with the hepatocellular type of drug-induced liver injury with concomitant jaundice (fulfilling Hy's rule criteria), the mortality rate varied by drug. The highest mortality was observed in patients with halothane-induced hepatitis (40%), whereas 32 patients with hepatotoxicity caused by erythromycin all survived the liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-induced hepatitis showed the highest mortality (40%) among patients fulfilling Hy's rule criteria (hepatocellular injury with serum ALT >=3x ULN plus bilirubin >=2x ULN without biliary obstruction), from the authors' study of prognostic markers in hepatocellular-type DILI with jaundice (reference 14).

raw_record.support_text: Halothane-associated DILI (hepatic necrosis) case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 49 individual case reports; median age 49 y; 36 female/13 male; median treatment duration not stated; HC 100%, Cs/mixed 0%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 47% (17/49 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 33% (18/49 reported); hepatic necrosis 89%; inflammatory reaction 70%; death or liver transplant 53%; liver biopsy reported in 45/49 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Serum samples were referred for patients clinically diagnosed with halothane hepatitis, who typically developed jaundice, increased serum liver enzymes, and other signs of hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia. Three samples were from male patients (one a 22-month-old infant), and two of the patients died of hepatitis. In most cases other potential causes of hepatitis (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, CMV, EBV) were reported excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of halothane hepatitis made on clinical grounds; patients developed jaundice, increased serum liver enzymes, and other signs of hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia. Three samples were from male patients (one a 22-month-old infant); two patients died of hepatitis. Sera tested negative for hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody to hepatitis C virus; other causes (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus) excluded in most cases. Article evaluates laboratory immunoassay methods (TFA-RSA based) for diagnosing halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old woman underwent elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on 18 July 2003 with halothane anesthesia, and by the fifth postoperative day developed malaise, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and progressive altered consciousness consistent with hepatic encephalopathy, leading to hospitalization with a diagnosis of fulminant hepatitis. Viral, metabolic, autoimmune, and other-drug etiologic study was negative, and she was admitted with the diagnosis of acute fulminant hepatitis due to halothane ('hepatitis aguda fulminante por halotano'), requiring urgent cadaveric ABO-incompatible liver transplantation; histopathologic study of the explant showed submassive necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 33-year-old female without prior morbidity; halothane used as anesthesia for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on 18 July 2003. Onset fifth postoperative day with malaise, nausea, vomiting, jaundice and progressive altered consciousness consistent with hepatic encephalopathy. Viral, metabolic, autoimmune, and other-drug etiologic workup negative. Diagnosis: acute fulminant hepatitis due to halothane. Explant histology showed submassive necrosis. Required urgent liver transplant (ABO-incompatible cadaver graft A to recipient O, 8 Aug 2003) with protocol including intra- and post-transplant plasmapheresis, splenectomy and quadruple immunosuppression (methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide, thymoglobulin, cyclosporine). At 5 years patient asymptomatic with normal liver enzymes on low-dose immunosuppression.

raw_record.support_text: The paper introduces a rare but severe form of hepatitis caused by the inhalation anesthetic halothane, and describes that a high proportion of patients with this toxicity had specific lymphocytes and antibodies in their blood directed against halothane-altered liver neoantigens. Examples include a leukocyte cell migration test suggesting that 8 of 12 patients with unexplained fulminant hepatic failure after halothane had specific T-cell lymphocytes, a direct lymphocyte cytotoxicity assay positive in three of four patients, and circulating IgG antibodies detected by indirect immunofluorescence (7 of 11 patients) or ELISA (16 of 24 patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Rare but severe form of hepatitis caused by this inhalation anesthetic (CF3CHClBr), still widely used in adults in the UK and Europe and an agent of choice for children. Immune-mediated mechanism: patients had specific lymphocytes and antibodies against halothane-altered liver neoantigens; leukocyte cell migration (T-cell) test positive in 8/12 patients with unexplained fulminant hepatic failure after halothane; direct lymphocyte cytotoxicity assay positive in 3/4; indirect immunofluorescence 7/11; ELISA 16/24.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane is given as an example of a drug with very well documented hepatotoxicity, with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge, and was commonly reported to be associated with hepatotoxicity in early DILI research.
raw_record.extra_details: Inhalational anesthetic; rechallenge reproduced DILI; listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported cases of drug-induced liver injury (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: Of the 40 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis included in the final data analysis, 4 developed fulminant hepatic failure as defined by Trey and Davidson. Of these, one died from a secondary cytomegalovirus infection 5 weeks after liver transplantation and another died before a donor organ became available; of the remaining two, one made a spontaneous recovery and the second died. All four fulminant cases developed grade 4 encephalopathy. The remaining 36 patients had no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis; 4 developed fulminant hepatic failure (Trey and Davidson criteria), all with grade 4 encephalopathy; among them one died from secondary cytomegalovirus infection 5 weeks after liver transplantation, one died before a donor organ became available, one recovered spontaneously, and one died; remaining 36 patients had no encephalopathy. In 12 patients (30%) there was a documented hepatitis-like reaction to a previous halothane anaesthetic, and at least 27 patients (68%) had received documented previous halothane anaesthetics (median 2). Interval between final anaesthetic and most recent previous anaesthetic was 2 weeks to 20 years (median 1 year). Interval between anaesthetic exposure and onset of hepatic injury was 1-24 days (median 6 days); peak recorded AST was 61-14,500 IU/l (normal 0-45), maximal prothrombin time prolongation 68 s. Previous operations were major in 9 patients and minor in the remainder, with no recorded surgical or anaesthetic complications. Peak AST for fulminant cases was 5990 (4140-14,500) IU/l versus 1000 (61-2000) for non-fulminant; survival 25% (1/4) in fulminant versus 100% (36/36) in non-fulminant.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies halothane as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 5 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Halothane produced both cytotoxic and cholestatic damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane was the causative agent in 5 of 53 patients; produced both cytotoxic and cholestatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane hepatitis is one of the more frequently occurring idiosyncratic drug reactions and accounted for 5% of the overall number of FHF cases in the series between 1973 and 1985. FHF typically develops within 5-15 days after the second or subsequent exposure to halothane, usually affecting obese, atopic, middle-aged females.
raw_record.extra_details: One of the more frequently occurring idiosyncratic drug reactions causing ALF; 5% of FHF cases in the unit 1973-1985; FHF typically develops 5-15 days after second or subsequent exposure; usually affects obese, atopic, middle-aged females; a specific halothane antibody test has been described as a potential discriminator from other causes of ALF after anaesthesia.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from three patients with halothane hepatitis reacted with halothane-induced neoantigens in rat liver microsomes by immunoblotting: patient 1 recognized 100 kDa and 76 kDa neoantigens, patient 2 the 100, 76, 59 and 54 kDa neoantigens, and patient 3 the 57 kDa neoantigen. These neoantigens were shown to carry the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) hapten derived from halothane metabolism, establishing the immune response to halothane-modified liver proteins in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated form of DILI. Antibodies in the sera of halothane hepatitis patients recognize TFA-modified neoantigens (100, 76, 59, 54, 57 kDa) that are formed when the reactive CF3COX metabolite of halothane covalently binds liver microsomal proteins. The 59 kDa-TFA neoantigen was identified as a microsomal carboxylesterase glycoprotein (EC 3.1.1.1); antibodies reacted only negligibly with the native unmodified protein. TFA-lysine only partially inhibits antibody binding, indicating epitopes comprise the TFA hapten plus portions of the carrier protein. Similar TFA-labeled proteins were detected in the liver of a halothane-treated patient (100, 76, 59, 54 and 57 kDa forms), supporting relevance of the rat neoantigens to human halothane hepatitis. TFA labeling occurs via direct reaction of CF3COX with proteins; sodium trifluoroacetate, ethyl trifluoroacetate, and trifluoroethanol administered to rats produced no detectable protein labeling.

raw_record.support_text: The study analyzed 20 cases of halothane hepatitis notified in institutional pharmacovigilance between 2012-2016, involving 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years. The injury was cholestatic in 12 cases and cytolytic in 8 cases; three cases turned out to be fulminant, resulting in death of the patient. Free radicals produced by liver metabolism of halothane can modify cellular proteins and introduce neo-antigens to the immune system; sensitization to these neo-antigens induces a more severe response after multiple exposures, with most type 2 hepatitis cases occurring after repeated contact.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 halothane hepatitis cases notified in institutional pharmacovigilance 2012-2016; 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years; cholestatic pattern in 12 cases and cytolytic in 8; 3 fulminant cases resulted in death. Mechanism: halothane metabolism in the liver produces free radicals that modify cellular proteins and create neo-antigens; immune sensitization to neo-antigens causes more severe response after repeated exposure, and most type 2 hepatitis cases occur after repeated contact. Paper notes newer halogenated anesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) are less metabolized in the liver and cause few cases of sensitization.

raw_record.support_text: The author discusses halothane-associated hepatitis and hepatic failure. In the Neuberger and Williams series, three of 46 patients with the most severe form of hepatic failure after halothane had been re-exposed after intervals of two, three, and six years, and about 60% of patients with adequate data had had a documented adverse reaction to halothane previously. Halothane associated hepatitis is described as an extremely rare problem that appears if enough patients are exposed, including in children.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes severe hepatic failure in 46 patients (Neuberger and Williams series) with three re-exposed after 2, 3, and 6 years; ~60% of patients with adequate data had a prior documented adverse reaction to halothane not brought to the anaesthetist's attention; problem first reported in 1958; also reported in children but not to the same extent as in adults; several patients known to have had halothane hepatitis have subsequently been successfully anaesthetised again with the agent.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical study the incidence of halothane-induced liver injury (halothane hepatitis) was compared between phenobarbital-treated and untreated patients. The incidence was significantly higher in phenobarbital-treated patients than in untreated controls (7/100 vs. 1/179, p < 0.01), and remained higher when restricted to patients not previously exposed to halothane anesthesia (4/71 vs. 1/168, p < 0.05). This explicitly attributes human liver injury to halothane anesthesia, with phenobarbital as an enhancing factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of halothane-induced liver injury reported higher in phenobarbital-treated patients (7/100) than untreated (1/179), p<0.01; and among patients without previous halothane exposure 4/71 vs 1/168, p<0.05. Previous halothane exposure noted as a risk factor for development of halothane-induced liver injury; male:female ratio and degree of obesity (percent of standard body weight) were comparable between groups.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane was the third most common cause of DILI (10.7% of patients). Halothane was mainly hepatocellular in 75% of cases, and 25% for both cholestatic and mixed forms, with short interval between drug intake and symptoms (8.3 ± 3.3 days).
raw_record.extra_details: 8 cases (10.7%); hepatocellular 6 (75%), mixed 2 (25%), cholestatic 0; time interval 8.3 ± 3.3 days; the only patient transferred to urgent liver transplantation due to DILI was a 30-year-old female with acute hepatocellular halothane-induced injury; biopsy in one case showed centrilobular necrosis with poor outcome.

raw_record.support_text: A 29 year old woman was transferred with fulminant hepatic failure secondary to halothane anaesthesia. Prior to transfer she had a normal plasma urea; on arrival she was unconscious with a plasma urea of 10.8 mmol/l, plasma creatinine of 496 µmol/l and grossly abnormal liver function tests. The case is presented as part of a series of patients with acute or acute-on-chronic liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anaesthesia in a 29 year old woman; case described in the context of diagnosing renal impairment. On transfer she was unconscious with plasma urea 10.8 mmol/l, creatinine 496 µmol/l, grossly abnormal liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: Between January 1968 and December 1983, 48 patients were referred to King's College Hospital with fulminant hepatic failure following halothane anaesthesia (31 female, ratio 1.8:1, age range 21-76 years, median 57). The interval between halothane exposure (anaesthetic) and onset of jaundice ranged from 2 to 26 days (median 5 days), and the median interval to onset of encephalopathy was 9 days. The paper attributes this fulminant hepatic failure causally to halothane anaesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis/fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anaesthesia. In the 1968-1983 series of 48 patients: 94% had at least one documented prior halothane exposure; 33 (69%) underwent only minor surgery (lasting <45 min) with no other operative cause for liver failure; 38 died including all with grade III/IV fulminant hepatic failure; 10 survived (5 with grade I/II hepatic encephalopathy, remainder non-encephalopathic); interval from anaesthetic to death 11-73 days (median 23). A serum antibody to a hepatocyte plasma membrane antigen associated with halothane metabolism is present only in patients with clinical halothane hepatitis, detectable in about 75% of cases; absent in halothane-exposed patients with no/minor liver-function abnormality or with liver failure from other causes (e.g., hepatitis A). In a 1983-1985 series of 40 tested sera (9 King's patients, 31 referred): 21 met fulminant hepatic failure definition (hepatic encephalopathy); age range 1-75 (median 59); ALT 127-4000 IU/l (normal <40); 65% had minor surgery; non-encephalopathic patients survived while 12 of 17 encephalopathic (71%, including all grade III/IV) died.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from 39 patients who developed hepatitis following halothane anaesthesia between January 1983 and December 1985 were tested for antibodies to halothane-induced liver antigens using an ELISA; 22 had hepatitis without encephalopathy. All patients had undergone previous anaesthesia 17 days to 13 yr (median 3 yr) earlier. Twelve of the patients died. In all patients, evidence of hepatic damage had appeared within 28 days of a documented halothane anaesthetic and no other cause for the liver damage was identified (hepatitis A and B, cytomegalovirus and toxoplasma excluded serologically, no history of alcohol excess), forming a case series of halothane-associated hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 39 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia; spectrum ranges from minor rises in serum aminotransferase to fulminant hepatic failure; 9 of 11 Liver Unit patients had fulminant hepatic failure overall (7 of 28 referred sera) and 12 of 39 patients died; hepatic damage appeared within 28 days of a documented halothane anaesthetic; all had prior halothane exposure 17 days to 13 yr (median 3 yr) earlier. Halothane antibodies detected in 12/16 (75%) patients with hepatic encephalopathy and 16/23 (70%) without. The study focused on diagnostic value of halothane antibodies, which are absent in other liver diseases and in patients with fulminant hepatic failure from other causes.

raw_record.support_text: All 38 Japanese patients had been diagnosed from clinical and biological evidence as having halothane hepatitis, with onset of jaundice or abnormal liver function within less than 3 weeks of anesthesia; none abused alcohol or took other known hepatotoxic drugs at illness onset. Five cases were fulminant hepatitis; two who received large fresh blood transfusions for fulminant hepatic failure developed secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis developed within <3 weeks of halothane anesthesia in all 38 cases. Jaundice group (24 cases) had female:male ratio 2:1 (4:1 among fulminant cases), pyrexia (>38°C) in all jaundice patients, eosinophilia (>=6%) in 64–68%, and 42% had prior halothane anesthesia; 5 cases of fulminant hepatitis were included. Two patients had secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis attributed to large fresh-blood transfusion for fulminant hepatic failure. HLA-Bw44 was increased in non-jaundice patients (RR 6.86, P<0.001) and HLA-Bw52 and DR2 in jaundice patients; Aw24-Bw52-DR2 haplotype frequency was high in jaundice patients (Hf=0.2362). All patients recuperated with complete recovery of liver function except the two with transfusion-related complications.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that considerable controversy has surrounded hepatic injury associated with halothane, but that the passage of time and accumulation of cases has led to near consensus regarding the reality of the clinical syndrome. The study analyzed a large number of cases with both biopsy and autopsy material, documenting spotty, submassive, and massive hepatic necrosis, with 13 fatal cases showing massive necrosis with nearly all hepatocytes destroyed.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia, with severity of liver injury related to repeated exposures within a 3-month interval. Necrosis included spotty (biopsy, n=12), submassive (biopsy n=16, autopsy n=30, biopsy n=8), and massive (autopsy, n=13 fatal cases). Inflammatory infiltrates predominantly lymphocytic with variable neutrophils, plasma cells, and eosinophils; cholangiolar proliferation, cholestasis, and endophlebitis of terminal hepatic venules in some cases; early fibrosis and postnecrotic cirrhosis in some cases. Authors note sharply outlined centrilobular necrosis as more characteristic of halothane injury than classical viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane hepatic necrosis as a human liver-injury entity with age-related morbidity and mortality similar to viral hepatitis. In the authors' small series of five patients with halothane hepatic necrosis, there was one death, in an adolescent female. Related text notes that unexplained postoperative fever is one of the most constant features indicating liver damage from halothane, and that jaundice is typically delayed unless there have been multiple exposures to halothane anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of five patients with halothane hepatic necrosis; one death in an adolescent female. Unexplained postoperative fever is a constant feature indicating liver damage; jaundice typically delayed unless multiple halothane anesthesia exposures. Age-related morbidity and mortality similar to viral hepatitis. Presented under the heading 'Halothane Hepatitis'.

raw_record.support_text: The review attributes acute hepatic necrosis to the anaesthetic halothane, which causes it in a very small proportion of cases in which it is administered. Halothane hepatitis is heralded by unexplained pyrexia about a week after anaesthesia, with jaundice appearing days to weeks later, is more frequent after multiple than single exposure, has a high mortality, and death occurs in fulminant hepatic failure; the authors describe a fatal hepatitis in a child who had received halothane for less than three minutes. Light and electron microscopy showed lesions similar, but not identical, to acute viral hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis occurs in a small proportion of administrations, unrelated to duration of anaesthesia; heralded by unexplained pyrexia about a week after anaesthesia, jaundice days to weeks later; more frequent after multiple exposure; fatal case in a child after <3 minutes exposure; mortality high with death in fulminant hepatic failure; lesions similar but not identical to acute viral hepatitis on light and electron microscopy.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-nine patients became jaundiced after three exposures to halothane anaesthesia; their ages ranged from 19 to 77 years (mean 55.7±16.0) and 17 (59%) died. In cases with three halothane exposures, the interval between the third exposure and onset of jaundice ranged from 1 to 25 days (mean 4.6 days). Fourteen additional patients exposed two times to halothane also developed jaundice, and among 16 patients with four to six halothane exposures, 10 (63%) were reported to have died from liver failure. The paper attributes these episodes of jaundice and deaths from liver failure to halothane anaesthesia exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of repeated halothane anaesthesia: 29 patients with three exposures (17 deaths, 59%); patients with two exposures (table V, including an anaesthetist with occupational exposure, case 33, who recovered); 16 patients with four to six exposures (10 died from liver failure, one died from coronary thrombosis). Interval between first and third exposure ranged from 14 days to five years (75% within 28 days); interval between third exposure and onset of jaundice 1-25 days, mean 4.6 days. Some patients were induced with propanidid (case 77) or methohexitone (case 97), which were not themselves attributed as causes. One case (case 80) became jaundiced days after each of three exposures. Occupational halothane exposure cases reported in cases 33 and 83.

raw_record.support_text: In the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study analysis of the first 150 cases from 73 centers, 35 of the patients developed massive liver necrosis less than three weeks after halothane anesthesia, and 27 (77 per cent) of these had multiple exposures to halothane. The paper describes halothane-associated fulminant hepatic failure as a small but clinically important risk, noting that this complication was present in nearly one quarter of the reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study; 150 cases collected from 73 centers; 35 patients developed massive liver necrosis less than 3 weeks after halothane anesthesia; 27 (77%) had multiple exposures to halothane; risk judged small but complication present in nearly one quarter of reported cases. Paragraph 57 notes postoperative 'unexplained' fever after halothane exposure is an important warning sign to investigate before further exposure, and advises avoiding multiple exposure when possible.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic necrosis, whether due to fulminant hepatitis or drug toxicity, carries an appalling mortality. In the latest account from the Fulminant Hepatic Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970) the mortality of the 284 patients who went into coma was 82%, with a figure of 96% for those with a halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The text explicitly attributes hepatic necrosis to halothane using an induced-injury construction.
raw_record.extra_details: From the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970); among the 284 patients who went into coma the overall mortality was 82%, and it was 96% among those with halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The 96% figure applies to halothane-induced hepatic necrosis cases who had progressed to coma.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old woman who underwent cholecystectomy under halothane anesthesia in 1967 developed postoperative vomiting, dark urine, jaundice and a tender enlarged liver, with marked eosinophilia and elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and SGOT; liver biopsy was interpreted as subacute hepatitis and the diagnosis was halothane-induced hepatitis. She recovered and a later cataract extraction under halothane-free anesthesia was uneventful.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane given in 1967 for cholecystectomy; symptoms began by postoperative day 13 (indigestion, chills, vomiting), dark urine day 18, jaundice day 22. Labs: eosinophils up to 37%, prothrombin time 29% of normal, alkaline phosphatase 24 KA units (normal 4-17), total bilirubin 3.0 mg/100 ml, SGOT 150 U/ml. Liver biopsy at day 38 showed subacute hepatitis; the patient recovered without specific treatment. Other drugs received during that episode included meperidine, atropine, thiopental, succinylcholine, gallamine, neostigmine, nitrous oxide, aspirin, codeine, propoxyphene, carbromal and barbiturates. Alias: Fluothane.

raw_record.support_text: A series of patients developed unexplained fever, jaundice, markedly elevated transaminases (SGOT and SGPT), hyperbilirubinemia, and prolonged prothrombin times following repeated halothane anesthesia exposure before surgery; multiple patients in the series died from hepatic failure during the necrotic phase of the illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Table of 8 biopsied surviving patients and 14 patients who died in the necrotic phase, 11 in the resorptive phase, 8 in the regenerative phase, plus 8 patients without tissues. Cases followed prior halothane exposure (1-4 exposures) with onset of fever and jaundice days to weeks after the last exposure. Illness often followed obesity and repeated exposure. Laboratory features included bilirubin up to ~40 mg%, SGOT/SGPT up to >4,000-8,000 units, prothrombin times below 25%, and reduced liver weights (e.g., 450-1,730 g) in fatal cases. Histology showed centrolobular swelling/necrosis, cholestasis, and pigmented macrophages.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe humans with halothane-induced liver injury: one patient recovered from severe hepatic failure after four halothane exposures and later bled from esophageal varices with liver fibrosis on biopsy; three patients in Boston developed postoperative cholestatic jaundice after multiple halothane exposures, with biopsy in one showing hepatocellular disease; and serum from seven patients with halothane-associated hepatitis tested negative for Australia antigen. The clinical and pathological diagnoses were 'massive hepatic necrosis, probably due to halothane', and halothane hepatitis was regarded as not dose-related but with occasional fatal sequelae.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury followed multiple/repeated anesthetic exposures (e.g., four exposures in one patient) and was described as not dose-related; presentations included postoperative cholestatic jaundice, hepatocellular disease on biopsy, hepatitis, hepatic fibrosis with esophageal variceal bleeding after recovery, and massive hepatic necrosis; occasional fatal sequelae were noted; serum of 7 halothane-hepatitis patients was negative for Australia antigen; halothane hepatitis to be suspected when unexplained postoperative fever or jaundice occurs.

raw_record.support_text: The National Halothane Study (1959-1962) evaluated ~850,000 anesthetic cases; halothane was used in 30% of cases. Among 82 fatalities with histologic confirmation of massive hepatic necrosis, nine had no obvious cause such as shock, overwhelming infection, or pre-existing hepatic disease; seven of the nine had received halothane and four had more than one exposure to halothane. Additional reported cases describe massive liver necrosis developing within three weeks of halothane anesthesia, with multiple exposures common, including a case of fulminant hepatocellular necrosis after three exposures despite corticosteroid treatment, and a series of 42 patients with hepatitis after halothane exposure in whom survival fell with repeated exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: National Halothane Study covered 1959-1962 with ~850,000 anesthetic cases; overall mortality 1.87% for halothane vs 1.93% for all agents. 82 fatalities with histologic confirmation of massive hepatic necrosis; 9 without other obvious cause (7 halothane-exposed, 4 with >1 exposure). Trey et al (1968) reported 150 cases of fulminant hepatic failure; in 35 patients massive liver necrosis developed in <3 weeks after halothane anesthesia, 77% with multiple exposures; unexplained post-surgical fever after halothane warranted investigation for hepatocellular damage. Aach and Kissane (1968) reported a patient with three halothane exposures who died of fulminant hepatocellular necrosis despite large-dose corticosteroids. Klion/Schaffner/Popper reported 42 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis, including two exposed occupationally rather than as patients; survival was 6/12 after one exposure, 7/22 (32%) after two, 0/5 after three, and 0/1 after four. Study concluded halothane was an extremely safe anesthetic relative to others used.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 42 patients with hepatitis after halothane anesthesia, 15 (33%) survived and 27 (67%) died; the material was biased toward fatal cases because most were referred for histologic diagnosis. Ages of survivors ranged from 26 to 77 years, with no significant difference between survivors and nonsurvivors.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis was described in 42 patients who underwent anesthesia for surgery; 15 (33%) survived and 27 (67%) died, with referral bias toward fatal cases. Survival was worse with more exposures: of 12 patients with one exposure half survived, of 22 with two exposures 7 (32%) survived, and all patients given halothane three or four times died; two individuals with multiple nonanesthetizing occupational vapour exposures survived (one factory worker, one anesthesiologist). Postoperative fever was noted in 37 patients (related to onset of hepatitis when persistent or recurrent), five patients remained afebrile before jaundice; the shortest interval between two exposures was 3 days. Fever after one exposure developed within 8-14 days, after multiple exposures from day 1 to 11.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 7, a 41-year-old woman developed jaundice and deep coma with progressive liver failure after halothane anesthesia used for a radium implantation and, three weeks later, for a total hysterectomy. The authors conclude that the clinical course and pathologic findings — a 1,580 gm pale yellow-tan, extremely firm liver with diffuse, primarily central necrosis and no evidence of regeneration — were consistent with toxic hepatitis caused by halothane anesthesia administered during the two surgical procedures. The patient ultimately died from infectious complications of hysterectomy in a debilitated state.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane general anesthesia given for two surgical procedures (cervical radium implantation followed three weeks later by total hysterectomy). Patient obese, deeply jaundiced (bilirubin 28 mg/100 cc, direct 19.2 mg/100 cc), SGOT 1,280 units, prothrombin time 26 s (control 12 s), serum ammonia 226 µg/100 cc, progressed to deep coma. Exchange transfusions transiently reversed coma on four occasions (12 units infused, 11 removed each time). Course complicated by ascites, peritonitis, candidemia (C. albicans), Klebsiella urine infection, and emergence of chronic liver disease. Death followed left-sided seizure, hemiplegia, and intracranial hemorrhage from a probable ruptured mycotic aneurysm. Postmortem liver 1,580 gm, pale yellow-tan, extremely firm, with diffuse primarily central necrosis, viable hepatocytes but no regeneration.

raw_record.support_text: Among 17 patients with acute hepatic failure (10 males, 7 females, aged 18-42 years), hepatic failure was due to fulminant viral hepatitis B in 10 patients, halothane-induced hepatitis in 3 patients, intoxication with Amanita phalloides in 3 patients, and fulminant viral hepatitis A in 1 patient. Halothane is thus explicitly attributed as the cause of hepatitis leading to acute hepatic failure in 3 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 of 17 patients with acute hepatic failure in the case cohort developed halothane-induced hepatitis; the cohort also included patients with viral hepatitis B (10), Amanita phalloides intoxication (3), and viral hepatitis A (1). The paper's main focus was measurement of the prostacyclin synthesis stimulating plasma factor, not causality assessment of halothane.

raw_record.support_text: In three cases, halothane-induced acute hepatitis was severe and accompanied by bridging necrosis and hepatic functional abnormalities persisting for 6 weeks to 3 months; the lesions healed within 10 to 14 months except for minimal residual portal fibrosis and fatty infiltration. In none of these surviving patients did the lesion progress to chronic aggressive hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: The three cases had severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis and hepatic functional abnormalities persisting 6 weeks to 3 months; lesions healed within 10 to 14 months, leaving only minimal residual portal fibrosis and fatty infiltration. A hypersensitivity reaction was considered the likely mechanism; corticosteroids were used in two patients with apparent benefit while the third recovered without them.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews the clinical features of halothane hepatitis in humans, describing fever as characteristically the first sign: among 42 cases reviewed by Klion et al., 37 had fever, and in 94 cases reported by Bottiger et al. the average delay in fever onset was 7 days after first exposure and 4 days after multiple exposures. Across many series some patients lacked fever (Walton et al. reported 21% never experienced postoperative fever). The paper further describes jaundice latency (jaundice appearing 10-28 days after single exposure, 3-17 days after multiple exposures), lab findings typical of parenchymal damage (transaminases 500-1500 IU or greater, bilirubin 5-15 mg/dl or greater), and prognosis, with 60% mortality in patients with bilirubin >10 mg/dl and 100% mortality when prothrombin time exceeded 20 seconds.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane administered as an inhaled anesthetic; liver injury termed halothane hepatitis. Fever present in 75% of cases, chills 30%, rash 10%, myalgia 20%, anorexia/nausea 50%. Jaundice never in the first 2 postoperative days unless prior halothane anesthesia within the prior 2 weeks; delayed jaundice distinguishes halothane hepatitis from benign postoperative cholestasis. Latency to first symptom/jaundice: 6/11 days (single exposure) and 3/6 days (multiple exposure); Klion series 10-28 days to icterus after single and 3-17 days after multiple exposures; Bottiger average jaundice at 8 and 7 days. Transaminases 500-1500 IU or greater, bilirubin 5-15 mg/dl or greater; SGOT and alk phos not predictive. 60% mortality with bilirubin >10 mg/dl vs none below 5 mg/dl; 100% mortality with prothrombin time >20 seconds. Eosinophilia in 32% (Walton, 76 patients); liver-kidney microsomal antibodies in 28%. Mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients with acute hepatitis, drug hepatitis was attributed to halothane in 1 patient with uncomplicated hepatitis, 1 survivor of fulminant hepatitis, and 6 patients who died of fulminant hepatitis, identifying halothane as a cause of drug-induced hepatitis, including fatal fulminant courses.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane drug hepatitis occurred in 1 uncomplicated hepatitis case and 8 fulminant hepatitis cases (1 survivor, 6 non-survivors who died). Fulminant hepatitis defined as acute hepatitis with encephalopathy stage 3 or 4.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial discusses halothane hepatitis as a form of human drug-induced liver injury occurring after halothane anesthesia, encompassing both severe or fulminant cases and more frequent mild, often asymptomatic cases. It notes that features of hypersensitivity are present in no more than approximately 25 per cent of cases and occur equally in severe and mild halothane-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases include fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anesthesia (11 patients, 14 serum samples); centrilobular necrosis seen in many cases is characteristic of true hepatotoxicity; the paper concludes that 'idiosyncrasy' is a more appropriate designation than 'hypersensitivity', accommodating both idiosyncratic allergic reactions and metabolic idiosyncrasy with enhanced toxic-metabolite production; halothane is also described as toxic to cultured hepatocyte membranes and hepatotoxic in several animal models.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined 35 sera from patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis. 17 of these sera recognized the trifluoroacetylated protein CF₃CO-RSA on immunoblots in a manner sensitive to competition by CF₃CO-Lys and lipoic acid, and these sera were further analyzed for reactivity against the lipoylated autoantigens (E2 subunits of the PDC, OGDC, and BCOADC, and protein X). The authors also analyzed liver biopsies of seven patients with halothane hepatitis and observed unusually low amounts of immunorecognizable 52 kDa proteins and the E2 subunit of the PDC in 5 of 7 patients, suggesting a possible association between low aberrant expression of these hepatic proteins and susceptibility to halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis (drug-induced hepatitis) with an apparent autoimmune component: sera from patients reacted with CF₃CO-RSA and with the lipoylated E2 subunits of the PDC (15/17 reactive sera), OGDC (13/17), BCOADC (9/17), and protein X (13/17). Two autoantibody populations were distinguished by competition with CF₃CO-Lys/lipoic acid. Liver immunoblots showed low immunodetectable amounts of 52 kDa proteins and PDC-E2 in 5 of 7 halothane hepatitis patients, suggesting HLA-like or expression-related susceptibility, mechanistically linked to lipoic-acid-containing autoantigens also involved in primary biliary cirrhosis. 35 patients with clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis studied.

raw_record.support_text: Specifically sensitized lymphocytes were demonstrated in a 27-year-old male patient with halothane-induced hepatitis. A strong proliferative response (stimulation index 8) was induced by serum collected from a healthy donor 60 min after halothane anaesthesia; sera taken before, 30 or 120 min after anaesthesia did not stimulate the patient's lymphocytes. The test was done in quintuplicate 10 days after halothane exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: 27-year-old male; halothane anaesthesia exposure; LTT demonstrated specifically sensitized T-lymphocytes; metabolite-containing serum (60 min post-anaesthesia) elicited stimulation index 8, 7-day culture, 3x10^5 cells/well, quintuplicate, performed 10 days after exposure. Halothane is also listed among substances known to have sensitizing potency that frequently give positive LTT results in patients with suspected drug-induced hepatic injuries (p:6).

raw_record.support_text: Clinical data are presented on 12 patients with presum ed halothane-associated hepatitis, each having had one or more previous halothane anaesthetics, with intervals between anaesthesia and jaundice of 3-14 days. Seven of the 12 patients died and the remainder survived. Postoperative pyrexia and autoantibodies (liver-kidney microsomal and smooth-muscle antibodies) were variable across cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 12 patients with presumed halothane-associated hepatitis; 7 of 12 died (patients 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12), rest survived. Each patient had 1-2 previous halothane anaesthetics, 6 days to 7 years before the index exposure; interval between anaesthesia and jaundice 3-14 days. Postoperative pyrexia and autoantibodies (LKM 1/80-1/120, SMA 1/20) variable. Leucocyte-migration test: with liver homogenate from halothane-exposed rabbits as antigen, migration index (sensitisation) was abnormal in 8 of 12 patients while normal for healthy controls (median 1.06, range 0.77-1.21), other liver diseases (1.0), and halothane-no-hepatitis (1.0); halothane-hepatitis group migration index 0.98 (0.81-1.19). Sensitisation was specific to the halothane homogenate, with normal indices using ether-anaesthetised-animal antigen.

raw_record.support_text: Among 62 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the etiology was considered viral in 26; in 5 other patients ALF was considered due to toxic hepatitis caused by the administration of ketoconazole, α-methyl dopa, halothane, pyroxicam, and disulfiram, respectively. Thus halothane was attributed as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to ALF in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution made in a single ALF patient within a 62-patient acute liver failure series; drug administration identified as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane-associated liver damage includes two distinct patterns. A rare but severe form termed 'halothane hepatitis' is characterized by extremely large serum transaminase elevations, jaundice, massive hepatic necrosis, and a significant fraction of patients develop liver failure in whom mortality is common. This rare severe form caused a marked reduction in halothane usage.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is a rare but serious dose-independent adverse reaction in anesthetized patients: serum transaminase elevations, jaundice, massive hepatic necrosis, liver failure with common mortality. In this study sera came from 56 patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis defined as otherwise unexplained severe, histologically confirmed hepatitis with normal preoperative liver function. Patients are frequently female, obese, and late middle age, though the syndrome is also described in males, non-obese patients, and children. Most patients had multiple halothane exposures; median interval from anesthesia to jaundice is 7 days; findings include pyrexia, eosinophilia, circulating immune complexes, autoantibodies, and antibodies to halothane-induced liver antigens. Halothane hepatitis is considered idiosyncratic and dose-independent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses patients with halothane hepatitis and contrasts their autoantibody patterns with those in patients with hepatic reactions caused by drugs other than halothane, describing cases of hepatitis caused by tienilic acid and dihydralazine. In halothane hepatitis, sera contain autoantibodies against multiple human hepatic microsomal proteins, with marked inter-individual variation in response intensity and in the number and nature of the microsomal proteins recognized; formation of TFA-modified protein antigens is proposed to cause immune dysregulation in exposed patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis studied in human patients; sera contain autoantibodies to multiple TFA-modified hepatic microsomal proteins with marked inter-individual variation in intensity and in the number/nature of proteins recognized; the most intense responses were seen in three patients with hepatitis; immune-mediated reaction proposed via covalent binding of TFA-groups and immune dysregulation; autoantibodies also seen in some halothane-treated patients without hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from 10 patients with halothane hepatitis stained TFA-labeled proteins in hepatocytes from a rat exposed to halothane, whereas sera from nine patients with multiple halothane exposures but no evidence of toxicity did not stain the same halothane-exposed rat liver. This identifies halothane as causing an immune-mediated hepatotoxicity directed against trifluoroacetylated hepatic proteins (halothane hepatitis).
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism is an immune response against hepatic proteins altered by the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) metabolite acting as immunogens. Evidence: sera from 10 patients with halothane hepatitis immunostained TFA-labeled proteins in halothane-exposed rat hepatocytes, while sera from 9 patients with multiple halothane exposure without toxicity did not.

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to amoxicillin in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 1 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999).

raw_record.support_text: A 42-year-old Caucasian female presented with ALF 21 days after receiving amoxicillin and underwent successful liver transplantation on hospital day 19. All competing causes were excluded, liver pathology was consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, and the case was deemed 'definite/highly probable' using causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was 42-year-old female; ALF with coagulopathy and encephalopathy; latency 21 days after amoxicillin; successful liver transplantation on hospital day 19; all competing causes excluded; pathology consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; causality scored definite/highly probable (CIOMS).

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data are compatible with a diagnosis of severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, probably due to amoxicillin. Symptoms appeared 6 days after stopping amoxicillin treatment; symptoms reappeared after the drug was discontinued and taken again, interpreted as a positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient presented 6 days after stopping amoxicillin with jaundice and malaise; laboratory showed increased direct bilirubin, ALP, and GGT. Viral hepatitis serology (HAV, HBV, HCV) and antinuclear/antismooth muscle antibodies negative; antimitochondrial antibodies positive but anti-M2 negative; abdominal ultrasound normal. Liver biopsy (4 weeks after jaundice onset) showed pronounced centrolobular cholestasis with inflammatory infiltrates and focal portal inflammatory infiltrate involving biliary epithelium, compatible with both toxic hepatitis and PBC. Bilirubin and ALP decreased after 1 month of jaundice and later normalized; patient well with no signs of liver damage at 2 years follow-up. Differential diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis considered but drug-mediated toxic hepatitis favored based on positive rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old woman was diagnosed with abdominal actinomycosis and received amoxicillin treatment. She displayed hepatocellular and bile-duct injury with elevated liver enzymes and was diagnosed with amoxicillin-induced cholestatic hepatitis. When amoxicillin was discontinued, her symptoms improved and liver enzyme levels reduced toward normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 39-year-old woman given oral amoxicillin 2 g/day for abdominal actinomycosis. Hepatocellular and bile-duct injury with elevated liver enzymes; diagnosed as cholestatic hepatitis; symptoms and enzyme levels improved/dechallenge response on amoxicillin discontinuation. Also described elsewhere in the paper as a very low-rate complication of amoxicillin with benign course typically resolving within months.

raw_record.support_text: Among antibiotic-related acute liver failure, amoxicillin was implicated in n=1 case of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: Among 81 patients with fulminant hepatitis, 11 (14%) were classified as fulminant drug-induced hepatitis. The cause was attributed to mercazole in 1 case.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed cause of fulminant drug-induced hepatitis in 1 of 11 drug-induced cases in a Japanese cohort (1980-1999).

raw_record.support_text: This letter describes a new case of acute cholestatic hepatitis secondary to treatment with methimazole (metimazol). Although this adverse effect has an incidence below 1%, its associated mortality of approximately 20-25% makes it an adverse effect to consider.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a single new case of acute cholestatic hepatitis secondary to methimazole, with a typical cholestatic syndrome of icterus, coluria, acholia and pruritus plus elevated cholestasis parameters; diagnosis supported by temporal sequence (typically 2 weeks to 3 months after thionamide start), exclusion of other causes, and progressive normalization of liver parameters after drug withdrawal. Histologically expected to correspond to hepatocanalicular cholestasis. This patient presented a dissociated cholestasis pattern and was asymptomatic, hindering early diagnosis. Mortality of this adverse effect estimated near 20-25%.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, a 67-year-old woman with Graves' disease, was started on methimazole (and propranolol), and she developed fulminant hepatitis, which after extensive workup was determined to be due to the methimazole. Methimazole was withdrawn, and the patient's liver tests had been elevated precipitably at presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Methimazole was given at 40 mg twice daily for Graves' thyrotoxicosis. LFTs elevated precipitously with features of fulminant hepatitis, and causality was determined after extensive workup. Methimazole was stopped. The patient was subsequently deemed unsuitable for thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine ablation.

raw_record.support_text: The summary states that in rare cases within the first few weeks of therapy, methimazole can cause severe and reversible cholestatic jaundice, which is described as a rare but serious adverse effect. Patients are also advised to watch for early symptoms of antithyroid drug adverse effects, including hepatic toxicity, and to stop the drug and contact their physician.
raw_record.extra_details: Rare adverse effect occurring within the first few weeks of antithyroid therapy; cholestatic jaundice described as severe but reversible. Generically classified alongside antithyroid drug hepatic toxicity adverse effects (also agranulocytosis).

raw_record.support_text: Thiamazole is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 4 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion states that methimazole (MMI) can induce cholestatic hepatitis after drug exposure ranging from 2 days to 3 months, and lists liver injury among MMI-related adverse events, including rashes, urticaria, arthralgias, vasculitis. A Taiwan study of 71,379 hyperthyroid patients reported ATD-induced hepatitis incidence of 3.17/1000 person-years with MMI/carbimazole and a 5.08-fold increased hepatitis risk with high-dose MMI/carbimazole compared with any PTU use; FDA data report that of 5 adult MMI patients who developed acute liver failure, 3 died.
raw_record.extra_details: MMI can induce cholestatic hepatitis with latency 2 days to 3 months; Taiwan cohort hepatitis incidence 3.17/1000 person-years for MMI/carbimazole (CBM) and 5.08-fold increased risk of hepatitis with high-dose MMI/CBM relative to any PTU use; FDA report: of 5 adult MMI patients who developed ALF, 3 died; MMI-related AEs include rashes, urticaria, arthralgias, vasculitis, and liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Zou et al reported 2 cases of cholestatic hepatitis caused by methimazole (Tapazole). Case 1: a 50-year-old female who initiated methimazole 10 mg daily and propranolol for newly diagnosed hyperthyroidism developed cholestatic hepatitis with severe icterus; after methimazole was stopped (propranolol continued), her liver tests were nearly normal in 4 weeks. Case 2: a 42-year-old female on methimazole 30 mg daily (reduced to 15 mg daily) had severe pruritus and icterus after 27 days of therapy; methimazole was discontinued and she recovered following methylprednisolone treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (phenotype as described by authors). Case 1 (50 y female, methimazole 10 mg/day for hyperthyroidism, with propranolol 10 mg TID): total bilirubin 105.86 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 54.21 µmol/L, ALP 200 U/L, GGT 104 U/L, AST 17 U/L, ALT 120 U/L; severe icterus, pruritus, diarrhea, weight loss; viral/autoimmune serologies and ultrasound negative/uneventful; labs nearly normal 4 weeks after discontinuation; switched to propylthiouracil. Case 2 (42 y female, methimazole 30 mg/day reduced to 15 mg/day): severe pruritus and icterus after 27 days; total bilirubin peaked at 348.2 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 262.12 µmol/L, ALP 353 U/L, GGT 255 U/L, AST 105 U/L, ALT 135 U/L; viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and primary biliary cirrhosis excluded; treated with methylprednisolone (12-week taper) with normalization of liver function. Both patients treated for hyperthyroidism; no alcohol use or liver disease history reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 34-year-old female Filipino with Graves' disease on methimazole presented with fever, sore throat and jaundice and was initially diagnosed with methimazole-induced agranulocytosis and drug-induced liver injury. The Authors' abstract states the case presents 3 rare life-threatening complications of methimazole: agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia and hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: methimazole 20 mg three times daily for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism); hepatitis and agranulocytosis appeared on approximately the 28th day of treatment. Liver tests showed total/direct/indirect bilirubin 6.90/4.03/2.86 mg/dL, ALT slightly elevated at 78 mg/dL (units reported as mg/dL), AST normal at 37; jaundice with icteric sclerae. Patient also developed aplastic anemia on day 4 of admission; treated with antibiotics, G-CSF, steroids, packed red blood cell, ursodeoxycholic acid and eltrombopag; discharged stable at 12th hospital day. Described as a rare life-threatening methimazole complication (hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: In an institutional case series, five cases of medically refractory severe cholestatic DILI were identified, defined by persistent serum bilirubin >20 mg/dL. Hepatotoxic medications included phentermine, methimazole, OxyElite, and two cases of the anabolic steroid methyl-1-etiocholenololepietiocholanolone. Cholestatic DILI was defined as ALP greater than two times the upper limit of normal secondary to a drug exposure known to cause intrahepatic cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: One case of severe cholestatic DILI (persistent bilirubin >20 mg/dL, ALP >2x ULN, >345 U/L) treated with 5 sessions of 8-hour MARS albumin dialysis; patient recovered with normalization of liver tests at outpatient follow-up. No hepatic encephalopathy or extrahepatic organ dysfunction; INR remained <2.

raw_record.support_text: A single-patient case report attributes cholestatic DILI to methimazole. The patient presented with signs and symptoms of cholestatic disease with concern for obstructive biliary pathology; malignancy, autoimmune, and infectious etiologies were ruled out, and choledochoscopy showed normal bile duct mucosa. The R-value at symptom onset was 0.64 (cholestatic pattern), the RUCAM score was 8 points, and the temporal relationship between methimazole initiation and symptom onset, together with improvement in symptoms and a downward trend in liver function tests after methimazole discontinuation, argued in favor of DILI. Six months after discontinuation the LFTs remained normal and the patient was symptom-free.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic DILI presenting like hepatobiliary obstruction. R-value 0.64 at symptom onset (cholestatic pattern); RUCAM score 8. Endoscopy showed a CBD stricture with distal narrowing and proximal dilation up to 14 mm; sphincterotomy/stenting initially performed; choledochoscopy spyglass showed normal bile duct mucosa within the narrowing; cytology negative for malignancy; autoimmune and infectious etiologies ruled out. Dechallenge: symptoms and LFTs improved after methimazole discontinuation, CBD stent later removed; LFTs remained normal and patient symptom-free 6 months later. Phenotype is cholestatic liver injury mimicking obstructive biliary pathology.

raw_record.support_text: The admitting diagnosis was methimazole-induced hepatitis, and use of the drug was stopped immediately. Despite stopping, the patient's total serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase continued to rise; prednisone therapy (up to 30 mg/day for four weeks) was tried without improvement. Surgical exploration showed a normal biliary system, and open liver biopsy showed cholestasis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis; the jaundice then receded and liver-function tests returned to normal by June 28, 1971.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Patient presented with deep jaundice; admission serum total bilirubin 13.6 mg/100 ml (direct 9.2), alkaline phosphatase 270 IµU/ml, with low/normal transaminases (SGOT 30). Total bilirubin rose to a peak of 31.0 mg/100 ml on 6/2 with direct 16.5. Liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis (dilated bile ducts with bile casts). Prednisone (max 30 mg/day for four weeks) was tried without improvement. Laparotomy revealed normal biliary system; open biopsy showed cholestasis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis. Jaundice receded after drug discontinuation and liver tests returned to normal by 6/28/1971. Causal wording uses 'methimazole-induced hepatitis' diagnosis with dechallenge recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that since the introduction of methimazole in 1949 a total of 20 cases of cholestatic jaundice have been described, 13 of which were caused by methimazole. The present case report describes methimazole-induced cholestatic liver injury mimicking sclerosing cholangitis, where the etiology was proven by a clear chronological relationship and the lack of other causative factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic liver injury mimicking sclerosing cholangitis (radiological picture of primary sclerosing cholangitis) during antithyroid therapy for hyperthyroidism. Etiology proven by clear chronological relationship and lack of other causative factors. Reported as a rare complication; a total of 13 prior cases of cholestatic jaundice caused by methimazole described in the literature since its introduction in 1949.

raw_record.support_text: A close temporal relationship between the first intake of risperidone and liver enzyme elevations, deterioration under continued risperidone treatment, a considerable decrease in liver enzyme abnormalities after switching to haloperidol, and exclusion of other causes make it highly probable that risperidone caused the initial hepatic injury. The liver biopsy result was consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude that the possibility of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatitis must be borne in mind.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of risperidone-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Liver needle biopsy was performed and was consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; an excess of eosinophils in the liver supported a possible immunoallergic reaction, while CYP2D6-dependent pharmacokinetic differences were discussed as possibly increasing risk of toxic liver injury. Rechallenge was not attempted due to the severity of the reaction. Elevations in AST, ALT, and γGT (γ-glutamyltransferase) resolved considerably after switching to haloperidol. Olanzapine caused deterioration of the hepatic injury in this case.

raw_record.support_text: The temporal relationship between risperidone exposure and serum liver enzyme elevations, deterioration under continuing risperidone treatment, immediate decrease in liver enzyme abnormalities after risperidone discontinuation, and exclusion of other causes led the authors to classify the case as probable risperidone-induced hepatotoxicity using the Naranjo scale. The patient's AST and ALT returned to normal on treatment with loxapine and oxazepam, while his transaminases remained normal after haloperidol.
raw_record.extra_details: Single male patient (Mr. A) with risperidone-associated hepatotoxicity; classified as 'probable' per the Naranjo scale. Elevated AST and ALT that deteriorated under continued risperidone and decreased immediately after discontinuation; transaminases normalized within 3 weeks on loxapine 200 mg/day and oxazepam 200 mg/day, and remained normal on haloperidol 20 mg/day. Eosinophilia (850 cells/mm³, normal <500), anti-smooth-muscle antibodies (1:640, decreasing to 1:100 after discontinuation); negative viral hepatitis A/B/C and autoimmune serologies except anti-smooth-muscle antibodies. Mechanism discussed as metabolic/immunoallergic idiosyncrasy; patient was CYP2D6 rapid metabolizer (CYP2D6*1/CYP2D6*5), so slow-metabolizer pharmacokinetic explanation not supported (metabolite 9-OH-risperidone formed by CYP2D6). Normal abdominal ultrasound, ceruloplasmin and copper.

raw_record.support_text: In a 41-year-old man (Mr. A) on outpatient risperidone monotherapy, elevated serum AST (83 U/L) and ALT (123 U/L) were noted after 7 weeks; levels rose during week 8 (AST=139 U/L, ALT=522 U/L) with nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain, prompting hospitalization and risperidone discontinuation. Viral hepatitis A/B/C serology, ultrasound, ceruloplasmin/copper, and autoimmune (ANA, AMA, LKM, SLA) tests were negative, but eosinophilia (850 cells/mm3) and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies (titer 1:640) were present, which resolved after discontinuation. Excluding other causes, the authors classified the case as probable risperidone-induced hepatotoxicity according to the Naranjo scale.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an adult on risperidone monotherapy for a psychiatric indication. Off-therapy AST/ALT normal on haloperidol 4 years earlier; AST/ALT returned to normal within 3 weeks of treatment with loxapine (200 mg/day) and oxazepam (200 mg/day), and remained normal on haloperidol (20 mg/day). Naranjo causality scale classified as probable. Laboratory highlights: cholestatic serum tests, WBC, RBC, and coagulation normal; negative hepatitis A/B/C serology, normal abdominal ultrasound, normal ceruloplasmin/copper; eosinophilia (850 cells/mm3) and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies (1:640, decreasing to 1:100) without actin/vimentin specificity; negative anti-LKM, anti-soluble liver antigen, ANA, and AMA.

raw_record.support_text: In table 2, risperidone (RIS 3 mg) was marked as the RUCAM highly-suggestive DILI drug (score 10) in a single patient (case 15).
raw_record.extra_details: Single RUCAM-adjudicated case (case 15) at 3 mg, RUCAM score 10; psychiatric inpatient; DILI moderate in severity.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old man with schizophrenia developed a sharp rise in liver enzyme levels during 13 days of treatment with risperidone, interpreted as hepatotoxicity, after which antipsychotic therapy was switched to paliperidone. Scoring with the Naranjo algorithm indicated a probable association between risperidone use and hepatotoxicity, with a score of 7. This is reported as the first case of a patient who developed hepatotoxicity during risperidone use that did not remit with a switch to paliperidone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme levels rose sharply during 13 days of risperidone therapy in a schizophrenic patient; therapy was then switched to paliperidone. Naranjo causality score 7 (probable). Hepatotoxicity resolved approximately 4 weeks after discontinuation of antipsychotics, with haloperidol initiated. First reported case of risperidone hepatotoxicity not remitting upon switch to paliperidone.

raw_record.support_text: In a 26-week randomized trial of 959 patients with type 2 diabetes, rosiglitazone (total daily dose 4 or 8 mg) produced dose-dependent HbA1c reductions, and the proportions of patients with at least one adverse event were comparable between rosiglitazone and placebo. The paper states there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in any treatment group.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized placebo-controlled trial, 959 patients, 26 weeks, total daily dose 4 or 8 mg; no evidence of hepatotoxicity in any treatment group; drug studied for efficacy in reducing hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes. Note: wording 'no evidence of hepatotoxicity' is an explicit negative conclusion regarding rosiglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that rosiglitazone was the only medication the patient used regularly, and state that the temporal association between rosiglitazone use, the presence of eosinophils in the granulomas, and resolution of both symptoms and elevated liver enzymes after drug withdrawal make it the most likely cause of the patient's granulomatous hepatitis. A liver biopsy showed a periportal mixed cellular infiltrate with granulomas in portal triads and hepatic parenchyma, inflammation crossing the limiting plate with focal hepatocyte degeneration, and fibrous portal expansion; symptoms resolved within 2 weeks and liver enzymes neared normal 2 months after rosiglitazone discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of granulomatous hepatitis attributed to rosiglitazone. Histology: periportal mixed infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, multinucleated giant cells), noncaseating granulomas in portal triads and parenchyma, lobular extension across the limiting plate with focal hepatocyte degeneration, fibrous portal expansion; stains for polarizing material, Giemsa, Gomori methenamine-silver, mucin and acid-fast negative. Presented with elevated bilirubin (total 5.0-5.9 mg/dL, direct 4.1-5.0 mg/dL), AST 49 U/L, ALT 82-84 U/L, ALP 125-162 U/L; ALT 33 U/L and AST 21 U/L near normal 2 months after cessation. Symptoms resolved within 2 weeks after discontinuation (dechallenge). Sarcoidosis excluded by normal chest radiograph and serum ACE; infectious causes considered less likely. Authors note uncertainty whether the high dose of 8 mg was a contributing factor, and recommend monitoring liver enzymes before and periodically during rosiglitazone therapy. Granulomas framed mechanistically as a delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman who had developed mild hepatotoxicity with troglitazone was prescribed rosiglitazone and over a few weeks developed abdominal pain and jaundice, with bilirubin 8.4 mg/dl, ALP 422 IU/l, ALT 86 IU/l, consistent with cholestatic hepatitis; liver biopsy showed granulomatous cholangitis with destructive bile duct lesions. Inadvertent rechallenge with rosiglitazone led to worsening liver tests, confirming causality as highly likely; after discontinuation the patient improved over 8 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (reference 111/112). Thiazolidinedione used for Type 2 diabetes. Labs: bilirubin 8.4 mg/dl, ALP 422 IU/l, ALT 86 IU/l; cholestatic hepatitis. Biopsy: granulomatous cholangitis with destructive bile duct lesions. Positive rechallenge worsened liver tests, causality highly likely. Improved over 8 months after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports cases of rosiglitazone- and pioglitazone-induced liver failure reported to the FDA from 1997-2006. For rosiglitazone (n=11 cases), the maximum recorded hepatic enzyme levels reflected a pattern expected with severe hepatocellular injury; nearly all patients had jaundice and encephalopathy, 8/10 were acute, and the overall outcome was 9/11 death, 1/11 transplant, and 1/11 spontaneous recovery. Negative viral serologies and absence of significant alcohol use were documented in most cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 FDA-reported cases. Median age 70, 63% male. Daily dose 2 mg (n=1), 4 mg (n=4), 8 mg (n=6). Median treatment duration 8 weeks (IQR 6-43, n=10). Acute in 8/10; jaundice 10/10; encephalopathy 10/10. Max AST median 2751 IU/L (n=10), max ALT 1194 IU/L (n=11), max AP 286 IU/L (n=9), max total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL (n=9). Pathology available 8/11, necrosis present 8/8. Eosinophilia noted in 5 cases overall. Outcomes: death 9/11, transplant 1/11, spontaneous recovery 1/11. 2/11 published in literature.

raw_record.support_text: Fosinopril induced severe cholestasis with high bilirubin levels (maximum 40 mg/dl) and a minor anicteric cholestasis persisting for 4 and 18 months, respectively. During hospitalization the patient developed severe disease with extreme anorexia, malnutrition and complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, renal failure and sepsis, without hepatic encephalopathy or biochemical features of impending hepatic failure; a low serum albumin that fell to 19 g/l was mainly attributed to anorexia and malnutrition.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fosinopril-induced cholestasis. Maximum serum bilirubin 40 mg/dl; minor anicteric cholestasis persisted 4 and 18 months (chronic cholestasis). Low serum albumin fell to 19 g/l, attributed mainly to anorexia/malnutrition. No fever, rash or eosinophilia (no hypersensitivity features); mechanism unknown. Hospitalization complicated by GI bleeding, renal failure and sepsis; no hepatic encephalopathy or impending hepatic failure. The authors conclude fosinopril, as a widely used ACE inhibitor, should be included in the list of potential causes of chronic liver disease; a MEDLINE search of important adverse reactions to fosinopril retrieved no other case.

raw_record.support_text: Based on the CIOMS scale result and the pathological characteristics of the liver, the authors concluded it was highly probable that fosinopril had induced cholestatic jaundice in the patient.
