The liver failure progressed, with serum bilirubin peaking at 25 mg/dL on hospital day 14 despite conservative treatment and withdrawal of fosinopril. The patient ultimately required plasma exchange and liver function returned to normal 2 months after discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of cholestatic jaundice attributed to fosinopril 10 mg once daily, an antihypertensive switched from prior therapy one month before presentation. CIOMS scale scored fosinopril as highly probable cause. Admission labs: total bilirubin 21.4 mg/dL (60% direct), ALT 41 IU/L, AST 47 IU/L, ALP 242 IU/L, GGT 136 IU/L, LDH 152 IU/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL; viral/metabolic/autoimmune markers negative. Liver biopsy on hospital day 10 showed marked cholestasis with hepatocyte swelling/damage and portal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, no piecemeal necrosis or portal fibrosis, interpreted as drug-related cholestasis. Bilirubin peaked at 25 mg/dL on day 14; treated with plasma exchange (20 units/day x 5 days), ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day, cholestyramine 8 g/day, cyproheptadine 4 mg 4 times/day; hypertension switched to amlodipine; glyburide discontinued and insulin used for diabetes. Liver function returned to normal 2 months after discharge.

raw_record.support_text: A phenprocoumon-induced necrotizing hepatitis was diagnosed in a 52-year-old woman on phenprocoumon for 7 months after prosthetic aortic valve replacement, based on clinical worsening after rechallenge with phenprocoumon, liver histology, and a positive lymphocyte transformation test. Liver values improved after discontinuing the oral anticoagulant and normalized with additional corticosteroid therapy; anticoagulation was continued with a low-molecular-weight heparin.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old female with right upper abdominal pain, impaired general condition, and markedly elevated serum transaminases indicating severe hepatitis; infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic causes excluded. Histology showed centrilobular subacute hepatitis without higher-grade fibrosis. Lymphocyte transformation test against phenprocoumon initially negative, later reactive. Clinical worsening after re-exposure supported causality. Indication: anticoagulation for prosthetic aortic valve replacement; heparin used subsequently. The paper notes hepatitis with phenprocoumon and other coumarin derivatives is a rare event to consider in differential diagnosis of unclear hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes Phenprocoumon-induced hepatopathy in a patient who developed clinically significant liver injury and (sub)acute liver failure after therapeutic oral anticoagulation with Phenprocoumon. The paper cites that latency to liver injury is 6-9 months, that rechallenge (reexposure) in all cases led to faster and more severe liver damage including one death from liver failure within 4 weeks and one case requiring liver transplantation, and that histology shows predominantly liver cell (perivenous) necrosis, supporting an immunologic idiosyncratic genesis with eosinophilia. The case conclusion states the patient's icterus was the expression of drug-induced liver failure (medikamentös-induziertes Leberversagen) attributable to Phenprocoumon, with improvement after conservative treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: postoperative worsening of liver function, patient declined liver transplantation, treated conservatively with lactulose, vitamin K, diuretic; discharged after 2-month hospital stay; final Quick 65% (INR 1.41); at follow-up asymptomatic with normal transaminases, bilirubin and liver function tests; mildly inhomogeneous liver echotexture on ultrasound. Literature: latency 6-9 months (occasionally much later, mimicking post-transfusion, viral or autoimmune genesis); rechallenge produced faster and more severe injury in all cases, with one reported death from liver failure within 4 weeks and one case needing liver transplantation; frequent blood eosinophilia; immunologic/molecular pathomechanism proposed (coumarin metabolite as hapten/neoantigen presented in Kupffer cells, genetic individual predisposition); histology predominantly perivenous liver cell necrosis with variable or minimal inflammation; lymphocyte stimulation tests can support the suspicion; steroids sometimes given with improvement; cross-reactivity with warfarin reported, though complication-free warfarin continuation also documented.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report eight cases of phenprocoumon-induced liver damage, three of which presented with (sub-)acute liver failure, two treated by orthotopic liver transplantation and one with a fatal outcome. Phenprocoumon-induced liver damage was diagnosed in 0.1% of patients presenting with liver disease at the First Department of Internal Medicine of the University of Mainz.
raw_record.extra_details: 8 reported cases; 3 with (sub-)acute liver failure, 2 treated by orthotopic liver transplantation, 1 fatal outcome; diagnosed in 0.1% of all patients presenting with liver disease at the University of Mainz; latency 6-64 months among (sub-)acute liver failure cases vs 3-11 months in others; histopathology ranged from severe hepatitis with massive hepatocellular bridging necrosis (cases 1-3) to only minor changes (case 4), with zone III accentuation in less severe cases; portal and periportal hepatitis in every case except case 4; marked bile-duct alterations with degenerative epithelial changes in cases 1 and 5; increase of eosinophilic granulocytes in most samples; primarily hepatitic (cytolytic) picture with rarely cholestatic features.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three women with phenprocoumon-induced liver injury in which cholestasis was clinically predominant. Latency from the start of oral anticoagulation was 6, 18, and 6 months. No liver-replacement therapy was needed and no corticosteroids were given; the course was prolonged in each patient but all three clinically recovered. The text frames coumarin treatment as a possible etiology of acute liver failure even after prolonged administration without prior problems.
raw_record.extra_details: Three women (aged 62 in the described representative case) treated with oral phenprocoumon (Falithrom brand) as anticoagulation, in one case started ~18 months before admission after a TIA with no other medication; no corticosteroids given, course prolonged but all three recovered, no liver-replacement therapy and no fatal or transplantation outcome. Cholestasis with jaundice clinically predominant; latency 6, 18, and 6 months. The authors note cross-reactions between different coumarin preparations can occur.

raw_record.support_text: This discussion of anticoagulation options states that hepatotoxicity is a very rare complication of coumarin therapy and documents liver toxicity reported for Warfarin, Phenprocoumon, and Acenocoumarol. Coumarin-induced liver damage frequently resembles viral hepatitis and can present with cholestasis, chronic aggressive hepatitis, subacute parenchymal inflammation, cirrhotic transformation, and cytolytic or necrotizing reactions; liver explants showed massive hepatocellular necrosis or complete fine-nodular cirrhosis with cholestasis and diffuse pericholangitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Cumarin-induced hepatotoxicity reported since the 1960s-70s; in a systematic evaluation of 10 coumarin-induced hepatotoxic reactions 4 patients had abnormal transaminases 2-7 days after therapy start while 6 required inpatient care with latencies from 10 days, 10 weeks, up to 6 years. Schimanski et al. reported 8 phenprocoumon patients with liver insufficiency, 3 with (sub)acute liver failure, the rest recovering after switch to another coumarin/heparin. Phenotypes attributed include cholestasis, chronic aggressive hepatitis, subacute inflammation with parenchymal destruction, cirrhotic remodeling, cytolytic and necrotizing reactions, and cholestasis with diffuse pericholangitis in explants; improvement after drug withdrawal is typical. A described case: rapid recurrence of hepatitis after phenprocoumon re-exposure (positive antinuclear and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies, lacking hypergammaglobulinemia) and a 56-year-old woman with hepatitis after 8 months of phenprocoumon.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man presented with jaundice 6 months after aortic valve replacement. The final diagnosis of phenprocoumon (Marcoumar®)-induced hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis was based on recurrence of jaundice after re-exposure to the drug, improvement after withdrawal, and centrilobular necrosis with eosinophilic infiltration in the liver biopsy; antibodies to hepatitis C virus were absent.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of the coumarin anticoagulant phenprocoumon (Marcoumar®) used for prophylaxis of thromboembolic disorders. Diagnosis rested on positive rechallenge (recurrence of jaundice within 4 weeks after drug re-institution), improvement after withdrawal (heparin substitution), and liver biopsy showing recent centrilobular liver cell necrosis with eosinophilic infiltration; the injury progressed to cirrhosis. Competing causes excluded: HAV, HBV, HCV (anti-HCV absent), EBV, CMV, HSV, toxoplasmosis, HIV serologies negative; ceruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin normal. Laboratory findings during relapse: bilirubin 138 µmol/l, ALAT 589 IU/l, ASAT 479 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 208 IU/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 566 IU/l, LDH 416 IU/l, serum bile acids 300 µmol/l, α-fetoprotein 700 µg/l; reduced ICG and antipyrine fractional clearances. Patient had changed from acenocoumarol (Sintrom®) to phenprocoumon 1 month after aortic valve surgery; recent blood-product exposure initially raised suspicion of non-A, non-B hepatitis. Liver functions were normal before surgery.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes phenprocoumon-induced liver damage (phenprocoumoninduzierter Leberschaden), first described in 1963. According to a BfArM analysis based on spontaneous reports it constitutes ~2% of all phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of all hepatopathies are phenprocoumon-induced. The clinical picture is extremely variable, ranging from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with fatal outcome, as in the presented case. Hepatopathy typically occurs 3-9 months after starting phenprocoumon, with latencies up to 7 years reported; in the presented case the patient had taken Marcumar (phenprocoumon) for 6 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Marcumar; anticoagulation indication. Latency typically 3-9 months, up to 7 years; present patient used phenprocoumon for 6 years. Clinical spectrum from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with death. BfArM spontaneous-report analysis: ~2% of phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of hepatopathies attributed to phenprocoumon. Four cases of this complication occurred in the authors' patient population during 2006-2008, two fatal; a Mainz case series illustrates the broad clinical spectrum. An immunologic genesis is considered likely (borderline ANA titer, exacerbation upon re-exposure, 'drug-allergic' course); cross-sensitization with other coumarins noted. Steroid therapy attempted without influence on outcome. Histology showed portal inflammatory infiltrate, group necrosis with cholestasis, collapse zone with clearing, and focal fiber increase; the course evolved into rapidly developing liver cirrhosis with subacute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Overview of hepatotoxicity caused by vitamin K antagonists based on 20 publications from 1980-2012 and 31 patients (24 women, 6 men; age median 60, range 30-90): 26 patients were on phenprocoumon therapy, 2 on warfarin, 2 on acenocoumarol, and 1 on dicumarol. Across the cohort there were 9 cases of (acute) liver failure, 4 liver transplantations, and 3 deaths.
raw_record.extra_details: Largest subgroup (26 of 31 total VKA hepatotoxicity cases) from 20 published reports (1980-2012). Latency to hepatopathy median 6.5 months (range 1-72); after rechallenge 4 weeks. Normalization of liver tests median 3 months after phenprocoumon discontinuation. Histology variable: portal and lobular hepatitis, inflammatory infiltrate, hepatocellular necrosis, bile duct proliferation, cholestasis; picture described as compatible with drug-toxic liver damage. Rechallenge repeatedly reported (refs 31,32,34,35,37,40,42,43) with earlier recurrence; initial injury sometimes misdiagnosed as non-A-non-B hepatitis or autoimmune hepatitis, and in one case verapamil was initially suspected. Pooled cohort outcomes (acute liver failure 9, transplant 4, death 3) reported for all VKA agents combined.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a thrombophilic patient with activated protein C resistance who was repeatedly treated with oral anticoagulants for recurrent venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and who twice developed a hepatitis-like clinical presentation following exposure to phenprocoumon. The patient improved and laboratory findings normalized within 3 to 4 months after withdrawal of the drug, and the authors note there are only few well-documented cases of liver toxicity due to coumarin derivatives such as phenprocoumon.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 38-year-old woman with APC resistance (heterozygous factor V R506Q/Leiden) and thrombophilia on phenprocoumon for venous thromboembolism. Episode 1: ~4 months after starting phenprocoumon developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 3,330 U/L, AST 2,090 U/L, AP 272 U/L, γ-GT 357 U/L, bilirubin 526 μmol/L); anticoagulation stopped (liver biopsy refused) and enzymes normalized within 3 months. Episode 2 (age 43): ~5 weeks after restarting phenprocoumon developed nausea, fatigue, jaundice (ALT 1,724 U/L, AST 1,219 U/L, AP 200 U/L, γ-GT 326 U/L, bilirubin 128 μmol/L); phenprocoumon stopped, switched to acenocoumarol, and the patient improved with decreasing liver values, indicating positive dechallenge and rechallenge. Viral hepatitis, CMV, and EBV serologies were negative; remote HBV infection (anti-HBc/anti-HBs) without active infection. Acenocoumarol was continued without new injury.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a 57-year-old female patient with chronic lumbago who died from the sequelae of acute liver failure induced by nimesulide medication. Nimesulide, an NSAID preferentially inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase 2, has been associated with a total of 13 reported cases of severe liver injury including this case.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old female with chronic low back pain (lumbago); nimesulide 100 mg once daily for 3 months (replacing ibuprofen 800 mg/day and mefenamic acid up to 1 g/week); presented with anorexia, malaise, arthritic finger pain and jaundice; died from the sequelae of acute liver failure. Part of a total of 13 reported cases of severe liver injury associated with nimesulide. Acute liver failure phenotype (hepatic necrosis not otherwise specified).

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old Arabic woman treated with nimesulide for chronic low back pain was admitted to the hospital with acute hepatitis confirmed by biopsy. Her liver function test results returned to normal within one month after nimesulide discontinuation, and an in vitro lymphocyte toxicity assay confirmed that the liver injury was due to nimesulide exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis in a 54-year-old Arabic woman treated with nimesulide for chronic low back pain; injury confirmed by liver biopsy and by an in vitro lymphocyte toxicity assay; liver function tests returned to normal within one month of discontinuation. Nimesulide is a relatively new NSAID commonly used in Europe with relative selectivity to cyclooxygenase type 2; it can cause a range of liver injuries from mild abnormal liver function to severe liver injuries, usually reversible on discontinuation but occasionally progressing to fatal hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide-associated hepatitis was diagnosed, and the patient was treated with methylprednisolone. Liver function tests and aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels improved rapidly and were within normal limits 3 weeks after admission; the patient was discharged asymptomatic. The paper reports this as the 12th case of nimesulide-associated liver injury published, with unclear frequency and mechanism, and notes nimesulide causes two characteristic histologic patterns: centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis resembling ethinyl estradiol- or androgen-induced cholestasis. This patient showed extensive centrilobular necrosis with a mixed eosinophil-rich infiltrate and a severe vasculitis of hepatic veins.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient admitted with nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, pleural effusions, and icteric sclerae. Symptoms recurred 5 days after nimesulide was restarted and the patient was readmitted after 12 days of repeated intake (positive rechallenge). Laboratory findings showed the typical pattern of acute liver failure (AST 1006 U/l, ALT 1115 U/l, prothrombin time 39%, bilirubin 2.2 mg/dl) with marked eosinophilia (35%). Cavography/duplex sonography excluded large-vein thrombotic outflow block (Budd-Chiari) but showed drop-out of hepatic vein branches and decreased portal flow; biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis in zones 3 and 2, mixed eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate, and severe vasculitis of hepatic vein branches. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes excluded. Concurrent medication was oral contraceptives (cyproterone acetate 2 mg/day and ethinyl estradiol 0.035 mg/day for 5 months). Treated with methylprednisolone (100 mg/day, tapering to 4 mg) and diuretics; recovered within 3 weeks. Reported as the 12th published case of nimesulide-associated liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes severe hepatic damage and hemolysis occurring in a patient receiving nimesulide. Drug involvement is supported by a temporal relationship between drug intake and the clinical picture, careful exclusion of other causes of liver injury, and histologic features compatible with drug-induced liver toxicity. CIOMS scale assessment yielded a score of 6 points, within the 'probable' category, though the fulminant outcome prevented assessment of the effect of dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of severe hepatic damage progressing to acute liver failure and fulminant liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy; patient received an orthotopic liver transplant on day 25 and was alive 20 months later with mild biochemical cholestasis. CIOMS causality score 6 points (probable). Prolonged drug exposure; accumulation of aberrant (reactive) metabolites (idiosyncratic metabolic mechanism) speculatively implicated. Co-occurring hemolytic anemia with negative Coombs test, no autoantibodies, and no response to steroids. Liver tests showed high bilirubin (up to 51.6 mg/dl), AST up to 240 U/l, ALT up to 110 U/l, AP up to 1099 U/l, GGT up to 565 U/l.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old previously healthy woman with no prior adverse drug reactions, adequate renal and hepatic function, and no history of alcohol or drug use took a single 100mg nimesulide tablet (Aulin) for a flu-like syndrome. About 8 hours later she developed nausea, vomiting and asthenia and was admitted. The paper reports this as a case of severe hepatotoxicity induced by nimesulide treatment, supported by a Naranjo adverse probability scale application that estimates a probable relationship between nimesulide use and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single 100mg oral tablet (Aulin, Roche SpA, Italy) taken for influenza-like illness; onset about 8 hours later with nausea, vomiting and asthenia. Laboratory findings: ALT 340 U/L (about 20-fold upper normal), AST 224 U/L (about 8-fold), γ-GT 53 U/L (about 2-fold). Serology negative for HAV, HBV, HCV, EBV, HIV, cytomegalovirus and autoimmune markers. Naranjo adverse probability scale applied, estimating a probable relationship; Naranjo score value not reported in the provided text.

raw_record.support_text: Three of the five reported cases (Cases 1, 3, and 4) were attributed to nimesulide taken for pain (dental, cervical, or lumbalgia) at 600, 100, and 200 mg/day respectively. All three women developed jaundice and acute liver failure with encephalopathy and required emergency liver transplantation, which was successful in cases 3 and 4. Liver histology showed panlobular necrosis with bile duct proliferation, acute hepatitis with about 90% necrosis, and centrilobular (zone 3) hemorrhagic collapses with bile plugs and mild macrovacuolar steatosis respectively.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases (women aged 22, 48, 49): Case 1, 600 mg/day for 2 days for dental pain, symptoms after 2 days (nausea, vomiting, jaundice), grade IV encephalopathy, transplant within 24 h, histology panlobular necrosis; Case 3, 100 mg/day for 4 days for cervical pain, acute hepatitis with abnormal coagulation, emergency transplant 1 week later; Case 4, 200 mg/day for 2 months for lumbalgia, acute hepatitis with subacute course, transplant within 2 weeks, histology zone-3 hemorrhagic collapses with cholestasis and mild macrovacuolar steatosis; viral causes and other causes ruled out in Case 4.

raw_record.support_text: In the NSAIDs group, 14 patients (70%) had liver damage attributable to nimesulide. Cases of fulminant and subacute hepatitis, sometimes fatal, have been documented, and two pathological patterns of nimesulide-induced DILI (hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis) have been documented. The only 3 patients with hepatic failure, encephalopathy and ascites due to DILI belonged to the nimesulide group; one of them died while on the waiting list for liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Potent anti-inflammatory/analgesic/antipyretic, widely used clinically; documented fulminant and subacute hepatitis, sometimes fatal; two DILI patterns (hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis) possibly related to patient gender; in this case series 50% were women with higher frequency of cytolytic and lower frequency of cholestatic patterns than males; majority of cases above age 40; highest mean aminotransferase values but shortest recovery time; the only 3 patients with hepatic failure, encephalopathy and ascites due to DILI belonged to this group, one dying on the waiting list for liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that in 2009 the authors' series included 43 well documented cases of nimesulide-induced liver damage associated with a wide clinical and histological spectrum of hepatotoxicity, the largest series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity ever reported. Main presenting symptoms were jaundice (70%), malaise (65%), and pruritus (50%); two thirds of patients started liver toxicity 15 to 90 days after drug intake, with only 11% having a latency shorter than 15 days, and normalization exceeded 90 days in 27% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Largest reported series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity (43 well documented cases). In the authors' institution, 5 of 30 cases (17%) had severe liver injury. Nine patients developed severe liver disease and fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) occurred in 6 cases, predominantly females older than 50 years (per Walker et al); 2 patients died before liver transplant due to multiorgan failure, and a 9-year-old girl successfully underwent orthotopic liver transplantation. ALT/aspartate transaminase: a wide range of variations; per Bjarnason, 33 case reports showed ALT elevation of at least 2-fold in 100% and 5-fold in 89% of patients. Liver damage spectrum included acute hepatitis, cholestasis, mixed forms, and massive and submassive hepatic necrosis: hepatocellular necrosis in 64%, cholestatic hepatitis in 27%, pure cholestasis in 9%. Symptoms: jaundice, malaise, pruritus; latency 15-90 days in two-thirds, only 11% shorter than 15 days; normalization exceeded 90 days in 27%; in cholestatic injury, alkaline phosphatase normalization can exceed 1 year. Proposed mechanism (unconfirmed): reactive metabolite formation and genetic variation in drug metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman presented at the emergency department with acute hepatic failure and a MELD score of 25.0, 2 weeks after taking nimesulide, with a probable diagnosis of toxic hepatitis. She was transferred to a liver transplant unit; after supportive care and acetylcysteine, a liver biopsy revealed micronodular cirrhosis associated with acute hepatitis with features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. She was then started on azathioprine 50 mg/day and prednisolone 30 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Nimesulide 100 mg twice daily for 3 days for oral pain, taken 2 weeks before admission; presented with worsening jaundice, soft stools and dark urine, then new-onset jaundice one week later. MELD score 25.0. Led to transfer to a specialist liver transplant unit with probable toxic hepatitis; treated with supportive care and acetylcysteine. Liver biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with acute hepatitis showing features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). After azathioprine 50 mg/day and prednisolone 30 mg/day, a biopsy 28 months later showed almost full remission with only mild fibrosis and no significant inflammatory infiltrate. The paper notes nimesulide is referred to in published reports as hepatotoxic but its association with triggering AIH symptoms is rare; cirrhosis reversibility after 2 years is highlighted.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 11 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists three patients (cases 2, 3 and 10) with DILI attributed to nimesulide taken at 200 mg/day for osteoarthritis. Case 2 showed jaundice, eosinophilia and hepatocellular injury (TB 24xULN, ALT 98xULN, ALP 2.5xULN), Moderate severity, CIOMS 'Probable'. Case 3 showed jaundice with hepatocellular injury and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 10 showed eosinophilia with cholestatic injury (TB 1.2xULN, ALT 1.2xULN, ALP 5xULN), CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases, all 200 mg/day for osteoarthritis. Case 2 (62/F), 30 days treatment, onset 30 days, no co-meds, jaundice, eosinophilia, hepatocellular, TB 24xULN, ALT 98xULN, ALP 2.5xULN, Moderate, resolution 90 days, CIOMS 'Probable'. Case 3 (61/F), 62 days, onset 62 days, co-meds fosinopril and torasemide, jaundice, hepatocellular, TB 15xULN, ALT 30xULN, ALP 1.7xULN, Moderate hospitalized, resolution 126 days, CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 10 (59/F), 25 days, onset 466 days, co-meds atenolol, captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, insulin, metformin, eosinophilia, cholestatic, TB 1.2xULN, ALT 1.2xULN, ALP 5xULN, Moderate hospitalized, resolution 284 days, CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Nimesulide was discontinued from the Spanish market due to liver safety.

raw_record.support_text: Among NSAID-related acute liver failure, nimesulide was attributed in n=3 cases of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF among patients transplanted for acute liver failure; n=3 cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the nimesulide-DILI series, a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury was present in all acute liver failure (ALF) cases except one that was classified as mixed (case 12). Liver histology from six patients showed severe hepatocellular necrosis ranging from submassive injury with extensive centrilobular necrosis and collapsed areas to massive multiacinar necrosis. Twelve patients developed ALF, of whom five died from multiorgan failure (cases 12, 22, 31, 52, 56), three were transplanted (cases 23, 35, 39), and four recovered spontaneously. The prescribed dose was 200 mg/day in 10 cases (83%) indicated for pain.
raw_record.extra_details: Nimesulide-DILI cases; prescribed dose 200 mg/day in 10/12 cases indicated for pain; 12 of the series developed acute liver failure (ALF); 5 died of multiorgan failure (3 while waiting for transplant), 3 were transplanted, 4 recovered spontaneously after 45-150 days (median 60 days). Latency longer in ALF patients (60 vs 30 days, p=0.108); cumulative dose median 10,500 mg (ALF) vs 6,000 mg (non-ALF), p=0.133. Histology showed centrilobular and multiacinar severe hepatocellular necrosis. ALF patients had higher mean TBL, AST, and INR (all p<0.001); most showed AST>ALT and ALP <= 4x ULN; half had AST/ALT ratio >1.5 vs 6.7% without ALF (p=0.002). Nine patients (75%) took concomitant drugs; transient ibuprofen (case 45) and diclofenac (case 12) intake had incompatible temporal relationships (no intake within 18 and 16 days, respectively, of symptom onset), leaving nimesulide as the attributed cause.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' six patients, nimesulide produced drug-induced hepatitis characterized by severe hepatocellular necrosis in 67% of cases (all women, three over 65 years of age), whereas a pure cholestatic pattern resembling ethinyl-estradiol or androgen-induced cholestasis was found in the two male cases. The nimesulide-induced liver injury is attributed to both idiosyncratic pathogenic mechanisms: immunoallergic hypersensitivity (two patients, 33%, had increased blood and tissue eosinophilia) and metabolic idiosyncrasy involving hepatotoxic metabolites such as 4-hydroxy-nimesulide.
raw_record.extra_details: Six patients; hepatocellular necrosis pattern in 67% of cases, all women, three above 65 years; pure cholestatic pattern in the two male cases (sex-dependent pattern distribution not previously reported for other NSAIDs); centrilobular lesion location; main metabolite 4-hydroxy-nimesulide; two patients had an underlying cholestatic disease diagnosed during the injury; blood and tissue eosinophilia in one hepatocellular and one cholestatic case suggesting immunoallergic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acute hepatitis induced by acarbose (acarbosa) is an infrequent but recognizable side effect, and recommends monitoring transaminase values during the first months of treatment. It also explains that because the incidence is low and unpredictable, the hepatic injury is believed to be idiosyncratic and dose-dependent rather than due to hypersensitivity, supported by the absence of concomitant allergic symptoms, the temporal relationship between drug intake and symptom onset, and the absence of eosinophils on biopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism unknown; believed dose-dependent with low and unpredictable incidence; not attributable to hypersensitivity based on absence of concurrent allergic symptoms, temporal relation between drug intake and symptom onset, and absence of eosinophils in the biopsy sample. Authors recommend monitoring transaminase values during the first months of treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on long-term glibenclamide, had acarbose (100 mg three times daily) added to her treatment in mid-1993. Two months later she developed jaundice, malaise, and anorexia, with elevated liver enzymes (AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 7.84 mg/dL, GGT 156 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L). Viral hepatitis and autoantibodies were ruled out, and ultrasonography showed a normal liver, so the authors attribute the hepatic injury to acarbose and describe it in the title as 'Hepatic Injury Caused by Acarbose.' After acarbose was stopped, bilirubin fell to 1.8 mg/dL and AST/ALT decreased within 4 weeks, with laboratory results normal within 9 months.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old woman with NIDDM; concurrent glibenclamide background therapy (indicated 7 years prior). Acarbose 100 mg three times daily; latency ~2 months. Symptoms: malaise, anorexia, jaundice. Labs: AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84 mg/dL), GGT 156 U/L, ALP 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and antinuclear/anti-smooth-muscle antibodies excluded; ultrasonography showed normal liver and no dilated bile ducts. Dechallenge: 4 weeks after stopping acarbose, bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, AST 159 U/L, ALT 155 U/L; normalized within 9 months. Outpatient management (patient refused hospitalization). Acarbose is a competitive α-glucosidase inhibitor that delays carbohydrate absorption and decreases postprandial glucose.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on glibenclamide, had acarbose (100 mg three times daily) added in mid-1993. Two months later she presented with malaise, anorexia, and jaundice; AST was 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84), γ-glutamyltransferase 156 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and autoimmune antibodies were excluded, and ultrasonography was normal. After acarbose was stopped, bilirubin decreased to 1.8 mg/dL within 4 weeks and laboratory values normalized within 9 months. The authors conclude that acarbose caused the hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Added to pre-existing glibenclamide therapy for non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; a co-medication, though causality was attributed to acarbose. Dose 100 mg three times daily; latency ~2 months; symptoms included malaise, anorexia, and jaundice; baseline transaminases AST 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84), GGT 156 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and antinuclear/anti-smooth-muscle antibodies excluded; ultrasonography normal; no liver biopsy performed. Injury classified as 'hepatocellular' per international consensus criteria; mechanism unknown, compatible with metabolic idiosyncrasy given long latency and absent hypersensitivity; dechallenge led to resolution (bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL at 4 weeks, laboratory values normal within 9 months). Managed as outpatient.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute liver toxicity due to acarbose in a diabetic patient. They conclude the acute liver damage was probably related to acarbose, fulfilling the three criteria of temporal relationship, favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease, and state that acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when liver test abnormalities develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus treated with acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months before onset; symptoms included right upper quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, lightened stool color, and scleral jaundice with slightly tender hepatomegaly. Peak enzymes on admission: ALT 1,580 IU/L, AST 1,090 IU/L, GGT 497 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, ferritin 1,290 ng/ml; viral and autoimmune serologies negative. Spontaneous recovery with all abnormalities subsiding within 5 weeks; no liver biopsy and no rechallenge; patient remained well on glipizide 8 months later. Concomitant medication ciclobutirol (laxative); cisapride started after acarbose was stopped.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of acute liver toxicity in a diabetic patient treated with acarbose (50 mg t.i.d. per os) that fulfills the criteria of a 'probable' adverse event related to the use of acarbose, i.e., a temporal relationship, a favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease. They conclude that acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when abnormal liver tests develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM); acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months. On admission: scleral jaundice, right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, light stools, slightly tender hepatomegaly. Peak ALT 1580 IU/L, AST 1090 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 IU/L, GGT 497 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, ferritin 1290 ng/ml. Serologies for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-EBV, anti-CMV IgM negative; autoantibodies negative; iron/copper, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin normal. No liver biopsy, no rechallenge. Clinical course spontaneously favorable; all biochemical abnormalities subsided within 5 weeks; patient well 8 months later on glipizide.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of acute liver toxicity in a diabetic patient that fulfills criteria of a 'probable' adverse event related to the use of acarbose. Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that is minimally absorbed in the gut, rarely inducing moderate aminotransferase elevations in treated patients, with more severe liver damage being very unusual. The case fulfills the three criteria of temporal relationship, favorable course after stopping the drug, and absence of other known causes of liver disease, so acute liver damage induced by acarbose should be suspected when liver-test abnormalities develop after starting acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old woman with noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus treated with acarbose 50 mg t.i.d. per os for 2 months; developed right upper quadrant pain, nausea, dark urine, lightening of stool color, and scleral jaundice 1 week before admission. Elevated ALT (1,580 IU/L), AST (1,090), GGT (497), alkaline phosphatase (220), bilirubin 3.8 mg/dl, and ferritin (1,290 ng/ml); viral and autoimmune serologies negative; abdominal ultrasonography normal. Spontaneous recovery within 5 weeks; liver biopsy not performed and no rechallenge. Causality rated 'probable' based on temporal relationship, favorable course after drug stopping, and absence of other known liver disease causes. Patient remained well on glipizide 8 months after the episode.

raw_record.support_text: In trials using methotrexate as an alternative to cyclophosphamide for remission induction in early systemic/limited Wegener's granulomatosis (ANCA-associated vasculitis), adverse effects related to methotrexate included pneumonitis (difficult to differentiate from pulmonary vasculitis), hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression, and these events were reversible.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in prospective open therapeutic trials of methotrexate for remission induction in early systemic disease/limited Wegener's granulomatosis (ANCA-associated vasculitis) without threatened vital organ function, used with or without steroids; hepatotoxicity was reversible.

raw_record.support_text: In a post-hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), hepatotoxicity leading to MTX withdrawal was associated with absence of folate supplementation and high body mass index. Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 36/137 (26%) of the placebo (no folate) group and 11/274 (4%) of the folate-supplemented group.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was defined as ALT >3x ULN (table footnote). Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 36/137 (26%) of the placebo group vs 11/274 (4%) of the folate group; with BMI 20-25 hepatotoxicity occurred in 16/190 (8%) and with BMI 30-35 in 10/51 (20%). Univariate OR for folate supplementation 0.12 (0.06-0.24), multivariate OR 0.10 (0.04-0.21); BMI multivariate OR 1.09 (1.01-1.17) per unit. MTX was withdrawn in 126 patients, 91 due to toxicity. Folate supplementation also reduced MTX withdrawal due to toxicity (multivariate OR 0.25, 0.14-0.42). Study population: rheumatoid arthritis patients on MTX therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In their series of patients with interstitial pregnancy treated with systemic methotrexate (MTX), side-effects of MTX therapy such as stomatitis, hepatotoxicity, or bone marrow depression were only mild, which the authors state is consistent with the literature.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity reported as a side effect of systemic MTX therapy given for interstitial pregnancy; only mild in the authors' series and consistent with the literature. Other concurrent side effects mentioned: stomatitis and bone marrow depression. MTX was applied systemically and/or locally for interstitial pregnancy, with total dosages similar to those used in gestational trophoblastic disease in some cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man with poorly differentiated acute lymphocytic leukemia received induction therapy in November 1998 achieving complete remission; consolidation therapy was discontinued after one cycle due to severe cytopenias, and maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months secondary to methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in a single 69-year-old man with acute lymphocytic leukemia; maintenance therapy was discontinued after 6 months because of the methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity, without further characterization of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In this comparative clinical trial of low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, hepatotoxicity was reported as a common toxic effect of methotrexate treatment: it occurred in 31/59 patients in the 8-day methotrexate-folinic acid (MTX-FA) regimen and 9/48 patients in the weekly methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m² without dose escalation). Drug toxicity necessitated changing chemotherapy in 13.6% (8/59) of the MTX-FA group and 2.1% (1/48) of the MTX group.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity counts: 31/59 in the 8-day methotrexate-folinic acid regimen and 9/48 in the weekly methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m², no dose escalation) for low-risk GTN. Comparison of weekly vs 8-day MTX-FA regimens in a single-institution trial of 107 patients; weekly regimen reported less toxic and better tolerated. Hepatotoxicity drug-necessitated change in chemotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the case report of a 51-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis, the patient was initially treated with methotrexate (7.5 mg twice a week). Because of hepatic toxicity, methotrexate was discontinued and the patient was switched to penicillamine 250 mg/day. This attributes drug-induced liver injury (hepatic toxicity) to methotrexate during therapeutic use in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Methotrexate was given at 7.5 mg twice a week for rheumatoid arthritis; hepatic toxicity led to its discontinuation, after which the patient was started on penicillamine 250 mg/day. No specific pattern, severity, or mechanistic detail was reported.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old seropositive rheumatoid arthritis patient on weekly low-dose oral methotrexate (MTX) developed ascites with normal serum transaminase and albumin levels. Liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with bridging fibrosis and piecemeal necrosis. After MTX was discontinued, ascites resolved and arthritis became more active. This is reported as the third case of reversible hepatic decompensation associated with prolonged MTX therapy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
raw_record.extra_details: Weekly oral MTX 10 mg beginning March 1983; cumulative dose 2,700 mg by admission February 1989 in a 54 kg patient. Pre-treatment biopsy was essentially normal. Patient denied alcohol use, was not diabetic or obese, no hepatitis/jaundice history. Ascites resolved upon discontinuation; biopsy findings of bridging fibrosis and piecemeal necrosis documented by a second biopsy. Third reported case of reversible hepatic decompensation with prolonged MTX therapy in RA.

raw_record.support_text: The 57-year-old male patient had a 13-year history of psoriasis treated with methotrexate which resulted in hepatic fibrosis, an explicitly attributed drug-induced liver injury presented as background in the case.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic fibrosis developed during chronic methotrexate treatment over a 13-year history of psoriasis in a 57-year-old male.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of psoriasis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), hepatotoxicity is described as one of the most significant methotrexate-induced adverse events, requiring continuous monitoring. Hepatotoxicity and symptomatic adverse events were the most frequently recorded AEs in the cohort, and the number of recorded hepatotoxicity cases was sufficient for logistic regression analysis of the association between MTX-related hepatotoxicity and candidate polymorphisms. A best-fit model identified the BHMT genotype as significantly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.18-8.49 for carrying the variant 742GA/742AA allele).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was the most frequently recorded MTX adverse event in the psoriasis cohort (safety group n=137, 24 with hepatotoxicity). MTX hepatotoxicity risk was significantly associated with the BHMT genotype (dominant model): patients carrying at least one variant BHMT allele (742GA or 742AA) were 3-fold more likely to experience MTX-induced hepatotoxicity than those with the 742GG genotype (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.18-8.49); other variables in the hepatotoxicity model (MTHFR activity, DNMT3b, FPGS, ABCC2, ABCB1 genotypes) did not reach significance. Indication: psoriasis.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists methotrexate as a RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with updated RUCAM scores of 6-8 (probable) and 9 or higher (highly probable) causality gradings, based on published cases evaluated with the updated RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Updated RUCAM scores 6-8 confer probable and scores ≥9 confer highly probable causality gradings; reported iDILI cases, reference [37].

raw_record.support_text: At Westminster Hospital, of fifteen patients with intractable psoriasis treated over 3 years, eight were methotrexate 'failures' and two had methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity before entering the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of fifteen patients with intractable psoriasis at Westminster Hospital were described as having methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity; these two were among eight patients who were methotrexate 'failures'. No further details on severity, laboratory values, or outcome are provided.

raw_record.support_text: In a single-institution series of osteosarcoma patients treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (OOS-A, OOS-B, and OOS-C regimens), methotrexate (MTX)-induced hepatitis was identified as a cause of delayed drug administration. The hepatitis was described as transient, and most patients recovered spontaneously.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX-induced hepatitis caused delayed drug administration during neoadjuvant osteosarcoma chemotherapy; hepatitis was transient and most patients recovered spontaneously. Second administration of consecutive weekly MTX tended to be delayed due to liver toxicity even at 8 g/m² doses. MTX was deleted from the OOS-C preoperative course because of this toxicity. Also noted as a co-therapy in regimens with doxorubicin (DOX) and cisplatin, which caused myelosuppression rather than liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Death was certified as being due to massive hepatocellular necrosis, consistent with sulphasalazine-induced fulminant hepatitis, based on the distinct temporal relation between the commencement of sulphasalazine therapy and the onset of fulminant hepatic failure. Multi-organ failure and brain death ensued but were deemed consequences of drug-induced liver failure, making the sulphasalazine-induced liver injury the primary cause of death.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulphasalazine (salicylazosulphapyridine) therapy preceded onset of fulminant hepatic failure; post-mortem showed massive hepatocellular necrosis; multi-organ failure and brain death considered consequences of the drug-induced liver failure. Pentobarbitone and thiopentone (and propofol) were also detected post-mortem but were not attributed as causes of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of fulminant hepatitis in a patient with sulfasalazine-induced DRESS syndrome (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) who survived without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: A 45-year-old woman with seronegative rheumatoid polyarthritis; oral corticosteroid was given before sulfasalazine (day 1). Sulfasalazine was stopped on day 15 due to generalized maculopapulous rash. On admission (day 22) she had abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, hepatic cytolysis (aminotransferases at 5 N); DRESS with hypereosinophilia (12.10%/l), major cytolysis (transaminases >2,000 IU/l), cholestasis (total bilirubin at 5 N) and liver failure (factor V 45%). Hepatic biopsy showed massive centrolobular necrosis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates, consistent with immunoallergic drug-induced hepatitis. Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy with cerebral edema, factor V fell to 17%; emergency liver transplantation proposed on day 33 but postponed after improvement. Patient came out of coma on day 40 and was discharged on day 74. Treated with intensive methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days then corticosteroids 2 mg/kg/day. The authors attribute establishment of DRESS syndrome to sulfasalazine; rare immunoallergic reactions including the 3-week sulfasalazine syndrome with some fulminant hepatitis cases are noted.

raw_record.support_text: Ten patients with serious hepatotoxicity on sulfasalazine were identified, eight during local surveillance. Eight patients were hospitalised, two in hepatic failure, one of whom died after a liver transplant. All but one event occurred within 6 weeks of treatment; seven had a skin rash, three eosinophilia and one interstitial nephritis. Liver enzymes showed a hepatocellular pattern in four cases and a mixed pattern in six. Drug-related hepatotoxicity was judged probable or highly probable in 8 patients, and the likely frequency of serious hepatotoxicity with sulfasalazine was estimated at 0.4% of treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Ten cases total, 8 occurring during local surveillance; 8 hospitalised, 2 in hepatic failure, 1 died after a liver transplant; all but one event within 6 weeks of treatment; 7 with skin rash, 3 eosinophilia, 1 interstitial nephritis; 5 patients of Black British African/Caribbean descent; hepatocellular pattern in 4 cases and mixed pattern in 6; causality assessed by two clinicians by consensus and with a causality assessment instrument, probable or highly probable in 8 patients; estimated frequency of serious hepatotoxicity 0.4% of treated patients; sulfasalazine used as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 15 patients with severe DRESS, patient 3 (a 30-year-old woman with ankylosing spondylitis) developed fulminant hepatitis attributed to sulfasalazine as the culprit drug, with 7 days from first drug intake to ICU admission; she was treated with glucocorticoids and underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 3, F/30, ankylosing spondylitis; fulminant hepatitis as a manifestation of DRESS; 7 days from first drug intake to ICU admission; treated with glucocorticoid and required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was admitted with probable sulfasalazine induced hepatitis 3 weeks after commencing the drug, consistent with the 3-week syndrome, characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, and widespread erythematous rash followed by rising liver enzymes and bilirubin, with rarely reported fatal fulminant hepatic failure. In a multicenter study of 1382 RA patients treated with sulfasalazine, only 1 patient had a similar reaction. Sulfasalazine is also a recognized cause of DRESS syndrome, a hypersensitivity reaction attributed to the sulfapyridine moiety.
raw_record.extra_details: Probable sulfasalazine-induced hepatitis occurring 3 weeks after starting the drug ('3-week syndrome'), with fever, lymphadenopathy, widespread erythematous rash, rising liver enzymes and bilirubin, transient anemia, raised IgM and atypical activated lymphocytes; patient also developed a rising INR with deteriorating liver function and was treated with N-acetyl cysteine, improved and was discharged 10 days after admission. The syndrome is rare, is rarely reported fatal from fulminant hepatic failure, and a multicenter study of 1382 RA patients treated with sulfasalazine recorded only 1 similar reaction. Sulfasalazine is a recognized cause of DRESS syndrome, a hypersensitivity reaction due to the sulfapyridine moiety.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had been on Azulfidine (sulfasalazine) for 19 days and developed a number of adverse effects, the most severe of which appeared to be diffuse hepatocellular injury with necrosis. The clinical presentation and pattern of hepatic injury were judged most compatible with acquired hypersensitivity as the basis for the drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Prompt recurrence of symptoms, fever, skin rash, and laboratory evidence of severe hepatocellular injury upon readministration of a small quantity of Azulfidine were taken as features supportive of acquired hypersensitivity; the latent period was 19 days on first exposure and 24 hr on reexposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Latent period 19 days on first exposure and 24 hr on rechallenge (readministration of a small quantity). Rechallenge reproduced symptoms, fever, skin rash, and laboratory evidence of severe hepatocellular injury, supporting drug-induced hepatotoxicity via acquired hypersensitivity. Additional features included significant lymphadenopathy and striking atypical lymphocytosis, described as part of a serum-sickness-like syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Among antibiotic-related acute liver failure, sulfasalazine was implicated in n=1 case of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old female presented with acute liver failure due to sulfasalazine and was listed for liver transplant. While awaiting a new organ, she developed progressive shock and worsening hepatic encephalopathy, leading to CRRT initiation. Following a rescue full hepatectomy with porto-caval shunt and an anhepatic period of 6 hours and 2 minutes, she received a liver transplant; hemodynamics improved but she developed bilateral mydriasis and confirmed cerebral death.
raw_record.extra_details: 37-year-old female; acute liver failure attributed to sulfasalazine, listed for liver transplant; progressive shock and worsening hepatic encephalopathy; CRRT initiated; rescue full hepatectomy with porto-caval shunt; anhepatic 6 hours 2 minutes; after transplant developed bilateral mydriasis with confirmed cerebral death.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old female with proctosigmoiditis was hospitalized three weeks after starting sulfasalazine with a temperature of 105°F, a diffuse maculopapular rash with subsequent desquamation, atypical lymphocytosis, and hepatitis (AST 726 units/L, ALT 1009 units/L). Hepatitis serology was negative, and all symptoms and laboratory abnormalities other than those related to her proctosigmoiditis resolved after discontinuation of the sulfasalazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution supported by dechallenge (resolution after sulfasalazine discontinuation); no rechallenge. Case patient was a 46-year-old female treated for proctosigmoiditis. Reaction included fever 105°F, diffuse maculopapular rash with desquamation, atypical lymphocytosis; hepatitis serology negative; AST 726 units/L, ALT 1009 units/L; hospitalized. Described as a severe allergic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide and valsartan 80 mg/day for 5 months developed progressive jaundice over 2 weeks with generalized pruritus. Liver tests showed AST 738 U/l, ALT 1664 U/l, GGT 352 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 385 U/l and total bilirubin 23.6 mg/dl (direct fraction); viral, autoimmune and metabolic studies were negative and a liver biopsy was reported as acute hepatitis of probable drug origin. Valsartan was withdrawn on the suspicion of drug-induced hepatitis, with progressive normalization of liver tests and complete enzymatic recovery two months after admission. The case was reported to the national pharmacovigilance service.
raw_record.extra_details: Valsartan 80 mg/day taken for 5 months for hypertension; biopsy showed acute hepatitis of probable drug nature with irregular lymphocytic, eosinophilic and polymorphonuclear infiltrate, focal hepatocyte necrosis, feathery degeneration and a canalicular bile thrombus; R-ratio-compatible markedly elevated transaminases with total bilirubin 23.6 mg/dl; dechallenge led to progressive normalization, bilirubin 4 mg/dl at hospital discharge (one month) and full enzyme normalization at two months. Case reported to the national pharmacovigilance service.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who developed acute hepatitis of probable drug origin attributed to valsartan. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with irregular inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils and polymorphonuclears with focal hepatocellular necrosis, hepatocytes with feathery degeneration and some bile canalicular thrombi. On admission, with suspicion of valsartan-induced pharmacological hepatitis, the drug was withdrawn and evolution was favorable with progressive normalization of liver tests; at one month bilirubin was 4 mg/dl and transaminases had normalized, with enzymatic normalization confirmed at two months. The case was reported to the National Pharmacovigilance Service.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case reported as the first described valsartan hepatotoxicity in the reviewed literature (MEDLINE 1998-2001). Biopsy reported acute hepatitis of probable drug origin with lymphocytic/eosinophilic/polymorphonuclear infiltrate, focal hepatocellular necrosis, feathery degeneration and bile canalicular thrombi. PCR for hepatotropic viruses and serology for CMV, EBV and HSV were negative; abdominal ultrasound, CT and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (CPRE) were normal; bilirubin 4 mg/dl at discharge one month later with normalized transaminases; normal enzymes at two months. Causality supported by chronological relationship, absence of other causes, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal; reported to national pharmacovigilance system.

raw_record.support_text: After 5 days of gatifloxacin therapy (prescribed for sinusitis), the patient developed acute hepatitis with subsequent symptomatic jaundice. Other causes of hepatitis (viral, autoimmune, functional) were ruled out, and biopsy revealed acute hepatitis with eosinophilic infiltrates consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; a complete blood count showed eosinophilia (7%).
raw_record.extra_details: Onset after 5 days of gatifloxacin for sinusitis; symptomatic jaundice; biopsy showed acute hepatitis with eosinophilic infiltrates consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; eosinophilia 7%; viral, autoimmune and functional causes ruled out; causality described as 'suggestive' based on onset and resolution and 'probable' by two adverse-effect probability estimation methods.

raw_record.support_text: Gatifloxacin was implicated as the cause of a fatal case of acute hepatitis progressing to fulminant hepatic failure. The patient had markedly elevated liver function tests with a normal alkaline phosphatase, consistent with hepatocellular injury, and jaundice appeared only a few days after initiation of gatifloxacin; the discussion states the onset corresponded with the time frame expected for fluoroquinolone hepatotoxicity. The patient died 25 days after completing the course of gatifloxacin due to multiple organ failure. An additional gatifloxacin case (hepatocellular pattern) with improvement at 5 weeks, plus a meta-analysis of 15 clinical trials finding liver-test alterations (>5xULN) in <0.1% (AST, ALT, ALP) and <0.4% (bilirubin) and 1 hepatitis case in >16,000 treated patients, was also reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 76-year-old, onset ~10 days (jaundice few days after gatifloxacin initiation); peak ALT 787 U/L, AST 743 U/L, ALP 150 U/L, total bilirubin 34.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 28.7 mg/dL; hepatocellular injury with normal alkaline phosphatase; progression to fulminant hepatic failure, INR peaked 7.04, hepatic encephalopathy with elevated ammonia (peak 274 microg/dL), renal impairment (creatinine peak 5.5 mg/dL), multiple organ failure; died 25 days after completing gatifloxacin. Additional reported case: 44-year-old, onset 5 days, peak ALT 669 U/L, ALP 297 U/L, bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL, hepatocellular, improvement at 5 weeks. Meta-analysis (Breen et al., 15 clinical trials): ALT/AST/ALP >5xULN in <0.1%, bilirubin in <0.4%; 1 hepatitis case linked to gatifloxacin in >16,000 postmarketing-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe 2 patients who developed acute cholestatic liver injury and acute pancreatitis while being treated with gatifloxacin (Tequin, Bristol-Myers Squibb), representing case reports of gatifloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: a 41-year-old woman treated orally at 400 mg/d for an upper respiratory tract infection (prior ciprofloxacin withdrawn for nausea/vomiting, not liver-related; no other medications). Presented 2 days after starting gatifloxacin with skin rash, dark urine, pale stools, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Laboratory findings: total bilirubin 87.2 µmol/L (5.1 mg/dL) with conjugated fraction 61.6 µmol/L (3.6 mg/dL), AST 139 U/L, ALT 145 U/L, albumin 30 g/L, alkaline phosphatase 8.03 µkat/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 8.62 µkat/L, amylase 1.38 µkat/L, lipase 6.5 µkat/L, prothrombin time 6.1 s. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis excluded; imaging showed no biliary obstruction. Liver biopsy showed portal edema and cholestasis with moderate macrovesicular steatosis. Abdominal pain resolved and prothrombin time normalized 2 weeks after gatifloxacin withdrawal; jaundice fully resolved after 1 year. Follow-up biopsy at 8 months showed increased portal fibrosis, early bridging fibrosis, and bile duct loss; persistent elevation of alkaline phosphatase and transaminases continued. Background note: less than 1% of exposed patients have increased bilirubin, aminotransferase, or amylase; 1 case of acute hepatitis previously reported.

raw_record.support_text: The COMMENT states that fusidic acid interferes with bile salt transport and secretion, and that hepatotoxicity (characterized by conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase) is common. Liver function tests return to normal when the drug is stopped, and jaundice is more frequently observed with intravenous than with oral administration. The paper also describes two case histories of hepatic dysfunction developing during fusidic acid therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case histories reported (Case 1 hepatic dysfunction with dechallenge: improved on stopping drug and returned to normal within one month; Case 2 derangement of liver function within one month of starting therapy). Comment characterizes hepatotoxicity as common, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase, and notes liver function tests normalize after drug withdrawal; jaundice more frequent with intravenous administration. Mechanism: interference with bile salt transport and secretion. A patient required dialysis for acute tubular necrosis attributed to severe hyperbilirubinaemia (up to 739 µmol/L) after fusidic acid therapy. Case 2 (oral fusidic acid 500 mg three times daily) died at home; no post-mortem, and death not directly attributed to the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the treatment of vertebral osteomyelitis, one patient developed cholestatic hepatitis attributed to (secondary to) fusidic acid therapy, reported among other adverse reactions in this case series.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient among a series treated intravenously and orally for vertebral osteomyelitis developed cholestatic hepatitis secondary to fusidic acid therapy; other noted adverse reactions were vancomycin-related vasculitis and persistent hearing loss, and interstitial nephritis possibly due to ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin.

raw_record.support_text: Idiosyncratic drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) is reported after clarithromycin use with exclusion of known causes of FHF. In this case the biopsy was consistent with drug-induced toxicity, other causes of FHF were absent, and the patient had no preceding liver dysfunction. Fever, eosinophilia, eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy, and a 1-week sensitization period support an immunologically mediated idiosyncratic reaction, and nonzonal panacinar necrosis is characteristic of an idiosyncratic phenomenon. The authors conclude the idiosyncratic drug reaction leading to FHF was associated with clarithromycin exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient developed FHF within 72 h; peak enzymes LDH 3529 U/L, ALP 1095 U/L, AST 2255 U/L, ALT 1974 U/L; total bilirubin rose to 33.4 mg/dl, unconjugated bilirubin 0.0 mg/dl, PT 21 s, activated PTT 51 s. Transjugular biopsy showed moderate cholestasis and microvesicular steatosis with increased eosinophilic infiltrate in portal tracts and hepatic lobules, ballooning degeneration and occasional hepatocyte dropout, no bile duct injury. Progressive encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, metabolic acidosis, and respiratory failure; terminal extubation on day 13. Same paper notes clarithromycin reported associated with cholestatic hepatitis in a patient treated for Mycobacterium chelonae lung infection, and that the manufacturer reports mild LFT elevations in <1% of patients. Acetaminophen-associated FHF was not supported (see separate record).

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a 63-year-old female who presented with fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation caused by a weight loss dietary supplement containing conjugated linoleic acid (CLA). Thorough investigation, including liver biopsy, revealed no other cause of hepatotoxicity, and the authors note only one prior reported case of CLA-induced toxic hepatitis worldwide.
raw_record.extra_details: 63-year-old female; fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation; toxic hepatitis attributed to a CLA-containing weight-loss dietary supplement; thorough investigation including liver biopsy excluded other causes; reported as the second case worldwide, with one prior CLA-induced toxic hepatitis case in the literature. The paper discusses CLA isomers (c9,t11 and t10,c12) and possible mechanisms involving lipid peroxidation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that their patient had elevations in liver enzymes after losartan use which returned to normal after discontinuation, re-elevations after rechallenge, no evidence of other hepatic disorders, a biopsy consistent with hepatic damage, and normal liver tests during a 2-year follow-up, and that these data clearly demonstrate the existence of losartan-induced hepatic injury in this patient. The majority of drug-related reactions are described as idiosyncratic and unpredictable.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old female treated with losartan 50 mg/d for 5 months; AST rose to 1,093 U/L, ALT 941 U/L, total bilirubin 8.9 mg/dL after rechallenge; liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with a mild-severe inflammatory response and mild fibrosis; enzymes normalized after discontinuation and rechallenge reproduced the injury; 2-year follow-up normal with recovery. A compiled table summarizes 5 reported cases of losartan-induced hepatic injury (additional prior cases from refs 7-9), all of whom improved.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed hepatocellular-pattern liver injury with aminotransferase elevations reaching ~50 times the upper normal limit, disproportionate bilirubin and minimal ALP elevation, after taking losartan. Alternative causes (acute viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, Wilson disease, malignant infiltration, biliary obstruction, and sepsis) were excluded, and there was rapid clinical recovery and laboratory normalization after losartan discontinuation. The CIOMS/RUCAM causality assessment scored >8 points ('highly probable') for losartan-related drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM score >8 ('highly probable'). Aminotransferases reached ~50x upper normal limit with disproportionate bilirubin and minimally elevated ALP; extra-hepatic obstruction considered unlikely. Other causes of acute hepatitis excluded by presentation and investigations (acute viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, Wilson disease, malignant infiltration, biliary obstruction, sepsis). Rapid clinical recovery and laboratory normalization after losartan discontinuation. Reported as the 6th case of losartan-induced hepatitis and possibly the first losartan-induced ischemic liver injury in an adult population.

raw_record.support_text: We present a case of severe hepatic injury and sub-fulminant hepatitis attributed to losartan use in a 54-year-old male patient with underlying hypertension. After ruling out all possible causes, he was diagnosed with drug-induced hepatotoxicity with losartan treatment. He started improving gradually after losartan discontinuation, N-acetylcysteine administration, and supportive management with close monitoring of liver enzymes, underscoring losartan as a potential cause of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 54-year-old male with hypertension (diagnosed 3 months prior) and type 2 diabetes mellitus, on 50 mg losartan daily. Presented with 14 days of severe abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, and vomiting, followed by altered sensorium/dizziness, lethargy, anorexia, intermittent fever; epigastric and right hypochondrium tenderness. Labs: ALT 1641 IU/L (ref <36), AST 1425 IU/L, ALP 150 (ref 35-95), total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl, INR 1.7, GGT 41 IU/L. No history of liver disease, smoking, alcohol, or illicit substance abuse; compliant with insulin. Treated by holding losartan, N-acetylcysteine, and supportive care with gradual improvement. Hepatotoxicity described as exceedingly rare with high morbidity and mortality; only a few prior cases reported. Phenotype reported specifically as sub-fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old man developed acute severe hepatic injury (malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly) while taking losartan, 50 mg/d, for hypertension. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, and total bilirubin 164 µmol/L; serologic, viral, autoimmune, iron, and copper studies were negative. Injury resolved after losartan was discontinued and atenolol substituted. On rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d, hepatotoxicity recurred within 3 weeks (mild jaundice, tender hepatomegaly; AST 206 U/L, ALT 254 U/L, total bilirubin 72 µmol/L), and liver tests normalized after losartan was again stopped. The case is presented under the heading 'Losartan-Induced Hepatotoxicity.'
raw_record.extra_details: Losartan 50 mg/d given for moderate essential hypertension after enalapril was stopped for cough. Initial episode: about 1 month of losartan exposure preceding admission, with 2-week symptom history; AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, GGT 266 U/L, total bilirubin 164 µmol/L (conjugated 152 µmol/L), moderately prolonged prothrombin time, normal eosinophil count; negative hepatitis A/B/C and other viral serologies, normal/negative iron, copper, and autoantibody tests. Dechallenge with atenolol substitution led to improvement (one month later AST 154 U/L, ALT 218 U/L, bilirubin 39 µmol/L) and full normalization 4 months after admission. Positive rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d after atenolol was stopped produced recurrence within 3 weeks; losartan was then definitively discontinued and the liver profile normalized 1.5 months later.

raw_record.support_text: Applying the Karch-Lasagna algorithm and Paris Consensus criteria, the causal relationship between the liver injury in this 56-year-old woman and treatment with tamoxifen is classified as probable, based on a compatible chronological relationship between drug administration and altered liver enzymes, absence of other potential causes of liver disease (alcohol, prior chronic hepatopathy, hepatotropic viruses), and persistence of the liver changes when all other medications except tamoxifen were withdrawn. The probability was not upgraded to 'definite' because there are no data on enzyme changes after tamoxifen discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman treated with oral tamoxifen 10 mg/12 h since 1996 after right mastectomy for intracystic papillary carcinoma. Presented with right hypochondrial pain, vomiting, coluria and slight mucosal jaundice; liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with marked portal inflammation and moderate macrovesicular steatosis. Lab values: total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, AST 199 U/l, ALT 184 U/l; later GGT 331 U/l and alkaline phosphatase 483 U/l. No alcohol intake or blood transfusions; hepatitis B surface antigen, HCV, ANA, AMA, anti-smooth muscle and ANCA all negative. Other potential hepatotoxic drugs (fluvastatin, lansoprazole, ofloxacin, omeprazole, metamizole) were withdrawn and re-introduced without any change in liver values, supporting tamoxifen as the cause. Biopsy findings concordant with a chronic hepatitis resembling a previously published case of tamoxifen hepatotoxicity; steatosis component and active chronic hepatitis pattern imply a mixed mechanism of metabolic idiosyncrasy and autoimmune phenomena. Discussion notes that published tamoxifen hepatotoxicity cases show two predominant injury patterns: cholestasis with or without cytolysis and steatohepatitis, including cholestatic jaundice without cytolysis, cholestasis with cytolysis, a case of hepatic peliosis, a case of fatty liver with liver failure and death, and several cases of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; additional cases collected by pharmacovigilance systems with little detail.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had evidence of tamoxifen-induced nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), as evidenced by an ALT/AST ratio greater than 1, steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of these tests after discontinuing tamoxifen. The paper also states that hepatitis A, B, and C serology were negative and alcohol and other known hepatotoxin intake were excluded. Tamoxifen is N-demethylated in the liver by CYP3A4, generating reactive metabolites capable of damaging protein and DNA.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a patient on tamoxifen. Evidence of tamoxifen-induced NASH included ALT/AST ratio greater than 1 (ALT 48 U/L, AST 42 U/L, normal 0-31), steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of liver toxicity tests after stopping tamoxifen. Paper notes six cases of tamoxifen-induced NASH have been reported, two progressing to cirrhosis. Hepatitis A/B/C serology negative; alcohol and other known hepatotoxins excluded. Proposed mechanisms: partial estrogenic activity and CYP3A4-mediated N-demethylation generating reactive metabolites (binding irreversibly to and damaging protein/DNA). Tamoxifen also implicated in porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) in this patient (urinary uroporphyrins 25,200 nmol/L, falling from 1570 to 359 nmol/mmol creatinine after stopping tamoxifen); PCT itself is not treated as a liver-injury phenotype here.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that the imputability of a 46-year-old patient's hepatic alterations to tamoxifen was established using criteria of drug-induced liver disorders, after exclusion of hepatic metastasis and bile duct obstruction and following normalization of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and aminotransferases upon tamoxifen discontinuation. They note tamoxifen hepatotoxicity is uncommon, previously reported as essentially steatosis and cholestatic syndrome, and that severe hepatotoxicity is a rare complication that can occur at any time of tamoxifen therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old woman with no history of hepatic disease, treated with tamoxifen as adjuvant hormonal therapy after mastectomy, four courses of doxorubicine and cyclophosphamide chemotherapy, and adjuvant radiation for lobular breast carcinoma; not taking other medicines. Jaundice appeared four weeks after tamoxifen initiation with elevated bilirubin, aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase consistent with acute hepatic injury; no hepatomegaly, no hepatic metastasis or main bile duct obstruction on ultrasound and CT. Negative serologic and immunologic tests. Bilirubin normalized one month after tamoxifen discontinuation; alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases returned to baseline in ~6 weeks. Rechallenge not attempted. Patient remained free of cancer relapse and hepatic disorders at 10 months. Paper notes previously reported tamoxifen-induced liver diseases are essentially steatosis and cholestatic syndrome, and severe hepatotoxicity is a rare complication.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman without prior hepatic disease started tamoxifen as hormonal therapy after mastectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy (doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide), and radiation, taking no other medicines. Four weeks after tamoxifen initiation she developed jaundice; labs showed elevated bilirubin, aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase consistent with an acute hepatic injury, while hepatic metastasis and main bile duct obstruction were excluded and serological/immunologic tests were negative. One month after tamoxifen discontinuation bilirubin normalized, and aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase returned to baseline in about 6 weeks; rechallenge was not attempted.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 4 weeks from tamoxifen start; jaundice with elevated bilirubin, aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase; hepatic metastasis and main bile duct obstruction excluded by ultrasound and CT; serological and immunologic tests negative; bilirubin normalized one month after discontinuation and aminotransferase/alkaline phosphatase returned to baseline in ~6 weeks; no rechallenge; imputability established using criteria of drug-induced liver disorders. Literature notes tamoxifen hepatotoxicity is rare and previously reported liver diseases are essentially steatosis and cholestatic syndrome; severe hepatotoxicity can occur at any time of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who had two episodes of severe hepatic dysfunction after two separate exposures to disulfiram, with liver biopsies showing extensive hepatocellular necrosis and no evidence of active alcoholic liver disease. Although they note that conclusive proof of a causal role would require rechallenge in a hospital setting, the extent of hepatic necrosis and the unpredictable effects of further exposure precluded rechallenge, and they describe the close temporal relation between disulfiram exposure and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two episodes of severe hepatic dysfunction after two separate exposures to disulfiram.
