Re-exposure at a rehabilitation center within 4 days produced jaundice and recurrent injury, effectively a rechallenge. First admission labs: bilirubin 43.0 mg/dl, SGOT 1650 nm/ml, alkaline phosphatase 220 nm/ml, LDH 504 nm/ml, SGPT 801 nm/ml; SGOT decreased to 278 nm/ml by day 4. Second episode: bilirubin 25.0 mg/dl, SGOT 1245 nm/ml, SGPT 407 nm/ml, LDH 397 nm/ml, alkaline phosphatase 211 nm/ml. Transcostal liver biopsies showed mononuclear cellular infiltrate, hepatocellular necrosis, Councilman-like bodies, and (second biopsy) bridging necrosis; no steatosis or hyaline degeneration. HBsAg negative by radioimmunoassay; hepatitis A antibodies (immune electron microscopy) absent; G6PD activity normal; hemoglobin A on electrophoresis. Recovery occurred over ~3 months after each exposure. Authors note a similar but less severe case reported by Keeffe and Smith.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of 82 patients with suspected disulfiram adverse liver reactions, four patients died during the initial hospitalisation and four underwent successful liver transplantation. Deceased or transplanted patients had higher serum bilirubin, AST, AST/ALT ratio and INR values than those who recovered, with no difference in age, sex, or duration of treatment. The study frames these as drug-induced liver injury cases attributed to disulfiram.
raw_record.extra_details: 82 patients with disulfiram suspected adverse liver reactions (1979-2004 reports); median ALT 46xULN and bilirubin 6.0xULN across the cohort. 49 patients fulfilled Hy's rule (ALT>=3xULN + bilirubin>=2xULN), with a 16% (8/49) mortality/transplantation rate. 4 patients died, 4 underwent liver transplantation. Liver biopsy in one patient who used alcohol showed eosinophilic infiltration and no evidence of alcohol-induced injury. In a multivariate analysis, bilirubin (P=0.0005, OR 1.214, CI 1.088-1.355) was the only independent predictor of death or liver transplantation. Median treatment duration 42 days (IQR 35-60). Two patients had documented alcohol use during treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Disulfiram-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 46 individual case reports (only patients reported individually per Björnsson et al.); median age 41 y; 21 female/25 male; median treatment duration 6 weeks; HC 100%, Cs/mixed 0%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 35% (23/46 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 50% (35/46 reported); hepatic necrosis 46%; inflammatory reaction 74%; death or liver transplant 37%; liver biopsy reported in 37/46 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 43 patients with drug-induced liver injury, disulfiram was the most frequent cause, responsible for 13 cases (30%). RUCAM scoring classified 20 patients as probable (6-8 points) and 23 as highly probable (>8 points), with none falling into possible, unlikely, or excluded categories, so all patients remained in the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Disulfiram was the most frequent cause of DILI in a Danish tertiary-center case series, accounting for 13 of 43 cases (30%). Patients were scored by RUCAM as probable (6-8) or highly probable (>8); none were possible, unlikely, or excluded.

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis are presented, both with prompt recurrence of abnormal liver function tests after rechallenge with small doses of the drug. All cases of disulfiram-induced hepatotoxicity reported in the English literature are reviewed.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports (Case 1: 30-year-old male, disulfiram (Antabuse) 250 mg daily for ~2.5 months for alcoholism treatment; presented with scleral icterus, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss, vomiting; prior normal liver tests). Both cases showed prompt recurrence of abnormal liver function tests after rechallenge with small doses. Paper also reviews all previously reported cases of disulfiram-induced hepatotoxicity in the English literature. Disulfiram = Antabuse, tetraethylthiuram disulfide.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman taking disulfiram for two months for alcohol addiction developed jaundice and malaise with AST 2020 IU/L, ALT 3467 IU/L, ALP 254 IU/L, GGT 80 IU/L and total bilirubin 16.4 mg/dl (INR 1.36). Other causes of acute hepatitis were ruled out, and liver biopsy showed acute necrotic lesions with numerous eosinophils consistent with acute toxic hepatitis. Disulfiram causality was rated probable on the CIOMS/RUCAM scale (7 points); she recovered with normal liver tests by April 2020.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter to the editor describing three cases of disulfiram-induced hepatotoxicity used as an alcohol deterrent for alcohol addiction/dependence. Case 1 (48-year-old woman, disulfiram for 2 months): AST 2020 IU/L, ALT 3467 IU/L, ALP 254 IU/L, GGT 80 IU/L, TB 16.4 mg/dl, INR 1.36; biopsy showed acute necrotic lesion with numerous eosinophils consistent with acute toxic hepatitis; CIOMS/RUCAM score 7 (probable); recovered with normal liver tests. Case 2 (44-year-old woman, disulfiram since August 2019): fatigue and nausea, AST 1709 IU/L, ALT 1406 IU/L, ALP 120 IU/L, GGT 111 IU/L, TB 15.1 mg/dl, INR 1.49; earlier October 2019 tests also abnormal (AST 1395, ALT 1134, ALP 154, GGT 191, TB 9.1); biopsy showed necrosis with inflammatory infiltration compatible with acute hepatitis; CIOMS/RUCAM score 7 (probable); liver enzymes normalized 6 weeks after discontinuation. Authors note difficulty reaching definitive diagnosis and potential underestimation of disulfiram hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report the authors state there is strong evidence that disulfiram was the cause of the patient's liver abnormalities: liver chemistries were normal before therapy, the patient was on no other medication and abstained from alcohol, liver biopsy showed no alcoholic liver disease, HBsAg was negative, reexposure to disulfiram reproduced the biochemical features of a hepatitis-like reaction, and both episodes improved with discontinuance of disulfiram. The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of disulfiram hepatitis and remained well.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report of disulfiram-induced hepatitis used for alcoholism treatment; liver chemistries were normal before therapy; patient on no other medication and abstaining from alcohol; liver biopsy (in a Raneck and Andreasen case) showed portal inflammation and eosinophilic infiltrate; rechallenge with disulfiram reproduced the biochemical features of a hepatitis-like reaction; both episodes improved with discontinuance; the authors note disulfiram is not a direct hepatotoxin but blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidation of acetaldehyde. The paper also cites Raneck and Andreasen's 6 cases of possible disulfiram hepatotoxicity, of which 5 were circumstantial and 1 showed abnormal liver chemistries on rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with a history of alcoholism, after three months of sobriety, began disulfiram therapy (0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily). Ten days into therapy he rapidly developed fatigue, malaise, and jaundice without fever. Disulfiram, chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, and methylphenidate hydrochloride (the latter two taken for months) were stopped; bilirubin peaked at 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT at 2,040 units with only slight serum alkaline phosphatase elevation, and hepatitis resolved in six weeks. After rechallenge with disulfiram 0.25 gm daily, the same biochemical and clinical sequelae recurred in ten days (with urticaria and no other medication), again improving after drug discontinuation, supporting disulfiram as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Two episodes reproducible on rechallenge. Standard dosage 0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily; rechallenge at 0.25 gm daily reproduced sequelae within ten days. Peak bilirubin 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT 2,040 units with only slight alkaline phosphatase elevation; no fever or eosinophilia on the first episode, urticaria present on rechallenge. Rapid resolution of hepatitis after withdrawal; liver tests normal in six weeks. HAA negative on two occasions. Patient had a prior episode of hepatitis after halothane anesthesia in 1968. First episode occurred with co-medications chlordiazepoxide and methylphenidate; rechallenge episode occurred without other medication, supporting disulfiram attribution.

raw_record.support_text: The liver toxicity section states that about thirty observations of hepatitis induced by disulfiram are collected in the literature, 18 of which are particularly studied. Sixty percent of patients are women; symptoms appear 10 days to 2 months after starting treatment, rarely after 8 weeks. The hepatitis is cytolytic, evolving in a third of cases toward death (fulminant hepatitis) by massive hepatic necrosis; in the other cases, improvement occurs within 2 weeks of discontinuing disulfiram exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: About 30 published cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis collected, 18 studied in detail; 60% of patients were female; latency 10 days to 2 months after treatment start, rarely after 8 weeks (one case); cytolytic hepatitis; fulminant hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis led to death in about one-third of cases; among survivors improvement occurred within 2 weeks of disulfiram discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Among 62 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the etiology was considered viral in 26; in 5 other patients ALF was considered due to toxic hepatitis caused by the administration of ketoconazole, α-methyl dopa, halothane, pyroxicam, and disulfiram, respectively. Thus disulfiram was attributed as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to ALF in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution made in a single ALF patient within a 62-patient acute liver failure series; drug administration identified as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Ein 49-jährige Frau starb an den Folgen einer fulminanten Hepatitis, die mit größter Wahrscheinlichkeit durch Disulfiram induziert worden war. Nach einjähriger stationärer Alkoholentziehungskur und normalen Leberwerten wurde eine Disulfiramtherapie in einer Dosierung von 250 mg/d eingeleitet; nach 13 Tagen trat ein Ikterus auf und nach 18 Tagen (Gesamtdosis 4,5 g) wurde ein akutes Leberversagen diagnostiziert. Die Patientin starb 25 Tage nach Therapiebeginn im Coma hepaticum mit hepatorenalem Syndrom. Die Autopsie ergab eine akute Leberdystrophie ohne Zirrhose mit Totalnekrose der Leber und dicht gelagerten entzündlichen Infiltraten mit zahlreichen eosinophilen Granulozyten, die als Hinweis auf eine medikamentös induzierte Hepatitis gewertet wurden. Der zeitliche Zusammenhang, der Ausschluss anderer Ursachen und die Leberhistologie sprechen für eine Disulfiram-induzierte fulminante Hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxische Wirkung von Disulfiram gilt als extrem selten, Häufigkeit geschätzt auf <1 Fall pro 25 000 behandelte Patienten. Eigener Fall: 250 mg/d, Latenz 13 Tage bis Ikterus, Gesamtdosis 4,5 g, akutes Leberversagen nach 18 Tagen, Tod 25 Tage nach Beginn. Aggregierte Serie aus 25 Fällen (inklusive 23 englischsprachige + 1 deutscher + eigener): mittlere Latenz 41 (10-183) Tage, mittlere Gesamtdosis 11,5 (3,75-48) g, Symptome einer akuten Hepatitis vom Virustyp (Appetitlosigkeit, Nausea, Erbrechen, Müdigkeit, Fieber, Ikterus, Pruritus, Abdominalbeschwerden), rascher Anstieg von Transaminasen und Bilirubin, gelegentlich Hautexanthem und Eosinophilie; Histologie mit ausgedehnten hepatozellulären Nekrosen, portal/periportalen mononukleären und eosinophilen Infiltraten sowie Cholestasezeichen; Autopsie meist akute Leberdystrophie. Bei allen 8 Re-Expositionsversuchen trat im Mittel nach 6 (1-14) Tagen erneut eine Hepatitis auf, die nach Absetzen abheilte; wegen Gefahr eines komplizierten Verlaufs wird von Re-Exposition abgeraten. Ausschluss anderer Ursachen (Hepatitis A/B/C/E serologisch, PCR, keine Autoimmun-/metabolische Leberkrankheit, negative Toxikologie).; liver_injury_short: Fulminant Hepatitis

raw_record.support_text: Metformin, a biguanide, has been associated in two reports with acute cholestatic hepatitis and in one case with bland cholestasis. Symptoms of acute hepatitis developed 2–4 weeks after taking metformin, and full recovery was observed in all three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases total: two acute cholestatic hepatitis reports and one bland cholestasis. Onset of symptoms 2–4 weeks after initiation; full recovery in all cases.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus developed jaundice, pruritus, and liver enzyme abnormalities four weeks after starting metformin (initially 500 mg twice daily, later increased to 850 mg twice a day). An extensive work-up (hepatitis screen, ultrasonography, MRI, ERCP) was normal, and liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis and mild portal inflammation. After metformin was discontinued the liver enzymes normalized except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase, attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect of metformin.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed diabetes. Metformin dosed 500 mg twice daily, later 850 mg twice a day; jaundice and pruritus appeared 4 weeks after initiation with liver enzyme abnormalities. Work-up including hepatitis screen, ultrasonography, MRI, and ERCP was normal. Liver biopsy revealed severe cholestasis and mild portal inflammation. Dechallenge: after discontinuing metformin, liver enzymes normalized except persistently increased alkaline phosphatase (AP), attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect. Phenotype termed 'cholestatic hepatitis'. Authors conclude metformin can rarely be responsible for inducing liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors' objective was to describe a patient with metformin-induced mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury who recovered after cessation of therapy and relapsed after rechallenge, attributing the liver injury to metformin.
raw_record.extra_details: A 67-year-old woman with an 8-year history of diabetes mellitus (treated by dietary restriction and acarbose) and coronary heart disease (isosorbide mononitrate, salicylic acid, diltiazem) began metformin 500 mg twice daily 6 weeks before admission and presented with 1-week jaundice, fatigue, weakness, and abdominal bloating. Labs: total bilirubin 82 µmol/L (4.8 mg/dL), direct bilirubin 60 µmol/L, ALT 905 U/L, AST 1152 U/L, ALP 121 U/L, GGT 248 U/L, INR 1.3. Negative viral and autoimmune serology except positive ANA (1:320 speckled). Liver biopsy showed marked portal inflammation with lymphocytes, monocytes and eosinophils, and acute lobular inflammation. Injury resolved on metformin cessation and relapsed after rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: After ruling out other etiologies (sepsis, ischemic hepatitis, low cardiac output), the case was attributed to pharmacological hepatotoxicity. Since no changes were made to the patient's treatment except for the introduction of metformin (metformina) 2 weeks earlier, metformin was considered the causal agent, supported by concurrent renal insufficiency and lactic acidosis, a known complication of metformin. The paper also noted 7 previously published cases of metformin hepatotoxicity (references 5-11), mostly cholestatic or mixed-pattern hepatitis appearing 2-6 weeks after starting metformin for diabetes, described as idiosyncratic reactions not associated with other drugs or triggering factors. Causality assessment gave Naranjo and María-Victorino scores of 10 points (definitive hepatotoxicity) and a CIOMS/RUCAM score of 9 points (very probable or defined pharmacological hepatotoxicity).
raw_record.extra_details: Diabetes treatment with metformin; reaction was early (within 2 weeks in this patient; 2-6 weeks in the 7 literature cases). Elevated aminotransferases (hyperaminotransferasemia) normalized fully within less than a month, with improvement starting one week after drug withdrawal; complete recovery in all described cases; no liver biopsy performed. Causality: Naranjo 10 (definitive), María-Victorino 10 (definitive), CIOMS/RUCAM 9 (muy probable or definido). Concurrent renal insufficiency and lactic acidosis present. Differential diagnoses excluded: septic shock (negative cultures), ischemic hepatitis/hepatic shock from heart failure, hepatic venous congestion. Patient had cardiac failure decompensation and hypotension at admission but these were excluded as the cause. Literature cases mostly cholestatic or mixed-pattern hepatitis (refs 5-11).

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that metformin can induce hepatic injury (hepatocellular and/or cholestatic), and notes that metformin hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported, with possible mechanisms being direct, idiosyncratic, or a drug–drug interaction leading to acute hepatocellular and/or cholestatic jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Search of PubMed yielded six published metformin hepatotoxicity reports (Table 2): two cases of acute hepatitis, two cases of cholestasis, and two cases of mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury; the paper's own patient is the third reported case of mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury. In all cases signs and symptoms resolved and liver enzymes normalized after metformin discontinuation, except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase in one case attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect. Liver biopsy was performed in three cases and rechallenge in one; no specific treatments were given. Bilirubin normalized after 2 months in the described case.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old white woman developed metformin-induced liver injury 5 weeks after starting metformin 500 mg twice daily for type 2 diabetes, and she was not on any other hepatotoxic agent. The case is reported to draw attention to this rare but important metformin side effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 70-year-old white woman with type 2 diabetes and hypothyroidism on only metformin 500 mg twice daily and levothyroxine, denying OTC medications, alcohol, or illicit drugs; injury developed 5 weeks after starting metformin, with no other hepatotoxic agent. Initial labs showed hepatocellular pattern: total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, ALT 1093 U/L, AST 1152 U/L, ALP 176 U/L, ALT/ALP ratio >5; normal INR and eosinophil counts. Metformin was discontinued with supportive care only; AST fell to 358 (day 2) and 71 (day 4), ALT to 747 (day 2) and 432 (day 4), bilirubin to 0.8 (day 3); labs normal 10 days after discharge. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, autoimmune and metabolic liver disease testing (iron, antimitochondrial/antinuclear/antismooth-muscle antibodies, ceruloplasmin, copper), abdominal ultrasound and MRCP were unremarkable. No rechallenge, causality instrument, or formal assessment reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 30 patients with metformin-induced hepatotoxicity, metformin was discontinued in all patients. Four patients (13.3%) were rechallenged with metformin and two of them relapsed with hepatotoxicity. Liver function returned to normal in all 30 patients (100%) at a median time of 6 weeks (range 2–16), while two patients had persistently high ALP levels.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality assessment: probable 16/30 (53.3%), highly probable 13/30 (43.3%), possible 1/30 (3.3%). Injury pattern: hepatocellular 14 (46.7%), cholestatic 9 (30.0%), mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic 7 (23.3%). Severity: mild 5 (16.7%), moderate 18 (60.0%), severe 3 (10.0%), NA 4 (13.3%). All patients recovered; rechallenge relapsed in 2/4. Laboratory values (median, range): ALT 694.5 U/L (47–4701), AST 382.5 U/L (36–8091), TBIL 4.5 mg/dl (0.5–25.6), ALP 437 U/L (94–1001). Clinical features included jaundice (50%), fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. Biopsy (13 patients) showed portal inflammation (61.5%), cholestatic hepatitis (38.5%), parenchymal inflammation (38.5%), bile duct inflammation with epithelial destruction (23.1%), fibrosis (15.4%). Maximum approved daily dose 2.5 g; hepatotoxicity seen in 20% of Asians in this analysis.

raw_record.support_text: Metformin-induced hepatotoxicity is described as a rare idiosyncratic reaction associated with marked elevations in serum liver transaminases and intrahepatic cholestasis. In the present and a previous case, hepatotoxicity resolved spontaneously within several weeks following discontinuation of the agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Rare idiosyncratic reaction with marked elevation in serum liver transaminases and intrahepatic cholestasis; hepatotoxicity resolved spontaneously within several weeks of drug discontinuation in the present and a previous case.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data in the reported case were described as compatible with a diagnosis of severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, probably due to atorvastatin, in a 69-year-old man treated for hypercholesterolemia. Symptoms appeared about 1 week after reinitiating atorvastatin 10 mg/day following a 5-month period of treatment without adverse reactions; after the drug was discontinued and later taken again, the symptoms reappeared, which the authors considered a positive rechallenge. Viral hepatitis serologies and autoantibodies were negative, the patient denied alcohol, and liver tests plus eosinophil count normalized after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 69-year-old man treated with atorvastatin 10 mg/day for hypercholesterolemia. Presenting symptoms were asthenia, nausea, pruritus and dark urine. Analytical changes during hepatitis: TB 2.6 mg/dl, AST 669, ALT 727, ALP 3767, GGTP 1359, eosinophil rise (1764). Positive rechallenge (symptoms reappeared after reinitiating therapy); symptoms first appeared ~6 days-1 week after reinitiation on Nov 17, 2000. Prior use of simvastatin, pravastatin, cholestyramine and gemfibrozil without attributed liver injury. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild steatosis. The paper notes atorvastatin has previously been associated with mild serum transaminase elevations and acute hepatitis; hepatitis also described with other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.

raw_record.support_text: In this three-patient case series, Patients 2 (J.K., 47-year-old man) and 3 (B.J., 51-year-old man) developed autoimmune hepatitis after about 4 months of atorvastatin therapy, with peak serum ALT 1170 and 1555 U/L and peak total bilirubin 3.4 and 5.5 mg/dL, AIH scores of 17 and 14, and Ishak fibrosis stages 4-5 and 4; two previously reported atorvastatin-triggered AIH cases (a 58-year-old woman who progressed to compensated cirrhosis and a 65-year-old woman) are also reviewed. The abstract further states that a patient developed severe atorvastatin-triggered hepatitis that persisted even after discontinuing medication. The authors conclude it is probable that atorvastatin (a statin) triggered the development of AIH.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients 2 (J.K., male, 47 y) and 3 (B.J., male, 51 y) developed AIH after 4 months of atorvastatin; peak ALT 1170 and 1555 U/L, peak total bilirubin 3.4 and 5.5 mg/dL, peak ALP 160 and 203 U/L, ASMA titers 1:40 and 1:160, AIH scores 17 and 14, Ishak fibrosis 4-5 and 4, DR-4/7 and DR-4 HLA; responded to azathioprine+prednisone (normal in 3 mo) and prednisone+mycophenolate (normal in 7 mo). Previously reported atorvastatin AIH cases (Ref 9: 58-y woman, bilirubin 32 mg/dL, progressed to compensated cirrhosis, tacrolimus/prednisolone/mycophenolate; Ref 1: 65-y woman, DR-7, ALT/AST <3x ULN after 67 d prednisone). Abstract notes a severe atorvastatin hepatitis that persisted after discontinuation. Patients were treated for hyperlipidemia/familial hypercholesterolemia.

raw_record.support_text: Among 73 cases included in the final causality-assessed analysis of statin-induced DILI, the vast majority were due to atorvastatin (n = 30) and simvastatin (n = 28). Other statin-associated liver injuries were due to fluvastatin (n = 11), pravastatin (n = 2) and rosuvastatin (n = 2). The biochemical types among the whole cohort were hepatocellular (59%), cholestatic (30%) and mixed (11%).
raw_record.extra_details: Largest contributor with 30/73 adjudicated DILI cases. Specific cases: F39 atorvastatin (10 mg) 120 days, causality possible, fatal outcome (death); F60 atorvastatin (40 mg) second treatment 30 days, highly probable, with positive rechallenge producing a similar liver-injury pattern ~1 month after re-exposure; F52 atorvastatin (10 mg) second treatment 30 days, highly probable, positive rechallenge. Causality grades across cohort: 52 possible, 14 probable, 7 highly probable. Median time to abnormal liver tests 3 months; ~35% jaundice at presentation; median ALT 10 x ULN. Rechallenge cases had negative viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/CMV/EBV) markers and no suspicion of alcoholic liver disease or hypotension.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 22 patients with statin-induced liver injury, 8 cases were attributed to atorvastatin (cases 1-8) at doses of 10-80 mg daily, with peak ALT up to 4560 U/L, mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns, autoimmune features in some cases, DILIN causality scores of 1-3 and RUCAM scores of 5-12, all resolving, with worst severity scored 4+ (severe).
raw_record.extra_details: 8 cases (cases 1-8); doses 10-80 mg/day; time to onset 2.2-120 months; peak ALT 222-4560 U/L; peak bilirubin up to 30.2 mg/dL; patterns included hepatocellular, cholestatic, and hepatocellular with autoimmune features (HC-AI-P); severity up to 4+; all resolved; autoimmune cases treated with prednisone and azathioprine (case 7).

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin is identified as one of five drugs present among the ten most common drugs causing DILI in at least two of three prospective studies (Icelandic and Spanish registries).
raw_record.extra_details: Statin; appears in the top ten drugs of the Icelandic and Spanish prospective DILI registries.

raw_record.support_text: The review reports statin-induced liver injury as an established clinical entity based on prospective DILI studies. In the Icelandic prospective population study, 2 of 96 DILI patients had liver injury associated with atorvastatin; in the DILIN US study 22/1188 DILI cases (2004-2014) with at least probable likelihood were associated with statins, and in Sweden a spontaneous-reporting cohort identified 73 statin DILI cases. During the 2-year Icelandic period 7385 patients were treated with atorvastatin and 2 developed DILI, a risk of roughly 1 in 3700 treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 atorvastatin DILI cases in the Icelandic study among 7385 treated users (~1/3700 risk). Atorvastatin is among statins implicated in Spanish Registry (47/858 statin cases) and DILIN (22/1188) series. More patients with statin injury had hepatocellular than cholestatic/mixed injury, but cholestatic/mixed pattern was more common with atorvastatin (56% of patients) than with simvastatin (24%, p=0.018) in the Swedish study. Documented positive rechallenge reported for atorvastatin. Statins as a class were implicated in 3 ALF-transplant-list cases (1990-2002, US) and 6/133 (4.5%) ALF cases (1998-2007, US).

raw_record.support_text: The Swedish DILI register reported a statin-related DILI episode in 1.2/100,000 users, with atorvastatin implicated in 30/73 (41%) cases, simvastatin in 28/73 (38%), and fluvastatin in 11/73 (15%), showing most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths due to acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation. In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, atorvastatin was implicated in 1.0%, rosuvastatin in 0.8%, pravastatin in 0.4%, fluvastatin in 0.2%, and lovastatin in 0.2% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases, with atorvastatin and rosuvastatin showing a long latency period (>60 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 30/73 (41%) of statin-DILI cases in the Swedish DILI register (statin DILI incidence 1.2/100,000 users); register statin DILI showed most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths from acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation across the 73 cases (not attributable to a specific statin). In the DILIN prospective study, atorvastatin was implicated in 1.0% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases and showed a long DILI latency profile (>60 days postexposure).

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, statins were initially implicated in 61 of 1188 suspected DILI cases, but after formal adjudication only 22 (1.85%) were accepted as true statin-induced DILI; injury was mostly mild-moderate and self-limited, with 4 severe and 1 fatal case, and a predominantly hepatocellular pattern (n=12). Atorvastatin accounted for 8 of these 22 adjudicated cases. The paper attributes statin DILI to an idiosyncratic timing of onset with variable presentation and a likely class effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated atorvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=8; Iceland study n=2 with estimated population risk of DILI of 27 per 100,000 (95% CI 4-98) persons treated with atorvastatin; Swedish study 1970-2004 n=8 (statin total) and 1988-2010 n=30 total atorvastatin with cholestatic-predominant phenotype; Spanish Registry n=16 (34%). Latency from exposure to clinically evident DILI ranged 34 days to >10 years. DILIN aggregate (all statins): 4 severe cases, 1 fatal, 15 (68%) jaundiced with total bilirubin ≥2.5 mg/dL, 4 (18%) with INR >1.5; hepatocellular (12) versus cholestatic (9).

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was given as the working diagnosis based on the timing of new drug therapies and the absence of pain. Using the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM), DILI secondary to atorvastatin was judged to be 'probable'.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality score: 'probable'. Working diagnosis supported by timing of new drug therapies and absence of pain. A wider differential diagnosis was considered.

raw_record.support_text: A case report attributes the patient's drug-induced liver injury to atorvastatin. The patient had an initial R-value > 5, classifying the injury as hepatocellular, and a Roussel-Uclaf causality assessment method (RUCAM) score placing them in the 'highly probable' category for drug-related liver injury. The patient was diagnosed with autoimmune-like DILI, with weakly positive ANA and ASMA (1:640 titers, decreasing to 1:80 after discontinuation of atorvastatin). Liver tests rose to ALT 3756 U/L, AST 3172 U/L, and total bilirubin 90.1 micromol/L at diagnosis and returned to normal after stopping atorvastatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for dyslipidemia/high LDL management. RUCAM score rated 'highly probable'; initial R-value > 5 (hepatocellular). Autoimmune-like DILI with weakly positive ANAs and ASMA decreased from 1:640 to 1:80 after drug discontinuation. At diagnosis: ALT 3756 U/L, AST 3172 U/L, total bilirubin 90.1, direct bilirubin 60.3, ALP 397 U/L. Liver tests normalized by 30 days after stopping atorvastatin and remained normal on follow-up. No immunosuppressants needed. Cites Russo et al. reporting 6 of 12 statin hepatocellular-injury cases as autoimmune-like DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was attributed to 16 DILI cases with hepatocellular (44%), cholestatic (25%) and mixed (31%) patterns. Seven cases (44%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria but had favourable outcomes without fatalities or liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 44%/Chol 25%/Mix 31%; female 44%, lymphopenia 0%, eosinophilia 19%; 7 (44%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law with no fatalities/liver transplantation; hepatocelluar subset had highest mean ALT and cholestatic subset high mean ALP.

raw_record.support_text: An adult female developed persistent fevers, abdominal and flank pain, malaise, and generalized muscle weakness without any cutaneous reaction after 20 days of atorvastatin therapy. Peak labs showed ALP 792 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 21 mg/dL, eosinophils 3100 cells/µL, and leukocytes 20.2 K/µL; serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, and autoimmune markers were negative. After being initially treated as pyelonephritis without improvement, a diagnosis of atorvastatin-induced DRESS syndrome was considered probable and atorvastatin was discontinued, after which the patient's clinical status improved and her liver enzymes and eosinophils normalized over about a month.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of probable atorvastatin-induced DRESS syndrome without cutaneous findings; regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction (RegiSCAR probable). Liver involvement shown by elevated ALP 792 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 21 mg/dL with eosinophilia and fever; no rash throughout the course. Injury resolved after drug discontinuation (dechallenge) with normalization of liver enzymes and eosinophils over about one month without further therapy; hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, ANA, RF, ANCA, mitochondrial and smooth muscle antibodies negative. Prior review reportedly found only 4 case reports of statin-associated DRESS.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin was one of the most commonly implicated conventional drugs in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry, adjudicated as the single cause of liver injury in 16 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 adjudicated single-cause cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry; ATC C10AA05; third most frequent culprit along with nivolumab-ipilimumab, accounting for 8% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists atorvastatin as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 9 conferring a highly probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 9, highly probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [15].

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular liver injury after taking atorvastatin, with jaundice and aminotransferases greater than five times the upper limit of normal. Liver biopsy showed features compatible with autoimmune drug-induced liver injury, and the diagnosis was atorvastatin-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 6 for the current admission, indicating atorvastatin was the probable causative agent, and a RUCAM score of 10 for a prior episode indicated atorvastatin was the highly probable causative agent. Symptoms improved with statin cessation alone, and the patient had a prior unexplained episode of elevated liver enzymes that resolved within three months after atorvastatin was held, with recurrence following the reintroduction of atorvastatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury with R value 3.32 on current admission and R value 7.47 during a prior episode. Jaundice, aminotransferases >5x ULN; Child-Pugh Class C, MELD score 26. Liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with periportal fibrosis, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, interface hepatitis, numerous plasma cells, severe portal inflammation, focal periportal fibrosis, and bile ductular proliferation; Simplified Autoimmune Hepatitis Score 8. ANA 1:160 (prior episode ANA 1:640), positive RNP, hypergammaglobulinemia; anti-LKM-1 negative. Hepatitis C antibody positive but PCR negative. RUCAM scores: 6 (current, probable) and 10 (prior, highly probable). Atorvastatin was held and LFTs downtrended; no corticosteroid used. Recurrence of DIAIH following reintroduction of atorvastatin. Patient died after discharge of unrelated causes. Latency of DIAIH highly variable (weeks to years).

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is described as a rare but well-documented life-threatening adverse event. In this report, a 57-year-old female prescribed atorvastatin 20 mg daily for dyslipidemia three months prior presented with worsening fatigue, jaundice, and deranged liver function tests; a liver biopsy confirmed a drug-induced autoimmune picture, and she was diagnosed with atorvastatin-induced AIH after ruling out all other possible causes, with improvement after prolonged treatment with prednisone.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin 20 mg daily for 3 months before presentation, used for dyslipidemia (patient also had type 2 diabetes mellitus). Labs: ALT 251 U/L (ref 0-55), ALP 391 U/L (40-150), AST 445 U/L (5-34), GGT 588 U/L (12-64), total bilirubin 6.9 mg/dL. ANA titer 1:180; IgG within normal range; smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial, and liver-kidney microsomal antibodies negative; negative hepatitis A/B/C, HIV, CMV, and EBV serology; normal MRCP. Liver biopsy confirmed a drug-induced autoimmune picture; other causes ruled out. Atorvastatin was discontinued and the patient improved after prolonged treatment with prednisone. Paper notes drug-induced AIH is a rare but documented cause of liver failure/transplantation, with a hepatocellular pattern of enzyme elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Case reports of ciprofloxacin-associated hepatotoxicity include 2 fatal cases of fulminant hepatic failure (Grassmick 1992: 66-year-old, onset 1 day, peak ALT 2608 U/L, hepatocellular; Fuchs 1994: 92-year-old, onset 2 days, hepatocellular), as well as several hepatocellular and cholestatic injury cases (Levinson, Aggarwal, Sherman, Villeneuve, Labowitz, Hautekeete, Smith) with full or partial resolution.
raw_record.extra_details: Case reports per Table 1: Grassmick (66y, onset 1d, ALT 2608/AST 2625/ALP 269/B 10.8, H, fulminant hepatic failure and death); Levinson (46y, CH, resolved over weeks); Fuchs (92y, onset 2d, H, fulminant hepatic failure and death); Aggarwal (36y, CH, LFTs baseline in 6 wk); Sherman (84y, CH, resolved over 3 mo); Villeneuve (44y, H, normalized after 8 mo); Labowitz (47y, CH, normal in 12 wk); Hautekeete (50y, onset 5d, CH); Smith (82y, onset 8d, H, full recovery in 4 wk). Discussion notes 2 fatal cases associated with ciprofloxacin.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old man treated with ciprofloxacin 2×250 mg daily for 7 days during a skin infection presented 14 days after intake with nausea and jaundice, and laboratory findings showed the typical pattern of acute liver failure (AST 907 U/l, ALT 890 U/l, AP 180 U/l, reduced PT-time 40%, bilirubin 16.9 mg/dl). Serology for viral hepatitis and autoimmune/mitochondrial antibodies was negative, there was no history of liver disease, alcohol, blood transfusion, or other medication, and liver biopsy revealed extensive hepatocellular necrosis involving zones 3 and 2 of hepatic acini with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils. A diagnosis of ciprofloxacin-associated hepatitis was rendered and the patient improved rapidly on methylprednisolone.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ciprofloxacin-induced acute hepatitis with extensive hepatocellular necrosis (zones 3 and 2) and mixed inflammatory infiltrate with abundant eosinophils; patient improved after corticosteroid (methylprednisolone) therapy and was discharged asymptomatic 8 days after admission. Authors note up to that time 14 cases of ciprofloxacin-associated liver injury were documented in the literature, with a direct causal association proven in only 2; ciprofloxacin can reportedly produce three histological patterns (pure hepatocellular cholestasis, zone 3 hepatocellular necrosis, or mixed pattern); most cases improved on cessation, while two resulted in fulminant hepatitis and death; mean time from drug start to injury 6.3±5.9 days. One additional case of chronic cholestatic liver disease occurred ~6.5 months after treatment with ciprofloxacin and ornidazol.

raw_record.support_text: Ciprofloxacin was among the antibiotics most often responsible for DILI with four cases in the series. The pattern distribution was two hepatocellular, one cholestatic and one mixed; three of the cases involved jaundice (bilirubin ≥2 ULN).
raw_record.extra_details: Four of 77 DILI cases; pattern 2 hepatocellular/1 cholestatic/1 mixed; duration of treatment median 7 (2-7) days, time to biochemical resolution 32 (26-45) days. Three jaundice cases listed (listed as Ciproxin), bilirubin 2.2-9.6 ULN.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old male with gastroenteritis developed elevated liver function tests (AST 520, ALT 582, ALP 1234, γ-GT 977 IU/L, direct bilirubin 1.48 mg/dL) three days after starting ciprofloxacin 400 mg twice daily IV. Ciprofloxacin was discontinued; enzymes gradually improved and returned to normal within 3 months. All common causes of acute hepatitis were excluded, and the Naranjo ADR Probability Scale indicated the hepatitis was probably due to ciprofloxacin. The authors conclude this is the first case providing clear evidence that ciprofloxacin by itself, at therapeutic doses, can cause acute cholestatic hepatitis, with no confounding factors present.
raw_record.extra_details: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg twice daily intravenously; liver enzymes rose 3 days after first dose (peak AST 550, ALT 515, ALP 1850, γ-GT 2410 at day 10), then improved after discontinuation; returned to normal within 3 months and remained normal during 10-month follow-up. Naranjo ADR Probability Scale indicated a probable association. Reported as the first case with no confounding factors (no additional drugs, pathogens, or environmental conditions); only four prior cases of ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic hepatitis in the literature. Gastroenteritis as presenting diagnosis; patient refused liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: In the three cases observed by the authors, the temporal relation and short latency (median 2 days) between use of ciprofloxacin (or levofloxacin) and liver damage, the absence of other hepatotoxic drugs, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, and a compatible liver histology in case 3 supported the diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury. Dechallenge was positive in all cases and rechallenge was not performed. RUCAM classified the cases as probable or highly probable and the Naranjo algorithm as possible or probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury in 3 cases; median latency 2 days; patients were not taking other hepatotoxic drugs; other causes of hepatitis (viral, autoimmune, alcohol) excluded; compatible liver histology in case 3; dechallenge positive, no rechallenge; RUCAM probable/highly probable, Naranjo possible/probable. SPC lists hepatotoxicity as a rare adverse reaction of ciprofloxacin related to both oral and intravenous administration.

raw_record.support_text: Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, was implicated as the cause of drug-induced liver injury in a 41-year-old woman treated for a urinary tract infection. After a few days of ciprofloxacin she developed jaundice and right upper quadrant discomfort with markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 1058 IU/L, ALT 806 IU/L, total bilirubin 11.5 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 315 IU/L). Other causes of acute hepatitis (acetaminophen intoxication, acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease), vascular obstruction, and cholelithiasis were ruled out; liver biopsy showed lobular disarray with lobular and portal lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils consistent with drug-induced liver injury. After ciprofloxacin was discontinued, symptoms and liver-injury markers improved. The discussion notes fourteen cases of ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury have been reported, two of which, similar to this case, occurred in patients not on any other medication, confirming this rare side effect.
raw_record.extra_details: 41-year-old woman with recurrent right kidney stones and prior UTI treated with Bactrim; treated with ciprofloxacin for a Streptococcus viridans UTI. Jaundice and RUQ discomfort developed a few days after starting ciprofloxacin, leading to hospital admission. Labs: AST 1058 IU/L, ALT 806 IU/L, total bilirubin 11.5 mg/L (direct 6.5 mg/L), alkaline phosphatase 315 IU/L. Ruled out: acetaminophen intoxication, acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease, vascular obstruction, cholelithiasis. Liver biopsy: marked lobular disarray, lobular and portal lymphocytes, occasional eosinophils, no plasma cells. Symptoms and liver-injury markers improved after withdrawal. Discussion notes 14 reported cases of ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury, only two patients (including this one) not on any other medication.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, ciprofloxacin accounted for 16 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases. DILI caused by ciprofloxacin had a 19% mortality rate, the highest among the compared agents, versus 0-1% for minocycline, cefazolin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate.
raw_record.extra_details: 16 adjudicated DILI cases; DILI-caused mortality 19%, the highest among compared agents.

raw_record.support_text: The CIOMS/RUCAM scale was assessed to be 8, defining the suspicion of ciprofloxacin as the cause of the patient's hepatotoxicity as highly probable. Factors included time of onset between medication use and symptoms, course of injury, risk factors, concomitant drug administration, potential non-drug origins of hepatic failure, documented information on ciprofloxacin hepatotoxicity, and response to readministration of the antibiotic. The patient presented with worsening fatigue, jaundice, ascites, and rising bilirubin (TBIL 22.6, INR 1.8). The background section states the background states that ciprofloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity proved fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 74-year-old female treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection; onset of nausea/vomiting on day 4-5 of first course; drug discontinued day 5; patient rechallenged with three days of ciprofloxacin during a later admission before ciprofloxacin was suspected. Liver biopsy showed active chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and portal and periportal fibrosis. Labs included AST 1,106-1,263, ALT 789-870, ALP 338-496, TBIL up to 22.6, INR 1.8. CIOMS/RUCAM score 8 (highly probable). Concurrent medications simvastatin (discontinued during workup), pantoprazole, levothyroxine were considered; competing causes (viral hepatitis A-E, HSV, CMV, EBV, autoimmune, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, malignancy) were ruled out. Fatal outcome from ciprofloxacin-induced liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Among antibiotic-related acute liver failure, ciprofloxacin was implicated in n=1 case of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute cholestatic liver injury attributed to ciprofloxacin in a 32-year-old female who developed pruritus, jaundice, and abdominal pain three days after completing a 10-day ciprofloxacin course for a urinary tract infection. Hepatic enzymes showed a cholestatic pattern, an extensive workup excluded other cholestasis causes, and liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced cholestasis. A diagnosis of ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury was made based on symptom onset after ciprofloxacin use, biochemical and clinical improvement after cessation, and biopsy findings; the patient recovered with liver enzymes returning to baseline six weeks after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 32-year-old female; a 10-day ciprofloxacin course for urinary tract infection; symptoms (pruritus, jaundice, abdominal pain) began three days after completing the course; hepatic enzymes showed a cholestatic pattern; liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced cholestasis; workup excluded viral, autoimmune, and imaging-based cholestasis causes; supportive treatment; liver enzymes returned to baseline six weeks after admission; patient advised to avoid ciprofloxacin and other quinolones. The paper notes 25 previously reported cases of ciprofloxacin-induced severe liver injury in the literature and that ciprofloxacin usually causes mild transient liver enzyme elevation in 2-3% of patients. Prior courses of fosfomycin and cefixime were taken three months before symptom onset and not implicated.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists ciprofloxacin as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 11 conferring a highly probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 11, highly probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [18].

raw_record.support_text: The objective states a case of probable ciprofloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity. A 44-year-old woman developed severe hepatitis 3 weeks after initiation of a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin; liver biopsy showed severe hepatic necrosis, other causes of liver injury were excluded, and liver function tests returned to normal 4 months after the appearance of jaundice. The paper concludes that ciprofloxacin can cause severe hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 44-year-old woman; 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin; severe hepatitis developed 3 weeks after initiating therapy; liver biopsy showed severe hepatic necrosis; other causes of hepatitis/liver injury were excluded; jaundice appeared and liver function tests returned to normal 4 months later; the adverse event was not currently labeled in the product literature; previous unpublished reports to the manufacturer of possible ciprofloxacin hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: An 84-year-old nursing-home woman developed acute cholestatic jaundice while taking ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for a urinary tract infection. On the sixth day of treatment a pruritic erythematous rash appeared on the chest and abdomen and ciprofloxacin was stopped because of a suspected allergic reaction; three days later she developed yellowish discoloration of skin and conjunctivae with abnormal liver function tests, elevated plasma cholesterol but normal prothrombin time and albumin. Liver function tests normalized within one month and remained normal at three months. The discussion and conclusions state this is considered a probable hepatic injury attributable to ciprofloxacin and, reportedly, the first case of an acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: 84-year-old woman in a nursing home; indication urinary tract infection; ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily; erythematous pruritic rash on chest and abdomen on day 6 prompted drug cessation; jaundice appeared 3 days later with disturbed liver function tests; elevated plasma cholesterol with normal prothrombin time and albumin; supportive fluids given; liver function normalized within one month and remained normal at three months; patient asymptomatic; authors call it probable hepatic involvement (atteinte hépatique imputable) and the first reported acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin; causality mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: A 50-year-old man treated for a urinary tract infection with oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice a day for 5 days developed asthenia, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, diarrhea, mild fever and jaundice on the last day of therapy, with ALT 202 IU/l, AST 111 IU/l, AP 314 IU/l, γGT 135 IU/l and bilirubin 82 µmol/l. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune antibodies and bile duct obstruction were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed pronounced centrolobular cholestasis with minimal portal lympho-eosinophilic infiltration. The patient recovered completely after jaundice lasting 9 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 of cholestatic hepatitis. No rechallenge performed; authors concluded the time course, exclusion of other causes and histology support cholestasis being induced by ciprofloxacin. Fever and eosinophilia argued for an idiosyncratic (immunoallergic) reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 159 µmol/l; severe pruritus; full recovery. Background literature noted: icteric cholestatic injury after ciprofloxacin (refs 5,6) and a reported case of fulminant hepatitis possibly related to ciprofloxacin (ref 9).

raw_record.support_text: Significant hepatotoxicity has been reported with the use of tacrine. All patients receiving tacrine should have baseline liver function tests performed, and liver function tests should be followed during weeks 4 through 16. Patients should be alert for symptoms of liver failure, and dosing guidelines are adjusted in response to liver function testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Tacrine (Cognex) is an acridine-derivative cholinesterase inhibitor FDA-approved in 1995 for Alzheimer's disease. In double-blind placebo-controlled trials, a significant percentage of patients, especially those at higher doses, withdrew because of intolerable hepatotoxicity and cholinergic side effects. Liver function test monitoring is recommended from weeks 4 through 16 with baseline testing; dosing is adjusted based on LFT results, and tacrine should be used with caution in hepatic insufficiency. Oral dosing divided into initial (10 mg four times daily for 4 weeks), titration up to maximum 160 mg total per day.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine hydrochloride (Cognex; Parke-Davis), the first FDA-approved AChEI (1993), causes serious hepatotoxicity: in approximately 27% of tested patients, alanine aminotransferase levels greater than three times the upper limit of normal occurred in clinical testing. The paper states that severe side effects including this hepatotoxicity and its short half-life limit its use in treating Alzheimer's disease.
raw_record.extra_details: In approximately 27% of tested patients serous hepatotoxicity with ALT >3x ULN occurred in clinical testing (Watkins et al., 1994). In a 30-week RCT of tacrine 40-160 mg/day in AD patients (Knapp et al., 1994), tacrine-treated patients frequently showed hepatotoxicity such as serum ALT exceeding 10x ULN plus cholinergic adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, dyspepsia, abdominal pain). Severe hepatotoxicity and short biological half-life limit clinical usefulness. Tacrine (Cognex) listed as having 'severe hepatotoxicity' among its side effects in the summary table.

raw_record.support_text: In the Knapp et al. trial, tacrine titrated to the maximum tolerated dosage (80–160 mg/day) was compared with placebo in 653 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease over 30 weeks, using the ADAS-noncog scale for behavioural symptoms. There were no statistically significant differences between treatment arms regarding behavioural symptoms, and the study had a very high withdrawal rate because of the hepatotoxic effects of the drug; of the 653 patients randomised, only 263 completed the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a reason for high study withdrawal in 653 randomized patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; tacrine dose titrated to maximum tolerated dosage (80–160 mg/day) over 30 weeks; only 263 of 653 patients completed the study.

raw_record.support_text: In controlled clinical trials of tacrine for Alzheimer's disease (Cognex package insert, Parke-Davis 1993), increased ALT occurred as an adverse effect in 29% of tacrine-treated patients (n=634) versus 2% of placebo recipients (n=342), described as tacrine hepatotoxicity. The paper further reports that of 145 patients with serum ALT increases 3-10 times the upper limit of normal, 127 were successfully rechallenged and continued tacrine, but rechallenge is considered imprudent for patients with ALT increases 20 times or greater than normal or with signs of allergic response (rash, fever, eosinophilia), and tacrine should be stopped if jaundice occurs or serum ALT reaches three times the upper limit of normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Increased ALT in 29% of tacrine patients (n=634) vs 2% placebo (n=342) in controlled trials for Alzheimer's disease. Of 145 patients with ALT 3-10x ULN, 127 were successfully rechallenged (Watkins), showing a more rapid rise but lower peak ALT with eventual return to normal; rechallenge discouraged for ALT >=20x ULN or allergic signs (rash, fever, eosinophilia). Tacrine should be stopped if jaundice occurs or ALT >=3x ULN; monthly ALT monitoring advised due to possibility of late hepatotoxicity. Contraindicated in patients with jaundice related to tacrine treatment when total bilirubin >50 umol/L.

raw_record.support_text: This paper characterizes tacrine-induced liver injury in humans. Of 636 patients developing elevated transaminases during clinical trials, 5 had jaundice; all had ALT >3x ULN, 3 had significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, and 1 significant bilirubin elevation, and 3 patients recovered on drug discontinuation. A Hammel et al. case reported acute hepatitis in a 76-year-old woman after 20 days of tacrine 75 mg/d (jaundice and fever, markedly elevated bilirubin and ALT), with a liver biopsy showing marked centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and mild inflammatory infiltration, and LFTs normal five days after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From NDA clinical-trial data: 636 patients developed elevated transaminases, 5 with jaundice (all ALT >3x ULN, 3 significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, 1 significant bilirubin elevation); 3 recovered on discontinuation. Manufacturer biopsy data for 7 patients with elevated transaminases showed hepatocellular necrosis in 6 and granulomatous hepatitis in 1; an Australian study of 4 patients with asymptomatic liver-enzyme increases found focal necrosis with slight fatty changes (1 with granulomatous hepatitis). Of 56 rechallenged patients in one study, 21.4% discontinued due to recurrence of elevated LFTs, with mean time to ALT elevation of 19 days (faster than initial onset). In the adverse-effects table (NDA trials), elevated transaminases occurred in 23.5% of 2706 tacrine-treated patients vs 1.5% of 342 placebo patients (difference 22.0%).; df: None

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine (Cognex) is described as causing clinically evident liver toxicity: of more than 8000 patients exposed in clinical studies and the treatment IND program, one documented patient had elevated bilirubin (5.3 × ULN), jaundice, and transaminase levels (AST/SGOT) nearly 20 × ULN. In the 30-week clinical study and all trials (2446 patients), approximately 50% had at least one ALT/SGPT elevation above ULN, about 25% developed elevations >3 × ULN, ~7% (>10 × ULN in trials) and 3% of 5665 treatment IND patients had ALT >10 × ULN; all transaminase levels returned to normal after discontinuation or dose reduction, usually within 4-6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand: Cognex. Intended for Alzheimer's disease. One case of jaundice with bilirubin 5.3 × ULN and AST/SGOT ~20 × ULN among >8000 exposed in clinical studies and the treatment IND program. In the 30-week study (N=479), ALT elevations: >ULN 54%, >2×ULN 38%, >3×ULN 29%, >10×ULN 6%, >20×ULN 2%; median time to first ALT elevation ~6 weeks, maximum ~1 week later; 95% of >3×ULN elevations within first 18 weeks under forced slow dose titration; 99% of 10-fold elevations by 12th week at ≤80 mg. All transaminases returned to normal on discontinuation or dose reduction, usually within 4-6 weeks. Transaminase monitoring and discontinuation criteria recommended (label WARNINGS: Liver Injury).

raw_record.support_text: Pemoline-induced hepatic injury is reported to range from an asymptomatic increase in serum transaminase levels, often reversible upon withdrawal of therapy, to cases of liver failure requiring liver transplantation or leading to death. Because of these findings the drug is recommended only as second-line treatment with careful monitoring of liver chemistries, indicating the paper's general claim that pemoline causes human hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Literature assertion: hepatic injury spectrum from asymptomatic serum transaminase increase (reversible on drug withdrawal) to liver failure requiring transplantation or death; drug recommended only as second-line with liver chemistry monitoring. Case report: 36-year-old female presented with 5 days of jaundice, hypocholic stools, dark urine, and developed acute liver failure requiring orthotopic liver transplantation; on admission no known causes of acute hepatitis including drugs were found, and after several days she admitted taking therapy from a 'non-traditional' physician for overweight, used for several years and recently modified by the introduction of pemoline. Admission liver chemistry: AST 460 U/l (normal <35), ALT 1000 U/l (normal <37), total bilirubin 22.5 mg/dl (normal <1), direct bilirubin 11.1 mg/dl, γGT 330 U/l (normal <40); negative serology for HAV, HBV, HCV; normal abdominal ultrasound. Pemoline (phenylisohydantoin) is a central nervous system stimulant indicated for attention/hyperactivity deficit disorders in children. Other side effects: insomnia, headache, mild depression, anorexia with weight loss.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of pemoline treatment for ADHD in 40 college students eligible for efficacy evaluation, routine laboratory measurements showed no hepatotoxicity in any of the students. No liver injury was reported among the treated students.
raw_record.extra_details: Open-label pemoline treatment of adult university students with ADHD; routine laboratory measurements showed no hepatotoxicity in any of the 40 students in the evaluable data set. An additional 5 students treated for fewer than 14 days were eligible only for safety evaluation.

raw_record.support_text: In the reviewed imatinib clinical trials, imatinib was discontinued because of serious adverse effects in up to 8% of patients with GISTs. Serious adverse effects requiring dose decreases and/or termination of imatinib therapy included severe hepatotoxicity in 1-3.5% of patients, alongside severe hematologic toxicity (46%), edema (1-5%), severe skin rashes, and nausea/vomiting.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 1-3.5% of imatinib-treated patients across the summarized CML and GIST clinical trials; this serious adverse effect required dose decreases and/or termination of treatment. Imatinib was discontinued because of serious adverse effects in 1% of chronic-phase CML, 2% accelerated-phase CML, 5% blast-crisis, and 8% of GIST patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that imatinib mesylate caused the acute cytolytic hepatitis observed in their patient because other potential causes were carefully excluded and a compatible chronological sequence with shortening of the exposure time after rechallenge was observed, giving the maximum likely causality score. In the absence of immunoallergic manifestations, an idiosyncratic type of drug-induced liver disease was judged probable, especially since rechallenge at only 2.5% of the usual therapeutic dose (10 mg/day) again produced an increase in aminotransferase activities.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib mesylate given at 400 mg/day for a pelvic mass (indication) starting 22 Oct 2003; cytolytic hepatitis with markedly elevated ALT (up to 66.3 x ULN) and AST (30.1 x ULN), serum bilirubin rising to 56 µmol/l, and prothrombin time nadir of 76%. Other drugs (pentoxifylline, naftidrofuryl, omeprazole, ketoprofen, paracetamol 1–3 g/day, aspirin 75 mg/day, atorvastatin, irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide) taken >1 year were excluded as causes; viral, autoimmune, and metabolic serologies were negative. Liver function normalized after drug cessation. Rechallenge with 300 mg/day (24–27 Feb 2004) and 10 mg/day (17–20 Mar 2004; 2.5% of usual dose) caused immediate biochemical relapse. Liver biopsy showed periportal necrosis, portal and periportal fibrosis with septa and bridging fibrosis, mild lymphocytic/neutrophilic infiltrate, and Councilman bodies, without steatosis or granuloma. Patient subsequently treated with sunitinib malate without detectable liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with imatinib mesylate developed hepatotoxicity including an increase in total bilirubin to a maximum of 513.4 µmol/l on hospital day 7, with normalization after 6 weeks following discontinuation of imatinib and short steroid therapy. After resuming imatinib mesylate at a reduced dose of 400 mg daily, the patient experienced no further hepatotoxicity. The authors attribute the liver abnormalities to imatinib mesylate.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib mesylate-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. Transaminase activity and bilirubin increased after 10 days of imatinib use; levels normalized after interruption for 6 weeks with minimal corticosteroid use. Bilirubin level and ALP activity reached grade 4 toxicity, aminotransferase and γ-glutamyltransferase activities grade 3. Liver biopsy (day 4) showed portal tract inflammation with cholestasis, acute hepatocyte injury, scattered acidophilic bodies, occasional ballooning degeneration, canalicular cholestasis, moderate inflammatory infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and many eosinophils, and eosinophil infiltration of interlobular bile ducts with ductal epithelial damage. Associated skin rash and hypereosinophilia (max 2.47 x 10^9/l, ~40% WBC) resolved after stopping imatinib. Rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg daily produced no further hepatotoxicity and patient continued imatinib for 18 months. Authors concluded the single dose of a Korean ginseng herbal remedy did not cause the hepatic function abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib mesylate is described as a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in CML, and the paper reports imatinib-induced fatal acute liver failure. The index CML patient developed fulminant liver failure with grade III encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy (clotting factor V 10%, prothrombin time 6%, bilirubin 360 mg/L), and multiorgan failure, and was referred for liver transplantation before dying of cardiac arrest ~48 h after intensive-care admission. The discussion aggregates prior human reports: grade 3/4 transaminase elevations in up to 5.1% of patients in phase 2/3 trials, three additional reported fatal acute liver failure cases following imatinib, and other imatinib liver-toxicity reports that resolved on discontinuation, with histology ranging from focal necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration to massive hepatic necrosis or cytolytic acute hepatitis, onset ranging from 11 d to 49 wk, and reappearance of toxicity on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Agent also used in Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia and gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Index case: progressive bilirubin increase and marked clotting factor V decrease, grade II then grade III encephalopathy, multiorgan failure, referred for liver transplantation, died after cardiac arrest ~48 h after ICU admission; blood, urinary and ascites cultures negative. Aggregated reports: grade 3/4 transaminase elevation in up to 5.1% of patients in phase 2/3 trials; fatal acute liver failure case in a phase 2 trial at 600 mg/d whose death was 'suspected to be related to treatment' (patient had prior bone marrow transplant and had taken 3000-3500 mg/d acetaminophen 1 mo before starting imatinib, died 12 d after start); fatal case in a 46-year-old CML woman after 18 mo at 400 mg/d, who received a liver transplant but died of sepsis, explanted liver showing severe hepatic necrosis; fatal case in a 61-year-old woman with polycythemia rubra vera in spent phase/myelofibrosis after 7 wk at 400 mg/d, dying of extensive hepatic necrosis, post-mortem showing microthrombi in liver/lung/spleen vasculature, mechanism postulated as exacerbation of underlying prothrombotic tendency. Other resolving reports: histology from focal necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration, marked periportal necrosis with mixed lymphocyte/neutrophil/plasmocyte infiltrate, to massive hepatic necrosis or cytolytic acute hepatitis; onset 11 d to 49 wk; rechallenge (including one at 2.5% of therapeutic dose) reproduced hepatotoxicity. Management: low-to-intermediate dose corticosteroids (prednisone 25-37 mg/d or methylprednisolone 40 mg/d) normalized aminotransferases in 2-4 wk in five patients, with imatinib resumed successfully.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that in their patient imatinib mesylate was a probable cause of acute severe hepatitis because other causes were excluded. They note hepatotoxicity has been observed in about 2-5% of patients receiving imatinib, mostly mild elevation of liver enzymes resolving after dose reduction or discontinuation, while imatinib-induced acute severe hepatotoxicity and death from hepatic failure were rarely reported (deaths due to imatinib-induced hepatic failure had been reported in four patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution for the reported patient is 'probable cause' by exclusion of viral, autoimmune, and other causes. Imatinib hepatotoxicity reported in about 2-5% of treated patients, usually mild enzyme elevation resolving after dose reduction or discontinuation; acute severe hepatotoxicity and hepatic-failure deaths rarely reported (four deaths documented). Latency to hepatic dysfunction ranged from 11 days to 18 months across 12 histologically studied cases (Table 2: diagnoses CML, GIST, PV), with histology spanning focal necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration, periportal/massive necrosis, cytolytic acute hepatitis, cholestasis, and autoimmune-hepatitis-like changes (positive anti-liver cytosol 1 and antinuclear antibodies in some cases). Case 6 required liver transplantation and died; case 10 (PV patient) died of extensive hepatic necrosis with microthrombi. Our patient (53, F, GIST) developed acute hepatitis 10 weeks after starting imatinib; after discontinuation she developed grade 2 encephalopathy and acute hepatic failure, which resolved upon prednisolone 0.8 mg/kg/day; biopsy showed sinusoidal congestion, perivenular hepatocyte necrosis, dropout and central hemorrhagic necrosis consistent with drug toxicity. Study reports 12 published cases with histology plus the index case, and cites corticosteroid (prednisone 25-37 mg/day or methylprednisolone 40 mg/day or prednisolone 40 mg/day) reversal of severe imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity in five patients.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was started on oral imatinib and developed imatinib-induced hepatitis. Because of the possibility of imatinib-induced hepatitis, imatinib was discontinued, leading to rapid resolution of clinical symptoms. On follow-up, liver function tests normalised over 3 weeks; imatinib was restarted but increased transaminases recurred after 1 week, and discontinuation again normalised liver function within 2 weeks. A rechallenge with oral imatinib 200 mg daily together with oral prednisone 25 mg daily was tolerated without liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: marked rise in transaminases (AST 1406 to 2364 IU/l during imatinib; ALT 2364 IU/l, AST 1406 IU/l), bilirubin 1.0-2.5 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase up to 131 IU/l; dechallenge resolved injury (ALT 95 IU/l at 3 weeks, ALT 83 at 2 weeks); positive rechallenge with imatinib 200 mg daily (ALT 654 IU/l, AST 332 IU/l after 1 week); tolerated upon rechallenge combined with oral prednisone 25 mg daily, then escalated to 400 mg daily with prednisone tapered over 8 weeks. Diagnosis was imatinib-induced hepatitis; histologically a drug-induced hypersensitivity/necrotic hepatitis with non-specific inflammatory infiltrate is described in the discussion.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib was discontinued in ten of sixty CML chronic-phase patients (16.6%): six (10%) due to intolerance, including hepatic toxicity grade 3 in three patients and hematological toxicity grade 4 in three patients, and four (6.6%) due to resistance. The three patients with hepatic toxicity after discontinuing imatinib were subsequently placed on nilotinib; all achieved major cytogenetic response and two achieved major molecular response.
raw_record.extra_details: In a monitored cohort of 60 CML chronic-phase patients, three patients developed hepatic toxicity grade 3 during imatinib treatment requiring discontinuation of imatinib; six of sixty (16.6%) discontinued imatinib overall due to intolerance (hepatic toxicity grade 3 in three, hematological toxicity grade 4 in three). All three patients with hepatic toxicity achieved major cytogenetic response after switching to nilotinib; two also achieved major molecular response.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 46-year-old woman with advanced GISTs who developed hepatotoxicity 11 days after initiation of imatinib mesylate (400 mg daily). Before therapy her liver function tests were normal; she had no risk factors for viral or alcoholic liver disease, imatinib was her only regular medication, and she had not used acetaminophen or over-the-counter medications. One week after imatinib discontinuation her liver function tests improved significantly, and the report confirms early-onset imatinib mesylate-induced liver failure in patients treated for GISTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of 46-year-old woman with advanced (relapsed) c-kit-positive GIST treated with imatinib mesylate 400 mg daily; hepatotoxicity developed 11 days after starting therapy, presenting with 2 days of nausea and weakness (no jaundice, fever, or abdominal pain). Labs: ALT 2520 UI/L, AST 1845 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 192 UI/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.3, INR 1.6. Abdominal CT showed mild diffuse fatty liver changes; ultrasound normal. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C all negative; no acetaminophen or herbal/OTC use. Liver tests began to decrease after imatinib discontinuation and were nearly normal 1 week later. Paper frames this as acute fulminant hepatitis/acute liver failure. Background context supplied: hepatotoxicity observed in ~2%–5% of patients in clinical trials (mostly mild transaminase elevation; grade 3–4 transaminase elevation in 1%–5%, grade 3–4 bilirubin elevation 0.4%–3.5%, usually resolving after dose reduction/interruption within 1–4 weeks); 5 deaths from hepatic failure reported (4 during CML treatment, 1 during polycythemia vera treatment); in the Demetri et al phase 2 trial of 147 GIST patients, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 5.4% and fatal liver disease in 0.3%. Reported histopathology varies from periportal necrosis with mixed lymphocyte/neutrophil/plasmocyte infiltration to massive hepatic necrosis or cytolytic acute hepatitis. Authors recommend early and continued surveillance of liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib-induced acute liver failure is reported as a rare and serious complication of imatinib therapy; the case shares features with 13 other reported cases (three in male patients) from eight case reports, with patient ages 22-79 years and imatinib treatment durations before toxicity recognition of 8 weeks to 1 year. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy was associated with poor outcome: of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplantation, and that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption. Successful liver transplantation for imatinib-induced hepatic failure in CML is described, and the paper reports the first use of dasatinib for CML after liver transplantation for imatinib-induced liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib-induced acute liver failure/fulminant hepatic failure in a CML patient who required liver transplantation within 24 hours of developing fulminant hepatic failure; the report aggregates 13 other reported cases (three male) in eight case reports. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy associated with poor outcome; of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplant (that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption, but this is a separate patient, not the index case). Six cases without coagulopathy received steroids and recovered; three other non-coagulopathic cases recovered without steroids. Duration of imatinib before recognition of toxicity 8 weeks to 1 year; age range 22-79 years. Dasatinib was subsequently used for CML after liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old woman treated for chronic myeloid leukemia with imatinib mesylate (selective Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase inhibitor) for 6 months developed imatinib-induced liver failure and subsequently underwent a successful liver transplant for acute liver failure. The authors also reviewed PubMed literature through September 2017 on imatinib-induced acute liver failure and highlight the role of liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Imatinib mesylate taken continuously for 6 months after delivery of a baby in a 36-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia. The patient's acute liver failure resolved after a successful liver transplant. Literature review (PubMed, through September 2017) identified that severe hepatotoxicity occurs in 1-4% of imatinib-treated patients but fulminant liver failure is rare, with only 8 known cases; all but one involved CML, most were fatal, and liver transplant was performed in four (one postoperative death). Dasatinib and nilotinib are mentioned only as alternative/sequential therapies after imatinib-associated liver failure, not as DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: The established diagnosis was 'Acute toxic (drug, imatinib-induced) drug-induced liver disease with cholestatic, cytolytic syndromes' in a patient with Philadelphia-chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia in early chronic phase. The liver injury (imatinib-induced DILI with both cholestatic and cytolytic patterns) developed during imatinib therapy, resolved after imatinib discontinuation, steroid (prednisolone) therapy, and hepatoprotective treatment, with recovery after about three and a half months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report in a CML (Ph-positive, early chronic phase) patient. Injury described as acute toxic drug-induced liver disease with cholestatic and cytolytic syndromes; bilirubin rose to ~400 µmol/L (23.40 mg/dL) on day 27 with severe jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy; AST/ALT elevated (peak AST 978.6 U/L day 16, ALT 1155 U/L day 0). Managed by imatinib cessation, prednisolone 40 mg/day IV, ursodeoxycholic acid 750 mg, ademetionine, and detoxification; recovered and switched to nilotinib 200 mg twice daily. No reported drug dose for imatinib in the provided window.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin (Zithromax), an erythromycin derivative of the macrolide azolide subgroup, is generally considered very safe but can uncommonly cause hepatic side effects including jaundice, fever, and right upper quadrant pain. The authors describe a patient who developed azithromycin-induced cholestatic hepatitis that resolved upon discontinuation of the drug. The diagnosis was established by the lack of other known causes for liver disease, the temporal relationship with the drug, and typical changes of liver histology.
raw_record.extra_details: Described as azithromycin-induced cholestatic hepatitis. Presenting features included jaundice, fever, and right upper quadrant pain. Liver injury resolved upon discontinuation of the drug.
