Diagnosis established by absence of other known causes of liver disease, temporal relationship, and typical cholestatic liver histology changes. Azithromycin (Zithromax) is an erythromycin derivative belonging to the azolide subgroup of macrolides and is generally considered a very safe medication with uncommon hepatic side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin was one of the macrolide antibiotics associated with DILI (the macrolides as a group accounted for three cases). In addition, a separate azithromycin-attributed jaundice case was documented with bilirubin 4.8 ULN, AST 8.4 ULN and ALT 8.4 ULN.
raw_record.extra_details: Part of the three macrolide cases (2 hepatocellular/1 mixed) with grouped duration mean 7 (4-10) days; separate jaundice case (58-year-old female, 10 days treatment, bilirubin 4.8 ULN, AST 8.4 ULN, ALT 8.4 ULN, ALP 1.9 ULN, resolution 60 days). Spelled Azitromycin in tables.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed features of hepatocellular toxicity and hepatic encephalopathy one week after the last dose of azithromycin, with markedly elevated ALT, AST, ALP and serum ammonia, elevated conjugated bilirubin and prolonged prothrombin time suggestive of subfulminant or fulminant necrosis. The diagnosis of azithromycin-induced hepatotoxicity was based on the temporal relationship between drug intake and symptom onset and the absence of other causes of liver disease; the Naranjo probability scale (score 6) and WHO causality assessment scale indicated azithromycin as the probable/likely cause of the drug-associated hepatocellular toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo probability scale score 6 and WHO causality assessment indicated probable/likely causation. Hepatocellular toxicity with hepatic encephalopathy one week after the last dose; markedly elevated ALT, AST, ALP and serum ammonia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged PT, suggestive of subfulminant/fulminant necrosis; normal serum LDH and no other organ dysfunction; ischemic hepatitis deemed unlikely. The discussion additionally notes (review assertion) that azithromycin has a long half-life with liver concentrations exceeding serum levels ~50-fold, with early injury possibly hypersensitivity-mediated and rare reported cases of cholestatic hepatitis and severe iatrogenic hepatitis requiring hepatic transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The study prospectively identified and adjudicated 18 cases of clinically apparent liver injury as probably, highly likely, or definitely owing to azithromycin. Hepatocellular injury outnumbered cholestatic injury, latency to onset was 1 to 3 weeks (recognized 2 weeks after stopping azithromycin in 16 patients), typical symptoms were fatigue, nausea and abdominal pain followed by itching and jaundice, and recovery usually was prompt (2 to 5 weeks) with complete resolution.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 prospectively identified, adjudicated cases of clinically apparent DILI (probable, highly likely, or definite). Latency 1-3 weeks after azithromycin; onset typically after completing the course (only 2 of 18 developed jaundice while taking it). Typical regimen 250-500 mg once daily for 4-7 days. At 6-month follow-up for 14 patients, 8 recovered, 4 had chronic injury, 1 died of multi-organ failure, 1 underwent liver transplantation. Four patients (1, 3, 6, 11) met chronic DILI definition; 3 had initial hepatocellular injury with jaundice and later mild-moderate ALT/Alk P increases. Histology showed ductopenic portal areas, zone 3 cholestasis with hepatocellular and canalicular bile accumulation, chronic hepatitis with perivenular inflammation and hemorrhage, and mild veno-occlusive changes. Recovery usually prompt, resolving in 2-5 weeks; median time to 50% reduction of peak bilirubin 12 days (8-27 d) and to normalization 35 days (25-46 d).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, azithromycin accounted for 18 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, one of the top 10 individual agents.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: Martinez et al. defined the clinical, histological features and outcome of azithromycin-induced liver injury based on 18 patients in the current DILIN registry. The injury was mostly hepatocellular and occurred within 1–3 weeks of exposure; outcomes were typically favorable but azithromycin caused chronic injury and associated cutaneous reactions, and in some cases resulted in liver transplantation or death.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 DILIN registry patients; onset 1–3 weeks after exposure; chronic injury and cutaneous reactions also reported; cases resulted in liver transplantation or death.

raw_record.support_text: Azithromycin has had accumulating reports of hepatotoxicity, some with serious consequences. In the DILIN study, 18 azithromycin cases were identified among patients enrolled 2004-2013: 89% presented with jaundice, 67% with abdominal pain and 56% with pruritus; mean duration of therapy was 4 days and median time to onset was 17 days. More than half had hepatocellular injury, with cholestatic and mixed patterns also observed; histology demonstrated veno-occlusive changes and ductopenia in a few patients. At 6-month follow-up, one patient required liver transplantation, one died of multi-organ failure and four had chronic biochemical injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 cases in DILIN 2004-2013; 89% jaundice, 67% abdominal pain, 56% pruritus; mean therapy duration 4 days (range 4-7), median onset 17 days; longer half-life than erythromycin; >half hepatocellular with cholestatic and mixed patterns; histology showed veno-occlusive changes and ductopenia; two reactions with severe hypersensitivity cutaneous reactions; at 6 months 1 transplant, 1 death from multi-organ failure, 4 chronic biochemical injury. Can be associated with severe cutaneous reactions, liver-related death and chronic injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old female admitted with new onset jaundice, yellow skin and conjunctiva, diffuse pruritus, and elevated hepatic enzymes had her acute jaundice ultimately attributed to an azithromycin-related, drug-induced liver injury that resolved with conservative management; she was discharged three days after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with jaundice, yellow skin and conjunctiva, diffuse pruritus, and elevated hepatic enzymes; injury resolved with conservative management. Occurred in context of a non-urologic diagnostic workup causing incidental detection of a ureteral mass.

raw_record.support_text: In the etiology table for 81 consecutive cases of acute liver failure, drugs and toxins accounted for 22 (27.2%) cases, with acetaminophen listed as the cause in 12 cases, isoniazide in 2, and salazopyrine, erythromycin, azithromycin, cyproterone, naproxen, germander, Amanita verosa, and carbon tetrachloride each in 1 case. The Results section notes that acetaminophen was the most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in this series.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as cause of acute liver failure in 12 of 81 consecutive ALF cases admitted to Hôpital Saint-Luc, Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal over nine years. Most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in the series.

raw_record.support_text: Using the UNOS liver transplant database from 1990 to 2002, 270 liver transplant recipients with drug-induced acute liver failure were identified. Acetaminophen (APAP) alone or in combination with another drug accounted for 133 (49%) cases, and in the non-acetaminophen group (n=137) the most frequently implicated drugs were isoniazid (n=24, 17.5%), propylthiouracil (n=13, 9.5%), and phenytoin and valproate (n=10, 7.3% each). These agents were implicated as causes of acute hepatic necrosis leading to liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: From UNOS liver transplant database 1990-2002. APAP alone or in combination with another drug accounted for 133 of 270 (49%) drug-induced acute liver failure transplant cases. APAP only implicated in 110/206 (53%) of Caucasian recipients and 12/48 (25%) of African-American recipients (P=.0004). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug. One-year patient and graft survival for the entire cohort was 77% and 71%.

raw_record.support_text: From 1998 to 2003, the ALF Study Group prospectively collected 610 detailed patient histories, including 262 cases of acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen (APAP, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol), an over-the-counter (OTC) drug product. These APAP patients had a median age of 36, median recorded peak ALT of 4310 IU/L, peak serum total bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL, and 67% survival without transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP = acetaminophen, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol; OTC drug product; 262 of 610 ALF cases attributed to it; median age 36 y, 74% female, jaundice mean 1 day, coma stage 3/4 in 52%, mean peak ALT 4055 IU/L, mean peak bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, 8% transplanted, 65% spontaneous survival, 71% overall survival.

raw_record.support_text: Russo et al. studied more than 51,000 liver transplants in the UNOS database (1990-2002) and identified 270 patients transplanted for documented drug-induced liver failure (15% of all liver transplants). Acetaminophen accounted for nearly half of these patients, either alone or in combination with another medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Identified as cause of ~half of 270 transplants for documented drug-induced liver failure in the UNOS database 1990-2002, alone or in combination with another medication. Of non-acetaminophen causes, leading were isoniazid, propylthiouracil, phenytoin, valproic acid, toxic mushrooms, nitrofurantoin, and herbal therapies.

raw_record.support_text: The study identified patterns of urinary metabolites that distinguished healthy subjects susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced liver injury from subjects who were not susceptible, during therapeutic acetaminophen dosing. The distinction appeared only after the start of acetaminophen treatment and not before it, and this robustness argument was extended in the discussion, where NAPQI metabolites tended to be higher in responders.
raw_record.extra_details: Metabolomics study comparing responders (susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced liver injury) vs nonresponders under therapeutic dosing. Pretreatment metabolome was not predictive; post-treatment endogenous metabolome distinguished groups. NAPQI metabolites tended to be higher in responders, providing biological plausibility. Glycine was elevated in responders on days 5-6 and 9-10, with a smaller fall in glycine excretion in responders than nonresponders (2.2% vs 17% from days 3 to 6; 1.5% vs 11% from days 3 to 10), though not statistically significant; creatine was generally higher in nonresponders. Endogenous-metabolite OPLS-DA models excluding acetaminophen metabolites retained predictive capacity (71.4% for days 5-6, P=0.01; 77.1% for days 9-10, P=0.001).; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: Among patients with acute liver failure resulting from drugs in the US who underwent liver transplantation, paracetamol (acetaminophen) was the most common causative drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Most common causative drug among US patients with drug-induced acute liver failure who underwent liver transplantation; followed in frequency by isoniazid, propylthiouracil, phenytoin and valproate. Also listed in the USA 1990-2002 series (Russo et al.) as 46% of 270 acute liver failure cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study enrolled 24 patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF) with hepatic encephalopathy on day 1, establishing acetaminophen as a cause of acute liver failure in humans. Outcomes among the AALF patients included 4 (17%) who underwent liver transplantation and 2 (8%) who died; 7 (29%) fulfilled the King's College Hospital criteria for poor prognosis on day 1. The diagnosis is explicitly framed as acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 24 AALF patients with hepatic encephalopathy studied at days 1, 4, and 7; day-1 median AST 5,696 IU/L, arterial ammonia 111 µmol/L, INR 6.7, MELD 37.9; 4 patients (17%) underwent liver transplantation and 2 (8%) died; 7 (29%) met King's College Hospital criteria for LT on day 1. The paper also refers to 'acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis' as the underlying event releasing DNA/cytokines and discusses elevated proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), hyperammonemia, impaired neutrophil phagocytosis, and increased neutrophil superoxide burst in these patients. Neutrophil TLR9 expression correlated with arterial ammonia and plasma IL-8 and was highest in those with severe SIRS and advanced HE.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the well-known paracetamol-associated hepatotoxicity is confirmed by a three-fold increase of risk in this case-control study, with an adjusted OR of 2.97 (95% CI 2.09-4.21) for acute serious liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjusted OR 2.97 (95% CI 2.09-4.21) described as confirming well-known paracetamol-associated hepatotoxicity; prevalence of use 16.7%; 69 cases (39%) and 309 controls (17%) exposed during the three months before the index day.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective population-based study of 62 patients with definite or possible ALF (32 due to acetaminophen or DILI), acetaminophen was implicated in 18 events (56%). In the ALFSG registry (1198 patients, 23 sites over 10 years), acetaminophen toxicity was responsible for 46% of ALF cases.
raw_record.extra_details: ALF is a syndrome whose causes include acetaminophen and idiosyncratic DILI. Acetaminophen implicated in 18/32 (56%) of acetaminophen/DILI ALF events in one retrospective study and in 46% of ALFSG cases. Latency of implicated DILI ALF agents was 1-2 weeks to 8 months; 65% of subjects did not stop the drug until after jaundice developed.

raw_record.support_text: This case represents the fourth published case describing drug-induced hepatitis temporally related to ingestion of celecoxib. A 41-year-old man developed jaundice and cholestasis after taking 2 doses of celecoxib 200 mg for knee trauma pain; histology showed bile plugs in the bile canaliculi and a mild portal infiltrate suggesting drug-induced cholestasis. The patient denied alcohol, natural products, or other medications, and per the Naranjo algorithm the causal relationship between the cholestatic hepatitis and celecoxib administration appears probable.
raw_record.extra_details: 41-year-old man hospitalized for jaundice after 2 doses of celecoxib 200 mg for right knee trauma pain. Laboratory findings: hyperbilirubinemia, cholestasis, and moderate transaminase elevation; abdominal imaging showed no bile duct dilatation. Histology: bile plugs in bile canaliculi and a mild portal infiltrate suggesting drug-induced cholestasis. Fourth published case of drug-induced hepatitis temporally related to celecoxib; patient denied alcohol, natural products, or additional medications. Causal assessment by Naranjo algorithm: probable. The paper notes celecoxib is considered to have low potential for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Among the five consecutively diagnosed cases of NSAID-induced fulminant hepatitis, one case was related to celecoxib at a dose of 100 mg/day, and the patient was successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. Diagnosis was based on exclusion of other potentially hepatotoxic medications and causes of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 5 cases of NSAID-induced acute liver failure; dose 100 mg/day; treated by orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant hepatitis. In the introduction celecoxib is described as a COX-2 inhibitor 'likely exhibiting less potential for hepatotoxicity'.

raw_record.support_text: Celecoxib was implicated in three cases, two with short latency (16 and 23 days), usually with a mixed pattern of liver enzyme elevations and without immunoallergic features. One patient developed a severe cholestatic hepatitis and ultimately recovered clinically, but had continued evidence of cholestatic injury 6, 12 and 24 months after onset, compatible with some degree of vanishing bile duct syndrome. The comparison table lists 3 celecoxib cases (1 definite, 1 very likely, 1 probable).
raw_record.extra_details: 3 implicated cases; two with short latency (16 and 23 days); usually mixed enzyme pattern without immunoallergic features; one patient with severe cholestatic hepatitis and persisting cholestatic injury at 6, 12 and 24 months compatible with some degree of vanishing bile duct syndrome. Initial ALT 656 U/L, Alk P 319 U/L, bilirubin 7.4 mg/dl (peak 11.1 mg/dl). Causality: 1 definite, 1 very likely, 1 probable.

raw_record.support_text: Celecoxib is a widely prescribed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that has been associated with rare instances of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The paper reviews and analyzes published cases of celecoxib DILI reported from 2000 through June 2016, totaling 18 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Celecoxib DILI reported in 18 patients, median age 54 (range 29-84), 15 (88%) female; median daily dose 200 mg (range 200-533); median duration and latency 13 days (1-730) and 17 days (2-730) respectively; 15 (83%) cases after short treatment (median 12 days) with rash and immunoallergic features, eosinophilia in 6 (40%); 3 cases after prolonged exposure (152-730 d) without immunoallergic features. Pattern of injury: hepatocellular 6, mixed 5, cholestatic 4, unknown 3. Outcomes: 2 (11%) required liver transplantation, 4 (22%) chronic liver injury, 12 (67%) recovered. NSAID class; women overrepresented.

raw_record.support_text: Using the Hanson conditions and CIOMS criteria, the authors concluded that their two cases matched the parameters for propylthiouracil to be causative of fulminating hepatitis. Viral hepatitis was ruled out via negative hepatitis A, B, and C markers, autoimmunity tests were largely negative, and neither patient had congestive heart failure or other extrathyroidal risk factors; fulminating hepatitis was diagnosed based on jaundice, severe clinical evolution like viral hepatitis, encephalopathy, terminal multiple organ failure, and autopsy-confirmed histologic hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (case series). Case 1: varying intermittent dose of propylthiouracil over 4 months, jaundice onset 92 days after start, death 30 days after icterus onset. Case 2: propylthiouracil 200 mg/day for 5 months plus constant 150 mg/day for 15 days, jaundice onset at 162 days, death 50 days after icterus. Hepatitis A/B/C ruled out; CMV and EBV not tested (optional per CIOMS). Autoantibody testing largely negative except low-titer antinuclear antibodies. Histology: extensive areas of necrosis with hemorrhagic infiltration, widened portal triads with edema and incipient fibrosis, perilobular cholestasis, slight ductal proliferation, lymphoplasmocytic portal infiltrate, centrolobular hepatocyte lysis, moderate cholestasis. No laboratory tests before propylthiouracil intake. Indication: thyrotoxicosis (mild to moderate).

raw_record.support_text: In the UNOS liver transplant cohort of drug-induced acute liver failure recipients, propylthiouracil was implicated in 13 of 137 (9.5%) non-acetaminophen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Second most frequently implicated non-acetaminophen drug. 13 of 137 non-APAP cases (9.5%). Diagnosis at transplant was acute hepatic necrosis from an implicated drug.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil (PTU) has been used to treat hyperthyroidism for over 50 years. The discussion notes that only a few cases of PTU-induced liver failure have been reported, with high mortality rates; the case presented failed to respond to stopping PTU with supportive care and required surgical management.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as PTU-induced liver failure in a hyperthyroidism patient; only a few such cases reported, with high mortality rates. The patient's liver failure resolved and she required thyroidectomy after failing to respond to stopping PTU plus supportive care and to steroids, lithium, propranolol, and radioactive iodine for thyroid control; preoperative Lugol's solution to achieve a euthyroid state followed by thyroidectomy was used safely.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary reports 33 published cases of severe propylthiouracil (PTU)-related liver failure in adults and 14 in children, plus 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children due to PTU-induced liver failure reported by UNOS between 1990 and 2007. FDA AERS data detail severe liver injury in 22 adults over 20 yr, nine of whom died and five received liver transplants, and 12 pediatric patients who sustained severe liver injury resulting in three deaths and six liver transplants. The average daily dose of PTU associated with liver failure was approximately 300 mg in both children and adults, with liver failure occurring after 6 to 450 d (median 120 d) of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease; also inhibits T4 to T3 conversion. Published reports: 33 severe liver failure cases in adults, 14 in children. UNOS reported 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children (1990-2007) due to PTU-induced liver failure; one to three PTU-related liver transplants per year over 17 yr. AERS: severe liver injury in 22 adults (9 died, 5 transplanted) and 12 pediatric cases (3 deaths, 6 transplants) over 20 yr. Two reports of serious maternal liver injury during pregnancy and two reports of liver injury in fetuses whose mothers took PTU. Average daily dose associated with liver failure ~300 mg in children and adults; latency 6-450 d (median 120 d). Estimated incidence of severe hepatic damage ~0.1% in adults; projected liver-failure (transplant or death) incidence ~1:10,000, giving 1-2 deaths/transplants per year in U.S. adults. Children: ~1 in 1000 incidence of liver failure. US PTU prescriptions: 101,000 patients in 2008, >340,000 prescriptions.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old female with Graves' disease initiated propylthiouracil (PTU) therapy; three months later she presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice with markedly elevated liver enzymes (total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dl, AST 1747 IU/L, ALT 1589 IU/L). She progressed to acute liver failure with coagulopathy and stage II encephalopathy and was the only medication taken; all serologic, autoimmune, and metabolic studies were negative. She underwent orthotopic liver transplant on hospital day 7 but succumbed to tonsillar herniation immediately after surgery; explant pathology revealed marked necrosis and collapse consistent with acute liver failure. The paper states PTU-associated hepatotoxicity is a well-recognized serious adverse effect, with PTU-related liver injury ranging from asymptomatic ALT elevations to fatal acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 19-year-old African American female treated for hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease; PTU started at 50 mg twice daily then increased to 100 mg three times daily; symptoms appeared about 3 months after starting PTU. Pretreatment liver enzymes normal; no routine liver-associated enzyme (LAE) monitoring was performed, consistent with 1995 US/ATA guidelines that deemed PTU hepatic necrosis rare enough to not require routine LAE monitoring. Presenting labs: total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, AST 1747 IU/L, ALT 1589 IU/L; on arrival INR 3.01, albumin low, total bilirubin 25.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 13.3 mg/dL, AST 1092 IU/L, ALT 1039 IU/L. Acute hepatitis/failure: admitted for acute hepatitis, transferred to tertiary center, listed status 1 for liver transplant, developed stage II encephalopathy, intubated, intracranial pressure reached 51 mm Hg; underwent orthotopic liver transplant on hospital day 7 but died of tonsillar herniation (brainstem herniation) immediately after surgery. Explant pathology showed marked necrosis and collapse. Excluded alternative etiologies include autoimmune, viral, and metabolic causes; acetaminophen and supplements not taken. Paper urges reconsideration of US monitoring guidelines for LAEs during PTU therapy and notes pediatric endocrinology centers recommend against PTU as first-line therapy due to liver failure risk.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman who was taking propylthiouracil died due to hepatic failure. Her laboratory results met the criteria for Hy's law. In the expired/transplanted patient table, propylthiouracil is given as the cause, with peak AST 781, ALT 1118, TB 28.6, ALP 989, and a RUCAM score of 6; she expired.
raw_record.extra_details: 46-year-old woman; died of hepatic failure; peak values AST 781 IU/L, ALT 1118 IU/L, TB 28.6 mg/dL, ALP 989 IU/L; RUCAM score 6; case met Hy's law criteria; propylthiouracil also appears in Table 4 among the 'Medications' (n=111) causal agents of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with propylthiouracil (PTU)-induced acute liver failure that was successfully managed with an artificial liver support system (ALSS), concluding that although PTU-induced liver failure is rare, liver function should be monitored during PTU treatment. The discussion attributes to PTU a spectrum of liver injury including PTU-induced hepatitis, severe liver injury, acute liver failure, and classic histologic changes of chronic lobular hepatitis with cholestasis and centrilobular necrosis; FDA data describe PTU-treated patients progressing to ALF, several of whom died or required liver transplantation, and a Taiwan cohort showed PTU-associated hepatitis at 1.19/1000 person-years.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of PTU-induced acute liver failure treated with four sessions of ALSS (plasma exchange plus plasma bilirubin adsorption); total bilirubin improved from 442.8 to 122.1 µmol/L and liver function normalized after 4 months; no biopsy obtained. Estimated ATD-associated hepatotoxicity incidence 0.1-0.2%; PTU-induced severe liver injury ~0.1% of ~15,000 treated adults/year in USA; Taiwan cohort (71,379 hyperthyroid patients) PTU hepatitis 1.19/1000 person-years; FDA report: of 32 PTU patients (22 adults, 10 children) who developed ALF, 13 died (12 adults, 1 child) and 11 required liver transplantation; children appear at higher risk for PTU liver injury; classic histology preserved architecture, chronic lobular hepatitis with cholestasis, centrilobular necrosis. Mechanism: inhibits thyroperoxidase and 5'-deiodinase.

raw_record.support_text: In a case report, a patient with hyperthyroidism/thyroid storm developed a severe elevation in serum transaminases rapidly after just a single dose of propylthiouracil (PTU). The Naranjo adverse drug reaction scale score was 5, rendering DILI a 'probable' adverse drug reaction of PTU in this case; the reaction was classified as an idiosyncratic drug reaction that is not dose-dependent. Alternate causes (acetaminophen, NSAIDs, viral hepatitis, autoimmune disease, shock liver) were excluded, and liver enzymes began to normalize while the patient's ejection fraction remained low during an episode of thyroid crisis.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient context: hyperthyroidism/thyroid storm with an acute episode of thyroid crisis and low ejection fraction. DILI occurred after just a single dose of PTU, with rapid severe elevation of transaminases and sudden clinically significant hepatic dysfunction that began to normalize. Naranjo scale score = 5 (probable). Other etiologies excluded: acetaminophen and NSAIDs not given, hepatitis panel and autoimmune markers normal, shock liver ruled out (patient remained normotensive).

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old female was treated with methimazole for hyperthyroidism, then switched to propylthiouracil after methimazole caused elevated liver transaminase. After propylthiouracil was started, she developed nausea, rash, high fever, acute toxic hepatitis and multiple organ dysfunction (liver, lung, heart) lasting 1 month. She was diagnosed with DRESS/DiHS syndrome induced by propylthiouracil, which resolved after drug withdrawal and treatment with adalimumab, corticosteroids and plasmapheresis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 38-year-old female with hyperthyroidism; DRESS/DiHS developed after propylthiouracil taken for 4 weeks, manifesting as acute toxic hepatitis with multiple organ dysfunction (liver, lung, heart); treated with adalimumab, systematic corticosteroids and plasmapheresis with symptom resolution 4 weeks later; propylthiouracil withdrawn. Literature context: only 3 prior cases of propylthiouracil-induced DRESS/DiHS reported. The patient first used methimazole (stopped for elevated liver transaminase that improved in 2 weeks) before switching to propylthiouracil.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes cases of propylthiouracil-induced hepatic injury and notes that clinically significant hepatotoxicity is a distinctly uncommon complication of propylthiouracil therapy, despite widespread use of the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Propylthiouracil is a thionamide used since 1946 to manage hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease). Hepatotoxicity is a rare side effect compared with more common rash, urticaria, arthralgia, fever, and transient leukopenia (1%-5%) and agranulocytosis (0.2%-0.5%). The author reports a new case (32-year-old woman) and reviews previously reported cases, noting that hepatic injury is rare but must be considered whenever hepatic dysfunction develops during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors identified 24 individual case reports of propylthiouracil-induced hepatic injury in the English-language literature, in patients aged 6 to 68 years (eight aged 18 or younger, 22 female, 20 with Graves' disease). Two additional studies noted hepatotoxicity during propylthiouracil therapy for hyperthyroidism (4/131 Graves' patients and 1/38 pediatric patients), and based on the number of case reports clinically significant hepatotoxicity appears distinctly uncommon.
raw_record.extra_details: Most patients presented with features similar to viral hepatitis (malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, abdominal pain/tenderness, sometimes rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, or agranulocytosis); one patient had isolated jaundice and one had asymptomatic hepatotoxicity. Laboratory abnormalities were elevated hepatocellular enzymes, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase, with frequent prothrombin time elevation. Biopsy in some patients showed predominantly hepatocellular damage, occasionally a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic picture, and less commonly a predominantly cholestatic pattern. Indication was hyperthyroidism, chiefly Graves' disease. Historically first reported in 1947 shortly after the drug became available.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil is widely used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism, and isolated hepatotoxicity due to propylthiouracil has been reported only rarely, with 13 adult and 5 pediatric cases reported in the English-language literature. Almost all patients with propylthiouracil-induced hepatitis had jaundice with nausea, vomiting, malaise, hepatic tenderness, or hepatomegaly; histology in 9 of 18 patients showed massive/submassive hepatic necrosis, chronic active hepatitis, or portal inflammation. In the patient of this report, propylthiouracil therapy was stopped and she developed propylthiouracil-induced hepatitis with dense portal inflammation and confluent zone 3 necrosis, later progressing clinically to cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of propylthiouracil-induced hepatotoxicity in a hyperthyroid woman treated for Graves disease; hepatic necrosis primarily involving zone 3 with dense portal inflammatory infiltration, bridging between lobules, and subsequent progression to cirrhosis (ascites and splenomegaly at 48 weeks, no follow-up biopsy due to prolonged prothrombin time). Course complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation and prolonged prothrombin time; hepatitis A/B/C serology negative. Discontinuation of propylthiouracil was followed by clinical deterioration eventually; lab values included AST up to 549 units/L, ALT up to 475 units/L, total bilirubin up to 3.2 mg/dL. Literature summary: 18 reported cases (13 adult, 5 pediatric, 16 female), onset 1 day to 15 months after starting therapy; histology in 9 cases: 5 massive/submassive hepatic necrosis (1 survived), 3 chronic active hepatitis, 1 portal inflammation with cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A literature review identified 28 cases of propylthiouracil (PTU)-associated hepatotoxicity, and including the 2 cases presented in this paper there were 30 total cases. The paper attributes the hepatic disease to PTU therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Combined analysis of 28 literature cases plus 2 new cases (n=30). Female:male ratio 8.3:1; PTU dose at presentation with hepatotoxicity 426±199 mg/day; months of continuous PTU therapy before hepatotoxicity 3.6±3.5; 7 fatalities and 21 survivors; age 27.9±17.1 yr. One additional case via transplacental passage (symptomatic at 5 days of age) was excluded from analysis, and the initial case report of hepatocellular jaundice was excluded because jaundice was not noted until after PTU discontinuation. PTU was discontinued in all reported cases once hepatotoxicity was recognized. 131I treatment of hyperthyroidism after presentation was associated with survival (P=0.024). Four cases received oral iodide; propranolol alone or methimazole was used without complication in seven cases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 430 patients treated for active TB between 1990 and 1999, side effects resulting in modification/discontinuation of therapy or hospitalization were attributed based on resolution after withdrawal and/or recurrence with rechallenge. The incidence of all major adverse effects was 1.48 per 100 person-months (95% CI, 1.31-1.61) for pyrazinamide. The paper concludes that the incidence of pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity and rash during treatment for active TB was substantially higher than with other first-line anti-TB drugs and higher than previously recognized.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of all major adverse effects 1.48 per 100 person-months (95% CI 1.31-1.61) among 430 patients treated 1990-1999 at Montreal Chest Institute; attribution based on resolution after withdrawal and/or recurrence with rechallenge. Pyrazinamide-associated adverse events (hepatotoxicity and rash) associated with age over 60 years (adjusted HR 2.6; 95% CI 1.01-6.6) and birthplace in Asia (adjusted HR 3.4; 95% CI 1.4-8.3).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the serial SGO-T pattern of toxic hepatitis, with a progressive rise if the drug is continued and rapid normalization on withdrawal, has been observed in patients with toxic hepatitis from pyrazinamide. Pyrazinamide is therefore explicitly reported as a cause of human drug-induced toxic hepatitis; a patient with toxic hepatitis due to pyrazinamide is also referenced elsewhere in the paper.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis (drug-induced); SGO-T (AST) rises progressively during continued pyrazinamide therapy and returns to normal on withdrawal. A figure caption also describes a patient with toxic hepatitis due to pyrazinamide.

raw_record.support_text: Pyrazinamide is listed among the drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases), a lesion resembling viral hepatitis with spotty, zonal, and massive/submassive necrosis patterns.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) hepatic injury (61 cases).

raw_record.support_text: The most serious toxic effect of pyrazinamide is upon the liver. The U.S. Public Health Service Tuberculosis Therapy Trial (1959) reported, in a series of 780 patients, an incidence of hepatic toxicity of 2-6%, depending upon the dosage employed. A summary by the Committee on Therapy of the American Trudeau Society covering 13 published clinic reports on 1,070 patients showed 33 (3.1%) instances of jaundice and 43 (4%) instances of increased bromsulphthalein excretion without clinical jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Antituberculous agent; recommended dosage 30-40 mg/kg body weight (total daily dose not exceeding 3 g). US PHS Tuberculosis Therapy Trial (1959) reported hepatic toxicity incidence of 2-6% in 780 patients depending on dosage. Trudeau Society summary of 13 published clinic reports on 1,070 patients: 33 (3.1%) instances of jaundice and 43 (4%) of increased bromsulphthalein excretion without clinical jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity was fatal in patient 74, and pyrazinamide was the drug incriminated. Cases were assessed with the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) scale, yielding a diagnosis of definite or highly probable in 96 cases and probable in 53 (149 ratings because of multiple drugs).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity in patient 74 of a 140-patient cohort of drug-induced liver disease; pyrazinamide was the drug incriminated. Cohort cases were graded with the CIOMS causality scale.

raw_record.support_text: In a consecutive series of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) and tuberculosis admitted to a liver intensive care unit between 1986 and 2008, 14 of 16 patients had an established diagnosis of anti-TB drug-induced ALF. The paper states that hepatitis was caused by pyrazinamide (PZA) in 10 patients and by isoniazid (INH) treatment in 4. Mean time from initiation of anti-TB treatment to the development of jaundice was 3.5 ± 3.1 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis attributed to PZA in 10 of 14 patients with anti-TB drug-induced ALF. Patients were receiving anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) for tuberculosis, initial regimens including combinations of RIF, INH, PZA, ETH, and sometimes streptomycin; some patients were immunosuppressed (renal transplant recipients, HIV infection).

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs, with pyrazinamide identified as the causative drug in 16 patients. Patients with pyrazinamide-induced liver injury showed no association with mitochondrial DNA variants.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, pyrazinamide was the attributed causative drug in 16. DILI defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. No association with mitochondrial DNA variants was found for pyrazinamide-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a study undertaken by the United States Public Health Service (1958) with pyrazinamide, hepatic toxicity developed in 21 of 645 patients: there were 6 cases of clinical jaundice, and 4 of these occurred after the twelfth week (from the nineteenth to twenty-third week).
raw_record.extra_details: US Public Health Service (1958) study: hepatic toxicity in 21 of 645 patients; 6 cases of clinical jaundice, 4 occurring between the nineteenth and twenty-third week, i.e., beyond the 12-week observation window of the present series.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis seen at Shinko Hospital, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis confirmed in liver biopsy during the acute episode. Drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one; pyrazinamide was the causative drug in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug for severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis in 1 of 9 affected patients; identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of drug withdrawal; repeat biopsies showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis; female preponderance (7 of 9) in this severe hypersensitivity-type group.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, 9 had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis on liver biopsy. In these patients, pyrazinamide was identified as the causative drug in one case; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one. The patient had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative in one of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis; bridging necrosis on liver biopsy; causality identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete recovery within 6 months after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was treated conservatively with bed rest and nutritional support; a 5-day course of prednisone produced no change. She improved gradually over a one-month hospitalization, with liver function tests returning toward normal. The final diagnosis at discharge was toxic hepatitis secondary to pyrazinamide.
raw_record.extra_details: A single patient case diagnosed as toxic hepatitis secondary to pyrazinamide. Elevated SGOT (peak 318 Reitman-Frankel Units on Jan 6), total bilirubin up to 26.4 mg/100 ml (conjugated 15.1 mg/100 ml), and prolonged prothrombin time (up to 22.9 sec vs 12 sec control) with bleeding tendency; liver biopsy deferred due to bleeding. Clinical features included jaundice (icterus), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, acneiform rash on face/chest/back, and nonpitting ankle edema. Patient improved over about one month with bed rest and nutritional support; prednisone (5 days) had no appreciable effect. Recovery with liver function tests nearing normal by March 8 (bilirubin 1.6 mg/100 ml, SGOT 50). Adjacent non-hepatic findings included acanthocytes (spur cells), target cells, abnormal lipid profile, and jejunal mucosal fold abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: The letter asserts that lower doses of pyrazinamide have reduced but not totally suppressed hepatotoxicity. The hepatitis is hepatocellular in type, is not associated with hypersensitivity manifestations, and regresses when pyrazinamide is withdrawn. The authors' patient was on pyrazinamide for a long time and developed fulminant hepatitis; even in reduced dosage pyrazinamide is hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Long-term pyrazinamide use in the reported patient led to fulminant hepatitis. Hepatitis is hepatocellular, not associated with hypersensitivity manifestations, and regresses with drug withdrawal. Lower doses reduce but do not suppress hepatotoxicity; the drug is hepatotoxic even in reduced dosage.

raw_record.support_text: In a 59-year-old woman, pyrazinamide (1500 mg/d) reintroduction during antituberculous therapy produced acute hepatitis with hypersensitivity symptoms (fever, pruritus, arthralgia, malaise) within 2 hours, marked transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l) and eosinophilia; symptoms resolved after withdrawal. The authors note that acute hepatitis associated with pyrazinamide has been described as dose-related direct (intrinsic) toxicity, but conclude that in this case the liver injury was secondary to a hypersensitivity mechanism and that hypersensitivity hepatitis should be included among the causes of pyrazinamide-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 59-year-old woman with tuberculosis. Pyrazinamide 1500 mg/day was reintroduced (day 28) after ethambutol and rifampicin had been resumed and tolerated; a positive rechallenge occurred 2 hours after the pyrazinamide dose with acute malaise, fever 40°C, generalized pruritus, arthralgia, perioral paresthesia, vomiting, eosinophilia (859 x 10^6/l eosinophils) and transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l); values fell after withdrawal (ALT 720 U/l, AST 120 U/l, eosinophils 280 x 10^6/l within 6 days). Initial episode had fever and hypereosinophilia. Patient remained healthy with normal laboratory data at 1-year follow-up. Authors note acute hepatitis with pyrazinamide is usually a dose-related predictable direct toxic mechanism, but attribute this case to a hypersensitivity mechanism involving antibodies and cytotoxic T-lymphocytes directed against hepatocyte proteins modified by reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: Ditercalinium, in which two molecules of 9-methoxyellipticine were linked by a substituted aminocyclohexane linker, was designed as a DNA bisintercalator and showed high activity against human cell lines in vitro. Accumulation of the drug in the mitochondria of the liver and the related high levels of liver toxicity resulted in its withdrawal from clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: DNA bisintercalator consisting of two 9-methoxyellipticine molecules linked by a substituted aminocyclohexane linker; accumulated in the mitochondria of the liver; high levels of liver toxicity led to withdrawal of the drug from clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: Ditercalinium was originally designed to bis-intercalate into DNA with high affinity and displayed strong cytotoxicity on experimental tumor cells. However, it turned out after a clinical trial that irreversible hepatotoxicity is a dose-limiting side-effect. The reagent specifically accumulates in mitochondria, depletes mtDNA, and the drug was ultimately abandoned as a clinical anticancer drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Irreversible hepatotoxicity was a dose-limiting side-effect; ditercalinium is a DNA bis-intercalator that specifically accumulates in mitochondria and depletes mtDNA; the drug was ultimately abandoned as a clinical anticancer drug. The cardiotoxic doxorubicin and myopathic AZT (mtDNA depletion) are mentioned in the same paragraph but are not attributed to liver injury, so no records are made for them.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old woman with no history of liver disease developed liver dysfunction with severe jaundice and general malaise following prolonged minocycline therapy for acne vulgaris (100 mg daily for about 1 year). Serum ANA was detected and IgG elevated; symptoms and liver function normalized after minocycline discontinuation and corticosteroids. The diagnosis was drug-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features, since liver histology revealed acute hepatitis. The paper notes drug-induced hepatitis should be considered when liver dysfunction develops during long-term minocycline therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 25-year-old Japanese woman with acne vulgaris treated with minocycline 100 mg/day for 12 months prior to onset; presented with deranged liver function, severe jaundice (icterus), and general malaise; serum anti-nuclear antibody detected and IgG elevated; liver histology revealed acute hepatitis; symptoms resolved and liver function normalized after minocycline discontinuation and corticosteroid administration; no history of drug/food allergy, transfusion, or significant alcohol consumption; only a few reports of minocycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis in Japan. Some reports indicate minocycline can induce abnormal immune reactions resulting in hepatitis and systemic lupus erythematosus-like syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of minocycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) cases (11 cases). Only 3 of 11 (27%) had jaundice at presentation, and two minocycline patients were not treated with immunosuppression. Histologically, minocycline cases showed lower inflammatory grade (median grade 2), with interface hepatitis 2.0, lobular hepatitis 1.0, and fewer confluent necrotic or rosette-forming lesions than nitrofurantoin cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 minocycline-induced AIH cases reported. 3/11 (27%) had jaundice at presentation; two patients were not treated with immunosuppression. AIH likelihood scores were at least 'probable' where complete data were available. Histology: median Batts-Ludwig grade 2, interface hepatitis 2.0 (1.0-2.8), lobular hepatitis 1.0, confluent necrosis 1/11, rosette formation 1/11, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate 9/11, zone 3 necrosis 6/11. Imaging abnormalities were not observed in any minocycline patient.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews 9 reported cases of minocycline-associated acute liver failure, including the authors' own patient, who had received minocycline for rosacea. Across the cases, 6 patients were under 25 years old; the duration of minocycline intake before acute liver failure was <35 days in 6 cases and 3 years in one. In addition to liver failure, exanthema was reported in 5 cases and renal failure in 3 (two required hemodialysis); 5 patients improved with supportive treatment while 4 required liver transplantation (one of whom died subsequently). Histopathology from 4 cases showed hepatic necrosis in 3 and severe hepatic steatosis in one, with eosinophilia, elevated IgE, and elevated ANA titers indicating a pseudoallergic/autoimmune-mediated pathophysiology.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 reported cases of minocycline-associated acute liver failure (1980-2009, including first reported case by Burette et al. 1980). Indications: acne vulgaris (7), rosacea (1), aspiration pneumonia (1). Duration before ALF <35 days in 6 cases, 3 years in one. Doses ranged from 50-400 mg/d, oral or IV. Exanthema in 5 cases, renal failure in 3 (2 on hemodialysis). 4 patients required liver transplantation, one of whom died subsequently; 5 recovered with supportive treatment. Histology available for 4 cases: hepatic necrosis (3) and severe hepatic steatosis (1); one case showed necrotising hepatitis. Eosinophilia, increased IgE, and elevated ANA in 3 patients each, and in vitro FACS showed drug-stimulated IFN-gamma, IL-17, and TNF responses, indicating immune-mediated severe liver failure. The paper advises reconsidering minocycline indications given rare but potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, minocycline accounted for 28 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases. It was a predominant cause (10 cases) among cases with latency greater than 1 year, and mortality for minocycline DILI was 0-1%.
raw_record.extra_details: 28 adjudicated DILI cases; predominant among cases with latency >1 year (n=10); mortality for minocycline DILI 0-1%.

raw_record.support_text: Of 1322 patients with suspected DILI enrolled in the DILIN Prospective Study, 94 (8%) were adjudicated as definitely, highly likely or probably due to nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa or hydralazine; the analysis cohort included 28 cases due to minocycline.
raw_record.extra_details: 28 adjudicated cases (DILIN Prospective Study). Younger patients (median age 19), female preponderance, majority non-Hispanic white. Latency above 6 months in 71% and above a year in 50%. Predominantly hepatocellular pattern. Fatality rate 0%.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes minocycline-induced hepatotoxicity/DILI as an established human entity and reports a genome-wide genotyping study in a well-characterized cohort of minocycline DILI cases, in which a significant association was noted between HLA-B*35:02 and risk for minocycline DILI (16% carrier frequency in DILI cases vs 0.6% in population controls). Most patients in the cohort were women and 90% had positive antinuclear antibodies.
raw_record.extra_details: Genome-wide genotyping in a well-characterized DILI cohort; 16% carrier frequency of HLA-B*35:02 in DILI cases vs 0.6% in population controls; most patients were women and 90% had positive antinuclear antibodies; HLA-B*35:02 carriers had presenting features and outcomes similar to non-carriers; in silico modeling supported direct binding of minocycline to this HLA risk allele as a possible initiating event.

raw_record.support_text: De Boer et al. characterized autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) secondary to minocycline in DILI cases, with an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score ≥2) present in the majority of cases (74%). In contrast, Urban et al. found that HLA-B 35:02 was associated with an increased risk of liver injury from minocycline.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases from the US DILIN prospective study; autoimmune phenotype present in 74% of minocycline cases. Urban et al. reported HLA-B 35:02 associated with increased risk of liver injury from minocycline, proposed as a potential diagnostic tool. One of the drugs for which the modified lymphocyte transformation test was not reliable for DILI diagnosis.

raw_record.support_text: Minocycline is recognized to cause an autoimmune hepatitis, generally appearing after a long period of exposure, with average onset within 2 years but possibly within a few months. Features include fever, polyarthralgia, rash, anorexia, fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice; serology resembles idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis with ANA, ASMA, and anti-LKM positivity, elevated IgG, and typical histology of chronic active hepatitis with periportal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and piecemeal necrosis. A higher frequency of HLA-B*35:02 is found in patients with minocycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis than in the general population, while HLA-DRB1*03:01 and *04:01 are not risk factors. Hepatitis occurs twice as often in women, who also develop symptoms after shorter therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported case: transaminitis persisted after minocycline discontinuation, peaking at ALT 3,422 U/L, AST 3,909 U/L and direct bilirubin 17.54 µg/dL about two weeks after stopping; improved with prednisone and lab values normalized within 12 weeks; hepatitis did not recur after prednisone. Minocycline hepatotoxicity risk is higher than other tetracyclines; symptoms/lab abnormalities typically resolve within 3 months of discontinuation; recurrence does not typically occur unless rechallenged. Serology: ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM, p-ANCA possible, IgG >1.5x ULN; eosinophils rare; bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis uncommon. Mechanism unknown but possibly immune-mediated via HLA-B*35:02 antigen presentation; onset average within 2 years of exposure.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort comparing patients with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and autoimmune hepatitis, one patient suffered from acute liver injury due to minocycline, which the authors note has been described to cause DILI with autoimmune features resembling autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) that responds well to corticosteroid treatment. Immunosuppressive treatment was initiated in this patient due to persistently elevated ALT levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with acute liver injury; DILI with autoimmune features resembling AIH that responds well to corticosteroids. Immunosuppressive therapy was initiated due to persistently elevated ALT levels despite withdrawal of the causative drug. Within a cohort of 18 DILI patients with autoimmune features receiving corticosteroid treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Among antibiotic-related acute liver failure, minocycline was implicated in n=1 case of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that certain drugs causing DILI are commonly associated with formation of serum autoantibodies, and cites the Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) Network prospective study in which de Boer et al. found positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at the onset of DILI caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine. This identifies minocycline as a human DILI-causing agent.
raw_record.extra_details: In the DILI Network prospective study, minocycline-induced DILI was associated with positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at onset of injury.

raw_record.support_text: Mechanistic proposals derived from 25 RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) caused by minocycline in association with HLA; direct molecular docking of minocycline to the HLA allele HLA B*35:02 was proposed as an important initiating step, supporting a role for adaptive immunity.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 25; proposed mechanism: direct molecular docking of minocycline to HLA B*35:02 as an initiating step, implicating adaptive immunity; study citation [57].

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed acute cholestatic hepatitis during treatment with propafenone. Viral infections, alcohol abuse, hepatotoxicity by other drugs, and biliary obstruction were excluded as causes. In one patient, liver biopsy showed changes consistent with a drug-associated injury, and another had serum autoimmune antibodies (ANA). Following propafenone withdrawal, the clinical and biochemical profiles of both patients improved. The authors describe hepatic toxicity from the antiarrhythmic drug propafenone as highly uncommon, noting that most cases reported had acute cholestatic hepatitis after a latency of two to four weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Two new cases added to seven previously published, for a total of nine (none fatal). Acute cholestatic hepatitis usually after a latency of two to four weeks; one new case had an extremely long latency period and circulating antinuclear antibodies (ANA). One patient's liver biopsy showed changes consistent with drug-associated injury. Both patients improved after propafenone withdrawal. Case 1: 67-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus type II and hypertension, on glibenclamide 5 mg/day and enalapril 20 mg/day for 5 years, started propafenone 450 mg/day 6 weeks before hepatitis symptoms for atrial fibrillation; other hepatotoxic drugs, viral infection, alcohol, and biliary obstruction excluded as causes. Mechanism unknown, proposed as either hypersensitivity reaction or idiosyncratic toxic reaction due to a propafenone metabolite; hepatic metabolism influenced by cytochrome P-450 2D6 activity with 5-hydroxy and N-desalkyl active metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: The authors performed a Naranjo evaluation to determine the probability that the clinical event was due to propafenone administration, obtaining a score of 7, which indicates a probable adverse drug reaction from propafenone use. A diagnosis of acute propafenone toxicity was based on temporal relationship with the drug, clinical and biochemical recovery after withdrawal, exclusion of other causes, and histology consistent with drug toxicity. This is reported as the eighth case in the world's literature of hepatotoxicity related to propafenone, with clinical presentation that can be cholestatic and/or hepatocellular, jaundice in all cases, a latency of two to six weeks, and no reported cases of fulminant liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo score 7 (probable ADR); dechallenge with withdrawal reduced alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase and normalized aminotransferases and CA19-9; latency 2-6 weeks (one case at 28 weeks); jaundice in all cases; no fulminant liver failure reported; eighth case in world literature; histology showed portal and periportal inflammatory infiltrate, macrovesicular steatosis, bile duct injury with ductular proliferation, mixed inflammatory infiltrate (eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells), mild periportal feathery degeneration, no fibrosis; antiarrhythmic indication.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient developed cholestatic liver injury approximately 2 weeks after starting propafenone, with development of jaundice and pruritus within 3 to 4 weeks thereafter. Three months after withdrawal, the patient was asymptomatic and all liver tests had normalised. The paper frames propafenone as a very rare cause of hepatotoxicity (DILI) and recommends discontinuing the drug when cholestatic and/or hepatocellular injury is suspected.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic liver injury with jaundice and pruritus, latency approximately 2 weeks from drug initiation; jaundice/pruritus developed 3-4 weeks after start; complete resolution ~3 months after withdrawal; RUCAM causality assessment performed (criteria tabulated: onset 5-90 days +2, ALT decrease >=50% within 8 days of withdrawal +3, age >=55 +1, all-cause exclusion +2); positive dechallenge; concurrent C. freundii gastroenteritis with sepsis/hypotension and meropenem use were evaluated and excluded as causes. Prior case reports show cholestatic injury with jaundice, latency generally 2-8 weeks; liver biopsies described portal tract enlargement with lymphocytic/monocyte/macrophage/granulocyte infiltrates, bile duct proliferation, hepatocyte ballooning, and macrovesicular steatosis; proposed mechanism includes hepatic toxic metabolite accumulation (p-quinone intermediates) and enterohepatic recirculation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 14 female patients with laxative-induced hepatitis (Laxantien-Hepatitis) over the last 18 months, in which the diagnosis was secured by re-exposure (durch Reexposition gesichert) to the incriminated laxative. The hepatic damage is attributed to phenolisatin (phenolisatin-bedingter Leberschaden), framed as continuing phenolisatin-induced hepatitis cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 female patients over 18 months; diagnosis confirmed by re-exposure; serum monitoring of GLDH, GOT, GPT and bilirubin; one or more liver biopsies in all cases. Note: section heading on p:8 refers to 'Oxyphenisatin-induced liver disease'.

raw_record.support_text: Oxyphenisatin has been reported as the cause of hepatic injury in more than 100 described patients, mostly female. In about one-third the injury resembled acute hepatitis with diffuse hepatocellular necrosis, acidophilic bodies, lobular disarray, Kupffer cell prominence and portal inflammation; the other two-thirds had histologic changes of chronic active hepatitis, many with features of cirrhosis, and a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis. Withdrawal usually produced rapid improvement, while readministration of oxyphenisatin to several patients led to return or increase of abnormal values.
raw_record.extra_details: More than 100 patients with hepatic injury attributable to the drug; a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis; prognosis good with withdrawal, most patients showing rapid improvement and complete or near-complete resolution of biochemical abnormalities; readministration (rechallenge) in several patients led to return or increase of abnormal laboratory values; affected patients were predominantly female, though the paper notes the data do not permit distinguishing disproportionate female susceptibility from greater exposure.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports two women, aged 53 and 65, in whom jaundice with the clinical, laboratory, and pathological picture of chronic active hepatitis developed after daily use of 5 to 7.5 mg of the laxative Prulets for 16 and eight months. In one, liver-function tests and biopsy returned to normal within a year of stopping the drug, and a challenge with Prulets (7.5 mg/day for four days) caused a definite rise in SGOT; in the other, liver function markedly improved two weeks after discontinuation. The accompanying paragraph states that these patients were taking laxatives with only one active ingredient, oxyphenisatin, providing additional proof that oxyphenisatin can be hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Laxative ingredient given as Prulets, 5-7.5 mg/day for 8-16 months. Both patients were women, ages 53 and 65. Jaundice and chronic active hepatitis clinical, laboratory, and pathological picture. In one patient liver-function tests and biopsy returned to normal within a year of discontinuation, and rechallenge with 7.5 mg/day for four days caused a definite rise in SGOT (AST); the other improved markedly two weeks after stopping. Laxative contained oxyphenisatin as the only active ingredient.

raw_record.support_text: After a first course of sertraline therapy was associated with symptomatic hepatitis and an elevated serum ALT, the patient resumed sertraline for worsening depression; three weeks later her serum ALT rose significantly. Sertraline was discontinued again and her ALT fell to the normal range over 89 days, and was later shown to have dropped near normal within four weeks of the first discontinuation. Inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline was followed by a prompt rise in ALT, a rechallenge phenomenon the authors consider diagnostic of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Persky and Reinus). Rechallenge (inadvertent) after resumption of sertraline produced a prompt rise in serum ALT, described as diagnostic of DILI. Liver biopsy during second admission showed lobular disarray with lymphocytic infiltrate, scattered neutrophils and eosinophils, spotty hepatocyte necrosis, and Councilman bodies, consistent with drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis. Diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis was made initially and treated with oral prednisone 20 mg daily; ALT did not permanently normalize on corticosteroids, and hepatitis was later presumed sertraline-induced rather than autoimmune. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic etiologies negative (anti-HAV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, ANA, ceruloplasmin, ferritin, CMV). Prior acetaminophen use was only at therapeutic doses with serum level <10 µg/ml at presentation. ALT normalized within 89 days after permanent sertraline discontinuation; depression subsequently treated with amitriptyline.

raw_record.support_text: Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Hepatotoxicity caused by sertraline is rare, with asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations reported in approximately 0.8% of patients, generally within the first 9 weeks of therapy, which normalize shortly after discontinuation. The paper presents a case of severe drug-induced hepatitis in a patient receiving sertraline, reported as the seventh case in the medical literature associated with severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 17-year-old man had taken sertraline 25 mg/day for 6 months for depression when he developed symptomatic hepatitis with nausea, fatigue, scleral jaundice, and dark urine. Peak labs: ALT 1,880 U/l, AST 810 U/l, ALP 483 U/l, GGT 124 U/l, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic work-up and abdominal ultrasound were negative; liver biopsy was refused. Sertraline was discontinued and transaminases declined to normal within 6 months with no relapse. Naranjo algorithm total score was 7 (Probable). Reported as the seventh case of severe sertraline-associated hepatotoxicity in the literature. Asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations occur in ~0.8% of sertraline-treated patients, usually within the first 9 weeks of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with major depressive disorder developed acute hepatocellular liver injury after treatment with sertraline 50 mg daily, presenting with elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and gastrointestinal distress. After discontinuation of sertraline, liver function tests gradually normalized over 90 days, confirming the diagnosis of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Sertraline 50 mg daily in a patient with MDD who had prior partial response to escitalopram and cognitive-behavioral therapy. Acute hepatocellular liver injury with elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and gastrointestinal distress; liver function tests normalized over 90 days after drug discontinuation. Paper also notes sertraline has been linked to transient asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations and rare clinically significant acute liver injury, with reports of acute hepatitis with or without jaundice (refs 15-23).

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' patient, acute hepatitis with cholestasis appeared within a DRESS syndrome after about 3 weeks of sustained-release bupropion for smoking cessation. Other causes of acute liver injury were excluded, and the similar elevation of serum transaminases with a cholestatic pattern and weakly positive ANA supported a drug-induced reaction; because serum acetaminophen was undetectable and liver synthetic function was preserved, the acute hepatitis was attributed to an idiosyncratic reaction to bupropion. Liver enzymes normalized more than 8 weeks after bupropion was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS syndrome presentation with fever, rash, angioedema, eosinophilia, and low serum complement; drug-induced liver injury and cholestatic pattern with weakly positive ANA; liver enzymes normalized >8 weeks after discontinuation without liver biopsy because synthetic function (normal coagulation) was preserved and encephalopathy was absent; acetaminophen as potential co-suspect was excluded by undetectable serum levels and preserved synthetic function; also developed myositis with myocardial involvement and possible rhabdomyolysis; complex history included corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia requiring intravenous insulin.

raw_record.support_text: A patient on bupropion SR presented six months after starting the drug with markedly elevated serum aminotransferases and bilirubin, showing a severe acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features. Enrolled in the DILIN prospective protocol with all other competing causes of liver injury excluded, the case scored 8 on RUCAM, categorized as a 'highly probable' case of DILI, and also scored 'probable' on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale. The authors concluded the patient presumably developed fulminant hepatitis with autoimmune features due to bupropion given the temporal course, exclusion of competing etiologies, and compatible histology.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: bupropion SR 150 mg BID for 180 days, peak ALT 20x ULN, peak bilirubin 37 mg/dl, positive ANA, liver biopsy showing acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features; progressed to fulminant liver failure and death with disseminated aspergillosis despite cessation and corticosteroids. RUCAM score 8 (highly probable DILI); scored probable on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale and probable autoimmune hepatitis on the International autoimmune hepatitis consensus scale. Table 1 lists prior published cases of bupropion hepatotoxicity (Oslin '93: 300-400 mg QD, 54 days, ALT 5.4x ULN, resolution; Hu '00: 200 mg QD, 42 days, ALT 6660 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8, resolution; D. Alvaro '01: 150 mg BID, 20 days, ALT 49x ULN, bilirubin 38, resolution; Humayun '07: 150 mg BID, 180 days, ALT 20x ULN, bilirubin 37, death), all occurring within the first 6 months of use with a hepatocellular injury pattern; this is described as the first reported fatal bupropion hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient case report, after acitretin 25 mg twice daily was started, liver function tests rose 2 days later (ALT 237 U/L, ALP 440 U/L, bilirubin 41 µmol/L) from normal baseline. Acitretin was discontinued and ALT returned to normal within 5 days; ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L 6 months later, consistent with acitretin-induced human liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient treated for erythrodermic/pustular psoriasis. Dose 25 mg twice daily, latency 2 days after start; baseline liver functions normal (ALP 93 U/L, ALT 12 U/L, bilirubin 8 µmol/L). Post-exposure ALT 237 U/L, ALP 440 U/L rising to peak 679 U/L, bilirubin 41 µmol/L; ALT normalized over 5 days after dechallenge, ALP still 191 U/L at 6 months. Same patient developed bone marrow features consistent with drug-induced agranulocytosis and total scalp alopecia. Paper notes that hepatic toxicity is a well-recognized retinoid side-effect, with up to 30% of acitretin-treated patients developing raised aminotransferases, 10% ALP elevations (generally mild/transient), and genuine toxic hepatitis rare; hepatotoxicity attributed to retinoids possibly via apoptosis or direct toxic necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient being treated for psoriasis was started on acitretin 25 mg twice daily. Two days later her ALT rose to 237 U/L, ALP to 440 U/L and bilirubin to 41 µmol/L from a normal baseline. Acitretin was stopped and ALT returned to normal over 5 days; ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L 6 months later. This indicates acitretin as the cause of the acute liver injury in therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient on acitretin 25 mg twice daily for pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis; ALT rose from 12 to 237 U/L, ALP from 93 to 440 U/L, bilirubin from 8 to 41 µmol/L with JAUNDICE-level bilirubin rise; ALT normalized within 5 days of discontinuation (dechallenge), ALP peaked at 679 U/L and stayed elevated at 191 U/L at 6 months. Same episode also involved drug-induced agranulocytosis (WCC 1.3 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.1 x 10^9/L) and subsequent total scalp alopecia. Elsewhere the paper notes hepatic toxicity is a well-recognized side-effect of acitretin, with up to 30% of patients developing raised aminotransferases and 10% ALP elevations, generally mild and transient, while genuine toxic hepatitis is rare; only isotretinoin (not acitretin) has prior retinoid-associated agranulocytosis reports.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old man with psoriasis developed a biopsy-verified toxic hepatitis probably due to acitretin, having used the drug for 5 months with a total dose of 7210 mg. Thorough examination found no other reason for his liver damage, and the liver changes normalized 10 weeks after stopping treatment. His psoriasis worsened and acitretin was reintroduced at a lower dose, with no evidence of liver damage during 15 months of follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: Psoriasis patient; biopsy-verified toxic hepatitis; used acitretin for 5 months, total dose 7210 mg; no other cause found for the liver damage; liver changes normalized 10 weeks after discontinuation; after rechallenge at a reduced dose there was no evidence of liver damage over 15 months of follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: Acitretin causes transient elevation of liver enzymes that is dose dependent and usually reverses to normal after dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy. Severe hepatotoxic reactions from retinoids are rare; in a dataset of 1877 patients receiving oral acitretin, only 0.26% showed overt chemical hepatitis, but severe hepatotoxic reactions are rare.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme elevation is dose dependent and usually reverses after dose reduction or drug discontinuation; severe hepatotoxic reactions are rare. In a dataset of 1877 patients on oral acitretin, only 0.26% showed overt chemical hepatitis (Katz, Waalen, & Leach, 1999).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the hepatotoxicity caused by dapsone in their patient, with liver biopsy showing focal destruction of bile ducts and intraepithelial neutrophils, features suggestive of acute cholangitis. They state this is the first report of dapsone as a cause of cholangitis, and describe the case as a dapsone syndrome with hepatic involvement in the form of acute cholangitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (dapsone syndrome) with hepatic involvement manifesting as acute cholangitis; liver biopsy showed focal destruction of bile ducts and intraepithelial neutrophils, not previously reported in dapsone syndrome. The patient had also received one dose of rifampicin, which the authors deemed unlikely to have caused such a severe reaction. Prior dapsone syndrome biopsy literature describes hepatitis, cholestasis, or granuloma formation. Indications noted: leprosy, AIDS, and dermatitis herpetiformis.

raw_record.support_text: Dapsone accounted for one patient in this DILI series. In the 22 definite DILI cases, one patient with dapsone-induced liver injury died of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient died of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS). Dapsone is described as one of the commonly implicated drugs in drug-induced systemic hypersensitivity syndrome, and DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect reported with dapsone use. Manifestations include hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and shock. In the presented patient, the diagnosis of DHS with hepatitis was made after typical clinical manifestations following 3 weeks of dapsone intake, after excluding other drug exposures and close differential diagnoses, and was supported by prompt response to systemic steroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS syndrome). DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect; latency several weeks to up to 6 months after treatment initiation; reported incidence 0.5%-3%. The patient had severe systemic manifestations including hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, shock and exfoliative dermatitis. Diagnosis followed 3 weeks of dapsone intake after excluding viral hepatitis, rickettsial infection, CMV, EBV, complicated malaria and leptospirosis; supported by prompt response to systemic steroids (prednisolone or methylprednisolone). Rechallenge not recommended. Mortality as high as 12%-23% reported in severe DHS. Pathogenesis proposed to involve dapsone metabolites (hydroxylamines via hepatic microsomal cytochrome P-450). Dapsone used for leprosy, Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, toxoplasmosis, malaria, dermatological conditions and immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

raw_record.support_text: Table of drugs implicated in causing drug-induced acute liver failure lists dapsone in 7 cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed in 7 of 128 drug-induced acute liver failure cases in a single-center Indian study. Conclusion notes dapsone DIALF is associated with hypersensitivity features in a majority of patients and lower mortality than anti-TB DIALF.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient with leukocytoclastic vasculitis who also had dermatitis herpetiformis, dapsone at 200 mg/day was effective, but a drug-induced hepatitis developed and the dapsone had to be discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg/day; patient also had dermatitis herpetiformis. Injury described as drug-induced hepatitis requiring discontinuation of dapsone.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed obstructive jaundice during chlorpromazine therapy. For the first, jaundice appeared after 16 days of chlorpromazine at 100 mg/day and lasted 27 days, with fever and a flu-like onset followed by severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, and a laboratory picture suggesting obstructive jaundice; recovery occurred with symptomatic management and drug withdrawal. The second received chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days and developed generalized pruritus, dark urine, light stools, and mild jaundice with obstructive liver-function findings and 21% blood eosinophils, recovering uneventfully 19 days after discontinuation. The authors state the jaundice in these cases is thought to be secondary to chlorpromazine therapy, and that jaundice from stone, other obstructive phenomena, or infectious hepatitis appears remote.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: chlorpromazine 100 mg/day, jaundice after 16 days persisting 27 days, fever and flu-like onset, severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, obstructive laboratory picture, active marginal ulcer and marked duodenal deformity; recovered after withdrawal and symptomatic management. Patient 2: chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days, generalized pruritus within a week, dark urine, light stools, mild jaundice at two weeks, obstructive liver-function tests, 21% eosinophils, duodenal spasm; icterus lasted about two weeks, uneventful recovery 19 days after stopping.
