Liver biopsy in the case reported by Zatuchni and Miller showed acute periportal inflammation, bile plugs in canaliculi, and numerous eosinophils, suggesting hypersensitivity as the principal mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Three cases of hepatitis produced by the drug chlorpromazine (Thorazine) are reported. Jaundice appeared after two weeks of drug therapy, preceded by fever, malaise and anorexia, and in one case was associated with right-upper-abdominal pain and a tender mass that led to surgery; the patients recovered in a few weeks. The jaundice was associated with intrahepatic biliary stasis, eosinophilia was present in one patient, and liver biopsy supported the diagnosis of Thorazine hepatitis in all patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Three attributed cases. Jaundice onset after ~2 weeks of chlorpromazine therapy, preceded by fever, malaise and anorexia; one case had right-upper-quadrant pain and a tender mass leading to exploratory surgery to exclude a surgical cause. Obstructive jaundice with intrahepatic biliary stasis; hepatocellular tests normal while serum cholesterol and alkaline phosphatase markedly elevated; eosinophilia in one patient; liver biopsy (Vim-Silverman needle, done in all cases) showed hepatitis with bile canaliculi plugged by inspissated bile. Patients recovered in a few weeks; jaundice cleared within 4-6 weeks, with alkaline phosphatase and cholesterol remaining elevated for considerably longer. No extrahepatic bile-duct disease demonstrable. Authors recommend reserving chlorpromazine for conditions where benefit outweighs risk because of the serious hepatitis.; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: A case of toxic hepatitis produced by chlorpromazine and later by iproniazid in the same patient is reported. The jaundice from chlorpromazine appeared after one day of therapy and was associated with intrahepatic biliary stasis and obstruction without evidence of hepatocellular damage, with the patient recovering completely.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis with jaundice after one day of chlorpromazine therapy; intrahepatic biliary stasis and obstruction without hepatocellular damage (cholestatic pattern); patient recovered completely from the episode. The paper also notes chlorpromazine can reportedly be reinstituted after jaundice disappears without relapse and that patients have recovered from jaundice while the drug was continued.

raw_record.support_text: In a large psychiatric hospital, nine patients with chlorpromazine jaundice (allergic cholangiolitis following administration of chlorpromazine) were studied in sufficient detail to warrant inclusion in the report; the authors state that liver cell damage is usual in this disease. They underwent intensive serial clinical, laboratory, and serial needle aspiration biopsy studies, documenting chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic liver injury with associated liver cell degeneration.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine psychiatric inpatients with chlorpromazine jaundice; 26 percutaneous needle aspiration biopsies. Histology showed liver cell damage typical of the disease: ballooning degeneration of liver cells, multinucleation, mitoses, unicellular and periportal focal necroses with Councilman-like bodies, and one fatal literature case (Rodin and Robertson) with diffuse non-inflammatory centrolobular necroses preserved supporting reticulum (feathery necrosis). Features of allergic cholangiolitis: jaundice, bile in urine, elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (Bodansky units) and cholesterol, eosinophilia; all nine present cases recovered, though some laboratory abnormalities persisted for months.

raw_record.support_text: Kelsey and associates observed three types of pathologic liver conditions associated with chlorpromazine: a diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis producing obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation, a type resembling acute hepatitis with parenchymal liver damage, and an uncommon early-cirrhosis type. Dreyfuss reported that the incidence of chlorpromazine jaundice was 4.4% in 362 patients given no extra fluids but dropped to 0.34% in 588 patients given about 2.3 L of additional fluids, supporting an inspissation-of-bile mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Kelsey's three liver types: (1) diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis, obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation and no abnormal parenchymal liver-function tests; (2) acute-hepatitis-like with elevated thymol turbidity and prothrombin deficiency; (3) uncommon early cirrhosis with marked azotemia and severe prolonged chronic liver disease. Dreyfuss fluid study: jaundice incidence 4.4% (362 patients, no extra fluids) vs 0.34% (588 patients, ~2.3 L extra fluids). Read/Harrison/Sherlock: 4 women developed obstructive jaundice after 1-4 weeks on 75 mg/day chlorpromazine, with very high serum cholesterol and xanthomas; clinical recovery in all, but serum cholesterol and phosphatase levels not normalized even 7-18 months later.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old female developed cholangiolitic (cholestatic) hepatitis / jaundice following chlorpromazine (Thorazine, Largactil); in a first episode (1955) she had fever, epigastric pain, anorexia, pruritus and dark urine after chlorpromazine 75 mg daily for ten days, symptoms subsiding on discontinuation; in a second episode (1960) she developed jaundice after only two doses (25 mg), with pruritus, dark urine, light-colored stools, icterus, a tender liver edge, mild eosinophilia, serum bilirubin rising to 3.3 mg/100 ml and alkaline phosphatase 33 King-Armstrong units, with normal SGOT; she made an uneventful recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical diagnosis of cholangiolitic (cholestatic) hepatitis consistent with findings and response to corticosteroid therapy; total serum bilirubin 3.3 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 33 King-Armstrong units, SGOT normal, cephalin flocculation and thymol turbidity negative, mild eosinophilia; serum electrophoretic pattern showed slight increase in alpha-2 globulin with normal gamma globulin despite presumed hypersensitivity; 51-year-old female.

raw_record.support_text: Clinically and biochemically the jaundice during chlorpromazine treatment is of obstructive type, but the liver in the fatal case showed central necrosis and biliary stasis, severe lobular atrophy, relative preservation of portal areas, and absence of exudate, interpreted as 'subacute toxic hepatitis of blood-borne type'. Ante-mortem passive congestion of the liver contributed to a significant degree to the central necrosis. Of 11 affected patients, 9 ran an uneventful course to recovery, while one died after thirteen weeks' remittent illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice clinically and biochemically of obstructive type; direct serum-bilirubin invariably 2-2.5x indirect component. Fatal case additionally showed central necrosis, biliary stasis, severe lobular atrophy, absent exudate, described as 'subacute toxic hepatitis of blood-borne type'; ante-mortem passive congestion contributed significantly to the central necrosis. 9 of 11 cases recovered uneventfully; 1 chronic encephalitic recovered after stormy 26 weeks with residual raised alkaline phosphatase (45 King-Armstrong units) and impaired bromsulphalein clearance (83%); 1 chronic rheumatic heart-disease patient died after thirteen weeks' remittent illness (Boardman 1954).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in the vast majority of subjects chlorpromazine hepatitis is benign and of relatively short duration, but describes a single patient in whom jaundice was extremely prolonged, with marked disturbance of lipid metabolism and a resulting syndrome indistinguishable from xanthomatous biliary cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (L.J.), 41-year-old white man with depressive reaction with anxiety. Chlorpromazine 25 mg orally QID, increased to 50 mg QID on hospital day 10; icterus, dark urine and light-colored stools appeared on hospital day 17 with enlarged liver 2 inches below right costal margin. Prolonged jaundice with marked lipid-metabolism disturbance resulting in a syndrome indistinguishable from xanthomatous biliary cirrhosis. Labs: leukocytes 11,700/cu mm with 9% eosinophils, urine bile-positive/urobilinogen-negative, serum total bilirubin rising to 41 mg/100 ml (20 mg direct), serum alkaline phosphatase 68 units (Shinowara-Jones), serum total cholesterol up to 1,164 mg/100 ml, normal protein electrophoresis, negative heterophil antibody.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpromazine is given as an example of a drug with very well documented hepatotoxicity with numerous case reports and case series and positive rechallenge, and in early DILI research it was commonly reported to be associated with hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Antipsychotic/phenothiazine; listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported cases of drug-induced liver injury (LiverTox) and in GPRD as most strongly associated with DILI (crude incidence 1 per 739 users, risk >100 per 100,000 users).

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies chlorpromazine as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 7 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Chlorpromazine produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 6 and diffuse necrosis in 1.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine was the causative agent in 7 of 53 patients; produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 6 and diffuse necrosis in 1.

raw_record.support_text: Marsilid (iproniazid) jaundice closely resembles viral hepatitis, with acute diffuse hepatocellular disease indicated by positive flocculation tests, hyperbilirubinemia, and considerable elevations in serum glutamic oxalacetic (SGOT) and glutamic pyruvic (SGPT) transaminases, while serum alkaline phosphatase and total cholesterol were elevated only slightly or not at all. The highest transaminase values observed in patients in whom Marsilid was reasonably suspected to cause jaundice were 357 units SGOT and 514 units SGPT (colorimetric method). The authors consider the hepatotoxicity produced by this drug a distinct problem from chlorpromazine jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Marsilid is the brand name for iproniazid. Jaundice closely resembled viral hepatitis with acute diffuse hepatocellular disease; positive flocculation tests (cephalin-cholesterol flocculation, thymol turbidity, 18-hour turbidity ratio, gamma globulin), considerably elevated SGOT and SGPT (highest 357 and 514 units, colorimetric); alkaline phosphatase and total cholesterol elevated only slightly or not at all. Mortality of jaundice from this drug reported as about 20% in over 100 cases. A fatal case treated with 100 mg daily (reduced to 50 mg daily 14 days before jaundice onset) died 12 days after jaundice onset with acute necrosis of the liver at autopsy. Histology in the authors' patient showed massive necrosis of liver cells. Summary notes the relative lack of emphasis in the literature on jaundice, and especially its possibly fatal outcome, from iproniazid administration.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 230 cases of hepatitis associated with iproniazid therapy, with 51 deaths among them, and states that a cause-and-effect relationship has been well established and accepted. The estimated incidence is one per 3,000 to 4,000 patients treated with iproniazid, with death occurring in 20 to 25 per cent of the afflicted. The hepatotoxicity has an insidious onset and a particularly fulminant course, is not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis, and no relationship of dose to incidence appears to exist.
raw_record.extra_details: 230 reported cases of hepatitis with 51 deaths. Estimated incidence 1 per 3,000-4,000 patients treated; fatality in 20-25% of the afflicted. Insidious onset and particularly fulminant course; not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis other than by severity. No dose-incidence relationship evident; hepatotoxic effects occurred only rarely within the first few weeks of therapy. Predictive susceptibility factors not identified; routine liver-function testing did not predict impending disease; course not immediately reversible after drug discontinuation. Iproniazid (Marsilid) was used in selected patients with mental depression and as adjunctive therapy in terminal malignancies and advanced collagen diseases.

raw_record.support_text: The occurrence of jaundice in a small fraction of patients receiving iproniazid (Marsilid) made necessary the study of biochemical features of the syndrome and evaluation of the incidence of hepatic dysfunction in patients receiving the drug. The paper explicitly frames this jaundice as a drug toxicity reaction, consistent with human iproniazid-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 86 patients developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid (data on 82 from manufacturer-submitted physician protocols, 4 from the Chicago, Ill. area). Jaundice was intense: 45% had bilirubin above 20 mg%, with values up to 60 mg%; in three quarters the direct-reading fraction was 40-65% of total bilirubin. Thymol turbidity was abnormal in 83% (range 4-41 units) and cephalin flocculation abnormal in 85%. Among substudies: serum iron elevated in all 6 patients; prothrombin time prolonged in 21/24; cholesterol esters below 60% of total in 9/13; serum albumin below 3 gm% in 8/27; globulins elevated (related table 1). GOT available in 50, GPT in 22 patients; 18 sera analyzed centrally. Iproniazid also known as Marsilid (Hoffmann-La Roche).

raw_record.support_text: In the viral-hepatitis-type group (61 cases of drug-induced hepatic injury), the drugs involved were iproniazid, metahexamide, B-phenyl-isopropyl hydrazine, isocarboxazid, amidosalicylic acid, pyrazinamide, and zoxazolamine. The histology resembled the acute icteric spotty necrotic form of viral hepatitis, with single-cell necrosis, mononuclear infiltrates, balloon cells, acidophilic bodies, and cholestasis prominent in half of the spotty necrosis cases; the group also included extensive zonal necrosis and massive/submassive necrosis (acute atrophy, subacute atrophy, transition to postnecrotic cirrhosis, postnecrotic cirrhosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases). Histology included spotty necrosis (13 cases, acute icteric form with cholestasis prominent in half), extensive zonal necrosis (9 cases), and massive/submassive necrosis (39 cases: 13 acute atrophy, 15 subacute atrophy, 7 transition to postnecrotic cirrhosis, 4 postnecrotic cirrhosis). Monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: Instances of jaundice were reported as associated with clinical and functional indications of hepatocellular injury following the intake of iproniazid (1-isonicotinyl-2-isopropylhydrazine, or Marsilid), an amine oxidase inhibitor used in the treatment of tuberculosis and various mental disorders. Biopsy and autopsy liver specimens from these patients showed histological manifestations usually considered characteristic of viral hepatitis, with no relationship observed between the dose of iproniazid and the extent of the lesion.
raw_record.extra_details: Material comprised 16 autopsy and 22 biopsy specimens from a total of 34 patients who developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid or up to 20 days after cessation of treatment; iproniazid was prescribed for depression in almost every instance. Histological findings were characteristic of viral hepatitis; no dose-relationship to extent of lesion was observed. Fourteen patients showed a severe spotty necrotic hepatitis on biopsy; of the fatal cases, 11 presented acute hepatitis with massive, submassive, or zonal necrosis and subsequent collapse, 7 showed subacute hepatitis and 1 chronic hepatitis of the same type with varying nodular regeneration; 2 showed almost complete histological recovery.

raw_record.support_text: Iproniazid, initially developed for tuberculosis and approved by the FDA for depression in 1958, was reported in several published cases of hepatic injury. In 1959, Zimmerman et al reported 86 patients who developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid; most had hepatocellular injury with a mortality rate of about 20%, and in most cases ALT or AST levels were above 7x ULN while ALP was not higher than 2x ULN in nearly 60%. Iproniazid was withdrawn from the market in 1961 due to hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the US market in 1961 due to hepatotoxicity; initial indication tuberculosis and subsequently depression; 86 jaundiced patients reported by Zimmerman et al in 1959; most cases had ALT/AST >7x ULN and ALP not higher than 2x ULN in ~60%; mortality rate ~20%.

raw_record.support_text: Iproniazid was incriminated as the cause of a highly fatal form of liver disease. Early reports indicated hepatitis that sometimes led to death in patients receiving the drug, and accumulated studies showed the syndrome was distinct from viral hepatitis: jaundice was intense with all cases presenting serum bilirubin greater than 20 mg per 100 ml, hepatitis incidence was higher than expected for coincidental viral hepatitis, and the fatality rate was about 20% versus under 1% for viral hepatitis. It was therefore concluded that iproniazid was the probable cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Incinmated as cause of a highly fatal form of liver disease via the specific clinical syndrome criterion; intense jaundice with all cases showing serum bilirubin >20 mg/100 ml (a level seen in <3% of viral hepatitis cases), hepatitis incidence much higher than expected for coincidental viral hepatitis, and a fatality rate of about 20% compared with a viral hepatitis fatality rate of under 1%; hepatitis sometimes led to death.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with zoxazolamine for almost 7 months at dosages quite small compared to those recommended developed jaundice and progressive hepatic insufficiency with an insidious onset of digestive disturbances. A juxtapyloric ulcer with gastric hyperacidity initially appeared as a possible cause, but the progression of jaundice and hepatic insufficiency, together with failure of the Sippy regimen, left no doubt that the liver disease and not the ulcer was the major and probably the only cause of the patient's symptomatology. Dr. Hans Popper interpreted the liver biopsy as a severe acute hepatitis with characteristics of viral hepatitis but considered it a zoxazolamine-induced lesion identical with that produced by iproniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case. Drug taken for almost 7 months at dosages quite small compared to those recommended; insidious digestive disturbances then jaundice deepened, weakness, inappetence, drowsiness, liver enlarged to 3 fingerbreadths below costal arch, moderate tenderness, hepatic insufficiency. Biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with features resembling viral hepatitis (liver cell variability, acidophilic bodies, mononuclear portal inflammation with plasma cells, proliferated ductules); described as more severe histologically than expected from clinical picture. Patient improved over ~2 months in hospital on hepatitis diet and bed rest, with complete recovery after an additional 6 weeks. A juxtapyloric (duodenal) ulcer with gastric hyperacidity was initially suspected but excluded as the main cause.

raw_record.support_text: Zoxazolamine was administered to 20 patients for its uricosuric action. Side effects were observed in two patients; one with probenecid skin sensitivity was also sensitive to zoxazolamine, and in another patient receiving the drug for control of hyperuricemia and recurring uric acid renal stones a rapidly fatal hepatitis developed after eight months of treatment with 250 mg daily. The authors note that three other cases of fatal hepatic necrosis after zoxazolamine and 32 instances of nonfatal hepatitis have been reported, attributing these liver injuries to zoxazolamine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Primary case: patient receiving zoxazolamine (250 mg daily, 8 months) for hyperuricemia and recurring uric acid renal stones developed rapidly fatal hepatitis. Additionally, three other fatal hepatic necrosis cases and 32 nonfatal hepatitis instances reported after zoxazolamine. Drug (brand name Flexin) used as uricosuric in daily dosages up to 1000 mg (250-1000 mg maintenance) for gout and recurring renal stones. Other side effect noted: skin sensitivity to zoxazolamine in a patient also skin-sensitive to probenecid.

raw_record.support_text: Zoxazolamine is listed among the drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) drug-induced hepatic injury (61 cases), a lesion resembling viral hepatitis with spotty, zonal, and massive/submassive necrosis patterns.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs involved in the viral-hepatitis-type (Group IV) hepatic injury (61 cases).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of hepatitis attributable to trifluoperazine, a recently introduced phenothiazine derivative. In a patient receiving the drug, clinical, laboratory, and biopsy findings of cholestatic hepatitis developed, identical to that seen with other phenothiazine compounds. The case details (48-year-old man, 1 mg twice daily) describe light stools, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, and icterus.
raw_record.extra_details: Trifluoperazine given as Stelazine (Smith Kline and French Laboratories), 1 mg twice daily for 3 weeks before admission; cholestatic hepatitis with icterus, light stools, dark urine, and dull aching right-upper-quadrant pain. Reported as the first published case of hepatitis attributable to this drug; injury identical to that seen with other phenothiazine compounds. No prior medications had been taken for 9 months (competing causes excluded).

raw_record.support_text: This case report attributes the initial hepatic injury to trifluperazine use. On the Naranjo ADR probability scale the likelihood of an ADR due to trifluperazine in this case was probable (score 6), based on elevation of liver enzymes after initiation of trifluoperazine, deterioration of liver function under continued treatment, and a considerable decrease in enzymes after stopping the drug. Other causes of cholestatic jaundice were ruled out, and the authors recognized trifluperazine as a cause; they note only a few cases of cholestatic jaundice induced by trifluperazine have been reported since its introduction in 1958.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo ADR probability scale score 6 (probable). Liver enzymes rose after therapy initiation, deteriorated on continued treatment, and decreased substantially after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Other causes of cholestatic jaundice ruled out. A prior 1968 case (Margulies et al.) reported jaundice in a 26-year-old woman with psychosis after 15 days of trifluoperazine. The drug has been marketed since 1958 with only a few reported DILI cases; small numbers of spontaneous reports are not necessarily a reliable risk indicator.

raw_record.support_text: Ten of 80 patients receiving propionyl erythromycin ester lauryl sulfate developed evidence of hepatic injury, and 2 of these developed jaundice. Clinical features in 4 of 10 patients developing hepatic abnormality while receiving erythromycin were similar to those of viral hepatitis; 2 were initially diagnosed as viral hepatitis until the physicians accepted drug induction. A rise of SGPT to a high level of 2,060 in one patient after challenge led the authors to conclude the hepatic abnormality is hepatocellular rather than cholestatic. One liver biopsy showed periportal infiltration with lymphocytes, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and many eosinophils with no bile stasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Administered as propionyl erythromycin ester lauryl sulfate (erythromycin estolate). Hepatic injury in 10/80 patients, 2 with jaundice; 4 of 10 resembled viral hepatitis; 1 presented like acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis. SGPT rose to 2,060 after challenge, supporting hepatocellular rather than cholestatic injury. One liver biopsy showed periportal lymphocytic infiltrate with polymorphonuclear leukocytes and many eosinophils, no bile stasis, in a non-jaundiced patient.

raw_record.support_text: Among 32 patients with hepatotoxicity caused by erythromycin within the cohort fulfilling Hy's rule (hepatocellular injury with jaundice), all survived the liver injury. The good prognosis in erythromycin liver injury is probably due to milder injury because these patients had significantly lower bilirubin and aminotransferase levels and were also significantly younger than the non-erythromycin cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 32 patients with erythromycin hepatotoxicity within the hepatocellular-type DILI with jaundice (Hy's rule) cohort; all survived the liver injury. These cases had significantly lower bilirubin and aminotransferase levels and were significantly younger than non-erythromycin cases (reference 14).

raw_record.support_text: Erythromycin-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 35 individual case reports; median age 45 y; 23 female/12 male; median treatment duration 1 week; HC 31%, Cs/mixed 69%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 34% (29/35 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 21% (14/35 reported); hepatic necrosis 20%; inflammatory reaction 67%; death or liver transplant 3%; liver biopsy reported in 15/35 cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes erythromycin-induced liver injury in humans, noting that thirteen liver biopsy reports are recorded in the literature and findings are comparable to those in the authors' nine patients: mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury with minimal to moderate portal and periportal inflammation including eosinophils. These pathological findings help differentiate erythromycin-induced liver injury from extrahepatic biliary tree obstruction.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis-like injury that can mimic extrahepatic biliary tree obstruction, viral hepatitis, and other conditions; distinguished histologically by absence of interlobular bile duct cholestasis, bile lakes, acute cholangitis, and periductal fibrosis, minimal cholangiolar proliferation, increased hepatocyte mitotic activity, and acidophilic/ballooning degeneration with focal necrosis. Phenotype includes marked mostly centrilobular cholestasis, mixed portal infiltrates with eosinophils, and eosinophils within sinusoids. Nine patients in the present series plus reported cases (31 recorded); 13 liver biopsy reports in the literature. Four reported patients underwent laparotomy with no extrahepatic biliary disease found. Prognosis always good with recovery within a few weeks after drug withdrawal; one reported case of jaundice lasting 10 weeks that led to laparotomy. One patient with prior gallstones had normal endoscopic retrograde cannulation of pancreatic and biliary ducts.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude erythromycin sensitivity is the likely cause of acute liver failure in this patient. They note that cholestatic jaundice due to erythromycin estolate is well known and that the patient had simple erythromycin BP, suggesting the erythromycin molecule itself, as well as the ester, is hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-case report of acute liver failure with an unusually selective factor X deficiency (1% of normal), a less marked factor VII deficiency (24%), and a prolonged prothrombin time that increased despite 11 units of fresh frozen plasma and 8 units of factor IX concentrate (also containing factors II and X). The patient improved and at 1-month follow-up factor X activity was 136%, prothrombin time 31 s, AST 48 iu/litre, alkaline phosphatase 399 iu/litre. Liver biopsy was declined. Erythromycin sensitivity proposed as likely cause; the paper argues the erythromycin molecule itself, in addition to its esters, is hepatotoxic.

raw_record.support_text: In the two episodes of hepatitis, clinical and biochemical features were suggestive of drug-induced toxicity, with no evidence of biliary obstruction, recent viral hepatitis, or concomitant drug intake. Erythromycin hepatotoxicity was confirmed by a positive rechallenge after the patient took two tablets of erythromycin ethylsuccinate and developed recurrent acute epigastric pain with ALT 324 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 112 IU/l, and bilirubin 0.04 µmol/l.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity confirmed by a positive rechallenge; two episodes at therapeutic dosing; acute epigastric pain; ALT 324 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 112 IU/l, bilirubin 0.04 µmol/l; no hypereosinophilia; liver function normalized after 2 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Dacarbazine has been associated with allergy-induced hepatic toxicity which has been fatal. Autopsy findings in reported cases revealed massive hepatic necrosis, thrombus in small hepatic veins, and frequently vasculitis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration. This allergic-induced Budd-Chiari syndrome usually occurred during the second cycle of dacarbazine and was associated with peripheral eosinophilia. The toxicity, although rare, indicates the drug should only be used where it has shown activity, such as in palliating metastatic melanoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Allergy-induced hepatotoxicity; autopsy findings of massive hepatic necrosis, thrombus in small hepatic veins, and vasculitis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration; allergic-induced Budd-Chiari syndrome usually occurring during the second cycle of dacarbazine; associated with peripheral eosinophilia; described as rare; used in palliating metastatic melanoma.

raw_record.support_text: Déticène (dacarbazine, DTIC), an alkylating agent used for over 15 years in palliative treatment of malignant melanoma, is generally considered low toxicity with minor side effects (nausea, vomiting, moderate marrow suppression, influenza-like syndrome). Since 1979, a rare but often fatal complication has been recognized: acute hepatic failure from extensive hepatic necrosis caused by acute occlusion of the hepatic veins, either at the suprahepatic level (Budd-Chiari syndrome) or at the intrahepatic level, classified as hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO). The mechanism of these events remains debated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 53-year-old woman on sequential dacarbazine monotherapy for malignant melanoma of the right leg (tumor resected 4 months earlier; untreated moderate arterial hypertension in history) developed acute hypovolaemic shock a few hours after the second chemotherapy infusion, with absent peripheral pulses, right hypochondrial pain/guarding, and slight flank dullness. Right-heart catheterization hemodynamic studies confirmed hypovolaemic shock. Diagnosis of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO) was established; after massive fluid resuscitation (4 L macromolecules over 2 hours) plus dopamine (10 µg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) and corticosteroid therapy, outcome was favorable. Liver injury was acute hepatic failure by extensive necrosis from acute hepatic vein occlusion (Budd-Chiari or MVO). Second course began 48 h prior. Paper notes such veno-occlusive complications are rare but often fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of fatal hepatic toxicity due to dacarbazine (DTIC), a drug used for 20 years in melanoma treatment, noting only few published cases of this complication. In the presented 50-year-old woman on her second course of DTIC (250 mg/m² daily for 5 days), acute vascular hepatic toxicity from DTIC was suspected; post-mortem histology confirmed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis and dilated hepatic veins, and the patient died 5 days later.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman with malignant melanoma; second course of dacarbazine (DTIC) 250 mg/m² daily for 5 days; pre-course basal labs were normal except eosinophilia (1.4x10⁹/L). On day 2 of second course developed abdominal pain, nausea, fever, then shock and respiratory failure/anuria. Peak labs: ALT 2348 IU/l, AST 5160 IU/l, LDH 20430 IU/l, INR 3.95, serum protein 2.8 g/100 ml. Treated with high-dose dexamethasone (250 mg/6 hourly) and recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (100 mg) without benefit. Patient died 5 days later; post-mortem showed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis, poor inflammatory infiltration, and dilated hepatic veins without thrombi or vessel-wall inflammatory infiltrate. Complications previously reported as Budd-Chiari syndrome, veno-occlusive disease, or small hepatic vessel thrombosis; allergic pathogenesis discussed given occurrence during second course and eosinophilia. Doppler sonography confirmed patent main hepatic and portal veins. Indication: melanoma treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In the chronic actinic dermatitis cohort, one patient treated with azathioprine (1.0–2.5 mg/kg/day) developed reversible azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity that necessitated cessation of the drug; the patient subsequently responded well to cyclosporin. The paper explicitly attributes the hepatotoxicity to azathioprine in a human patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient in a retrospective study of 44 chronic actinic dermatitis patients; the azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity was reversible, required drug cessation, and the patient subsequently responded well to cyclosporin. Azathioprine was dosed at 1.0–2.5 mg/kg/day and was used in 12 patients overall with partial to good clinical response.

raw_record.support_text: A male patient receiving azathioprine for discoid lupus erythematosus developed severe cholestatic hepatitis 14-21 days after starting treatment, with a peak bilirubin of 62.4 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatic dysfunction were clinically and serologically excluded, and liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatocellular damage. Liver function began to improve 14 days after azathioprine was stopped, although alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase remained elevated after 4 months. The authors conclude the case argues for an idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatocellular damage caused by azathioprine.
raw_record.extra_details: 67-year-old male treated for discoid lupus erythematosus; latency 14-21 days after initiation; peak bilirubin 62.4 mg/dL; liver biopsy revealed cholestatic hepatocellular damage; onset of improvement in transaminases and bilirubin 14 days after discontinuation, with alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase still elevated after 4 months; viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatic dysfunction excluded; patient also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, gastroesophageal reflux, hip arthrosis, smoking (~20 cigarettes/day) and moderate alcohol intake. The named hepatic phenotype is cholestatic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a myasthenia gravis patient, azathioprine was reported to cause hepatotoxicity with jaundice, after a thymectomy and failed treatment with pyridostigmine and prednisone had not controlled his condition.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity presented with jaundice in a single myasthenia gravis patient receiving azathioprine as an immunosuppressant; no dose, duration, or latency specified.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a retrospective cohort of IBD patients with azathioprine (AZA)-induced liver injury in whom mercaptopurine (MP) was subsequently used. 87% of patients eventually tolerated MP, most at full doses, without further toxicity after a mean follow-up of close to 3 years. This passage frames AZA as the cause of the initial liver injury that defined the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Thiopurine therapy for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); retrospective cohort defining AZA-induced liver injury; liver injury is described as a dose-independent idiosyncratic phenomenon, more frequent in the first months of exposure (initial AZA toxicity after a median of 2 months); basis for subsequently evaluating MP tolerance.

raw_record.support_text: In Table 5, listing the main adverse effects of azathioprine (AZA) in 35 ulcerative colitis patients, hepatotoxicity was reported in 8 patients (23%). All 5 patients with AZA hepatotoxicity who were shifted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) were 6-MP-tolerant, indicating the hepatotoxicity was attributed to AZA rather than 6-MP. A separate patient case noted that AZA was discontinued due to hepatotoxicity after which the patient tolerated 6-MP.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a main adverse effect of AZA in 8 of 35 (23%) ulcerative colitis patients (Table 5). Five of the 8 were shifted to 6-MP and all tolerated it (5 6-MP-tolerant). In one illustrative case, a patient discontinued AZA due to hepatotoxicity and was successfully treated with 6-MP with improved endoscopic findings. No biochemical pattern, histology, or severity grade beyond hepatotoxicity requiring drug discontinuation is reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective multicenter study of 220 Slovak IBD patients treated with azathioprine, adverse drug reactions to AZA therapy were observed, including hepatotoxicity in 10.9% of patients. The hepatotoxicity was attributed to AZA therapy, with the high frequency partly explained by meticulous monitoring including regular hepatic enzyme biochemistry.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective multicenter study of 220 Slovak IBD patients treated with azathioprine; hepatotoxicity occurred in 10.9% of patients (myelotoxicity 14.5%, dyspepsia 3.2%, pancreatitis 2.7%, allergic reactions 0.9%). High frequency partly due to meticulous monitoring including regular hepatic and pancreatic enzyme biochemistry; analysis of TPMT genotype effects on ADRs. Concomitant mesalazine (5-ASA) use did not affect occurrence of ADRs (73.9% of ADR patients vs 66.3% of AZA patients without ADRs, p=n.s.).

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine, an immunosuppressant used for myasthenia gravis, can cause hepatotoxicity. The paper presents a 47-year-old man on azathioprine for 1 year who developed painless jaundice; azathioprine was discontinued due to potential acute liver failure secondary to azathioprine toxicity, and a liver biopsy showing drug-induced liver injury with high serum 6-methylmercaptopurine nucleotide confirmed azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 47-year-old man with myasthenia gravis, azathioprine 200 mg orally daily for about 1 year. On presentation: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools; AST 165 U/L, ALT 102 U/L, total bilirubin 16.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL; negative viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E), autoimmune (ANA, ASMA, AMA), CMV, EBV assays, normal iron panel, no peripheral eosinophilia. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis, pericholangitis, mild bile duct injury, and lobular apoptotic hepatocytes consistent with toxic/drug-induced injury. Diagnosis confirmed by high serum 6-methylmercaptopurine nucleotide levels. Transaminases and bilirubin improved steadily over 4-day hospital course after discontinuation; no transplant or death reported.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine is among the top ten drugs in the Icelandic prospective DILI registry and among the drugs most strongly associated with DILI in GPRD, with a crude incidence of 1 per 1,103 users and the highest Icelandic incidence of 1 of 133 users among potentially hepatotoxic drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Immunosuppressive agent; top-ten drug in Icelandic registry; strongly associated with DILI in GPRD (crude incidence 1 per 1,103 users); highest Icelandic incidence of 1 of 133 users; listed in Table 1 with >100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: Over the initial ten-year period of the prospective DILIN cohort study, 1434 cases of drug-induced liver injury were enrolled and underwent causality assessment, of which 27 were attributed, at least in part, to a thiopurine, including 15 to azathioprine (Aza), 12 to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and none to 6-thioguanine (6-TG). After excluding 5 cases in which liver injury was considered only possibly related to the thiopurine, 22 cases (12 attributed to Aza and 10 to 6-MP) fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria and were analyzed.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 of 22 included DILIN cases were attributed to azathioprine (10-year prospective DILIN cohort, total 1434 DILI cases). Combined Aza/6-MP expert DILIN causality was definite in 2 (9%), very likely in 12 (54%), and probable in 8 (36%); RUCAM median 6.5 with 4 highly probable, 14 probable, and 4 possible. Most patients were adults with autoimmune conditions; most common indication was inflammatory bowel disease (55%). Presenting features included symptoms attributable to liver injury in all but one patient (jaundice 73%, nausea 64%, fatigue and abdominal pain 50%); viral serologies for HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV were negative except one patient with stable pre-existing chronic hepatitis C; imaging showed no biliary obstruction. Ten patients (46%) were receiving corticosteroids when liver injury developed.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine was attributed to 11 DILI cases with a predominantly cholestatic pattern (64%). No cases met nR-based Hy's law criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 9.1%/Chol 64%/Mix 27%; female 54%, lymphopenia 20%, eosinophilia 36%; 0 fulfilled nR-based Hy's law.

raw_record.support_text: Among seven patients with recalcitrant vasculitis or steroid-induced side effects treated with azathioprine 150 mg/day, all had a good clinical response within four to eight weeks, but azathioprine-induced hepatitis developed in one of these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 150 mg/day; injury described as azathioprine-induced hepatitis in one of seven treated patients, used for recalcitrant disease or steroid-induced side effects.

raw_record.support_text: According to the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences scale, the case scored six points ('probable') for Enalapril-induced liver injury. The adverse effect occurred 2 years after starting Enalapril; a first episode of drug-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis was followed by severe prolonged cholestasis several days later. The authors regard hepatotoxicity of Enalapril as not dose-dependent and based on idiopathic late hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case (CIOMS score 6, 'probable'). Latent period 2 years after starting Enalapril. Presented as drug-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis followed by severe prolonged cholestasis several days later. Reported as the first case of hepatotoxicity with ductopenia by Enalapril. Histology showed hepatocanalicular perivenular cholestasis, mild portal inflammation, and bile duct loss. Patient was placed on the waiting list for liver transplantation but was removed 40 days after discontinuation due to optimal resolution; jaundice disappeared within 2 months and liver function tests normalized in 6 months. Asymptomatic and biochemically normal at 2.5 years follow-up. Mechanism proposed as non-dose-dependent idiopathic late hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: Among the 9 patients with drug-induced liver injury in the AIH criteria validation cohort, one case was related to the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor enalapril.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient with drug-induced liver injury attributed to enalapril in a validation cohort of 549 patients used to compare the 1999 and simplified IAIHG criteria for autoimmune hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a previously healthy 41-year-old woman who developed liver cirrhosis as a sequela of acute hepatic injury induced by ketoconazole administration (200 mg/day for 5 months) to treat onychomycosis. The initial presentation was a typical acute hepatitis with nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and jaundice that developed during ketoconazole administration; other causes of hepatitis were excluded. The authors conclude that ketoconazole can cause liver cirrhosis through acute hepatic injury under certain circumstances.
raw_record.extra_details: 41-year-old woman treated with ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 5 months for onychomycosis; acute hepatitis developed (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice) with onset about 2 weeks before admission; AST 1461 IU/L, ALT 1318 IU/L, total bilirubin 211 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 268 IU/L, INR 1.21 at presentation; viral, autoimmune, metabolic (Wilson, alpha-1-antitrypsin, iron) causes excluded; hepatitis resolved gradually over months but liver function did not fully recover; ascites at week 17; follow-up CT and liver biopsy at 6 months showed markedly reduced liver volume, splenomegaly, and definite cirrhotic change persisting for more than 5 years.

raw_record.support_text: Three female patients were hospitalized for acute hepatitis related to repeated therapeutic use of ketoconazole prescribed for leucorrhea. The first patient had received 10 courses over 7 years and developed jaundice and anaphylactic shock within 24 hours of a 200 mg ketoconazole tablet; the second and third developed acute hepatitis within 1-3 days of ketoconazole rechallenge. The first two had prolonged prothrombin time (INR >1.2), and injury responded to corticosteroids. The authors describe this as consistent with the previously described idiosyncratic liver reaction to ketoconazole (dose-independent, hepatocellular damage with ballooning degeneration) yet with features more suggestive of an immunoallergic response.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity reported to appear within 1.5 to 24 weeks after drug administration; postulated mechanisms include glutathione chelation with active metabolites and formation of drug-protein adducts. Injury required repeated ketoconazole treatments and appeared within 1-3 days of rechallenge. First patient had jaundice and anaphylactic shock within 24 h of one 200 mg tablet after 10 courses over 7 years; first two patients had prolonged prothrombin time (INR >1.2) and 2-3-fold eosinophilia; ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes in the first patient; response to corticosteroids; absence of antinuclear antibodies did not support autoimmune hepatitis. Controlled cohort study (Chien et al) reported ~20% of patients had asymptomatic liver enzyme increases and 5% developed overt hepatitis, with biochemical alterations returning to normal after discontinuation; authors recommended continuing therapy with caution in the absence of symptoms/hyperbilirubinemia but discontinuing if overt hepatitis occurs.

raw_record.support_text: Symptomatic hepatitis from ketoconazole use was documented as early as 1981. In several cases a cause-effect relationship with ketoconazole was established by rechallenge. The reaction is described as idiosyncratic rather than immunoallergic or toxic and is unrelated to daily dosage, cumulative total dose, or duration of therapy. Jaundice occurred in 63% to 100% of cases. The most serious side effect of ketoconazole is hepatitis, which has proved fatal in seven reported cases; the present report describes a 45-year-old Japanese-American woman who developed fulminant hepatic failure leading to liver transplantation after 58 days of ketoconazole 200 mg daily for candidal onychomycosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis that has proved fatal in seven reported cases (literature review); present index case of fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplant in a 45-year-old woman treated with ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 58 days for candidal onychomycosis. Cause-effect established by rechallenge in several cases. Reaction is idiosyncratic, unrelated to daily dose, cumulative dose, or therapy duration. Incidence estimated by manufacturer as 1 in 10,000 and later 1 in 15,000 exposures, with a Dutch review suggesting closer to 1 in 2000. Onset from 2 to 365 days, mean ~2 months; jaundice in 63% to 100% of cases; anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise common. Index case laboratory peak values: SGOT 2561 U/L, SGPT 3811 U/L, LDH 709 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 157 U/L, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dl. Hepatitis A/B serology and ANA negative; concurrent levothyroxine (Synthroid) not attributed as cause.

raw_record.support_text: The first case of hepatitis with ketoconazole was reported in September 1981, involving a patient in her sixties with onychomycosis who developed clinical hepatitis during therapy; after recovery she was rechallenged and liver enzymes immediately increased again, clearly pointing towards a ketoconazole-induced reaction. In February 1982 a 67-year-old woman with onychomycosis died in hepatic coma after continuing ketoconazole for more than a month after becoming jaundiced. The overall incidence of clinical hepatitis for all indications combined was about 1:10000, with most patients treated for onychomycosis (~70%), female (~67%), and over 40 years old (~75%).
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case September 1981: patient in her sixties with onychomycosis, clinical hepatitis, positive rechallenge with immediate rise in liver enzymes. Fatal case February 1982: 67-year-old woman with onychomycosis (toe nails) died in hepatic coma after continuing ketoconazole >1 month after becoming jaundiced without telling her usual doctor. Overall incidence of clinical hepatitis for all indications combined about 1:10000; majority onychomycosis (~70%), female (~67%), over 40 years (~75%); most had received griseofulvin prior to ketoconazole.

raw_record.support_text: Ketoconazole is reported to have the highest incidence of hepatotoxicity among the azoles, usually presenting initially as an asymptomatic increase in liver enzymes, with an estimated incidence of one in 1000 to 3000 patients. In a cohort study by Garcia Rodriguez et al. among 69,830 patients treated with oral antifungal agents, ketoconazole carried the highest relative risk of acute liver injury (RR 228.0; 95% CI 33.9-933.0) relative to nonusers, followed by itraconazole (RR 17.7; 95% CI 2.6-72.6).
raw_record.extra_details: Estimated incidence of hepatotoxicity 1 in 1000-3000 patients, usually starting as asymptomatic liver enzyme increase. Cohort (Garcia Rodriguez et al., 69,830 oral antifungal patients): RR 228.0 (95% CI 33.9-933.0) for acute liver injury vs nonusers. Chien et al. (137 onychomycosis patients): 17.5% asymptomatic transaminase elevation; 4 patients (2.9%) developed hepatotoxicity that resolved after treatment discontinuation; asymptomatic biochemical changes returned to normal despite continuing ketoconazole. Biochemical pattern predominantly hepatocellular, less frequently cholestatic or mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular; mechanism more consistent with metabolic (not hypersensitivity) injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the largest retrospective study to date (FReSKO), 200 patients with Cushing's disease received ketoconazole at 200-1200 mg daily. Generally reversible upon drug withdrawal, up to 5-fold increases in liver enzymes were found in 13.5% of patients while severe hepatotoxicity (>5-fold elevation) was observed in 2.5%. The authors recommend close liver function monitoring and advise dose reduction or discontinuation when liver enzymes are 3-fold elevated. The drug treatment table also lists hepatitis among ketoconazole's possible adverse events.
raw_record.extra_details: Adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitor used for Cushing's disease; FReSKO retrospective cohort of 200 patients, oral 200-1200 mg/day; up to 5-fold liver enzyme increases in 13.5% and severe hepatotoxicity (>5-fold elevation) in 2.5%, generally reversible on withdrawal; liver monitoring advised and dose reduction/discontinuation when enzymes 3-fold elevated; listed under 'Hepatitis' in adverse-event treatment table.

raw_record.support_text: In 50 patients receiving ketoconazole for onychomycosis or dermatomycosis, a causal relationship to hepatic injury was considered likely, adjudicated as 'definite' in 1, 'probable' in 26 and 'possible' in 23 cases. The biochemical pattern was hepatocellular in 67% of 'probable' (n=18) and 39% of 'possible' cases; most 'possible' cases had mild-to-moderate liver enzyme elevations (48%). The daily dose was 200 mg in 90% of cases; the mean latent period from first intake to onset was 68 days (probable) and 52 days (possible). In almost all 'probable' cases ALAT exceeded ASAT; jaundice was reported in 63% of 27 probable cases. None of the 50 cases had a fatal course, and in 13 probable cases other drugs were continued or reinstituted without aggravation or relapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality adjudication across 50 'likely' cases: 1 definite, 26 probable, 23 possible. Indications were onychomycosis (54%) and dermatomycosis (30%); daily dose 200 mg (90% of cases); mean latent period 68 days (probable) and 52 days (possible), onset within 6 weeks in 44% and 79% respectively. Female predominance (81.5% probable, 87% possible); mean age 48.4 and 53 years. Biochemical pattern in this study: hepatocellular 54%, cholestatic 16%, LEE/mixed 30% (Table 2); hepatocellular in 67% of probable and 39% of possible cases. Symptoms in 27 probable cases: jaundice 63%, malaise 59%, nausea/vomiting 41%, hepatomegaly 33%, fever 11%, eosinophilia 9%, rash 4%; ALAT>ASAT in 89%. Eosinophilia (>=7%) in 2/22 probable cases. Histology (n=14 this study): mostly necrosis 57%, cholestasis 43% (centrilobular cholestasis, cholangiolitis, cholangitis, bridging necrosis, beginning fibrosis). In 13 probable cases co-medications were continued/reinstituted without relapse; griseofulvin ingestion was explicitly excluded in cases with early (≤6 weeks) onset; only 2/50 had prior idiosyncratic reaction to another drug. No death in the 50-case group; literature subgroups in the comparison table reported fatal courses (19% and 3%).

raw_record.support_text: In response to Sobel's report on a possible new use for oral ketoconazole, the authors address which patients are subject to ketoconazole hepatotoxicity. They note that Lewis et al. reported 33 cases of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity, including 13 patients under 50 (40%) with a 5-year-old and a 17-year-old boy, and 11 male patients (33%). They also state that three of the four fatal cases of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity reported in the literature occurred in women over 50, and that there is no solid evidence that acute-phase morbidity among survivors is more severe in women or in patients over the age of 50.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter to the editor responding to Sobel's proposed therapeutic use of oral ketoconazole; disputes that hepatotoxicity predominantly affects women over 50. Cites Lewis et al. series of 33 ketoconazole hepatotoxicity cases: 13 patients under 50 (40%), including a 5-year-old and a 17-year-old boy; 11 male patients (33%). Four fatal ketoconazole hepatotoxicity cases reported in the literature (references 2-4), three in women over 50 and one of unreported age; no solid evidence that survivors' acute-phase morbidity is more severe in women or in patients over 50.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two patients who developed fulminant hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis, which they state 'can be reasonably ascribed to ketoconazole.' Patient 1 received only ketoconazole; patient 2 received other drugs (cytarabine, zorubicin, colistin, amikacin, amphotericin B) none of which was judged likely responsible, as cytarabine and zorubicin were stopped 26 days before jaundice and amikacin/amphotericin B are not considered hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with fulminant hepatitis; marked increase in serum ALT, hepatic encephalopathy developing 19 days (patient 1) and 1 day (patient 2) after jaundice onset, low prothrombin, massive predominantly centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Viral hepatitis (except non-A, non-B) excluded. Patient 1 received only ketoconazole; patient 2's co-medications (cytarabine, zorubicin, colistin, amikacin, amphotericin B) considered unlikely responsible. Mechanism considered direct or reactive-metabolite-mediated rather than immunoallergic, consistent with relatively high prevalence of asymptomatic serum ALT increase. Liver function continued deteriorating despite cessation; patient 2 died of fulminant hepatitis less than a month after starting the drug. Authors recommend bimonthly/weekly serum ALT monitoring and immediate interruption on ALT increase. Increased wedged-to-free hepatic venous pressure gradient (portal hypertension) and ascites also observed.

raw_record.support_text: Ketoconazole has caused elevation of liver enzymes and hepatitis. Hepatotoxicity is estimated to occur in 0.1-1.0% of patients receiving ketoconazole, with no correlation with dose observed. The first report (1980) concerned a biopsy-proved mild acute hepatitis in a 17-year-old patient that developed after 6 months of therapy but was mild and reversible, and Petersen's group described four further cases of elevated transaminases.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity estimated to occur in 0.1-1.0% of patients; no correlation with dose observed. First literature report in 1980 was a biopsy-proved mild acute hepatitis in a 17-year-old with no previous history of drug abuse or hepatitis, developing after 6 months of therapy but mild and reversible. Petersen's group described four cases of elevated transaminases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the reappearance of liver impairment shortly after ketoconazole treatment was restarted strongly supports the evidence for ketoconazole-induced liver damage. Because no liver toxicity was found in animal experiments, they classify the hepatotoxicity as a type II (idiosyncratic) reaction per the National Institutes of Health classification: unpredictable from animal experiments, rare in humans, and dose-independent.
raw_record.extra_details: A 68-year-old woman treated for recalcitrant Trichophyton rubrum dermatophytosis; started on 200 mg ketoconazole daily for 12 weeks then increased to 400 mg daily. Two weeks later she developed pruritus, rhinorrhoea, tiredness, dizziness, dark urine, and pale faeces. LFTs (serum alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) were compatible with parenchymal liver damage. First biopsy showed enlarged portal tracts with slight bile duct proliferation, moderate mononuclear infiltration, focal parenchymal necroses, and condensed reticulin with ceroid in Kupffer's cells. Symptoms and LFTs normalized on withdrawal. On rechallenge 17 weeks later at 200 mg daily, symptoms and abnormal LFTs reappeared within two weeks; biopsy showed less prominent parenchymal changes, rare necroses, and no Kupffer cell proliferation; again resolved on stopping. Hepatitis B surface antigen and antibodies to hepatitis B and A viruses negative; eosinophilia absent; she received no other drugs. Histology resembled methyldopa-induced hepatitis (enlarged portal tracts, mononuclear infiltration, piecemeal necrosis as in chronic active hepatitis). Classified as a dose-independent, unpredictable type II idiosyncratic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Transient elevations in liver enzymes have occurred in patients receiving ketoconazole, and a case of hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation of therapy has been reported and documented by rechallenge with ketoconazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported case required discontinuation of therapy and was confirmed by rechallenge with ketoconazole; transient liver enzyme elevations also occurred in other patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in a human patient in whom slight elevation of serum transaminases appeared 4 weeks after starting ketoconazole treatment and progressed to severe hepatitis because medication was continued. It also cites an FDA report of three cases of fatal massive hepatic necrosis attributed to ketoconazole, which prompted a warning about its rare but potentially serious hepatic danger. In an accompanying mechanistic discussion (paragraph 32), the authors classify the hepatic injury as a form of host idiosyncrasy with metabolic abnormality, inferring that a centrilobular hepatotoxic metabolite of ketoconazole is responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Single reported patient; slight transaminase elevation noted 4 weeks after starting therapy, progressing to severe hepatitis because the drug was continued. No fever, rash, itching, or increased peripheral/liver-parenchymal eosinophils; LST (delayed hypersensitivity test) negative, arguing against hypersensitivity. The authors categorize the injury as host idiosyncrasy with metabolic abnormality (Zimmerman classification) and infer that a hepatotoxic metabolite formed in the centrilobular zone is responsible. FDA reportedly described three cases of fatal massive hepatic necrosis and warned of the drug's rare but potentially serious danger; this is described as the first report of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that ketoconazole has been associated with liver toxicity (citations 9, 10), but in the 13 patients treated with high doses of ketoconazole for advanced prostatic cancer the authors noted no evidence of hepatotoxicity: no patient had clinical hepatitis and there were no changes in serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase, serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase, lactic dehydrogenase, or total bilirubin throughout the course of treatment (table 3).
raw_record.extra_details: In 13 patients treated with high doses of ketoconazole (400 mg every 8 hours) for advanced prostatic cancer, the authors explicitly noted no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no clinical hepatitis; liver function tests (SGOT/SGPT, LDH, total bilirubin) were unchanged over 12 weeks of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A second case of toxic hepatitis with ketoconazole is reported: a 48-year-old physician treated for fingernail onychomycosis with ketoconazole 200 mg/day orally developed fatigue, nausea, icterus, and marked elevation of ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase after about 81 days of therapy, with viral hepatitis A and B excluded and no history of liver disease or other medications. A single extra 200 mg ketoconazole dose 48 hours before day 86 testing further accelerated the rise; findings returned to normal within 2 months of drug cessation. The letter also cites a prior biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case with ketoconazole and the manufacturer's advisory reporting the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: fingernail onychomycosis (open multicenter study), unresponsive previously to griseofulvin. Dose: single oral 200 mg daily. Hepatitis onset after ~81 days of therapy; fatigue and nausea at ~day 78 leading to cessation. Laboratory: AST 1030 U/L on day 84 rising to 1900 U/L on day 86 (normal 10-40); total bilirubin 107-111 µmol/L (normal 2-17); alkaline phosphatase 450-480 U/L (normal 50-275); LDH 600-800 U/L (normal 150-450); icterus and marked malaise. Viral hepatitis A and B excluded; liver/pancreas ultrasound and CT normal; patient refused biopsy. Rechallenge-like acceleration after a single 200 mg dose 48h before day 86. Recovery to normal within 2 months after stopping. Prior communication reported a biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case with ketoconazole; manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Estimated ~300,000 prescriptions since licensing in the US in 1981.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician treated with ketoconazole (single oral daily dose of 200 mg) for fingernail onychomycosis, with no history of liver disease and no other medications, developed sudden fatigue and nausea after 81 days of therapy, followed by markedly elevated ALT that accelerated after a single 200 mg ketoconazole dose on day 86, accompanied by icterus and markedly elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded, and abnormal findings subsided to normal within 2 months. The accompanying discussion notes that hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole therapy has been reported in only a few cases and is probably an idiosyncratic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Single oral daily dose of 200 mg for 81 days for fingernail onychomycosis (following griseofulvin unresponsiveness). ALT rose to 1030-1900 U/L (baseline 13), total bilirubin up to 111 umol/L, alkaline phosphatase up to 480 U/L, lactic dehydrogenase up to 800 U/L; icterus and malaise at day 86. Viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology; ultrasound and CT of liver/pancreas showed no abnormalities; liver biopsy refused; laboratory values returned to normal within 2 months. Re-exposure with a single 200 mg dose accelerated the rise (associated with day 86 tests). A prior communication from the same institution described biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient, and a manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Incidence estimated between 0.1% and 1%, with many subclinical cases; about 300,000 prescriptions in the US since 1981 licensure. Author recommendation to do liver function tests before and monthly during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician treated with a single oral daily dose of 200 mg ketoconazole for fingernail onychomycosis developed fatigue, nausea, icterus and marked malaise after 81 days of therapy, with markedly elevated serum ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and lactic dehydrogenase. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded by serologic studies; the patient refused a liver biopsy. Abnormal laboratory findings subsided to normal within 2 months after cessation of ketoconazole, and a single rechallenge dose (200 mg) 48 hours before day-86 testing further accelerated the enzyme rise.
raw_record.extra_details: Case follows a previously reported biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in another ketoconazole-treated patient, so the paper aggregates at least two cases. Ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 81 days for onychomycosis; no other medications, no history of liver disease, no excessive ethanol. Peak labs: aspartate transaminase 1900 U/L (day 86), total bilirubin 107 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L, lactic dehydrogenase 600-800 U/L. Icterus, malaise, nausea, fatigue; viral hepatitis A/B excluded; liver/pancreas ultrasound and CT normal; biopsy refused; full recovery within 2 months. The paper states ketoconazole hepatic damage is probably an idiosyncratic reaction with an estimated incidence of 0.1%-1%, many cases subclinical. A manufacturer (Janssen Pharmaceutica) advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician without prior liver disease or other medications was treated with ketoconazole (a single oral daily dose of 200 mg) for fingernail onychomycosis. After 8 weeks a slight ALT increase appeared; one month later fatigue and nausea led to stopping therapy after 81 days, with markedly elevated ALT, icterus, and marked malaise. A single 200 mg ketoconazole dose further accelerated the ALT rise; serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase were markedly elevated. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded and the abnormal findings resolved within 2 months. The accompanying text notes that hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole therapy is probably an idiosyncratic reaction, estimated at 0.1%-1% incidence, and that a prior patient in the institution had biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Second case in the institution; a prior communication described a biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis patient on ketoconazole. Ketoconazole 200 mg daily for 81 days. Peak values: ALT ~1900 U/L, aspartate transaminase 1900 U/L, total bilirubin 111 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase ~480 U/L, lactic dehydrogenase 800 U/L. Presented with fatigue, nausea, icterus, malaise; viral hepatitis A/B excluded; rechallenge with a single 200 mg dose (day 86) accelerated the ALT rise; recovery within 2 months. The paper describes hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole as probably an idiosyncratic reaction with estimated incidence 0.1%-1%, many cases subclinical; recommends liver function tests before and monthly during therapy; notes a manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reporting death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician developed sudden fatigue and nausea during daily oral ketoconazole 200 mg for fingernail onychomycosis, with cessation of therapy after 81 days. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated ALT (aspartate transaminase up to 1900 U/L), icterus, and markedly elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase; viral hepatitis A and B were excluded and recovery occurred within 2 months. The authors note a previously reported biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient and conclude that hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole therapy is probably an idiosyncratic reaction, with estimated incidence of 0.1% to 1% and many subclinical cases. The paper also cites a manufacturer advisory reporting the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Second reported case of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in a 48-year-old physician treated for fingernail onychomycosis (a prior biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case was reported from the same institution). Dose 200 mg/day for 81 days; onset of fatigue and nausea after ~8 weeks with an ALT increase still within normal limits, then marked elevation (aspartate transaminase 1900 U/L, bilirubin 107-111 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 450-480 U/L, LDH 600-800 U/L); a single rechallenge dose (200 mg, 48 h before day 86 studies) appeared to accelerate the ALT rise. Icterus and marked malaise present; viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology; ultrasonography and CT of liver and pancreas normal; liver biopsy refused; findings returned to normal within 2 months. Estimated incidence of hepatic damage 0.1% to 1%, many cases subclinical. Manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Authors recommend liver function tests before and during ketoconazole treatment. Prior griseofulvin treatment was discontinued due to diarrhea; no other medications, no history of liver disease or excessive ethanol.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician with fingernail onychomycosis was treated with ketoconazole as a single oral dose of 200 mg daily. He had no history of liver disease, no excessive ethanol intake, and took no other medications. After 81 days of therapy he developed fatigue and nausea, with markedly elevated ALT and later the appearance of icterus and marked malaise; serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase were all markedly elevated. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded serologically, and imaging of the liver and pancreas was normal. He refused biopsy, and laboratory findings returned to normal within 2 months after the episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Second reported case from the authors' institution; the earlier communication described a case of biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient. The paper states hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole is 'probably an idiosyncratic reaction' with estimated incidence between 0.1% and 1%, many cases subclinical. In this case a single 200 mg ketoconazole dose on day 86 appeared to further accelerate the ALT rise. Case details: ALT peaked near 1900 U/L (normal 10-40), total bilirubin peaked at 111 µmol/L (normal 2-17), alkaline phosphatase peaked at 480 U/L (normal 50-275). Abnormal findings resolved within normal limits 2 months after the episode. Also notes a manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reporting death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy, with an estimated 300,000 prescriptions since 1981 licensing.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician receiving ketoconazole (single oral 200 mg daily) for fingernail onychomycosis, with no history of liver disease, no other medications, and normal baseline ALT, developed fatigue and nausea after 8 weeks, leading to cessation at day 81. Liver tests then rose markedly (ALT 1030 U/L on day 84 and 1900 U/L on day 86, with elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LDH and icterus); a single 200 mg ketoconazole dose 48 hours before the day-86 tests further accelerated the ALT rise. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded and liver/pancreas imaging was normal; liver biopsy was refused. Lab values returned to normal 2 months after the episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 of an institution's ketoconazole hepatitis series; a prior case of biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient had been reported. Dose 200 mg oral once daily for fingernail onychomycosis. Marked malaise and icterus; marked elevations of ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (450 U/L) and lactic dehydrogenase (800 U/L). A single rechallenge dose of 200 mg 48 hours before hospital day 86 further accelerated the ALT rise. Viral hepatitis A and B serologies negative; ultrasonography and CT of liver and pancreas normal; patient refused liver biopsy; complete recovery within 2 months with no change in hematologic values or sedimentation rate.

raw_record.support_text: Among 62 patients with acute liver failure (ALF), the etiology was considered viral in 26; in 5 other patients ALF was considered due to toxic hepatitis caused by the administration of ketoconazole, α-methyl dopa, halothane, pyroxicam, and disulfiram, respectively. Thus ketoconazole was attributed as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to ALF in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution made in a single ALF patient within a 62-patient acute liver failure series; drug administration identified as the cause of toxic hepatitis leading to acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A case series reported ornidazole-induced hepatic injury across three new patients: Case 1 (38/F, ornidazole 1.5 g/day for 7 days then 1 g/day for 4 days) had chronic autoimmune hepatitis and improved in 20 weeks; Case 2 (50/F, 1 g/day for 3 days) had total bilirubin 47.9 mg/dl, ALT 3042 U/l, AST 1665 U/l, with mild cholestasis, focal and bridging parenchymal necrosis and moderate portal inflammation, improving in 7 weeks; Case 3 (25/F, ornidazole 1 g/day for 3 days for vaginitis) presented with jaundice (bilirubin 10.1 mg/dl, ALT 1160, AST 790) and biopsy showing mild cholestasis with focal and confluent necroses, improving in 4 weeks. Case 2 also had a history of a previous reaction following ornidazole use, consistent with rechallenge recurrence.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were adult women; indication vaginitis in Case 3; prior ornidazole reaction (rechallenge recurrence) in Case 2; negative viral/autoimmune serology; MR cholangiography normal in Case 3; all three improved without liver failure or death. The authors describe DILI features of absence of baseline liver abnormality, temporal relationship to drug use, and improvement upon withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Ornidazole, a nitroimidazole antibiotic, is reported to cause ornidazole-induced liver injury (OILI). In a retrospective analysis of 101 OILI cases from eight tertiary centers (2006-2023), causality was assessed with RUCAM: highly probable in 42.6% (n=43), probable in 51.5% (n=52), and possible in 5.9% (n=6). The predominant pattern was acute hepatocellular injury (83.2%, n=84). The authors conclude that ornidazole can cause serious idiosyncratic liver injury, including autoimmune phenotypes, and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective multicenter study of 101 OILI patients (Turkey, Dec 2006-Nov 2023). RUCAM grading: highly probable 42.6% (n=43), probable 51.5% (n=52), possible 5.9% (n=6). Acute hepatocellular injury in 83.2% (n=84). Autoimmune-like hepatitis in 5% (n=5); ANA positivity in 16.8% (n=17). Corticosteroids used in 24.8% (n=25), associated with higher ANA positivity and 20% (n=5) relapse after discontinuation. Outcomes: recovery 87.7% (n=88), liver transplantation 7.9% (n=8), death 4% (n=4). Some OILI cases resemble autoimmune hepatitis or severe cholestatic injury leading to liver failure [10]. Indications include amoebic dysentery, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, and dental infections.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of granulomatous hepatitis probably due to the administration of aprindine. Although drug rechallenge was not done, the hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved rapidly after drug withdrawal, which the authors state is suggestive of aprindine-induced liver toxicity. The patient had received no other medication during the past year, had no history of liver disease or sarcoidosis/tuberculosis, and was negative for HBV/HCV/HAV markers.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis is the named phenotype. Drug rechallenge was not performed. Hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved after withdrawal. A liver biopsy 5 days after withdrawal showed moderate inflammatory infiltration consisting predominantly of eosinophils and granulomata in most portal tracts and lobules, without caseous necrosis or fibrosis; 6 months later granulomata had disappeared and fibrosis was present in expanded portal tracts. No competing medications, liver disease history, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, hypotension, blood transfusion, or HBV/HCV/HAV markers were present. The paper also cites at least eight previously published cases of aprindine-induced hepatitis with mild to moderate clinical illness occurring within 12 days to 6 weeks of starting therapy and resolving after drug withdrawal, with rechallenge reproducing hepatitis in all four rechallenged patients; no granulomatous hepatitis was identified in the four prior biopsied cases.

raw_record.support_text: Viral-hepatitis-like hepatic damage ('aprindin hepatitis') developed in a 50-year-old woman after taking aprindin, the cause of the jaundice being confirmed by the same signs recurring when the drug was taken again after initial withdrawal. A rechallenge confirmed the drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman; viral-hepatitis-like hepatic damage termed 'Aprindin-Hepatitis'; jaundice present; injury reproduced on re-administration after initial withdrawal (positive rechallenge). Aprindin (Amidonal) is an oral antiarrhythmic of the local-anesthetic class; no hepatotoxic side effects had been observed in prior clinical testing.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old woman with aspirin-sensitive asthma and allergic rhinitis began montelukast therapy after baseline liver function tests were normal. After 3 weeks of montelukast, she developed jaundice, severe pruritus, and nausea, with elevated total bilirubin (181.3 µmol/L), alkaline phosphatase (231 IU/L), AST (123 IU/L), ALT (174 IU/L), and γ-glutamyltransferase (224 IU/L); serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C was negative.
