Therapy was stopped and jaundice and pruritus resolved, with most liver test results normalizing over 5 months though aminotransferases remained elevated; a liver biopsy 14 months after starting montelukast showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis. The authors report this as the first case of montelukast-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~3 weeks after starting montelukast 10-mg/day (standard therapeutic use); jaundice, severe pruritus, nausea; bilirubin/elevated enzymes normalized over 5 months after dechallenge but aminotransferase levels remained ~2x ULN; eosinophil count 8%; liver biopsy 14 months after start showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis; patient concurrently used inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting inhaled beta-2 agonist, allergy immunotherapy, and occasional oral corticosteroids, with theophylline stopped at montelukast initiation. Clinical trials of montelukast showed no significant difference in liver function abnormalities vs placebo (2.1% of 1955 montelukast vs 2.0% of 1180 placebo recipients had increased ALT; 1.6% vs 1.2% had self-limited transient AST increases).

raw_record.support_text: One subject (patient 5) developed drug-induced hepatitis after 4 weeks' treatment with montelukast. The cause was attributed to montelukast because there was no history of other causes; the patient's pre-treatment liver function tests and follow-up liver ultrasonography were normal, and serum bilirubin, ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase, which rose to 10 µmol·L⁻¹, 326 U·L⁻¹, 262 U·L⁻¹ and 318 U·L⁻¹, respectively, returned to normal within 3 days of stopping montelukast treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Montelukast 10 mg daily for 4 weeks in a randomized, controlled, double-blind crossover study in steroid-resistant asthmatic subjects with sputum eosinophilia. Patient 5: serum bilirubin 10 µmol·L⁻¹, ALT 326 U·L⁻¹, AST 262 U·L⁻¹, alkaline phosphatase 318 U·L⁻¹; values returned to normal within 3 days of stopping montelukast. Attribution supported by no other causes, normal pre-treatment liver function tests, and normal follow-up liver ultrasonography.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman presented with jaundice, pruritus, anorexia and vomiting, with elevated liver enzymes (AST 676 U/L, ALT 425 U/L, ALP 384 U/L, GGT 406 U/L, total bilirubin 19.87 mg/dL). Her history included a recently completed 2-month course of terbinafine 250 mg/day for onychomycosis ending 6 weeks before admission, with no other drug intake, liver disease, alcohol, or parenteral drug abuse. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C and autoantibodies were negative. A liver biopsy obtained during the eighth week after terbinafine discontinuation revealed cholestatic hepatitis, and use of the Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship between terbinafine and cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 56-year-old woman, terbinafine 250 mg/day for ~2 months for onychomycosis, stopped 6 weeks before admission; jaundice and pruritus starting one week before admission. Peak serum bilirubin 60.2 mg/dL at ~8 weeks after discontinuation; liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis. Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship. UDCA (1000 mg/day) was given for elevated liver enzymes and intractable pruritus; liver tests normalized by 15 weeks after terbinafine cessation (AST 30, ALT 32 U/L, total bilirubin 1.17 mg/dL). Competing viral/autoimmune causes ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver disease accounts for about 50% of acute or subacute liver failure in the United States. The authors report a case of terbinafine-induced severe liver failure requiring liver transplantation. A variety of antifungal medications are known to cause a range of liver injury from mild hepatocellular-cholestatic injury to acute/subacute liver failure, and terbinafine (Lamisil), a widely prescribed antifungal for onychomycosis, is one antifungal associated with such liver injuries.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old African American male with onychomycosis treated with terbinafine for approximately 3 months. At the 3-month outpatient visit he was jaundiced with dark urine, acholic stools, weight loss, anorexia, myalgias, and pruritus; labs showed AST 95 IU/L, ALT 149 IU/L, total bilirubin 29 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. After 33 days, at outside hospital admission: AST 228 IU/L, ALT 144 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 497 IU/L, albumin 2.2 mg/dL, bilirubin 68.6 mg/dL, BUN 114 mg/dL, creatinine 14.2 mg/dL. Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, ANA, ASMA, AMA, HIV; undetectable serum acetaminophen; normal ceruloplasmin. His condition deteriorated, requiring hemodialysis and orthotropic liver transplantation. Explant pathology showed portal areas lacking corresponding bile ducts (cholestatic liver disease). The report notes terbinafine usually produces mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury that is reversible after discontinuation, with previous reports of prolonged cholestasis and disappearance of interlobular bile ducts. Brand: Lamisil (Novartis).

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old man treated with 250 mg terbinafine daily for onychomycosis developed anorexia and dark urine after 2 weeks, and a diagnosis of terbinafine-induced hepatitis was made a month later. He denied other medications, alcohol, previous hepatitis, tuberculosis or other infections. He was clinically jaundiced, with ALT 580 U/L, AST 324.7 U/L, GGT 499.9 U/L, TBil 322.7 µmol/L, DBil 170.9 µmol/L; hepatitis A/B/C/D/E serologies were negative. A diagnosis of drug-induced hepatitis was made; hemodialysis and plasmapheresis gave unsatisfactory results and liver transplantation was recommended.
raw_record.extra_details: Representative case within a meta-analysis of terbinafine liver injury. Dose 250 mg daily for onychomycosis; icterus onset ~2 weeks into treatment; laboratory values ALT 580 U/L (n<40), AST 324.7 U/L (n<40), GGT 499.9 U/L (n<85), TBil 322.7 µmol/L (n<19), DBil 170.9 µmol/L (n<8), ALB 40 g/L; serologies negative for hepatitis A-E; hepatitis A/B/C/D/E and tuberculosis/infection ruled out; hemodialysis and plasmapheresis were unsatisfactory and liver transplantation was recommended (recommended, not confirmed performed).

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male on Terbinafine 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis for 1 month developed progressive jaundice and pruritus. LFTs showed a mixed cholestatic hepatitis picture (bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL, AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3) with negative viral serologies, autoimmune markers, and negative biliary obstruction workup. A liver biopsy showed extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, and portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate and Kupffer cell hyperplasia, with no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. A diagnosis of Terbinafine-induced liver injury was made (RUCAM score 9, highly probable); he was given ursodeoxycholic acid for 3 months and recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis; jaundice latency ~1 month after start. Bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 11.7), AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3 (mixed). RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). Biopsy showed maintained lobular architecture, extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate, Kupffer cell hyperplasia; no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 300 mg three times daily until LFT normalization (~3 months), with a prolonged recovery phase of 3 months after drug discontinuation. Discussion notes Terbinafine DILI incidence 0.5-3/100,000 exposed; reported phenotypes include acute hepatitis, cholestasis or mixed picture, acute liver failure, and vanishing bile duct syndrome; latency to jaundice generally 2-6 weeks, bilirubin peaks 3-5 weeks after discontinuation, normalization 2-12 months; rarely acute/subacute liver failure requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors characterize terbinafine-induced DILI as a rare but serious, idiosyncratic and rapidly evolving event that clusters in the first 6 weeks of treatment, occurring in patients treated for a mean of 30 days (range 5-84 days). They identified 69 patients with clinical presentation, all symptomatic, none detected through monitoring, including one with symptom onset after drug discontinuation. In the same systematic review, three patients developed fulminant liver failure attributed to terbinafine and required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Literature-based critical appraisal topic (CAT) assessing usefulness of laboratory monitoring for early DILI detection; 69 patients (65 of 69 clinically obviously sick by 6 weeks), symptomatic only and none found on monitoring; mean 30 days treatment, onset 5-84 days; symptoms included jaundice (most common per FDA), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, anorexia, dark urine, with pruritus added as a potentially isolated symptom (in >20%, n=16). Three case reports of fulminant liver failure requiring successful liver transplant (48-year-old female symptomatic within 5 days; 50-year-old male with jaundice, dark urine, acholic stools followed by weight loss, anorexia, myalgias, pruritus, deteriorated after discontinuation; 41-year-old female no further details). Three reports of death associated with terbinafine-induced hepatic dysfunction occurred but in complex patients with multiple medications or disease and without clear attribution to terbinafine. Authors conclude routine blood monitoring is not helpful for detecting this DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Fifteen well characterized patients with liver injury attributed to terbinafine who were enrolled into the ongoing DILIN Prospective registry study are presented. Most patients were symptomatic with pruritus and jaundice, 2 were hospitalized and 1 required eventual liver transplantation, and most had either a cholestatic or mixed liver injury pattern at onset with a generally favorable prognosis. One potential fatal case had a distinctly severe hepatocellular injury at onset and underwent liver transplantation within 3 weeks of presentation. During follow-up, 6 patients were treated with corticosteroids, and the majority (54%) had protocol-determined chronic liver injury, far above the overall DILIN cohort rate (18%).
raw_record.extra_details: 15 DILIN registry cases of terbinafine-attributed DILI; 2 hospitalized; 1 liver transplant (a potential fatal case with severe hepatocellular injury at onset, transplanted within 3 weeks); cholestatic or mixed pattern at onset; chronic liver injury in 54% of followed patients vs 18% overall DILIN; median BMI 24.2 vs 27 kg/m2 overall; 6 treated with corticosteroids; no patients with chronic injury had underlying chronic liver disease. HLA-A*33:01 present in 10 of 11 European ancestry cases. FDA removed the need for liver biochemistry monitoring with terbinafine in 2001 due to favorable post-marketing safety profile.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients taking terbinafine, monitoring laboratory test results identified one asymptomatic patient with grade 3 ALT and AST elevation who was diagnosed with terbinafine-induced hepatotoxicity 45 days into treatment; the ALT and AST elevations resolved after terbinafine was discontinued. Overall, 6 patients discontinued terbinafine because of grade 1 to 3 terbinafine-attributed liver function test abnormalities.
raw_record.extra_details: One asymptomatic patient developed grade 3 ALT and AST elevation diagnosed as terbinafine-induced hepatotoxicity 45 days into treatment; elevations resolved after terbinafine discontinuation (dechallenge). Six patients overall discontinued terbinafine due to grade 1-3 terbinafine-attributed LFT abnormalities. Monitoring ALT: 4 cases (0.2%) of grade >=2 ALT elevation, 1 case (0.1%) grade >=2 AST elevation. No significant adult vs pediatric differences.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported case, cholestasis was well documented as attributable to terbinafine, which had been prescribed for its usual indication (therapeutic antifungal use). The paper emphasizes the need for a high level of clinical suspicion for early diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury and presents this case to raise awareness of pharmacological hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity prescribed for its usual indication. Usual toxicity pattern is cholestatic, typically prolonged (2-12 months), with possible progression to ductopenia. Latency (exposure-jaundice/icterus) ranges from 2 to 6 weeks; maximum bilirubin peak typically occurs 3-5 weeks after drug discontinuation. Resolution after withdrawal is usually the rule. No specific treatment exists, though ursodeoxycholic acid has been tried with success. Recent description of an association between HLA-A*33:01 and susceptibility to terbinafine cholestatic hepatotoxicity. Exact mechanisms not yet fully elucidated; some metabolites can bind hepatobiliary proteins and promote an immune reaction. Figure 1 shows chronological evolution of liver biochemistry abnormalities in relation to terbinafine use and withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies Terbinafine as a known hepatotoxic agent used to treat onychomycosis. It recommends that if terbinafine is the suspected agent of hepatic injury, prompt discontinuation should be considered, and frames the case as illustrating symptoms, diagnostic measures, and suspected pathophysiology of terbinafine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Terbinafine indicated for onychomycosis. The paper describes a case of terbinafine-induced hepatotoxicity and advises prompt discontinuation of the drug when it is the suspected agent of hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes a previously healthy 24-yr-old man prescribed terbinafine 250 mg daily for onychomycosis who, at the end of a 3.5-week course, developed progressive loss of appetite, jaundice, and severe pruritus. Serum bilirubin peaked at 30.9 mg/dl 3 weeks after discontinuing terbinafine, and a liver biopsy showed hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis with a mild-to-moderate mixed portal cellular infiltrate, portal tracts lacking bile ducts, and necrotic bile duct changes with features of cholangitis. Liver tests normalized 100 days after stopping terbinafine, and the paper identifies this as terbinafine-induced icteric hepatitis, the fourth reported case.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (fourth reported case of terbinafine-induced icteric hepatitis). Terbinafine 250 mg daily for onychomycosis; injury appeared at end of a 3.5-week course. Peak serum bilirubin 30.9 mg/dl (peaked 3 weeks after discontinuation). Initial tests: AST 296 IU/L, ALT 584 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 222 IU/L, GGT 318 IU/L, prothrombin time 11.1 s. Histology: hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis, pseudoxanthoma/cholate-stasis foamy hepatocytes, mild-to-moderate mixed portal infiltrate with eosinophils, bile duct paucity in some portal tracts, necrotic bile ducts with mild neutrophil infiltration, ductular proliferation, hepatocyte pleomorphism/mitoses/apoptotic bodies; predominantly cholestatic picture with cholangitis. Symptoms improved ~6 weeks after discontinuation; liver tests normalized 100 days after stopping terbinafine. No acute viral hepatitis or biliary tract disease; no other medications or alcohol. Biochemically a mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two new cases of hepatotoxicity probably induced by amiodarone, with evocative histology; in the first case the course was fatal and in the second there was improvement after discontinuation of the treatment. The introduction notes that abnormal liver tests and sometimes severe liver injury can occur during prolonged amiodarone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Two reported cases of hepatotoxicity probably induced by amiodarone during prolonged therapy, with evocative histology; liver function monitoring is recommended during amiodarone treatment because of the toxic risk of sometimes severe evolution. First case had a fatal course; second case improved on treatment discontinuation. Includes abnormal liver tests and sometimes severe liver injury described in the introduction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with classical features of amiodarone hepatotoxicity who died of progressive liver failure of over 2 months duration. It states that hepatotoxicity due to amiodarone is well documented, with rare fatalities reported. A 67-year-old man had been on amiodarone 400 mg/day for 3.5 years for ventricular arrhythmia; five months after starting amiodarone, asymptomatic elevation of serum aspartate aminotransferase to 64 U/L was noted, and liver biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis, bile ductular proliferation, active hepatocyte destruction, abundant Mallory bodies, and parenchymal polymorphonuclear inflammatory infiltrate, with EM showing lysosomal lamellar inclusion bodies consistent with amiodarone phospholipid complexes. The patient died of progressive liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic oral dosing of amiodarone 400 mg/day for 3.5 years for ventricular arrhythmia in a 67-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and ventricular aneurysm. Asymptomatic AST elevation (64 U/L, normal 0-45) noted 5 months after starting amiodarone; at admission AST 134 U/L, ALT 47 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 208 U/L (normal 30-115), total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dl. Liver biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis, bile ductular proliferation, active hepatocyte destruction, abundant Mallory bodies, and polymorphonuclear infiltrate; EM revealed lysosomal lamellar inclusion bodies consistent with amiodarone phospholipid complexes. Patient died of progressive liver failure over 2 months; no autopsy. Co-medications included diltiazem HCl, warfarin sodium, and isosorbide dinitrate. Authors also raise the question of possible amiodarone-induced pancreatitis due to persistent mild-moderate serum/peritoneal amylase and lipase elevation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of amiodarone-induced hepatic dysfunction in a patient on long-term low-dose amiodarone therapy (standard loading dose followed by 18 months of low-dose maintenance without medical follow-up). The patient had elevated GGT (239 u/L), mildly elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL), serum ammonia 127 µmol/L, and a hepatobiliary function test showing mildly delayed tracer clearance suggesting some degree of hepatic dysfunction, with negative hepatitis profile. After amiodarone discontinuation (with lactulose added), ammonia normalized by day 4, symptoms resolved by day 6, and liver function tests were normal at 1-month follow-up. The discussion states amiodarone has established hepatotoxic properties, with reported hepatotoxicity mainly at large loading doses (usually fulminant hepatitis) or prolonged high maintenance doses (usually cirrhotic liver disease), and a low-dose case with micronodular cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: atrial fibrillation. Patient received standard loading dose then low-dose amiodarone maintenance for 18 months. Laboratory findings: ALT 32 u/L, AST 54 u/L, ALP 189 u/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, GGT 239 u/L, serum ammonia 127 µmol/L; hepatobiliary test showed mildly delayed tracer clearance; hepatitis profile negative. Clinical course: nausea, ataxia, wide-based gait, weakness, confusion (signs partly multifactorial given amiodarone's neurotoxic properties); lactulose added, ammonia normalized by day 4, symptoms resolved by day 6, normal liver function tests with no asterixis/cognitive impairment/proximal weakness at 1 month. Discussion (references): hepatotoxicity reported mainly with large loading doses (usually fulminant hepatitis) or prolonged high maintenance doses (usually cirrhotic liver disease); one reported low-dose case of ascites and micronodular cirrhosis after 22.5 months; one report of low-dose therapy causing aminotransferases to rise then normalize despite continued hepatic insult, with cumulative dose hypothesized as toxic factor; AHA Circulation publication on 140 long-term low-dose patients noted slight AST increase and GGT increase with none developing clinical hepatic dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 39 amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports published between 1984 and 2007 found that 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis attributed to amiodarone, with low ALT, AST and TB values observed in these patients but no statistically significant differences versus non-cirrhotic patients; the cumulative amiodarone dose was significantly higher in patients who developed cirrhosis (p = 0.01). A Likelihood Ratio model was constructed comparing these published cases with LFT abnormalities of any other etiology in a general population.
raw_record.extra_details: 39 published amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports (1984-2007); 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis, 15 patients died (20 did not, 4 not registered). Mean age 68.77 y (SD 11.15), mean latency period 1021 days, mean cumulative dose 300.70 g. Cirrhotic patients had significantly higher cumulative dose (382.8 vs 222.7 g, p=0.01). Likelihood-ratio model compared published cases with LFT abnormalities of any other cause in a general population; LRs >1 for AST 1-3×ULN (1.98), ALT 1-3×ULN (1.70), age >65 y (2.27), and AP >8×ULN (4.42) categories.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report one case of acute hepatitis induced by an acute loading dose of amiodarone, with a positive accidental rechallenge test, adding to previously reported cases of cytolytic and cholestatic hepatitis and cirrhosis during chronic amiodarone therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis was induced by an acute 1200 mg amiodarone IV infusion in saline over 24 hr given to restore sinus rhythm in a 59-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and atrial fibrillation. ASAT rose from 15 to 145 IU/l and ALAT from 25 to 265 IU/l within 24 hr, then peaked at 1470 and 2090 IU/l three days later; total bilirubin rose to 22 µmol/l. Values declined after amiodarone withdrawal. Three years later an inadvertent rechallenge with amiodarone infusion (1200 mg over 24 hr) produced the same liver-function changes, confirming causality. Liver biopsy 13 days after rechallenge showed major parenchymal damage with hepatocyte atrophy and peliosis-like sinusal ectasia, polymorph portal infiltrate with eosinophilic lymphocytes; electron microscopy was normal. Viral hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, mononucleosis, herpes, non-A/non-B hepatitis markers, tissue antibodies, and stool cultures were negative on both episodes.

raw_record.support_text: The characteristic morphologic features of amiodarone (AD) hepatotoxicity include changes mimicking alcoholic hepatitis ('pseudoalcoholic hepatitis') and secondary phospholipidosis. The incidence of hepatic disease in recipients of AD is approximately 1% for pseudoalcoholic liver disease, 25% for lesser parenchymal injury deduced from elevated hepatic-related serum enzymes, and an unknown but probably high incidence of phospholipidosis after chronic administration. The complete histologic spectrum of alcohol-like liver injury includes steatosis, steatonecrosis, Mallory bodies, megamitochondria, portal inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; at least two of these features were present in most of the authors' cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 17-case series; incidence of hepatic disease ~1% for pseudoalcoholic liver disease and ~25% for lesser parenchymal injury (elevated hepatic-related serum enzymes); histologic spectrum includes steatosis, steatonecrosis, Mallory bodies, megamitochondria (42% of cases), portal inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis (2 cases); Mallory bodies located in zone I; steatosis microvesicular, macrovesicular, or both; ALT equal to or greater than AST in several cases; foam cells (PAS with diastase) in 9 of 17 cases; no cirrhosis in 9 patients who died while receiving AD; resembles pseudoalcoholic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, amiodarone was suspected as the cause of drug toxicity and the dosage was decreased to 200 mg daily; other causes of hepatitis were investigated and excluded by serology. Liver biopsy showed marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen hepatocytes with foamy cytoplasm, focal hepatocellular necrosis with inflammatory infiltrates, Mallory's bodies, proliferated bile ductules, and portal inflammatory infiltrate, with lysosomal phospholipid inclusions on electron microscopy. After amiodarone was discontinued the patient's condition deteriorated, and he died on day 21 of hospitalization; a postmortem biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with amiodarone and metabolite tissue levels of 180 and 1060 µg/g.
raw_record.extra_details: Elderly patient with arrhythmia treated with amiodarone; serum amiodarone and N-desethylamiodarone levels on admission were 3.0 mg/L (normal 1.0-2.5 mg/L) and 2.6 mg/L, respectively (were 2.0 and 1.6 mg/L 2 months after initiation of therapy in November 1986, when hepatic enzymes were normal). Laboratory findings at admission: total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl, AST 223 IU/L, ALT 124 IU/L, GGT 738 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 459 IU/L, prothrombin time 39 sec (control 12.1 sec). Histology: marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen foamy hepatocytes, focal necrosis, Mallory bodies, proliferated bile ductules, portal inflammation, lysosomal phospholipid inclusions in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells and bile duct epithelium; postmortem micronodular cirrhosis. Hepatitis B surface/core antibodies positive with no active disease; hepatitis A IgG positive. Amiodarone discontinued on admission; patient transferred to ICCU, given encainide which was stopped for negative inotropic effects, developed congestive heart failure, and died on day 21. Discussion notes amiodarone commonly causes asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations (15-55% frequency) and rarely clinically apparent hepatic disease (symptomatic hepatotoxicity in 6/2122 patients, 0.28%, treated mean 13 months); symptoms such as hepatomegaly, jaundice, cirrhosis, or chronic hepatitis generally subside on discontinuation, with reversal time 20 days to 17 months. Six deaths have been attributed to amiodarone-induced liver toxicity (patients aged 8-76 years; dosages 400 and 600 mg/day; durations 2 months to 4 years). Case presented at ASHP 45th annual meeting.

raw_record.support_text: 17 cases of amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) confirmed by transmission electron microscopy from 1990-2020 were identified, with a mean amiodarone usage of 20.4 months and a mean dose of 300 mg. AILI histologically mimics alcoholic steatohepatitis and can be definitely diagnosed by identifying characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.
raw_record.extra_details: 17 EM-confirmed AILI cases (1990-2020); mean usage 20.4 months at mean dose 300 mg. Histology: steatohepatitis with ballooning degeneration, periportally located Mallory hyalines, satellitosis, periportal pericellular fibrosis, sinusoidal Kupffer cell lipidosis (1 case); less frequently ductular reaction, macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis than ASH. A histologic scoring system (score <10 suggestive of AILI) correctly classified 100% of cases, with all AILI cases scoring <8. Diagnosis confirmed by characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) is described as a rare occurrence that histologically mimics alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH), presenting with steatohepatitis, ballooning degeneration, Mallory hyalines, and satellitosis. The abstract states that a definite diagnosis of AILI can be made by identifying characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy (EM).
raw_record.extra_details: 17 cases of AILI confirmed by EM (identified from 1990 to 2020) were reviewed by two pathologists blindly; diagnosis confirmed by characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy. Histologic presentation mimics alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) with steatohepatitis, ballooning degeneration (BD), Mallory hyalines (MH), and satellitosis; histologic differentiation from ASH is challenging.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation taking clopidogrel and amiodarone presented with elevated liver tests (total bilirubin 0.71 mg/dL, AST 358 U/L, ALT 177 U/L, prothrombin time 27.1 s) and diffuse increased liver intensity on CT. The authors diagnosed amiodarone-induced hepatic, pulmonary, thyroid, and ophthalmologic toxicity, and liver function was restored after cessation of amiodarone. The same narrative states that amiodarone causes liver damage ranging from asymptomatic serum aminotransferase elevation to hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation; concurrent clopidogrel use; presented with general weakness, nausea, visual disturbance, heat intolerance, and non-productive cough. Baseline liver tests: total bilirubin 0.71 mg/dL, AST 358 U/L, ALT 177 U/L, prothrombin time 27.1 s; CT showed diffuse increased liver intensity. Liver function restored after amiodarone cessation. Multi-system toxicity also involved lungs (fibrinoid interstitial inflammation with atypical type II pneumocytes and intra-alveolar foamy macrophages), thyroid (TSH <0.008 μIU/mL, free thyroxine 4.67 ng/dL, treated with methimazole), and eyes (bilateral vortex corneal deposits). Amiodarone is an iodine-containing benzofuran derivative, class III antiarrhythmic. Narrative notes liver damage range up to hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present two patients with amiodarone-induced liver injury. In case 1, perivenular aggregates of granular cells are described as the earliest morphological manifestation of amiodarone hepatotoxicity, and on withdrawal of amiodarone the hepatic function tests became normal with complete recovery. In case 2, cirrhosis of the liver is reported as a rare complication of amiodarone treatment. The granular cells contained iodine, supporting the presence of amiodarone or a metabolite, and electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal inclusions consistent with known amiodarone hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients: case 1 with subtle perivenular granular-cell foci and hepatic function test abnormality that normalized on amiodarone withdrawal with complete recovery; case 2 with liver cirrhosis (rare complication of amiodarone). Lysosomal inclusions (mainly lamellar) on electron microscopy; granular-cell cytoplasm contained iodine (presumptive evidence of amiodarone or a metabolite). Varma et al. described similar lysosomal bodies in two patients with mild increases in AST whose biopsies were essentially normal. Perivenular site is the main area of hepatocellular necrosis and fibrosis in amphophilic drug toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The patient discontinued amiodarone, which was considered the most probable cause of acute hepatitis. The modified RUCAM score was 9 points, indicating that amiodarone was a highly probable cause of acute liver injury in this case. Liver tests improved by more than 50% within a week of withdrawal; a final diagnosis of DILI caused by amiodarone was made.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication was atrial fibrillation (Holter monitoring confirmed sinus conversion); amiodarone ceased on cardiology consultation and no other antiarrhythmic started. Initial liver biopsy (H&E) showed severe lobular, portal and periportal inflammation with hepatocyte necrosis, marked centrilobular necrosis, ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory bodies, and a red granule; electron microscopy showed phospholipid-laden lysosomal lamellar bodies and fatty deposition. One week after cessation liver tests decreased >50%: AST 92 U/L, ALT 120 U/L, total bilirubin 5.51 mg/dL; bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, and γ-GTP normalized by 3 months, and follow-up biopsy 5 months later confirmed recovery without fibrosis. Reduced RUCAM score 9. General review note: amiodarone DILI is most commonly a sole aminotransferase elevation without liver dysfunction, but rare severe liver injury, fulminant hepatitis, or progression to cirrhosis with decompensated hepatic failure can occur; large apparent volume of distribution slows total body-store decline after discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The DILIN identified 10 cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity. Amiodarone toxicity occurred after a longer latency than dronedarone (387 vs 119 days), and amiodarone patients were more likely to be symptomatic, with nausea and abdominal pain most frequent. Cases were attributed to the drug by DILIN adjudication.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN case series, N=10, median age 70 (range 59-89). Daily dose 100 mg BID to 200 mg BID PO. Days from drug start to DILI onset median 388 (21-3112). Latency 387 days. Pattern at onset: cholestatic 4/9, mixed 4/9, hepatocellular 1/9; R value median 2.1 (0.2-13.8). Peak ALT median 229 U/L, peak alkaline phosphatase 402 U/L, peak total bilirubin 8.6 mg/dL. Jaundice in 80%. Biopsy (5 cases): fibrosis/advanced bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis (3), steatosis, numerous Mallory-Denk bodies (one periportal), one burned-out cirrhosis. 9 hospitalized, 5 died (1 liver-related) at median 32 days, 3 fatal DILI, 0 liver transplants, chronic DILI 1/6.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case series titled 'Amiodarone Hepatotoxicity' describing five patients who developed drug-induced liver injury while on therapeutic amiodarone. In Patient 1, biopsy showed moderate to marked panlobular steatosis with occasional hepatocellular degenerative changes and no fibrosis or Mallory bodies; liver tests improved after amiodarone was discontinued, and upon rechallenge with amiodarone 400 mg/d, anorexia returned and ALT rose to 61 U, resolving again after drug withdrawal. Patient 2 developed rising aminotransferases during amiodarone 800 mg/d with biopsy showing mild focal steatosis and minimal hepatocellular degeneration, followed by enzyme improvement after dose reduction. These findings explicitly attribute hepatic steatosis-associated injury to therapeutic amiodarone use in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients (58/M, 51/M, 73/F, 64/M, 63/M) developed amiodarone hepatotoxicity after 2-18 months of therapy at usual daily doses of 400-800 mg. Liver biopsies showed moderate-to-marked panlobular steatosis (Patient 1) and mild focal steatosis with minimal hepatocellular degeneration (Patient 2), with occasional sinusoidal monocyte aggregates and portal round-cell infiltrates, and no Mallory bodies, fibrosis, or cirrhosis. Elevated AST/ALT and alkaline phosphatase (e.g., Patient 2 ALT 5x normal, ALP 1.5x ULN; Patient 4 AST 500, ALT 1320, ALP 234) and hepatomegaly in Patients 3 and 5; bilirubin, PT, and PTT normal in all five. Patient 1 showed positive dechallenge/rechallenge (ALT 61 U on rechallenge), with clinical and biochemical recovery after withdrawal. Concurrent cardiac/other medications included digoxin, furosemide, KCI, propylthiouracil, dyazide, warfarin, thyroxine, and lubricant eye drops. Indications: coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, aortic valve disease. No specific biochemical R-based pattern classification is stated.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with amiodarone-induced liver injury, which led to liver failure. Computed tomography revealed a gradual increase in hepatic density over a long period following initiation of amiodarone. Despite discontinuation of the drug, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy and subsequently died, which the authors attribute to the drug's extended half-life causing persistent end-organ damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic used for atrial fibrillation. The molecular structure includes iodine; hepatic accumulation increases hepatic density on CT, which correlates with blood level of desethyl-amiodarone metabolite. 74-year-old woman; oral amiodarone 200 mg started perioperatively (after mitral valvuloplasty for severe mitral regurgitation) and continued after discharge; referred ~6 years later for elevated liver enzymes. Also taking atorvastatin (10 mg), vonoprazan (20 mg), diltiazem (90 mg), and warfarin (1 mg); no drinking/smoking. Patient progressed to liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy and died despite drug discontinuation, reflecting amiodarone's extended half-life; authors recommend lowest effective dose and annual liver function monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: Patient number 9, a 58-year-old woman with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia who had been taking a maintenance oral dose of 300 mg amiodarone (AMD) for over 3 years, was found to have abnormal liver tests compatible with cholestatic liver injury. Alcohol consumption and injection drug abuse were excluded; hepatitis A, B and C tests were negative, and antinuclear, anti-LKM and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were not detected. The serum amiodarone concentration was 1012 ng/mL (therapeutic range 500-1000 ng/mL). The patient was diagnosed with AMD-induced hepatotoxicity, the drug was discontinued, and a liver biopsy two weeks later showed moderate fibrosis and steatosis with periportal Mallory bodies. Liver enzymes gradually returned to normal after about three months, and amiodarone was not resumed.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old woman with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; maintenance oral dose 300 mg amiodarone for over 3 years before detection. Laboratory values: total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL (normal 0.7-1.1), AST 160 U/L (normal 19-35), ALT 174 U/L (normal 7-45), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 105 U/L (normal 6-29). Serum amiodarone concentration 1012 ng/mL (therapeutic range 500-1000 ng/mL). Alcohol and injection drug abuse excluded; hepatitis A/B/C negative; ANA, anti-LKM and anti-mitochondrial antibodies absent. Liver biopsy 2 weeks after discontinuation showed moderate fibrosis and steatosis and periportal Mallory bodies. Dechallenge led to gradual normalization of liver enzymes within about 3 months; drug not resumed.

raw_record.support_text: The summary emphasizes the potential severity of amiodarone toxicity: transient increases in liver enzyme activity that abate with dosage reduction or drug cessation are common, while rarely there is progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Toxicity shows no consistent relationship with dose, duration, cumulative dose, or serum/tissue concentrations, current data on fatal hepatic failure are limited to case reports, and the contribution of concomitant medications is unclear.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic oral amiodarone use (maintenance 200-400 mg/d) for refractory arrhythmias. Mild asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations are common and generally abate with dose reduction or cessation; rarely there is progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Fatal hepatic failure reports are limited to case reports. Toxicity lacks a consistent relationship with dose, duration, cumulative dose, or serum and tissue concentrations; contribution of concomitant medications is unclear. Monitoring of liver function tests at baseline and every 6 months is recommended. No evidence supports routine monitoring of serum concentrations of amiodarone or N-desethylamiodarone.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone, commonly used for arrhythmias, causes adverse effects in up to 55.3% of patients, and hepatotoxicity is described as a known but uncommon complication of amiodarone treatment. The authors report a fatal case of severe hepatic failure due to prolonged amiodarone treatment in a 62-year-old woman who had taken amiodarone 800 mg/day for one year for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, with no history of alcoholism or previous hepatitis; histology showed micronodular cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 62-year-old woman treated with amiodarone 800 mg/day for one year for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (resistant to digoxin, verapamil, and quinidin); no alcoholism or prior hepatitis. Presented with jaundice, enlarged tender liver (span 20 cm), ankle edema; labs included bilirubin 3.9-5.4 mg%, SGOT 520 U/L, SGPT 131 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 329 U/L, gamma-GT 1493 U/L, prolonged prothrombin time. Histology showed regenerative nodule with fibrosis (micronodular cirrhosis). Fatal outcome from severe hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: An observational study collecting all cases of dantrolene-associated hepatic injury reported to the manufacturer, regulatory authorities, or in published literature using prespecified inclusion criteria found 122 cases of dantrolene-associated hepatic injury, with 27 fatalities. The risk of hepatic complications was estimated at less than 9.0 cases per 100,000 prescriptions and fatal hepatic reactions at 0.83 cases per 100,000 prescriptions.
raw_record.extra_details: 1990 study collected all dantrolene-associated hepatic injury cases reported to the manufacturer, regulatory authorities, or the literature using prespecified inclusion criteria: 122 cases of hepatic injury with 27 fatalities, of which 52% (14/27) occurred in multiple sclerosis patients. Fatalities associated with higher mean dantrolene dose (582 mg/day) than nonfatal cases (263 mg/day). Risk estimated <9.0 hepatic complications and 0.83 fatal hepatic reactions per 100,000 prescriptions. An earlier 1977 study estimated 1.8% (16/1044) any hepatic injury and 0.3% (3/1044) fatal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: After exclusions, a total of 50 patients (19 from category 1 controlled trials and 31 from category 2 postmarketing) who developed liver injury during dantrolene therapy were analyzed. Hepatic adverse reactions were categorized into four groups: transaminase elevation only; transaminase elevation with mild hyperbilirubinemia (1-2.5 mg/100 ml); icteric hepatitis (bilirubin above 2.5 mg/100 ml) with recovery; and fatalities caused by acute or subacute hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 50 patients with liver injury during dantrolene therapy (19 from category 1 premarketing controlled efficacy/safety trials including up to 7 years of follow-up, covering 2191 trial patients; 31 from category 2 postmarketing, an estimated 30,000 long-term users). Hepatic reactions included transaminase elevation only; transaminase elevation with mild hyperbilirubinemia (1-2.5 mg/100 ml); icteric hepatitis (bilirubin >2.5 mg/100 ml) with recovery; and fatalities from acute or subacute hepatic failure. Hepatic tissue available from 9 patients (6 liver biopsy, 3 autopsy). Indication: spasticity; drug used as dantrolene sodium (talc crystal evidence and alcoholism and baseline SGOT elevation were exclusion reasons in some patients).

raw_record.support_text: The authors of one observational study reported one case of reversible hepatotoxicity associated with chlorzoxazone and found 23 additional cases of hepatotoxicity reported to the FDA since 1970. Eight cases (two fatal) were judged to be probably related to chlorzoxazone, while the rest were possibly or doubtfully related. Most cases were mild and resolved after discontinuation of the medication, but a few were associated with very high elevations of serum transaminases, severe hepatitis, or permanent liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 additional FDA-reported cases of hepatotoxicity since 1970; 8 cases (2 fatal) probably related to chlorzoxazone, remaining cases possibly or doubtfully related; most cases mild and resolved on discontinuation, some with very high serum transaminase elevations, severe hepatitis, or permanent liver damage; one case of reversible hepatotoxicity. No data estimating rates of serious hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute liver failure attributed to chlorzoxazone (CZ), requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Histopathologic findings were consistent with drug-induced injury (necrosis, ballooning degeneration, mixed inflammatory infiltrate). The paper states hepatic toxicity of CZ appears idiosyncratic, that there is no clear dose- or time-dependent relationship, that hepatotoxicity is sustained with rechallenge, and reviews a 1986 series in which CZ hepatotoxicity varied from mild reversible jaundice to fulminant liver failure and death. It also notes the FDA strengthened its hepatotoxicity warning for CZ in 1995 and that this is the first reported CZ-induced ALF requiring transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of CZ-induced acute liver failure requiring orthotopic liver transplantation; typical dosage 500 mg three to four times daily. Histology (pre-transplant and explant) showed massive hepatic necrosis, ballooning degeneration, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Literature review: clinical liver injury recognized since 1967, ranging from mild reversible jaundice to fulminant liver failure and death; 1986 series with age range 25-74 years and therapy duration 2 days to years, with short-latency (mean 15 days) and long-latency (mean 10.4 months) groups, the latter older with more co-medications and higher death frequency. Hepatotoxicity sustained with rechallenge; FDA strengthened hepatotoxicity warning in 1995; no identified risk factors for CZ-induced hepatotoxicity; no routine liver chemistry monitoring recommended. CZ metabolized by CYP2E1 to 6-hydroxychlorzoxazone, used as a probe of CYP2E1 activity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case report of acute cholestatic hepatitis caused by flutamide, an oral antiandrogen used for advanced prostate cancer. They note that flutamide is described as capable of producing severe hepatotoxicity in a very low percentage of cases, and report a case that resolved favorably after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an 82-year-old man with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma treated with flutamide 250 mg every 8 hours (started October 2001, jaundice noted early January 2002). Labs: GPT 1369 U/l, GOT 1102 U/l, bilirubin 13.6 mg/dl, GGT 586 U/l, LDH 400 U/l, platelets 97,000, prothrombin time 51.5%. Negative HAV/HBV/HCV/EBV serologies, normal abdominal ultrasound. Comedications: amiloride, hydrochlorothiazide, acetylsalicylic acid, lovastatin, atenolol, and leuprorelin (analog of GnRH). Jaundice with coluria clinically; recovered and discharged at 2 weeks with improving labs, flutamide treatment prohibited thereafter. Flutamide marketed since 1989; also mentioned as sometimes used in benign prostatic hyperplasia and hirsutism, with debatable use given risk of severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old man on flutamide therapy (unknown dose) presented with jaundice, choluria, and 2 weeks of asthenia/anorexia. At admission, liver tests showed total bilirubin 20.9 mg/dL, AST 739 IU/mL, ALT 262 IU/mL, AP 103 IU/mL, GGT 200 IU/mL, and a prothrombin index of 35%. Acute hepatitis with severe hepatocellular insufficiency was suspected to result from flutamide, which was withdrawn; viral, autoimmune, thyroid, iron, and tumor etiologies were excluded. Bilirubin peaked at 23.2 mg/dL and liver tests recovered to near normal before discharge after 20 days. In the discussion, the CIOMS causality scale yielded 9 points for this episode (highly probable drug-induced liver injury), with 90 days from treatment start to symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Prostate cancer indication. Latency 90 days; recovery 20 days. CIOMS scale 9 points. Prothrombin index 35% (low). Acute hepatitis with severe hepatocellular insufficiency; other causes of liver injury excluded. Abdominal ultrasound showed increased liver echogenicity with normal gallbladder and biliary tract. No dose stated in the window.

raw_record.support_text: For flutamide, the major adverse effects include gastrointestinal disorders, hematological disorders, muscle cramps, and gynecomastia, with acute liver failure highlighted as the most relevant adverse effect due to high mortality and frequent need for liver transplantation. A 14-year retrospective observational study observed 10 cases of acute and fulminant hepatitis induced by flutamide; two of these patients were treated for acne vulgaris and developed fulminant flutamide-induced hepatitis that responded well after discontinuation. A separate retrospective study of 230 patients on flutamide for acne and seborrhea initiated at 250 mg daily (annually halved to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily) found that only 5% discontinued due to increased liver enzymes at 250 mg daily, with no enzyme elevation at 125 mg and 62.5 mg.
raw_record.extra_details: In a 14-year retrospective observational study, 10 cases of flutamide-induced acute and fulminant hepatitis were observed; 2 of the 10 cases were patients treated with flutamide for acne vulgaris, both developing fulminant hepatitis with good response after discontinuation. In another retrospective study of flutamide tolerability in 230 patients with acne and seborrhea (started at 250 mg daily, annually reduced by half to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily), only 5% discontinued at 250 mg daily due to increased liver enzymes, and no enzyme elevation was seen at 125 mg and 62.5 mg daily. Acute liver failure from flutamide is associated with high mortality and necessity of liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, a 79-year-old man with prostatic adenocarcinoma developed jaundice 5 weeks after starting oral flutamide (750 mg/d) post-transurethral prostatectomy. Laboratory findings showed elevated bilirubin (74 µmol/L), AST (120 U/L), ALT (158 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (1070 U/L), and GGT (405 U/L); hepatotropic viral causes were excluded, and liver enzymes and bilirubin declined rapidly after flutamide was discontinued, with all values returning to normal within 3 weeks. The authors concluded that 'Flutamide was the most likely cause of hepatic injury in this patient' and that flutamide caused cholestatic hepatitis, noting a predominantly cholestatic biochemical pattern, peripheral eosinophilia possibly compatible with an immunoallergic reaction, and uncertainty about the exact mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide (4'-nitro-3'-trifluoromethyl-isobutyranilide), a nonsteroidal antiandrogen without estrogenic, antiestrogenic, progestational, antiprogestational, androgenic, adrenocortical, or antigonadotropic activity, used for prostate adenocarcinoma. Dose 750 mg/d oral; jaundice appeared after 5 weeks. Laboratory values: bilirubin 74 µmol/L (normal <20); AST 120 U/L; ALT 158 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 1070 U/L (normal <110); GGT 405 U/L. Peripheral eosinophilia (16% of leukocytes, with 10%–16% reported) disappeared on dechallenge; full clinical and laboratory recovery within 3 weeks with unremarkable follow-up at 4 months, 1 year, and 18 months. Viral (hepatitis A/B, cytomegalovirus, infectious mononucleosis), extrahepatic, hemolytic, and metastatic causes excluded; non-A non-B hepatitis considered less likely. Authors unsure of mechanism, speculating androgen-related cholestasis or immunoallergic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male with Gleason 9 prostatic adenocarcinoma started treatment with flutamide 250 mg t.i.d. and planned radical prostatectomy. Three weeks after the first flutamide dose he developed jaundice, choluria, and altered liver tests (AST 2008 U/L, ALT 3660 U/L, bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL, INR 3.5) and was transferred for acute liver failure (ALF) work-up. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis serology were negative, and a flutamide-induced ALF was diagnosed.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg t.i.d. for prostate cancer; onset of jaundice, choluria and elevated liver tests three weeks after first dose (AST 2008 U/L, ALT 3660 U/L, bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL, INR 3.5 at presentation; on admission AST 2046 U/L, ALT 3829 U/L, total bilirubin 9.39 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.15 mg/dL, INR 2.7, prothrombin time activity 25%, ammonia 84.4 umol/L). N-Acetyl-cysteine therapy initiated; patient developed progressive jaundice, INR elevation and mild encephalopathy, was listed and underwent orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) from a deceased donor three weeks after admission. Liver pathology showed portal and lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis, portal-portal bridging hepatocyte necrosis with lympho-plasmacytic inflammation, ductular proliferation and bile plugs. Viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV, EBV/CMV/HIV) and autoimmune (AMA/ASMA) serology negative. Patient had rapid recovery of liver function after OLT.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide was attributed to 22 DILI cases, predominantly hepatocellular (64%). Of these, 12 (57%) met nR-based Hy's law criteria and 4 patients (33%) died or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 64%/Chol 9.1%/Mix 27%; female 14%, lymphopenia 5.6%, eosinophilia 4.8%; 12 (57%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 4 (33%) died or required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide has a potent antiandrogenic action and was frequently used to treat acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, and female pattern hair loss, but its use for this purpose was prohibited after cases of severe acute hepatotoxicity were described. This frames flutamide as a human causative agent of severe acute hepatotoxicity in the setting of therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Off-label use of flutamide for acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, and female pattern hair loss (indication outside its package-insert prostate cancer indication) was prohibited following descriptions of severe acute hepatotoxicity. Acts by inhibiting androgen nuclear receptors (NR3C4).

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports that a 20-year-old woman given flutamide for hirsutism, who had no other known causes of liver disorder and recovered after withdrawal of the drug, developed serious hepatotoxicity, and the authors call this confirmatory evidence that flutamide can cause serious hepatotoxicity. They also cite their earlier case series of two 58-year-old men treated with flutamide for benign prostatic hypertrophy who developed serious hepatotoxicity, noting the estimated incidence of this disorder is less than 1%.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases: a 20-year-old woman treated with flutamide for hirsutism (an unapproved indication) who recovered after drug withdrawal, and two 58-year-old men treated for benign prostatic hypertrophy; incidence of this 'serious hepatotoxicity' estimated at less than 1%. Letter advises patients to immediately report nausea, vomiting, fatigue, discolored urine, jaundice, and other signs of liver injury so the drug can be withdrawn promptly.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old woman given flutamide for hirsutism, with no other known causes of liver disorder, developed serious hepatotoxicity and recovered after drug withdrawal; the authors describe this as confirmatory evidence that flutamide can cause serious hepatotoxicity. They also cite their prior case series in which two 58-year-old men treated with flutamide for benign prostatic hypertrophy developed serious hepatotoxicity, and note the incidence of this disorder has been estimated at less than 1%.
raw_record.extra_details: New case: 20-year-old woman treated for hirsutism (an unapproved/off-label indication) who recovered after drug withdrawal; supporting prior case series of two 58-year-old men treated for benign prostatic hypertrophy with serious hepatotoxicity. Incidence of serious hepatotoxicity estimated at less than 1%. Letter recommends caution in off-label prescribing and instructing patients to report nausea, vomiting, fatigue, discolored urine, and jaundice. Views are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the Food and Drug Administration.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 65 patients with prostate cancer receiving a total androgen suppression (TAS) regimen, flutamide was discontinued because of liver function test (LFT) elevations in 14 patients (22%), and hepatotoxicity contributed to discontinuation in others. ALT elevation was the most sensitive finding (37/60 evaluable patients had ALT ≥41 U/L), and grade 3-4 toxicity with ALT >5 times normal occurred in 4/60 patients. AST and ALT were significantly elevated relative to baseline during flutamide therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 65 prostate cancer patients on a TAS regimen; flutamide discontinued for LFT elevation in 14 (22%); median time to discontinuation 8 weeks (range 1-16). ALT elevation most sensitive: 37/60 (62%) ≥41 U/L; grade 3-4 toxicity (ALT >5x normal) in 4 (7%) of 60. AST: 24/61 (39%) ≥41 U/L. Median AST/ALT rose from 21/25 to 35/50 U/L; no rise in alkaline phosphatase. Baseline only 4/65 had AST/ALT ≥41. P<.02 for AST, P<.005 for ALT. In 12/14 discontinued patients transaminase elevation noted; one isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation; one patient had pruritus with bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL and GGT 112 U/L with normal transaminases.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man presented with jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, and anorexia of 2 weeks duration after completing a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally 3 times daily) started for a postoperative wound infection. Approximately 3 days after starting cephalexin he noted dark urine and pale stool, and within 24 hours of completing therapy developed fever, hives, pruritus, and jaundice. The report is framed as cephalexin-induced cholestatic hepatitis, documenting the temporal, clinical and biochemical course.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with a mild panacinar hepatitis and eosinophils plus extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs on liver biopsy. Laboratory values: total bilirubin 17.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL, AST 40 U/L, ALT 87 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 272 U/L. No increased hepatic iron. Prior exposure included cefazolin 1 g preoperatively, single doses of meperidine and morphine, a wound bupivacaine pump, and a short course of hydrocodone/acetaminophen for postoperative pain, but the patient took no other medications at the start of cephalexin and had previously tolerated penicillin. Infectious hepatitis A, B, C serologies and autoimmune/antimitochondrial antibodies were negative; imaging (ultrasound, CT, ERCP) unremarkable. Onset of symptoms about 3 days into cephalexin with progression after completion.

raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man developed jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, and anorexia after starting a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally 3 times daily) for a postoperative wound infection, about 3 days after starting therapy with dark urine and pale stool, followed within 24 hours of completing therapy by fever, hives, pruritus, and jaundice. Liver biopsy showed mild panacinar hepatitis with eosinophils and extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs. A diagnosis of cephalosporin-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made; pruritus responded to ursodeoxycholic acid and symptoms resolved by 7 weeks postexposure, with biochemical abnormalities resolving 5 weeks later.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis. 10-day course, 500 mg orally 3 times daily; onset ~3 days after starting (dark urine, pale stool), then within 24 hours of completing therapy fever, hives, pruritus, jaundice. Labs at presentation: total bilirubin 17.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL, AST 40 U/L, ALT 87 U/L, ALP 272 U/L. Liver biopsy: mild panacinar hepatitis with eosinophils and extensive cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs, no increased hepatic iron. Pruritus responded to ursodeoxycholic acid; all symptoms resolved by 7 weeks postexposure, biochemical abnormalities resolved 5 weeks later. Patient took no other medications at the start of cephalexin therapy and had previously tolerated penicillin; had received 1 g cefazolin preoperatively and single doses of meperidine and morphine, a wound bupivacaine pump, and a short course of hydrocodone/acetaminophen before cephalexin.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer took cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days after tumor resection and a repeat course at the same dose for cellulitis. About one month later she developed fatigue and syncope, with a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 587 U/L, R-factor 0.7). After excluding viral and autoimmune etiologies and biliary obstruction, a biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate and marked bile-duct damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days, repeated for cellulitis two weeks later; cholestatic pattern with R-factor 0.7, total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, ALP 587 U/L; cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with marked bile duct damage and bile plugs in canaliculi; follow-up biopsy showed minimal ductular proliferation and resolution of bile duct damage/inflammation. Liver enzymes remained elevated, prompting budesonide initiation 142 days after onset.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient case report, acute hepatotoxicity was attributed to repaglinide. Three observations supported the causal relationship: the temporal relationship between starting repaglinide and the onset of hepatic abnormalities, the resolution of symptoms after therapy was stopped, and the absence of alternative explanations. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale indicated a probable relationship between acute hepatotoxicity and repaglinide therapy. No hypersensitivity symptoms were reported and eosinophilia was not observed. The authors concluded that repaglinide-induced liver toxicity can occur.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale indicated a probable relationship. No hypersensitivity symptoms and no eosinophilia; mechanism of hepatotoxicity unknown. Symptoms resolved after therapy discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old man with a 2-year history of type 2 diabetes developed itching and jaundice after taking repaglinide (1 mg/day for 1 month, then increased to 2 mg/day) for a total of about 2 months. Laboratory tests showed elevated transaminases (AST 83 U/l, ALT 183 U/l), alkaline phosphatase (307 U/l), γ-GT (303 U/l), and total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl; viral serology, autoantibody screening, and MR cholangiography were negative. A liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with bile duct proliferation, a moderate lymphocytic/eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate, and hepatocyte ballooning. After repaglinide was discontinued, laboratory findings normalized within a month. The authors report this as the first published case of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide, with the drug's role strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histological features, and rapid improvement after withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled initially) with normal prior liver function. Repaglinide dosing: 1 mg/day initially, increased to 2 mg/day one month before presentation; 2-week history of itching and jaundice before admission. No other drugs or herbal remedies, no toxic habits. Labs: AST 83 U/l (<37), ALT 183 U/l (<40), ALP 307 U/l (<136), γ-GT 303 U/l (<85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl (direct 9.4 mg/dl), serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Viral causes and autoantibodies ruled out; MR cholangiography normal. Biopsy: expanded portal areas, mild bile duct proliferation, moderate lymphocytic infiltrate with some eosinophils, hepatocyte ballooning. Recovery (normal labs) within a month after discontinuation. Authors note presence of eosinophils suggesting a possible immune mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's acute liver dysfunction was attributed to anesthetic-induced hepatotoxicity after investigations ruled out viral and metabolic causes and ischemic hepatitis. The authors state that a diagnosis of anesthetic-induced hepatotoxicity is secure, and that desflurane was the agent that resulted in acute drug hepatotoxicity in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Third reported case of desflurane-induced hepatitis. Jaundice and malaise/anorexia began on postoperative day 6; markedly abnormal liver biochemistry (ALT 2188 U/L, AST 425 U/L, GGT 130 U/L, ALP 149 U/L, total bilirubin 118 umol/L); INR 2.29 on POD 8 and bilirubin 214 umol/L on POD 12; stage I/IV hepatic encephalopathy on POD 10; treated with methylprednisone 60 mg IV daily for 5 days; recovered and discharged on POD 21. Fulfills definition of fulminant liver failure; unlike the two prior desflurane cases, this patient developed hepatic encephalopathy. Mechanism considered immunologic via reaction with CYP system and trifluoroacetylated (TFA) protein adducts, with likely sensitization from prior volatile-anesthetic exposure (possibly halothane 36 years earlier); CYP metabolism of desflurane reported as 0.01%. Patient had advanced age and extra-hepatic malignancy and was not a transplant candidate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe desflurane-induced acute liver failure in a 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia who underwent a Heller myotomy. After the initial desflurane (1.2 MAC) anaesthesia her ALT peaked at 943 U/L (initially attributed to antibiotic toxicity), and after a repeat myotomy 10 days later with desflurane (0.9 MAC) she developed acute liver failure 96 hours after surgery (ALT 11,600 U/L; pH 7.06; INR 3.7) and died despite supportive management. Postmortem confirmed massive hepatic necrosis and significantly elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies (OD 0.585; ref <0.233), consistent with an inhalational agent being the cause of the necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia, undergoing Heller myotomy; desflurane given at 1.2 MAC then 0.9 MAC via Datex-Ohmeda Aestiva/5 anaesthesia delivery system; ALT peaked at 943 U/L after first operation (attributed to antibiotic toxicity); after redo myotomy developed acute liver failure 96 h post-surgery (ALT 11,600 U/L; pH 7.06; INR 3.7) and died despite supportive management; postmortem showed massive hepatic necrosis and elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies (OD 0.585; ref <0.233).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe desflurane-induced acute liver failure in a 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia who underwent a Heller myotomy. She received desflurane (1.2 MAC) anaesthesia, and 10 days later a repeat myotomy under desflurane (0.9 MAC) anaesthesia. She developed acute liver failure 96 hours after surgery (serum ALT 11,600 U/L, pH 7.06, INR 3.7) and died despite supportive management. Postmortem confirmed massive hepatic necrosis and significantly elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies, consistent with an inhalational anaesthetic agent being the cause of the necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman with achalasia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia; desflurane at 1.2 MAC during first Heller myotomy and 0.9 MAC at repeat surgery 10 days later; serum ALT peaked at 943 U/L after first surgery (attributed to antibiotic toxicity); acute liver failure 96 h after second surgery (ALT 11,600 U/L, pH 7.06, INR 3.7) with death despite supportive management; postmortem showed massive hepatic necrosis and elevated trifluoroacetyl chloride-specific IgG4 antibodies (optical density 0.585; reference range <0.233). Desflurane is metabolised to inorganic fluoride and trifluoroacetyl chloride but, owing to its low blood:gas partition coefficient and resistance to degradation, is metabolised less than halothane, enflurane and isoflurane.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that drug-induced hepatitis and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis are recognized complications of NSAIDs, and that COX-2 inhibitors have been implicated in prior case reports of AIN and hepatitis, but simultaneous presentation of both with a single therapeutic agent had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor. Given the temporal sequence, clinical findings, and liver and renal biopsy histology, they believe there is good evidence to implicate rofecoxib as the causative agent of this combined drug-induced hepatitis and acute interstitial nephritis in the patient. The liver biopsy demonstrated zone 3 cholestasis, a mixed periportal infiltrate of neutrophils and eosinophils, and mild bile duct proliferation; hepatic dysfunction and cholestasis resolved over weeks and liver function tests fully recovered within months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Simultaneous combined drug-induced hepatitis (zone 3 cholestasis, mixed periportal neutrophil/eosinophil infiltrate, mild bile duct proliferation on liver biopsy) and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis attributed to rofecoxib. Hepatic dysfunction produced a coagulopathy (returned to normal within ~4 weeks, permitting renal biopsy), persistent leucocytosis with eosinophilia (1.8e9/L), and cholestasis that resolved over 4 weeks; liver function tests fully recovered over ~3 months and remained normal at 12 months. Patient also developed renal failure requiring haemodialysis, heavy proteinuria and acute tubular necrosis. Authors note this combined presentation had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report being confident that a causal relationship exists between rofecoxib therapy and liver dysfunction in two described cases, both rated highly probable of drug-induced liver injury on the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) causality scale. The temporal association was appropriate (symptoms within two to six weeks of drug initiation) and clinical and biochemical improvements occurred rapidly upon rofecoxib discontinuation. Other causes including viral hepatitis, other toxins, and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of severe hepatotoxicity attributed to rofecoxib. In the presented case, ALT 995 U/L, ALP 243 U/L, GGT 99 U/L, total bilirubin 207 µmol/L, INR 1.1, positive ANA (1:320 speckled), slightly elevated IgG; histology showed mild macrovesicular steatosis with established portal and perivenular fibrosis and mononuclear portal/lobular infiltrate, interpreted as acute drug-induced hepatotoxicity superimposed on previously subclinical liver injury. Symptoms resolved within a week of discontinuation and liver biochemistry normalized over the following month. The first patient had previously received rofecoxib on brief occasions without hepatotoxicity; the authors speculate sensitization by repeated use with toxicity on prolonged exposure. Authors cite 4 additional reported rofecoxib cases of severe hepatic injury in the English literature.

raw_record.support_text: Rofecoxib was implicated in a single case of DILI in the series. This case was jaundiced, with bilirubin 5.6 ULN, AST 6.9 ULN, ALT 10.9 ULN, resolving in 60 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (35-year-old female, 1 day treatment) with jaundice; bilirubin 5.6 ULN, AST 6.9 ULN, ALT 10.9 ULN; time to biochemical resolution 60 days.

raw_record.support_text: Rofecoxib showed a low rate of hepatic events in several studies, with increased ALT (≥3x ULN) in only 1.8 per 100,000 exposed persons per year. Yan et al. reported two well-documented cases of cholestatic hepatitis induced by rofecoxib: one with high serum alkaline phosphatase and marked periportal (zone 1) necrosis on histology, the other with a marked ALT increase and minimal ALP abnormality, with mild damage in zones 1 and 3. In addition, 6 other rofecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity cases were reported, all predominantly cholestatic, with liver test normalization within 6 months of drug withdrawal; the main indication was osteoarthritis and arthralgia.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis: case 1 with high ALP and periportal/zone 1 necrosis on histology; case 2 with marked ALT increase and minimal ALP, mild zone 1 and 3 damage. Six additional rofecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity cases, predominantly cholestatic clinical presentation; liver tests normalized within 6 months of drug withdrawal; ursodeoxycholic acid given in 4 and steroids in 1 due to intense cholestasis; main indication osteoarthritis and arthralgia. Altogether a low hepatic-event rate, ALT >=3x ULN in 1.8 per 100,000 exposed persons/year.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists one patient (case 8) with DILI attributed to rofecoxib taken therapeutically: an 82-year-old man on 12.5 mg/day for osteoarthritis who presented lymphopenia and a cholestatic injury pattern (TB 2.6xULN, ALT 4.9xULN, ALP 4.4xULN), classified Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (82/M, osteoarthritis), 12.5 mg/day for 60 days, onset 59 days, co-meds nimodipine, omeprazole, paracetamol, troxerutin, insulin, vitamins, folic acid, lymphopenia, cholestatic pattern, TB 2.6xULN, ALT 4.9xULN, ALP 4.4xULN, Moderate severity, resolution at 94 days, CIOMS 'Highly probable'.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports a case of acute liver toxicity induced by sildenafil citrate (Viagra). While therapeutic dosages (25–100 mg/day) are usually well tolerated, the authors describe a case of acute liver toxicity attributed to sildenafil.
raw_record.extra_details: A 49-year-old man with diabetes (treated with glibenclamide) and no liver disease risk factors took Viagra 50 mg/day for erectile dysfunction; routine blood tests were normal when sildenafil was started. Four weeks later he developed right hypochondriac pain without fever, jaundice, or encephalopathy, with palpable hepatomegaly and an increase in serum aminotransferases (AST 7.4x normal, ALT 1.2x) while GGT, ALP, and total bilirubin remained normal. Prothrombin time, hematocrit, leukocyte and eosinophil counts were normal; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, IgM and total anti-hepatitis A, anti-hepatitis C, and IgM anti-cytomegalovirus were negative, and anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies were absent. Liver tests normalized after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 58-year-old man developed jaundice, pruritus, and malaise about 1 month after taking sildenafil 50 mg; no other medications, including NSAIDs, were used and tests for viral hepatitis, autoantibodies, and bile duct obstruction were negative. A liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with marked bile stasis. On the basis of criteria for drug-induced liver disorders and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, the authors diagnosed probable sildenafil-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity, and laboratory values returned to normal 4 months after symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity attributed to sildenafil in a 58-year-old man treated for erectile dysfunction. Dose 50 mg; onset about 1 month before symptoms. Labs: ALP 476 IU/l, ALT 64 IU/l, AST 42 IU/l, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, eosinophils 2.8%, prothrombin time 95%. Laparoscopy showed a green, enlarged, non-nodular liver. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with marked pericentral canalicular bile stasis and minimal portal necroinflammation. Diagnosis supported by drug-induced liver disorder criteria and the Naranjo scale. No rechallenge; liver tests normalized without treatment by 4 months. The authors note a prior literature case (Daghfous et al.) of acute hepatotoxicity attributed to sildenafil with an uncertain causal relation and no recurrence on rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old previously healthy man who took sildenafil 50 mg 1 month before symptom onset was diagnosed, on the basis of criteria for drug-induced liver disorders and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, with probable sildenafil-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity. He used no other medications, and his laboratory values improved without treatment, returning to normal 4 months after onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Presenting with jaundice, pruritus, and malaise. Labs: AST 42 IU/l, ALT 64 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 476 IU/l, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, eosinophils 2.8%. Liver biopsy showed marked intrahepatic cholestasis with bile stasis in canaliculi around the peripheral area and minimal portal necroinflammation. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune, and obstructive etiologies excluded. Symptom onset about 1 month after a single 50 mg dose; recovered without treatment by 4 months.

raw_record.support_text: A patient who had completed an oral course of levofloxacin therapy developed acute hepatitis; histopathologic examination of the liver revealed hepatic necrosis and acute hepatitis was diagnosed. Despite supportive measures including plasmapheresis and hemodialysis, the patient's condition deteriorated with grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, metabolic acidosis, and hepatorenal syndrome, and she died 104 days after finishing her oral levofloxacin course (paragraph 13). Elevated serum transaminases and bilirubin with normal serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase were compatible with hepatocellular-type liver injury, confirmed histopathologically (paragraph 17).
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case report of levofloxacin-induced acute hepatitis. Patient developed hepatic necrosis (confirmed histologically), hepatic encephalopathy up to grade IV, progressive metabolic acidosis and hepatorenal syndrome; treated with consecutive plasmaphereses and hemodialysis. Elevated serum transaminases and bilirubin with normal serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase were consistent with hepatocellular-type injury. Patient died 104 days after finishing the oral levofloxacin course. Context review notes fluoroquinolone-class reversible liver enzyme abnormality rate of 2-3%; worldwide surveillance data give a hepatitis/hepatic-failure rate <1 per million levofloxacin prescriptions, and clinical trial data show 0.3% abnormal liver function tests, with occasional reports of acute hepatocellular injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a patient who developed acute toxic hepatitis probably associated with the use of levofloxacin. The report is notable for the performance of a liver biopsy during the course of the illness, providing histologic aspects of this toxicity, and the patient survived. The authors note the well-known safety profile of levofloxacin but advise clinicians to be aware of the rare possibility of several grades of hepatic injury related to its use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of acute toxic hepatitis; a liver biopsy was performed during the course of the disease providing histologic aspects of the toxicity; the patient survived; authors describe the possibility of several grades of hepatic injury and acknowledge levofloxacin's generally well-known safety profile. Causality was described as 'probable.'
