raw_record.support_text: In a case report, the liver injury classified by the International Consensus Conference criteria gave an R = 0.37 corresponding to a cholestatic pattern. The CIOMS scale, which assesses the probability that a drug produces hepatic damage, classified levofloxacin as probable (total score 8) as responsible for the damage in this case.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported cholestatic levofloxacin DILI case (prior cases were hepatocellular or mixed). CIOMS causality score 8 (probable); International Consensus Conference criteria R = 0.37 = cholestatic. Onset at day 5 of exposure; marked elevation of GGT (basal 151 to peak 1094 U/l) and alkaline phosphatase (basal 174 to peak 1445 U/l) with modest AST/ALT rises; liver tests normalized at 24 days.

raw_record.support_text: In the three cases observed by the authors, the temporal relation and short latency (median 2 days) between use of levofloxacin (or ciprofloxacin) and liver damage, absence of other hepatotoxic drugs, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, and a compatible liver histology in case 3 supported the diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury. Dechallenge was positive and no rechallenge was performed; RUCAM classified the cases as probable or highly probable and Naranjo as possible or probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of fluoroquinolone-associated liver injury in 3 cases; median latency 2 days; no other hepatotoxic drugs; other causes of hepatitis excluded; compatible liver histology in case 3; dechallenge positive, no rechallenge; RUCAM probable/highly probable, Naranjo possible/probable. SPC lists hepatotoxicity as a rare adverse reaction of levofloxacin related to both oral and intravenous administration.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old female patient developed toxic hepatitis due to levofloxacin after receiving a single 750 mg dose of levofloxacin tablets for a pulmonary infection 10 days earlier. She experienced itching, redness, and rash, followed on day 5 by abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice. She was deemed a liver transplant candidate but suffered cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer; multiple organ failure was secondary to the toxic hepatitis. The authors emphasize that hepatotoxicity and death due to levofloxacin are uncommon.
raw_record.extra_details: Single 750 mg oral levofloxacin dose for pulmonary (lower respiratory tract) infection; began with pruritus, redness, and rash that regressed over 3 days with whole-body desquamation; from day 5 onward abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice (icterus). Presented at emergency department 10 days post-dose with confusion (GCS 12), acute hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia (53 mg/dL), and multiple organ failure. Toxic hepatitis resulted in fatal outcome: patient was a liver transplant candidate but had cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer to a transplant center. Hepatic necrosis described in the general context of drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No other co-suspect drug is reported.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, levofloxacin accounted for 13 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, one of the top 10 individual agents.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN registry.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed acute liver injury a day following initiation of IV levofloxacin therapy. Laboratory values included ALT of 4525 (ULN 49) and ALP of 52 (ULN 107), yielding an R-factor of 190, indicating a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. The paper concludes this is a case of quinolone-induced acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: IV levofloxacin started on Day 3 and discontinued immediately upon recognition of acute liver failure on Day 4. Peak labs on Day 4: AST 9334 U/L, ALT 4525 U/L, PT 24.6 s, INR 2.22, ammonia 157 umol/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL; ALP remained near normal (52 U/L on Day 4). R-factor of 190 calculated from ALT/ULN vs ALP/ULN. Patient presented with Grade III hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy. Notable improvement in liver function testing in the days following discontinuation with supportive care, supporting quinolone-induced ALF. Short latency (injury one day after initiation), consistent with fluoroquinolone hepatic injury. Mechanism described as not clear; severity ranges from transient mild LFT elevation to ALF.

raw_record.support_text: BCNU (carmustine) at higher doses in humans is known to lead to long-term hepatic and pulmonary toxicity, in some cases causing death as a result of pulmonary fibrosis. In a recent phase II study, patients with recurrent glioblastoma and no prior chemotherapy received 80 mg/m² BCNU; two of 40 patients developed grade 4 pulmonary toxicity after four cycles, while hepatic toxicity grade 3 was observed in two patients at the third cycle and grade 2 in two patients at cycles 2 and 3, as measured by serum bilirubin. BCNU was discontinued in four patients because of grade 2 or 3 pulmonary and hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Higher-dose BCNU is known to cause long-term hepatic and pulmonary toxicity in humans, with possible death from pulmonary fibrosis. Phase II study in recurrent glioblastoma patients (no prior chemotherapy) at 80 mg/m²: 2 of 40 patients developed grade 4 pulmonary toxicity (by DLCO) after four cycles (8 weeks between cycles); hepatic toxicity grade 3 in two patients at the third cycle and grade 2 in two patients at cycles 2 and 3, measured by serum bilirubin; BCNU discontinued in four patients for pulmonary and hepatic toxicity grade 2-3; pulmonary toxicities were irreversible and possibly under-reported, with only 10 of 40 patients completing four or more cycles.

raw_record.support_text: Abnormal liver function studies developed in 29 of 93 (31.2%) evaluable patients treated with BCNU (carmustine). Ten patients (10.8%) had severe, delayed hepatotoxicity (median onset day +40, range +19 to +76) that was fatal in eight patients (8.6%). Clinically this was painless cholestatic jaundice with ascites and progressive hepatic insufficiency; two patients slowly improved. Pathology in eight of nine patients showed massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, while one melanoma patient with prior dacarbazine exposure had veno-occlusive disease at necropsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity was significantly dose-related: 6/17 (35.3%; 95% CI 14.2-61.7%) patients at BCNU 1500-2850 mg/m2 vs 4/76 (5.3%; 95% CI 1.5-13.0%) at 600-1200 mg/m2 (P<0.01). At 1200 mg/m2 the incidence of severe was 6.1% and fatal hepatic necrosis 3.0%. CNS tumor diagnosis was also associated (9/44, 20.5% vs 1/49, 2.0%; P<0.01). A transient asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation pattern was seen in 19 patients. Fatal in 8/10 (8.6%); 2 recovered. Pathology: massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis (8/9); veno-occlusive disease in one patient with prior dacarbazine exposure (co-suspect). No correlation with mannitol, anticonvulsants, or corticosteroids. BCNU hepatic toxicity grading scale defined (grades 0-4).

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET trial, nine cases of serious liver abnormalities were judged to be probable drug-induced hepatitis, of which one (0.02%) was associated with the use of naproxen; raised transaminase levels reversed after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: One of nine adjudicated cases of probable drug-induced hepatitis in the TARGET trial (0.02%); raised transaminase levels reversed after drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists one patient (case 6) with DILI attributed to naproxen taken therapeutically: a 65-year-old man on 1000 mg/day for pain who developed jaundice with a mixed injury pattern (TB 4.5xULN, ALT 9.7xULN, ALP 3.4xULN), classified Moderate severity and CIOMS 'Highly probable'. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (65/M, pain), 1000 mg/day for 44 days, onset 48 days, co-meds tetrazepam, ranitidine, heparin, bisoprolol, metamizole, jaundice, mixed pattern, TB 4.5xULN, ALT 9.7xULN, ALP 3.4xULN, Moderate hospitalized, lost to follow-up, CIOMS 'Highly probable'.

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET trial, nine cases of serious liver abnormalities were judged to be probable drug-induced hepatitis, of which two (0.05%) were associated with the use of ibuprofen; raised transaminase levels reversed after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Two of nine adjudicated cases of probable drug-induced hepatitis in the TARGET trial (0.05%); raised transaminase levels reversed after drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had been taking an OTC agent containing ibuprofen for headaches. Time until onset of liver injury, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, liver biopsy findings, and DLST results indicated a diagnosis of DILI, and the DDW-J 2004 diagnostic scale score was 8 or 'highly probable.' Clinical symptoms and liver function tests completely resolved after discontinuation of the OTC medication and corticosteroid administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Taken as an OTC agent for headache; DLST positive for ibuprofen (stimulation index 195, positive) while famotidine, azulene sodium sulfonate, and domperidone were negative; DDW-J 2004 score 8 ('highly probable'); admission labs AST 1,492 U/L, ALT 1,860 U/L, T-Bil 15.3 mg/dL, PT (INR) 1.76; diffuse erythema (erythema multiforme-type eruption) on lower limbs, face, and upper limbs; treated with 1,000 mg/day IV methylprednisolone for 3 days then tapered oral corticosteroid; rash and liver tests normalized within 4 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Ibuprofen is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 7 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized 26 ibuprofen DILI cases from the Spanish DILI Registry, noting that ibuprofen-induced liver injury usually develops within four weeks of treatment initiation and presents as hepatocellular type liver damage, though characteristics varied considerably between patients. The paper concludes the risk of developing ibuprofen-induced liver injury is low given the drug's extensive worldwide use but can have life-threatening consequences. Registry data showed hepatocellular injury in 15 (58%) and cholestatic/mixed in 11 (42%) cases, with 2 fatal and 1 liver transplantation outcome among the ibuprofen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 ibuprofen DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry (N=26 ibuprofen vs 76 other NSAIDs vs 844 non-NSAIDs). Median time to onset 15 days (range 3-1767), median treatment duration 16 days (1-1826). Clinical presentation: jaundice 17 (65%), hospital admission 14 (58%), eosinophilia 6 (24%), lymphopenia 4 (17%), positive autoantibody titers 6 (27%). Prior to this, ibuprofen was considered to have very limited hepatotoxicity. Higher OTC doses marketed in Spain (200 and 400 mg) vs US (200 mg only) hypothesized to explain higher ibuprofen DILI frequency in Spain; threshold dose for idiosyncratic DILI and reactive-metabolite/oxidative-stress/JNK mechanism discussed. A multicenter Italy study reported higher adjusted risk of liver damage for ibuprofen than for diclofenac. Severity: mild 9 (35%), moderate 14 (54%), severe 0, fatal 2 / liver transplant 1 (12%). Hy's law criteria met in 11 (42%). 11 of 13 (85%) resolved within 1 year. No characteristic drug signature; diabetes mellitus trend more common in ibuprofen DILI patients (7, 27%); lower hypertension prevalence (2, 10%).

raw_record.support_text: In this 40-year-old woman who had a history of taking ibuprofen, clinical diagnosis was an ibuprofen-induced liver injury resulting in persistent cholestasis and hyperlipidemia, supported by a RUCAM score of 6 (modest probability of DILI) with severe liver injury (stage III) and a pathology diagnosis of DILI at stage IV with features of bile duct injury and loss of bile duct structures consistent with vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS).
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6 with R=0.32 (grade III/severe liver injury); pathology DILI stage IV; liver biopsy on day 28 showed biliary injury and absence of small terminal bile ducts around hepatic arteries in >50% of portal tracts with bile salt deposition; Ishak necroinflammatory activity score 5 and fibrosis score 2; second biopsy day 213 showed acute VBDS with some autoimmune-hepatitis features; persistent hyperbilirubinemia and hyperlipidemia with no significant improvement after 10-month follow-up; normal PT; viral serology and autoantibodies negative excluding hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, PBC, PSC; concurrent diabetes treated with acarbose and metformin; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid, polyene phosphatidylcholine, silibinin, glutathione.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 lists five patients (cases 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13) with DILI attributed to ibuprofen taken therapeutically for pain or rheumatoid arthritis. The cases show hepatocellular or mixed injury patterns with CIOMS 'Highly probable' or 'Probable' and severity ranging from Mild to Moderate. The study is framed as NSAIDs-induced idiosyncratic liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Five cases. Case 5 (64/F), 600 mg/day for 17 days, onset 10 days, co-meds enalapril, insulin, jaundice, ASMA 1/40, mixed, TB 9xULN, ALT 5.9xULN, ALP 1.7xULN, Moderate hospitalized, resolution 180 days, CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 7 (18/M), 600 mg/day single day, onset 2 days, no co-meds, jaundice, lymphopenia, mixed, TB 7.9xULN, ALT 5.5xULN, ALP 2.6xULN, Moderate hospitalized, lost to follow-up, CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 9 (57/M), 1200 mg/day for 31 days, onset 50 days, co-med glibenclamide, elevated enzymes, hepatocellular, TB 1xULN, ALT 24xULN, ALP 0.9xULN, Mild, lost to follow-up, CIOMS 'Highly probable'. Case 11 (43/M), 1200 mg/day for 8 days, onset 8 days, co-med metronidazole, jaundice, hepatocellular, TB 1.9xULN, ALT 8.2xULN, ALP 1.3xULN, Mild hospitalized, resolution 308 days, CIOMS 'Probable'. Case 13 (41/F, rheumatoid arthritis), 600 mg/day for 3 days, onset 7 days, co-meds diclofenac, paracetamol, diazepam, fluoxetine, elevated enzymes, hepatocellular, TB 1.6xULN, ALT 14xULN, ALP 1.8xULN, Mild, resolution 31 days, CIOMS 'Probable'.

raw_record.support_text: Ibuprofen was attributed to 25 DILI cases with hepatocellular (44%) and mixed (44%) patterns. Fatal cases were reported for ibuprofen among the most frequent causative drugs; 6 (25%) cases met the nR-based Hy's law criteria and 2 (33%) of these had death/liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 25 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 44%/Chol 12%/Mix 44%; female 48%, lymphopenia 23%, eosinophilia 17%; 6 (25%) fulfilled nR-based Hy's law, 2 (33%) true Hy's law (death/liver transplantation).

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of tea-colored urine, jaundice, and anorexia with impaired liver function after taking a single ibuprofen-sustained release capsule the day before onset due to headache. The authors made a diagnosis of liver failure due to taking ibuprofen-sustained release capsules. After 9 days of hepatoprotective and nutritional therapy the symptoms improved, liver function returned to near normal, and follow-up at 2 weeks showed normal liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man; single ibuprofen-sustained release capsule taken the day before symptom onset for headache. Presenting features: 4-day history of tea-colored urine, oil avoidance, jaundiced skin, anorexia, impaired liver function. Diagnosis of liver failure attributed to ibuprofen; hepatotoxic drugs discontinued, then hepatoprotective agents, nutritional support, correction of acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities. Marked improvement after 9 days (no discomfort, subsided jaundice, clear urine, near-normal liver tests), discharged, normal liver function at 2-week follow-up. No formal causality instrument reported.

raw_record.support_text: In the TARGET trial (52-week, double-blind outcomes trial), nine cases of serious liver abnormalities were judged to be probable drug-induced hepatitis: six (0.07%) were associated with the use of lumiracoxib, two (0.05%) with ibuprofen and one (0.02%) with naproxen. The difference between lumiracoxib and the NSAIDs was not statistically significant, and in all cases raised transaminase levels reversed after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Six of nine adjudicated cases of probable drug-induced hepatitis in the TARGET trial (0.07%); raised transaminase levels reversed after drug discontinuation; difference versus NSAIDs not statistically significant. Commentary notes lumiracoxib was studied at a supratherapeutic dose.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA issued a nonapprovable letter for lumiracoxib in 2007, and postmarketing surveillance identified serious instances of DILI not foreseen in clinical trials. In the large TARGET trial, 2.6% had aminotransferase elevations >3× ULN, with six cases of probable or possible clinical hepatitis that all resolved on drug cessation and no reports of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA nonapprovable letter (2007); postmarketing surveillance identified serious DILI not foreseen in trials. TARGET trial: 2.6% AT >3× ULN; six cases of probable/possible clinical hepatitis all resolved; no liver failure. Pharmacogenetic GWAS (Affymetrix 6.0, >900,000 SNPs) in 41 cases (ALT/AST >5× ULN) vs 176 matched controls, validated in 98 cases vs 405 lumiracoxib-exposed controls (ALT/AST >3× ULN), associated lumiracoxib DILI with MHC class II SNPs on chromosome 6 (leading rs9270986, P = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) and extended haplotype HLA-DRB1*1501-HLA-DQB1*0602-HLA-DRB5*0101-HLA-DQA1*0102 (most significant allele P = 6.8 × 10⁻²⁵, OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6-7.0). No similar relationship seen in ibuprofen (n=18) or naproxen (n=9) DILI control cases. All patients with ALT >20× ULN and all three Hy's law (ALT/AST >3× ULN, bilirubin >2 ULN) cases carried the implicated haplotype. HLA-DQA1*0102 had best negative predictive value (99%) and sensitivity (73.6%). Curated table lists HLA-DQA1*0102 OR 6.3 (4.1-9.6) for lumiracoxib DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary states that lumiracoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor, joins the list of NSAIDs withdrawn due to their association with DILI, and reports that lumiracoxib has the potential for rare but serious hepatotoxicity. Worldwide at least 20 cases of severe DILI associated with lumiracoxib have been reported, including 14 with acute liver failure, two deaths, and three liver transplants; most cases occurred several months after starting lumiracoxib, many at daily doses exceeding 100 mg, but severe DILI was also reported at 100 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Selective COX-2 inhibitor developed for osteoarthritis and acute pain; hepatotoxicity contributed to withdrawal/nonapproval in most major markets. At least 20 reported cases of severe DILI, including 14 with acute liver failure, 2 deaths, and 3 liver transplants. Most cases occurred several months after starting lumiracoxib, with early presentations also noted; many cases involved daily doses exceeding 100 mg, but severe DILI also occurred at 100 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: A GWAS on 41 cases of DILI resulting from the NSAID lumiracoxib found a highly significant association (p=6.8×10^-25; allelic OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6–7.0) with an HLA class II haplotype that includes DRB1*1501, and the association was replicated in a further 98 lumiracoxib DILI cases. No independent HLA class I association was found, and lumiracoxib shows good clinical utility apart from rare incidences of DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. GWAS of 41 DILI cases with allelic OR 5.0 (95% CI 3.6–7.0), p=6.8×10^-25, associated with HLA class II haplotype including DRB1*1501; replicated in 98 additional cases. No independent HLA class I association. Pattern of liver injury generally differs from that of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Consideration of genotyping for DRB1*1501 to exclude at-risk patients.

raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor registered in Australia in 2004 at 200 mg daily for osteoarthritis, was associated with severe liver injury: in March 2007 the first Australian patient with fulminant liver failure was admitted and died within a week, followed by two further cases of serious liver injury at the same hospital, one requiring liver transplant. Two cases were reported to the Australian TGA and contributed to eight reports of severe liver injury leading to lumiracoxib's withdrawal from the Australian market in August 2007.
raw_record.extra_details: Three Australian adult female patients treated for osteoarthritis; doses 200-400 mg daily for 3-6 months before symptom onset. Case 1 (63F, 200 mg x 3 months, ~20 g/day alcohol): AST 2123, ALT 3016, AP 754, GGT 393, bilirubin 274 U/L, PT 24 s, ANA 1:640 speckled + anti-ENA (SSA/Ro, SSB/La); biopsy sub-massive hepatic necrosis; fatal. Case 2 (53F, 200-400 mg x 6 months): AST 2150, ALT 1180, AP 393, bilirubin 300 U/L, PT 29 s, ANA 1:2560 nucleolar; severe hepatic necrosis; liver transplant. Case 3 (49F, 200 mg x 6 months): AST 817, ALT 652, AP 344, bilirubin 82 U/L, PT 15 s, ANA 1:640 speckled, IgG anti-cardiolipin 24 U/mL; hepatocellular necrosis; post-necrotic cirrhosis. Jaundice with nausea, dark urine, pale stools, grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy (case 1). Two cases reported to TGA; total 8 TGA reports of severe liver injury; Australian market withdrawal August 2007.

raw_record.support_text: Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced COX-2 inhibitor. All had histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis; one patient died from acute liver failure and another needed a liver transplant. A further five cases of liver injury were reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three women with severe hepatotoxicity and histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis; one died from acute liver failure and another needed a liver transplant. A further five liver-injury cases were reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Lumiracoxib is a cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor; drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity, and many affected individuals were women (noted as not unusual in DILI case series).

raw_record.support_text: Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced COX-2 inhibitor, all with histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis. One patient died from acute liver failure, another needed a liver transplant. Five further cases have been reported to the Australian TGA, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported index cases, all with significant histologic hepatocellular necrosis; one died from acute liver failure, one required liver transplant. Five additional cases reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, with two deaths and two liver transplants. Anti-nuclear antibodies noted in all three cases. GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced liver injury cases vs 176 exposed controls found association with HLA class II markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 had highest sensitivity (73.6%). Health regulators called for withdrawal of lumiracoxib from clinical use. Structurally similar to diclofenac, sharing proclivity for forming reactive hepatotoxic metabolites and glutathione adducts.

raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor developed for osteoarthritis, was shown to be superior to nonselective NSAIDs at reducing ulcer complications, but data from the phase 3 clinical trial showed hepatotoxicity in 2.6% of individuals receiving lumiracoxib. The drug was withdrawn from the market due to rare but fulminant hepatitis. A GWAS carried out in a subgroup of the pivotal efficacy trial identified a significant association between an HLA haplotype (HLA-DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602-DRB5*0101-DQA1*0102) and lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity (P = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁰).
raw_record.extra_details: Selective COX-2 inhibitor for osteoarthritis; hepatotoxicity in 2.6% of individuals in the phase 3 clinical trial; withdrawn from market due to rare but fulminant hepatitis. GWAS in a subgroup of the pivotal trial found HLA-DRB1*1501-DQB1*0602-DRB5*0101-DQA1*0102 haplotype association (P=2.8e-10); DRB1*1501 OR 5.0 (95% CI 3.6-7.0); DQA1*0102 screening sensitivity 74%, negative predictive value 99%; predicted hepatotoxicity incidence would fall to 1.0% for non-carriers.

raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a COX-2 inhibitor, was found to cause idiosyncratic DILI in clinical trials. In the TARGET trial 2.6% of 9,117 randomized patients developed ALT elevations >3x ULN versus 0.6% in the naproxen/ibuprofen arms, with nine cases consistent with Hy's law. It was not approved in the United States; in 2007 Australia's TGA received eight reports of serious liver injury including two deaths and two liver transplants, and several countries withdrew approval in 2007-2008.
raw_record.extra_details: COX-2 inhibitor; TARGET trial 9,117 patients, 2.6% ALT>3x ULN vs 0.6% in naproxen/ibuprofen arms; nine Hy's law cases; cases with ALT increases >5x, 8x, 10x, 15x, 20x ULN. Not approved in the United States; approved and marketed abroad; 2007 Australia TGA received 8 reports of serious liver injury including 2 deaths and 2 liver transplants; approval withdrawn in several countries in 2007-2008.

raw_record.support_text: Detectable titres of serum autoantibodies, mostly antinuclear antibodies, were present in 3 cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity, suggesting an immune-mediated mechanism in the pathogenesis of coxib-induced DILI. A genome-wide association study in 41 cases of lumiracoxib-induced DILI and 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls found a strong association with HLA class II markers, with HLA-DQA1*0102 being the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity had detectable antinuclear antibodies, suggesting an immune-mediated/immune mechanism in the pathogenesis. Genetic susceptibility is supported by a GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced DILI cases versus 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls, with strong association to HLA class II region markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 was the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk. Proposed mechanisms include reactive metabolites generating antigenic drug-protein adducts presented by HLA complexes triggering a T-cell-mediated immune response, or direct interaction of lumiracoxib with the HLA complex.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude by reporting 3 cases of severe drug-induced liver injury secondary to telithromycin, stating it includes, to their knowledge, the first related death and need for orthotopic liver transplantation, and advise caution in prescribing this drug pending further postmarketing surveillance data.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 cases of severe drug-induced liver injury reported by the authors, including the first related death and orthotopic liver transplantation. Pharmacovigilance (FDA AERS) described 10 postmarketing hepatic adverse events with telithromycin, severity from serious to fatal (2 patients died), involving cholestatic hepatitis, abnormal aminotransferase levels, increased bilirubin, liver disorder, cholestatic jaundice, and hepatocellular damage; duration of use 1-30 days, patient ages 35-85 years. Phase III data (Sanofi-Aventis) described 7 cases of hepatitis or hepatocellular damage, with alcohol use, baseline aminotransferase elevations, and hepatitis B virus infection as confounders in 4 cases; all but 1 resolved without sequelae. Prescribing information: ALT>3x ULN in 1.6% and reversible hepatitis with or without jaundice in 0.07%; labels advise caution in patients with a hepatitis or jaundice history. Postmarketing reports of infrequent hepatocellular or cholestatic hepatitis with and without jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: In January 2006, three reported cases of severe telithromycin hepatotoxicity prompted an FDA label revision warning of potential severe liver injury. The cases developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes within 2-7 days of starting telithromycin; one had enzymes >10x ULN that normalized within 8 weeks, a second required orthotopic liver transplantation, and a third died. Three additional cases were reported to FDA Medwatch. An editorial compared the reported acute liver failure rate with telithromycin as greater than trovafloxacin and troglitazone and similar to bromfenac. FDA removed bronchitis and sinusitis indications in February 2007.
raw_record.extra_details: Three index cases of severe hepatotoxicity: jaundice and elevated liver enzymes within 2-7 days of therapy; one normalized within 8 weeks after stopping, one required orthotopic liver transplantation, one died. Three additional FDA Medwatch cases. Reported acute liver failure rate described as greater than trovafloxacin and troglitazone and similar to bromfenac. FDA label revision Jan 2006; Feb 2007 removed bronchitis and sinusitis indications, now only for community-acquired pneumonia.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old male patient presented with jaundice, malaise, and vomiting shortly after receiving telithromycin, and reported similar complaints 11 months prior when he was diagnosed with telithromycin-related toxic hepatitis. At the second occurrence the diagnosis was confirmed by liver biopsy, and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale gave a score of 8, indicating telithromycin was the probable cause of acute hepatitis in this patient. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were excluded, and histology showed hydropic degeneration, hepatic necrosis around the central vein, and hepatocellular and canalicular bile cholestasis; the patient recovered after telithromycin was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 25-year-old male; dechallenge-rechallenge (two separate exposures to telithromycin) with hepatic event recurred on rechallenge ~11 months later, supporting causality. Telithromycin 400 mg/d was used for an upper respiratory tract infection and for community-acquired pneumonia. Naranjo score 8 = probable cause of acute hepatitis. Liver biopsy at second event showed hydropic degeneration, hepatic necrosis around the central vein, and hepatocellular and canalicular bile cholestasis, suggesting drug-induced toxic hepatitis. Viral (hepatitis A/B/C, mononucleosis, HIV), autoimmune (ANA, AMA, ASMA, liver-kidney microsomal) and metabolic (ceruloplasmin, iron, ferritin) causes excluded; abdominal ultrasound showed a benign hemangioma. Lab peaks at second exposure: AST 71 U/L, ALT 98 U/L, TB 20.08 mg/dL, DB 14.75 mg/dL, ALP 513 U/L, GGT 32 U/L; recovery of bilirubin within ~2 months. Patient also had jaundice, malaise, and vomiting.

raw_record.support_text: An ad hoc group adjudicated 42 spontaneous reports of liver injury associated with telithromycin reported to the FDA as of April 2006. Five cases had severe outcomes (4 deaths, 1 liver transplantation); more than half were considered highly likely or probable in causal association with telithromycin. Typical clinical features were short latency (median 10 days) with abrupt onset of fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice, sometimes with ascites. The paper concludes that telithromycin is a rare cause of drug-induced liver injury with a distinctive clinical signature and associated high mortality rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Ketolide antibiotic approved by the FDA in 2004 for upper and lower respiratory infections, dosed 800 mg once daily. 42 cases comprehensively reviewed and adjudicated by an expert group; 5 severe outcomes (4 deaths, 1 liver transplantation); >half considered highly likely or probable. Typical features: median latency 10 days, abrupt onset fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, sometimes ascites. In December 2006 FDA indications reduced to community-acquired pneumonia only. Pre-marketing development included one case of significant hepatocellular injury with eosinophilia and high aminotransferases 10 days after a 10-day course, and mild cholestatic liver injury in European/Latin American post-marketing reports. About 5.2 million US prescriptions dispensed July 2004-April 2006.

raw_record.support_text: Telithromycin is the first and only ketolide approved for clinical use. In Phase III trials mild-to-moderate ALT increases occurred at higher frequency than placebo. After US launch, three cases of serious liver injury with jaundice and significantly elevated liver enzymes occurred in patients given telithromycin for minor upper respiratory infections; one recovered, one required liver transplantation, and one died. The FDA issued a boxed warning and drastically restricted the indication to community-acquired pneumonia.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious liver injury with jaundice and significantly elevated liver enzymes (>10x ULN in one case) in three patients treated for minor upper respiratory infections; one recovered, one required liver transplantation, one died. An analysis of 12 cases showed a rare unusual form of hepatotoxicity with short latency, systemic symptoms and, in some cases, significant ascites. FDA boxed warning and restriction to community-acquired pneumonia; EMA added alterations in hepatic enzymes, severe hepatitis, and liver failure to Special warnings. Designed against macrolide-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; mild-to-moderate ALT increases more frequent than placebo in Phase III trials.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA strengthened its warning on the risk of liver toxicity when using telithromycin, the first FDA-approved ketolide. De novo hepatotoxicity developed within a few days following treatment with telithromycin in three individuals with previously normal liver test results, and the authors judged the adverse drug reactions as probably but not definitely related to telithromycin. The ketolide class (telithromycin, cethromycin, solithromycin) is discussed, but the liver-toxicity warning specifically concerns telithromycin.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA strengthened its warning on the risk of liver toxicity for telithromycin, the first FDA-approved ketolide. De novo hepatotoxicity developed within a few days following treatment in three individuals with previously normal liver test results; the authors judged the adverse drug reactions as probably but not definitely related to telithromycin. The FDA also strengthened warnings on telithromycin-related visual disturbances and loss of consciousness. The ketolides include telithromycin, cethromycin and solithromycin; fluoroketolides K-1602, K-1636, K-1835, K-1804, HMR-3562 and HMR-3787 are also mentioned, but no liver-toxicity claim is made for them.

raw_record.support_text: AstraZeneca decided to withdraw its anticoagulant Exanta (ximelagatran) following safety concerns related to liver toxicity. Phase III trials had raised questions about liver toxicity, and AstraZeneca pulled the drug after discovering a new case of serious liver injury in an ongoing trial examining use over 35 days. All clinical trials were ended and regulatory applications withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Exanta; anticoagulant positioned as an alternative to warfarin. Phase III trials showed efficacy comparable to warfarin and low-molecular-weight heparin for deep vein thrombosis and stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, but raised liver toxicity questions. Withdrawal triggered by a new case of serious liver injury in an ongoing trial examining treatment over 35 days; all clinical trials were ended and all regulatory applications withdrawn.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran (36 mg bid) was as effective as warfarin in preventing stroke and systemic embolism in the SPORTIF III and V trials, but a higher proportion of treated patients had alanine aminotransferase levels three times the upper limit of normal with associated bilirubin elevation (6.1% vs 0.8% on warfarin). Three of these patients developed fatal hepatotoxicity, which led to FDA rejection and termination of drug development.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral prodrug of melagatran, direct thrombin inhibitor. SPORTIF III and V trials; ALT at least 3x ULN with associated bilirubin elevation in 6.1% of ximelagatran-treated patients versus 0.8% on warfarin; three patients developed fatal hepatotoxicity; FDA approval not granted due to liver toxicity and development terminated. Table 1 lists ximelagatran as not granted FDA approval due to liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: During the ximelagatran trial programme, cases of severe hepatic toxicity were recorded, along with a risk of abnormal liver enzyme elevations (alanine aminotransferase, ALT, at least three times the upper limit of normal) in 6.1% of treated patients vs 0.8% on warfarin. In 2004 ximelagatran was rejected by the US FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee and subsequently withdrawn by AstraZeneca following the EXTEND study data due to fear of severe liver toxicity; the EXTEND study was terminated after just 3 weeks of recruitment because of one case of severe acute liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Ximelagatran (pro-drug of melagatran) investigated in clinical trials since 1999 for acute DVT with/without PE. Severe hepatic toxicity cases and ALT >=3x ULN risk (6.1% vs 0.8% for warfarin) emerged during the trial programme; numerical but non-significant increase in myocardial infarction events after cessation. Rejected by US FDA Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee in 2004 and withdrawn by AstraZeneca following EXTEND data; EXTEND (evaluation of extended prophylactic treatment with melagatran/ximelagatran vs enoxaparin) was terminated after 3 weeks due to one case of severe acute liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor formerly investigated for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, is no longer marketed because of liver toxicity, although it demonstrated efficacy in two large phase III clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: No longer marketed because of liver toxicity; demonstrated efficacy in two large phase III clinical trials for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that Exanta 3 (ximelagatran), the prodrug of melagatran 2 and the only orally available drug for treating thrombosis disorders at the time, was approved for limited uses in Europe but was withdrawn from the market overall because of the liver toxicity found in recent clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Ximelagatran (Exanta 3) is the orally available prodrug of melagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor; liver toxicity observed in clinical trials led to its overall market withdrawal. It had been approved for limited uses in Europe.

raw_record.support_text: In the search for novel anticoagulants, ximelagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, caused unacceptable rates of liver toxicity compared with warfarin in the SPORTIF V trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct thrombin inhibitor; hepatic safety evaluated in the randomized SPORTIF V trial for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation/stroke prevention; rates of liver toxicity were unacceptable and comparable to warfarin, prompting the pursuit of alternative agents.

raw_record.support_text: When compared with warfarin in the SPORTIF III and V trials, the oral direct thrombin inhibitor ximelagatran was found to be effective with an acceptable bleeding risk, but its development was stopped due to liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor under evaluation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; reported effective with acceptable bleeding risk in SPORTIF III and V trials relative to warfarin, but clinical development was halted due to liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study of 74 cases and 130 controls, AstraZeneca identified HLA-DRB1*0701 as the major genetic risk factor associated with ximelagatran drug-induced liver injury (DILI), which led to the drug's withdrawal soon after its introduction on the market.
raw_record.extra_details: HLA-DRB1*0701 identified as the major genetic risk factor for ximelagatran DILI in a retrospective study (74 cases, 130 controls; OR 4, PPV 61%, NPV 73%); DILI led to market withdrawal shortly after introduction, highlighting the need for systematic DNA banking during drug development.

raw_record.support_text: In the section on direct thrombin inhibitors, the paper states that the first DTI phase III trial was with ximelagatran, but hepatotoxicity, in the absence of adequately planned follow-up laboratory checks in the study design, led to the forced withdrawal of the drug from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: First DTI phase III trial; hepatotoxicity occurred in the absence of adequately planned follow-up laboratory checks in the study design, and led to the forced withdrawal of the drug from the market. No clinical severity (e.g., liver failure) is stated.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelgatran (ximelagatran), the first novel direct thrombin inhibitor developed in 2006 following warfarin, was found to cause significant hepatic injury during phase III clinical trials and as a result never achieved United States marketing approval.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct thrombin inhibitor developed in 2006; described as causing significant hepatic injury during phase III clinical trials, after which it never achieved US marketing approval. The paper spells the drug name 'ximelgatran'; matched to ximelagatran.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary states that 'Ximelagatran was stopped because of hepatic injury during clinical trials,' indicating that the drug's development was halted due to drug-induced liver injury observed in clinical trial subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Ximelagatran's development was stopped because of hepatic injury (drug-induced liver injury) encountered during clinical trials, which prevented marketing.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, developed for long-term and short-term use, caused serious hepatotoxicity in long-term clinical trials. Among 6,948 treated patients, 7.6% and 1.1% developed ALT increases >3x and >10x ULN respectively, and 0.5% had concurrent total bilirubin >2x ULN versus 0.08% for warfarin. Among the 37 ximelagatran-associated cases (13 with no alternative etiology) there were three deaths linked to liver injury, and a comprehensive review judged ximelagatran-induced serious hepatotoxicity 'highly likely' a cause in one death. The initial NDA was not approved in 2004 and the drug was withdrawn from all markets in 2006 after a severe hepatotoxicity case in an orthopedic surgery trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Direct thrombin inhibitor; indications included secondary prevention of VTE, prevention of atrial fibrillation-associated thromboembolism, and postoperative thromboembolic risk after total knee replacement. In long-term trials 7.6% ALT>3x ULN, 1.1% ALT>10x ULN, 0.5% concurrent bilirubin>2x ULN vs 0.08% warfarin; 37 cases, 13 without alternative etiology, 3 deaths linked to liver injury; causality review found 'highly likely' cause in one death. NDA not approved by FDA in 2004; withdrawn from all markets in 2006 after severe hepatotoxicity case in an orthopedic surgery trial during extended treatment over 35 days.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor developed for prevention and treatment of thromboembolic conditions, had its pending FDA and EMA marketing applications withdrawn in February 2006 due to reports of abnormal liver tests and DILI during clinical trials. In trial data, 7.9% of treated patients had ALT >3x ULN versus 1.2% of the comparator group; combined ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN occurred in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 of whom had no alternative cause, and one of these patients sustained severe liver damage with liver failure and eventually died.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor for prevention/treatment of thromboembolic conditions; pending FDA and EMA applications withdrawn February 2006 due to abnormal liver tests and DILI in clinical trials; ALT>3x ULN in 7.9% vs 1.2% comparator; combined ALT>3x ULN plus TBL>2x ULN in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 with no alternative cause, one of whom had severe liver damage with liver failure and died; already approved in several European and South American countries at time of FDA withdrawal; animal studies and primary human hepatocyte cultures showed no hepatotoxic effects even at concentrations considerably above therapeutic plasma levels; cellular mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor, was found to cause severe hepatic injury, with several cases meeting Hy's Law criteria, in longer-term clinical trials. Pharmacogenomic studies identified increased risk of serum ALT elevations in patients with HLA-DRB1*07 and DQA1*02 genotypes, possibly through activation of the host's immune response.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatic injury with several cases meeting Hy's Law criteria in longer-term clinical trials; genetic predisposition - HLA-DRB1*07 and DQA1*02 genotypes increase risk of serum ALT elevations, possibly via activation of the host's immune response; exact cause of injury unknown.

raw_record.support_text: In discussing DOACs and liver injury, the paper states that early clinical trials showed Ximelagatran (factor IIa inhibitor) resulted in significant hepatotoxicity and that the drug was subsequently withdrawn from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Factor IIa inhibitor; resulted in significant hepatotoxicity in early clinical trials and was subsequently withdrawn from the market. Contrasted with a meta-analysis of more than 29 RCTs finding no significant DILI risk for currently used DOACs.

raw_record.support_text: In 2006, after reports of hepatotoxicity, the FDA halted clinical development of ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor intended for prevention or treatment of thromboembolic conditions, due to concerns about DILI. The paper uses this programme's extensive clinical trial data to describe the clinical signature of ximelagatran-associated liver injury and confirms that the DILI-CAT algorithm clearly identified a DILI signal for ximelagatran.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor (Factor IIa inhibitor) designed for prevention or treatment of thromboembolic conditions; FDA halted clinical development in 2006 after reports of hepatotoxicity due to DILI concerns. DILI-CAT (data-driven algorithmic causality tool) identified a DILI signal for ximelagatran using clinical trial data. The intended setting was early drug development signal detection; ximelagatran is used as an example drug with a known potential hepatotoxicity phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with bone mycetoma being treated with oral voriconazole developed cholestasis after the first month (alkaline phosphatase 616 IU/l; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1126 IU/l) with mild cytolysis (AST up to ~3N, ALT 2–3N). After 18 months of treatment she presented right hypochondrium tenderness and significant cytolysis (ALT 17N, AST 8N) with normal prothrombin time; infectious and autoimmune causes were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed lesions compatible with toxic hepatitis. Voriconazole was stopped on 25 September; hepatic enzymes returned to normal within one week and cholestasis markedly diminished within four weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dosing was 400 mg twice daily for 2 days then 200 mg twice daily (Pfizer, Paris, France). raw_record.support_text: This cohort study of voriconazole-treated patients found that voriconazole-related liver injury was associated with serum trough concentration; in the present study the critical trough concentration above which liver injury likely occurred was 4.375 mg/L, consistent with published meta-analyses and prior reports showing increased liver injury incidence at troughs above 3.0-6.0 mg/L.

Adding voriconazole early after lung transplantation increased liver injury risk (OR 4.37, 95% CI 1.53-12.43, p=0.006). Transplant status was negatively related to liver injury, attributed to closer monitoring. Patients with severe infections showing systemic inflammation (n=64) were excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The RUCAM score was 6 for the first case, which would make atomoxetine a probable cause of liver injury. The first case patient showed marked improvement coincident with discontinuation of the medication.

These cases were deemed sufficient evidence of an increased risk of liver toxicity to warrant a 2004 label change for atomoxetine. Considering the now extensive exposure (>4 million patients after 4 years), these reactions are very rare and fit the pattern of an idiosyncratic drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the death of a 64-year-old man from acute hepatic failure attributable to beclobrate, a lipid-lowering agent. raw_record.support_text: A non-alcoholic, previously healthy 49-year-old man was put on tienilic acid 250 mg daily for mild hypertension. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, cytomegalovirus, herpesvirus) and HIV serology were negative, and high titres (500) of liver/kidney microsomal type 2 autoantibodies, considered specific for tienilic acid hepatotoxicity, were detected. Authors note the drug has a poor risk/benefit ratio and puts patients at risk of severe acute or chronic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (Ticrynafen), a uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension, was associated with drug-associated hepatotoxicity characterized by fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, raised serum transaminases, and a histological picture resembling viral hepatitis. raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used for hypertension; withdrawn from US sale in 1980. 340 reported instances of hepatic injury likely drug related in ~265,000 exposed (US frequency ~1 in 800 vs France ~1 in 10,000; difference attributed in part to a slightly greater amount of tienilic acid isomer in the US preparation). Features: fever, jaundice, elevated serum transaminases (max rise 2013 IU/l), histology resembling viral hepatitis, prompt recurrence on rechallenge, eosinophils on liver histology, and anti-LKM2 autoantibodies (ceasing within 3-9 months of stopping drug). Patients in the antibody study: 40 with presumed tienilic acid hepatotoxicity (17 men, ages 32-84, median 69; median dose 250 mg/day, range 125-500; abnormal LFTs first noted 30 days to 4 years after start, median 3 months; 24 had jaundice; 25 had anti-LKM2). Sera from 16/36 tested induced significant ADCC against hepatocytes from rabbits pretreated with BNF then tienilic acid, suggesting sensitization to drug-altered liver cell determinants.

raw_record.support_text: Case 51 was attributed to tienilic acid-induced hepatitis, with chronic active hepatitis (CAH) on biopsy, maximum serum bilirubin 361 µmol/l, 2 years of treatment, and the diagnosis supported by the presence of serum anti-liver/kidney microsome antibodies of type 2 specifically associated with hepatitis due to tienilic acid.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (ticrynofen), 2,3-dichloro-4-(2-thenoyl)phenoxy acetic acid, is a uricosuric diuretic whose association with severe liver damage was analyzed in 340 cases by Zimmerman et al. The high frequency of hepatotoxicity led to withdrawal of the drug in the United States and other countries. Homberg and colleagues reported as many as 67 cases, with death in the acute phase in 11; histology in 36 biopsies did not correspond with chronic active hepatitis, and anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response occurred in about 50% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic; 340 cases analyzed by Zimmerman et al.; 67 cases reported by Homberg with 11 acute-phase deaths; histologic changes in 36 biopsies not consistent with chronic active hepatitis; delayed recovery in 14 cases responded to prednisolone and azathioprine; anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response in ~50% of cases; high hepatotoxicity frequency led to drug withdrawal in the US and other countries.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (TA), a uricosuric diuretic used to treat hypertension, was first marketed in Europe in 1976 and introduced in the US in 1979, then rapidly withdrawn from the US market in 1980 because of its hepatotoxic secondary effects. The incidence and clinical features of 340 reported cases supported an immune mechanism for TA-induced hepatitis, and a specific autoantibody (anti-LKM2, directed against a liver-kidney microsomal component) was detected only in patients with TA-induced hepatitis, serving as a specific marker.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension; marketed in Europe 1976, US 1979, withdrawn from US market 1980 due to hepatotoxic effects; 340 reported cases of hepatitis supporting an immune (immunoallergic) mechanism; specific anti-LKM2 autoantibody against a liver-kidney microsomal (endoplasmic reticulum) component, a specific marker of TA-induced hepatitis; TA was devoid of direct hepatotoxic effect in laboratory animals.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid, an uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension, was withdrawn from the market because of cases of rare but severe hepatotoxicity. Between 0.1% and 0.7% of treated patients developed clinical hepatitis; the reaction occurred with significant delay and was dose independent. Liver damage resolved after discontinuation and recurred on rechallenge. In 60% of patients with severe hepatitis after tienilic acid, a specific anti-liver/kidney microsome type 2 (LKM-2) autoantibody targeting cytochrome P450 2C9 was detected.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic formerly used for hypertension; withdrawn from market for hepatotoxicity. Clinical hepatitis in 0.1-0.7% of treated patients; reaction delayed and dose independent; resolved on discontinuation, recurred on rechallenge. LKM-2 autoantibody against unmodified liver/kidney microsomal proteins detected in 60% of severe cases, target cytochrome P450 2C9 (major tienilic acid metabolizing enzyme).

raw_record.support_text: An 80-year-old man developed symptomatic liver disease 6 weeks after 1 x 75 mg/day clopidogrel intake as adjunctive antiplatelet therapy for a renal artery stent implantation. Histological examination revealed severe acute hepatitis with extensive hepatocanalicular cholestasis and focal cell necrosis with preferential zone-3 distribution, and the case is presented as clopidogrel-induced acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 80-year-old man; 75 mg/day clopidogrel for 43 days after percutaneous transarterial angiography with renal artery stent implantation; symptomatic disease (weight loss, lack of appetite, jaundice, nausea) at 6 weeks. Liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with hepatocanalicular cholestasis, focal necrosis in zone 3, cholestatic pseudorosettes, apoptosis, moderate portal/periportal inflammation with eosinophils, and suppurative cholangiolitis. Five prior clopidogrel-associated liver injury cases discussed in the literature (mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic or predominantly hepatocellular by lab findings without histologic confirmation); clopidogrel is a thienopyridine activated by CYP3A4.

raw_record.support_text: A score of 14 out of 20 on the Maria and Victorino scale (temporal relationship, exclusion of alternate causes, positive rechallenge test, prior case reports) established a probable diagnostic relationship between clopidogrel and mixed hepatocellular injury and cholestatic jaundice in the patient, who was reexposed to clopidogrel after drug-eluting stent placement. The paper reviews 13 total published cases of clopidogrel-induced hepatotoxicity (12 prior plus this case), with onset 3 days to 6 months after starting clopidogrel for coronary artery disease; nine cases were mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic injury, three predominantly hepatocellular, and one presented with systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of clopidogrel-induced hepatocellular injury and cholestatic jaundice with positive rechallenge (drug reintroduced on day 5, discontinued again on day 9 with subsequent improvement of AST to 193 U/L, ALT to 326 U/L, and total bilirubin to 5.5 mg/dl by day 12). Maria and Victorino validated scale score 14/20 (probable) applied to the index patient; scale was also applied in six of the reviewed cases and liver biopsy in three. Among 13 published cases (6 men, 7 women, age 50-89, mean 70.4 +- 12.3 yrs, clopidogrel 75 mg/day), one patient (hepatocellular pattern) died; all others recovered over 1 week-6 months. Nine cases were mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic injury, three predominantly hepatocellular, one SIRS. Possible dose-independent idiosyncratic and dose-dependent toxic reactions postulated in one biopsied patient. Concomitant drugs (simvastatin, omeprazole, lansoprazole, metoprolol, allopurinol, valsartan) were ruled out as culprits by prolonged prior use without adverse effects; clopidogrel and allopurinol were initially discontinued together. Pharmacologic background: second-generation thienopyridine inhibiting P2Y12 receptor after hepatic cytochrome P450 biotransformation.

raw_record.support_text: A patient's liver histopathology, initially thought consistent with primary biliary cirrhosis, was reviewed after his medication chart revealed he had received clopidogrel intermittently since Day 10 despite a request to cease it. Clopidogrel-induced granulomatous hepatitis was then diagnosed; clopidogrel was ceased permanently and the patient was discharged, with liver function completely normalised at follow-up about 2 months later.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosed granulomatous hepatitis (histology showed poorly formed granulomas in hepatic lobules, marked cholangiolitis with neutrophils surrounding small bile ducts in portal tracts, and relatively mild hepatocyte death), accompanied by systemic inflammatory response syndrome. Direct temporal relationship between clopidogrel administration and symptoms/signs/LFT abnormalities on three separate occasions was highly suggestive of causality, with clinical improvement each time clopidogrel was ceased. LFTs normalised at ~2-month follow-up with no recurrence. Reported as the second documented case of clopidogrel-induced hepatic injury histopathology (first reported 2006). Paper notes clopidogrel-associated LFT derangement has included hepatocellular and mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns, and that 15 cases of hepatic injury associated with clopidogrel were reported to the Australian ADRAC since 2000; this adverse effect appears rare. Other differential diagnoses of hepatic granulomas (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, primary biliary cirrhosis) were excluded.

raw_record.support_text: According to the International Consensus Meeting, the type of liver damage in this case was hepatocellular. Applying the CIOMS (Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences) score, the causality assessment of clopidogrel-induced liver injury was probable, based on no history of liver or biliary disease, negative diagnostic work-up excluding other causes of acute hepatitis, clopidogrel being the recently added drug, worsening of liver injury during drug administration, and resolution-linked evidence; the presence of thrombocytopenia (a known clopidogrel side effect) provided additional evidence of drug involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: A 63-year-old man with diabetes and ischaemic disease, on chronic human insulin, captopril, molsidomine, simvastatin and aspirin (>3 years without adverse reaction), started clopidogrel 75 mg daily for percutaneous coronary stenting. Nineteen days after starting clopidogrel he developed tea-coloured urine and jaundice; he was hospitalized on day 54 (clopidogrel and all other drugs stopped) and died on day 56 after grade IV encephalopathy, significant haemoptysis, and 2 days after hospitalization. Autopsy not performed. Liver biochemistries on day 54/day 56: total bilirubin 78/80 µmol/L, ALT 336/297 U/L, AST 303/208 U/L, GGT 160/156 U/L, ALP 186/185 U/L, prothrombin time 27%/28%. Thrombocytopenia 90×10³/mm³; negative viral/autoimmune serologies; normal liver and biliary tract on ultrasound; CIOMS causality score = probable.

raw_record.support_text: Only 12 cases of clopidogrel hepatotoxicity are described in the literature, in eight men and four women aged 56-89 who developed liver injury 4 days to 6 months after clopidogrel intake. The liver injury pattern was mainly mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic, though hepatocellular injury and systemic inflammatory response syndrome with hepatic injury also occurred. The reported index case exhibited liver failure documented by factor V and prothrombin time alterations, and a separate recent published case of clopidogrel liver injury had a fatal outcome.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 reported human cases (8 men, 4 women, aged 56-89) with onset 4 days to 6 months after intake; patterns: mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic (mainly), hepatocellular, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome with hepatic injury; one index case with liver failure (low factor V, prolonged prothrombin time) at the peak of cytolytic lesion; one separate fatal case with fulminant hepatitis; authors note this rare adverse reaction can evolve to fulminant hepatitis if the drug is not discontinued early.

raw_record.support_text: Clopidogrel (Plavix) is reported to cause a rare severe cholestatic hepatitis. The authors describe a 34-year-old male on aspirin and clopidogrel for coronary artery disease who developed jaundice 4 months after re-starting clopidogrel, with AST peaking at 2,107 U/L, ALT at 1,562 U/L, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL, and prothrombin time 19.8; other etiologies (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, immune panel) were negative. Liver biopsy showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate mainly of neutrophils with plasma cells and proliferation of bile ducts. After clopidogrel discontinuation, progressive cholestasis led to a trial of steroids plus ursodiol, followed by rapid normalization of liver tests. The discussion states the patient had severe cholestatic hepatitis due to clopidogrel, with onset in reports ranging from 4-180 days and a possible idiosyncratic toxic-metabolic mechanism with a superimposed immune-mediated component.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 34-year-old male with coronary artery disease (and remote coronary stent) treated with aspirin and clopidogrel; prior 2-month clopidogrel course 12 years earlier without adverse effect. Latency approximately 4 months after re-starting. Peak AST 2,107 U/L, ALT 1,562 U/L, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 19.8; no peripheral eosinophilia. Imaging (ultrasound, CT, ERCP) negative for obstruction. Biopsy showed mixed inflammatory infiltrate predominantly neutrophils with plasma cells and bile duct proliferation. Co-medications aspirin and metoprolol had been used for years with normal liver tests (aspirin, metoprolol and other etiologies excluded). Received empiric vitamin K; progressive cholestasis and rising INR led to steroids plus ursodiol with rapid normalization of LFTs. Literature-reported onset 4-180 days; one prior case associated with rash, fever, and leukopenia. Mechanism proposed as idiosyncratic toxic-metabolic with possible superimposed immune-mediated component.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with clopidogrel-induced severe hepatitis. After discontinuing clopidogrel, AST increased to 2,107 U/L, ALT to 1,567 U/L, and bilirubin to 37 mg/dL (predominately direct), and INR rose to 2.1 despite empiric vitamin K. A brief course of prednisone and ursodiol led to normalization of liver biochemistries.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with mixed inflammatory portal tract infiltrates (plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils), bile ductular reaction, patchy hepatocyte ballooning degeneration, and extensive periportal hepatocyte dropout without fibrosis. Peak ALT 1,567 U/L, AST 2,107 U/L, bilirubin 37 mg/dL (predominantly direct), INR 2.1 with coagulopathy and jaundice. Naranjo and RUCAM scores both 8, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis. Patient treated with prednisone and ursodiol and recovered with normalization of liver biochemistries. Prior reported clopidogrel-induced hepatitis cases range from reversible injury and recovery to acute hepatic failure and death, with onset between 3 and 180 days and rechallenge-confirmed injury in some cases; clopidogrel liver injury has been reported as cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed.

raw_record.support_text: A 50-year-old woman developed jaundice and right upper quadrant pain after taking nitrofurantoin 50 mg once daily for 12 months. Liver biopsy revealed autoimmune chronic active hepatitis with mild fibrosis, consistent with immune-mediated drug-induced liver injury. After nitrofurantoin was suspended and prednisolone started, ALT declined and liver function normalized within two months.

Viral serology negative; gallstones on ultrasound but otherwise unremarkable; MRCP excluded biliary obstruction. Treatment with prednisolone 20 mg daily led to recovery with normal liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, nitrofurantoin was the third most common individual DILI agent, accounting for 42 of 899 adjudicated cases. It was a predominant cause (16 cases) among the 60 cases with latency greater than 1 year.
raw_record.extra_details: 42 adjudicated DILI cases; predominant cause (n=16) among cases with latency >1 year.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin is identified among the most common single implicated antimicrobial agents causing DILI in the DILIN cohort and appears in the top ten drugs of the DILIN, Icelandic, and Spanish prospective studies (in at least two of the three studies).
raw_record.extra_details: Antibiotic; among most common single implicated antimicrobial agents in DILIN (with amoxicillin–clavulanate, isoniazid, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole); listed in Table 1 with more than 100 reported DILI cases (LiverTox).

raw_record.support_text: Of the 82 patients identified with AIH, 11 (13.4%) were considered to have drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH), with RUCAM scores probable for all 11 cases (6-8). The implicated drugs included nitrofurantoin (n=4), statins (n=4), herbal remedies (n=2; Echinacea and valerian), and diclofenac (n=1).
raw_record.extra_details: 4 of 11 DIAIH cases attributed to nitrofurantoin, with RUCAM causality 'probable' (score 6-8) for all DIAIH cases. Mean duration of drug use prior to DIAIH diagnosis was 23.1 +/- 15.6 months for the DIAIH group. Nitrofurantoin cases were older, had lower ALT and higher fibrosis stage at presentation; the drug was discontinued only after specialist review, and none relapsed despite shorter immunosuppression duration.

raw_record.support_text: In an ALFSG cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF and APAP-ALF groups, nitrofurantoin was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity progressing to acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized clinical and autoimmune features of liver injury caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine, using 88 cases of DILI attributed to these agents in the DILIN prospective study (2004-2014).
raw_record.extra_details: 82% of cases attributed to nitrofurantoin had an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score >= 2). 74% of all 88 cases had hepatocellular injury and 25% had severe injury; 91% of cases were women. Autoimmune features (ANA, SMA, IgG) decreased with recovery; no association with HLA-DRB1*03:01 or *04:01 vs controls.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 11 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: A female patient who previously scored 6 points on the simplified AIH score (a false positive) had her hepatitis detected in relation to use of nitrofurantoin. The patient suspended the drug and received a short course of corticoids with an excellent response; after 5 years of follow-up she is asymptomatic with normal liver tests, and for that reason the definitive diagnosis was DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case identified as a false positive in the simplified AIH diagnostic score (6 points). Drug was discontinued and patient received a short course of corticosteroids with an excellent response; she was asymptomatic with normal liver tests after 5 years of follow-up. The 'hepatitis' was reported as hepatitis without a canonical biochemical pattern. Corticosteroid and ursodeoxycholic acid are mentioned only as treatments for other cases, not as DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: De Boer et al. characterized autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) secondary to nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine in DILI cases, defining an autoimmune phenotype as an autoimmune score ≥2. For nitrofurantoin, an autoimmune phenotype was present in the majority of cases (83%), and the typical AIH HLA alleles HLA-DRB1*03:01 and HLA-DRB1*04:01 were found at rates similar to the general population.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases from the US DILIN prospective study; autoimmune phenotype (score ≥2 based on ANA, SMA, SLA, IgG) present in 83% of nitrofurantoin cases; AIH-associated HLA-DRB1*03:01 and HLA-DRB1*04:01 allele frequencies similar to the general population. Nitrofurantoin is one of the drugs for which the modified lymphocyte transformation test was found not reliable for diagnosing DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Among antibiotic-related acute liver failure, nitrofurantoin was implicated in n=1 case of DILI leading to ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin was implicated in 4.5% of drug-induced liver injury cases in the Pro-Euro-DILI registry.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 4.5% of Pro-Euro-DILI cases; also among leading causes in DILIN (4.7%) and Icelandic (4.2%) columns.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of definite causality of nitrofurantoin with autoimmune-like hepatitis, concurrent with interstitial lung disease, describing it as an uncommon combination of nitrofurantoin toxicity present in 10-18% of nitrofurantoin-associated hepatotoxicity series.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as definite causality in a case of nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis concurrent with interstitial lung disease. Autoimmune hepatitis shows female predominance (86-100%), and 38.5% occur in elderly patients >65 years, with age a possible risk factor for chronic injury. Liver biochemistry showed a hepatocellular injury pattern as most frequent (67-71%) with occasional cholestasis; nuclear antibodies (80-82%), smooth muscle antibodies (55-73%), and lupus erythematosus cells (50%) were frequent in chronic cases. A mechanism involving a breakdown product or nitrofurantoin presented to class I HLA activating cytotoxic T cells was proposed. EudraVigilance data: from 7,868 nitrofurantoin adverse reactions, 740 (9.4%) had hepatobiliary disorders, including 78 autoimmune hepatitis cases, with most reported as acute or chronic unspecified liver injury. Recovery after 1-2 months following withdrawal in almost all reviewed cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study's case series describes DILI induced by nitrofurantoin. 52% of patients were asymptomatic at presentation with liver profile elevations, while jaundice (55%) was the most frequent clinical manifestation. A predominance of hepatocellular-type liver injury was found (83%), and positive autoantibodies were frequent (antinuclear antibodies in 64% of cases, of which 29% also had positive ASMA titres). Most cases were mild to moderate, with neither deaths nor liver transplantations, and nitrofurantoin-induced liver injury is rarely associated with severe liver injury and cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of nitrofurantoin-induced DILI. 52% asymptomatic at presentation; jaundice was most frequent clinical manifestation (55%); hepatocellular pattern in 83%; positive ANA in 64% of cases (29% also ASMA-positive). Most cases mild to moderate with no deaths or liver transplantations; rarely associated with severe liver injury and cirrhosis. Time to full liver-profile recovery was >90 days in 44% of cases, with 17% not recovered within six months; longer recovery group included cholestatic cases with ALP elevations decreasing less rapidly than ALT. Five cases were classified as nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (NI-AILH) after prospective expert evaluation, with characteristics similar to 42 nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune-phenotype cases in the US DILIN registry; one NI-AILH case relapsed four years later without reexposure and received long-term corticosteroid plus azathioprine. Extended nitrofurantoin therapy (>180 days) was associated with increased risk of severe pulmonary and hepatic events in a meta-analysis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that certain drugs causing DILI are commonly associated with formation of serum autoantibodies, and cites the Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) Network prospective study in which de Boer et al. found positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at the onset of DILI caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine. This identifies nitrofurantoin as a human DILI-causing agent.
raw_record.extra_details: In the DILI Network prospective study, nitrofurantoin-induced DILI was associated with positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at onset of injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 28 drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-AILH) patients, nitrofurantoin was the most frequent implicated drug (n=7) followed by tetracycline antibiotics (minocycline n=4 and lymecycline n=2). The commonest drug classes were antibiotics (n=18), biologics (n=4, comprising infliximab and adalimumab), and herbal products (n=4). Most patients scored RUCAM 6-8 (probable DILI) and the rest 3-5 (possible DILI).
raw_record.extra_details: Most frequent drug implicated (n=7 cases, patients 5,13,14,15,16,17,18); doses 50-100 mg with durations up to 1843 days; RUCAM scores 6-8 (probable DILI); RUCAM ≥9 highly probable, 6-8 probable. Biopsies showed autoimmune hepatitIS features whereas simplified and new histology criteria were typical/compatible (and one atypical case, patient 14). Median exposure to presentation across cohort was 116 days (IQR 31-762).

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 26 RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) caused by nitrofurantoin was described; no mechanistic proposals were presented for these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 26; no mechanistic proposals presented; study citation [58].

raw_record.support_text: The authors confidently diagnosed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune hepatitis in their case, presenting a rapid-onset drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis occurring 18 days after a therapeutic 5-day course of nitrofurantoin (100 mg twice daily) for an uncomplicated UTI. Diagnosis was supported by elevated liver enzymes, positive smooth muscle antibodies, normal IgG levels, and a liver biopsy showing acute hepatitis with moderate necroinflammatory activity and no fibrosis after ruling out other causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Rapid-onset drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis appearing 18 days after exposure to nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days for an uncomplicated UTI; presentation included jaundice, lethargy, and elevated liver enzymes, with positive smooth muscle antibodies and normal IgG; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with moderate necroinflammatory activity and focal portal fibrosis (no advanced fibrosis). Treated with prednisone 40 mg daily, tapered with azathioprine added as steroid-sparing agent; asymptomatic with normal liver biochemistry at 1-year follow-up. Noted as unique because of acute DIAIH after a brief 5-day course, contrasting with the widely recognized long-term prophylaxis association.

raw_record.support_text: Chronic active hepatitis is described as a recognized complication of treatment with nitrofurantoin; the letter reports the first case in a man. A 65-year-old man had taken nitrofurantoin 100 mg at night for 12 months for recurrent urinary tract infections and was admitted for nonresolving jaundice and developing liver failure. Biopsy showed severe architectural disturbance with extensive liver cell necrosis, reported as chronic active hepatitis with bridging hepatic necrosis. After nitrofurantoin was stopped (and prednisolone started), liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks and ascites and oedema resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case in a man; all previously described cases occurred in women. Dose 100 mg at night for 12 months for recurrent urinary tract infections. Bilirubin 55 mmol/L with moderately raised transaminase and alkaline phosphatase; total protein 92 g/L, albumin 28 g/L; fourfold increase in IgG, IgA, and IgM; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; antinuclear factor and smooth-muscle antibody titers 1:640. Biopsy: severe architectural disturbance, extensive liver cell necrosis, chronic active hepatitis with bridging hepatic necrosis. After nitrofurantoin was stopped and prednisolone started, liver function tests returned to normal within 4 weeks and ascites/oedema resolved.

raw_record.support_text: Case reports of chronic active hepatitis with prolonged use of nitrofurantoin have included biochemical and liver biopsy evidence for direct hepatocellular toxicity, as well as immunologic reactions including hyperglobulinemia and antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies in some patients. Some patients also had evidence of pulmonary damage. The role of immune phenomena in the hepatic damage is unclear; antinuclear antibodies have persisted in some patients after drug discontinuation despite improved hepatic function. The paper frames this within an increasing recognition of nitrofurantoin's potential for hepatic injury in an idiosyncratic drug reaction context.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic active hepatitis reported with prolonged therapeutic use of nitrofurantoin. Immunologic features included hyperglobulinemia and antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies in some patients; antinuclear antibodies persisted in some patients after discontinuation despite improvement in hepatic function. Some patients also had pulmonary damage.
