Proposed mechanisms: metabolism to a reactive electrophilic intermediate capable of covalent binding to cell macromolecules, possibly via nitroreduction of the furan ring, and/or superoxide formation from redox cycling.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old woman developed hepatic failure after receiving nitrofurantoin 200 mg po bid for one month for urinary-tract infection prophylaxis; symptoms began after two weeks of therapy. After other causes of hepatic failure (viral infection, autoimmune disorder, concomitant medications, cancer, Wilson's disease, ethanol abuse, pregnancy) were ruled out, the authors concluded that she appeared to have developed hepatic failure secondary to nitrofurantoin, ultimately requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Acute and chronic hepatic injury has previously been reported with nitrofurantoin use.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 200 mg po bid for one month; symptoms after two weeks; progressed to stage I hepatic encephalopathy; orthotopic liver transplantation two days after admission; liver histology showed extensive hepatocyte necrosis, moderate cholestasis, and bridging necrosis; lab values: AST 17.7, ALT 19.7, alkaline phosphatase 4.1, total bilirubin 436 umol/L, GGT 3.0 ukat/L, ammonia 156 umol/L. Nitrofurantoin has been associated with acute and chronic liver injury at a rate of 0.02-0.035%; reaction described as idiosyncratic or hypersensitivity, not dose related, proposed mechanism immunoallergic or metabolic; small number of fatalities previously reported.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed erythema multiforme, cholestatic hepatitis, and acute pulmonary toxicity secondary to nitrofurantoin administration, culminating in death. The authors recommend promptly discontinuing nitrofurantoin when evidence of skin, lung, or liver adverse reactions manifests.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of cholestatic hepatitis attributed to nitrofurantoin administration; the patient also developed erythema multiforme and acute pulmonary toxicity and died. Authors advise prompt discontinuation of nitrofurantoin when skin, lung, or liver adverse reactions appear.

raw_record.support_text: A case of fatal fulminant hepatitis caused by cyproterone acetate was reported by Friedman et al. in Canada. The case profile seemed similar to that of flutamide, and the authors mention at least seven previous reports of fatal hepatic failure with this compound, believed to be due to an idiosyncratic reaction. No evidence of hypersensitivity was reported, suggesting injury is probably the result of a toxic metabolite or possibly a direct drug effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatitis; at least seven previous reports of fatal hepatic failure with the compound; mechanism thought to be a toxic metabolite or possibly direct drug effect rather than hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: Cyproterone acetate is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 9 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 9 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; spelled 'cypropterone acetate' in the paper; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a new case of a male patient treated with cyproterone acetate (CPA) for advanced prostate cancer who developed acute liver failure (ALF) during treatment, with a fatal outcome. The authors note that CPA has been evidentially correlated with a wide spectrum of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and is frequently related to ALF, that the first CPA-induced case of fulminant hepatitis with fatal outcome was described in 1989, and that 18 cases of ALF have been reported to date.
raw_record.extra_details: Steroidal synthetic progestagen and anti-androgen used in advanced prostate cancer. Injury manifested as fulminant (acute) hepatitis progressing to acute liver failure with encephalopathy in a patient without cirrhosis or preexisting liver disease, and resulted in death. First fatal case described in 1989; 18 cases of CPA-associated ALF reported to date. The presented new case involved a male patient; the letter does not specify causality scores, histology, laboratory values, or rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient with Graves' disease treated with carbimazole, both the minor effects and the major adverse effects (agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity) were reported to be probably related to the carbimazole therapy by the Naranjo probability scale. The patient developed cholestatic jaundice with hepatocellular damage that resolved and liver enzymes normalized after carbimazole was withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Graves' disease/hyperthyroidism; carbimazole 30 mg/day started at day -21 and stopped at day 0. Hepatic injury presented as cholestatic jaundice (total bilirubin up to 28.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin up to 23.8 mg/dL) complicated by hepatocellular damage (ALT up to 164 U/L, AST up to 225 U/L); referred to as severe hepatotoxicity with significant cholestatic enzyme elevations and moderate aminotransferase elevations. Naranjo probability scale = probable. Other causes excluded (normal hepatobiliary ultrasound; negative IgM for EBV, CMV, VZV, HSV). No liver biopsy performed; clinical evolution favorable with normalization of liver enzymes. Co-managed for coexisting agranulocytosis (WBC 0 granulocytes) with G-CSF; propranolol 160 mg/day and 131I ablation started day 8 with enzyme/granulocyte recovery despite continued propranolol, argued against interaction. The authors concluded cholestatic jaundice and secondary hepatocellular damage were attributable to carbimazole.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old female with severe hyperthyroidism was treated with Carbimazole 30 mg/day. Within six weeks of starting therapy, she developed potentially life-threatening acute cholestatic hepatitis and agranulocytosis as adverse effects to carbimazole; her symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the offending drug was withdrawn. The report describes carbimazole-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis together with agranulocytosis as an extremely rare idiosyncratic side effect of carbimazole treatment that is considered dose- and age-related.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 30 mg/day for hyperthyroidism; onset within six weeks of therapy; acute cholestatic hepatitis with concurrent agranulocytosis (presented with bluish skin discoloration, right hypochondriac pain, high-grade fever, deep jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, semi-conscious state, Glasgow coma scale 11/15); symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after drug withdrawal. Authors describe the cholestatic hepatitis plus agranulocytosis combination as extremely rare, idiosyncratic, and dose- and age-related.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old male developed jaundice and severe hyperbilirubinemia beginning about 1 year after starting carbimazole (40 mg with levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily as block-and-replace) for Graves' disease. He had no prior history of liver disease and had taken no other prescribed, over-the-counter, or illicit substances. Carbimazole was stopped; liver biopsy showed a mixed cholestatic-hepatitic injury (cholestatic more prominent), and it was considered most likely to represent a drug-related liver injury. Liver function slowly improved and the jaundice resolved completely.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 38-year-old male with Graves' disease/hyperthyroidism; block-and-replace carbimazole 40 mg + levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily; late onset about 1 year after commencement (jaundice for 6 weeks, mild abdominal pain, malaise); bilirubin rose from 129 to 459 with prothrombin time 15 then 18.6; normal US liver structure and normal MRCP biliary tree; liver biopsy showed mixed cholestatic-hepatitic injury with cholestatic component more prominent; no evidence of hepatic necrosis on biopsy mentioned in case; recovered completely; propylthiouracil avoided due to hepatotoxicity risk, total thyroidectomy performed.

raw_record.support_text: Cases of chronic hepatocellular-type idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity are tabulated. Bentazepam was attributed as the sole culprit drug in two cases: case 2 (hepatocellular damage, persistent at 10 months, antinuclear antibody titer 1/80) and case 4 (chronic hepatitis with portal inflammatory infiltrate, piecemeal necrosis, bile duct proliferation, and portal-to-portal fibrosis showing regenerative nodules; recovery at 26 months). Another bentazepam case (case 11) in the cholestatic/mixed table showed mixed-pattern injury persistent at 16 months with anti-smooth muscle antibody 1/160. These cases were classified definite or probable by causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic idiosyncratic DILI registry. Case 2: F/51, raised enzymes, 152 d therapy, 28 d onset, persistent (10 mo). Case 4: F/60, jaundice, 277 d therapy, 150 d onset, chronic hepatitis histology, recovery (26 mo). Case 11: F/47, raised enzymes, mixed pattern, persistent (16 mo), anti-smooth muscle antibodies 1/160.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that a causal relation between the use of bentazepam and hepatic injury can confidently be established because alternative explanations were ruled out and withdrawal was followed by rapid clinical improvement and return of laboratory findings to normal. Bentazepam is a benzodiazepine marketed in Spain since 1981 for anxiety disorders; rechallenge was not attempted for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man with prior peptic ulcer, chronic constipation, and transient ischaemic attacks; previously stopped triflusal due to gastrointestinal bleeding and took only oral lactulose during bentazepam therapy. Bentazepam given at the manufacturer's recommended dose of 25 mg three times daily for severe anxiety; symptoms (abdominal discomfort, progressive asthenia, anorexia, weight loss) appeared ~4 months after start, with no improvement after dose reduction to 25 mg/day, and the drug was stopped at 13 months. At presentation AST 152 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, total bilirubin 18.6 µmol/L (direct 6.8), γ-GT 109 U/L, with normal alkaline phosphatase, plus leukopenia (3.5 × 10⁹/L) and thrombocytopenia (130 × 10⁹/L). Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with dense lymphocytic/monocytic infiltrate disrupting the limiting plate, lymphoid aggregates, marked portal-to-portal fibrosis with transition to cirrhosis in some areas, and marked parenchymal collapse. Viral (Hep A/B/C, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune serologies were negative. After stopping the drug, symptoms improved dramatically; by the eleventh week AST fell to 66 U/L, ALT to 53 U/L, and γ-GT to 85 U/L, and counts normalized by 4 months. Authors attributed the injury to an idiosyncratic metabolic mechanism (no rash, fever, eosinophilia, or granulomatous infiltrate; long latency), and noted benzodiazepines generally have very low hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial reports that todralazine, a hydralazine derivative used to treat hypertension, induces hepatic failure in humans: seven cases of todralazine-induced hepatic failure were previously reported, and a further case progressed to fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation 20 days after admission. Histology of the explant revealed submassive hepatocyte necrosis with little inflammation and little hepatocyte proliferation.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases of todralazine-induced hepatic failure previously reported; the new case had fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation 20 days after admission. Explant histology showed submassive hepatocyte necrosis with little inflammation and little hepatocyte proliferation. Todralazine is a hydralazine derivative used to treat hypertension. Murata et al. hypothesized reduced histone acetylation with subsequent failure of liver regeneration as mechanism; in a mouse model 4 months of todralazine feeding induced mild hepatitis with ALT rise (67 vs 27 control) and reduced acetylated H4, PCNA positivity, cyclin D1, and HAT activity; in vitro todralazine, isoniazid and hydralazine dose-dependently inhibited core histone acetylation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the clinical course of seven patients who developed fulminant hepatic failure caused by ecarazine hydrochloride, an antihypertensive agent. Course details include massive hepatic cell necrosis (Case 1, fatal), zonal hepatic cell necrosis with a positive rechallenge and positivity for ANA (Case 2), a fatal case with jaundice, hemorrhage and renal failure (Case 3), and Case 4 with elevated ALT/AST to 1,090 IU/L and 1,205 IU/L after being prescribed ecarazine with warfarin and dilazep.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients developed fulminant hepatic failure attributed to ecarazine hydrochloride given as an antihypertensive agent. Case 1 (69-year-old man) died after hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure; necropsy showed massive hepatic cell necrosis. Case 2 demonstrated zonal hepatic cell necrosis on biopsy, ANA converted to positive (1:80), and rechallenge 2 weeks later produced fatigue with AST 1,305 IU/L, ALT 1,197 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL that normalized after discontinuation; anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA were negative. Case 3 (74-year-old man) died from exacerbated jaundice, hemorrhagic tendency and renal failure. Case 4 (postpartum woman) had ALT 1,090 IU/L and AST 1,205 IU/L with concurrent warfarin and dilazep co-medication. Cases treated with plasma filtration, plasma exchange and prednisolone.

raw_record.support_text: In two patients with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury, fluvastatin (patients 22, male 45 and 23, male 68, exposure 7 and 6 months) was recorded as causative, presenting with jaundice (and in one case ascites, nausea, dark urine) and canalicular cholestasis on histology.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 cholestatic cases; ALT 1.5-9 ULN, AP 1.8-2.2 ULN, gamma-GT 4.7-9.5 ULN; jaundice, ascites (pt22); histology canalicular cholestasis (pt22); no comedication. Fluvastatin also tested as BSEP inhibitor in-vitro.

raw_record.support_text: The Swedish DILI register reported statin-related DILI with fluvastatin implicated in 11/73 (15%) of cases, showing most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern; separately, in the DILIN prospective study fluvastatin was implicated in 0.2% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 11/73 (15%) of statin-DILI cases in the Swedish DILI register (register statin DILI showed most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths from acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation across the 73 cases, not attributable to a specific statin); implicated in 0.2% of adjudicated DILI cases in the DILIN prospective study.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted after adjudication as true statin-induced DILI, described as mostly mild-moderate, self-limited injury with idiosyncratic timing as a likely class effect. Fluvastatin accounted for 2 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated fluvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=2; Swedish 1988-2010 n=11; Spanish Registry n=12 (25.5%). DILIN aggregate (all statins): hepatocellular 12/22, cholestatic 9/22, 4 severe, 1 fatal; latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: Fluvastatin was attributed to 11 DILI cases with a predominantly mixed pattern (64%), the highest proportion of mixed cases among the frequent causative drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 of 843 registry DILI cases; Hep 18%/Chol 18%/Mix 64%; female 54%, lymphopenia 0%, eosinophilia 18%; 0 fulfilled nR-based Hy's law.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with fluvastatin-induced cholestatic liver injury and acute renal failure, and was identified as a possible candidate for liver transplant; a liver biopsy was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of fluvastatin-induced cholestatic jaundice/liver injury with concurrent myositis (elevated creatine phosphokinase) and acute renal failure; considered a possible liver transplant candidate; no liver biopsy performed. Naranjo algorithm causality score of 7 for fluvastatin (probable ADR); Maria and Victorino scale score of 16 (possible). Co-suspects metformin and gliclazide were separately assessed (Naranjo 4 each, Maria-Victorino 14 points each = possible) but fluvastatin was concluded to be the cause. Hepatobiliary laboratory results recovered fully with supportive treatment; patient subsequently diagnosed with stage 3 chronic kidney disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver toxicity is a potentially serious effect of treatment with niacin (nicotinic acid), first reported by Rivin, and that liver toxicity of time-release niacin preparations has also been recognized for many years. Additional cases of adverse hepatic effects of unmodified and time-release niacin have been reported, with severe cases resulting in fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Also called niacin/NA. Compiles multiple reported patient cases of hepatic toxicity for unmodified and time-release preparations. Doses mostly 3-4.5 g/day for hyperlipidemia with toxicity latency 1-18 months; patients typically experienced nausea and vomiting, sometimes jaundice, with more severe cases showing elevated bilirubin, ammonia and prolonged prothrombin time. Table II cases: 3.0 g/day JA/AST/alk phos/bilirubin elevation normalizing in 20 days; 3.0 g/day peripheral edema, increased SBP retention; 0.75 g/day with cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy (in a man who had attempted suicide by carbon monoxide inhalation 3 days earlier); 0.9-4.5 g/day nausea/vomiting/jaundice; 3.0 g/day; 3.0 g/day case with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy resolving in <10 days; time-release cases include aluminum nicotinate 3 g/day for 48 months with intrahepatic cholestasis and chronic portal inflammation/fibrosis, and 0.5 g/day for 2 months with fulminant liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy (taken as 'super timed-release' tablets for health effects). Most severe cases (refs 10,11,13) led to fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The letter argues that the hepatotoxic potential of niacin has been understated and cites three human cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity: a 46-year-old man with clinical and biochemical hepatotoxicity on unmodified niacin 3 g/d for one month who, on rechallenge six weeks later, developed fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy that resolved on discontinuation; a 32-year-old man taking SR niacin 500 mg/d for two months who developed acute liver failure with stage 4 encephalopathy and recovered on discontinuation; and a 44-year-old man on niacin 6 g/d who, three days after being switched to an SR formulation, developed fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation. The letter concludes that severe hepatotoxicity occurs with both unmodified and sustained-release (SR) niacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter responding to an earlier DIAS Rounds column; argues SR niacin offers no adverse-effect profile advantage over unmodified niacin and that hepatotoxic potential is understated. Cases: (1) 46-year-old man, unmodified niacin 3 g/d for 1 month, clinical/biochemical hepatotoxicity; positive rechallenge 6 weeks later leading to fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy, resolved on niacin discontinuation; (2) 32-year-old man, SR niacin 500 mg/d for 2 months, acute liver failure progressing to stage 4 encephalopathy, recovered on discontinuation; (3) 44-year-old man, niacin 6 g/d, fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation, onset 3 days after switch to SR formulation. Both unmodified and SR niacin implicated.

raw_record.support_text: In six patients (18%, all nontransplant) a definite overall diagnosis of medication-induced hepatitis was made, based on liver injury occurring after use of a specific medication, improvement upon discontinuation, and exclusion of other etiologies. Niacin (1 g, twice/day) was the inciting agent in three patients, all with panacinar hepatitis; cholestasis was present in two of these three patients. Hepatitis developed within 1–16 weeks and significant improvement occurred within 3–12 weeks of discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 1 g twice/day; inciting agent in 3 patients, all panacinar hepatitis; cholestasis present in two of the three niacin cases; latency 1–16 weeks; significant clinical and biochemical improvement within 3–12 weeks of discontinuation; diagnosis rendered by definite overall diagnosis with exclusion of viral, autoimmune, systemic and GI etiologies.

raw_record.support_text: A patient taking 6 g/day of nicotinic acid for 7 days developed toxic hepatitis with peak total bilirubin 41 µmol/l, ALT 12.21 µkat/l, and AST 7.80 µkat/l, plus a prothrombin time that peaked at 22 s and returned to normal by day 3. Discontinuing the nicotinic acid led to rapid clinical improvement, and at 9 days after discharge liver function tests continued to normalize (ALT 2.0 µkat/l, bilirubin 18 µmol/l). Serologies for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and EBV were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 6 g/day for 7 days; peak PT 22 s returning to normal by day 3; nonicteric; AST 7.80 µkat/l, ALT 12.21 µkat/l (normal 0-0.58 µkat/l), total bilirubin 41 µmol/l (normal 2-18); marked improvement within 9 days of discharge on discontinuation; no biopsy performed; other causes (hepatitis A/B, EBV, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) ruled out by serology.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a patient receiving nicotinic acid 3 g daily for hypercholesterolemia who developed severe hepatocellular liver injury that progressed to clear-cut fulminant hepatic failure. The patient was on no other drugs and had no exposure to other hepatotoxic agents, and liver injury developed on two separate occasions in direct conjunction with nicotinic acid administration, which clearly implicates that drug as the causative agent of his hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 3 g daily for hypercholesterolemia; injury appeared within weeks of starting therapy. On re-presentation about 10 weeks after reinstituting nicotinic acid: dark urine, lethargy, somnolence, confusion, icterus; total bilirubin 6.6 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 239 IU/L, LDH 8,176 IU/L, AST 14,140 IU/L, ALT 6,220 IU/L, prothrombin time 90 s (control 12 s), blood ammonia 93 µg/dl, 6% eosinophils; progressed to stage 2-3 hepatic encephalopathy (bilirubin 10.7 mg/dl) and recovered, discharged on hospital day 10; at 4 months bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase/AST/PT normal but gammaglutamyl transpeptidase 99 IU/L (normal 15-85). Discussion notes no evidence of hypersensitivity, dose dependence (most reported cases >=3 g daily), and evidence of direct hepatotoxicity as the fundamental mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Nicotinic acid is associated with flushing and pruritus, and liver toxicity is a well-recognized adverse effect of treatment at pharmacologic doses (1.5 to 6 g/day), reported as more common with slow-release than immediate-release (crystalline) nicotinic acid. In the current report, 3 cases of hepatic toxicity induced by treatment of dyslipidemia with crystalline nicotinic acid are described, characterized by signs of generalized synthetic dysfunction of the liver out of proportion to transaminase elevation, manifesting as a striking decrease in apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and plasma LCAT, and in some cases increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin. In 2 of the 3 patients these changes occurred without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal or only mildly elevated transaminases.
raw_record.extra_details: Treatment for dyslipidemia with crystalline (immediate-release) nicotinic acid. Novel presentation of generalized hepatic synthetic dysfunction out of proportion to transaminase elevation: decreased plasma apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and LCAT activity, increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin; in 2 of 3 patients without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal/mildly elevated transaminases. At 3.0 g/d, LCAT activity fell (Patient 1: 320 to 147; Patient 2: 355 to 151; Patient 3: 394 to 133 nmol/h/ml), AST/ALT rose mildly, and recovery of LCAT/transaminases followed dose reduction (1.5 g/d) or cessation. Liver toxicity noted as more common with slow-release than immediate-release nicotinic acid.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 60 individual case reports; median age 45 y; 32 female/28 male; median treatment duration 5 weeks; HC 40%, Cs/mixed 60%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 27% (49/60 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 32% (38/60 reported); hepatic necrosis 37%; inflammatory reaction 100%; death or liver transplant 17%; liver biopsy reported in 38/60 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Anticonvulsants were the most common offending drugs (21 of 27 definite DRESS/DIHS cases; 77.7%). Phenytoin was the most common individual drug (12 cases; 44.4%), followed by carbamazepine (8 cases; 29.6%). Hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement, present in 23 patients (85.1%).
raw_record.extra_details: Carbamazepine identified as culprit drug in 8 of 27 definite RegiSCAR-scored DRESS/DIHS cases (29.6%); indications included epilepsy, prophylaxis after cranioencephalic trauma or neurological surgery, chronic pain, insomnia, and drug dependency treatment; hepatitis was the most common visceral involvement (23/27 patients, 85.1%).

raw_record.support_text: In an Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) cohort, which categorized patients into DILI-ALF (drug-induced liver injury progressing to acute liver failure) versus APAP-ALF groups, carbamazepine was named among the causative drugs responsible for non-APAP hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among causative drugs for non-APAP hepatotoxicity in the ALFSG DILI-ALF cohort (this study subgroup N=39; larger study N=52).

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine is listed among the main 10 drugs leading the Latin American DILI Registry with n = 5 cases, with RUCAM-based causality assessment.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 cases in the Latin American DILI Registry; RUCAM-based causality assessment used.

raw_record.support_text: High-confidence DILI cases due to carbamazepine (n=9) from the DILIN studies were analyzed. The previously reported association between HLA-A*31:01 and carbamazepine DILI was confirmed (n=6, OR=11.7, 95% CI 3.17-43.4, P=0.001, FDR=0.008).
raw_record.extra_details: High-confidence DILI cases (n=9, n=6 tested) from DILIN. Confirmed association with HLA-A*31:01 (AF cases=0.25, AF controls=0.03). Antiepileptic drug class.

raw_record.support_text: Carbamazepine was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: In the causative-agents analysis, carbamazepine (13%), anti-tuberculosis medications (isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, alone or combined, 13%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), and allopurinol and lamotrigine (7.6% each) were the most common agents implicated in DILI-DRESS. Among 15 carbamazepine-induced liver injury cases, 47% were DILI-DRESS, and four of six lamotrigine cases (67%) were DILI-DRESS.
raw_record.extra_details: Most common agent implicated in DILI-DRESS (13% of cases). Individual cases listed include hepatocellular (nR 12.1), mixed (4.3, 3.8), and cholestatic (0.2-0.5) patterns; severities ranged mild to moderate; all recovered or lost to follow-up. 47% of 15 carbamazepine-induced liver injury cases were DILI-DRESS.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a patient who developed a severe hypersensitivity reaction to carbamazepine, presenting as DRESS syndrome, which further complicated into hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS). The authors state this is, to their knowledge, the first reported case of carbamazepine-induced HLH and VBDS, attributing the bile duct injury (ductal/cholangiopathy-type liver injury) to carbamazepine.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-epileptic drug (AED) causing DRESS syndrome, which complicated into HLH and vanishing bile duct syndrome. DRESS typically manifests 2-6 weeks after drug initiation. Liver biopsy showed areas of missing bile ducts; no CK19-positive small bile ducts were detected, only CK7-positive cholestatic liver cells; bilirubin fluctuated during treatment. HHV-6 immunofluorescence staining in liver tissue was negative. No eosinophilia was observed despite fever, dark urine, and rash on admission. DRESS-associated immune dysregulation (T-cell proliferation, cytokine storm including IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, IL-2) and elevated IL-1, IL-2, IL-6 by carbamazepine are proposed mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports two patients who developed granulomatous hepatitis while receiving carbamazepine (Tegretol). Both had hepatitis within one month of starting the drug and rapid, complete resolution after the agent was discontinued; liver biopsies showed granulomas with acute portal inflammation. The authors state these cases are most likely a result of carbamazepine therapy and recommend adding carbamazepine to the list of drugs causing granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis with acute portal inflammation, focal acute cholangitis/pericholangitis, and intralobular bile stasis on biopsy. Onset of hepatitis within one month of drug start in both patients; rapid and complete resolution after discontinuation (within four weeks for Patient 1, liver no longer palpable and transaminases/alkaline phosphatase returned to normal). Patient 1: 54-year-old male given carbamazepine 200 mg orally three times daily for trigeminal neuralgia; presented with nausea, anorexia, malaise, fatigue, night sweats, dark urine, jaundice, hepatomegaly (liver 5 cm below right costal margin); admission labs bilirubin 3.4 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 236 IU, SGOT 110 IU, SGPT 145 IU; serum carbamazepine 7.9 mg/liter (therapeutic range); HBsAg negative; no eosinophilia. Prior literature notes drug-induced hepatitis in three patients receiving carbamazepine. The authors additionally reviewed adverse effects including aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, rash/Stevens-Johnson syndrome, neurologic effects, water-balance disturbances, and pulmonary fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatitis developing from carbamazepine use is distinctly uncommon and can take the form of hepatocellular jaundice, cholestatic jaundice (as in the patient), or a mixture of both. Six previous cases of carbamazepine-caused hepatitis had a sensitization period of about 4 weeks before fever and jaundice, with liver biopsies showing granulomas with or without eosinophilic infiltrates; one patient rechallenged with the drug had recurrence of fever and abdominal pain that resolved on discontinuation. The index patient had been on carbamazepine for 5 weeks (total dose 18.9 g) before fever and jaundice, with skin rash and eosinophilia supporting drug hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis from carbamazepine is uncommon (references 2-4). Liver injury presented as hepatocellular jaundice, cholestatic jaundice (index patient), or a mixture. Mechanism attributed to immunologic hypersensitivity supported by ~4-week sensitization period, fever, and granulomas on liver histology; index patient had skin rash and eosinophilia. Six prior literature cases; one rechallenge reproduced fever and abdominal pain that resolved on drug stoppage. One fatal hepatitis case reported (reference 6). Prognosis good if drug discontinued, with reversal of biochemical and histological abnormalities. Baseline liver function tests and blood counts recommended; about 5-10% of patients develop transient liver enzyme elevation resolving within first months; monthly LFT monitoring for the first year recommended. Index patient was treated for 5 weeks (total carbamazepine dose 18.9 g) before fever and jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Sulindac-associated DILI case reports were analyzed for liver-injury pattern, eosinophilia, hepatic necrosis, inflammatory reaction, and death/liver transplantation outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 individual case reports; median age 51 y; 18 female/5 male; median treatment duration 3 weeks; HC 10%, Cs/mixed 90%; peripheral eosinophilia present in 12% (17/23 reported); hepatic eosinophilia present in 40% (19/23 reported); hepatic necrosis 22%; inflammatory reaction 82%; death or liver transplant 4%; liver biopsy reported in 12/23 cases.

raw_record.support_text: Early clinical trials reported increased serum alkaline phosphatase, and in 1979 the first report of sulindac hepatitis appeared, followed by eleven further published cases of acute sulindac hepatitis plus the three cases in the present report. In five published cases sulindac was definitely implicated on the basis of rechallenge; in the others it was implicated by association of drug administration with symptom onset, resolution on cessation, and exclusion of other causes. The present cases were implicated on the same grounds, with rechallenge considered unjustifiable due to a report of a potentially life-threatening reaction on inadvertent re-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulindac (Clinoril, Charles E. Frosst) is a substituted indene structurally related to indomethacin; the parent drug is metabolised in the liver to the sulphide analogue, the major pharmacologically active anti-inflammatory agent. Reacts at recommended dosages of 200-400 mg/day; two reports described intermittent non-usual dosing for four to six months with reaction only after recommended dosing, indicating some degree of dose dependency. Initial symptoms occurred within one week to one month of commencement: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, then fever and jaundice; some cases had diffuse pharyngitis or stomatitis, facial swelling, or generalised rash; tender hepatomegaly occasionally present. 14 published cases plus 3 present cases are tabulated; one published case (Park et al. 1982) died. Histology showed focal lobular hepatitis with lipofuscin-laden macrophages in centrilobular regions, canalicular bile plugging in a predominantly cholestatic case, and hepatocyte regeneration (thickened plates, binucleated hepatocytes) in a late-resolution biopsy; sulindac hepatitis did not progress to irreversible structural injury. Reaction independent of age, sex, and underlying rheumatic disorder, and independent of prior adverse reactions to other NSAIDs including aspirin; lack of reactions to other NSAIDs (naproxen, aspirin, indomethacin) did not preclude sulindac hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two women who developed reversible hepatic dysfunction with sulindac. Sulindac had been started one month before admission for back pain and was stopped one week after developing jaundice. Case 1 was similar to previous reports in biochemical presentation, while Case 2 demonstrated a predominantly cholestatic picture. The authors note three prior cases of hepatitis associated with sulindac use.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female patients; sulindac started one month before admission for back pain, stopped one week after jaundice developed (dechallenge). Clinical jaundice without chronic liver disease stigmata; liver enzymes took seven months to return to normal (recovery). Case 2 showed a predominantly cholestatic picture; Case 1 similar to previous reports. Labs (case presented): SGOT 65 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 278 IU/l, bilirubin 213 µmol/l (12.6 mg/dl), normal albumin and thyroid indices, negative hepatitis markers, normal ultrasound/ERCP. Liver biopsy showed zone III (centrilobular) hepatocellular damage with acidophil bodies, focal hepatocyte drop-out with mononuclear infiltrates, mild small and large droplet steatosis, pigmented Kupffer cells, and dilated bile canaliculi with bile plugs. NSAID therapeutic indication.

raw_record.support_text: The strongest evidence linking NSAIDs with liver disease is for sulindac. Multiple reports described sulindac therapy leading to hepatitis on rechallenge, and the incidence of acute liver injury was 148.1 per 100 000 sulindac users and 27.2 per 100 000 sulindac prescriptions. An association with liver disease was found in one study (odds ratio 5.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 18.5) and was borderline in a second (odds ratio 4.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 22.4).
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge reproduced hepatitis in multiple reports. Incidence of acute liver injury 148.1 per 100 000 users and 27.2 per 100 000 prescriptions; odds ratio 5.0 (95% CI 1.3-18.5) in one study and borderline odds ratio 4.1 (95% CI 0.8-22.4) in a second.

raw_record.support_text: Erlotinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for non-small-cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer, was reported to cause fulminant hepatic failure. The paper describes a patient with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer who died of fulminant hepatic failure as a result of treatment with erlotinib.
raw_record.extra_details: A 67-year-old Caucasian female with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer and an EGFR L858R mutation received erlotinib 150 mg/day orally as part of a phase II trial. After mild liver test elevation (ALT 80 U/L at 2 weeks), erlotinib was stopped and restarted at 100 mg/day; 10 days after restart she developed anorexia with painless jaundice and was hospitalized. Peak ALT 2210-2171 U/L, AST 1888 U/L, total bilirubin up to 28.7 mg/dL, INR up to 9.5. A liver biopsy was performed on 05-05-2006. The patient died on 05-13-2006 of fulminant hepatic failure attributed to erlotinib. Report notes erlotinib liver toxicity is usually mild to moderate and that two large NSCLC trials (731 and 1059 patients) reported no hepatotoxicity; overall trial experience did not report severe systemic toxicity before this case.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient who died of acute liver failure most likely due to erlotinib. The patient showed a rapidly progressive hepatopathy that led to hospitalization 17 days after starting erlotinib, presented with a clinical picture of acute hepatitis, and from the seventh hospitalization day developed massive liver necrosis and a blood coagulation disorder.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure developed 17 days after initiating erlotinib; massive liver necrosis and blood coagulation disorder appeared from the seventh hospitalization day. Erlotinib is hepatically metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2. Co-medication with phenprocoumon during the first week was evaluated and explicitly excluded as the cause of the toxicity ('we do not think that the combination was the cause'). The time course was noted to correlate with other documented erlotinib case reports.

raw_record.support_text: After gefitinib withdrawal, the patient was treated with erlotinib 150 mg once daily; after 10 weeks serum transaminases again rose (AST 100 U/L, ALT 262 U/L). Erlotinib was interrupted for 2 weeks and resumed at 100 then 50 mg/day, but liver enzymes remained elevated at each dose; terminating erlotinib normalized the liver enzymes. The paper also states that hepatotoxicity due to erlotinib is considered less frequent than that of gefitinib but that clinical trials show some patients experience hepatotoxicity, roughly 3-8% with grade 3-4 aminotransferase elevation; a pooled analysis found grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 5.4% of erlotinib-treated patients versus 18% for gefitinib (OR 3.71) and 1.7% for afatinib (OR 3.36, 95% CI 1.11-10.2, P=0.037).
raw_record.extra_details: EGFR-TKI; in the case, ALT 262 U/L and AST 100 U/L after 10 weeks at 150 mg daily, with elevated enzymes persisting at reduced doses of 100 and 50 mg daily and normalization on discontinuation; pooled analysis of EGFR-mutation-positive NSCLC phase II/III trials found grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 5.4% of erlotinib-treated patients, with ~3-8% experiencing grade 3-4 aminotransferase elevation in trials; no differential between Asian and non-Asian patients.

raw_record.support_text: This letter to the editor reports a case of methyldopa-induced granulomatous hepatitis with positive rechallenge. Methyldopa, a widely used antihypertensive agent, is stated to cause chronic or acute hepatitis in about six percent of patients, and much more infrequently granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 78-year-old woman on methyldopa 250 mg once or twice daily for three years for hypertension; also had diabetes mellitus treated by diet and insulin. Presented with right-upper-quadrant tenderness, fever, hepatomegaly; labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase (359 IU/L), GGT (179 IU/L), normal AST/ALT and bilirubin; biopsy showed moderate steatosis and multiple nonnecrotizing epithelioid granulomas. Improved on withdrawal, then relapsed with jaundice one week after rechallenge (bilirubin 4651.2 umol/L, ALP 696 IU/L, GGT 252 IU/L, normal transaminases), resolving after permanent withdrawal. Causality attributed via compatible temporal sequence, improvement on dechallenge, relapse on rechallenge, and exclusion of other causes (hepatitis B, CMV, toxoplasmosis, Q-fever, syphilis, rheumatic serology negative). The paper notes methyldopa hepatitis is generally thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity manifestation (auto-antibodies against endoplasmic reticulum), spanning acute forms indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, and less common forms such as bridging necrosis, cholestasis with necrosis, submassive periportal fibrosis, regenerative nodules, and cirrhosis; a 1982 Bezahler case of fatal granulomatous hepatitis and myocarditis is also referenced.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of patients diagnosed with methyldopa hepatitis, Case 2 (H.M., a 38-year-old hypertensive housewife) developed jaundice and severe hepatitis while taking methyldopa 1500 mg/day for 6 weeks along with long-term hydrochlorothiazide; she progressed to hepatic encephalopathy and died 41 days after admission, with postmortem bridging and multilobular necrosis of the liver. Other cases (e.g., Case 3) improved after methyldopa was discontinued, and the authors present methyldopa as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple hypertensive patients on methyldopa; Case 1 had two bouts of hepatitis with prompt resolution and return of liver tests to normal within 1 month; Case 2 died of hepatic encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal failure, and seizures, with postmortem bridging and multilobular necrosis and bile stasis; Case 3 improved after discontinuation of methyldopa with resolution on follow-up biopsy minus acute necrosis but residual portal inflammation and fibrosis. Laboratory findings included markedly elevated transaminases (SGOT up to 1460 MIU, SGPT up to 710 MIU) and hyperbilirubinemia; some cases showed positive smooth muscle/antinuclear antibodies and extracellular material on LE cell preparations. Histology showed diffuse hepatocellular injury, inflammation, bridging/multilobular necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized clinical and autoimmune features of liver injury caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine, using 88 cases of DILI attributed to these agents in the DILIN prospective study (2004-2014).
raw_record.extra_details: 55% of cases attributed to methyldopa had an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score >= 2). 74% of all 88 cases had hepatocellular injury and 25% had severe injury; 91% of cases were women. Autoimmune features decreased with recovery; no association with HLA-DRB1*03:01 or *04:01 vs controls.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old patient with severe cholestatic liver disease had been receiving methyldopa 250 mg daily for 6 years. Evaluation excluded extrahepatic obstruction and viral hepatitis; liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis without hepatitis, compatible with a rare methyldopa-induced liver injury. Drug cessation led to slow but complete recovery, and the paper states this was a rare manifestation of methyldopa hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Methyldopa 250 mg daily given for 6 years (unusually long latency) before onset; presented with jaundice, dark urine, severe pruritus, abdominal pain and anorexia; liver biopsy showed marked cholestasis without hepatitis; no extrahepatic obstruction or serologic viral hepatitis; complete recovery after withdrawal. Patient's concurrent medications included nifedipine, isosorbide dinitrate, furosemide and spironolactone; past history of angina pectoris, mild renal failure and hypertension. Phenotype is pure cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: De Boer et al. characterized autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) secondary to methyldopa in DILI cases, with an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score ≥2) seen in about one-half (55%) of the cases with methyldopa.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases from the US DILIN prospective study; autoimmune phenotype present in 55% of methyldopa cases.

raw_record.support_text: Rehman et al. reported a 51-year-old female who developed hepatitis 12 weeks after initiation of methyldopa therapy; she recovered after drug withdrawal but the drug was reintroduced after 4-5 months and severe hepatitis led to her death 9 weeks later, with submassive hepatic necrosis at postmortem. Thomas et al. reported a 55-year-old female who developed jaundice 12 weeks after beginning methyldopa, with liver biopsy showing chronic aggressive hepatitis with features of subacute hepatic necrosis; she died 4 months later and postmortem showed postnecrotic cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Rehman case: hepatitis 12 weeks after start, recovered after withdrawal, reintroduced after 4-5 months, severe hepatitis with death 9 weeks later, submassive hepatic necrosis at postmortem. Thomas case: jaundice 12 weeks after start, anorexia/nausea/occasional vomiting throughout, biopsy showing large areas of hepatocellular necrosis and collapse compatible with chronic aggressive hepatitis with subacute hepatic necrosis, transaminases fell after discontinuation, hepatic encephalopathy and death 4 months later despite corticosteroids, postnecrotic cirrhosis with small droplet fat accumulation.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine, diclofenac, isoniazid, metamizole sodium, methotrexate, methyldopa, methylepitiostanol, ribociclib and terbinafine were each implicated in 1.5% of drug-induced liver injury cases in the Pro-Euro-DILI registry.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated at 1.5% frequency in Pro-Euro-DILI and 1.2% in the Spanish DILI Registry; also implicated in drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the Toxic Hepatitis group (D), three patients had biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis caused respectively by diphenylhydantoin, INH (isoniazid), and methyldopa. Liver biopsies in each case showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation, and all three had extremely high GGTP values (1018, 980, and 645 mU/ml) with alkaline phosphatase values of 284, 560, and 251 IU.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis attributed to methyldopa; histology showed hepatobiliary necrosis with eosinophils and occasional fat accumulation; GGTP 645 mU/ml and AP 251 IU.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that certain drugs causing DILI are commonly associated with formation of serum autoantibodies, and cites the Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) Network prospective study in which de Boer et al. found positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at the onset of DILI caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine. This identifies methyldopa as a human DILI-causing agent.
raw_record.extra_details: In the DILI Network prospective study, methyldopa-induced DILI was associated with positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at onset of injury.

raw_record.support_text: An HLA study comprising 4 RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) due to methyldopa was described; no mechanistic proposals were made for these cases.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 4; no mechanistic proposals presented; study citation [50].

raw_record.support_text: Sera from five of nine patients with methyl dopa associated hepatotoxicity induced significant antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity to hepatocytes isolated from rabbits pretreated with Arachlor and methyl dopa. None of the sera from patients with other forms of liver disease or from patients taking methyl dopa without liver damage induced significant cytotoxicity. The methyl dopa related antibody was present in one patient with methyl dopa associated chronic active hepatitis and in two of three patients with an acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine patients with methyl dopa associated hepatotoxicity were studied. A circulating IgG antibody reacting with a methyl dopa-related hapten/neo-antigen on rabbit hepatocytes was detected in five of nine patients; antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity dropped from 44±15% to 8±8% with F(ab)2 to human Fc of IgG and to 6±4% after absorption. Immunofluorescence on patient liver sections showed peripheral hepatocyte staining. Clinical spectrum included acute hepatitis and chronic active hepatitis. Evidence supports an immune-mediated mechanism; methyl dopa is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P450 to a reactive quinone/semi-quinone that covalently binds macromolecules, with lymphocytes from patients sensitized to the quinone derivative. Arachlor (enzyme inducer) and phenobarbitone were used only in the rabbit target-cell preparation, not implicated as human DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: Methyldopa, a centrally acting antihypertensive, was associated with rare but serious hepatotoxic effects. A 31-year-old woman with hypertension developed acute hepatitis with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes about six weeks after starting methyldopa; viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were excluded, and liver function normalized after discontinuation with full recovery, supporting DILI. RUCAM scoring gave a score of 9, indicating a 'highly probable' link between methyldopa and the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used for hypertension, including in pregnancy. Case: 31-year-old woman (class III obesity, asthma). Onset ~6 weeks after start; symptoms fatigue, jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, RUQ pain, malaise, nausea. RUCAM score 9 ('highly probable'). Diagnosed as DILI mimicking autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) clinically and histologically. Viral, autoimmune, metabolic causes excluded; full recovery after dechallenge. Estimated incidence of methyldopa-induced hepatitis 0.1%-0.5%. Mechanism discussed as immune-mediated (reactive metabolites creating neoantigens driving T-cell autoimmune response, autoantibodies, AIH-like histology) and less prominent direct toxic injury via oxidative stress/mitochondrial dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A patient is described who developed hepatocellular jaundice after methyldopa was administered, and hepatitis recurred when the drug was again prescribed. This exacerbation, along with transient arthritis, antinuclear antibodies and positive LE cell tests, is documented as a case of hepatotoxicity due to methyldopa.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; hepatocellular jaundice with recurrence of hepatitis upon rechallenge (re-prescription of methyldopa). Accompanying transient arthritis, antinuclear antibodies and positive LE cell tests documented as supporting drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Because of uncertainty about the patient's liver disease, methyldopa rechallenge was performed as a diagnostic test, with 250 mg three times a day started on September 12, 1972. Eight days after beginning methyldopa, her SGOT rose to 325 Karmen units per ml and SGPT to 500 Karmen units per ml; the medication was stopped immediately and transaminase activity returned to pretreatment levels. The paper frames her acute liver disease as 'methyldopa-induced hepatic necrosis', with a positive rechallenge confirming methyldopa as the cause of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of methyldopa-induced hepatic necrosis. Acute phase showed jaundice, total bilirubin up to 8.2 mg/100 ml, SGOT 1200 and SGPT 720 Karmen units/ml; liver biopsy showed hepatocellular destruction around portal regions with swollen hepatocytes and deranged cord pattern, later followed by fibrosis. Rechallenge with methyldopa 250 mg three times a day reproduced transaminase elevation (SGOT 325, SGPT 500 Karmen units/ml) after 8 days, resolving on discontinuation. Patient also had positive LE prep, positive direct Coombs test, and smooth-muscle/antinuclear antibodies; liver tests returned to near normal by September 1972.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that methyldopa is undoubtedly hepatotoxic, based on a strong temporal relation between drug administration and the development of jaundice, and in four patients the reappearance of liver damage after a second exposure (rechallenge) provided ultimate proof. They acknowledge that coincidental viral hepatitis cannot always be excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: The resulting hepatic reaction to methyldopa spanned a wide spectrum clinically and histologically. Case 9 showed typical features of chronic aggressive hepatitis with lobular distortion, irregular septa, bridging, and plasma cells in the infiltrate. Case 13, examined at necropsy, showed massive hepatic necrosis with a 540 g liver and surviving islands indicating attempted regeneration with nodule formation. Two patients in the series had predominantly cholestatic hepatitis, described as unusual. Rechallenge reproduced liver damage in four patients. A mixed inflammatory portal infiltrate with eosinophils was noted to help distinguish methyldopa liver damage from viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old woman on reserpine, chlorothiazide, guanethedine, digitalis, and chlordiazepoxide for hypertension had methyldopa 250 mg twice daily substituted for reserpine on November 10, 1970. About 10 weeks later she developed loss of appetite, fatigability, dark urine, and later palpitations and orthopnea; on hospitalization she was mildly icteric. A liver biopsy on February 6, 1971 revealed necrosis, mononuclear-cell infiltration, and portal exudate with a histologic diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis. Methyldopa was continued despite jaundice; the drug was briefly suspended February 8-12 but resumed on February 13. She became more severely jaundiced and was rehospitalized on March 25 with the liver extending 4 cm below the costal margin, a positive direct Coombs test, and diffuse antinuclear antibodies (1:10). After discontinuation she improved over 4 weeks, and a June 8, 1971 biopsy showed a chronic active hepatitis-like lesion.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 (E.M., female, age 55). Methyldopa 250 mg twice daily started Nov 10, 1970; jaundice appeared ~10 weeks later (late Jan 1971). Drug continued despite jaundice; suspended Feb 8-12 but resumed Feb 13 on histologic diagnosis of 'viral hepatitis', followed by progressive worsening jaundice and rehospitalization March 25. Serology: direct Coombs negative initially then positive on rechallenge; no Australia antigen; antinuclear antibodies 1:10; negative LE cells, latex fixation, antithyroid antibodies. Histology: initial biopsy acute viral hepatitis-like (necrosis, acidophilic bodies, portal exudate); follow-up biopsy chronic active hepatitis-like (parenchymal collapse, cicatization, chronic inflammatory exudate, condensation of portal tracts). Improvement within 4 weeks of drug discontinuation; LFTs returned to normal in clinic.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman with hypertension was started on methyldopa (Aldomet), 250 mg every 8 hours, and 41 days later developed conjunctival icterus, nausea, fatigue, and malaise, with elevated SGOT (up to 2,070 units) and bilirubin (15.0 mg/100 ml) about 53 days after starting therapy. Liver function tests returned to normal two months after discontinuing methyldopa, though alkaline phosphatase remained elevated for six months. The authors conclude 'There seems little doubt that methyldopa can cause hepatitis,' noting a nonspecific syndrome resembling viral hepatitis, with liver biopsy showing mononuclear infiltrates and focal liver cell necrosis, similar to drug-induced hepatitis, an immunologic basis, rechallenge recurrences in several reported patients, and no permanent hepatic changes or fatalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg every 8 hours; onset of jaundice at ~41 days, maximum liver-test abnormalities (SGOT 2,070 units, bilirubin 15.0 mg/100 ml) at ~53 days; tests returned to normal 2 months after discontinuation, alkaline phosphatase elevated for 6 months; liver biopsy showed nonspecific changes with mononuclear infiltrates and focal liver cell necrosis; rechallenge produced recurrence in several reported patients; no permanent hepatic changes or fatalities; incidence of liver-function abnormalities between weeks 4 and 48 of therapy reported as high as 35% while hepatitis itself is unusual; proposed immunologic basis was supported by positive direct Coombs, fever, arthritis, and lupus cell phenomena.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient the relationship between Aldomet (methyldopa) and liver damage was unequivocally established. Within 1 week of starting Aldomet, gastrointestinal symptoms appeared followed by jaundice and pruritus; these remitted and recurred twice as the drug was withdrawn and readministered. After the third withdrawal, severe liver injury resolved within 7 weeks, and two further challenges each caused mild recurrences that were clinically and biochemically less severe than prior relapses. The paper notes the clinical picture of Aldomet-induced liver injury is clinically, biochemically, and histologically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, often detected only by routine liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: gastro symptoms within 1 week of starting Aldomet, followed by jaundice and pruritus; recurred on two readministrations, then severe liver injury resolved within 7 weeks after third withdrawal; two further challenges caused mild recurrences, each less severe than the prior (dechallenge/rechallenge demonstrates causality). Onset after Aldomet start ranges from 1 week to 1 year, most severe examples within the first 3 months. Mild cases often show only elevated SGOT or serum alkaline phosphatase with normal or nonspecifically abnormal liver histology; 'obstructive' phase with alkaline phosphatase elevation, jaundice, pruritus, and hypercholesterolemia. Incidence of abnormal liver function tests varies from 0% to 35% (mean 6%) across studies using routine liver tests; among first 1,500 recipients only 11 instances of hepatic dysfunction (less than 1%). In more severe cases syndrome resembles typical viral hepatitis with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, fever, hepatomegaly. One fatal case has been described (Perret: elderly man with fulminant fatal jaundice, autopsy showing massive fatty change and perilobular liver cell necrosis) where an association was assumed but not proved; no postnecrotic cirrhosis instances reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a fatal human case, a man with mild chronic renal failure but no prior hepatic dysfunction developed fulminating hepatic failure after sevoflurane administration. He had no previous general anesthesia, viral hepatitis, known allergies, or other hepatotoxic drugs, and operative hepatic hypoperfusion, hypotension, or ischemia were excluded. Microscopic liver examination showed extensive and confluent hepatic necrosis with large calcium deposition in hepatocyte cytoplasm, and the findings were interpreted as sevoflurane-induced hepatotoxicity consistent with earlier reports that cytoplasmic calcium elevation underlies it.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case; exitus preceded by symptoms of fulminating hepatic failure. Patient had mild chronic renal failure but no hepatic dysfunction before sevoflurane administration; no previous general anesthesia, viral hepatitis, allergies, or other hepatotoxic drugs; operative hepatic hypoperfusion, hypotension, and ischemia excluded. Microscopy revealed extensive confluent hepatic necrosis with large calcium deposition in hepatocyte cytoplasm, confirmed by confocal laser microscopy and 3-D visualization. Mechanism previously reported as elevation of cytoplasmic calcium underlying sevoflurane-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: After autopsy microscopic study and dismissing other causes of hepatic damage, a diagnosis of DILI was made. After studying each administered drug and contemplating the chronologic and morphologic characteristics of this case, the authors considered that the liver injury was probably caused by sevoflurane. The patient had received sevoflurane, propofol and fentanyl as anesthetics for an arthroscopic lavage, and died within 3 days; the autopsy showed a necroinflammatory lesion with perivenular predominance affecting about 70% of the organ and hepatocellular necrosis with ceroid deposits, without bilirubin accumulation, and no evidence of viral, bacterial or fungal infection.
raw_record.extra_details: Single autopsy-diagnosed case of fulminant hepatitis in a 59-year-old patient with hypertension and Friedreich's ataxia. Anesthesia for arthroscopic lavage comprised sevoflurane, propofol and fentanyl; the other anesthetic agents were considered and dismissed as causes. Histology: necroinflammatory lesion, perivenular predominance, affecting approximately 70% of liver parenchyma, hepatocellular necrosis with ceroid material deposit and without bilirubin accumulation; no viral, bacterial or fungal infection; blood and synovial fluid cultures negative. Patient deteriorated rapidly, lapsed into coma and died within 3 days despite CPR; no liver enzyme analyses were performed. Liver injury identifier is the DILI disease entity.

raw_record.support_text: Among the five consecutively diagnosed cases of NSAID-induced fulminant hepatitis, one case was related to piroxicam at a dose of 20 mg/day, and the patient was successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. Diagnosis was based on exclusion of other potentially hepatotoxic medications and causes of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 of 5 cases of NSAID-induced acute liver failure; dose 20 mg/day; treated by orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report the authors state that, in their patient who received piroxicam, the temporal sequence together with exclusion of viral hepatitis A and B and an initially normal autoantibody screen all point to a drug induced hepatitis. Despite withdrawing piroxicam after the onset of jaundice, the illness progressed to fatal subacute hepatic failure, and the patient died 105 days after the onset of jaundice with a biopsy showing severe confluent centrilobular necrosis with extensive bridging collapse and an inflammatory infiltrate (subacute hepatic necrosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with severe jaundice, grade II hepatic coma and gross ascites; bilirubin 407 umol/l, aspartate transaminase 730 IU/l, alanine transaminase 258 IU/l, prothrombin time 39/13s; antinuclear antibody titre rose to 1/160 and was associated with hyperglobulinaemia; the authors propose a self-perpetuating autoimmune reaction triggered by piroxicam. Treated with corticosteroids then suffered gastrointestinal bleeding; died 105 days after onset of jaundice; post-mortem biopsy showed subacute hepatic necrosis. The report separately notes one published report of probable piroxicam-induced cholestatic jaundice and that mild transient rises in serum transaminase have been described in piroxicam clinical trials. Patient age not stated in this window.

raw_record.support_text: In this case series of acute hepatitis patients, toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis was attributed to intake of nitrofurantoin, efavirenz, amphetamine, prophylthiouracil, sirolimus, flumatid, lamictal (lamotrigine), and opipramol.
raw_record.extra_details: Listed among drugs causing toxic (drug-induced) hepatitis in a case series of acute hepatitis patients; liver stiffness measured with FibroScan.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old Latino male newly diagnosed with HIV started efavirenz-based HAART (tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, efavirenz 600 mg once daily). Eleven days after beginning therapy he developed a hypersensitivity reaction with rash and fever preceding severe drug-induced hepatitis, with peak liver enzymes of AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L. Hepatitis resolved with HAART discontinuation. Rechallenge with tenofovir and emtricitabine one year later produced no adverse reactions. The Naranjo probability scale demonstrated a probable relationship between this adverse reaction and efavirenz, and the authors concluded efavirenz is the most probable cause of the rash and acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: 30-year-old Latino male, newly diagnosed HIV, efavirenz 600 mg once daily with tenofovir 300 mg and emtricitabine 200 mg. Onset 11 days after starting therapy; hypersensitivity with erythematous maculopapular rash and fever preceding hepatitis; peak AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L; resolved on discontinuation; rechallenge with tenofovir+emtricitabine one year later caused no adverse reaction. Naranjo score = probable. MEDLINE search (2004–Sept 2007) found 2 prior cases of rash preceding hepatitis with efavirenz, both in women. Mechanism speculated to involve efavirenz half-life/auto-induction and CYP2B6-mediated clearance (CYP2B6 responsible for ~90% of efavirenz clearance); higher efavirenz concentrations reported in black and Latino patients.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with a massive increase of efavirenz-based first-line antiretroviral therapy. Three patterns of injury were observed, the most severe being submassive necrosis. A high baseline CD4+ count seemingly predicted risk for submassive necrosis, with female sex and younger age as additional factors, and the associated morbidity and mortality were noted as a serious concern. Clinicians were advised to manage suspected efavirenz DILI with rapid cessation of efavirenz.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with massive expansion of efavirenz-based first-line ART in a developing-world program. Three patterns of injury observed; the most severe was submassive necrosis. High baseline CD4+ count predicted risk for submassive necrosis, with female sex and younger age as additional factors; associated morbidity and mortality noted as a serious concern. Authors recommend rapid cessation of efavirenz when DILI is suspected. Efavirenz is the prescribed antiretroviral, hepatotoxic in human therapeutic use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of probable efavirenz-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) in a patient with HIV. The Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale was used to assess drug causality and yielded a total score of 7 (probable). The VBDS was assessed as secondary to the efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Atripla) therapy, and the cause was narrowed to efavirenz because the patient had previously tolerated emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate without hepatotoxicity. VBDS was confirmed by liver biopsy (ductopenia), ruling out other causes such as Hodgkin lymphoma, infection, autoimmune disease, and primary biliary cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7 (probable); described as the first reported case of efavirenz-induced VBDS in an HIV patient. Patient received Atripla (efavirenz, emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) with no prior prescription or OTC hepatotoxic medications and denied alcohol use. VBDS confirmed on liver biopsy by ductopenia. Received ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) and cholestyramine for cholestasis/pruritus management but progressed to end-stage liver disease and required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a histologically confirmed case of an acute drug-induced liver injury related to citalopram, noting the drug's datasheet only hints in some countries at pathological liver function tests and that isolated cases of SSRIs and hepatotoxicity have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman took citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/day for 3 weeks and presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss, jaundice, and mild hepatomegaly; no alcohol, other drugs, blood transfusion, or history of liver disease. Labs: bilirubin 11 mg/dL (<1), AST 5.7, ALT 14.2, GGT 6.9 µmol/s/L (normal 0.1-0.60, 0.17-0.60, <1.10 respectively); autoantibodies and viral hepatitis screening normal. Abdominal ultrasound compatible with acute hepatitis. Biopsy histology consistent with drug-induced liver injury showing subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis (zones 2 and 3 complete necrosis, zone 1 vital with lymphocytic/macrophage infiltrate; picture indistinguishable from acute viral hepatitis). Causality established by temporal relationship, histology, and rapid improvement upon discontinuation; serum liver function tests normalized completely in 3 months. Prior literature (Lopez-Torres et al) reported a possibly related case where the patient also received 2 further drugs suggesting possible cross-reactivity with citalopram.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks developed weakness, asthenia, weight loss, and jaundice, with elevated bilirubin (11 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and γ-glutamyltransferase. Liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced liver injury showing subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis; citalopram was stopped and serum liver function tests fully normalized within 3 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose of 20 mg/d for 3 weeks; symptoms included jaundice with mild hepatomegaly; bilirubin 11 mg/dL (<1), AST 5.7 µmol/s/L (0.1-0.60), ALT 14.2 µmol/s/L (0.17-0.60), GGT 6.9 µmol/s/L (<1.10); acute hepatitis pattern on ultrasound; no metabolic, viral, hereditary liver disease or bile duct obstruction; autoantibodies and viral hepatitis screens normal; histology showed subacute liver dystrophy with complete necrosis of hepatocytes in zones 2 and 3, incompatible picture consistent with drug-induced liver injury; full normalization of liver tests within 3 months of drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) at 20 mg/d for 3 weeks presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss, and jaundice; she reported no other drugs or alcohol and no liver disease history. Labs showed elevated bilirubin (11 mg/dL), AST, ALT, and GGT, and a liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced liver injury showing subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis. Stopping citalopram led to complete normalization of liver function tests within 3 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks. Histology showed subacute liver dystrophy with complete necrosis of hepatocytes of zones 2 and 3 and a picture indistinguishable from acute virus hepatitis (degenerating hepatocytes, focal and confluent necrosis, apoptotic bodies). Labs at presentation: bilirubin 11 mg/dL (ref <1), AST 5.7 µmol/s/L (ref 0.1-0.60), ALT 14.2 µmol/s/L (ref 0.17-0.60), GGT 6.9 µmol/s/L (ref <1.10). Mild hepatomegaly; abdominal ultrasound compatible with acute hepatitis. No viral, metabolic, hereditary, or autoimmune liver disease. No other drugs or alcohol; no prior DILI. Full recovery with normalization of liver tests in 3 months after drug discontinuation (dechallenge).

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman who had taken citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss, and jaundice, with elevated bilirubin (11 mg/dL), AST (5.7 µmol/s/L), ALT (14.2 µmol/s/L), and GGT (6.9 µmol/s/L). She reported no alcohol or other drug use, had no prior liver disease, and had no metabolic, viral, hereditary, or biliary disease. Liver biopsy showed histology consistent with drug-induced liver injury, with subacute liver dystrophy and liver-cell necrosis. After citalopram was stopped, liver function tests normalized completely within 3 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Histologically confirmed acute drug-induced liver injury in a single patient (Cipramil brand of citalopram). Dose 20 mg/d for 3 weeks; jaundice with bilirubin 11 mg/dL and elevated transaminases; histology showed subacute liver dystrophy and liver-cell necrosis; authors state causal association can be established on temporal relationship, histological confirmation, and rapid improvement after discontinuation, with complete normalization of liver function within 3 months. Laboratory values in µmol/s/L: AST 5.7, ALT 14.2, GGT 6.9 (reference ranges 0.1-0.60, 0.17-0.60, and <1.10 respectively). No alcohol, other drugs, prior liver disease, or metabolic/viral/hereditary/biliary disease identified.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) at 20 mg/d for 3 weeks presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss and jaundice, with elevated bilirubin (11 mg/dL), AST, ALT and GGT. Biopsy showed subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis consistent with drug-induced liver injury; all other causes (alcohol, other drugs, metabolic, viral, hereditary, bile duct obstruction) were excluded. Stopping citalopram led to complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months. The authors establish a causal association for this acute hepatic injury based on temporal relationship, histology and improvement after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Female, 56 years old; citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks. Symptoms: weakness, asthenia, weight loss, jaundice, mild hepatomegaly; abdominal ultrasound compatible with acute hepatitis. Labs: bilirubin 11 mg/dL (<1), AST 5.7 µmol/s per L (0.1-0.60), ALT 14.2 µmol/s per L (0.17-0.60), GGT 6.9 µmol/s per L (<1.10). Histology: subacute liver dystrophy with complete necrosis of hepatocytes of zones 2 and 3, indistinguishable from acute virus hepatitis; lymphocytes and macrophages infiltrate zone 1 at the necrosis border. No alcohol, no other drugs, no transfusion, no pre-existing liver disease; metabolic, viral, hereditary and autoimmune causes and bile duct obstruction excluded. Complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months after drug discontinuation; no rechallenge. The paper notes a prior report (Lopez-Torres et al) of possibly citalopram-related hepatotoxicity in a patient receiving two other drugs. Authors do not recommend routine liver function monitoring due to long cohorted clinical experience without previously described hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks who presented with weakness, jaundice, and hepatomegaly, an acute hepatic injury developed while on treatment. Authors state the causal association with citalopram can be established based on a temporal relationship between drug administration and hepatic injury that was subsequently histologically confirmed, and the patient rapidly improved after the drug was stopped, with complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months. Histology showed subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis consistent with drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman took citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks; presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss, jaundice, mild hepatomegaly; no alcohol or other drugs, no prior liver disease; abdominal ultrasound compatible with acute hepatitis. Elevated bilirubin 11 mg/dL (<1), AST 5.7 µmol/s/L (0.1-0.60), ALT 14.2 µmol/s/L (0.17-0.60), GGT 6.9 µmol/s/L (<1.10); autoantibodies and viral hepatitis screens normal. Liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced liver injury showing subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis of zones 2 and 3, histologically indistinguishable from acute viral hepatitis. Complete normalization of liver function tests in 3 months after citalopram cessation. Authors note citalopram data sheets only in some countries mention pathological liver function tests, and no recommendation for routine liver monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old male with adenocarcinoma of unknown primary treated once daily with 8 mg oral gemcitabine was considered to have a toxic death. Nine days after starting the second cycle he developed fever, grade 4 liver and kidney failure with steep rises in ALT (2,424 U/L), AST (2,781 U/L), γ-GT (237 U/L) and LDH (3,360 U/L), and died 5 days later. Obduction revealed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis which was likely related to the study drug. Other possible causes (viral hepatitis B and C, liver metastasis, alcohol abuse) were excluded and an interaction with comedication (simvastatin, irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide, oxazepam, omeprazol) was deemed unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: Single fatal case from a phase I trial of oral gemcitabine (30 patients; dose levels 1-8 mg part A, 8-20 mg part B). Onset 9 days after start of second cycle of 8 mg daily oral gemcitabine; grade 4 liver and kidney failure; ALT 2,424 U/L, AST 2,781 U/L, γ-GT 237 U/L, LDH 3,360 U/L; treated with i.v. prednisone 1 mg/kg; died 5 days after deterioration. Autopsy showed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis. Viral hepatitis (B, C), liver metastasis, and alcohol abuse excluded; interaction with comedication judged unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists gemcitabine as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 10 conferring a highly probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 10, highly probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [21].

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with no apparent risk factors for liver injury developed acute hepatitis one week after the final dose of a long-term course of pulse itraconazole therapy (200 mg orally twice daily, 1 wk on, 3 wk off, for 24 wk) for onychomycosis. Liver function tests showed alanine aminotransferase 3330 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 3250 U/L, and bilirubin 21 mg/dL. The patient underwent liver transplantation 17 days after admission; histology showed massive panlobular necrosis, and the patient died about 4 months later. The Naranjo probability scale graded the relationship of itraconazole therapy and the acute hepatitis as probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Pulse-dosed regimen of 200 mg orally twice daily, 1 week on, 3 weeks off, for 24 weeks for onychomycosis; liver enzyme monitoring not performed during treatment.
