Lab values: ALT 3330 U/L, AST 3250 U/L, bilirubin 21 mg/dL. Histology: massive panlobular necrosis; reduced liver volume and mild ascitic fluid accumulation. Liver transplantation performed 17 days after admission; the patient died about 4 months later after post-transplant complications and a rejection crisis. Naranjo probability scale rated causality as probable. Serologic evaluation ruled out infectious or other etiological causes.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports two patients with itraconazole (ITZ)-induced cholestatic liver injury who had markedly high serum ITZ concentrations. The paper then characterizes the mechanism using ITZ-treated rats and MDR3-expressing LLC-PK1 cells, showing that ITZ inhibited MDR3-mediated biliary phospholipid secretion, which the authors conclude is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients presented with itraconazole-induced cholestatic liver injury with markedly high serum ITZ concentrations; the specific clinical phenotype is cholestatic liver injury/cholestasis. Mechanistic work in ITZ-treated rats and MDR3 (ABCB4)-expressing LLC-PK1 cells showed drastically reduced biliary phospholipids (rather than bile acids) and significantly reduced MDR3-mediated efflux of [14C]phosphatidylcholine at clinically relevant ITZ concentrations, whereas BSEP-mediated [3H]taurocholate transport was not significantly affected. The authors conclude MDR3 inhibition is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman with onychomycosis treated with itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 weeks developed jaundice, elevated transaminases (AST 2571, ALT 3789 IU/L), and progressive hepatic failure with ascites and coagulopathy. A liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with bile plugs, hepatocellular ballooning, and patchy necrosis, and the condition was judged consistent with acute cytotoxic and cholestatic injuries caused by drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Her hepatic failure was attributed to itraconazole and improved with corticosteroid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Onychomycosis indication; itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 weeks. Liver tests rose to AST 2571 IU/L and ALT 3789 IU/L at admission; later total bilirubin 12.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.3 g/dL, INR 2.77 with ascites and coagulopathy. Biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with canalicular bile plugs, pericentral zonal ballooning, and patchy hepatocyte necrosis. Negative viral hepatitis and autoimmune serology; patient developed erythema multiforme. Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg q8h, tapered), then oral prednisolone; condition stabilized and liver chemistries returned to normal by ~2 weeks after discharge; discharged 36 days after admission.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective, randomized, single-blinded multicentre trial of 221 women with acute candida vulvovaginitis treated with oral itraconazole 200 mg bid (one-day course) or vaginal clotrimazole 500 mg single dose, adverse events were recorded and evidence of hepatotoxicity was sought. Results reported 'No evidence of hepatotoxicity was found.'
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective, randomized, single-blinded multicentre trial of 221 women with acute candida vulvovaginitis; one-day course of oral itraconazole 200 mg bid. Adverse events were transient and mild; itraconazole was more often associated with gastrointestinal or central nervous system complaints. No evidence of hepatotoxicity was found.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, treated for disseminated histoplasmosis, was started on oral itraconazole 100 mg twice per day in addition to fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone. After six months, itraconazole was continued. The report states that up to the time of follow-up the patient showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity related to the itraconazole therapy, though he developed generalized body pigmentation about three months into therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient receiving itraconazole 100 mg twice daily for disseminated histoplasmosis with adrenal involvement; the authors explicitly report no evidence of hepatotoxicity related to itraconazole therapy during follow-up, while noting generalized body pigmentation developed after about three months.

raw_record.support_text: In a 72-year-old woman treated with itraconazole plus corticosteroids for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, the patient developed jaundice and significantly abnormal liver tests (AST=485 IU/L, ALT=182 IU/L, gamma-GT=933 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase=758 IU/L) after four months of antifungal treatment; the diagnosis of an acute liver failure due to a drug-induced hepatitis associated with the antifungal treatment was established and itraconazole was stopped immediately, with the authors explicitly attributing the hepatitis to itraconazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Drug-induced hepatitis with jaundice arising about four months after starting itraconazole for ABPA; laboratory values AST=485 IU/L, ALT=182 IU/L, gamma-GT=933 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase=758 IU/L indicate significant hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis; itraconazole was immediately stopped; the authors excluded intake of any other treatment associated with drug liver toxicity before establishing the diagnosis of acute liver failure due to drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In the safety outcomes of this ABPA attack-treatment study, itraconazole was switched to voriconazole in two patients due to hepatotoxicity, i.e., the hepatotoxicity was clinically attributed to itraconazole during the 4-month attack treatment period (100 or 200 mg twice daily).
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients required a switch from itraconazole to voriconazole because of hepatotoxicity during the 4-month attack treatment period for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Itraconazole was given at 200 mg twice daily, with 100 mg twice daily in 40/174 (23.0%) patients after monitoring and adaptation to residual concentrations. No formal causality score, biochemical pattern, or severity detail beyond attribution of clinically apparent hepatotoxicity is reported.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone has caused published cases of hepatotoxicity (four published cases of hepatitis), and the drug was removed by Sanofi-Synthélabo because of hepatotoxicity. Risk factors for hepatotoxicity are difficult to determine because only a few cases are available for examination, and the four published cases do not indicate the rate at which the hepatitis developed.
raw_record.extra_details: Four published cases of hepatotoxicity/hepatitis attribute injury to benzbromarone at therapeutic urate-lowering doses; the drug was removed by Sanofi-Synthélabo because of hepatotoxicity; risk factors are hard to determine from the few available cases; using the drug only for recurrent gout (not asymptomatic hyperuricaemia) would have prevented three of the four published cases of hepatotoxicity; monitoring of liver function tests was recommended because the cases do not indicate the rate at which hepatitis developed.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone (BBR) was withdrawn from many countries in 2003 as a result of 11 unexplained cases of hepatotoxicity, of which nine patients died of fulminant hepatic necrosis. Subsequent analysis effectively excluded other causes of liver failure, and all patients who were re-challenged with BBR developed hepatotoxicity within weeks of restarting the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzbromarone (BBR) and its metabolite 6-hydroxybenzbromarone block renal uric acid reabsorption by inhibiting URAT1; used for gout, particularly in renal impairment. Withdrawn in many countries in 2003 after 11 unexplained hepatotoxicity cases (refs 50-53); nine of 11 patients died of fulminant hepatic necrosis; other causes of liver failure effectively excluded; all rechallenged patients developed hepatotoxicity within weeks of restarting.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone is a powerful uricosuric drug; after reports of several serious hepatotoxicities, benzbromarone was withdrawn by Sanofi in 2003. It is mainly used in Japan, China, Singapore and other Asian countries for gout and hyperuricemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzbromarone is a uricosuric agent used at ~50-200 mg/d for gout/hyperuricemia. Withdrawn by Sanofi in 2003 after reports of several serious hepatotoxicities. Hepatotoxicity mechanism proposed as mitochondrial toxicity (decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced state 3 oxidation and respiratory control ratios, decreased beta-oxidation, increased ROS, altered mitochondrial structure) and cytochrome-P450-mediated epoxidation; CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 catalyze 1'-hydroxy and 6-hydroxy benzbromarone formation, and 5,6-dihydroxy benzbromarone forms via CYP2C9/CYP1A2.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone hepatotoxicity is reported in humans. A 1994 case report from the Netherlands described a woman who developed acute hepatitis attributed to benzbromarone, confirmed when she was rechallenged with the drug two years later. In the late 1990s and early 2000s in Japan, several cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death were attributed to benzbromarone, and the drug was eventually withdrawn from the market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 1994 case report from the Netherlands of acute hepatitis in a woman was confirmed on rechallenge with the drug two years later; multiple cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death in Japan (late 1990s-early 2000s); drug withdrawn from market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity; still marketed in some European countries, not available in the US. Used as a uricosuric for gout at standard daily doses of 100 mg, with dose increases to 150-200 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc (AK602/ONO4128/GSK-873140), an investigational CCR5 antagonist in development with Ono Pharmaceuticals and GlaxoSmithKline, was the lead analogue studied for HIV-1. During phase IIb trials three subjects developed severe hepatotoxicity deemed secondary to drug-induced hepatitis. Additionally, 1 of the first 44 subjects enrolled in a phase III trial of aplaviroc developed severe hepatotoxicity, and the trials and development of aplaviroc were stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Investigational CCR5 antagonist (AK602/ONO4128/GSK-873140) developed by Ono Pharmaceuticals and GlaxoSmithKline for HIV-1. Severe hepatotoxicity deemed secondary to drug-induced hepatitis occurred in 3 subjects in phase IIb trials and in 1 of the first 44 subjects enrolled in a phase III trial; trials and development of aplaviroc were stopped as a result.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc (formerly GSK 873140), a CCR5 antagonist, demonstrated antiviral activity in short-term monotherapy studies, producing up to a 1.6-log10 reduction in plasma HIV-1 RNA levels during 10 days of treatment. However, drug-induced hepatitis occurred in 5 subjects in phase 2b and 3 trials; no deaths were noted, the hepatitis resolved upon aplaviroc discontinuation, and clinical development of the drug was terminated.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist formerly known as GSK 873140, studied in HIV-1-infected patients. Drug-induced hepatitis occurred in 5 subjects in phase 2b and 3 trials; no deaths occurred, hepatitis resolved upon drug discontinuation, and clinical development was terminated. Antiviral effect up to 1.6-log10 reduction in plasma HIV-1 RNA during 10 days of treatment; blocks MIP-1alpha at nanomolar concentrations while RANTES-mediated signaling is less susceptible to inhibition.

raw_record.support_text: Among three CCR5 inhibitors with preliminary clinical trial data, aplaviroc had its development halted after the development of severe hepatotoxicity in one individual, which necessitated liver transplantation, and a 1% rate of grade 3/4 alanine aminotransferase elevation among other patients on therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 inhibitor (chemokine receptor 5 antagonist) for HIV. Severe hepatotoxicity in one individual necessitated liver transplantation; a 1% rate of grade 3/4 alanine aminotransferase elevation was seen among other patients on therapy. Development of the drug was halted.

raw_record.support_text: Among the CCR5 antagonists that entered clinical development for HIV/AIDS, aplaviroc (GW873140) was discontinued due to observed hepatotoxicity in a Phase III trial; vicriviroc was in Phase III and maraviroc (Selzentry) gained regulatory approval in 2007.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist (GW873140) developed for HIV-1 infection; discontinued from development because of observed hepatotoxicity during a Phase III trial. No causal grading, severity, or phenotype details are provided.

raw_record.support_text: Development of aplaviroc was discontinued in 2006 following reports of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity in Phase IIb treatment-naive and Phase III treatment-experienced studies. Reported cases included simultaneous increases in serum alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin breaching the 'Hy's Law' threshold, which the US FDA considers indicative of drug-induced hepatotoxicity of particular clinical concern, and one case of increased alanine aminotransferase that demonstrated a clear dechallenge-rechallenge reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity leading to discontinuation of development in 2006. Cases included simultaneous increases in serum alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin breaching the Hy's Law threshold (considered by the US FDA to identify drug-induced hepatotoxicity of particular clinical concern), and a case of increased alanine aminotransferase with a clear dechallenge-rechallenge reaction. Sourced from Phase IIb treatment-naive and Phase III treatment-experienced studies.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc, a GlaxoSmithKline CCR5 antagonist compound, demonstrated antiviral activity with minimal toxicities in short-term monotherapy studies. In phase 2b trials, four out of roughly 300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity that, on liver biopsy, was consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to cessation of the trial. Similarly, one out of 26 patients in a phase 3 trial had alanine aminotransferase elevated to 24 times normal; no deaths occurred, the hepatitis resolved with aplaviroc discontinuation, the trial was stopped, and clinical development of aplaviroc was terminated.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist (GlaxoSmithKline). Phase 2b: 4 of ~300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to trial cessation. Phase 3: 1 of 26 patients showed ALT elevation to 24 times normal; no deaths, hepatitis resolved on aplaviroc discontinuation; trial stopped and clinical development terminated. Aplaviroc produced 1.0-1.6 log10 viral load reduction in 10-day monotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc (GSK873140, ONO-4128, AK-602), a small-molecule CCR5 antagonist licensed from Ono Pharmaceuticals, appeared well tolerated on short-term administration apart from mild/moderate gastrointestinal effects. However, chronic administration produced cases of severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005. A further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient from the Phase III trial ended all development activities on aplaviroc. The authors note the absence of reported human hepatotoxicity with the other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports the idea that these findings are compound specific rather than due to CCR5 blockade.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist for HIV-1 therapy. Chronic administration produced severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005; a further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient in the Phase III trial ended all development. In a Phase IIa study, 600 mg b.i.d. for 10 days gave mean viral load reduction of 1.66 log10 copies/ml; short-term administration showed only mild/moderate GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain). No hepatotoxicity attributed to CCR5 blockade itself; absence of hepatotoxicity with other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports compound specificity.

raw_record.support_text: A clinical trial with the CCR5 antagonist Aplaviroc was terminated prematurely due to treatment-associated hepatotoxicity, which was considered to be compound-related and idiosyncratic. In contrast, the original anti-HIV trials with Plerixafor were discontinued because of cardiac disturbances, not liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Aplaviroc is a CCR5 antagonist (used in anti-HIV trials). The trial was terminated prematurely due to treatment-associated hepatotoxicity regarded as compound-related and idiosyncratic. Plerixafor, also mentioned in the same passage, caused cardiac disturbances, not DILI, and is therefore not extracted as a liver-injury agent.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc, a small molecule CCR5 antagonist developed by GlaxoSmithKline as a spiro diketopiperazine moiety that inhibits HIV infection with a half-life of more than 100 hours, was halted at Phase IIB because of severe hepatotoxicity observed in patients under Aplaviroc therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist developed by GlaxoSmithKline; spiro diketopiperazine moiety; half-life over 100 hours; development halted at Phase IIB due to severe hepatotoxicity reported in patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes it is possible that pregabalin induced the liver injury in this patient, obtained a 'probable' classification using the causality assessment from the International consensus criteria, and reported the acute liver injury as being of hepatocellular type. Pregabalin was given as 75 mg twice daily for herpes zoster starting 12 days before admission, following unsuccessful tramadol and acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old male with 1-2 weeks history of sickness, nausea, vomiting, and itching. Peak labs: aspartate aminotransferase 50x ULN, alanine aminotransferase 35x ULN, bilirubin 354 µmol/l, peak INR 4.2 (normalized by discharge, INR 1.2 and bilirubin 75 mmol/l at 6-week follow-up; all liver tests normal at 6 months). Concomitant jaundice noted as carrying ~10% risk of death or liver transplantation. Nausea began ~8 days into pregabalin. Hepatitis and autoantibody serologies negative; no hepatic vein thrombosis on CT. Hepatocellular type per International consensus criteria; 'probable' causality classification. Prior treatment with tramadol and acetaminophen (unrelated to injury onset). Pregabalin is not subject to hepatic metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of hepatic adverse reaction associated with pregabalin and assess causality with the CIOMS scale: their case obtained a score above 8, which per CIOMS classifies the causal relationship of the hepatic adverse reaction to pregabalin as 'very probable' (muy probable). In the Maria and Vitorino scale the case scored 15, categorized as 'probable', although because it is a predominantly cholestatic case this scale is not considered ideal. Both cases of pregabalin-associated hepatotoxicity were reported to the regional pharmacovigilance center.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS score >8, classified as 'muy probable' (highly probable). Maria and Vitorino scale score 15, categorized as 'probable'. Case described as predominantly cholestatic (predominio colestásico). A comparison case by Orive Calzada et al was graded 'probable' (CIOMS score 6-8). Two cases of pregabalin-associated hepatotoxicity were reported to the Centro de Farmacovigilancia of each autonomous community.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that the absence of hepatic metabolism does not prevent drug-induced hepatotoxicity, and states that pregabalin (PGB)-induced hepatotoxicity has been described in limited case reports, each of which classified PGB as a probable cause of liver injury. This is presented alongside the observation that PGB rarely, if ever, is associated with hepatic dysfunction and is only minimally metabolized in the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Limited case reports each classified pregabalin as a probable cause of liver injury (references 113-116). The same text notes PGB is only minimally hepatically metabolized (major N-methylated metabolite accounts for ~1% of dose), rarely if ever associated with hepatic dysfunction, and does not inhibit or induce major cytochrome P450 isoenzymes, but that absence of hepatic metabolism does not preclude hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman developed a severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with jaundice, pruritus, elevated bilirubin and transaminases, and 2 spontaneous reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal; liver biopsy showed perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis and eosinophilic necrosis. The biochemical pattern was initially cytolytic and later mixed. The patient improved and normalized fully by week 20.
raw_record.extra_details: Escitalopram is the pure S enantiomer of citalopram, ~300x more selective for serotonin reuptake than noradrenaline, in the SSRI class. Dose 10 mg/day; symptoms began ~8 weeks after start. Labs: total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl rising to 10.8 mg/dl and 6.3 mg/dl at flares; initial ALT 2,400 U/dl, AST 1,065 U/dl, GGT 224 U/dl, ALP 116 U/dl; later mixed pattern ALT 1,624-2,714 U/dl, GGT 703-1,145 U/dl. Biopsy: perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, eosinophilic necrosis, moderate periportal round-cell/eosinophil infiltrate with lobular sparing, no bile duct lesion or cholestasis. CIOMS causality score 7 = 'probable'. Negative viral and autoimmune serology; no prior liver disease, alcohol, or herbal use. Dechallenge with subjective improvement but 2 icteric reactivation flares; full normalization at week 20. Reported as the first described case of escitalopram-induced toxic hepatitis, supporting that even severe hepatotoxicity can occur during escitalopram treatment. Underlying case: female, 49 years old.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a 49-year-old woman who developed severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with initially cytolytic and then mixed biochemical pattern, two spontaneous cholestatic/jaundice reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal, and biopsy showing perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, and eosinophilic necrosis consistent with hepatotoxicity. CIOMS causality assessment scored 7, corresponding to 'probable'. The authors state this is the first described case of toxic hepatitis due to escitalopram and caution that hepatotoxicity, even severe, should be considered during escitalopram treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 10 mg/day; symptoms present from 7 days before presentation, treatment started 8 weeks earlier; CIOMS causality score 7 ('probable'). Biopsy: perivenular balloonized hepatocytes, discrete microvacuolar steatosis, eosinophilic necrosis, moderate mixed inflammatory infiltrate (round cells and isolated eosinophils) in portal and lobular areas, no ductal injury or cholestasis. Biochemical pattern initially cytolytic then changed to mixed (max ALT 2,714 U/L, GGT 1,145 U/L, total bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl). Prolonged course with 2 spontaneous reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal; complete normalization at 20 weeks. Author reports this as the first described case of toxic hepatitis from escitalopram.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a probable case of escitalopram-induced liver injury. A 56-year-old Chinese lady presented with fever and cholestatic liver injury two weeks after initiation of escitalopram for the treatment of psychotic depression. Investigations for stones, viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver disease were unyielding, and upon stopping escitalopram repeat liver function tests showed downtrending liver enzymes with eventual normalization of serum aminotransferase levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 56-year-old Chinese lady with psychotic depression; cholestatic liver injury with fever developed two weeks after escitalopram initiation; CT abdomen/pelvis and hepatitis A, B, C and autoimmune liver disease workup were unyielding; after drug cessation, AST and ALT downtrended and normalized by one week post-discharge. Probable causality per case report. Clinical phenotype: cholestatic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old man was admitted with clinical jaundice with hepatitis, pruritus and dark urine; after an etiologic work-up for jaundice was negative, an adverse drug reaction with escitalopram was the sole possible explanation. Two days after escitalopram withdrawal pruritus resolved, clinical jaundice disappeared at ten days, and liver function tests normalized one month and three weeks after withdrawal. The authors state this is the first reported case where escitalopram was the only possible cause of cholestasis, with highly probable causality.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic and cytolysis liver injury; clinical jaundice, pruritus and dark urine; dechallenge with resolution of pruritus at 2 days, jaundice at 10 days, and normalized liver function tests at ~7 weeks after withdrawal. Etiologic study for hemolysis, viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, carcinoma, cholangitis, cholelithiasis and obstruction was negative. Reported as the first case of escitalopram as the only possible cause of cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: Across the four RECORD studies of rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin for VTE prevention after major orthopedic surgery, the authors report no evidence of drug-induced liver injury attributable to rivaroxaban. The incidence of predefined abnormal liver function tests (ALT elevated to three times the upper limit of normal and bilirubin >2-times ULN) was similar in the rivaroxaban and enoxaparin groups, and there was no evidence of compromised liver function attributable to rivaroxaban.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative finding in four phase III RECORD studies in patients undergoing major orthopedic surgery (TKR/THR) comparing oral rivaroxaban 10 mg od with subcutaneous enoxaparin 30 mg bid (10-14 d). Predefined abnormal LFTs (ALT >3x ULN and bilirubin >2x ULN) were similar between rivaroxaban and enoxaparin; the paper states no evidence of compromised liver function or drug-induced liver injury attributable to rivaroxaban.

raw_record.support_text: A report of 14 postmarketing cases of liver injury associated with rivaroxaban, including two with liver biopsy. Formal causality assessment classified rivaroxaban as the 'probable' cause in 7 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 14 postmarketing cases, 7 patients classified as 'probable' by formal causality assessment; 2 cases had liver biopsy; cases reported to a regional pharmacovigilance center for thromboembolic disorder treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 2 cases of rivaroxaban-induced DILI in patients, with alanine aminotransferase >5x ULN and serum bilirubin >2x ULN, most symptomatic, who recovered after discontinuing rivaroxaban. It cites a Swiss Regional Pharmacovigilance Center series of 14 rivaroxaban-induced DILI cases (10/14 with ALT >5x ULN, 9 with bilirubin >2x ULN, 13 recovered), stating the similarity strengthens the conclusion that rivaroxaban was causing liver injury. The conclusion states that treatment with rivaroxaban can be associated with severe hepatocellular liver injury, with some patients fulfilling Hy's law criteria, and complete recovery after discontinuation; renal reexposure is discouraged.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 index cases plus reference to a separate Swiss series of 14 rivaroxaban-induced DILI cases; 10/14 had ALT >5x ULN, 9/14 had serum bilirubin >2x ULN, most symptomatic, 13 recovered after discontinuation. Some patients fulfilled Hy's law criteria. Rapid clinical and biochemical improvement and complete recovery after discontinuation; authors recommend rapid discontinuation for symptomatic liver injury and avoiding reexposure, and propose a symptomatic-liver-injury warning in drug labels.

raw_record.support_text: A publication described 14 patients with rivaroxaban-associated liver injury reported to a Swiss regional Pharmacovigilance Center. Patients had a median age of 71 years (9 female, 5 male), treated for atrial fibrillation (n=4) or after knee/leg surgery (n=10); median dose was 10 mg/day, and median latency was 15.5 days. All but one were symptomatic and 11 were jaundiced; ALT exceeded 2x ULN in all (median 7.8x ULN). Eight had hepatocellular, four cholestatic and one mixed liver injury; median bilirubin was 6.6x ULN. RUCAM causality was highly probable in 4, probable in 7 and possible in 3 patients; one patient died, all others recovered. Author database searches found rivaroxaban as a suspected DILI cause in WHO (179 reports), EMA (375) and FDA FAERS (87) databases. A second Swiss case report described two further patients (10 mg rivaroxaban after surgery) presenting with jaundice 1-2 months later; one had hepatocellular and one mixed injury, causality probable/possible, with full recovery 2 weeks after stopping.
raw_record.extra_details: First series of 14 patients: median age 71 y (range 41-91), 9 female/5 male; indications AF (n=4) and knee replacement/leg surgery (n=10); median dose 10 mg/day (range 10-20); latency 15.5 d (range 3-62); 13/14 symptomatic, 11 jaundiced; ALT >2x ULN in all (median 7.8x, range 2.5-53.7); ALP <2x ULN in 5 and >2x ULN in 9 (median 2.5x); 8 hepatocellular, 4 cholestatic, 1 mixed; bilirubin in 10 patients median 6.6x ULN (range 1-21.6); RUCAM: highly probable 4, probable 7, possible 3; one death, others recovered. Two patients biopsied showed cholestatic injury with centroacinar cholestasis, focal hepatocyte ballooning, portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltration and biliary epithelial alterations. Pharmacovigilance database searches: WHO VigiBase 179 DILI-compatible reports, EMA EudraVigilance 375 events, FDA FAERS 87 cases with rivaroxaban as suspected cause. Second case series (2 patients, 52 y man and 73 y woman, 10 mg after surgery): jaundice 1-2 months later, massively raised transaminases with slight ALP rise; 1 hepatocellular and 1 mixed injury; causality probable/possible; full recovery ~2 weeks after stopping; biopsy in the hepatocellular case showed confluent centroacinar hepatocyte necrosis with macrophage infiltration and minimal portal lymphocytic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported patient, liver injury occurred after initiation of rivaroxaban therapy and resolved after dechallenge, with a strong chronologic relationship between rivaroxaban and hepatocellular injury resulting in a RUCAM score of 8 (time to onset, course, risk factors, concomitant drugs, exclusion of other causes, previous information of hepatotoxicity, and response to readministration). The authors additionally note that in daily practice hepatotoxicity is a rare unpredictable adverse effect of rivaroxaban highlighted by post-marketing spontaneous reporting systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. RUCAM score of 8 (probable causality), with components including time to onset (+2), course (+2), risk factors (+1), concomitant drugs (0), exclusion of other causes of liver injury (+2), previous information of hepatotoxicity of the drug (+1), and response to readministration (0). Liver injury resolved after dechallenge. Post-marketing spontaneous reporting systems highlight hepatotoxicity as a rare unpredictable adverse effect; authors advise hepatic enzyme monitoring during the first weeks of treatment because asymptomatic forms are the most common expression.

raw_record.support_text: The compiled case series (Table 1) reports numerous patients who developed drug-induced liver injury during therapeutic rivaroxaban treatment at doses of 10-30 mg/day for indications including knee replacement surgery, atrial fibrillation, and venous thromboembolism prevention. Latencies ranged from about 2 to 180 days, with symptoms of jaundice, nausea, pruritus, and fatigue; hepatocellular (H), cholestatic (C), and mixed (M) biochemical patterns were documented, and most cases recovered after rivaroxaban discontinuation, while one 89-year-old patient died of acute liver failure. RUCAM causality scores ranged from 3 to 9 across cases. The two new cases presented in this article (an 79-year-old man and an 84-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation) showed hepatocellular injury with ALT >35× ULN and >9× ULN respectively, negative viral and autoimmune serology, and recovery within 1-4 weeks after rivaroxaban withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses 10-30 mg/day; latencies approximately 2-180 days across cases; symptoms included jaundice, nausea, pruritus, fatigue, vomiting, and right hypochondrial pain. Most patients recovered after discontinuation (within 1-4 weeks in the two new cases), one 89-year-old female died of acute liver failure (RUCAM 6), and one elderly male died of paralytic ileus. Liver histology in some cases showed cholestasis with portal inflammation and eosinophilic infiltration, centrilobular cholestasis with mixed portal inflammation, or severe lobular hepatitis with perivenular confluent necrosis. RUCAM scores 3-9. Naranjo score 7 (probable) for case 1 and 4 (possible) for case 2. No rechallenge performed. The discussion notes a meta-analysis of 29 phase III trials (152,116 patients) with DOACs including rivaroxaban found no increased risk of hepatotoxicity, but argues trial populations are too small and short-term to capture rare idiosyncratic DILI. Case 2's concurrent drugs (lansoprazole, amlodipine, carvedilol, furosemide) were continued and considered unlikely alternative causes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of hepatitis and synthetic liver failure secondary to rivaroxaban in a 39-year-old patient with no past medical history, which resolved rapidly after drug withdrawal and for which no alternate cause of liver injury was identified. The patient had been on rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for a left peroneal deep vein thrombosis attributed to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, which was ceased; liver function tests were normal at initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for a left peroneal deep vein thrombosis attributed to contraceptive depot medroxyprogesterone acetate use (which was ceased); normal liver function tests at initiation; injury manifested as hepatitis and synthetic liver failure; resolved rapidly after drug withdrawal with no alternate cause identified; 39-year-old female with no past medical history. The paper notes a prior meta-analysis of 29 phase III trials of new oral anticoagulants reported no hepatotoxicity association.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with elevated transaminases while on rivaroxaban for 13 days. After ruling out thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis B reactivation, and transient hypotension-related ischemia, a calculated RUCAM score of 8 indicated rivaroxaban as the 'probable' cause of DILI. A preliminary diagnosis of DILI due to rivaroxaban was made; rivaroxaban was switched to apixaban on the sixth day of admission, and liver enzymes trended downward, further supporting the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality assessment score of 8 (probable). Hepatocellular pattern with calculated R-factor of 18.8. Patient on rivaroxaban for 13 days at presentation; median time to liver injury reported as 15 days. Elevated AST/ALT peaked around day 7 (ALT 1702 U/L, AST 810 U/L) then downtrended after discontinuation, normalizing by 2 months. Patient had malaise but no jaundice or vomiting. Competing causes (thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis B reactivation, ischemia) ruled out. Tenofovir already being taken for hepatitis B. Mechanism likely idiosyncratic and possibly immunologic; no CYP3A4 inhibitor co-medication present. Rivaroxaban has dual elimination (one-third renal, two-thirds hepatic, CYP3A4-dependent). Rarely reported to cause acute liver failure and, very rarely, death.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who developed isolated acute hepatitis after propofol administration and had spontaneous resolution of the hepatitis. The liver biopsy results and rapid normalization of the transaminases were consistent with hepatitis from drug or toxin injury, and the validated Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method gave a drug causality score of +6 (scale -9 to +15), indicating a probable relationship between propofol and the acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality score +6 (scale -9 to +15) indicating probable relationship, in a patient given propofol for sedation during colonoscopy. Hepatocellular pattern supported by AST and ALT >50x normal with a normal/slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase; hepatitis resolved spontaneously with supportive measures. Two prior literature cases of isolated acute hepatitis after propofol (a 66-year-old male after therapeutic ERCP and a 17-year-old female one day after femoral hernia repair) also resolved spontaneously; neither had liver biopsy confirmation. The presented patient's liver biopsy showed findings consistent with drug/toxin injury.

raw_record.support_text: Propofol is commonly used as an anesthetic agent for invasive procedures. The paper reports a case of idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury (DILI) in a 39-year-old female after a brief exposure to propofol during routine endoscopy. Within 48 hours of discharge she was hospitalized with abdominal pain, nausea, and laboratory abnormalities consistent with hepatocellular injury; serologic workup for viral and autoimmune etiologies was negative, and the transaminase abnormalities improved by hospital day three and resolved by two week follow up. The RUCAM score was highly suggestive of an adverse drug reaction, and this was described as only the fourth case report of propofol-related DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old female; brief exposure during routine endoscopy; hospitalized within 48 hours with abdominal pain and nausea; serologic workup for viral and autoimmune etiologies negative; transaminase abnormalities improved by hospital day three and resolved by two week follow up; Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score highly suggestive of an adverse drug reaction; reported as the fourth case report of propofol-related DILI; INR was 1.5 on day of admission then ranged from 1.1 to 1.2 throughout hospital stay.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's changes in laboratory test values and corresponding symptoms of nausea and vomiting were thought to be related to enoxaparin-related hepatotoxicity, and enoxaparin was discontinued. Symptoms subsided over the following days with complete resolution by hospital discharge, and AST and ALT returned to normal around two months after discharge with no other changes to the drug regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: On the Naranjo scale (Naranjo et al.), hepatotoxicity was rated as probably related to enoxaparin administration. Patient had no prior enoxaparin or heparinoid use; no other drugs known to elevate AST/ALT were given on admission, and viral hepatitis testing and abdominal ultrasound were negative. Peak labs after enoxaparin initiation on day 21 (continued to day 24): AST 228 units/L, ALT 465 units/L, LDH up to 346 units/L, ALP up to 194 units/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL; onset of enzyme changes within 48 hours of enoxaparin with peak on days 5-6 (1-2 days after discontinuation). Symptoms of nausea and vomiting developed within the first days after initiation. Levels decreased shortly after discontinuation and returned to baseline within two months. Warfarin was initiated on the same day (day 21) and continued. A prior episode of elevated transaminases was related to acute cholecystitis and laparoscopic cholecystectomy two years earlier, with subsequent return to normal.

raw_record.support_text: The reported case is consistent with the established clinical signature of enoxaparin liver injury: short latency, rapid reversibility, and no accompanying hypersensitivity symptoms such as fever, rash, or eosinophilia. In this patient, aminotransferase elevations peaked by day 7 and began to normalize quickly thereafter, with liver injury completely resolving after the drug was discontinued; the replacing fondaparinux showed no cross-reactivity and liver tests remained normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Aminotransferase elevations peaked by day 7 and resolved after discontinuation; peak values were higher than in other published reports. Fondaparinux, started on day 7, showed no cross-reactivity with normal liver tests. Authors note a similar hepatic pattern is associated with UFH and presume heparin-induced liver injury is a class effect.

raw_record.support_text: Tanespimycin (17-AAG) was evaluated in Phase I clinical trials. The dose-limiting toxicity of the daily × 5 schedule was hepatotoxicity with elevations in transaminases and bilirubin, which led to abandonment of this schedule. The weekly schedule was better tolerated without significant hepatotoxicity, and the commonest toxicities of the weekly and twice-weekly schedules included mild hepatotoxicity reflected as reversible transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Tanespimycin is 17-AAG (17-allyl-aminodemethoxygeldanamycin), an HSP90 inhibitor used as an antitumor agent. In the daily × 5 schedule (every 3 weeks), hepatotoxicity with transaminase and bilirubin elevations was the dose-limiting toxicity and led to abandonment of this schedule; weekly and twice-weekly schedules showed only mild reversible hepatotoxicity (transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia). Other common toxicities were diarrhea, fatigue, nausea, and myalgia. Reported recommended Phase II doses were 220 mg/m² (twice weekly), 295 mg/m² (weekly × 3), 308 mg/m², 450 mg/m² (weekly), 40 mg/m² (daily × 5), and 112 mg/m² (daily × 3). In a combination study with docetaxel, the 17-AAG dose was 300 mg/m².

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials of 17-AAG (the first HSP90 inhibitor to reach the clinic), toxicity increased gradually with dose and schedule; in addition to diarrhea and fatigue, severe hepatotoxicity of 17-AAG posed a prominent and inevitable challenge. This is presented as a human clinical-trials finding for 17-AAG used as a single agent and in combinations against solid tumors and lymphomas/leukemias.
raw_record.extra_details: 17-AAG (tanespimycin) is a first-generation ansamycin-based HSP90 ATPase inhibitor used against relapsed/refractory solid tumors, lymphomas, and leukemias, and in combination (e.g., with sorafenib) for unresectable or metastatic solid tumors; most trials halted at Phase I/II due to poor efficacy and treatment-related toxicity; also reported poor water solubility, short half-life, and uneven distribution.

raw_record.support_text: A case of hepatitis attributed to moxifloxacin is presented, with the diagnosis supported by known hepatotoxic potential of the drug, a compatible temporal sequence, reasonable exclusion of alternative causes, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal. Re-exposure was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM causality score of 8 points (probable). Of 16 Spanish notifications of moxifloxacin hepatitis, 2 were fatal (12.5%); symptoms appear in most cases between 3 and 10 days of treatment, with late hepatotoxic effects also described. The European Medicines Agency published a July 2008 press release concluding moxifloxacin should only be used in its authorized indications when no other antibiotic can be used, and recommending caution regarding certain adverse effects including fatal hepatic reactions. Probable genetic determinants of some idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity reactions are noted. The case diagnosis was based on known hepatotoxic potential, compatible temporal sequence, exclusion of alternative causes, and rapid improvement on withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of fatal hepatotoxicity caused by Moxifloxacin in a 72-year-old man who received Moxifloxacin for treatment of an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis. He developed jaundice and epigastric tenderness one week after treatment, with marked elevation in liver enzymes and bilirubin, and his condition deteriorated despite ICU supportive care. Acute hepatic failure resulting in death was attributed to an idiosyncratic reaction to Moxifloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: 72-year-old Caucasian man with COPD, rheumatoid arthritis, and remote squamous cell carcinoma of skin. Moxifloxacin given for 5 days for acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, along with steroids and bronchodilators, by primary care physician. Jaundice appeared about one week after treatment. Labs showed WBC 2.6, platelets 13000 (pancytopenia), AST 150, ALT 193, alkaline phosphatase 337, total bilirubin 29.0, Cr 2.8, albumin 2.8. Admitted to ICU; acute hepatic failure led to death despite supportive care. Concurrent home medications included tiotropium bromide, salmeterol/fluticasone inhaler, albuterol, folic acid, and low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. Authors note scant literature on severe Moxifloxacin hepatotoxicity and few case reports of fatal hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Figure 1c shows a patient with a cholestatic pattern of serum enzyme elevations and prolonged, severe cholestasis arising 8 days after starting a course of moxifloxacin (Case 3 in Table 2). She developed prolonged jaundice (1.3 years) ultimately leading to hepatic failure and liver transplantation, with histology of the explanted liver showing vanishing bile duct syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic pattern of enzyme elevation per R-ratio; injury arose 8 days after starting a moxifloxacin course; prolonged jaundice (1.3 years) progressing to hepatic failure and liver transplantation; explant histology showed vanishing bile duct syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in its serial measurement of liver function, no evidence of hepatotoxicity with dabigatran was found. This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion for dabigatran.
raw_record.extra_details: RE-LY randomized trial (dabigatran 110 mg and 150 mg vs warfarin). Liver-function monitoring showed ALT or AST >3x ULN in 124 (2.1%) of 110-mg and 117 (1.9%) of 150-mg dabigatran patients vs 132 (2.2%) with warfarin; ALT/AST >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN occurred in 13 (0.2%) on each dabigatran dose vs 21 (0.3%) on warfarin; hepatobiliary disorders (mostly cholelithiasis/cholecystitis) were similar across groups. Authors concluded no evidence of dabigatran hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Serial measurement of liver function in both the phase 2 and 3 trials of dabigatran showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity (Fig. 3). The paper therefore explicitly concludes that dabigatran was not associated with hepatotoxicity in these clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Serial measurement of liver function in both phase 2 and phase 3 trials (up to 150 mg bid in RE-LY) showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Table 3 lists ALT or AST >3xULN with Bili >2xULN within 30 days rates of 0.2% for dabigatran 150 mg bid and 110 mg bid versus 0.3% for warfarin, interpreted by the authors as no hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the RE-LY study of over 18,000 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation randomized to dabigatran 110 mg twice daily, dabigatran 150 mg twice daily, or dose-adjusted warfarin for 2 years, dyspepsia occurred in 12% of the dabigatran patients, and no evidence of hepatotoxicity was reported. The paper states this as an explicit finding that dabigatran showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: RE-LY trial (n > 18,000) in non-valvular atrial fibrillation; dabigatran 110 mg twice daily and 150 mg twice daily vs dose-adjusted warfarin (target INR 2-3) for 2 years. Dyspepsia occurred in 12% of dabigatran patients; the paper explicitly reported no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily was approved by the FDA for AF patients except those with severe renal impairment (an exclusion criterion of RE-LY).

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 52-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia who developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine. Approximately 1 week after starting titration (clozapine 25 mg AM / 75 mg PM) she developed abdominal pain and malaise with elevated ALT (75 IU/L) and AST (198 IU/L). Clozapine was discontinued after 8 days; LFTs peaked the next day (ALT 308, AST 119, GGT 78 IU/L), then improved by day 5 and normalized by 4 weeks. On rechallenge with slower titration, LFTs remained normal for 1 month, then on clozapine 100 mg AM / 250 mg PM she had elevated AST 44, ALT 107, and GGT 37 IU/L that persisted despite a 50 mg dose reduction; she was asymptomatic. Clozapine was discontinued with subsequent normalization of LFTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1. First episode: abdominal pain and general malaise, ALT 75 IU/L (ref 10-40), AST 198 IU/L (ref 10-42); clozapine discontinued after 8 days; day after discontinuation ALT peaked at 308, AST 119, GGT 78 IU/L (ref 0-35); after 5 days off drug ALT 77, AST 24, GGT 53; normal at 4 weeks; abdominal ultrasound normal. Rechallenge: after ~1 month normal LFTs, on clozapine 100 mg AM/250 mg PM elevated AST 44, ALT 107, GGT 37; remained elevated despite 50 mg dose reduction; asymptomatic with normal physical exam; discontinued with normalization, ALT slightly elevated at 64. Psychosis worsened on withdrawal; chlorpromazine restarted for agitation.

raw_record.support_text: The letter states that hepatic adverse effects of clozapine are under-recognized: increased liver enzymes are reported to affect between 30% and 50% of patients, most commonly aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT), with 60% of increases resolving in the first 13 weeks of treatment. To date, 2 cases of mortality due to hepatic failure and 1 case due to hepatitis secondary to clozapine have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic used in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Increased liver enzymes affect 30-50% of patients, with AST and ALT most commonly involved; 60% of increases resolve in the first 13 weeks. Cases reported include 2 deaths due to hepatic failure and 1 due to hepatitis secondary to clozapine. Case Report 1: a 52-year-old woman (paranoid schizophrenia) developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine, which discontinued and on later rechallenge produced similar hepatotoxicity; Case Report 2 remained on clozapine with the abnormalities resolving spontaneously.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, a patient on clozapine 250 mg/day developed marked liver test abnormalities (ALT 1914, AST 830, bilirubin 76, gamma-GT 99 U/L, albumin 35 g/L, WCC 21.4, Hb 107). Clozapine was stopped immediately and the patient was transferred to a gastroenterology unit for observation. The authors describe the case as illustrating the treacherous nature of a rare fulminant hepatotoxic reaction, with no pre-existing liver disease or indicator of vulnerability, and rapid progression of liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Young male treated for a first psychotic episode; described as the youngest such case in the literature with good recovery. Peak transaminases (ALT 2282, AST 1056) occurred the day after clozapine cessation, gamma-GT peaked at 164, bilirubin peaked at 112 on day 3, INR raised to 1.3 for 5 days, albumin below normal for 2 weeks, CRP peaked at 45.5 mg/L. All enzymes returned to normal 3-4 weeks after cessation, bilirubin last to normalise; recovery so complete that liver transplant, otherwise to be considered, was not needed. Patient was subsequently restarted on amisulpride 200 mg twice daily with normal liver function tests. Clinical course included only sedation despite severe injury; no pre-existing liver disease or vulnerability indicator identified.

raw_record.support_text: Clozapine associated hepatitis is characterized by clinically significant elevated transaminases (ALT and/or AST >3 fold above ULN), eosinophilia, and elevated serum bilirubin (>2 fold above ULN) in over 50% of cases, with jaundice in a minority. Hepatitis onset was within 8 weeks of clozapine initiation in all but three cases (mean onset 34.2 days), with a mean time to recovery of 25.9 days. The severe inflammatory (hypersensitivity) form was associated with death in three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis presented with fever, abdominal pain, nausea, and lethargy; clinically significant ALT and/or AST >3-fold ULN in all cases; mean ALT 629 U/L; elevated bilirubin (>2-fold ULN) in over 50%; onset within 8 weeks for most (range up to 90 days), mean 34.2 days; recovery mean 25.9 days; death in three cases; 50% had other internal organ involvement; immune-mediated hypersensitivity mechanism postulated; five of seven rechallenged cases had recurrence of inflammatory disorder at mean 3.5 days.

raw_record.support_text: Clozapine is associated with a spectrum of human drug-induced liver injury in therapeutic use. The most common abnormality is an isolated asymptomatic increase in aminotransferase levels (ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 clozapine-treated patients; an increase in one enzyme in 61% of 125 patients). Icteric hepatitis has been reported twice, with biopsy-confirmed zone 3 (piecemeal) necrosis in one case and normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within 4 weeks. Cholestatic or mixed hepatitis has been reported in two cases, with jaundice within 8 weeks and confirmed cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy is very rare, with only 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients in the manufacturers' database over 6 years. The mechanism is unclear, but the drug is hepatically metabolized via cytochrome P450 and reactive metabolites are presumed to mediate the damage, with insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic from immunoallergic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Common isolated asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation: ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 patients; in 125 patients an increase in one of AST, ALT, GGT, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase in 61%, with ≥2-fold increase in 31%; no jaundice reported in that cohort; regulatory data reported aminotransferase increase in 30%. Icteric hepatitis reported twice, associated nausea within 4 weeks, biopsy-confirmed zone 3 necrosis in one case, bilirubin/aminotransferase normalized in 4 weeks; manufacturers reported icteric hepatitis in 84/136,000 (0.06%). Two cases of cholestatic or mixed hepatitis with jaundice within 8 weeks and biopsy-confirmed cholestatic hepatitis; liver tests normalized upon discontinuation. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy: 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients over 6 years, including the present case. Mechanism unclear; predominantly hepatic cytochrome P450-dependent metabolism; reactive metabolites presumed, insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic vs immunoallergic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded the patient's diagnosis was compatible with tubular dysfunction, drug-induced hepatitis, and hypersensitivity reaction due to deferasirox. The patient, on deferasirox for iron overload, had elevated aminotransferases (peaking at about 8 times normal on hospital day 4 with progressive decrease over the next month), jaundice (total bilirubin 3.79 mg/dL), and fever; she had discontinued deferasirox before admission, symptoms persisted then resolved, and she was discharged in good health 8 days after admission. Infectious and other causes were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Female patient with beta thalassemia major (splenectomy 28 years earlier) treated with orally active iron chelator deferasirox. Shortly after the initial dose she developed fatigue, malaise and fever (38.5 C); initial aminotransferase elevation about 2x normal, peaking about 8x normal on hospital day 4 with gradual normalization over one month. Liver tests: aspartate aminotransferase 167 U/L (ref 9-36), alanine aminotransferase 250 U/L (ref 10-28), gamma-glutamyltransferase 102 U/L, total bilirubin 3.79 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 494 U/L, elevated CRP. Concurrent findings included hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (tubular dysfunction), hypokalemia, leukocytosis. Dechallenge: deferasirox stopped, symptoms initially persisted then resolved. Infectious etiologies (Epstein-Barr virus, toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, Brucella melitensis, HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV) and blood cultures negative; autoimmune serologies negative. Patient continued iron chelation with deferoxamine one month later.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that there have been several case reports of clinically apparent liver injury associated with deferasirox (DFX) therapy, which was often severe and occasionally fatal. Onset of acute liver injury ranged from a few days to 8 weeks after starting DFX, the pattern of injury was typically hepatocellular with marked elevations in serum aminotransferase levels, recovery was usually rapid once DFX was stopped, but some cases were associated with progressive liver injury and hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Iron chelator given to iron-overloaded, regularly transfused patients (thalassemia, sickle cell disease, myelodysplastic anemia, aplastic anemia, hereditary hemochromatosis, congenital dyserythropoetic anemia). Onset of acute liver injury a few days to 8 weeks after starting DFX; typically hepatocellular pattern with marked aminotransferase elevations; rapid recovery on discontinuation, but some cases had progressive liver injury and hepatic failure. Summary table lists 3 previously reported acute liver failure cases (ages 12-63 y): one full recovery with conservative management, one death with management of sepsis/multiorgan failure, one full recovery after N-acetylcysteine. DFX-treatment stopped liver-test elevation occurred in 6% of patients and led to drug discontinuation in 1-2%. Underlying diagnoses in the case table were hereditary hemochromatosis, sickle cell disease, and congenital dyserythropoetic anemia type I.

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of hepatotoxicity occurred after high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone treatment of a demyelinating disease. The first patient developed a histologically documented acute hepatitis and recovered after 3 weeks; the second showed a mild augmentation of liver enzymes that normalized within a few days. The causal relationship between hepatotoxicity and methylprednisolone treatment was deemed probable in both cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 33-year-old man with first episode of demyelinating encephalopathy, 4-day high-dose IV methylprednisolone (total 2.5 g); 5 weeks later AST 349 U/L and ALT 1042 U/L; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with focal liver cell necrosis in acinar zones 2-3, monocyte/macrophage infiltration, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, acidophil bodies, and focal microvesicular steatosis; recovery within 20 days. Case 2: 27-year-old woman treated for retrobulbar optic neuritis with 6-day high-dose IV methylprednisolone (total 4.5 g); on day 6 AST 39 U/L, ALT 122 U/L, normalizing in 4 days. Both patients had no prior liver disease, denied alcohol and any drug use for the previous 6 months, and had negative hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and autoantibody markers.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of a 24-year-old female treated with pulsed methylprednisolone (MT) for multiple sclerosis who developed icteric hepatitis and impaired liver synthetic function. Hepatotoxicity developed several weeks after drug exposure, and the causal association with MT was confirmed by an unintentional rechallenge test.
raw_record.extra_details: 24-year-old female with multiple sclerosis (retrobulbar optic neuritis history). Treated with pulsed IV methylprednisolone for MS exacerbation: initial 6-day course at 0.5 g/d, then later pulses totaling 3.0 g. Icteric hepatitis with impaired liver synthetic function and prothrombin synthesis; jaundice developed ~4 weeks after the second MT pulse and ~1 week after the last Betaferon dose. Laboratory: AST 900 IU/L, ALT 1740 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 186 IU/L, GGTP 50 IU/L, bilirubin 17.9 mg/dL (direct 16.1), prothrombin index 35.1% (INR 2.52), AFP 17.18 ng/mL, MELD score 26 (potential liver transplantation candidate). Elevated SMA (>1:320). No liver biopsy due to low prothrombin. Spontaneous recovery and discharge after 3 weeks. Causal association with MT confirmed by unintentional rechallenge (a later 6-day MT pulse of total 3.0 g without Betaferon reproduced acute hepatitis 4 weeks later, AST 1488 IU/L, ALT 1129 IU/L, bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL, then recovery). Betaferon (beta-1b interferon) and acetaminophen were initially considered but MT was the confirmed cause. Brief literature review notes corticosteroids occasionally linked to severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that hepatotoxicity after corticosteroid pulse therapy has been increasingly acknowledged in the literature but is not yet in the information leaflet. It cites Gutkowski et al., who reported a 24-year-old female who received a total of 3 g of IV methylprednisolone (MP) over 6 days and developed hepatotoxicity several weeks after exposure, with the causal association confirmed by an unintentional rechallenge. The authors further summarized 12 additional case reports of corticosteroid-induced hepatotoxicity, five of them in multiple sclerosis patients, with clinical courses ranging from asymptomatic hypertransaminasemia to fulminant hepatic failure that led to death in three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred after IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy (3 g total over 6 days), manifesting several weeks after exposure; confirmed by unintentional rechallenge. Paper also summarizes 12 additional corticosteroid-induced hepatotoxicity case reports (5 in MS patients), with courses from asymptomatic hypertransaminasemia to fulminant hepatic failure, fatal in 3 cases. The authors note hepatotoxicity after CS pulse therapy is not yet incorporated in the drug information leaflet.

raw_record.support_text: Methylprednisolone was adjudicated as a single causative agent in 2 DILI cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry.
raw_record.extra_details: 2 adjudicated single-cause cases; ATC D07AA01 (corticosteroid).

raw_record.support_text: The lower dose of lapaquistat (50 mg/day) had relatively few commonly reported side effects such as headache and back pain. Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Ltd. discontinued clinical development of lapaquistat because of hepatotoxicity. Although almost every known antihyperlipidemic drug, including all statins, is hepatotoxic at high doses, the dose-dependent hepatotoxicity of lapaquistat was a major reason that terminated its clinical development, and the major threat was that hepatotoxicity was observed at low doses, 50 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Squalene synthase inhibitor tested in Phase II and Phase III clinical trials in Europe and the United States; hepatotoxicity was dose-dependent and, importantly, observed at the low therapeutic dose of 50 mg/day, prompting discontinuation of clinical development by Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Ltd.; the compound is no longer pursued as a statin complement. Lower-dose side effects included headache and back pain.

raw_record.support_text: Lapaquistat, an inhibitor of squalene synthase, showed promising results in preclinical and early clinical studies, but in a broad clinical Phase III trial severe increases in liver enzymes and hepatotoxicity occurred, leading to discontinuation of its development.
raw_record.extra_details: Squalene synthase inhibitor tested for hypercholesterolemia; severe increases in liver enzymes and hepatotoxicity occurred in a broad Phase III trial, after which drug development was discontinued.

raw_record.support_text: In the context of the RE-LY trial comparing dabigatran etexilate with warfarin for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, dabigatran etexilate showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. The trial findings on bleeding and myocardial infarction risk did not include any report of liver injury for dabigatran.
raw_record.extra_details: Finding reported within the RE-LY trial, a randomized blinded trial comparing two dabigatran etexilate doses (150 mg twice daily and lower dose) with warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation; dabigatran was associated with increased gastrointestinal bleeding (higher dose only), myocardial infarction, and fewer intracranial bleeds, but no hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Dabigatran etexilate showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity in the RE-LY trial. There was no statistically significant difference in the frequency of transaminase rise, defined as an AST or ALT rise greater than three times the upper limit of the normal range, between either dose of dabigatran etexilate (110 mg or 150 mg BID) and warfarin.
raw_record.extra_details: RE-LY trial of atrial fibrillation patients (mean CHADS2 score 2.1); no significant difference in transaminase rise (>3x ULN for AST or ALT) between dabigatran etexilate 110 mg BID or 150 mg BID and warfarin.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old patient treated with doxycycline (100 mg/d) for bacterial bronchitis for one week developed malaise, jaundice, markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 4670 U/L, ALT 5350 U/L, bilirubin 226 µmol/L) and impaired liver function (INR 1.45). After exclusion of viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease and paracetamol intoxication, the authors concluded that doxycyclin-induced liver damage seemed to be probable. Thirteen years earlier the patient had a similar jaundice episode with elevated liver enzymes after intake of doxycycline (100 mg/d), suggesting repeat doxycycline exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Doxycycline 100 mg/d for one week for bacterial bronchitis. First exposure episode 13 years earlier produced jaundice (total bilirubin 224 µmol/L) and elevated liver enzymes (AST 309 U/L, ALT 763 U/L); liver histology then showed portal lymphoplasmacellular and eosinophilic inflammation with slight bile duct epithelial lesions. Current episode progressed to acute liver failure (AST 2134 U/L, ALT 2820 U/L, INR 3.0, bilirubin up to 380 µmol/L) with renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy; liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis and 40% liver cell necrosis; patient underwent liver transplantation (MELD 40). Explanted liver revealed giant cell hepatitis with severe cholestasis and siderosis, incomplete micronodular cirrhosis with perisinusoidal and porto-central fibrosis. Extensive workup negative for viral hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, EBV, HIV, autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, SLA, LKM, SMA, AMA, pANCA), ferritin/transferrin saturation hemodromatosis (C282Y, H63D negative), Wilson's disease, alpha1-antitrypsin, and paracetamol intoxication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report what they believe to be the first definitive case of doxycycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis, occurring in the setting of chronic systemic tetracycline therapy for acne vulgaris. They note that while this rare serious adverse event is well described with minocycline, there have been no prior cases linking doxycycline to drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: A 22-year-old female with acne vulgaris had taken doxycycline 100 mg daily for 4 months before presentation with 2 weeks of jaundice, diffuse pruritus, and fatigue. ALT 1,559 IU/L, AST 938 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 101 IU/L. ANA positive >1:640, anti-smooth muscle antibody positive 1:80; soluble liver antibody 1.1U, anti-LKM negative, IgG 1210 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C) and CMV/EBV PCR negative. Liver biopsy compatible with chronic, Batts-Ludwig grade 3 autoimmune hepatitis without fibrosis. After doxycycline discontinuation and methylprednisolone 60 mg IV for two doses followed by an 8-week prednisone taper, AST normalized within 14 days and complete liver chemistry normalization within 20 days; chemistries normal 6 months after steroid discontinuation. Concurrent only blueberry extract and a daily probiotic; ~1.2 oz alcohol weekly. Authors note drug-induced AIH can be difficult to differentiate from idiosyncratic DILI.

raw_record.support_text: After excluding infectious, malignant, vascular, and autoimmune liver diseases, a diagnosis of a hepatocellular pattern of idiosyncratic DILI due to doxycycline was established. The patient presented with significant elevation of liver enzymes (AST 814 IU/L, ALT 758 IU/L) with normal bilirubin and INR, and a consistent temporal association between doxycycline intake and liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality score was 8 and Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 6, defining the case as probable DILI. Liver enzymes improved and normalized within one month after doxycycline withdrawal when the patient was switched to amoxicillin for a 14-day course. The paper notes antibiotics are the most common drug class causing DILI, and cites an Iceland study in which amoxicillin-clavulanate was the most common cause followed by nitrofurantoin, with doxycycline causative in only 2 of 32,677 cases. AST was 814 IU/L (reference <20) and ALT 758 IU/L (reference <20); total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL and INR 1.1 were normal.

raw_record.support_text: Niperotidine is an H2 antagonist structurally related to ranitidine. Twenty-five cases of acute hepatitis (including one death from fulminant hepatitis) associated with niperotidine use were reported in Italy between March and August 1995, and the drug was withdrawn from the market. The methylenedioxy group of niperotidine (absent in ranitidine) is known to undergo metabolism to catechol and quinone metabolites.
raw_record.extra_details: H2 antagonist structurally related to ranitidine; 25 cases of acute hepatitis reported in Italy between March and August 1995, including one death from fulminant hepatitis; drug withdrawn from the market. Methylenedioxy group (absent in ranitidine) metabolizes to catechol and quinone metabolites, implicated in toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-five cases of acute hepatitis, probably related to the use of niperotidine, were reported in Italy between March and August 1995. The diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury was supported by the chronological correlation (onset after therapy, dramatic improvement on withdrawal) and by exclusion of viral hepatitis, other drugs, alcohol, biliary obstruction, and travel-related causes. One patient had a positive rechallenge that confirmed the reaction was most probably niperotidine-related. The paper concludes the liver injury is idiosyncratic, with no dose-relationship, rarity and unpredictability, and variable latency, possibly related to a toxic metabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: 25 patients treated with niperotidine (daily doses 23-920 mg, treatment duration 15-210 days) had acute hepatitis; causal assessment followed International Consensus Meeting criteria (reference 3), with a positive rechallenge in one patient (115 mg/day; ALT, AST, bilirubin rose to 1000 UI/l, 1200 UI/l, 15 mg/dl and normalized 7 days after withdrawal). Liver injury patterns in the 25 cases were hepatocellular (3), cholestatic (9), or mixed (13). One 54-year-old woman on 230 mg/d for 2 months developed fulminant hepatitis (bilirubin 30 mg/dl, grade 2 encephalopathy, ascites, prothrombin time 18%) and died following an acute episode of digestive haemorrhage. Pathogenesis proposed as idiosyncratic, possibly via a toxic metabolite; niperotidine is an H2-receptor antagonist structurally related to ranitidine (furan ring) with a piperonyl side chain.

raw_record.support_text: N-methylformamide (NMF) was evaluated as a potential cancer chemotherapeutic agent in a number of phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials. The paper states that the outcome of these trials did not support a role for NMF in therapy of human malignancies, 'not least due to the hepatotoxicity, occasionally very severe, which was observed as one of the dose-limiting toxicities in patients treated with NMF.'
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a dose-limiting toxicity during phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials of NMF as an antineoplastic agent, described as occasionally very severe; these trials failed to support NMF efficacy in human malignancies partly because of this hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In the early 1950s, a clinical cancer trial of N-methylformamide (NMF) was begun at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. Severe, reversible hepatotoxicity was reported in all of the five patients treated on this trial, and because of the severity of the hepatotoxicity additional clinical studies were not conducted.
raw_record.extra_details: NMF (NSC 3051), a polar solvent evaluated by the NCI as an antineoplastic agent. In phase I studies dose-limiting toxicities included reversible hepatotoxicity, generalized malaise syndrome, and nausea and vomiting. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, and beagle dogs showed reversible hepatotoxicity as dose-limiting. Given orally and by IV; oral bioavailability 90-95%. Reports from the early-1950s trial and later phase I trials are merged for this therapeutic-use claim.

raw_record.support_text: An early clinical trial of N-methylformamide (NMF) in man showed hepatotoxicity, which was described as an unacceptable side effect, and as a result interest in further chemotherapeutic studies of NMF was lost. NMF later regained attention due to its lack of myelotoxicity. A subsequent report (paragraph 5) notes that the most frequent side effects in man are anorexia, nausea and hepatotoxicity, based on two recent phase I clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: N-methylformamide (NMF) is an antineoplastic agent; early clinical trial in man demonstrated hepatotoxicity that was an unacceptable side effect, leading to loss of interest in further chemotherapy studies. NMF lacks myelotoxicity. In man the most frequent side effects are anorexia, nausea and hepatotoxicity, reported from two recent phase I clinical trials. Confusingly, a separate entity in the input entity list maps the 'NMF' surface form to N-methyl-D-aspartate; the paper text unambiguously refers to N-methylformamide.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials anastrozole has shown a good liver safety profile, but the reported patient developed acute liver damage during treatment with this aromatase inhibitor and recovered fully after drug discontinuation. Considering the time lapse between drug exposure and onset of hepatitis, patient age, exclusion of other non-drug-related causes, improvement after withdrawal and other reported anastrozole-related hepatitis cases, the case achieved a score of 7 on the Roussel-Uclaf Causality Method, suggesting a probable correlation between anastrozole and liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 70-year-old woman on anastrozole 1 mg/day for ER-positive breast carcinoma; liver injury appeared ~4 months (January 2009) after start (August 2008). Baseline liver tests were normal. At onset: AST 640 U/l, ALT 1344 U/l, ALP 355 U/l, total bilirubin 3.54 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 2.29 mg/dl, GGT 234 U/l. Hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV serologies and autoimmune Abs negative (ANA 1:80 speckled). Liver biopsy showed mild steatosis (10%), moderate inflammatory activity and moderate-to-severe fibrosis (Ishak 5-6). Prompt normalization of liver parameters within one month and ANA became undetectable after 12 months after anastrozole withdrawal; switched to tamoxifen without side effects. RUCAM score 7. Two prior reported cases of anastrozole-related hepatitis (patients aged 58 and 89 years, acute mainly cholestatic injury improving after withdrawal, anastrozole considered most probable cause); in the de la Cruz case biopsy showed diffuse zone-3 liver cell necrosis without inflammation, considered metabolically-mediated hepatocellular injury. Anastrozole is extensively metabolized by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation and glucuronidation; potential and mechanisms of hepatotoxicity remain uncertain.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists anastrozole as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI (iDILI) cause, with a RUCAM score of 6 conferring a probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 6, probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [14].

raw_record.support_text: Among 73 cases included in the final causality-assessed analysis of statin-induced DILI, the vast majority were due to atorvastatin (n = 30) and simvastatin (n = 28). Simvastatin cases included highly probable causality with severe outcomes: one patient required liver transplantation and one died, and another had a positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: 28/73 adjudicated DILI cases. Specific cases: M63 simvastatin (20 mg) 90 days, highly probable, liver transplantation; M78 simvastatin (20 mg) 92 days, highly probable, death; M58 simvastatin (20 mg) 28 days second treatment, highly probable, positive rechallenge producing a similar liver-injury pattern ~1 month after re-exposure. Rechallenge cases had negative viral markers (HAV/HBV/HCV/CMV/EBV) and no suspicion of alcoholic liver disease or hypotension.

raw_record.support_text: In this case, according to the CIOMS scale, the causality relationship between simvastatin (simvastatina) and the described clinical picture is probable (8 points); after discontinuation of the drug the problem resolved within one month, as reflected in the medical literature. The distinction between autoimmune-like hepatitis and other forms of drug-induced liver injury is made on the basis of the presence of autoantibodies.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality scored as probable (8 points) on the CIOMS scale; liver injury resolved within one month after discontinuation. Described as autoimmune-like hepatitis distinguished by presence of autoantibodies. Pathogenic basis described as loss of immune tolerance initiated by a reactive drug metabolite that covalently binds a hepatocyte surface protein to form a neoantigen that activates the immune system, with injury persisting only while the drug is administered. Treatment consists of stopping the causal agent, adding corticosteroids if the damage is significant; continued administration would produce chronic progressive liver injury, and long-term surveillance for autoimmune diseases is recommended.

raw_record.support_text: In the Icelandic prospective population study, 1 of 96 DILI patients had liver injury associated with simvastatin. During the 2-year Icelandic period, 27845 patients were treated with simvastatin and one was diagnosed with liver injury. Statins as a class accounted for 5.5% (47/858) of Spanish Registry DILI cases and 1.9% (22/1188) of DILIN cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 1 simvastatin DILI case among 27845 treated users in the Icelandic study (~1/3700 risk; ~1 per 11,000 when combined with atorvastatin cases). Cholestatic/mixed pattern occurred in only 24% of simvastatin injury cases (vs 56% for atorvastatin, p=0.018), indicating predominantly hepatocellular injury. Documented positive rechallenge reported for simvastatin.
