raw_record.support_text: The Swedish DILI register reported statin-related DILI with simvastatin implicated in 28/73 (38%) of cases, showing most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths due to acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation among the 73 statin DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 28/73 (38%) of statin-DILI cases in the Swedish DILI register (statin DILI incidence 1.2/100,000 users); register statin DILI showed most commonly a cholestatic/mixed pattern, with 2 deaths from acute liver failure and 1 liver transplantation across the 73 cases (not attributable to a specific statin).

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, after formal adjudication only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted as true statin-induced DILI; injury was mostly mild-moderate and self-limited, and the paper describes statin DILI as a likely class effect with idiosyncratic timing of onset. Simvastatin accounted for 5 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated simvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=5; Iceland study n=1; Swedish total for statins with jaundice 1970-2004 n=8 and 1988-2010 n=28 simvastatin; Spanish Registry n=13 (27.7%). DILIN aggregate (all statins) showed hepatocellular pattern in 12/22 (54%), cholestatic in 9/22 (41%), 4 severe and 1 fatal case, latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluated the side-effects of long-term cyclosporin A (CyA) treatment in 26 patients with severe psoriasis treated for 7-37 months (mean 19.5 months). The paper explicitly states that there was no hepatotoxicity with CyA treatment across all dose groups (<2, 2-3, and >3 mg/kg per day).
raw_record.extra_details: CyA given for a mean 19.5 months (range 7-37 months) to 26 patients with severe (and one palmoplantar pustulosis) psoriasis, initially 3 mg/kg per day with dose adjusted across three groups (<2, 2-3, >3 mg/kg per day); liver function tests were among the laboratory investigations.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient receiving cyclosporine, the report notes severe tremors and mild renal toxicity (slight elevations of blood pressure and serum urea nitrogen and creatinine), but explicitly states there were no signs of hepatic toxicity. The paper attributes no liver injury to cyclosporine in this case.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit report of no hepatic toxicity in a cyclosporine-treated patient who instead experienced severe tremors and mild renal toxicity (slight elevations of BP and serum urea nitrogen and creatinine).

raw_record.support_text: In the adverse effects section of this cyclosporine clinical study, the authors state explicitly that no hepatotoxicity was observed among the treated Crohn's disease patients. The passage reports no hepatotoxicity, central nervous system toxicity, or infectious episodes, distinguishing these from the renal, neurologic, and other side effects that were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of cyclosporine in 16 patients with Crohn's disease (parenteral administration); explicit statement that no hepatotoxicity was observed during the study.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old man with gout, chronic renal failure, and hypertension was treated with allopurinol and presented after 3 months with fever, jaundice, dyspnea, and generalized maculopapular rash; blood analysis showed eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes (ALT 429 IU/L, AST 369 IU/L, GGT 481 IU/L, ALP 773 IU/L), hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated IgE. Skin biopsy was consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity and he was diagnosed with DRESS syndrome. Allopurinol was stopped and steroids started; acute renal failure and acute liver failure developed, and the patient died on day 24 of admission. The text states that allopurinol can cause DRESS syndrome and that DRESS involves hepatitis/liver involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol prescribed for gout (hyperuricemia); rash and liver involvement appeared after 3 months of therapy (paper notes allopurinol can cause DRESS typically 2-6 weeks after initiation). Diagnosed as DRESS with hepatitis and acute liver failure; eosinophilia 7300/mm3; skin biopsy consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity; allopurinol stopped and steroid treatment initiated; acute renal failure and acute liver failure developed; hemodialysis performed; patient died of DRESS/multiple organ failure on day 24. Comorbidities: chronic renal failure and hypertension. Viral, autoimmune, and brucella work-up negative; ERCP and abdominal ultrasound (grade-2 hepatosteatosis, gallbladder sludge) not mechanistic.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old man was diagnosed with allopurinol-induced hepatic injury. He developed severe cholestatic liver failure without hepatic encephalopathy, and because medical treatment was transiently effective and his renal function and coagulation deteriorated, a living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) with a right lobe graft was performed four months after onset. The explanted liver was severely enlarged (2,480 g) and cholestatic, and microscopically compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. He was discharged 55 days after LDLT, with persistent renal dysfunction at 6 months. The authors note allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and even fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 39-year-old man with hyperuricemia who started allopurinol 2 months before onset of jaundice; after detailed examination no cause of liver dysfunction other than allopurinol-induced hepatic injury was found (nondrinker, no hepatitis virus infection, no blood transfusion). Serum TB reached >40 mg/dL; MELD score 31 at transfer (AST 382 IU/L, ALT 238 IU/L, TB 60.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.74 mg/dL). Histology showed severe cholestasis around the central vein, hepatic cord atrophy, sinusoidal/pericentral venous fibrosis, atypical bile ductule proliferation, and lymphocyte infiltration, compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. Bilirubin adsorption and corticosteroid therapy were ineffective. Living-donor LT performed; discharged 55 days post-LT with TB 2.8 mg/dL; renal dysfunction remained at 6 months. Authors state allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and fatal; reported as first case of successful LDLT for allopurinol-induced cholestatic liver failure without DRESS syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: In a Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network study, 11 patients with allopurinol hepatotoxicity (adjudicated definite, highly likely, or probable) presented at a median of 52 days after starting allopurinol; all were hospitalized, six were jaundiced, and three died including two from liver failure at 38 and 45 days after onset, while the remaining eight recovered. Nine were treated with corticosteroids including five of six with suspected DRESS. The conclusion states allopurinol hepatotoxicity is associated with systemic hypersensitivity, short latency, African-American race, and three HLA risk alleles (HLA-B*58:01, HLA-B*53:01, HLA-A*34:02).
raw_record.extra_details: 11 adjudicated cases of allopurinol hepatotoxicity; causality graded definite, highly likely, or probable (11 of 17 suspected). Median age 60 years; 54% male; 63% African-American, 27% Caucasian, 9% Hispanic; median latency 52 days. All hospitalized; six jaundiced. Median peak ALT 525 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 521 U/L, total bilirubin 7.8 mg/dl; median R ratio 2.7 at onset. Nine treated with corticosteroids including five of six with suspected DRESS. Three died, including two from liver failure at 38 and 45 days after onset; eight recovered. HLA overrepresentation: HLA-B*58:01, HLA-B*53:01, and HLA-A*34:02, particularly in African Americans.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a single patient who developed hepatic granulomatosis (granulomatous hepatitis) as an idiosyncratic adverse reaction to allopurinol, tel with no other cause identified despite physical, skin, microbiological, biochemical, and radiological investigation. After re-exposure to the drug the patient showed a prompt exacerbation of previous symptoms and abnormal liver function values; the reappearance of a dose-independent reaction when medication was resumed after a drug-free interval was considered consistent with a 'definitive' adverse allergic reaction, and the authors conclude the hepatic adverse effect of allopurinol in susceptible hosts is probably immunologically mediated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Hepatic granulomas consisted of multinucleated giant cells (up to 50 nuclei) surrounded by epithelioid cells and mononuclear infiltrate, located in portal tracts and throughout the three zones of Rappaport's acinus, with readily shown eosinophils; mild large-droplet fatty change but no focal necrosis; special stains for acid-fast bacteria and fungi negative. Latency of 6 years before allergic symptoms (fever, malaise, eosinophilia, granulomas) became manifest. On re-exposure there was prompt exacerbation of symptoms and abnormal liver function values, interpreted as a 'definitive' allergic reaction. Liver function and eosinophilia returned to normal 16 days after allopurinol discontinuation; follow-up liver biopsy at 6 months showed no granulomas or inflammatory infiltrate; patient well at 10 months. Hypothesis of oxypurine (hypoxanthine/xanthine) crystal deposition considered unlikely since no crystalline material seen.

raw_record.support_text: Pfizer announced voluntary worldwide withdrawal of sitaxsentan from the market after 2 cases of fatal hepatotoxicity during the Sitaxsentan Efficacy and Safety Trial With Randomized Prospective Assessment of Adding Sildenafil (SR-PAAS) clinical trial (NCT00795639). This attribution of fatal hepatotoxicity to sitaxsentan precipitated the market withdrawal and forced transition of stable PAH patients from sitaxsentan to other ERAs.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of fatal hepatotoxicity occurred during the SR-PAAS clinical trial (NCT00795639), leading to Pfizer's voluntary worldwide market withdrawal on December 15, 2010. Agent is a highly selective ET-A antagonist used for pulmonary arterial hypertension; patients were transitioned to bosentan or ambrisentan after withdrawal. Specific hepatic histopathology, biochemical pattern, and causality-instrument scores were not reported.

raw_record.support_text: Sitaxentan therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension was associated with hepatotoxicity; there have been seven documented cases of a more severe and apparently idiosyncratic hepatitis resulting in two deaths from acute liver failure (one during an early premarketing trial, the second in a recent case report). In December 2010, following a further two cases of fatal hepatitis during clinical trials, sitaxentan was withdrawn from the global market.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for pulmonary arterial hypertension; seven documented cases of severe apparently idiosyncratic hepatitis with two deaths from acute liver failure (one death in an early premarketing trial, one in a recent case report); withdrawn from the global market in December 2010 after two further fatal hepatitis cases in clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: Sitaxentan (Thelin), a selective endothelin-A receptor antagonist marketed for pulmonary arterial hypertension, was withdrawn worldwide in December 2010 after severe, apparently idiosyncratic liver toxicity that included four deaths and one case of liver transplantation (the introduction cites eight deaths). Some reported cases were characterized by elevated bilirubin levels with histological evidence of lymphocytes and eosinophils, typical of idiosyncratic liver toxicity. The paper investigates whether this idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity can be rationalized by formation of a reactive ortho-quinone metabolite via P450 3A4-mediated bioactivation.
raw_record.extra_details: Marketed as Thelin in several European countries and Canada for pulmonary arterial hypertension; withdrawn worldwide by Pfizer in December 2010. The abstract reports four deaths and one case of liver transplantation from severe liver toxicity, while the introduction reports eight deaths from severe liver toxicity, both attributed to withdrawal. Some cases showed elevated bilirubin with histological evidence of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Sitaxentan has a 1,3-benzodioxole ring undergoing demethylation to an ortho-catechol metabolite that oxidizes to a reactive ortho-quinone; P450 3A4 shows time-dependent inhibition; sitaxentan appeared to have a lower incidence of liver function test abnormalities than bosentan.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a fatal case of nafcillin-induced hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy, with total bilirubin peaking to 21.8 mg/dl and an extensive negative evaluation for other causes of hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman receiving nafcillin 12 g/day IV for MSSA bacteremia/osteomyelitis; jaundice with mild disorientation appeared on day 15 with total bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL, direct 7.3 mg/dL, ALP 388 IU/L, AST 67 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, GGTP 878 IU/L; peak total bilirubin 21.8 mg/dL. Dechallenge produced a mild transient drop in AST/ALT/ALP/GGTP. Extensive workup negative (coombs, ANCA MPO/PR3, RF, ASMA, ANA, HLA B27, complement, LKM, AFP, anti-TPO); ultrasound and MRCP excluded obstruction. Liver biopsy showed diffuse hepatocanalicular cholestasis with focal centrizonal bile infarct, periportal hepatocellular swelling and mild nodular hyperplasia-like changes; diagnosis of cholestatic jaundice secondary to nafcillin was made and ursodiol (10 mg/kg) started. No fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy at that time; GGTP and ALP remained >1500 IU/L on follow-up. Prior ertapenem had been discontinued before nafcillin. Patient had pre-existing renal insufficiency (creatinine 2 mg/dL, GFR 26 mL/min).

raw_record.support_text: The case report highlights early recognition of nafcillin-induced acute liver injury. Complete withdrawal of nafcillin resulted in complete recovery of liver function and the drug effects were proven reversible, adding to the literature supporting the finding of DILI. The current opinion is that nafcillin is generally well tolerated, with the most common side effects being mild to moderate gastrointestinal and hematological toxicities.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case. Due to the acute nature of presentation, the cholestatic pattern of the liver injury, and eosinophilia, there was high suspicion for DILI; pathology further confirmed the diagnosis. Patient presented with painless jaundice, marked transaminitis, and hyperbilirubinemia. Thorough workup found no underlying etiology, no prior hepatic or renal disease, and no other hepatotoxic drugs at the time. Following discontinuation, symptomatology dramatically improved and liver function normalized. The case concerned prolonged use of nafcillin (long-term treatment); authors recommend serial liver function testing in patients on long-term nafcillin and class-equivalent narrow-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotics.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of nafcillin-induced liver injury in a patient treated with nafcillin 12 g/day for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus infection, with onset of liver injury on day 27. The patient's liver panel showed a cholestatic pattern (ALK and bilirubin elevated out of proportion to ALT/AST), evidence of immune-mediated idiosyncratic liver injury supported by peripheral eosinophilia (11.7%, absolute eosinophil count 1100), a liver biopsy showing lobular necrosis, portal inflammation and mild bile stasis without steatosis, no encephalopathy, and normal INR/PT. LFTs declined with supportive treatment and the patient was discharged on day 42.
raw_record.extra_details: Nafcillin 12 g/day IV for MSSA bacteremia; onset of liver injury day 27; peak labs on day 30-40: total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dl (7.0 direct), ALK 865 IU/L, AST 206 U/L, ALT 415 U/L; eosinophilia 11.7% (absolute 1100); biopsy showed lobular necrosis, severe portal tract inflammation with mixed infiltrate, mild bile stasis, mild periportal fibrosis, no steatosis; no encephalopathy, INR/PT normal; recovered with supportive care after ERCP (day 33) for biliary sludge; discharged day 42. Authors describe the cholestatic pattern as drug-induced liver injury and direct causality to nafcillin.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of etodolac-induced acute liver failure without confounding factors such as chronic liver disease or concomitant hepatotoxic agents. In the described 73-year-old patient, extensive laboratory, histopathological and radiological investigations, together with spontaneous recovery following etodolac withdrawal, strongly support a diagnosis of etodolac-induced acute liver failure, defined as hepatic impairment associated with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Etodolac 600 mg twice daily was the patient's only medication, started 6 months prior and discontinued 1 week before admission. 73-year-old female with inflammatory polyarthritis presented with worsening jaundice, malaise and abdominal pain; developed grade II encephalopathy. Admission labs: bilirubin 525 µmol/l, ALT 1400 IU/l, ALP 274 IU/l, prothrombin time 16.7 s. Viral, autoimmune, metabolic, radiological and Doppler work-up negative. Liver biopsy showed severe acute portal and lobular hepatitis with confluent necrosis and bridging collapse, compatible with drug-induced liver injury. Spontaneous recovery, liver function normalized within 3 months and stable at 2 years. Prior hepatic impairment reported in <0.3% of patients; one prior liver failure report was confounded by alcohol-related chronic liver disease and cocaine abuse.

raw_record.support_text: Etodolac was implicated in two cases of DILI, both with a long latency (166 and 216 days), a mixed and hepatocellular pattern of serum enzyme elevations (R-values 2.8 and 19.3), moderate severity in that both were jaundiced, but peak bilirubin levels were 3.8 and 4.0 mg/dl and neither patient was hospitalized or had INR elevations. The comparison table lists 2 etodolac cases (1 definite, 1 probable causality).
raw_record.extra_details: 2 implicated cases with long latency (166 and 216 days); mixed and hepatocellular enzyme pattern (R-values 2.8 and 19.3); both jaundiced (peak bilirubin 3.8 and 4.0 mg/dl); neither hospitalized nor with INR elevations; no immunoallergic or autoimmune features. Causality: 1 definite, 1 probable. Propionic acid derivative NSAID.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity induced by gefitinib (an EGFR TKI) was reported in the IDEAL 1 trial, with grade 1/2 ALT elevation in 10.7% of patients at 250 mg/day and 17.9% at 500 mg/day, and gefitinib was discontinued in 4% of patients due to grade 3/4 hepatic enzyme elevations. The authors' own study found elevated ALT in 6.5% (6/92) and elevated AST in 5.4% (5/92) of gefitinib-treated patients, consistent with the prior trial. In paragraph 24, the authors note gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity was generally mild to moderate and self-limiting in their 6 patients, with one grade 2 case, a case of severe liver impairment reported by Ho et al., and grade 3/4 ALT elevation in 1.9% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: IDEAL 1 trial: grade 1/2 ALT elevation 10.7% at 250 mg/day and 17.9% at 500 mg/day; discontinuation in 4% for grade 3/4 hepatic enzyme elevations; grade 3/4 ALT elevation in 1.9% of patients. Authors' study: elevated ALT 6.5% (6/92) and AST 5.4% (5/92); transaminase elevation observed from 7 days to 6 months after starting gefitinib, returning to normal within 3-7 months; each case generally mild and self-limiting, one grade 2 (moderate) case managed by dose reduction; 250 mg every other day used in one patient with moderate hepatic impairment. Ho et al. reported a case of severe liver impairment with chronic hepatitis and active necrosis on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: A total of 55 patients with NSCLC in whom gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity had developed were enrolled. Median serum ALT was 236 IU/L (range 100-1119 IU/L), median time to onset after taking gefitinib was 41 days (range 7-228 days), and there were 25/28/2 grade 2/3/4 hepatotoxicity cases. Gefitinib rechallenge at reduced dose in 40 patients caused recurrence of hepatotoxicity in 19.
raw_record.extra_details: 55 adult NSCLC patients (11 men, 44 women; median age 73 y; 52 adenocarcinoma; EGFR mutations in 35). CTCAE v3.0 grade 2/3/4 hepatotoxicity counts 25/28/2; median ALT 236 IU/L; median onset latency 41 d (7-228 d). Rechallenge with reduced-dose gefitinib (alternate-day 250 mg) recurred in 19 of 40 patients. CYP2D6 *5/*10 allele analysis showed no significant enrichment (69.1% vs 62.6% in Japanese controls, P=.824).

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old Chinese female with EGFR-mutant (exon 19 deletion) stage IV NSCLC developed severe gefitinib-induced grade 4 hepatotoxicity after 14 months of gefitinib 250 mg/day, with ALT 1,130 U/l (grade 4) and AST 629 U/l (grade 3) by CTCAE v3.0. Because liver metastasis and other diseases were ruled out and no other medications were administered, the hepatic enzyme elevation was attributed to gefitinib. Liver function improved after gefitinib discontinuation (ALT falling to 98 and 69 U/l at 6 and 10 weeks), and a gefitinib rechallenge with hepatoprotective therapy maintained disease control with normal liver function for more than 6 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg/day (Iressa; AstraZeneca), injury appeared after 14 months of long-term administration. ALT 1,130 U/l (grade 4) and AST 629 U/l (grade 3), CTCAE v3.0. Liver metastasis and other diseases excluded; no co-medications. Dechallenge: ALT fell to 98 and 69 U/l at 6 and 10 weeks after discontinuation. Rechallenge at same dose with hepatoprotective therapy maintained normal liver function >6 months with disease control. Case of a 61-year-old non-smoking female NSCLC patient with EGFR exon 19 deletion, first-line therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of grade 3 (CTCAE v4.03) cytolytic hepatitis occurring in a patient treated with gefitinib, with recurrence of the hepatitis upon gefitinib reintroduction; switching to erlotinib did not lead to reappearance of hepatic toxicity. The case was notified to the Grenoble (France) pharmacovigilance center on 6 October 2011 and analyzed by the French imputability method. Transaminases rose on rechallenge (ASAT up to 6.7 N, ALAT up to 10.5 N), etiologic work-up (viral hepatitis B and C serologies, imaging) was negative, and no self-medication was reported.
raw_record.extra_details: 71-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (EGFR exon 21 mutation, KRAS wild-type) treated with gefitinib 250 mg/day first line; grade 3 (CTCAE v4.03) cytolytic hepatitis with transaminase elevation (peak ASAT 6.7 N, ALAT 10.5 N) starting ~9 weeks after initiation; recurrence upon reintroduction (rise within 4 days); switching to erlotinib caused no hepatic toxicity; negative hepatitis B/C serologies and imaging work-up; concurrent doxycycline prescribed for cutaneous toxicity prevention (not attributed as cause); causality analyzed by French imputability method; notified to Grenoble pharmacovigilance center.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 239 NSCLC patients harboring EGFR mutations who were treated with gefitinib, severe hepatotoxicity was graded per CTCAE v4.0 and defined as grade 3+ transaminase elevation (ALT >=210 U/L or AST >=165 U/L) with any total-bilirubin elevation (>=1.2 mg/dL), or grade 2+ transaminase elevation with grade 2+ total-bilirubin elevation (>=1.8 mg/dL), based on the FDA Guidance for Industry on DILI. The study endpoint was the severe hepatotoxicity rate, defined as the proportion who experienced gefitinib-induced severe hepatotoxicity during treatment, which is the cause of gefitinib withdrawal; the study examined associations between this gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity and SNPs in metabolic enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 239 NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations treated with gefitinib at a single institution (Jan 2009-Dec 2012); endpoint was severe hepatotoxicity rate per CTCAE v4.0 and the FDA DILI Premarketing Clinical Evaluation guidance (grade 3+ ALT>=210 U/L or AST>=165 U/L with any total-bilirubin elevation, or grade 2+ transaminases with grade 2+ bilirubin); severe hepatotoxicity is the cause of gefitinib withdrawal. Study examined SNPs in CYP1A2, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A5, NAT2 and UGT1A1 as potential determinants (these gene/HLA associations themselves are not extracted as DILI causes). Blood samples were available for 60 of 239 patients from the National Cancer Center Biobank.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old Japanese woman with EGFR-mutation-positive lung adenocarcinoma was treated with gefitinib 250 mg once daily and after 16 weeks showed a substantial rise in transaminases (AST 112 U/L, grade 1; ALT 223 U/L, grade 3 per CTCAE v4). A liver biopsy histologically revealed drug-induced liver injury, and a drug lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for gefitinib, suggesting the hepatitis was from drug allergy rather than dose-dependent toxicity. Gefitinib was discontinued; liver function normalized within 11 weeks. The paper further states that gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity is widely recognized, with Japanese clinical trials reporting pronounced serum hepatic-enzyme elevations that required cessation of treatment in 24-30% of patients, and a pooled trial analysis showed grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 18% of gefitinib-treated patients versus 5.4% for erlotinib (OR 3.71, 95% CI 2.12-6.49, P<0.0001).
raw_record.extra_details: EGFR-TKI; alkylation-independent idiosyncratic (allergic) mechanism inferred from a positive drug lymphocyte stimulation test and biopsy-confirmed drug-induced liver injury; ALT 223 U/L (grade 3) and AST 112 U/L (grade 1); resolution within 11 weeks of withdrawal; Japanese EGFR exon-19-deleted lung adenocarcinoma case in a patient with no prior liver disease; pooled phase II/III trial analysis found grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 18% of gefitinib-treated EGFR-mutation-positive NSCLC patients, higher in Asian than non-Asian patients, with a trial-incidence of grade 3 hepatotoxicity of 24-30%.

raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity is an emerging issue in the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, and pazopanib is emphasized as having a higher incidence of high-grade liver toxicity than other VEGFR inhibitors. A recent phase III trial (COMPAZ) directly compared pazopanib to sunitinib in 1002 RCC patients, finding ALT elevation significantly higher with pazopanib (31% vs. 18%).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe and fatal hepatotoxicity listed as an FDA black box warning. COMPAZ phase III trial (1002 RCC patients) showed ALT elevation 31% with pazopanib vs 18% with sunitinib. High-grade AST incidence 6.9% (95% CI 5.5-8.6) and high-grade ALT incidence 9.4% (95% CI 7.8-11.4) from this meta-analysis. Package insert notes two fatal outcomes from initial studies attributed to disease progression and hepatic failure; four pazopanib-arm treatment-related fatal adverse events including two with abnormal hepatic function. Meta-analysis found low risk of fatal hepatotoxicity, not a significant increase in fatal hepatic AEs (incidence 0.7%, 95% CI 0.2-2.7%; RR 2.51, 95% CI 0.12-51.91, p=0.552). Pazopanib primarily hepatically metabolized (<4% renal clearance); contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment with dose adjustment for baseline moderate impairment. Metabolized by liver, eliminated in feces.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman with angiosarcoma on pazopanib (recently increased from 400 to 600 mg daily) presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice, with AST 719 U/L, ALT 910 U/L, and total bilirubin 10.1 mg/dL (direct 7.8 mg/dL); ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Pazopanib was believed to be the causative agent and was stopped, after which symptoms and hepatic function returned to baseline. The authors note that pazopanib has potentially fatal hepatotoxicity among its side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Patient with stage II angiosarcoma undergoing chemotherapy; pazopanib dose increased from 400 to 600 mg daily shortly before symptom onset (temporal association). Labs: AST 719 U/L, ALT 910 U/L, total bilirubin 10.1 mg/dL (direct 7.8 mg/dL); jaundice; nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary pathology. Clinical and laboratory improvement on drug cessation (dechallenge); patient discharged stable and asymptomatic. Pazopanib is a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for renal cell carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma; its GI side effects range from diarrhea, nausea, vomiting to potentially fatal intestinal perforation and hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The case report concludes that reversible severe liver toxicity with pazopanib treatment is a known rare side effect of pazopanib, and that low-dose personalized rechallenge in responding patients is a therapeutic option in experienced hands, though this conflicts with the current Summary of Product Characteristics and requires close monitoring of liver function, e.g., weekly liver function testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver toxicity described as severe and reversible. Low-dose personalized rechallenge was performed in this responding patient with a YWHAE-FAM22A/B translocated endometrial stromal sarcoma, which the authors present as a therapeutic option despite conflicting with the current SmPC; patients should be closely monitored for liver function abnormalities with e.g., weekly liver function testing.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma was started on oral pazopanib 800 mg/day. Two weeks later he showed signs of liver dysfunction (elevated serum liver enzyme levels) and pazopanib was stopped; after 1 week he was restarted at 400 mg/day and 6 days later presented with fever, malaise, fatigue, and appetite loss together with severe liver dysfunction (elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin). He was admitted, pazopanib was stopped, and liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis; after treatment with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone he recovered from drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe pazopanib-associated liver dysfunction in a 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma. Initial dose 800 mg/day produced liver enzyme elevation within 2 weeks (treatment stopped); rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg/day led 6 days later to fever, malaise, fatigue, appetite loss, and severe liver dysfunction with elevated transaminases and bilirubin. Liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis. Treated with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone; recovered and discharged. Tumor showed complete response but regrew 4 months after cessation. Pazopanib is an orally bioavailable VEGFR-1/2/3, c-kit, and PDGFR-alpha/beta tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: Pazopanib is associated with various safety concerns and dose-limiting adverse effects, and severe and fatal hepatotoxicity has been observed in clinical trials. Hepatic function must be monitored, and treatment should be interrupted, dose reduced, or discontinued as clinically indicated; package labeling recommends dose adjustments in 200-mg increments depending on tolerability.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe and fatal hepatotoxicity observed in clinical trials; hepatic function monitoring required; treatment interruption, dose reduction, or discontinuation as clinically indicated; package labeling recommends 200-mg dose increment adjustments for tolerability. Pazopanib used as systemic therapy for soft-tissue sarcoma.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists pazopanib as a RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with an updated RUCAM score of 8 conferring a probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the updated RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Updated RUCAM score 8, probable causality grading; reported iDILI case, reference [41].

raw_record.support_text: The paper states explicitly that pazopanib is known to cause liver toxicity and that a relationship between pazopanib exposure and alanine transaminase (ALT) elevations has been described in clinical trials. The study investigated this exposure-liver toxicity relationship in real-world patients and evaluated management of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity in routine care.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective observational cohort study (Pazopanib Exposure and Liver Toxicity). Liver toxicity observed in 25 of 133 patients (19%); pazopanib exposure was comparable in patients with vs without liver toxicity (27.7 mg/L vs 28.1 mg/L). The study did not demonstrate a clear relationship between pazopanib exposure and occurrence of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity. Seven patients permanently discontinued pazopanib after liver toxicity; of the remaining 18, continuation/restart was successful in 16, with half continuing at the same dose as prior to liver toxicity. Liver toxicity definition centered on ALT elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity, as measured by alanine aminotransferase increases, has been observed in 13% of patients, with grade 3 and 4 alanine aminotransferase increases occurring in 5% of patients. Fatal hepatotoxicity was rare, occurring in less than 1% of patients in clinical trials. Concurrent elevations in ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN with normal alkaline phosphatase occurred in less than 1% of patients. ALT >5x ULN occurred in 7% (study A) and 4% (study B) of patients; these findings were generally asymptomatic and reversible upon treatment interruption, and crizotinib should be permanently discontinued for more severe hepatotoxicity, with routine monthly monitoring of liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in clinical trials leading to FDA approval (NSCLC indication); hepatotoxicity measured as ALT increases in 13% of patients, grade 3-4 ALT increases in 5%; fatal hepatotoxicity <1% of patients; concurrent ALT >3x ULN with total bilirubin >2x ULN and normal alkaline phosphatase (Hy's Law-like) in <1%; ALT >5x ULN in 7% (study A) and 4% (study B); generally asymptomatic and reversible upon treatment interruption; most resumed lower dose without recurrence; permanent discontinuation required in 2% (study A) and <1% (study B); monitoring with ALT and total bilirubin monthly recommended; symptoms counseled include weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (especially right upper quadrant), jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, and bleeding diathesis.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old female with non-small-cell lung cancer treated with crizotinib presented with acute liver failure after 24 days of therapy. AST and ALT rose from normal to 2053 IU/L and 6194 IU/L, total bilirubin and PT-INR increased up to 443 µmol/L and 5.33, and hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome emerged. Despite crizotinib discontinuation and supportive therapy, the patient died 40 days after treatment initiation due to acute liver failure with massive liver cell necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of fatal fulminant acute liver failure due to liver cell necrosis in a Caucasian patient with ALK-positive stage IV NSCLC, described as the first such reported case. Dose 250 mg twice daily; onset of fulminant failure ~24 days after start. Peak ALT 6194 IU/L, AST 2053 IU/L, total bilirubin up to 443 µmol/L, PT-INR 5.33; coagulation factor V 11%; ferritin 10756 µg/L; hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome; MELD 36; met King's College criteria for poor prognosis but not a transplant candidate due to poor cancer prognosis; died on day 40. Other causes excluded (biliary obstruction, viral hepatitis A/B/C, alcohol, concomitant medication). Plasma crizotinib levels within expected range after discontinuation; estimated t1/2 ~50 h. No autopsy/biopsy. Authors note crizotinib-induced fatal hepatotoxicity occurs in 0.2% of patients and grade 3-4 ALT elevations in ~15% in pivotal phase III trials.

raw_record.support_text: Sato et al. reported a case of fatal fulminant hepatitis due to crizotinib administration. The patient did not respond to supportive therapies and died on the 36th day of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatitis; patient died on the 36th day of treatment despite supportive therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity with fatal outcome was observed in 0.1% of patients. Grade 3 or 4 transaminase elevations were observed in 11% and 6% of patients, respectively. Concurrent elevation in ALT and/or AST ≥ 3 × ULN and total bilirubin ≥ 2 × ULN without significant ALP elevation occurred in < 1% of patients. Transaminase elevations generally occurred within the first 2 months of treatment, were manageable by dose interruption/modifications, and crizotinib should be discontinued with grade 2 or higher AST/ALT plus bilirubin elevation in the absence of cholestasis or hemolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity in 0.1% of patients; grade 3 transaminase elevations in 11% and grade 4 in 6%; concurrent ALT/AST ≥ 3x ULN plus total bilirubin ≥ 2x ULN without significant ALP elevation in <1%; elevations generally began within the first 2 months of treatment, manageable by dose interruption/modification; recommendation to discontinue on grade ≥2 AST/ALT plus bilirubin elevation without cholestasis or hemolysis; liver function test monitoring recommended weekly for first 2 months.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib received FDA accelerated approval for ALK-positive NSCLC in August 2011. A meta-analysis of clinical trials showed the dose had to be reduced or treatment discontinued in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity, and the most clinically significant toxicities of crizotinib included hepatotoxicity. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient following closure of the FDA safety database, prompting investigation of the mechanism of crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper presents this as established human hepatotoxicity and studies its mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: ALK-positive NSCLC. A meta-analysis of clinical trials reported crizotinib dose reduction or treatment discontinuation in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity. Severe hepatotoxicity is observed with most receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors in clinical applications. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient after the FDA safety database closed. The paper's mechanistic work (HL-7702 cells and human primary hepatocytes) indicates ALK, ROS1 and MET are not targets of crizotinib-induced hepatocyte death/apoptosis.

raw_record.support_text: During crizotinib therapy in a patient with ROS1-rearranged pleomorphic pulmonary carcinoma, grade 4 treatment-related hepatotoxicity was observed, with peak AST and ALT of 865 U/L and 2451 U/L, respectively, while total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase remained within normal limits. Her liver enzymes returned to normal levels at day 39 after crizotinib discontinuation (AST 19 U/L, ALT 20 U/L), after which treatment was changed to ceritinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report within a serial-ROS1-TKI treatment narrative for ROS1-rearranged pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (PPC), young non-smoker female. Grade 4 (CTCAE) treatment-related hepatotoxicity; peak AST 865 U/L and ALT 2451 U/L with normal total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; enzymes normalized by day 39 after crizotinib discontinuation (AST 19 U/L, ALT 20 U/L) with no rechallenge; treatment then switched to ceritinib.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of ramipril-induced liver injury proven by positive rechallenge, and (per the RUCAM assessment) the case was classified as 'highly probable' with a score of 12 of 15. The patient presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP (mixed pattern), developing 10 months after starting ramipril, with normalization after rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: First ramipril DILI case proven by positive rechallenge; RUCAM score 12/15 ('highly probable'); time to onset 10 months; presented with jaundice and highly elevated ALT and ALP; outcome was normalization after dechallenge/rechallenge. Pattern expected to include cholestasis but hepatocellular damage also possible.

raw_record.support_text: This case report is described as the fifth known case of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity. Following discontinuation of ramipril, the patient's alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin began declining promptly, though biochemical markers had not yet returned to baseline at one month post-discharge. The biopsy revealed bland cholestasis with no ductular changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity, the fifth known case. Current case: bland cholestasis with no ductular changes on biopsy; onset 8 weeks after beginning ramipril (latency range 5 weeks to 10 months across cases); ALP and bilirubin declined after discontinuation but not returned to baseline at one month; prior cholestatic cases (biopsies showing cholestasis and bile duct necrosis) returned to near baseline at 6 and 14 months. Two other prior cases: one mixed pattern (markedly elevated ALT and ALP, minimal bilirubin increase, parenchymal inflammation on biopsy, unintended positive rechallenge confirming diagnosis) and one unclassifiable (mild liver enzyme increases, no biopsy). Symptomatic presentation varied from incidental blood-work findings to jaundice and severe pruritus. Cholestasis described as the most common liver injury pattern in ACEI-induced hepatotoxicity. First described cross reactivity between ramipril and methimazole in recurrent DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old Hispanic woman was diagnosed with albendazole-induced granulomatous hepatitis after ruling out other possible causes, based on laboratory studies, liver biopsy, medical history, detailed drug history, and spontaneous improvement of her liver biochemical profile after medication withdrawal. The diagnosis was supported by the CIOMS-Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method, which showed a likely correlation between hepatocellular damage and drug toxicity as the etiology. The histologic pattern was granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis (granulomatous inflammatory reaction with epithelioid macrophages and mononuclear cells) as the attributed phenotype in a 25-year-old Hispanic woman in Colombia. Diagnosis supported by CIOMS-Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method showing a likely correlation; other causes (infectious, autoimmune, sarcoidosis) ruled out; liver biochemical profile improved spontaneously after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The CIOMS/RUCAM scale was used to objectively evaluate the probability of toxic hepatitis; it showed a 'likely' correlation with a 5-point score, which confirmed the diagnosis of albendazole-induced toxic hepatitis with a pattern of hepatocellular damage. The case documents sub-acute toxicity with progressive improvement of the hepatic profile over time after discontinuing the medication as the only intervention; only two other similar human cases have been reported worldwide.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis; CIOMS/RUCAM score 5 ('likely') supporting albendazole causality. First described case documenting sub-acute toxicity, with progressive improvement of the hepatic profile after drug discontinuation as the sole intervention; only two other human cases of albendazole-induced toxic hepatitis reported worldwide. Case ruled out ischemic liver damage, infectious causes (serology negative), and liver cystadenocarcinoma.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of albendazole-induced fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation, noting that while albendazole-induced liver injury and jaundice had been previously documented, a case of fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation had not yet been described. Albendazole was used in treatment of echinococcosis (as monotherapy for small hydatid cysts < 5 cm or adjunct to percutaneous drainage/surgery), and the authors advise monitoring liver function tests throughout treatment and considering transplant evaluation when liver function continues to deteriorate despite stopping the offending agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. Albendazole used to treat Echinococcus (hydatid) disease, as medical monotherapy for small cysts <5 cm or as adjunct therapy in percutaneous drainage or surgery. Authors advise monitoring liver function tests throughout the treatment course and seeking transplant evaluation when hepatic function continues to deteriorate despite drug cessation. Previously documented albendazole-induced liver injury and jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that hepatotoxicity is a possible side effect of albendazole and that the case patient experienced hepatocellular injury after six weeks of treatment. The rapid decline of liver enzymes after discontinuation of the drug and recrudescence after rechallenge clearly defined albendazole as the cause of hepatotoxicity, and a high Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score supported this observation. A prior meta-analysis (2003) reported liver enzyme elevation in 0.7% (13/1681) of patients and liver fibrosis or failure in 0.7% (7/952) of patients, with acute severe hepatitis and liver failure described as extremely rare.
raw_record.extra_details: Case patient developed hepatocellular injury after six weeks of albendazole therapy, with rapid decline of liver enzymes after discontinuation and recrudescence after rechallenge; high RUCAM score. Meta-analysis from 2003: liver enzyme elevation in 0.7% (13 of 1681 patients) and liver fibrosis or failure in 0.7% (7 of 952 patients); acute severe hepatitis and liver failure are extremely rare. Patient was subsequently switched to mebendazole until pathology result was available (18 days total).

raw_record.support_text: In a series of forty patients with Echinococcus granulosus cysts treated with albendazole and followed for at least 24 months after therapy, the most serious complication of albendazole therapy was hepatotoxic jaundice, which occurred in 5% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxic jaundice occurred in 5% of 40 patients (about 2 patients) treated with albendazole for hydatid disease caused by E. granulosus. Twenty-one patients (53%) with 37 cysts (59%) showed evidence of healing; recurrence during observation occurred in 9.5% of patients with a positive response. The paper presents clinical phenotyping as hepatotoxic jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: During the Berlin Case-control Surveillance Study, eight cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) associated with flupirtine were identified, all leading to hospitalisation. Based on the RUCAM scale, two cases were classified as highly probable, five as probable, and one as possible; only the seven cases judged at least probable were examined. The liver damage was hepatocellular in all cases (based on ratio R and liver biopsies showing liver cell necroses without cholestasis), three patients developed acute liver failure, and two developed hepatic encephalopathy. Discontinuation of flupirtine was followed by ALT normalisation in five patients within the first two months.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven of eight RUCAM-adjudicated cases (>= probable) included; RUCAM grades: two highly probable (scores 8, 9), five probable (scores 6-7), one possible. Mean age 55±16 years; six female, one male; indications osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, depression/back pain, vertebral disc herniation, post-surgical. Flupirtine dosages 100-400 mg/day; time from therapy start to symptom onset 11 days to 8 months. All cases led to hospitalisation; three developed ALF (jaundice with severe coagulopathy), two hepatic encephalopathy; five patients had jaundice or dark urine; all had fatigue. Liver biopsies (4 patients) showed liver cell necroses without cholestasis; no autoimmune hepatitis or hypersensitivity signs (no rash, fever, eosinophilia). Peak ALT up to 1887 U/l (patient 2) and 1308 U/l (patient 4). ALT normalised within 2 months in five patients after stopping flupirtine; flupirtine was the only drug common to all cases and the only medication with compatible time course in three cases.

raw_record.support_text: Flupirtin (Flupirtine) is reported in association with hepatotoxicity: Puls et al. [34] published five cases of severe liver damage and one case of acute liver failure requiring transplantation in conceivable connection with flupirtine. The liver damage became manifest three weeks to 24 months (median 4 months) after starting flupirtine. Causality was adjudicated by RUCAM as probable in four cases and highly probable in the remaining two cases. During follow-up of 5–25 months (average 16, median 9 months), the liver injury was reversible in five of the six cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported by Puls et al. (reference [34]): five cases of severe liver damage and one case of acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation; detailed histological assessment of liver biopsies from five patients. Onset 3 weeks to 24 months (median 4 months) after flupirtine initiation; RUCAM causality: probable in 4 cases, highly probable in 2 cases. Follow-up 5–25 months (average 16, median 9); injury reversible in 5 of 6 cases. Medically indicated chronic pain analgesic use.

raw_record.support_text: Flupirtine is described as the first in-class selective neuronal potassium channel opener used for pain, and the paper states that its use can be associated with severe drug-induced liver injury (sFILI). The injury is framed as severe idiosyncratic flupirtine-induced liver injury; the paper also notes that since its 1984 approval in Germany over 12 million patients were exposed, that increased reports prompted a 2013 EMA safety re-evaluation examining nearly 600 case reports including 49 cases of liver failure with 15 resulting in liver transplantation or fatal outcome, and that in the reported cohort a case with fatal outcome occurred despite NAC treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved in Germany in 1984 with reportedly >12 million patients exposed. EMA/PRAC/310015/2013 safety re-evaluation in 2013 examined nearly 600 case reports including 49 cases of liver failure with 15 resulting in liver transplantation or fatal outcome. Reported management with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and prednisolone; two patients with late NAC/prednisolone start developed hepatic encephalopathy and required liver transplantation, while remaining patients recovered without long-term sequelae; sFILI cases resolved more rapidly (p<0.01) compared with untreated sFILI patients, and one treated case had fatal outcome. Presented mechanism invokes reactive quinine diamine metabolites detoxified via glutathione conjugation.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 30 patients with clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH), initial liver biopsies mostly showed acute hepatitis, with 17 cases (68%) being acute cytolytic hepatitis (centrolobular clarified and balloonized hepatocytes, two with multinucleated giant hepatocytes and two with moderate eosinophilic infiltration). Seven patients (28%) showed stigmas of chronic active hepatitis, and one case showed micronodular cirrhosis. A repeat biopsy after rechallenge with clometacin in one patient showed severe acute hepatitis with aggravation of hepatic lobule lesions. Mortality related to the first hepatitis was 13% (4/30), with three patients dying in the acute phase of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 30-patient case series of clometacin-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features. Histology: 68% acute cytolytic hepatitis, 28% chronic active hepatitis, 1 case micronodular cirrhosis; rechallenge in one patient aggravated lesions. First-hepatitis mortality 13% (4/30): 3 died rapidly of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy, 1 in the 4th month after downhill progression. The 26 survivors clinically and biochemically recovered within ~2 months of drug withdrawal, with anti-tissue antibodies (anti-actin cable, anti-N, anti-M2) becoming undetectable 3-9 months after clometacin withdrawal. Autoimmune markers: anti-smooth muscle (anti-actin cable) antibody present in 70% (21/30); anti-actin cable positivity in 19; anti-N in 16 (14 in common with anti-SM); transient drug-induced anti-M2 in 2; anti-LKM absent. Mean serum gammaglobulin 23 g/l, >18 g/l in 73%.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatitis induced following treatment with clometacin, an arthritis medication, was described in 30 patients: 75% had hepatocellular injury and 25% had cholestatic injury. Hepatitis was reported as directly responsible for death in three patients. Of seven patients with clometacin DILI, four had HLA-B*08 antigens, and four had chronic active hepatitis with autoantibodies in three cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Arthritis medication; 30 patients with 75% hepatocellular and 25% cholestatic injury; hepatitis directly responsible for death in three patients; HLA-B*08 antigens in four of seven DILI patients; chronic active hepatitis with autoantibodies in three cases; postulated as a model for autoimmune drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Clometacin is described as a cause of drug-induced hepatitis (DIH), classified with drugs such as oxyphenisatin that produce antiorganelle antibodies similar to those in autoimmune hepatitis I. The paper reports a series of clometacin-induced hepatitis with 29 females and 1 male (30:1 female:male ratio), 68 females and 2 males accumulated from several pharmacovigilance centers, hypergammaglobulinemia of 23 g/L, and antiorganelle antibodies (anti-N 28%, anti-M2 10%, anti-SM 59%). Acute forms showed centrilobular necrosis on biopsy, unknown in autoimmune hepatitis I.
raw_record.extra_details: Clometacin-induced hepatitis shows female predominance (29 females/1 male in this series; 68 females/2 males in pharmacovigilance accumulation), female consumers represent 73% so ratio only partially explained by differential consumption; hypergammaglobulinemia 23 g/L ±10; antiorganelle antibodies (anti-N 28%, anti-M2 10%, anti-SM 59%); acute form showed centrilobular necrosis on liver biopsy; individuals treated with ~4x lower than usual dose in 20% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: The Homberg et al. series of 157 cases of drug-induced hepatitis identified the major culprit drugs causing hepatotoxicity as clometacin (29 cases), α-methyldopa (12 cases), troleandromycin (11 cases), ajmaline (8 cases), halothane (6 cases) and perhexiline (6 cases), with the drugs most often associated with autoimmune serologic reactions being clometacin (17/29), fenofibrate (4/4), papaverine (4/5) and tienilic acid (3/3).
raw_record.extra_details: Most common culprit in Homberg series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis cases (29 cases); 17/29 also had autoimmune serologic reactions characterized by antismooth muscle antibody (ASMA) and antinuclear antibody (ANA).

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with severe atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis was started on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 500 mg three times daily as a corticosteroid-sparing agent. After a month she developed a biochemical hepatitis with ALT rising from 22 to 418 IU/L and AST from 20 to 139 IU/L; after dose reduction to 500 mg twice daily, ALT and AST rose to 821 and 203 IU/L. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative, ANA was positive (speckled 1:160), and she denied alcohol or herbs; hydroxyzine was taken only intermittently. The hepatology consult agreed with MMF-induced hepatitis, and liver enzymes were normal 1 month after stopping MMF.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Dose 500 mg three times daily, reduced to 500 mg twice daily. ALT rose from 22 to 418 IU/L then to 821 IU/L; AST rose from 20 to 139 IU/L then to 203 IU/L. Asymptomatic (no abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice). Negative hepatitis A/B/C serologies; antinuclear antibodies positive speckled 1:160. Resolution to normal ALT/AST one month after discontinuation. Paper frames MMF-associated hepatitis as rare and as hepatitis due to drug hypersensitivity; authors conclude MMF is relatively safe but physicians should monitor for rare hepatitis. References supporting MMF-induced transaminase elevation: Balal et al (79 transplant patients, 11 with modest liver enzyme elevations, median onset 28 days, resolution 16 days after withdrawal or 50% dose reduction), Hantash and Fiorentino (2 atopic dermatitis patients), a toxic hepatitis case (AST/ALT up to 750 IU/L) in ANCA-positive vasculitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 449 cadaveric renal transplant recipients (mycophenolate mofetil 2 g/day, n=167; 3 g/day, n=166; or azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day, n=166), no hepatotoxicity was reported in the mycophenolate mofetil groups. In a separate randomized trial of 49 renal allograft patients given mycophenolate mofetil (100–3500 mg/day), bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity were not observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Mycophenolate mofetil evaluated for prevention of acute rejection after renal transplantation, given with antithymocyte globulin or Minnesota antilymphocyte globulin, cyclosporine, and prednisone. The 449-patient US Renal Transplant Mycophenolate Mofetil Study Group trial reported no hepatotoxicity; the 49-patient dose-ranging trial explicitly stated hepatotoxicity was not observed. Reported adverse effects were GI (diarrhea, esophagitis, gastritis, GI hemorrhage), anemia, hypertension, and opportunistic infections; neutropenia and thrombocytopenia occurred infrequently. Mycophenolate mofetil is primarily eliminated renally as the glucuronide metabolite mycophenolic acid glucuronide (MPAG).

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective registry, cefazolin accounted for 20 of 899 adjudicated DILI cases, and mortality for DILI caused by cefazolin was 0-1%.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 adjudicated DILI cases; mortality for cefazolin DILI 0-1%.

raw_record.support_text: In the 19 cases in which cefazolin was the primary implicated agent, final adjudication by the DILIN Causality Committee scored the cases highly likely in all except 3, two of which were considered definite and one probable. Cefazolin was initially considered a potential responsible agent in only 10 of 19 patients, and other drugs were sometimes initially suspected. Laboratory documentation of liver injury was obtained 6 to 31 days after exposure, with mixed or cholestatic serum enzyme patterns; the injury was scored severe (INR transiently ≥1.5) in 2 patients, moderate in 16, and mild/anicteric in 1, with no deaths or liver transplantation. Liver biopsies in 10 patients showed cholestatic patterns (5 reviewed centrally) and one mild acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 DILIN cases of cefazolin-attributed DILI; latency 6-31 days after exposure, 2-23 days after symptom onset; total serum bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL in 18 (95%) and >10 mg/dL in 7 (37%); two bilirubin-peak curves (before or after 25 days); DILIN causality scores highly likely (16), definite (2), probable (1); severity scored severe (INR ≥1.5) in 2, moderate (2+/3+) in 16, mild (anicteric) in 1; no deaths, liver transplant, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, or variceal hemorrhage; 3 patients had minimal liver test abnormalities at 6 months that eventually resolved; 10 biopsies (6 centrally reviewed) most with cholestatic injury (cholestatic hepatitis, acute cholestasis, chronic cholestasis with duct injury) and one mild acute hepatitis; eosinophil infiltrates in 2 of 6 reviewed biopsies; other agents initially considered possible causes included tramadol, propofol, sevoflurane, azithromycin, clindamycin, oxcarbazepine, ketorolac, chaparral, and oxycodone/acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: The orally active CGRP receptor antagonist MK-3207, which proved effective for migraine attack treatment, also showed hepatotoxicity in some cases and its development was thus discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Effective for acute migraine attack treatment; hepatotoxicity reported in some cases and led to discontinuation of development.

raw_record.support_text: In a pivotal Phase 2 clinical study, MK-3207 caused ALT >3-fold ULN after 2 weeks in 1% of subjects at daily doses <100 mg and in 42% (5/12) at doses >500 mg; among these 5 patients, 3 had >20-fold ALT rises, including 1 symptomatic patient meeting Hy's Law. ALT rises were delayed in onset (up to 2–3 months) and slow to resolve, and MK-3207 was discontinued in Phase 2 because of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT >3-fold ULN in 1% at daily doses <100 mg and 42% (5/12) at >500 mg; 3 subjects with >20-fold ALT rises and 1 symptomatic Hy's Law case; ALT rises delayed in onset (up to 2–3 months) and slow to resolve; discontinued in Phase 2. DILIsym predicted hepatotoxicity driven by competitive bile salt export pump inhibition and mitochondrial electron transport inhibition, with oxidative stress a minor contributor.

raw_record.support_text: Across idelalisib clinical trials, serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 109/760 (14%) patients, with one fatality (1/1192) in a patient receiving idelalisib in combination with ofatumumab in an ongoing phase 3 trial; the cause of death was determined to be acute liver failure, and the patient also had grade 4 sepsis at the time of death. Most (74%) patients with ALT/AST elevation resumed idelalisib at a lower dose without recurrence, while 26% had recurrent ALT/AST elevation despite the lower dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious, including fatal, hepatotoxicity reported in idelalisib-treated patients. ALT/AST elevations >5x ULN usually within first 12 weeks of treatment, mostly reversible with dose interruption. Across clinical trials serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 109/760 (14%) with 1 fatality (1/1192) attributed to acute liver failure in a patient receiving idelalisib plus ofatumumab (grade 4 sepsis present at death). In the relapsed CLL phase 3 trial (idelalisib + rituximab, n=110) any-grade ALT/AST increase was 35%/25% (placebo group 10%/14%) and grade 3-4 elevations 8%/5% (placebo 1%/0%). In iNHL patients on idelalisib 150 mg monotherapy (n=146), any-grade ALT increase was 50% (grade 3 in 14%, grade 4 in 5%) and AST in 41% (grade 3 in 8%, grade 4 in 4%); transaminase elevations were a common cause of interruption/discontinuation (10%). Residual elevations led to dose reduction; 26% recurred despite lower dose. US prescribing information advises against concomitant use with other hepatotoxic drugs and mandates ALT/AST monitoring (every 2 weeks for first 3 months, then every 4 weeks for 3 months, then every 1-3 months; weekly for ALT/AST >3x ULN; withhold idelalisib at >5-20x ULN and resume at reduced 100 mg BID once levels <=1x ULN; permanently discontinue if >20x ULN).

raw_record.support_text: Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 14% of patients treated with idelalisib during clinical trials, including one reported fatality associated with acute liver failure. Additionally, 13% and 8% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 increases in ALT and AST levels, respectively, and marked elevations in these hepatic enzymes typically occurred within the first 12 weeks of idelalisib treatment. The preceding paragraph notes that labeling for idelalisib includes a black-box warning for hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 14% of patients in clinical trials; includes one reported fatality associated with acute liver failure; 13% had grade 3 or 4 ALT increases and 8% had grade 3 or 4 AST increases; marked hepatic enzyme elevations typically occur within the first 12 weeks of treatment. Labeling carries a black-box warning for hepatotoxicity (and separate black-box warnings for severe diarrhea or colitis, intestinal perforation, and pneumonitis).

raw_record.support_text: Elevation in ALT and AST levels can occur during treatment with idelalisib, and hepatotoxicity was one of the most common reasons for discontinuation of the drug in clinical trials. It typically manifests 4–12 weeks after treatment initiation in asymptomatic patients, is reversible in most cases after dose interruption, and grade 3–4 ALT/AST elevation (>5x ULN) was reported in 14% of patients, leading to death in one case. In the phase I trial 28% of patients experienced liver enzyme elevation of any grade, and in the phase III study transaminase elevations were more common in the idelalisib plus rituximab arm, with grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increases in 25–35%.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a common reason for idelalisib discontinuation in clinical trials. ALT/AST elevation typically manifests 4–12 weeks after treatment initiation in asymptomatic patients and is reversible after dose interruption; about 75% of patients do not experience recurrence upon resumption at a lower dose. Grade 3–4 ALT/AST elevation (>5x ULN) reported in 14% of patients, with one associated death. Phase I trial: 28% any-grade liver enzyme elevation, one grade 3. Phase III (idelalisib plus rituximab): grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increase in 25–35%; drug withheld and successfully reinitiated in two thirds of patients. Prescribing information recommends against concomitant hepatotoxic drugs and close ALT/AST monitoring (3–5x ULN maintain with monitoring; 5–20x ULN interrupt until resolution; >20x ULN permanently discontinue). In frontline trials grade ≥3 elevations occurred in 67% (O'Brien) and 57% (Lampson); liver biopsies in the Lampson study showed increased activated cytotoxic T cells within the liver parenchyma.

raw_record.support_text: Idelalisib is reported to induce hepatotoxicity. Fatal and/or serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 18% of patients treated with idelalisib monotherapy and 16% treated in combination with rituximab or unapproved combination therapies. ALT or AST elevations greater than 5x ULN occurred, generally within the first 12 weeks of treatment, were reversible with dose interruption, and recurred in 26% of patients after resumption at a lower dose. The FDA-approved label includes a black box warning on its potential for hepatotoxicity, and discontinuation is advised for recurrent hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal and/or serious hepatotoxicity in 18% of monotherapy patients and 16% with rituximab combination or unapproved combinations; ALT/AST >5x ULN generally within first 12 weeks, reversible with dose interruption; 26% recurrence of ALT/AST elevations after resumption at lower dose; recurrent toxicity rates lower with corticosteroids at re-initiation; hepatic monitoring recommended pre- and during treatment; discontinue for recurrent hepatic injury; FDA black box warning on hepatotoxicity potential; reader referred to review [41] for mechanisms and histological changes.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies chlorpropamide as a drug implicated in inducing liver injury, being the causative agent in 8 of 53 patients with drug-related liver disease. Chlorpropamide produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 5 cases and diffuse necrosis in 3.
raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpropamide was the causative agent in 8 of 53 patients; produced hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 5 cases and diffuse necrosis in 3.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpropamide is estimated to produce cholestatic hepatitis in some 0.5% of patients, and signs of hypersensitivity with eosinophilia frequently accompany this reaction; it is presented as an example of idiosyncratic, non-dose-dependent drug hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 42-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes developed rash, pruritus, jaundice, shivering and cholestatic hepatitis after 4 weeks on chlorpropamide (Diabinese, 500 mg daily); marked improvement on dechallenge and abrupt exacerbation on rechallenge; liver tests indicated a cholestatic type of injury with elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGTP and bilirubin; eosinophilia rose to 31%; estimated population incidence of cholestatic hepatitis about 0.5%; hypersensitivity with eosinophilia frequently accompanies the reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Trabectedin was reported to have a favorable safety profile with low rates of febrile neutropenia (0.8%), although potentially fatal hepatotoxicity was observed. The hepatotoxicity is attributed to direct necrosis of the biliary epithelial cells, with rates as high as 32% grade 3 AST elevations (trial [33]). Pretreatment with dexamethasone 20 mg IV was shown to markedly reduce the risk of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity described as caused by direct necrosis of biliary epithelial cells; rates up to 32% grade 3 AST elevations in the Demetri et al. Phase II trial of anthracycline/ifosfamide pre-treated soft tissue sarcoma; potentially fatal; pretreatment with dexamethasone 20 mg IV markedly reduced the risk; low rate of febrile neutropenia (0.8%).

raw_record.support_text: Trabectedin (ecteinascidin-743, ET-743, Yondelis®), an alkaloid isolated from the marine squirt Ecteinascidia turbinata, is used in the treatment of soft tissue sarcoma, breast, ovarian and other cancers. The paper states that its major drawback seems to be its hepatotoxicity observed in clinical trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Marine alkaloid (ecteinascidin-743, ET-743, Yondelis®) from Ecteinascidia turbinata, used for soft tissue sarcoma, breast, ovarian and other cancers; hepatotoxicity observed in clinical trials as the major drawback.

raw_record.support_text: Of 1322 patients with suspected DILI enrolled in the DILIN Prospective Study, 94 (8%) were adjudicated as definitely, highly likely or probably due to nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa or hydralazine; the analysis cohort included 7 cases due to hydralazine.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 adjudicated cases (DILIN Prospective Study). Typically elderly (median age 60), female preponderance, African Americans accounting for 43% of cases. Latency beyond 6 months uncommon (14%), all within 1 year. Predominantly hepatocellular pattern. Fatality rate 14%.

raw_record.support_text: De Boer et al. characterized autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) secondary to hydralazine in DILI cases, with an autoimmune phenotype (autoimmune score ≥2) seen only in about one-half (43%) of the cases with hydralazine.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases from the US DILIN prospective study; autoimmune phenotype present in 43% of hydralazine cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a woman with no previous liver disease who developed drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis from hydralazine, which had been prescribed for hypertension. Despite discontinuing the medication, she developed acute liver failure and subsequently underwent successful liver transplantation, with a good clinical outcome and survival.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 51-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease requiring stent placement, and prior cerebrovascular accident. Hydralazine 10 mg PO three times daily was started for blood pressure control three months before admission. Injury persisted despite drug discontinuation, progressing to acute liver failure; the patient underwent successful liver transplantation and survived. Clinical findings included scleral icterus, altered mental status, and asterixis. The patient had no pre-existing liver disease. Concurrent home medications (amlodipine 10 mg PO daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg PO twice daily, lisinopril 5 mg PO daily, aspirin 325 mg PO daily) were not attributed as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that certain drugs causing DILI are commonly associated with formation of serum autoantibodies, and cites the Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) Network prospective study in which de Boer et al. found positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at the onset of DILI caused by nitrofurantoin, minocycline, methyldopa, or hydralazine. This identifies hydralazine as a human DILI-causing agent.
raw_record.extra_details: In the DILI Network prospective study, hydralazine-induced DILI was associated with positive ANA and SMA (72% and 60%, respectively) at onset of injury.

raw_record.support_text: The product labeling warns that cases of hepatotoxicity, including granulomatous hepatitis, due to quinidine hypersensitivity have been reported. Unexplained fever and/or elevation of hepatic enzymes, particularly early in therapy, warrant consideration of possible hepatotoxicity, and monitoring of liver function during the first 4-8 weeks should be considered. Cessation of quinidine in these cases usually results in the disappearance of toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported liver injury is described as hepatotoxicity including granulomatous hepatitis, attributed to quinidine hypersensitivity. Presenting features include unexplained fever and/or elevation of hepatic enzymes, especially in the early stages of therapy; liver function monitoring is recommended during the first 4-8 weeks, and discontinuation of quinidine usually leads to resolution of toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatic toxicity secondary to quinidine is an uncommonly reported event. In the author's series, serial liver function tests were available in 5 of 11 patients with fever, and in one of these patients granulomatous hepatitis was demonstrated after biopsy (case 6). The authors also cite four previously reported cases of quinidine-related hepatic abnormality, including one with chemical evidence of both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury, and two cases with biopsy evidence of reversible noncaseating hepatic granulomas. The current case had similar histology during fever with resolution of granulomas one year later. The paper supports routine hepatic function testing in all patients with quinidine fever to clarify the frequency of quinidine-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient in the current series had biopsy-demonstrated granulomatous hepatitis (Appendix, case 6), which resolved one year later. Four previously reported cases of quinidine-related hepatic abnormality include one with chemical evidence of both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury and two with biopsy evidence of reversible noncaseating hepatic granulomas. Serial liver function tests were available in 5 of 11 patients with quinidine fever. The paper describes hepatitis occurring in association with quinidine fever and allergic origin.

raw_record.support_text: The study subjects are patients with amineptine hepatitis, i.e., humans who developed hepatitis from therapeutic use of amineptine. The paper further discusses 'amineptine hepatotoxicity' throughout, and reports that this susceptibility was constitutional and inherited based on in vitro lymphocyte testing of 9 patients (8 tested after complete recovery) and their relatives.
raw_record.extra_details: About 9 patients with amineptine hepatitis; hepatotoxicity attributed to a reactive amineptine metabolite (cytochrome P-450/NADPH dependent, detoxified by glutathione/epoxide hydrolase). Susceptibility was constitutional and inherited, not related to debrisoquine/dextromethorphan (CYP2D6) poor-metabolizer phenotype, and not due to impaired glutathione synthesis (basal lymphocyte glutathione and acetaminophen-metabolite cytotoxicity were similar to controls). In vitro lymphocyte cytotoxicity test (amineptine 1-2.5 mM) positive in first-degree relatives, some never exposed to amineptine. Phenotype reported as hepatitis (acute/chronic not specified).

raw_record.support_text: The described hepatic injury is attributed to amineptine: an anicteric acute hepatitis developed 15 days after the onset of amineptine (300 mg daily for depression) and improved rapidly after its cessation, with no other cause of liver disease. Multiple cases of amineptine-induced hepatitis with similar features (abdominal pain, fever) had been reported, and at therapeutic dose amineptine hepatotoxicity is described as likely immuno(activating) — a hypersensitivity pattern.
raw_record.extra_details: Tricyclic antidepressant given at 300 mg daily for depression in a 39-year-old woman. Anicteric acute hepatitis appeared 15 days after amineptine start, with nausea, abdominal pain, chills, fever (40°C), dark urine, tender 12 cm hepatomegaly. Labs on admission: ALT 1360 U (N 5-40), AST 560 U (N 5-30), GGT 205 U (N 10-40), AP 5.5 U (N 2-5), 6% eosinophils; HBsAg/HBV markers/HCV and M-, SM-, nuclei-, DNA-autoantibodies negative; normal biliary ultrasound. Improved after amineptine interruption (bilirubin 7 µmol/l, ALT 426 U, AST 120 U, GGT 152 U). Authors note several previously reported amineptine-induced hepatitis cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that the patient's course incriminates amodiaquine as the cause of the fatal hepatic injury: hepatitis appeared 5 weeks after beginning amodiaquine, regressed when the drug was stopped, and the symptoms (asthenia, pruritus, vomiting, worsened jaundice) recurred only 3 days after readministration of 600 mg amodiaquine, progressing to hepatic encephalopathy and death with massive hepatic necrosis on autopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a fatal fulminant hepatitis in a patient who developed hepatitis 5 weeks after starting treatment with amodiaquine (600 mg rechallenge dose). Injury regressed on drug withdrawal and recurred sharply 3 days after rechallenge, with worsening jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, respiratory disturbance, and death on March 12. Autopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis with isolated lymphocytic clusters. Laboratory findings at the time of repatriation: total bilirubin 372 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 280 µmol/L, SGPT 965 IU/L, SGOT 1180 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 313 IU/L (N 30-120), prothrombin 20%, factor V 23%, fibrinogen 1.5 g/L. No competing etiology found (no alcohol, no other medications, negative viral A and B hepatitis serology, no reason to suspect non-A, non-B hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: The drug amodiaquine, a 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial, became of importance when some P. falciparum strains resistant to chloroquine retained sensitivity to amodiaquine. In 1986 it was shown that 1 in 2000 subjects taking amodiaquine for prophylaxis of malaria developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both, illustrating idiosyncratic (Type B) drug toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for prophylaxis of malaria; 1 in 2000 subjects developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both. Mechanism attributed to an unstable reactive quinoneimine metabolite formed in liver and white cells that acts as a hapten, and high titres of specific antibodies to the reactive metabolite were found in the blood of patients who developed myelotoxicity or hepatotoxicity, giving evidence for an immunological basis. Whereas chloroquine retained sensitivity in resistant strains, amodiaquine was toxic.
