raw_record.support_text: The patient, with no specific past medical history and negative serologic/radiologic findings, developed jaundice-related liver injury after taking LCZ (levocetirizine) for 2 months, with normalization of all liver enzymes within 3 weeks of discontinuation and biopsy showing portal inflammation, hepatitis, and apoptotic hepatocytes. Based on timing of LCZ administration and clinical course, the authors suspected, and then confirmed after biopsy and recovery on drug withdrawal, an LCZ-induced liver injury, which was considered an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: LCZ is the R-enantiomer of cetirizine dihydrochloride, used for allergic diseases and not listed in prescribing information for hepatotoxicity. The patient presented with jaundice after ~2 months of LCZ. Laboratory findings: AST 1,208 IU/L, ALT 2,043 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.68 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.23 mg/dL, ALP 184 U/L, GGT 253 IU/L. No extrahepatic obstruction or biliary ductal disease on imaging; viral, autoimmune, ceruloplasmin and copper markers negative. Liver biopsy showed portal inflammation and hepatitis with apoptotic hepatocytes and increased portal connective tissue. All liver enzymes normalized within 3 weeks after LCZ discontinuation, and liver function remained normal at follow-up. The paper also cites a prior report of LCZ-induced hepatitis with milder elevation (AST 113 IU/mL, ALT 115 IU/mL) detected by routine LFT after 2 weeks of use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute liver injury (DILI) attributed to levocetirizine, describing a highly probable association with the use of levocetirizine according to the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method based on a score of 9.4. They classified the injury as idiosyncratic (rare, typically dose-independent with variable onset) and noted that the patient had previously taken levocetirizine for very short periods without injury but developed clinically relevant liver injury when taking it for 11 consecutive days. After ruling out other etiologies, they concluded the most likely diagnosis was idiosyncratic levocetirizine-induced liver injury, supported by timing of drug administration, improvement of clinical and laboratory parameters after drug discontinuation, and histological findings similar to another reported case.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 9.4 (highly probable). Patient developed injury only after 11 consecutive days of use despite multiple prior short-term exposures without injury, consistent with dose-independent idiosyncratic mechanism. Acute DILI confirmed by liver biopsy showing portal inflammation (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils), intrahepatic cholestasis and prominent cholestatic injury, intralobular and periportal collapse, and mild periportal fibrosis on trichrome stain; abdominal ultrasound showed no cholelithiasis/ductal obstruction, MRI showed periportal edema. Laboratory trends showed elevated total bilirubin, AST, and ALT. Treated with prednisone 60 mg daily, with dramatic improvement in symptoms and transaminases within 2 days. Authors note limited evidence for corticosteroid therapy in DILI/ALF generally.

raw_record.support_text: Clinically evident idiosyncratic hepatitis has been observed with suloctidil, and since its introduction in France in 1981, sixty-seven cases had been reported up to July 1985; in cases where liver biopsy was performed the findings were similar to those of the reported patient. Growing concern regarding the hepatic adverse effects of suloctidil led to its withdrawal from the market in August 1985. Asymptomatic elevations of liver enzymes had also been noted in a number of trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Suloctidil is a calcium antagonist with alleged anti-platelet, antithrombotic, and vascular antispasmodic activity. In the index patient, jaundice cleared and liver tests (AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, prothrombin time) and eosinophil count returned to normal within eight weeks after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Peripheral eosinophilia was considered compatible with an idiosyncratic drug reaction; cirrhotic cold agglutinins and haemolytic anaemia were found but not felt to account for the severe jaundice. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with eosinophilic leucocyte infiltrate suggesting a drug aetiology, plus confluent centrilobular necrosis, acidophilic individual cell necrosis, cholestasis, and ballooned degeneration of hepatocytes; histology was not consistent with contraceptive steroid-induced liver disease. Competing causes considered and excluded included choledocholithiasis, oral contraceptive pill, autoimmune hepatitis (CRST syndrome, smooth muscle antibody positivity), viral hepatitis, and hemolysis. Sixty-seven suloctidil hepatitis cases reported in France up to July 1985; drug withdrawn from market in August 1985; extensive necrosis described in other reports.

raw_record.support_text: After excluding viral, toxic, alcohol-related and transfusion-related hepatitis, and noting that despite concurrent long-term ibuprofen therapy the liver enzymes returned to baseline while ibuprofen continued, while all abnormalities appeared soon after suloctidil initiation and returned to normal 2 months after discontinuing it, the authors conclude this is a case of hepatotoxicity caused by suloctidil, with no evidence of toxicity to other organ systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Index patient received suloctidil 300 mg; SGOT rose from baseline to 390 IU/L, SGPT to 565 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase to 202 IU/L, total bilirubin peaked at 1.2 mg/dl, with recovery to normal by 2 months after discontinuation; liver biopsy showed intact lobular pattern, scattered individual necrotic hepatocytes, focal Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and increased round cells in portal areas without piecemeal necrosis. Concurrent ibuprofen was excluded as cause (taken for years, enzymes returned despite continued therapy). At least 15 other reported cases: Schouten and Westerman reported 3 cases of elevated liver tests in hyperlipoproteinemia patients on 1200 mg/day suloctidil, with transaminase abnormalities between 8-10 weeks and peak elevations of 2- to 40-fold, all resolving after discontinuation; Perrin et al. reported a case progressing to cirrhosis and death after two rechallenges (early biopsy showed hepatitis with mild eosinophilic infiltrate; postmortem showed fibrosis and regenerating nodules); additional biopsy-proven cirrhosis and significant-fibrosis cases reported; Verneau et al. reported fatal fulminant hepatitis. In the Gent et al. trial of suloctidil in patients with recent thromboembolic stroke, 6 of 216 patients (2.7%) developed a twofold serum transaminase elevation that resolved after drug discontinuation; dose-relatedness and relative risk not established.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma started osimertinib 80 mg once daily. One month later she developed grade 2 hepatotoxicity (AST 106 U/L, ALT 63 U/L); after discontinuation her liver function improved to near normal within 10 days. Rechallenge at a reduced dose (40 mg) produced grade 2 deterioration within a week and, after a second discontinuation, worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). The hepatotoxicity was considered osimertinib related because she had no history of liver disease, viral hepatitis, or habitual alcohol intake, and her liver metastases were improving on osimertinib. Osimertinib was later successfully readministered using a desensitization method.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 66-year-old woman with EGFR L858R/T790M metastatic lung adenocarcinoma treated for pleural-effusion and liver progression after erlotinib. Osimertinib started at 80 mg once daily; grade 2 hepatotoxicity (AST 106 U/L, ALT 63 U/L) after 1 month; improved to near normal in 10 days after discontinuation. Rechallenge at reduced 40 mg dose caused grade 2 deterioration within 1 week; after second discontinuation enzymes worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). No viral hepatitis, liver disease, or alcohol intake; liver metastases were improving, supporting causality. Osimertinib withheld 5 weeks until enzymes normalized, then successfully restarted via a desensitization method; at 5 months after rechallenge brain metastases, pulmonary tumor, and pleural effusion had decreased.

raw_record.support_text: Osimertinib (80 mg/day) was started as sixth-line therapy in a 62-year-old woman with EGFR T790M-mutated NSCLC. On day 15 she developed general malaise; after reduction to 40 mg/day she was admitted with high fever and elevated serum AST (284 IU/L) and ALT (183 IU/L). No other cause was found, and fever and transaminase elevations improved immediately after discontinuation, leading to the diagnosis of drug-induced fever and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 62-year-old woman with relapsed stage IV NSCLC harboring EGFR L858R and acquired T790M, receiving osimertinib as sixth-line therapy. Initial dose 80 mg/day; reduced to 40 mg/day after day-15 general malaise; hepatotoxicity (AST 284 IU/L, ALT 183 IU/L) with high fever noted three days after the reduced dose, prompting emergency ward admission. No other cause identified; fever and transaminase elevations resolved after osimertinib discontinuation (dechallenge). Oral desensitization with milled osimertinib tablets mixed in lactose was performed over ~2 weeks (0.1 mg/day up to 40 mg/day on day 17) with no recurrence of hepatotoxicity or fever for the following 6 months on 40 mg/day. The paper notes osimertinib treatment is permanently stopped in 7–13% of patients due to drug-induced toxicities and that severe hepatotoxicity was the most common drug-induced side effect in clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: The case is presented as the first report of ibrutinib-induced acute liver failure (ALF), defined by the AASLD as acute hepatic injury of less than 26 weeks duration with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy in a patient without preexisting cirrhosis. RUCAM was used to attribute causality.
raw_record.extra_details: First report of ibrutinib-induced acute liver failure. RUCAM causality score 7, stated as consistent with 'probable'. R-ratio of 7.3 indicated hepatocellular injury. ALF evidenced by coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy without preexisting cirrhosis in a patient with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. Coagulopathy resolved within 30 days of discharge and liver chemistries normalized by 60 days; patient was not re-challenged with ibrutinib; WM disease markers (M-spike 2.8 g/dL, IgM 4330) increased and alternative treatment was pursued.

raw_record.support_text: In this prospective trial of ibrutinib monotherapy in treatment-naive Waldenström macroglobulinemia patients, one patient discontinued the study for drug-induced hepatitis that resolved 2 months after ibrutinib discontinuance. The adverse-event table lists grade 3 drug-induced hepatitis (1 of 31 patients, 3%) as well as grade 3 alanine transaminase and aspartate transaminase elevations (each 1 of 31, 3%), all events being those investigators deemed possibly, probably, or definitively associated with protocol therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Ibrutinib monotherapy (treatment-naive Waldenström macroglobulinemia, prospective single-arm trial). Drug-induced hepatitis reported as grade 3 (1 of 31, 3%), categorized by investigators as possibly, probably, or definitively related to protocol therapy; the affected patient discontinued study drug and the hepatitis resolved 2 months after discontinuance (dechallenge response). Grade 3 alanine transaminase (1/31, 3%) and aspartate transaminase (1/31, 3%) elevations also reported as possibly/probably/definitively related. No grade 4 protocol-related toxicities occurred.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, rosuvastatin was implicated in 0.8% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases and showed a long latency period profile of DILI (>60 days postexposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 0.8% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases in the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases; long latency profile (>60 days postexposure).

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with icteric sclera, generalized jaundice, mild right upper quadrant tenderness and a palpable liver edge; LFTs on arrival showed AST 1,400, ALT 2,253 and TB 9.9. The RUCAM/CIOMS causality scale, a validated tool for assessing causality in suspected DILI, gave a score of 9, suggestive of a highly probable adverse drug reaction. The patient was only taking rosuvastatin and admitted no other drugs, supplements, or herbal products.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of rosuvastatin-associated DILI. RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). LFTs on presentation: AST 1,400, ALT 2,253, TB 9.9, normal CBC and electrolytes; later AST 942, ALT 1,312, ALP 167, TB 17.2. Liver biopsy showed acute severe hepatitis with portal and lobular mixed inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils) with interface activity and bile duct damage, interpreted as a likely immune-mediated drug reaction. Workup for chronic liver disease, autoimmune antibodies (ASMA, ANA, anti-LKM), hepatotropic viruses, HSV/CMV/EBV, and copper/iron/trichrome stains was unrevealing. Treated with IV N-acetylcysteine for 5 days and Ursodiol without enzyme improvement; evaluated for possible liver transplantation; patient remained stable without hepatic encephalopathy. Abdominal ultrasound showed nonspecific hepatitis findings and CT showed mild periportal edema. Patient denied alcohol and other co-medications.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted after adjudication as true statin-induced DILI, with mostly mild-moderate self-limited injury and a likely idiosyncratic class effect. Rosuvastatin accounted for 4 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated rosuvastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=4; Swedish 1988-2010 n=2. DILIN aggregate (all statins): hepatocellular 12/22, cholestatic 9/22, 4 severe, 1 fatal; latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists rosuvastatin as a RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with an updated RUCAM score of 9 conferring a highly probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the updated RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Updated RUCAM score 9, highly probable causality grading; reported iDILI case, reference [40].

raw_record.support_text: In the ROAD study, a prospective observational study of 14,243 rosuvastatin-treated patients with dyslipidemia in the Republic of Korea conducted over ~4.6 years, the overall adverse event rate was notably low (1.63%) and no clinically significant incidences of statin-associated myopathy, hepatotoxicity, or diabetes were observed during the study period. The authors conclude there was no clinically significant hepatotoxicity associated with rosuvastatin use.
raw_record.extra_details: ROAD study (ROsulord® sAfety for patients with Dyslipidemia), non-interventional, multicenter, prospective observational study in the Republic of Korea; 14,243 participants; ~4.6 years; overall adverse event rate 1.63%; no clinically significant statin-associated hepatotoxicity observed. Indication: dyslipidemia.

raw_record.support_text: In the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases, lovastatin was implicated in 0.2% of the definitive, highly likely, or probable total DILI cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Implicated in 0.2% of adjudicated (definitive, highly likely, or probable) DILI cases in the DILIN prospective study of 899 idiosyncratic DILI cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the US DILIN prospective study, only 22 of 1188 suspected DILI cases were accepted after adjudication as true statin-induced DILI, described as mostly mild-moderate, self-limited injury with idiosyncratic timing as a likely class effect. Lovastatin accounted for 1 of these 22 adjudicated cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated lovastatin DILI cases: US DILIN n=1; Spanish Registry n=4 (8.5%). DILIN aggregate (all statins): hepatocellular 12/22, cholestatic 9/22, 4 severe, 1 fatal; latency 34 days to >10 years.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an adult patient who developed clinical hepatitis three months after starting lovastatin, with asthenia, jaundice, and increased aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase activities. Liver histology showed centrilobular necrosis, centrilobular cholestasis, and infiltrates of mononuclear and polymorphonuclear cells including eosinophils. Withdrawal of lovastatin led to complete normalization of liver tests within two months, and the paper notes lovastatin is known to induce asymptomatic liver dysfunction in a few patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency: clinical hepatitis three months after lovastatin onset. Symptoms: asthenia, jaundice, increased aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase activities. Histology: centrilobular necrosis, centrilobular cholestasis, infiltrates with mononuclear and polymorphonuclear cells including eosinophils. Dechallenge: complete normalization of liver tests within two months after withdrawal. Paper notes lovastatin is known to induce asymptomatic liver dysfunction in a few patients; authors recommend monitoring liver tests during the first year of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical trial of LY3031207, all six cases of DILI were judged to be related to LY3031207 dosing based on negative viral hepatitis serologies, negative serology for autoimmune hepatitis, limited alcohol consumption during the trial, and denial of use of medications with known hepatotoxicity (including acetaminophen). A retrospective analysis showed that females and older subjects were more susceptible to DILI than males and younger subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Six cases of DILI in the trial; five showed a hepatocellular pattern (R ratio 10-38) and one a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern (R ratio 4); eosinophilia 6-21% (normal 0-6%) in all; 2 patients had generalised urticaria; 4 patients female and all but one aged >50 years. Three patients developed DILI symptoms after 225 mg daily dosing was stopped early (Patients 3-5: urticaria, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite); Patient 6 completed 28 days of 75 mg daily with modest ALT increases and remained asymptomatic. Total dose ranged from 2100 mg over 28 days (Patient 6) to 4950 mg over 22 days (Patient 3). Dose-dependent increase in likelihood of DILI; plasma concentrations in DILI patients were comparable with subjects in the same dose group without DILI and lower than the NOAEL exposure in both dog and rat. Patients were monitored as outpatients until liver tests returned to predose ranges. Females and older subjects were more susceptible (P ≤ 0.05).

raw_record.support_text: Drug candidate 1 (LY3031207), an mPGES-1 inhibitor, was evaluated in a multiple ascending dose clinical trial (25, 75, and 225 mg per day for one month). Several human subjects experienced significantly increased ALT levels (5–45× ULN) and DILI-related symptoms such as hepatocellular injury and hypersensitivity. These clinical observations led to its termination from clinical development due to the emergence of liver safety signals.
raw_record.extra_details: mPGES-1 inhibitor (inhibition of PGE2 formation in human whole blood IC50 = 0.24 µM); phase 1 multiple ascending dose trial at 25, 75, and 225 mg/day for one month; ALT elevations 5–45× ULN; DILI-related symptoms included hepatocellular injury and hypersensitivity; clinical development terminated due to liver safety signals; 2-aminoimidazole-based agent.

raw_record.support_text: The mPGES inhibitor LY3031207, assessed in Phase 1 clinical trials, was found to cause DILI. Preclinical models indicated formation of an epoxide on the 3,4 double bond that gave rise to adducts with glutathione, and for these reasons a 2-aminoimidazole becomes a new and relevant structural alert.
raw_record.extra_details: mPGES (microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1) inhibitor evaluated in Phase 1 clinical trials. Preclinical models indicated epoxide formation on the 3,4 double bond with glutathione adducts; this finding underlies the designation of the 2-aminoimidazole substructure as a new structural alert.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 65-year-old patient who developed jaundice, fever, and hepatocellular insufficiency that led to death at the beginning of treatment with regorafenib (3 tablets per day) for metastatic colon cancer, with no liver metastases. No concomitant treatment was given and other causes of liver damage were eliminated. Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with lymphocyte infiltration, illustrating the risk of severe hepatic involvement typically occurring within the first 2 months of treatment. Hepatotoxicity is described as a frequent side effect of regorafenib.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported case: 65-year-old female with sub- and diaphragmatic ganglionic metastases of colon adenocarcinoma; jaundice, fever, and hepatocellular insufficiency; fatal liver failure at regorafenib 3 tablets/day (subtherapeutic dosage noted in the discussion); no concomitant treatment; competing causes of liver damage eliminated; liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with lymphocyte infiltration; no liver metastases. Aggregate trial data: severe drug-induced liver injury with fatal outcome occurred in 0.3% of 1,100 regorafenib-treated patients across all published clinical trials; fatal hepatic failure in 1.6% (regorafenib) vs 0.4% (placebo) in the phase III CORRECT trial, all affected patients having metastatic liver disease; 0.8% fatal hepatic failure in the GRID trial; in the CONCUR Asian trial hepatotoxicity was associated with a cytolysis syndrome (elevated ALT in 7%, elevated AST in 6%). Monitoring liver biology every 2 weeks during the first 2 months recommended.

raw_record.support_text: Regorafenib, an oral multi-kinase inhibitor approved for unresectable GIST and previously treated metastatic colorectal cancer, caused severe drug-induced liver injury seen only in the regorafenib group in a phase 3 trial (Grothey et al.), described as potentially life-threatening, with elevated bilirubin, AST and ALT in 2% vs 1% of patients compared to placebo. In a separate phase 3 trial for advanced GIST (Demetri et al.), one death due to hepatic failure was described. Regorafenib carries an FDA black box warning for hepatotoxicity, with recommended dose reduction from 160 mg to 120 mg for grade 3 AST/ALT elevations and defined discontinuation criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved for unresectable GIST progressed on imatinib/sunitinib and for metastatic colorectal cancer previously treated with fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, anti-VEGF and (if KRAS wild-type) anti-EGFR therapy. Inhibits VEGFR 2 and 3, Ret, Kit, PDGFR and Raf kinases. In Grothey et al. phase 3 mCRC trial, elevated bilirubin, AST and ALT in 2% vs 1% vs placebo; severe DILI seen only in regorafenib group and can be life-threatening. In Demetri et al. phase 3 GIST trial, one death due to hepatic failure. FDA black box warning for hepatotoxicity. Dose reduced from 160 to 120 mg for grade 3 AST/ALT; discontinue if AST/ALT >20x ULN, AST/ALT >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN, recurrence of AST/ALT >5x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN, recurrence of AST/ALT >5x ULN at 120 mg, or grade 4 adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: In the single-arm CONSIGN study (2,864 treated patients with treatment-refractory mCRC receiving regorafenib 160 mg once daily for the first 3 weeks of each 4-week cycle, median three cycles), ongoing monitoring identified one nonfatal case of regorafenib-related severe drug-induced liver injury per DILI Working Group criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: One nonfatal case of regorafenib-related severe drug-induced liver injury per DILI Working Group criteria identified during ongoing safety monitoring. Regorafenib given at 160 mg once daily for the first 3 weeks of each 4-week cycle; median treatment duration three cycles. Separately reported grade 3-4 laboratory toxicities (ALT 6%, AST 7%, bilirubin 13%) were not themselves labeled as DILI/hepatotoxicity. Study: CONSIGN, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01538680.

raw_record.support_text: Among 1229 patients with confirmed DILI, 7 cases (0.6%) were attributed to fenofibrate. Laboratory results at presentation showed hepatocellular, mixed and cholestatic injury, 6 cases presented with jaundice, and causality scores were highly likely in 5 and probable in 2. Outcomes included hospitalization in 4 patients, liver transplantation in 1, and chronic injury and death in another.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were definite, very likely and probable DILI attributed to fenofibrate enrolled in the DILI Network study 2004-15; 7/1229 (0.6%) confirmed DILI cases. Median age 43 years (range 37-61). Latency 5-8 weeks in 4 patients and 18-56 weeks in the rest. No patient had routine monitoring. 6 presented with jaundice. 4 required hospitalization. 2 with delayed drug discontinuation had severe outcome: 1 liver transplantation, 1 chronic injury and death. Liver biopsy in 4 patients showed diverse injury patterns. HLA-A*33:01 present in 3 patients (43% vs 1% in control populations). Causality highly likely in 5 and probable in 2. Fenofibrate is a hypolipidemic with rare instances of hepatotoxicity and routine liver biochemistry monitoring recommended.

raw_record.support_text: Ho et al. reported a 61-year-old man on fenofibrate 300 mg/day who developed jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue two weeks after treatment initiation, with ALT 249 U/L, AST 259 U/L, and bilirubin 9.3 mg/dL. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis, steatosis, and portal inflammatory cells with mild fibrosis. No other explanation for the hepatic injury was found (acute hepatitis markers negative, no autoantibodies, no biliary obstruction), and liver function tests improved after fenofibrate discontinuation, supporting fenofibrate-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old man; fenofibrate 300 mg/day; symptoms (jaundice, dark urine, fatigue) appeared 2 weeks after initiation; ALT 249 U/L, AST 259 U/L, bilirubin 9.3 mg/dL; biopsy showed cholestasis, steatosis, portal inflammatory cells with mild fibrosis; acute hepatitis markers negative, serum autoantibodies absent, no biliary obstruction; dechallenge: liver function tests improved after discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of fenofibrate-induced acute severe drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with sudden onset and rapid recovery, and recommend measuring hepatic enzymes at least two weeks after initial fenofibrate treatment, followed by monitoring every 3 months within the first year of therapy, to avoid delayed diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute severe DILI with sudden onset and rapid recovery; the authors recommend hepatic enzyme monitoring starting at two weeks after initial fenofibrate treatment and every 3 months during the first year of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes the patient's liver injury to fenofibrate. A standardized RUCAM causality assessment gave a score of 7 ('probable'). The calculated R-ratio was 12.8 with ALT ≥3 ULN, fitting a hepatocellular damage pattern. The patient was a first-time fenofibrate user and developed liver damage within 2 days of taking the drug, with jaundice (elevated bilirubin), fatigue, and anorexia; liver tests normalized after fenofibrate withdrawal (bilirubin normal by 6 days; AST and ALP normal by 10 days). Fenofibrate was not re-challenged because of the severity of the liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: male patient (BMI 27.76 kg/m2, BSA 2.21 m2) with gallstones and fatty liver on ultrasound. RUCAM score 7 ('probable'). R-ratio 12.8 with ALT >=3 ULN classified as hepatocellular damage. Jaundice with raised bilirubin; bilirubin normalized 6 days and AST/ALP normalized 10 days after fenofibrate withdrawal; fatigue and anorexia resolved. No rechallenge (fenofibrate not re-applied) due to severity. Literature context: a report of 1229 confirmed DILI patients included 7 (0.6%) attributed to fenofibrate, with short latency (5-8 weeks) in 4 and longer latency (18-56 weeks) in the rest; a separate report described a 53-year-old female with severe abdominal pain 36 h after fenofibrate re-application. This case is notable for first-time use and injury within 2 days.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis consistent with toxic hepatitis. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 6 (time to onset 2 points, ALP course after cessation 2 points, age risk factor 1 point, alternative causes 1 point), indicating fenofibrate as the probable cause of DILI. The patient was diagnosed with severe DILI due to fenofibrate, a fibric acid derivative taken at 135 mg daily for 6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man with jaundice and pruritis, latency 6 wk at 135 mg daily; initial ALT 172 U/L, ALP 1182 U/L, total bilirubin 15.99 mg/dL, INR 0.92; biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with zone 3 cholestasis/necrosis, bile pigment deposition, portal vein fibrosis; recovery in 3 wk after treatment with prednisolone. The paper also compiles 11 published fenofibrate DILI case reports (older men, median age 54 yr, BMI overweight/obese, several with diabetes) with variable latency (2 d to 2 yr) and outcomes including one liver transplant and one death (renal failure at 26 months). DILI associated with fenofibrate occurs in only 0.6% of patients; mild transient aminotransferase elevations in 5-10%.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists fenofibrate as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 10 conferring a highly probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 10, highly probable causality grading; reported iDILI case evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [19].

raw_record.support_text: Although disopyramide has fewer gastrointestinal side effects, cases of hepatotoxicity have been reported, as well as hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure by passive congestion. Rarely, disopyramide can cause cholestatic jaundice that in most cases appears within the first week of taking the medication and generally resolves promptly on discontinuation. A case of severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation was reported, which improved after discontinuation of disopyramide.
raw_record.extra_details: Comparison of disopyramide-induced hepatotoxicity cases (Scheinman et al. two cases: hepatic necrosis with congestion on biopsy, elevated AST/ALT/LDH, improved on day six after discontinuation, recurrence of symptoms on rechallenge with the drug switched to procainamide; second case improved with diuresis, liver enzymes normalized, and recurred on rechallenge). Doody case: severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation (prolonged PT, elevated fibrin split products), liver enzymes and functions improved 14 days after discontinuation. Barkins et al. case: jaundice and abnormal liver enzymes after one week, prompt clinical resolution on discontinuation. Also noted hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure/passive congestion (indirect mechanism) and negative inotropic effect worsening heart failure. Generally cholestatic jaundice appears within first week.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three new patients with cholestasis probably related to disopyramide (Norpace). The patients had no hepatosplenomegaly, fever, abdominal pain, or heart failure; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients: a 63-year-old man on digoxin, isosorbide dinitrate, and disopyramide 400 mg/d who became jaundiced 10 days after starting, with cholestasis lasting 4 months; a 60-year-old man on dipyridamole, K-strophanthin, and disopyramide 300 mg/d with jaundice 10 days later clearing after 7 months; and a 79-year-old woman on K-strophanthin, oxazepam, furosemide, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate who developed pruritus (without jaundice) 15 days after adding disopyramide 300 mg/d. Surgical exploration/IV cholangiography confirmed a normal biliary system in each. The authors attribute the cholestasis to disopyramide because no cholestatic reactions have been reported for the concurrent drugs, patients were on different drugs except disopyramide, there was a fixed 10-15 day interval between starting the drug and onset of cholestasis, and doses were within the normal therapeutic range.

raw_record.support_text: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), a GPR40 partial agonist with clinical efficacy comparable to sulfonylureas but no propensity for hypoglycemia or weight gain, was terminated during Phase III trials due to drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that was presumably idiosyncratic in nature. The formation and accumulation of a reactive acyl glucuronide (AG) in hepatocytes, and inhibition of TAK-875/AG elimination by MRP2/3/4 transporters, are proposed key contributors to the DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875 is a GPR40 partial agonist that showed clinical efficacy comparable to sulfonylureas without hypoglycemia or weight gain. Phase III program terminated due to DILI. Proposals: formation and accumulation of a reactive acyl glucuronide (AG) in hepatocytes; inhibition of elimination of TAK-875 and its AG by MRP2/3/4 transporters as key contributors. This motivated mitigation efforts in the authors' own series.

raw_record.support_text: Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a potent and highly selective GPR40 agonist being developed for the treatment of T2DM, provided significant glycemic control in clinical trials. However, because of liver safety concerns, clinical development of fasiglifam was terminated in December 2013, a decision that resulted from liver test data in patients enrolled in phase III studies indicating drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Fasiglifam (TAK-875) is a potent, highly selective GPR40 agonist developed for treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus; its novel mechanism amplifies agonism of the endogenous ligand gamma-linolenic acid at an allosteric GPR40 site. It provided significant glycemic control and was well tolerated with low hypoglycemia incidence in trials. Clinical development was terminated in December 2013 due to liver safety concerns based on liver test data in phase III patients indicating drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), a drug candidate developed by Takeda Pharmaceutical Company as an adjunct to improve glycemic control and treat Type 2 diabetes mellitus, was discontinued at Phase III due to liver toxicity. Data from clinical studies indicated TAK-875 was an orally available, potent and selective ago-allosteric modulator of human GPR40 receptor. The paper notes the hepatotoxicity mechanism of TAK-875 is still unknown, and that a computational bSDTNBI prediction found 19 of 30 predicted off-targets have connections with DILI-related liver conditions, explaining the Phase III failure.
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), developed by Takeda as adjunct glycemic control for Type 2 diabetes mellitus; orally available potent selective ago-allosteric modulator of human GPR40; discontinued at Phase III due to liver toxicity; hepatotoxicity mechanism unknown; computational bSDTNBI predicted 30 possible off-targets, 19 of which have connections with DILI including biliary liver cirrhosis, intrahepatic cholestasis, acute liver failure, liver failure, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, liver cirrhosis, and fatty liver.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that phenylpropanoic acid GPR40 agonists such as TAK-875 and AMG-837 were estimated in clinical trials, but the hepatotoxicity found in these clinical trials led to abrogation of the studies. For instance, TAK-875 (fasiglifam) was terminated in Phase III trials despite good pharmacokinetic profiles and potency; the mechanism of its hepatotoxicity is still under research and is generally considered not related to the target because of low GPR40 expression in the liver.
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875 (fasiglifam) was terminated in Phase III trials for type 2 diabetes due to hepatotoxicity despite good PK profiles and potency; mechanism of hepatotoxicity still under research; generally considered not target-related because of low GPR40 (FFA1) expression in the liver.

raw_record.support_text: Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a partial GPR40 agonist, effectively lowered HbA1c in people with type 2 diabetes in a phase III placebo-controlled study. However, due to off-target liver toxicity, the clinical development of fasiglifam was terminated, despite successfully lowering HbA1c.
raw_record.extra_details: Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a partial GPR40 agonist, was evaluated in a phase III placebo-controlled study and effectively lowered HbA1c in people with type 2 diabetes; its clinical development was terminated because of off-target liver toxicity. Indication: type 2 diabetes.

raw_record.support_text: Fasiglifam (TAK-875), an oral FFAR1 (GPR40) agonist for glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes, had its development discontinued because of the rare DILI incidence detected in a phase 3 study. The investigators recruited 43 patients with TAK-875 DILI and 129 matched treated controls from the clinical trials for a GWAS; ALT was elevated after treatment and total bilirubin was also increased, consistent with experimental models showing inhibition of bile acid transporters by TAK-875. No genome-wide significant association signal was found.
raw_record.extra_details: Development discontinued due to rare DILI incidence in a phase 3 study; DILI cases and controls recruited from the clinical trials for a GWAS (43 cases, 129 matched controls). ALT and total bilirubin both increased, consistent with inhibition of bile acid transporters (cholestatic/mixed pattern). GWAS (with 1000 Genomes Phase 3 imputation, 13,477,278 autosomal variants) yielded no genome-wide significant signals; TAK-875 DILI shared genetic aetiology with the cholestatic/mixed (CM)-DILI iDILIC-DILIN GWAS more than with all-DILI or hepatocellular-DILI; a CM-PRS exactly distinguished TAK-875 DILI cases from controls with AUROC 0.61 (95% CI 0.51-0.71). Indication/class: glucose-lowering FFAR1 agonist in type 2 diabetes.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that TAK-875 (fasiglifam), an example of a GPR40/FFA1 agonist, had its development terminated during phase III of clinical trials due to hepatotoxicity, underscoring that the safety profile should be examined early in structure optimization. In paragraph 70, the authors discuss proposed mechanisms of TAK-875 hepatotoxicity after multiple administrations in humans, including its long half-life and accumulation in the liver at high doses, and note the half-life is longer in patients with type 2 diabetes compared with healthy volunteers (51.6 hours vs. 36.6 hours for a 50-mg dose).
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), a GPR40/FFA1 agonist, had its development terminated during phase III clinical trials due to hepatotoxicity. Proposed mechanism of hepatotoxicity after multiple administrations in humans includes a long half-life and accumulation in the liver at high doses (Wolenski et al., 2017). Half-life was longer in type 2 diabetes patients than in healthy volunteers (51.6 h vs. 36.6 h for a 50-mg dose) (Leifke et al., 2012; Naik et al., 2012). Plasma-protein binding is high (99.8% in rats) (Otieno et al., 2018). Preclinical data showed TAK-875 reduced viability of rat and mouse insulinoma cells at higher concentrations, suggesting a narrow safety window.

raw_record.support_text: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), a selective G-protein-coupled receptor 40 agonist in development for type 2 diabetes, was associated during Phase 3 clinical trials with rare but serious incidents of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), leading to discontinuation of development of the compound. The pattern of liver injury observed was a delayed acute hepatocellular injury characteristic of idiosyncratic DILI (IDILI). Mechanisms including hepatocellular oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, bile acid accumulation, and immune response were implicated, and a GWAS analysis from TAK-875 clinical trials supported genetic susceptibilities to DILI from this drug.
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875/fasiglifam (fasiglifam); selective GPR40 agonist; indication type 2 diabetes; Phase 3 clinical trials associated with rare but serious incidents of DILI leading to discontinuation of development; delayed acute hepatocellular injury pattern; mechanistic factors (hepatocellular oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, bile acid accumulation, immune response); GWAS analysis of clinical trial data supported genetic susceptibility (polygenic risk score overlap, enrichment of oxidative stress and mitochondrial pathways).

raw_record.support_text: TAK-875 was discontinued due to liver toxicity, and Marcinak et al. published post hoc results of a Liver Safety Evaluation Committee pooling 15 double-blind phase II/III trials totaling 9,139 patients with type 2 diabetes. Patients treated with TAK-875 had an increased incidence of serum ALT elevations above 3-, 5-, and 10-fold ULN versus placebo or comparators (ALT >3x ULN was 2.7% in the TAK-875 group vs 0.8% comparator and 0.5% placebo), with no dose response seen at 25 and 50 mg/day, and the elevated ALT resolved upon discontinuation. Shavadia et al., analyzing 7,595 patients across 8 trials before program termination, reported a greater frequency of possible Hy's law cases and a 3–7-fold higher risk of ALT/AST increase in the TAK-875 group, with an overall probability of drug-induced liver injury of 0.64% versus 0.06% in placebo/comparator.
raw_record.extra_details: GPR40 (FFAR1) partial agonist (fasiglifam). Terminated at phase III due to liver toxicity. Post hoc pooled analysis of 15 phase II/III trials (9,139 T2D patients): ALT >3x ULN 2.7% vs 0.8% comparator and 0.5% placebo; no dose response at 25 vs 50 mg daily; ALT resolved after discontinuation. Second analysis (7,595 patients, 8 trials): possible Hy's law cases more frequent, 3-to-7-fold higher ALT/AST increase risk, overall DILI probability 0.64% vs 0.06% placebo/comparator. Proposed mechanisms (preclinical): acyl glucuronidation (TAK-875AG reactive metabolite), inhibition of mitochondrial respiration, bile acid transporter inhibition, ROS generation, increased bile acid biosynthesis.

raw_record.support_text: The FFA1-selective agonist TAK-875, also named fasiglifam, exhibited promising antidiabetic effects in clinical studies but failed in phase III trials due to liver toxicity. The paper cites this liver toxicity as the reason the drug failed in phase III trials in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Fasiglifam (TAK-875) is described as an FFA1 (GPR40)-selective agonist pursued for type 2 diabetes mellitus that showed antidiabetic effects in clinical studies but was discontinued/failed in phase III trials because of liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old South Korean man with hypertension developed drug-induced liver injury after his ARB was changed to fimasartan 30 mg then 60 mg. He was referred with acute liver dysfunction (AST 233 U/L, ALT 424 U/L, INR 1.09); viral, autoimmune, iron and copper etiologies were excluded, the modified RUCAM score was 8, and liver biopsy showed hepatocellular necrosis in zones 2 and 3 with spared periportal hepatocytes (zone 1), suggesting toxic hepatitis. The authors state this is the first published report of fimasartan-induced hepatotoxicity, that the patient had no side effects from other ARBs, that injury appeared 10 months after first dose, and that the causative agent was clearly identified after accidental rechallenge with fimasartan caused the episode to recur.
raw_record.extra_details: First published case of fimasartan-induced hepatotoxicity; RUCAM score 8; accidental rechallenge with fimasartan produced recurrence and recurrence, confirming causality; latency of 10 months after first dose; biopsy showed hepatocellular necrosis in zones 2 and 3 with spared periportal hepatocytes (zone 1) and severe lobular inflammation consistent with toxic hepatitis; laboratory values AST 233 U/L, ALT 424 U/L, INR 1.09, total bilirubin 1.22 mg/dL, ALP 112 U/L, GGT 118 U/L; viral and autoimmune etiologies excluded; patient previously tolerated candesartan, irbesartan, and telmisartan without liver side effects; patient took aspirin for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; hypertension indication.

raw_record.support_text: Park et al. reported a case of DILI in fimasartan, an angiotensin-receptor blocker; workup included exclusion of other liver infections, trending of liver enzymes, and a liver biopsy demonstrating hepatocellular necrosis, with a calculated RUCAM score of 11 (highly probable).
raw_record.extra_details: First published case of fimasartan-induced liver injury (an angiotensin-receptor blocker); hepatotoxicity had previously been associated with other ARBs. RUCAM score of 11 (highly probable); liver biopsy demonstrated hepatocellular necrosis; other liver infections excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The authors ascribe three episodes of acute hepatitis in their patient to terfenadine; there was no other cause of liver disease and the patient took no other drug. The first episode occurred 5 months after beginning terfenadine, and the second and third episodes occurred while the patient continued taking terfenadine intermittently. Liver function tests returned to normal after interruption of the drug, and the mechanism of liver injury in this patient was unknown.
raw_record.extra_details: Three recurrent episodes of acute hepatitis; first episode 5 months after start of therapy, subsequent episodes during continued intermittent use. Liver function tests returned to normal after drug interruption. Mechanism of injury unknown. No other cause of liver disease and no other drug taken.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman taking terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria developed two episodes of jaundice and elevated liver enzymes that resolved when off the drug; the second episode occurred during intermittent continued terfenadine use, with viral hepatitis, infectious mononucleosis, and biliary disease excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 43-year-old woman treated with terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria, started 15 Sep 1983. First episode Feb 1984: asthenia and jaundice, bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100), eosinophils 3%, HBsAg absent, normal ultrasonography; jaundice resolved and liver tests normalized by July 1984. During intermittent terfenadine use, a second episode on 5 Sep 1984: bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alk phos 484 U, eosinophil count normal, serologies negative (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, IgM anti-HAV, infectious mononucleosis); resolved Oct 1984. Recurrent injury pattern with rechallenge-like exposure during intermittent continued use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman started terfenadine 60 mg/day for recurrent urticaria and developed jaundice with elevated serum bilirubin (160 µmol/L), ALT (920 U; normal 5-40 U) and alkaline phosphatase (188 U); HBsAg was absent. Jaundice resolved when the drug was withdrawn, but recurred when she resumed taking terfenadine intermittently, and liver tests normalized again after the drug was finally stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of a 43-year-old woman treated with terfenadine 60 mg/day for recurrent urticaria. Episodes of jaundice and asthenia with elevated serum ALT and alkaline phosphatase resolved on drug withdrawal and recurred on re-exposure (dechallenge/rechallenge pattern), with liver test normalization after final drug cessation. Reported elevations: bilirubin up to 160 µmol/L, ALT up to 920 U, alkaline phosphatase up to 484 U. Serologic evaluation excluded hepatitis A/B, infectious mononucleosis, and autoantibodies (mitochondrial, smooth muscle, endoplasmic reticulum) were negative. No history of prior liver/biliary disease, blood transfusion, or recent surgery.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that three episodes of acute hepatitis in their patient can be reasonably ascribed to terfenadine. There was no other cause of liver disease and the patient took no other drug. The first episode occurred 5 months after beginning terfenadine, and the second and third episodes occurred with continued intermittent use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report (case report authorship). Three episodes of acute hepatitis; first occurred 5 months after starting terfenadine, subsequent episodes with continued intermittent use. Serum ALT reached 820 U and alkaline phosphatase 233 U; antimitochondrial, anti-smooth-muscle, and anti-endoplasmic-reticulum antibodies were negative. Liver tests returned to normal after drug discontinuation and the patient felt healthy by end of February 1985. No other drug was taken and no other cause of liver disease was identified; mechanism of injury unknown.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes while taking terfenadine 60 mg/d, with recurrence on intermittent readministration and normalization of liver tests after the drug was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: 43-year-old woman on terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria; first episode September 1983 with onset February 1984 (asthenia, jaundice), bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40 U), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100 U), HBsAg absent; recurrence September 1984 (bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, ALP 484 U) despite intermittent terfenadine use; ALT peaked at 820 U in January 1985; jaundice resolved and liver tests normal after drug cessation in February 1985; serologies for hepatitis A/B, infectious mononucleosis, and autoimmune markers negative; liver/biliary ultrasonography normal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman taking terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria developed asthenia and jaundice, with elevated serum bilirubin (160 µmol/L), ALT (920 U), and alkaline phosphatase (188 U); HBsAg was absent and ultrasonography was normal. After jaundice resolved and liver tests normalized, she again took terfenadine intermittently and developed a second episode of jaundice with elevated bilirubin (70 µmol/L), ALT (512 U), and alkaline phosphatase (484 U), with viral serologies negative; this also resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria. First episode: latency about 5 months (started 15 Sep 1983; jaundice Feb 1984) with bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100), 3% eosinophils, HBsAg absent, normal liver/biliary ultrasound. Resolved by July 1984. On intermittent rechallenge, second episode (jaundice 5 Sep 1984) with bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alkaline phosphatase 484 U, negative viral serology (HBV, HAV IgM, mononucleosis); resolved by October 1984. Jaundice (icterus) and asthenia were the presenting features. Causality attributed as 'probably caused.'

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman started terfenadine, 60 mg/d, for recurrent urticaria and later developed asthenia and jaundice with elevated serum bilirubin (160 µmol/L), ALT (920 U), and alkaline phosphatase (188 U). After resolution, she continued intermittent terfenadine and developed a second episode of jaundice with ALT 512 U and alkaline phosphatase 484 U, resolving again with normal liver tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria (H1-receptor antagonist). First episode ~5 months after starting (Sep 1983 to Feb 1984): bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100), 3% eosinophils, HBsAg absent, normal liver and biliary ultrasound. Second episode (Sep 1984) during intermittent re-administration (rechallenge-like): bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alkaline phosphatase 484 U, normal eosinophil count, viral serologies negative. Both episodes resolved with normal liver tests (jaundice disappeared July 1984 and October 1984). No history of prior liver disease, blood transfusion, surgery, or drugs other than terfenadine noted.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old man (case 2) developed jaundice, pruritus, and epigastric discomfort after taking terfenadine 60 mg twice daily for 4 weeks (he had no other medications, herbal remedies, or risk factors for hepatitis). Initial liver tests were AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, and total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; a liver biopsy showed centrilobular intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes, compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. After terfenadine was stopped, bilirubin rose to a maximum of 909 µmol/L but liver function tests returned to normal within 3 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases (case 1 and case 2) of acute cholestatic hepatitis attributed to terfenadine; case 2 took 60 mg twice daily for 4 weeks. Latency of a few weeks. Initial laboratory values case 2: AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; peak bilirubin 909 µmol/L during recovery. Liver biopsy showed preservation of architecture with centrilobular intra- and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal tract fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes. No rechallenge performed in either case due to severity of the initial episode; causality supported by temporal relation, absence of other identifiable causes of hepatitis, and compatible histology. The paper notes the reaction is rare and 'probably idiosyncratic', that a product monograph (Seldane) reported isolated cases of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis and hepatitis without clear causality, and that only one prior report of possible terfenadine hepatitis (without histology) was found. Recovery within 3 months.

raw_record.support_text: In two presented cases, terfenadine administration was followed within a few weeks by acute cholestatic hepatitis. Rechallenge was not performed because of severity, but the temporal relation between drug administration and jaundice, absence of other identifiable causes of hepatitis, and liver histology compatible with drug-induced disease argued in favour of a causal relation between terfenadine and the observed liver abnormalities. The authors state that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare and probably idiosyncratic reaction to terfenadine.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports; rechallenge not performed in either case; no previous personal or family history of liver disease and no hepatitis risk factors; initial liver tests AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; liver biopsy showed preservation of architecture, intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis in a centrilobular pattern, mild portal tract fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes, compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; total bilirubin rose to a maximum of 909 µmol/L over 6 weeks after stopping; liver tests returned to normal within 3 months; product monograph (Seldane) notes isolated reports of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis and hepatitis from marketing experience but without clear causal relationship; only one previous possible terfenadine hepatitis report found on MEDLINE.

raw_record.support_text: The causality of fluconazole inducing hepatotoxicity was established by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM)/CIOMS score. Components included a hepatocellular pattern, second exposure, onset <5 days (+1), satisfactory dechallenge (+1), alcohol as a risk factor (+1), age <55 (0), >50% improvement within 8 days (+3), no concomitant therapy (0), nondrug-related causes ruled out (+2), and positive response to re-administration (+3), giving a total score of 11, interpreted as 'Highly Probable' (>8).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; RUCAM/CIOMS score 11 ('Highly Probable', >8) with hepatocellular pattern, positive rechallenge, and satisfactory dechallenge. The conclusion states fluconazole is a known cause of elevated liver function tests but is rarely reported in the literature as an agent associated with acute liver failure (ALF); it is generally linked to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity and concurrent risks such as chronic liver disease, renal impairment, and HIV. This patient developed ALF with none of these apparent risk factors, and further investigation was warranted specifically for IV administration.

raw_record.support_text: Given the close temporal relation between initiation of fluconazole therapy (400 mg orally daily from March 12, 1992) and the acute increase in serum hepatic transaminases, the previously reported association of fluconazole with abnormal transaminase elevations, and exclusion of other potential causes of acute hepatic necrosis, the authors conclude the report most likely represents a case of fatal fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. The patient died on April 6, 1992.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report in an AIDS patient. Fluconazole 400 mg orally daily initiated March 12, 1992; acute rise in transaminases (ALT up to 1,825 IU/L, AST up to 2,770 IU/L), bilirubin up to 28.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time up to 33.0 s. Histology showed massive hepatic necrosis with portal lymphocytic infiltrate and spared hepatocyte islands; viral, Amanita phalloides, and acetaminophen-overdose causes excluded; prochlorperazine differential not consistent because hepatocellular necrosis was not reported for it. Patient died April 6, 1992. Authors note fatal hepatotoxicity also reported with related azole ketoconazole and recommend transaminase monitoring during fluconazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the OPAL Beyond study of tofacitinib, elevations in liver enzymes (ALT & AST) greater than the upper limit of normal were seen in 30% and 32% respectively of patients in the continuous tofacitinib groups, and elevations of 3 or more times the upper limit of normal were seen in 6 patients during the trial. Notably, there were no cases of drug-induced liver injury in these trials, and liver enzyme elevations were also observed in the OPAL Broaden study.
raw_record.extra_details: In OPT OPAL Beyond, ALT and AST elevations above ULN occurred in 30% and 32% respectively of patients in continuous tofacitinib groups; elevations of >=3x ULN occurred in 6 patients during the trial; similar elevations were observed in OPAL Broaden. Despite these liver test abnormalities, no cases of drug-induced liver injury were reported.

raw_record.support_text: In the tofacitinib 5 mg two times per day group up to week 48, there were no deaths and no cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). Adjudicated hepatic events were reported in one (0.8%) patient up to week 16 and three (2.3%) patients up to week 48; one event was assessed as unlikely DILI and the other two as unrelated DILI, and none met the criteria for potential or definite Hy's law.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 3 trial of tofacitinib 5 mg two times per day in axial spondyloarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis (N=133). No DILI cases through week 48 (double-blind and open-label phases). Adjudicated hepatic events: one (0.8%) up to week 16, three (2.3%) up to week 48; one assessed unlikely DILI and two unrelated DILI; none met potential or definite Hy's law criteria. ALT increased was reported in 4 (3.0%) to week 16 and 8 (6.0%) to week 48. Two sequential AST or ALT elevations >5×ULN in 1 (0.8%) to week 16 and 2 (1.5%) to week 48.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of TB patients, 38 developed DILI due to anti-TB drugs, with rifampicin identified as the causative drug in 14 patients. Patients with rifampicin-induced liver injury showed no association with mitochondrial DNA variants.
raw_record.extra_details: In 38 TB patients who developed DILI during anti-TB therapy, rifampicin was the attributed causative drug in 14. DILI defined as ALT >=5x ULN, or ALT >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >=2x ULN. No association with mitochondrial DNA variants was found for rifampicin-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: After the patient's antituberculous treatment was switched to the first-line regimen, he coincidentally developed rifampicin-induced hepatotoxicity with aspartate aminotransferase 848 IU/L (range 15–48 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase 1067 IU/L (range 10–40 IU/L), total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (range 0.2–1 mg/dL) with direct bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL (range 0–0.2 mg/dL), and normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase levels. This necessitated replacement of rifampicin with moxifloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report during first-line antituberculous therapy for tuberculosis. Liver tests showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 848 IU/L, ALT 1067 IU/L) and elevated bilirubin (total 6.4 mg/dL, direct 3.5 mg/dL) with normal GGT and alkaline phosphatase. Hepatotoxicity necessitated replacement of rifampicin with moxifloxacin in the subsequent non-rifampicin based regimen (isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, moxifloxacin). Rifampicin resistance genotypically suspected (rpoB S512T / Xpert probes A and B) but phenotypically pan-susceptible on DST.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed severe and progressive jaundice 53 days after starting cyclophosphamide, with normal liver function before therapy and no evidence of viral hepatitis A/B/C/E, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, cholelithiasis, biliary tract disease, or hepatic/biliary metastasis on MRI. Liver abnormalities resolved completely 3 months after cyclophosphamide was withdrawn, and the authors concluded that the patient suffered from severe and prolonged hepatotoxicity caused by cyclophosphamide.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of 53 days after starting cyclophosphamide; liver function normal before therapy; viral hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, and EBV ruled out; no cholelithiasis, biliary tract disease, or hepatic/biliary ductal metastasis on MRI. Liver abnormalities resolved completely 3 months after drug withdrawal. Prior reported cases of severe cyclophosphamide hepatotoxicity in patients with rheumatologic diseases or hematological malignancies mostly recovered after stopping the drug, though one case required liver transplantation and one died from acute coronary syndrome. Strong indications link 4-OHCP exposure to veno-occlusive disease of the liver, and increased carboxyphosphamide exposure has been associated with increased liver toxicity and mortality.

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old woman with SLE developed severe and progressive jaundice a few days after starting cyclophosphamide, with normal liver function before therapy. Viral hepatitis, cholelithiasis/biliary disease, and lupus hepatitis were excluded, while other signs of cyclophosphamide toxicity (leukopenia, severe monomorphic haematuria) were present. Liver abnormalities resolved only months after cyclophosphamide withdrawal, and the authors concluded the patient suffered from severe hepatic toxicity caused by cyclophosphamide.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: severe cholestasis with minimal hepatocellular injury on biopsy, severe monomorphic haematuria and leukopenia (bladder toxicity). Literature aggregate of 13 total cases: severe hepatotoxicity became clinically evident after 2-40 weeks of oral or IV cyclophosphamide; two patients died of hepatic failure (Aubrey 1970, massive hepatic necrosis; Arai 1992), the rest recovered after drug withdrawal. Biopsy patterns varied: perivascular/perivenous hepatocyte necrosis, diffuse hepatocellular destruction with mild fatty infiltration, massive hepatic necrosis, small hepatic vein damage and fibrosis, drug-induced hepatitis, and (in index case) severe cholestasis. Indications included breast carcinoma, Still's disease, SLE, polymyositis, Sjögren's, Wegener's syndrome, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, minimal-change glomerulonephritis. Mechanism hypothesized to involve abnormal hepatic conjugation of acrolein metabolite. Authors advise monitoring of liver enzymes/bilirubin and prompt discontinuation on liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: Tolvaptan, the only drug approved to treat ADPKD patients at high risk of progression, is only moderately effective and is associated with a high incidence of poorly tolerated side effects mainly due to increased aquaresis. Monthly monitoring of liver function is mandated in all countries where tolvaptan has been licensed due to idiosyncratic liver toxicity seen in the pivotal trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Used to treat ADPKD patients at high risk of progression; idiosyncratic liver toxicity was observed in the pivotal trials, leading to a mandate for monthly liver-function monitoring in all countries where tolvaptan is licensed; drug also associated with side effects mainly due to increased aquaresis.

raw_record.support_text: Causality of tolvaptan in trial subjects with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease who experienced liver injury in the TEMPO 3:4 or TEMPO 4:4 trials was adjudicated by the expert Hepatic Adjudication Committee (HAC), the gold standard for DILI causality, as at least 'probable' for all nine recruited subjects. All patients exhibited a positive dechallenge, with liver injury resolving upon cessation of tolvaptan treatment, and recurrence of injury was observed in the two subjects rechallenged with tolvaptan, with a more rapid onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury occurred in a small number of ADPKD patients on therapeutic tolvaptan in the randomized phase 3 TEMPO 3:4 (NCT00428948) and open-label follow-on TEMPO 4:4 (NCT01214421) trials; delayed onset 3-18 months with rapid recurrence of symptoms on rechallenge, suggestive of adaptive immune-mediated pathogenesis. Most subjects had ALT >7x ULN and two met Hy's law, with transient enzyme elevations (ALP, ALT, AST, bilirubin) resolving on dechallenge. Tolvaptan- and metabolite (DM-4103, DM-4107)-responsive T cell clones (predominantly CD4+) were detected in 6/8 trial subjects, with dose-dependent IFN-γ, IL-13, and granzyme B secretion. No ethnic/race susceptibility was seen (5 Asian, 4 non-Asian).

raw_record.support_text: The TEMPO 3:4 trial illuminated a serious hepatotoxic side effect of tolvaptan, which is thought to be idiosyncratic in nature and accompanied by elevated transaminases with possible elevation of bilirubin. In most cases ALT/AST and bilirubin elevations returned to baseline after stopping the drug, but tolvaptan can cause severe liver damage in some patients; some patients required liver transplantation due to acute liver failure. Supporting trial data include the TEMPO 3:4 comparison of elevated AST (4.4% vs 3.1%), ALT (1.0% vs 0.8%) and bilirubin (0.9% vs 1.9%) in tolvaptan vs placebo (transaminases >3x ULN, bilirubin >1.5x ULN), and the REPRISE trial in which 11% of 681 tolvaptan patients versus 5% of 685 placebo patients developed hepatic side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity reported in ADPKD patients on tolvaptan therapy. In most cases ALT/AST and bilirubin elevations reversed after drug discontinuation; some patients developed severe liver damage and required liver transplantation due to acute liver failure. TEMPO 3:4 trial elevations: AST 4.4% vs 3.1%, ALT 1.0% vs 0.8%, bilirubin 0.9% vs 1.9% (tolvaptan vs placebo; transaminases >3x ULN, bilirubin >1.5x ULN). REPRISE double-blinded trial: hepatic side effects in 11% of 681 tolvaptan patients vs 5% of 685 placebo patients. Tolvaptan is a vasopressin (V2) receptor antagonist.

raw_record.support_text: For five hepatic standardized MedDRA queries (cholestasis and jaundice of hepatic origin; hepatic failure, fibrosis and cirrhosis and other liver damage-related conditions; noninfectious hepatitis; liver-related investigations/signs/symptoms; and liver-related coagulation and bleeding disturbances), there was one treatment-emergent AE (increased blood bilirubin) in the placebo group during phase A. No participant experienced elevated transaminases, and there were no cases of drug-induced liver injury in the tolvaptan group.
raw_record.extra_details: In a phase A trial of tolvaptan (n=48) vs placebo (n=43) in a pediatric population, none of the five hepatic standardized MedDRA query categories were met in the tolvaptan group; the only liver-related treatment-emergent AE (increased blood bilirubin) occurred in the placebo group. No participant experienced elevated transaminases, and there were no cases of drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the TEMPO 3:4 and 4:4 clinical trials, a hepatic adjudication committee concluded that in 17 patients presenting with liver injury a causal role of tolvaptan in the liver injury was 'probable' or 'highly likely.' Three of these patients met Hy's Law criteria (ALT >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN). Nineteen of twenty-one rechallenged patients were not mentioned, but of 21 patients with ALT elevations rechallenged after ALT normalization, 10 had eventless rechallenge permitting continued therapy while 11 exhibited rapid ALT elevations, a positive rechallenge rate comparable to immuno-allergic DILI compounds such as halothane.
raw_record.extra_details: Adjudicated causality graded 'probable' or 'highly likely' for 17 patients on TEMPO 3:4 and 4:4. Three patients met Hy's Law (ALT >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN). Latency to hepatic injury 3–18 months; ~75% of affected individuals had hepatic cysts; female predominance (60% of 'probable' or higher category, and all 3 Hy's Law cases). Of 21 patients rechallenged after ALT normalization, 10 rechallenges were eventless and 11 showed rapid ALT elevations; positive rechallenge rate comparable to immuno-allergic DILI-causing compounds such as halothane. Precautionary measures include limiting tolvaptan duration to 30 days in non-ADPKD indications and avoiding use in patients with underlying liver disease or cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: In the tolvaptan safety population (n = 2074), 223 (10.8%) patients experienced ALT or AST ≥3 times the ULN or an adverse event consistent with hepatotoxicity; 75 (3.6%) had ALT or AST ≥3 times the ULN and 200 (9.6%) had an adverse event consistent with hepatotoxicity. At the time of initial elevation, 10 participants had ALT/AST ≥3 times the ULN at 60 mg/day, 19 at 90 mg/day and 46 at 120 mg/day. Of 69 liver-related adverse events in patients with confirmed elevations, investigators considered 63 related and 6 unrelated to tolvaptan.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence in safety population of 2074 tolvaptan-treated patients: 223 (10.8%) with ALT or AST ≥3x ULN or a hepatotoxicity-consistent adverse event; 75 (3.6%) with ALT/AST ≥3x ULN; 65 participants (3.1%) had confirmed elevations after data review excluded 10 with incorrect reference ranges. Among 84 confirmed events (15 isolated transaminase elevations ≥3x ULN and 69 liver-related adverse events), by investigator severity 41/69 (59.4%) mild, 18 (26.1%) moderate, 10 (14.5%) severe; 63 of 69 judged tolvaptan-related. Elevation timing by dose: 10 events at 60 mg/day, 19 at 90 mg/day, 46 at 120 mg/day. Management: interruption (39 events) or withdrawal (20 events); tolvaptan interrupted/withdrawn per labelling for 59/65 (90.8%) participants. Outcomes: 66/84 resolved, 7 resolving, 6 not resolved, 5 not reported; tolvaptan restarted in 27 participants, 20 of whom continued for >6 months.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 154 DILI cases admitted to a tertiary care centre in Hamburg (2008-2017), metamizole was the second most frequent putative agent causing DILI, accounting for 23 of 154 cases (14.9%, after phenprocoumon). The biochemical pattern on admission was hepatocellular, with median ALT 779 U/L (64-3532 U/L) far exceeding median ALP 131 U/L (42-578 U/L). Liver biopsy in 17/23 cases showed moderate-to-severe inflammatory activity and severe centrilobular necrosis (>30%) in 76.5% and 35.3%, respectively. Metamizole was involved in 2 DILI cases progressing to acute liver failure that received liver transplantation and were alive at assessment; re-exposure supported causality in 4 patients. A search of the EMA database identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic frequently prescribed in Germany, Russia and South America; off-market in the UK, USA and Scandinavia due to side effects including agranulocytosis. Liver side effects are not mentioned in the German drug label. Second most frequent putative DILI agent after phenprocoumon in the series (23/154, 14.9%). Infiltration of immune cells on liver histology; 2 cases progressed to acute liver failure and received liver transplantation, alive at assessment; causality supported by re-exposure in 4 patients. EMA (European Medicines Agency) database search identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients with metamizole-induced DILI, clinical characteristics showed a slight female predominance, a median age at onset of 41 years, a mostly hepatocellular pattern of injury, and a relatively large proportion presenting with necrosis and eosinophilic cell infiltration (85% respectively) on histopathology.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 32 patients with metamizole-induced DILI; metamizole suspected as cause in 13% of all DILI patients; slight female predominance; median age at onset 41 years; jaundice in 66% and acute liver failure in 22%; 22% reported mostly unintentional positive rechallenge; histology showed necrosis and eosinophilic cell infiltration (85% respectively) and immune cell infiltration in all specimens; high ANA and AMA positivity; cholestasis and higher fibrosis frequency associated with more severe/jaundiced cases; latency of ~2-3 months from initiation of metamizole associated with more severe evolution; causality assessed by RUCAM (probable/highly probable >=6 vs possible 3-5); proposed immune-mediated mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Metamizole is increasingly recognized as hepatotoxic at normal doses and without concomitant hepatotoxic treatment, based on published case reports and case series of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) following metamizole. Four patients required liver transplantation; reported RUCAM scores ranged 3-11, with at least 13 cases considered probable or highly probable (RUCAM ≥6); a positive rechallenge was recorded in nine patients; and some 18 cases were supported by a positive monocyte-derived hepatocyte-like (MH) cell test. The authors conclude there is growing evidence that metamizole can cause DILI and it has been proposed that metamizole qualifies as a medicine with definite hepatotoxic potential.
raw_record.extra_details: At normal therapeutic doses and in the absence of concomitant hepatotoxic treatment. Reported RUCAM scores varied between 3 and 11; at least 13 cases had RUCAM ≥6 (probable or highly probable). Positive rechallenge in 9 patients. ~18 cases supported by positive MH cell test (sensitivity 92%, specificity 100% for causative agent in DILI patients with positive rechallenge). Positive LTT in a few further cases suggesting immune-mediated reaction. Proposed to qualify as a medicine with definite hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: Metamizole sodium was adjudicated as a single causative agent in 3 DILI cases in the Pro-Euro DILI Registry.
raw_record.extra_details: 3 adjudicated single-cause cases (metamizole sodium); ATC N02BB02; most cases came from Germany.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists metamizole as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a median RUCAM score of 7 conferring a probable causality grading, based on published cases evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Median RUCAM score 7, probable causality grading; reported iDILI cases evaluated with the RUCAM, reference [23].

raw_record.support_text: The study characterizes a cohort of 61 metamizole DILI patients. Most patients with metamizole DILI presented with a hepatocellular type of injury (83.6%). The median RUCAM for metamizole was 6 (range 2–11), and 43 of 61 cases (70.5%) scored RUCAM ≥6, indicating a 'probable' or 'highly probable' cause of DILI, while 18 (29.5%) scored below 6 ('unlikely' or 'possible'). Patients showed high ALT (36.5×ULN), AST (26.9×ULN), and TBIL (8.2×ULN) elevations.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 61 metamizole DILI cases; RUCAM ≥6 in 70.5% (probable/highly probable) and <6 in 29.5% (unlikely/possible); median RUCAM 6 (2–11), significantly higher than non-metamizole DILI (4 [2–6], p=0.009). Hepatocellular injury in 83.6%. ALT 36.5×ULN, AST 26.9×ULN, TBIL 8.2×ULN; no relevant ALP increase; R-ratio at onset 20.5. Jaundice developed in 86.9%. Remission in 77.0%, time to remission 10 weeks. DILI severity index, Hy's law positivity, coagulopathy, and ALF similar to AIH but higher than non-metamizole DILI. Rechallenge recurrence in 9 patients (14.8%): 5 (8.2%) with metamizole alone, 4 (6.6%) with concomitant medication. A characteristic metamizole DILI signature pattern (high AST/ALT at recognition, rapid decline, rising TBIL after onset) was observed in 70.5% (n=43).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of a 29-year-old patient who developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that progressed to vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) after administration of the NSAID pelubiprofen. VBDS is characterized by ductopenia and cholestasis, triggered in this case by an adverse drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: 29-year-old female patient; no history of other drugs or herbal medication and was a social drinker. Pelubiprofen given for 2 days (90-180 mg) for mild fever, runny nose, sputum, and muscle pain. Patient then had more than 10 episodes of vomiting and nausea and was admitted to the emergency department; DILI progressed to VBDS, requiring liver transplantation. The authors state no prior case of VBDS related to pelubiprofen has been reported.

raw_record.support_text: Bak et al. reported a 29-year-old female patient with osteoarthritis treated with pelubiprofen who was hospitalized 2 days after ingesting it and had markedly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 6479 IU/L, AST 4254 IU/L on day 2 of admission). Tbili rose from 3.12 mg/dL on admission to a peak of 11.81 mg/dL on day 23.
