Initial liver biopsy was consistent with cholestatic injury; a repeat biopsy on day 124 revealed chronic cholestatic hepatitis with absent bile ducts in more than 50% of portal tracts, and CK19 immunostaining confirmed bile duct loss and bile ductular proliferation, leading to a diagnosis of vanishing bile duct syndrome with a RUCAM score of 6 indicating low 'probable' causation by pelubiprofen.
raw_record.extra_details: 29-year-old female; COX-2 selective NSAID primarily used in South Korea for osteoarthritis; hospitalized 2 days after ingesting pelubuprofen; ALT 6479 IU/L and AST 4254 IU/L on day 2; Tbili 3.12 mg/dL on admission rising to peak 11.81 mg/dL on day 23; initial liver biopsy consistent with cholestatic injury; repeat biopsy on day 124 showed chronic cholestatic hepatitis with absent bile ducts in >50% of portal tracts; CK19 immunostaining confirmed bile duct loss and bile ductular proliferation; RUCAM score 6 (low probable); aminotransferase height is atypical of other vanishing bile duct syndrome cases.

raw_record.support_text: A breast cancer patient treated with ribociclib in 21-day cycles developed pruritus and ALT elevation after the first cycle; liver enzymes continued rising after discontinuation (ALT >1000 U/L) with jaundice and coagulopathy (INR 2.1) but no encephalopathy. A second patient treated with ribociclib 600 mg in 4-week cycles developed significantly elevated liver enzymes after three cycles; after ribociclib was discontinued the enzymes continued to rise, peaking at ALT 1112 U/L, with nausea and fatigue but no jaundice or encephalopathy (INR 1.3). Neither patient had viral hepatitis, autoimmune serology, alcohol/drug abuse, or herbs, and both normalized after prednisolone treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female breast cancer patients (ER-positive/Her-2 negative; case 2 also received fulvestrant) developed liver injury after ribociclib (600 mg) therapeutic dosing in 4-week cycles. ALT peaked >1000 U/L (case 1) and 1112 U/L (case 2); case 1 had jaundice and coagulopathy (INR 2.1) without encephalopathy. Liver enzymes continued to rise after ribociclib discontinuation and normalized after prednisolone (40 mg) tapered. Hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, HSV, ANA, and SMA were negative; alcohol/drug abuse and herbal use excluded. Both patients later tolerated palbociclib (125 mg daily) with normal liver enzymes, supporting ribociclib as the culprit.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a real-world experience of rechallenging with abemaciclib after a prior reaction of grade 4 liver toxicity to ribociclib, describing high transaminase values of more than 27 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) that occurred while the patient was receiving ribociclib for HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer. After switching to abemaciclib the patient later had grade 3 neutropenia and diarrhea, but after two years hepatic enzymes and complete blood count were normal with stable oncological disease.
raw_record.extra_details: 67-year-old female with HR+/HER2- metastatic (inflammatory) breast cancer on CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy; grade 4 hepatic toxicity with transaminases >27x ULN while on ribociclib. She was subsequently rechallenged by switching to abemaciclib, which caused grade 3 neutropenia and diarrhea but not liver injury; after two years hepatic enzymes and complete blood count normalized and oncological disease was stable.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old female with metastatic HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer developed liver enzyme elevation under ribociclib treatment. Ribociclib was withdrawn 8 weeks after initiation due to enzyme elevation. A liver biopsy performed after further enzyme increase (peak ALT 2836 U/l), jaundice (peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l) and coagulopathy (INR 1.8) revealed acute hepatitis with 30% parenchymal necrosis; the RUCAM score was 7 points (probable).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI grade 3 (International DILI Expert Working Group) in a 41-year-old female with primary metastatic HR-positive HER2-negative breast cancer. Ribociclib withdrawn 8 weeks after initiation. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with 30% parenchymal necrosis; peak ALT 2836 U/l, peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l, INR 1.8. RUCAM score 7 (probable). Managed with prednisone 60 mg and N-acetylcysteine (Prescott regimen); liver enzymes normalized within 8 weeks with prednisone tapering. Peak ALT, bilirubin, and INR values and treatment details recorded.

raw_record.support_text: In the current case of DILI attributed to ribociclib, ALT/AST peaked at 1,967/1,621 U/L and liver biopsy demonstrated significant parenchymal confluent necrosis, representing one of very few reports of submassive hepatocyte necrosis secondary to ribociclib. This pattern was compared with the Schaeffer et al case (41-year-old female with 30% zone III parenchymal necrosis, ALT 2,896 U/L, AST 875 U/L, bilirubin 353 µmol/L) and with a retrospective analysis of 22 DILI cases secondary to CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib and abemaciclib) by Meunier et al, in which 12 liver biopsies showed centrilobular hepatitis with some foci of necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Current case ALT/AST peak 1,967/1,621 U/L with significant parenchymal confluent/submassive hepatocyte necrosis; causality supported by RUCAM, R-factor, and Naranjo in conjunction with histopathologic correlation, all strengthening ribociclib as the offending agent. Schaeffer et al case: 41-yo female, 30% zone III necrosis, ALT 2,896 U/L, AST 875 U/L, bilirubin 353 µmol/L. Meunier et al retrospective: 22 DILI cases secondary to CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib and abemaciclib), 12 liver biopsies showing centrilobular hepatitis with some foci of necrosis (necrosis extent not quantified). Proposed mechanisms: reactive-metabolite formation and piperazine hydroxylation generating iminium ions (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis), bile salt export pump (BSEP) inhibition causing cholestatic features with jaundice and elevated bilirubin, CYP3A4 metabolism with drug-drug interactions (azole antifungals, macrolides) exacerbating hepatotoxicity, and immune-mediated injury (ANA and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, response to glucocorticoids). Some patients showed marked LFT improvement following NAC supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: Duloxetine was one of the other agents (n=1 each) implicated in DILI-ALF in a Brazilian registry of 12 transplant centers.
raw_record.extra_details: Attributed as a cause of DILI-ALF; n=1 case.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy showed inflammatory changes with portal, periportal, and lobular inflammation, focal eosinophils, and perivenular cholestasis, which the authors state further supports a diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury. The patient's duloxetine was discontinued, with a persistent decline and return of hepatic enzymes toward baseline. The patient, admitted for acute liver failure, had a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic picture with markedly elevated aminotransferases (ALT 3365 U/L, AST 1347 U/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (237 U/L), and elevated total bilirubin (7.3 mg/dL); competing etiologies (viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, autoimmune, alpha-1 antitrypsin) were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a female patient admitted and treated for acute liver failure. Mixed injury pattern: disproportionate aminotransferase elevation (ALT 3365 U/L, AST 1347 U/L) versus alkaline phosphatase, elevated total bilirubin (7.3 mg/dL), with perivenular cholestasis on biopsy and portal/periportal/lobular inflammation with eosinophils. Dechallenge: duloxetine discontinuation led to persistent decline of hepatic enzymes toward baseline. No formal causality instrument or rechallenge reported. Viral hepatitis panel, hemochromatosis HFE variants, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies negative or normal. Liver biopsy and discharge labs reported on hospital days 1 and 11.

raw_record.support_text: In the pivotal phase III trials of rimegepant (75 mg) for acute migraine treatment, no serious adverse events related to treatment occurred and no hepatotoxicity was described; nausea and urinary tract infections were the most common adverse events. A companion open-label study (NCT03266588) with up to 75 mg rimegepant taken as needed for up to 52 weeks likewise reported that hepatotoxicity was not observed with long-term and high-frequency dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: NURTEC ODT 75 mg; approved by the US FDA for acute migraine treatment in February 2020. In phase III trials (NCT03235479, NCT03237845, NCT03461757) no hepatotoxicity was described; in the long-term open-label study (NCT03266588) hepatotoxicity was not observed with high-frequency dosing up to one tablet per day for 52 weeks. Use should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment due to higher plasma rimegepant concentrations, but no DILI-related injury is attributed.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized controlled trial of a single 75 mg rimegepant oral tablet for the acute treatment of adults with migraine, the authors state that safety and tolerability with rimegepant were excellent and that liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Transaminase elevations comparing rimegepant (serum AST or ALT >ULN in 2.0%, 11/546) versus placebo (3.6%, 20/549) showed no signal, one participant in each group had levels >3x ULN, none >5x ULN, and no bilirubin elevations >2x ULN were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase safety assessment of rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet for acute migraine. Serum AST or ALT >ULN: 2.0% (11/546) rimegepant vs 3.6% (20/549) placebo; >3x ULN in 0.2% each group; none >5x ULN; total bilirubin >2x ULN in 0.0% both groups. Authors explicitly concluded liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Most common AE was nausea (0.9% vs 1.1% placebo).

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old man with ALK-positive, EML4-ALK fusion lung adenocarcinoma (stage IVB) treated with alectinib 600 mg/day as first-line therapy developed serum AST and ALT elevation to CTCAE grade 3 on day 79. The injury was determined to be alectinib-induced hepatotoxicity of the cholestatic type (Digestive Disease Week Japan 2004 scale and R value), with hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV excluded. After recovery with UDCA and glycyrrhizin, rechallenge with reduced alectinib (150 then 300 mg/day) caused recurrent grade 2 and then grade 3 elevations, requiring discontinuation and a switch to lorlatinib on day 235.
raw_record.extra_details: ALK-positive NSCLC patient. Onset of AST/ALT elevation on day 79 (CTCAE v5.0 grade 3), readmitted on day 107 for alectinib-induced hepatotoxicity; abdominal CT/ultrasonography showed no liver abnormality; cholestatic-type injury by Digestive Disease Week Japan 2004 scale and R value; treated with oral UDCA 600 mg/day and IV glycyrrhizin (SNMC), improving to grade 1; positive rechallenge at 150 mg/day (day 128) then 300 mg/day (day ~149) with recurrence to grade 2 on day 191 requiring discontinuation, then grade 3 on day 219 requiring readmission and IV SNMC; switched to lorlatinib on day 235. Paper notes approximately 1-5% of patients experience alectinib-induced liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: On clinical and paraclinical grounds the authors oriented towards the diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) manifested by acute liver failure, attributed to a history of alectinib intake. Alectinib was stopped, supportive measures and treatment with N-acetylcysteine and corticosteroids were given, with favorable clinical evolution; the hepatotoxicity gradually improved to grade 1.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Differential diagnosis of hepatocellular injury excluded viral hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, NAFLD, alcohol hepatitis, biliary disease, malignancy, and herbal hepatotoxicity. DILI manifested as acute liver failure and improved to grade 1 after alectinib withdrawal; treated with N-acetylcysteine and corticosteroids with favorable evolution.

raw_record.support_text: In the exposure-response analysis of hepatic safety (increased ALT, AST), there was a probable relationship between increased pexidartinib exposure and the risk of hepatic events, with the relationship most apparent in the first 2 weeks of treatment. The risk of liver transaminase elevations was lower in men versus women, in non-TGCT disease versus TGCT, and in placebo crossover patients versus patients originally assigned to pexidartinib. The paper further notes an unpredictable risk of serious mixed or cholestatic hepatic injury seen in the clinical trials, which requires weekly liver test monitoring for the first 8 weeks and biweekly for the third month.
raw_record.extra_details: Population exposure-response analysis of pexidartinib clinical-trial data in adult patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) with locally advanced disease; hepatic risk (ALT/AST elevations) was most apparent in the first 2 weeks; a 1000-mg initial dose during the first 2 weeks increased aminotransferase risk; model-predicted ALT>3xULN event rates ranged from 0.18 (95% CrI 0.12-0.24) at 400 mg/day to 0.22 (0.15-0.29) at 800 mg/day and 0.22 (0.15-0.30) at 1000/800 mg/day, with similar AST>3xULN rates; recommended dose 800 mg/day (400 mg b.i.d.); liver tests monitored weekly for first 8 weeks and biweekly for third month, with dose modifications (withholding, 200-mg dose reductions, discontinuation); lower transaminase-elevation risk in men vs women, non-TGCT vs TGCT, and placebo crossover vs pexidartinib-assigned patients.

raw_record.support_text: Serious adverse reactions caused by PEX (pexidartinib) were reported in 13% of patients, including life-threatening hepatotoxicity occurring in 3.3% of patients. Due to the potential for severe and even fatal liver injury, the FDA issued a boxed warning for PEX hepatotoxicity, and PEX is only available through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) with monitoring of liver function prior to initiating treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved by the FDA for treatment of tenosynovial giant cell tumor in adults not likely to benefit from surgery. Life-threatening hepatotoxicity occurred in 3.3% of patients and serious adverse reactions in 13% of patients. FDA issued a boxed warning due to potential for severe and even fatal liver injury; available only through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) with liver-function monitoring prior to treatment initiation. The paper's investigational findings (metabolic activation studied in HLM/MLM/PHH with GSH and NH2OMe trapping, 11 PEX-GSH and 7 PEX-NH2OMe adducts, CYP3A4/CYP3A5-mediated reactive metabolite formation) concern possible mechanisms and do not constitute an additional human DILI claim; the authors state the association of reactive metabolites with PEX hepatotoxicity needs further study.

raw_record.support_text: In pooled analyses of the ENLIVEN trial and phase 1 extension (N=130, median follow-up 39 months), 92% of pexidartinib-treated patients experienced aminotransferase elevations (dose-dependent, resolved with treatment interruption), and 4 (3%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity occurred within the first 8 weeks of treatment, all recovering within 1-7 months after discontinuation. A further pooled analysis of the clinical program (N=140) found 91% with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations (66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN) and 5 (4%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity, all recovering after discontinuation. The US prescribing information includes a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, and a retrospective analysis of 3-year hepatic safety data from the tREMS program (N=451) found 21 (4.7%) patients met criteria for a hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of a serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with event onset within 2 months of starting pexidartinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Pooled analyses of ENLIVEN (phase 3 trial) + phase 1 extension (N=130; median follow-up 39 mo): 92% aminotransferase elevations, 4 (3%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity within first 8 weeks, recovered within 1-7 months after discontinuation. Clinical program pooled analysis (N=140): 91% dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations resolved with interruption, 66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN, 5 (4%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity recovered after discontinuation. Final ENLIVEN analysis (median follow-up 31 mo, cutoff April 2021): no new safety signals, no additional mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity cases. Indication: diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor. USPI carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity; drug available only through the TURALIO REMS (tREMS) program. tREMS retrospective hepatic safety analysis (N=451): 21 (4.7%) met criteria for hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury; onset within 2 months; treatment interrupted in 1, permanently discontinued in 20. Both ALT (UMLS:C0151905) and AST (UMLS:C0151904) elevations reported.

raw_record.support_text: Cumulatively through June 2024, 45 (5.7%) patients receiving pexidartinib in the tREMS Program met criteria for AEs or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury; 32/45 (71.1%) recovered, 6/45 recovering, 6/45 not yet recovered, and 1/45 status unknown. Of 158 liver adverse event report forms for 114 patients, there were 19 (12.0%) hospitalizations due to liver AEs. Pexidartinib was discontinued in a VBDS-suspect case.
raw_record.extra_details: tREMS Program (FDA-mandated REMS for pexidartinib in adult TGCT patients), data through June 2024; 45/785? (5.7%) patients with serious/potentially fatal liver injury; 158 LAERFs for 114 patients, 22 hepatology referrals, 27 liver ultrasounds, 1 liver biopsy, 19 liver-AE hospitalizations, 7 medically managed, 59 resolved/88 ongoing/1 resolved with sequelae/10 missing. Frequency and pattern of liver injury consistent with ENLIVEN trial and prior 3-year REMS assessment; no irreversible liver injury and no new safety signals identified.

raw_record.support_text: In the phase 2 safety analysis, namodenoson was well-tolerated at both doses (12.5 mg BD and 25 mg BD), no patient withdrew due to toxicity, no severe treatment-related adverse events were reported, and no hepatotoxicity was observed during the study.
raw_record.extra_details: Multicentre phase 2 study in NAFLD patients (with or without NASH); doses 12.5 mg BD (n=21) and 25 mg BD (n=19) versus placebo (n=20). No hepatotoxicity was observed and no deaths occurred during the study. The few TEAEs considered possibly related to treatment were myalgia, muscular weakness, and headache, none hepatic.

raw_record.support_text: In the phase 2 MASLD/MASH trial, treatment with either dose of namodenoson (12.5 mg BID and 25 mg BID for 12 weeks) was well tolerated, and no drug-emergent severe adverse events, drug-related withdrawals, hepatotoxicity, or deaths were reported. The text explicitly states that no hepatotoxicity occurred with namodenoson treatment in this human clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized 1:1:1 double-blind phase 2 study in 60 patients with MASLD (ALT >= 60 IU/L); compared namodenoson 12.5 mg BID and 25 mg BID for 12 weeks with 16-week follow-up versus placebo. No hepatotoxicity reported at either dose in this trial.

raw_record.support_text: Based on RUCAM causality assessment of 70 tigecycline-treated patients with abnormal liver function, 15 cases (scores 3–5) were possible, 46 cases (scores 6–8) were probable, and 9 cases (scores ≥9) were highly probable. After excluding the 15 possible cases, 55 patients had confirmed tigecycline-associated DILI, an incidence of 5.7% (55/973).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective EMR cohort of 1,250 tigecycline-treated patients; 277 excluded (incomplete labs n=74, <72 h exposure n=201, Child C liver function n=2); 95/973 had abnormal biochemical values, 25 explained by alternatives (severe sepsis n=12, active hepatitis n=5, multiple organ failure n=1, obstructive jaundice n=3, surgery n=4). RUCAM causality grading: 15 possible, 46 probable, 9 highly probable; confirmed DILI incidence 5.7% (55/973). Liver injury patterns: hepatocellular n=10 (3 highly probable, 7 probable), mixed n=4 (all probable), cholestatic n=41 (6 highly probable, 35 probable). Median latency 4.5 (Hep), 6.5 (Mix), 12.0 (Chol) days; liver injury during treatment in 70–78%; re-exposure with recurrent ALT/ALP increase in 2 cholestatic cases. Outcomes: recovery/improvement in most; time to recovery 11–24 days; 30-day all-cause mortality 7–25% by pattern (not attributed to liver injury). One patient had liver biopsy. 46.3% of cholestatic cases showed no improvement.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of inpatients who received tigecycline treatment from January 2018 to January 2020 assessed Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) using biochemical criteria and the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM), retaining cases with a probable or highly probable causality grading. The author found that tigecycline was associated with liver injury, with a slightly higher incidence (5.7%) than the frequency of "frequent" (5%) defined by the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Tigecycline-associated DILI was related to a high maintenance dose, prolonged treatment duration, and a number of concomitant medications with known hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Inpatients treated January 2018 to January 2020; DILI diagnosed by biochemical criteria with RUCAM probable or highly probable causality grading; incidence 5.7% versus the MedDRA 'frequent' threshold of 5%. DILI was associated with a high maintenance dose, prolonged duration of treatment, and a number of concomitant medications with known hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists tigecycline as a RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with updated RUCAM scores (mean 6.8 ± 0.7) conferring probable and (mean 9.1 ± 0.3) highly probable causality gradings, based on published cases evaluated with the updated RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Updated RUCAM scores, mean ± SD: 6.8 ± 0.7 (probable) and 9.1 ± 0.3 (highly probable) causality gradings; reported iDILI cases, reference [43].

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis started teriflunomide 14 mg orally once daily (plus vitamin D 60,000 IU daily) and after 54 days reported abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, and nausea, with worsening for a week. Laboratory results showed ALT 1384 U/L, AST 612 U/L, GGT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 1.20 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.50 mg/dL. The case was considered probable hepatotoxicity associated with teriflunomide and treatment was suspended. The adverse reaction was notified to the Brazilian Pharmacovigilance Service, and the Naranjo causality score was 7, indicating the drug was probably associated with the reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Relapsing-remitting MS patient; teriflunomide 14 mg/day orally for <2 months (54 days) before symptoms; also daily vitamin D 60,000 IU (not implicated as cause). Symptoms: abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, nausea. Labs: ALT 1384 U/L, AST 612 U/L, GGT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 1.20 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.50 mg/dL. Treatment suspended; adverse drug reaction notified to Brazilian Pharmacovigilance; Naranjo causality score 7 (probable). Patient denied alcohol, other medications, herbal medicines; no prior liver disease. Background: transient ALT elevation up to 3x ULN expected in first 6 months of teriflunomide at frequencies 14.2%–15.8%, with discontinuation described in up to 3% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of probable teriflunomide-induced liver injury as assessed for causality using the updated RUCAM. The liver injury occurred approximately nine months after teriflunomide initiation and improved with discontinuation of the drug and treatment with cholestyramine.
raw_record.extra_details: 60-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis treated with teriflunomide 14 mg daily; onset ~9 months after initiation with initially normal liver tests. On presentation: AST 1,499 U/L, ALT 777 U/L, AP 478 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, INR 1.20; jaundice, fatigue, anorexia, altered mental status. Causality assessed with updated RUCAM (probable score). Liver biopsy most consistent with drug-induced injury with a minor steatohepatitis component; treated with cholestyramine 4 g every 6 hours for accelerated elimination starting hospital day 7; liver tests improved and teriflunomide discontinued indefinitely. Competing causes (hepatitis/herpes serologies, autoimmune markers, iron overload, acetaminophen) largely excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The review lists teriflunomide as a new RUCAM-based idiosyncratic DILI cause, with a RUCAM score of 8 conferring a probable causality grading, based on a published case evaluated with the RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 8, probable causality grading in one report [24]; a second report [42] mentions teriflunomide iDILI with score and causality grading not reported.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients suffered reversible hepatic injury with jaundice within a month of starting treatment with feprazone. Liver biopsies showed changes similar to those reported with phenylbutazone, including granulomas in one case (Wiggins and Scott, 1981).
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients with reversible hepatic injury and jaundice within a month of starting treatment; liver biopsies showed changes similar to those reported with phenylbutazone, including granulomas in one case (Wiggins and Scott, 1981).

raw_record.support_text: The letter describes four cases of sulphonamide hepatitis occurring within 11 months in one clinic. In all four cases sulphonamethoxypyridazine was one component, and it was confirmed to be the causal agent in the case tested. The author states this sulphonamide seems to be specially hepatotoxic, noting that drugs containing this sulpha comprise only 29% of the total amount of sulphonamides sold in Finland.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases of sulphonamide hepatitis occurred within 11 months in a single non-hepatology clinic, suggesting the condition is more common than generally thought. Sulphonamethoxypyridazine was a component in all four cases and was confirmed as the causal agent in the one case rechallenged/tested. Drugs containing this sulphonamide accounted for only 29% of total sulphonamides sold in Finland, supporting the claim that this sulpha is especially hepatotoxic.

raw_record.support_text: Sotorasib had a manageable tolerability profile in 359 patients with solid tumours treated with sotorasib 960 mg once daily in the CodeBreaK 100 trial. Increased ALT, increased AST and drug-induced liver injury (all 1%) were the most common ADRs leading to discontinuation of sotorasib. For the drug-induced liver injury portion of paragraph 40: DILI was reported as an adverse drug reaction and was among the most common ADRs leading to sotorasib discontinuation (1% of 359 patients). 26% of patients who had hepatotoxic reactions were treated with corticosteroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor, 960 mg orally once daily) for solid tumours/NSCLC. CodeBreaK 100 (n=359 solid tumour patients): drug-induced liver injury was an ADR leading to discontinuation in 1%; increased ALT (6%), increased AST (6%) and DILI (1%) were the most common ADRs leading to dose modification/discontinuation; increased ALT/AST elevation was transient with median time to onset of 8 weeks; 26% of patients with hepatotoxic reactions were treated with corticosteroids. Phase II CodeBreaK 100 (n=126 KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC patients): grade >=3 liver-related TRAEs included ALT increase 6.3%, AST increase 5.6%, GGT increase 2.4% and drug-induced liver injury 1.6%; dose modification due to all-grade TRAEs 22.2%, discontinuation due to all-grade TRAEs 7.1%.

raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old woman with KRASG12C-mutated NSCLC was started on sotorasib 960 mg orally daily about six weeks after her last chemoimmunotherapy cycle. Six weeks after starting sotorasib, her AST and ALT rose to 356 U/L and 518 U/L; the hepatitis virus panel was negative and imaging showed no liver metastases or biliary obstruction, so the transaminitis was attributed to sotorasib, and the drug was withheld for 2 months. LFTs subsequently normalized, but repeat trials of sotorasib at 480 mg and 240 mg each caused LFT elevations, and sotorasib was ultimately discontinued. On a later rechallenge at 480 mg daily the patient developed diffuse abdominal pain, distension, and jaundice with grade 3 hepatotoxicity (AST 157 U/L, ALT 199 U/L, total bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL), and sotorasib was permanently discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: Recurrent dose-related elevation of AST/ALT reproducible on rechallenge at 960 mg, 480 mg, and 240 mg daily, with normalization of LFTs upon discontinuation. Final rechallenge at 480 mg daily produced grade 3 hepatotoxicity with jaundice (AST 157 U/L, ALT 199 U/L, total bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL) within 48 hours. Hepatitis viral panel negative; no liver metastases or biliary obstruction on imaging; steroids not administered during the first episode. Patient had a history of prior chemoimmunotherapy with pembrolizumab and recent ICI discontinuation. Occurred in a 52-year-old woman with metastatic KRASG12C-mutated NSCLC.

raw_record.support_text: In the phase 3 trial of the endothelin receptor antagonist aprocitentan (12.5 mg and 25 mg) versus placebo in patients with resistant hypertension receiving standardised antihypertensive treatment, safety monitoring found no signs of hepatotoxicity in any treatment group (table 2).
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 3 randomized study in patients with resistant hypertension receiving standardised antihypertensive treatment including a diuretic; aprocitentan 12.5 mg and 25 mg compared with placebo; explicit statement that no signs of hepatotoxicity were observed.

raw_record.support_text: In the PRECISION study of Aprocitentan for resistant hypertension, treatment was associated with dose-dependent mild-to-moderate fluid retention and increases in NT-proBNP and MR-proANP, but the paper explicitly states 'There was no evidence of hepatotoxicity' in the studied participants.
raw_record.extra_details: PRECISION randomized trial in resistant hypertension; doses 12.5 mg and 25 mg across parts 1-3 (up to 48 weeks); explicit negative conclusion that there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity in the studied population.

raw_record.support_text: For the reported patient, the RUCAM (Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method) score was +6, breaking down as follows: time to onset +1, course +3, risk factors 0, concomitant drugs 0, nondrug causes search +1, previous information on the hepatotoxicity of the drug +1, and response to rechallenge +0. This score made 'probable' the correlation between ceftriaxone and liver injury. The text also notes treatment with antibiotics has been reported as a rare cause of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score +6 (time to onset +1; course +3; risk factors 0; concomitant drugs 0; search for nondrug causes +1; previous information on hepatotoxicity +1; response to rechallenge +0). Antibiotic treatment noted as a rare cause of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: We report a patient who developed severe acute hepatitis following a single dose of 2 g ceftriaxone within one day; apart from a fever of 101.9 F, no other insult was noted to explain his severe hepatocellular injury. On stopping ceftriaxone, symptoms resolved and liver enzymes normalized within a week. RUCAM score was 6, suggesting DILI was a probable cause of his acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, situs inversus, and obesity; single 2 g intravenous dose for suspected tooth infection. Symptom onset within 12 hours (bloatedness, fatigue, dark urine). Initial labs: ALT >5,000 U/L (Ref 4-33), AST >10,000 U/L (Ref 13-39), ALP 159 U/L (Ref 34-104), elevated urine bilirubin, serum bilirubin/INR/albumin normal, eosinophilia 11% (Ref <7%). Serological, viral, iron, and autoimmune workups were negative for competing causes (alcohol, acetaminophen, salicylate, viral hepatitis, etc.). CT showed mild fatty liver, no cirrhosis or focal lesion. RUCAM score 6 = probable DILI; liver enzymes normalized within a week. Authors note this is a rare side effect needing larger-scale surveillance.

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old female treated with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) for cholesterol gallstones developed jaundice with increasing pruritus; liver biopsy demonstrated feathery degeneration and vacuolated nuclei of hepatocytes, intrahepatic cholestasis, focal liver cell necrosis and bile thrombi with little portal inflammation, findings the authors state are compatible with toxic liver injury. After CDCA was discontinued and taurine (TS-201) was prescribed, T-Bil, TBA and Al-P normalized and itching improved; a scratched patch test with CDCA was fairly positive. The paper attributes the intrahepatic cholestatic liver injury to CDCA.
raw_record.extra_details: CDCA used to dissolve cholesterol gallstones; the patient presented clinically with jaundice and generalized itching (no hypochondralgia) with elevated T-Bil, TBA and Al-P. Liver biopsy on August 23 showed feathery degeneration, vacuolated hepatocyte nuclei, focal liver cell necrosis, bile thrombi in dilated canaliculi and intrahepatic cholestasis with little portal inflammation, compatible with toxic liver injury; extrahepatic bile duct obstruction was excluded by ultrasonography/CT and the cholangiogram. Values normalized after CDCA discontinuation plus taurine (TS-201, Taisho). Positive scratched patch test with CDCA on September 25. Patient also underwent cholecystectomy with choledocholithotomy for cholesterol gallbladder stones and common bile duct sands. Bile acid analysis showed marked increases in serum CDCA and hyocholic acid during maximum cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: In the National Cooperative Gallstone Study (NCGS), frequent mild diarrhea and slight transient elevations of serum aminotransferases due to chenodiol were confirmed. Chenodiol at 750 mg/day caused clinically significant hepatic injury in 3% of patients; this injury was reversible biochemically in each instance, and the reports concluded serious liver disease should be preventable by careful monitoring and management.
raw_record.extra_details: NCGS (National Cooperative Gallstone Study) findings. Dosed at 750 mg/day for gallstone dissolution (cholelithiasis); clinically significant hepatic injury in 3% of enrolled patients, reversible biochemically in each instance; concurrent slight transient aminotransferase elevations attributed to chenodiol; no data beyond 2 years of treatment or for doses above 750 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: In comparative controlled trials of acute healing of duodenal ulcers, 1 patient taking ranitidine and 1 taking cimetidine developed hepatitis out of 1786 and 1743 treated patients respectively (0.06% on both drugs). In placebo-controlled trials, 2 patients on ranitidine out of 2332 treated (0.08%) had hepatitis; 2 ranitidine patients with jaundice had baseline features giving confirmatory evidence of alcoholism.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of hepatitis: 0.06% (1/1786) in comparative controlled duodenal-ulcer healing trials; 0.08% (2/2332) in placebo-controlled trials; 0% (0/1658) among alternative dosage schedules (150 mg twice daily or 300 mg); 0.09% (1/1049) in placebo-controlled maintenance trials; no cases among 675 ranitidine patients in comparative maintenance trials. Postmarketing surveillance of 9600 ranitidine users showed no hepatitis cases attributed to the drug. Two ranitidine jaundice patients had baseline evidence of alcoholism. Overall hepatitis regarded as a rare and idiosyncratic clinical occurrence.

raw_record.support_text: The authors argue H2-antagonists only rarely cause hepatitis and that clinical characteristics are similar with ranitidine and cimetidine. Clinical case reports indicate a hypersensitivity reaction rather than direct liver toxicity, and the authors conclude that hepatitis can be confidently regarded as a rare and idiosyncratic clinical occurrence with both drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: In comparative controlled trials of acute healing of duodenal ulcers, 1 patient taking ranitidine developed hepatitis out of 1786 treated (0.06%). In placebo-controlled trials, 2 patients on ranitidine out of 2332 treated (0.08%) had hepatitis; no cases occurred among 1658 patients on alternative dosage schedules (150 mg twice daily or 300 mg), and no cases in comparative (675) or placebo-controlled maintenance (1049) trials beyond the above. Postmarketing surveillance of 9600 ranitidine users showed no cases of hepatitis attributed to the drug. Two ranitidine jaundice patients had baseline features giving confirmatory evidence of alcoholism. The authors characterize the reaction as a hypersensitivity reaction rather than direct liver toxicity, and ranitidine was not hepatotoxic in rodents treated over 2 years at doses 800 times higher than therapeutic ones.

raw_record.support_text: The author, referring to his own earlier report, states that his report of ranitidine hepatitis describes a definite case based on positive dechallenge, liver biopsy findings, and rechallenge, not merely a possible case, and criticizes misinterpretation of that case by Bredfeldt and von Huene.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral use of ranitidine; defined case supported by positive dechallenge, liver biopsy findings, and rechallenge; pathogenesis of liver injury in orally reported cases compatible with a hypersensitivity-type drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient who developed hepatitis with systemic symptoms, fever, eosinophilia, prompt recurrence on rechallenge with ranitidine (150 mg twice daily, onset about 36 hours), and a variable latency, consistent with a hypersensitivity-type, dose-unrelated drug reaction. The initial bout of hepatitis resolved within 1 week after cessation of ranitidine, was unaffected by substitution of cimetidine, and was reproduced on rechallenge (positive dechallenge followed by recurrence); the authors state the causative link between ranitidine and the liver injury was definite. On rechallenge, AST was 1310 U/L, ALT 860 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 451 IU/L, with normal bilirubin, and the absolute eosinophil count rose to 0.48 × 10⁹/L; symptoms resolved within 24 hours and laboratory values normalized within 2 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with ranitidine 150 mg twice daily reproduced the reaction about 36 hours after onset; positive dechallenge and recurrence on rechallenge; features of hypersensitivity: systemic symptoms, fever, chills, eosinophilia (0.38–0.48 × 10⁹/L), eosinophils on liver biopsy; initial hepatitis resolved within 1 week after withdrawal and was unaffected by cimetidine substitution; symptoms resolved within 24 hours after discontinuation and laboratory values returned to normal within 2 weeks; AST 1310 U/L, ALT 860 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 451 IU/L, bilirubin normal, prothrombin time normal, ANA/mitochondrial/smooth muscle antibodies negative, circulating ranitidine antibodies not detected by ELISA or radioimmunoassay. Authors note clinical studies show occasional small, usually isolated aminotransferase elevations and the patient here represents clinical hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis associated with rash and hypereosinophilia, in which the absence of transfusion, intercurrent viral infection, alcohol consumption or other hepatotoxic drugs is suggestive of ranitidine-induced hepatotoxicity. They note the lack of a dose-effect relationship, the rarity and unpredictability of the reaction, and the clinical signs, concluding hypersensitivity is involved and that physicians should be aware of this rare and idiosyncratic side-effect of ranitidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute cholestatic hepatitis with rash and hypereosinophilia. Injury developed on a second course of oral ranitidine therapy; no hepatotoxicity was apparent on the first contact. Supporting features: absence of transfusion, intercurrent viral infection, alcohol consumption, and other hepatotoxic drugs; no dose-effect relationship; clinical hypersensitivity signs. Pathogenesis attributed to an allergic/hypersensitivity mechanism rather than reactive-metabolite-mediated toxic hepatitis (in vitro/high-dose animal studies considered unlikely to cause toxic hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with cimetidine 300 mg four times a day for peptic ulcer developed transaminase elevation. A liver biopsy showed scattered foci of liver cell necrosis, acidophilic cytoplasmic changes, perivenular cytolysis and collapse, bile inclusions, and mononuclear infiltration, interpreted as consistent with toxic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case. Cimetidine 300 mg four times a day; biopsy showed scattered foci of liver cell necrosis, acidophilic cytoplasmic changes, perivenular cytolysis and collapse, bile inclusions, mononuclear infiltration, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, mild portal inflammation. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative. Cimetidine was stopped after the first episode.

raw_record.support_text: A causal relationship between cimetidine and acute hepatic injury was established through rechallenge in a case reported by Lorenzini and associates. The patient was initially diagnosed with acute hepatitis by liver biopsy after 70 days of cimetidine therapy; liver enzymes normalized within 24 days of stopping the drug, but five days after restarting cimetidine the aminotransferases reached six times the upper limit of normal with pruritus and myalgia. After discontinuation the patient clinically and enzymatically returned to normal within 10 days.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosed as acute hepatitis by liver biopsy after 70 days of cimetidine therapy; aminotransferases reached 6x ULN upon rechallenge with pruritus and myalgia; complete clinical and enzymatic recovery within 10 days of discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: In a recent phase III clinical trial, zavegepant 10 mg was evaluated against placebo for acute migraine treatment. The most common adverse events (≥2%) in either treatment group were dysgeusia (21% zavegepant vs 5% placebo), nasal discomfort (4% vs 1%), and nausea (3% vs 1%). The authors explicitly state that no hepatotoxicity associated with zavegepant was identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase III trial of zavegepant 10 mg for acute migraine (623 patients) vs placebo (646 patients); explicit statement that no hepatotoxicity was identified. Most common AEs were dysgeusia, nasal discomfort, and nausea.

raw_record.support_text: In a completed phase II/III study of zavegepant 10 mg and 20 mg (FDA-approved in 2023 for acute migraine), no hepatotoxicity was detected. The most common adverse effects were dysgeusia, nausea, and nasal discomfort.
raw_record.extra_details: Formerly known as vazegepant; first intranasally administered CGRP receptor antagonist approved by FDA in 2023. Phase II/III trial at 10 mg and 20 mg; no hepatotoxicity detected; most common adverse effects dysgeusia, nausea, and nasal discomfort.

raw_record.support_text: Under isoxazolyl penicillins, the paper lists RUCAM-based cases of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) for cloxacillin (n = 2), included in the HLA study; no specific mechanistic aspects were presented.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM-based iDILI cases, n = 2; grouped within isoxazolyl penicillins; no mechanistic proposals presented in the HLA study.

raw_record.support_text: The report is framed as 'Features of cloxacillin-induced cholestasis', attributing cholestatic liver injury to cloxacillin. The accompanying case table records multiple patients given cloxacillin, including one receiving cloxacillin alone (the present report), with time to onset of symptoms ranging from 3 to 27 days, jaundice duration from 15 to 100 days, and time to recovery from 23 to 180 days. The paper states the hepatotoxic effect of cloxacillin does not appear to be dose related and is reversible, and that rechallenge is not recommended because of the severity and duration of the toxic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism of hepatic injury is presumably hypersensitivity, though the exact mechanism is not clear; in the present report fever, rash, and eosinophilia were not present. Hepatotoxic effect is not dose-related and is reversible; rechallenge is not recommended due to severity and duration. Case table (refs 1-5 plus present report) details patients with cloxacillin alone or with concomitant drugs (nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, penicillin G, triamterene/Dyazide, digoxin/furosemide, isosorbide, azathioprine/prednisone); onset of symptoms 3-27 days, jaundice duration 15-100 days, recovery 23-180 days. Cloxacillin is a penicillin antibacterial agent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that captopril is a cause of drug-induced liver injury in humans, reporting 14 cases of jaundice associated with captopril. Of these, 9 showed 'pure' cholestatic injury, 4 mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury, and only 1 'pure' hepatocellular injury. The authors describe the index case as a clear instance of captopril-induced cholestatic jaundice, with the mechanism appearing to be a hypersensitivity reaction, as jaundice and fever appeared within 2 weeks of starting the drug and subsided promptly upon withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 icteric patients reviewed (including the authors' case; 3 previously reported). Jaundice was the most striking feature; 9 cases considered cholestatic with prominent pruritus; ERCP done in 4 and ultrasound in 7 to exclude extrahepatic obstruction. 5 patients had fever and rash, 3 had eosinophilia. Bilirubin ranged 4-35 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase >3x ULN in all but two patients. Per the pattern categorization, 9 cholestatic (hepatocanalicular), 1 'pure' hepatocellular, 4 mixed. Biopsy reports: two consistent with drug reaction, two cholestasis without inflammation, one intrahepatic cholestasis with mild parenchymal injury and portal eosinophilic infiltrate, one submassive necrosis (the pure hepatocellular patient), one ballooning degeneration and acidophilic bodies without cholestasis. Jaundice lasted 1 week to 6 months; 8 recovered, 3 died of other medical problems, 3 lost to follow-up. Index case: deep jaundice, pruritus, bilirubin >20 mg/dL, slight aminotransferase elevation, 11-fold alkaline phosphatase elevation; fever, chills, marked eosinophilia; jaundice and fever subsided on drug withdrawal (dechallenge). Dose of captopril at onset mean 225-800 mg/d; time to onset mean 46-150 d across subgroups. Mechanism proposed as hypersensitivity to captopril.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who developed hepatocellular jaundice while being treated with captopril. They conclude that the jaundice was probably the result of captopril, interpreted as an idiosyncratic drug reaction, based on dechallenge (gradual improvement in liver function tests after captopril was discontinued) and exclusion of hepatitis A, B, cytomegalovirus, and infectious mononucleosis. The liver disorder was primarily hepatocellular with secondary cholestatic elements.
raw_record.extra_details: 64-year-old man with essential hypertension; captopril started June 1979 at 25 mg three times daily, increased to 150 mg three times daily; propranolol added July 1979 as co-medication. In December 1979 he developed jaundice with pale stools and dark urine; total bilirubin 143 µmol/l, direct bilirubin 114 µmol/l, AST 780 i.u./l, LDH 615 i.u./l, alkaline phosphatase 338 i.u./l, γGT 64 i.u./l. No liver biopsy performed; patient improved clinically after captopril cessation. HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HAV, CMV titres, and Monospot were negative; ultrasound of liver, gallbladder and pancreas was normal. Authors advise regular liver function testing in captopril-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a real-world academic cohort, follow-up liver biochemistries available in 24 patients who initiated resmetirom for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) showed no evidence of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), constituting an explicit negative DILI conclusion for resmetirom in this patient group.
raw_record.extra_details: Eighty-three patients initiated resmetirom (liver-specific thyroid hormone receptor beta agonist, brand name Rezdiffra) at an average of 30 days after prescription; follow-up liver biochemistries in 24 patients showed no evidence of DILI. Adverse events were reported by 41% of patients (mainly gastrointestinal and pruritus/rash, no hypersensitivity), with 13 patients (16%) discontinuing (mean 25.5 days, range 2-68 d), 11 due to adverse events such as nausea/diarrhea/vomiting, right upper quadrant discomfort, left lower quadrant pain, rash with pruritus, pruritus with rash and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, dizziness, and mental fogginess.

raw_record.support_text: In Phase 3 trials, resmetirom demonstrated a favorable safety profile, with mostly mild to moderate gastrointestinal symptoms. Serious adverse event rates were comparable between resmetirom and placebo, and no drug-induced liver injury was reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved in the US in 2024 for noncirrhotic NASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis, alongside diet and exercise; marketed as Rezdiffra in 60 mg, 80 mg, and 100 mg tablets; prescribed daily dose 80 mg (<100 kg body weight) or 100 mg (>=100 kg). No drug-induced liver injury was reported in Phase 3 trials.

raw_record.support_text: In a clearly documented case, a patient being treated with sulfamethoxazole was admitted with arthralgia and hepatitis; symptoms subsided when the drug was discontinued and liver function tests returned to normal. Rechallenge with the congener drug sulfisoxazole resulted in recurrence of hepatitis with jaundice and an elevated serum transaminase level within one day, which again subsided on withdrawal. The temporal association between the second drug and the reappearance of hepatitis, together with rapid resolution on withdrawal, made it almost certain that sulfamethoxazole was a cause of hepatitis in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as Gantanol. Case with rechallenge evidence: recurrence of hepatitis with jaundice and elevated serum transaminase within one day of sulfisoxazole (congener) re-exposure, resolving rapidly on withdrawal; initial presentation with arthralgia. Soluble sulfonamide implicated with four other temporally associated patients.

raw_record.support_text: Jaundice and elevated serum transaminases and alkaline phosphatase developed during sulfamethoxazole administration. Readministration of a small test dose reproduced the clinical and laboratory manifestations of hepatic injury, confirming the drug's hepatotoxic effect in this patient. The features conformed to the generally accepted criteria for drug-induced hepatic injury on the basis of acquired hypersensitivity, except for the absence of rash.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report with positive rechallenge: oral test dose of sulfamethoxazole (4 doses of 250 mg over 24 h) reproduced generalized malaise, nausea, back pain, chills, fever (102°F), blood eosinophilia, and elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases; symptoms resolved within 2 days and laboratory abnormalities within 12 days. During the original episode both transaminases exceeded 200 Karmen units (glutamic pyruvic transaminase rose to 500 units after test dose), alkaline phosphatase was in the range generally seen in obstructive jaundice, and biopsy showed multiple focal areas of parenchymal necrosis and prominent bile casts. The jaundice was designated 'mixed hepatocellular' type. History of prior exposure without adverse effect, prompt recurrence on rechallenge, blood eosinophilia, and hepatic eosinophilic infiltration supported an acquired-hypersensitivity mechanism. Administered as Gantanol (Roche).

raw_record.support_text: This case is the third report of sulfamethoxazole-induced liver injury in which the causal role of the sulfonamide was proven by readministration of a test dose, along with biochemical abnormalities associated with two courses of treatment and a challenge dose of 1 g sulfamethoxazole. The patient developed fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, and arthralgias that were followed after a few days by jaundice. Liver biopsy showed a 'pure' cholestatic picture with canalicular bile plugs and accumulation of bile pigment in hepatocytes, with no hepatocellular necrosis evident.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality proven by rechallenge with a 1 g test dose of sulfamethoxazole and by readministration across two treatment courses. Clinical features: fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, arthralgias, and jaundice that appeared a few days later. Biopsy showed pure cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs and bile pigment accumulation without hepatocellular necrosis. The pattern of response to challenge was interpreted as characteristic of an immunologically-mediated hypersensitivity reaction; the patient's lymphocytes did not undergo blast transformation to sulfamethoxazole, sulfisoxazole, or plasma from volunteers after ingestion. All sulfonamide drugs were subsequently proscribed due to reported cross-sensitization.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis seen at Shinko Hospital, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis confirmed in liver biopsy during the acute episode. Drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one; mefenamic acid was the causative drug in one patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug for severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis in 1 of 9 affected patients; identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of drug withdrawal; repeat biopsies showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis; female preponderance (7 of 9) in this severe hypersensitivity-type group.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, 9 had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis on liver biopsy. In these patients, mefenamic acid was identified as the causative drug in one case; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one. The patient had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after drug withdrawal.

In these patients, kanamycin was identified as the causative drug in one case; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one. raw_record.extra_details: Causative in one of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis; bridging necrosis on liver biopsy; causality identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete recovery within 6 months after withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis seen at Shinko Hospital, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis confirmed in liver biopsy during the acute episode. Drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one; N-Methyl carbamate was the causative drug in four patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug for severe drug-induced hepatitis with bridging necrosis in 4 of 9 affected patients; identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; all nine patients had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months of drug withdrawal; repeat biopsies at 3-34 months showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis; effective hepatic blood flow per blood volume was low at 15.7-20.1%/min (normal controls 32.7 ± 6.0); female preponderance (7 of 9) in this severe hypersensitivity-type group.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, Kobe, Japan, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis as determined in liver biopsy during the acute episode (two males, seven females). Causative drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight patients and by an in-vitro test in one. N-Methyl carbamate was the causative drug in four patients and mefenamic acid, kanamycin, pyrazinamide, difenamizole, and pyrithioxin hydrochloride in one each. All nine recovered fully within 6 months after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative drug in 4 of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis showing bridging necrosis; part of a series of 35 drug-induced hepatitis patients at Shinko Hospital. Causality assigned by cautious rechallenge (8 of 9 cases overall) or in-vitro test (1 case). Severity: bridging necrosis on liver biopsy during acute episode. Complete clinical and biochemical recovery by 6 months after withdrawal; repeat biopsy at 3-34 months showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis. Female preponderance (7 of 9); described as a severe hypersensitivity response. Steroids not prescribed. Effective hepatic blood flow per blood volume 15.7-20.1%/min (normal controls 32.7±6.0).

raw_record.support_text: Among 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, 9 had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis on liver biopsy. In these 9 patients, N-Methyl carbamate was identified as the causative drug in four cases; drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight and by an in-vitro test in one. All nine patients had complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Causative in 4 of 9 patients with severe drug-induced hepatitis; bridging necrosis on liver biopsy; causality identified by cautious rechallenge or in-vitro test; complete clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months after withdrawal; repeat liver biopsies at 3-34 months showed normal lobular structure with minor fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the clinical and biochemical picture of alpha-methyldopa-induced hepatic injury in 36 patients, which occurred in two phases: acutely after beginning treatment (group A, cases 1–14, mean 3.4 ± 0.4 months) and after several years of alpha-methyldopa treatment (group B, cases 15–36, mean 36.5 ± 2.9 months). One patient (case 8) died with hepatic coma and belonged to group A.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 36 patients with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver damage; two phases: group A (cases 1-14) acute onset (mean latency 3.4 ± 0.4 months, bilirubin elevated, ALAT/ASAT high) and group B (cases 15-36) chronic course (mean latency 36.5 ± 2.9 months, initially mild epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, colic); total drug consumed before onset was about 10 times higher in group B; one fatal case with hepatic coma (case 8). Histology showed hepatitis with or without necrosis and chronic active hepatitis (CAH), with fatty liver accumulation ranging 20-40% of the biopsy typical in prolonged onset; 5/7 group A patients had acute hepatitis (71%) and 2/7 a CAH-type reaction (29%), versus 10/16 (63%) and 6/16 (37%) in group B. Occurrence of injury in four members of one family (cases 5, 6, 12, 13) noted. One death with hepatic coma.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes alpha-methyldopa-induced liver injury occurring after short-term (1.5 to 6 months) and long-term (1 to 11 years) exposure in 31 patients. Short-exposure patients were acutely ill with weakness, malaise, nausea, and abdominal pain, and four had icterus; occasional fever was noted.
raw_record.extra_details: 31 patients with alpha-methyldopa-induced liver damage. Short-term group (n=7): mean dose 750 mg/day, mean duration 3.5 months; long-term group (n=24): mean dose 739.5 mg/day, mean duration 60 months (1-11 years). Liver histology included mesenchymal reaction, reactive hepatitis, chronic persistent hepatitis-like and chronic active hepatitis-like reactions. Short-term group showed reactive hepatitis (3 biopsies), chronic aggressive hepatitis-like reaction with massive necrosis (3 cases), and mesenchymal reaction (1 biopsy). Long-term group had chronic progression with epigastric pain, discomfort, nausea, and weakness. Liver function tests (bilirubin, ASAT, ALAT, A-P, albumin, Thrombotest) and degree of hepatic fat accumulation were reported, with greater fat accumulation in the long-term group.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman taking quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps presented with episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia, and granulomatous hepatitis was diagnosed with no common cause found. Upon rechallenge with quinine sulphate her temperature rose and symptoms returned within hours, transaminase activities rose within 48 hours along with erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and after withdrawal symptoms abated and transaminase activities returned to normal. The paper concludes that the biochemical response to quinine challenge implicates the drug as the cause of the liver disturbances and that quinine should be added to the list of drugs known to cause granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of quinine-induced granulomatous hepatitis (case report of a 65-year-old woman). Administered as quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps; four episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia over five months, each spontaneously subsiding after 3-28 days. No common cause for granulomatous hepatitis found. Rechallenge with quinine sulphate reproduced fever within hours and returned symptoms; transaminases and ESR rose within 48 hours; dechallenge led to symptom resolution and normalization of transaminases. Concurrent daily medications (pindolol, methyclothiazide) and rare alcohol use were noted but not implicated. Granulomatous hepatitis is the attributed specific phenotype, recorded under other_specific_phenotype. Related optical isomer quinidine was noted as a previously reported cause of granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 58-year-old man with repeated episodes of thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, lymphocytopenia, and a typical picture of granulomatous hepatitis after ingestion of quinine, following prior reports of quinine-induced granulomatous hepatitis. The association between the episodes and quinine ingestion was established by a quinine challenge that reproduced the complete clinical picture, with liver biopsy during an attack showing granulomatous hepatitis. Multiple quinine-dependent antibodies to platelets, neutrophils, and lymphocytes were detected, indicating an immune-mediated mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old man with recurrent attacks over a 2-year period; liver biopsy during an attack showed a typical picture of granulomatous hepatitis; GPT and GOT 4-6 times normal during attacks; quinine challenge reproduced fever, vomiting, and diarrhea with profound platelet and leukocyte diminution within hours; quinine-dependent IgG antibodies to platelets, neutrophils, T lymphocytes, and B lymphocytes detected by flow cytometry; specific phenotype is granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report quinine-induced hepatotoxicity and emphasize that a single dose of quinine can cause onset of symptoms and liver enzyme abnormalities within 24 hours. A summary of four published cases (Katz 1983, Punukollu 1990, Mathur 1990, Perez 1994) shows quinine-induced hepatotoxicity with markedly elevated aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT; liver biopsies showing intralobular microgranulomas and epithelioid cell granulomas; resolution of symptoms within days of discontinuation; and reappearance of symptoms on rechallenge. The authors' own index case (a 57-year-old woman on chronic quinine therapy) resolved within 48 hours of discontinuation, with liver enzymes decreasing within 72 hours.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapeutic quinine used for muscle spasms in the index case. Four published cases summarized: 65-woman (5 mo, dose unknown, Bil 0.53, AlkPhos 306, AST 129, ALT 298, GGT 238; biopsy intralobular microgranulomas and eosinophils); 37-woman (3 wk 300 mg po bid, Bil 1.8, AlkPhos 327, AST 288, ALT 128; resolution in 2 d); 67-man (2 mo 300 mg at hs, Bil 0.65, AlkPhos 1668, AST 100, GGT 1140; biopsy small epithelioid cell granulomas); 74-woman (1 mo 260 mg at hs, Bil 7.23, AlkPhos 314, AST 209, ALT 241; biopsy microgranulomas). Symptoms included malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, arthralgia, myalgia, headache, jaundice. Rechallenge produced reappearance of symptoms. Index case enzyme elevations in alkaline phosphatase, LDH, AST, ALT, and GGT.

raw_record.support_text: Felbamate was initiated at 600 mg three times a day on June 27, 1994 and increased weekly by 900 mg/d to a total daily dose of 3,600 mg. The patient developed marked liver test abnormalities starting 24 days after felbamate initiation (AST up to 1,258 U/L, elevated direct bilirubin and protime), and autopsy showed massive to sub-massive hepatic necrosis. The authors attribute the injury to felbamate after excluding viral hepatitis (A, B, C, CMV, EBV, HSV) and deeming metoprolol, nifedipine, and phenytoin unlikely or non-fulminant causes. The patient died on August 4 due to multisystem organ failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of felbamate-induced fulminant hepatic failure. Latency 24 days after initiation; dose escalated weekly by 900 mg/d to 3,600 mg/d, later decreased to 1,800 mg/d due to GI irritation, then discontinued on hospital day 9. Peripheral eosinophilia 12.4% (abs 0.7 K/CUMM), elevated AST (601-1,258 U/L), GGT, direct bilirubin up to 18.7 mg/dL, protime rising to 22.4 sec; negative hepatitis A IgM, B, C, CMV, EBV, HSV serologies and cultures; ANA negative. Ultrasound showed enlarged liver. Autopsy: small liver (940 g), massive to sub-massive necrosis, lymphocytic portal infiltrate with few eosinophils, no fibrosis, no viral inclusions. Patient died August 4 from multisystem organ failure; liver transplant not considered. Metoprolol, nifedipine, and phenytoin considered and excluded as unlikely/alternative cause.

raw_record.support_text: Felbamate therapy reportedly causes liver failure, with 18 cases of acute liver failure reported to date. Wallace Laboratories and the FDA recommended weekly monitoring of complete blood counts, reticulocyte counts, and liver function tests in patients receiving felbamate. This hepatotoxicity is presented as a serious, known side-effect risk of felbamate used for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or medically refractory seizures.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 cases of acute liver failure reported; felbamate is largely banned for most epileptic conditions and approved only for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or medically refractory seizures with no reasonable alternative. FDA and Wallace Laboratories recommended weekly monitoring of CBCs, reticulocyte counts, and LFTs. Aplastic anemia (31 reported cases, mostly adults, with concurrent medications) is also an associated side effect. The dosage is 20-35 mg/kg/day (maximum 90 mg/kg/day).
